15789-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number thirty-six, dated July 15, 1897. Five cents bought news, science, and stories in words young readers could follow. Subscribers who sent one new name earned a book, bound in red buckram on laid paper. The paper mixed learning with prizes, as many children's papers did.

This number leads with books as premiums, then turns to the week's events abroad and at home. Nature notes, serial tales, and picture items keep the pace brisk. Editors explain treaties and inventions in short, clear paragraphs. Seen now, the issue captures a summer of 1897 for American children: curious, loyal, and eager for the next week's news.
5939-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
One chapter carries this Don Quixote installment toward Barcelona: chapter sixty, on what happened to Quixote on his way there. It was a fresh morning promising a cool day when Quixote quitted the inn, first taking care to learn the most direct road to Barcelona without touching Saragossa. He is anxious to make out a new history, avoiding the false sequel that claimed his name, and the road itself becomes his argument.

Here follows a knight deliberately steering away from a rival book, toward a city where his fame precedes him. The single chapter favors travel, purpose, and literary self-awareness over battle. It suits readers nearing volume two's end, since the Barcelona road leads to Roque, the enchanted head, and the final defeat that awaits.
arxiv-2412-00036:
Andrew Lesniewski and Giulio Trigila use diffusion models to make fake financial market data. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such data can stand in for real data in tests, if it matches well. Monte Carlo runs are the classic route, but they are slow.

Their fake data pass a strict two-sample test for asset groups. Plots show the fake and real data match across the whole range, tails as well. Spread matrices built from much fake data are also better shaped than those from real data, so they can serve as cleaned stand-ins. Training uses a fast numeric method, not Monte Carlo. Tests run on a large set of share data.
arxiv-2412-00936:
Gregor Skok and Katarina Kosovelj made it practical to grade global weather forecasts with spatial scores that reward near misses. Forecast checking usually compares values point by point, punishing a rain band that is slightly misplaced as harshly as one that is absent. Smoothing-based scores fix this, but smoothing on a sphere, with uneven grid cells and missing data, was too slow for global use.

The pair present two fast global smoothing methods that respect each grid point's true area and handle gaps cleanly. With them, scores such as the Fractions Skill Score can finally be computed worldwide. They demonstrate the approach on the European weather center's high-resolution global rainfall forecasts, opening spatial verification to operational global modeling.
arxiv-2412-02136:
Dillon Chen, Mingyu Hao, Sylvie Thiébaux, and Felipe Trevizan present a 2024 survey of graph learning for planning tasks. Planning means finding a step order that reaches a goal, a task full of links between objects. Graph learning fits that shape well, since it reads links and handles any count of objects. Their survey asks how choices in setup change both learning and planning results.

Three choice lines get the focus: how a task becomes a graph, which network design learns from it, and how training is set up. The work ties into the team's GOOSE frame, which learns from small tasks to solve far larger ones. The authors close with five open challenges for the wider field. Their map shows where graph methods help planners and where the hard problems sit.
arxiv-2412-02336:
Zhenyu Li and co-authors tackle in 2024 amodal depth estimation in real photos: guessing the depth of object parts hidden behind others. Earlier methods leaned on synthetic data and exact metric depth, which transfers poorly outdoors. They reframe the task around relative depth, which generalizes better across varied natural images and scenes.

They built a large new data set by compositing segmented images and blending depth maps from strong pretrained models. Two systems follow: a direct model based on a leading depth network, and a generative flow-based one. Accuracy improved about seventy percent over the prior best on their benchmark.
arxiv-2412-02436:
Xiao-Bin Chen and six co-authors report a new gamma-ray source near the Coma galaxy cluster in a 2024 paper. Gas falling onto clusters slams into shocks that can accelerate cosmic rays. Those particles then shine in gamma rays, leaving a detectable glow.

Sixteen years of space telescope data revealed a source well outside the cluster's core. Its hard spectrum fits light scattered by fast electrons. The spot sits in a long filament of galaxies feeding the cluster. That placement points to an external accretion shock, where fresh gas first crashes in. The team argues this is the shock's signature rather than inner cluster activity. The find helps map how the cosmic web dumps energy into clusters.
arxiv-2412-02536:
Adrian William Romero Jorge, Elena Bratkovskaya, Taesoo Song, and Laura Sagunski use heavy-ion collision data to constrain dark photons, in a two thousand twenty-four particle physics paper. Dark photons are hypothetical vector bosons that could mediate interactions with dark matter.

The analysis runs the PHSD transport model, which reproduces measured dilepton spectra from proton and nucleus collisions across a wide energy range. Hypothetical dark photons are added, produced in meson and resonance decays and themselves decaying into electron pairs. Comparing with data yields an upper limit on the kinetic mixing parameter as a function of dark photon mass. The study also quantifies the precision future dilepton experiments need to push the search further.
arxiv-2412-02836:
Miranda Caputo and co-authors census the young star clusters of NGC 1614, a luminous infrared galaxy forming stars in extreme, dusty conditions. Cluster demographics test theories of how stars are born, but dating clusters is treacherous: an old dust-free cluster and a young dusty one can share the same colours. In a galaxy this dusty, naive dating puts nearly every cluster in the youngest bin.

Using Hubble images in eight filters, plus hydrogen emission data, the team capped each region's allowed dust by its location. The correction emptied the youngest bin and spread massive clusters fairly evenly across ages. The mass distribution follows a power law with no clear top-end cutoff. About 22 percent of stars are born in clusters, but the share still clustered falls to under 2 percent by a few hundred million years: clusters dissolve fast.
arxiv-2412-02936:
Jhordan Silveira de Borba and Sebastian Gonçalves model a simple food web in Patagonia, in two thousand twenty-four. One predator, the puma, hunts two prey: the native guanaco and sheep brought by European settlers. Ranchers often see both wild species as threats to their income, which makes the balance a live issue.

The pair build an equation model from earlier work, then shrink it to the fewest key parameters. Two tools help read the model's behavior. A learning tool shows how each parameter shapes survival or loss of each species. A new kind of three-way graph shows the system's response to many parameter mixes in one picture.
arxiv-2412-03636:
Hao Geng addressed a foundational puzzle of quantum gravity in a 2024 letter. In normal quantum field theory, local operators describe what an experimenter at one place can measure. When gravity is dynamical, its gauge symmetries tie varied spacetime locations, apparently blocking any sensible notion of a local reading. One classic escape is to define everything relative to an actual reference system, such as the galaxies, but those rods and clocks are themselves quantum objects that fluctuate.

Geng shows the relational idea survives quantization, and more: the reference system's quantum swings are not an obstacle but a needed ingredient in making relatively defined observables work. The letter gives an affirmative answer to whether empirical, local physics can be reconciled with quantum gravity in this way, turning a suspected problem into part of the answer.
arxiv-2412-03736:
Dewang Sultania, Zhaoyu Lu, and Twisha Naik are the first names on this paper from two thousand twenty-four, whose text lists a long author roster. It shows that a hybrid search beats a lone retriever at domain-specific question answering for firms.

The system blends a fine-tuned dense retriever with keyword search. A weighted mix joins three signals: dense match scores, BM25 keyword scores, and a boost when the source host matches. Each weight can be tuned. Tests show the blend tops the single-retriever build on accuracy while keeping answers tied to source text. The authors say the mix handles the quirks of niche domains well.
arxiv-2412-03836:
Jian-Ying Wu wrote a review from 2024 unifying the phase-field models used to simulate cohesive fracture, where cracks open gradually against a softening grip. The approach smears a sharp crack into a band so computers can track it. Every model in the family is set by three functions: one shapes the crack profile, one degrades the material law, and one defines the driving force. Wu shows how choices among them decide what a model can and cannot do.

A demand is that the band's width never shrink as failure proceeds, or the crack law gets distorted. Older models crack the problem only in a vanishing limit or for one softening curve. The phase-field cohesive zone model largely fixes this with a length-aware degradation rule. With the profile choice, its two variants cover nearly any softening law. Wu clears up misreadings and shows worked examples.
arxiv-2412-05036:
Andronikos Paliathanasis, in a 2024 paper, studies how to rewrite the equations of motion for a particle so that they take a simple linear form. The work deals with Newton's second law for a particle moving on a line under a force that does not change with time. Instead of the better known route based on symmetries of the equation, the author uses a geometric method called the Eisenhart lift.

The method recasts the motion so that, in the new picture, the particle behaves like a free particle with no force acting on it. The author shows this works for the oscillator, for the Ermakov potential with or without the oscillator term, and for the Morse potential. The paper closes by pointing to new directions for this geometric approach.
arxiv-2412-05536:
Cailian Ruan, Chengyue Huang, and Yahe Yang evaluate multimodal AI for medical image diagnosis in a 2024 study. Hospitals hope these models can read scans alongside clinical notes. Fair comparison needs a shared yardstick, which the field still lacks.

Their pipeline expands five hundred real cases to three thousand through controlled augmentation. Models then produce assessments from images plus observations. A leading language model graded the outputs against doctor-written diagnoses in blind preference tests. One large model was preferred over human diagnoses in most cases. Two specialist vision models scored far lower on the same test. The framework exposes wide gaps between general and specialist systems in this setting.
arxiv-2412-06036:
Jeong-Eun Heo and Miji Jeong reported an astronomy observation in 2024 on the symbiotic star V366 Carinae. Using the GHOST instrument on the Gemini South telescope, they detected faint spectral features known as Raman-scattered carbon lines at two wavelengths in the visible range. These features begin as ultraviolet carbon lines and are transformed as their light passes through surrounding gas.

Such lines are rare. Before this detection they had been seen in only two other symbiotic stars, V1016 Cygni and RR Telescopii. The authors stress the sensitivity of the GHOST instrument, which made spotting these subtle features possible. Having a third example opens the way to comparing the features across systems and learning what conditions produce them.
arxiv-2412-07536:
Nir Gavish finds that two competing disease strains can keep an epidemic pulsing forever under far milder conditions than theory previously allowed. When infection with one strain partly protects against the other, the standard belief was that strong cross-immunity and strong lopsidedness between strains were needed for self-sustained waves. Writing in twenty twenty-four, Gavish analyzes a two-strain model with asymptotic methods. Shows the settled coexistence state loses stability along specific curves in parameter space, giving oscillations for any basic reproduction number above one, even with weak cross-immunity and near-symmetric strains.

Computer simulations back the analysis and reveal an unexpected oscillatory region in the parameter map. The author argues earlier studies overlooked this regime, and that real multi-strain diseases, from flu to dengue, may oscillate under broader conditions than modelers assumed. Public health forecasts built on settled-endemic assumptions could miss such cycles.
arxiv-2412-08436:
Piotr Pokora, a solo author, studied Poincaré polynomials for arrangements of conics and lines in two thousand twenty-four. Such arrangements are patterns of curves in the plane whose crossing points can have special singular forms. A polynomial can encode key counts for an arrangement.

Pokora defines a combinatorial version of that polynomial for arrangements with ordinary singularities. He proves a factorization result, in the spirit of Terao, when the arrangement is free and its singularities are ordinary and quasi-homogeneous. The polynomial then splits over the rational numbers. He then focuses on a family called d-arrangements and derives a combinatorial constraint that any free such arrangement with those singularities must obey.
arxiv-2412-08636:
Ya Deng, Chikako Mese, and Botong Wang wrote a 2024 mathematics paper on a question first posed in 2001. The question asks whether having a big fundamental group stays true when a smooth projective variety is bent a little. Earlier work settled the point for surfaces and for some threefolds.

The authors prove the claim for varieties that carry a big complex local system. They also tackle a broader claim about a size measure for such varieties. As a payoff, they show a form of hyperbolicity stays open under small changes in this setting. Their tools track special maps into buildings and symmetric spaces as shapes vary.
arxiv-2412-08836:
Sean Pike and eight co-authors measure how proton radiation damages germanium cross-strip detectors in a two thousand twenty-four detector paper. Such detectors fly on gamma-ray telescopes like COSI, and trapped charges degrade their spectral resolution.

First the team spelled out a spare detector, finding electron trapping from dirt dominates before any damage. Two rounds of proton irradiation then gauged, for the first time, how fast hole traps accumulate with proton fluence. The trap density grows in a straight line with fluence at a measured rate. Finally, calibration fixes using the measured trapping parameters clawed back much of the lost spectral resolution, a useful recipe for operating irradiated detectors.
arxiv-2412-09536:
Simon Demange and co-authors report a 2024 lab study on which air flow shapes make the noise at a wing's back edge. That noise is the main part of the sound from air over a wing. It comes from rough flow in the thin layer near the wing skin as it meets the sharp back edge.

The team ran a standard wing shape at mid flow speeds and took sound and surface pressure reads at once with spanwise mic rows. Splitting the sound by spanwise wave size showed only broad waves reach the far field as sound. Flow shapes that stay in step across the span linked strongly to the sound sent out. At peak noise tones, the shapes in charge span more than 60 in 100 of the wing chord. A paired paper probes those shapes with fine computer runs.
arxiv-2412-09936:
Dongyu Yao, Keling Yao, Junhong Zhou, and Yinghao Zhang built a system that estimates calories from a single photo of food. Their paper came out in 2024. Standard calorie tools need special data formats or long processing chains, which limits daily use.

The team first built a large dataset of food images paired with text that names ingredients and gives nutrition facts. Their system trains a vision-language model, a model that reads both images and words, on those pairs. A light tuning method adapts the model without retraining all of it. Users can also chat with the system to refine an estimate, which keeps the tool flexible for real meals.
arxiv-2412-10536:
Von Witte and a large team studied in twenty twenty-four how spin spread sets boost strength in tiny silicon grains. Such grains can hold a strong spin boost for more than half an hour at room warmth. Past thought held that grain size rules that boost and its life.

Their sums and sims show both are near free of grain size in fact. Spin spread from near flaws to the bulk drives the slow pace and long life. Line width reads match their spread counts well. They give plain rules to call spread in like grains from a few known traits.
arxiv-2412-11336:
Anton Grishechkin, Abhirup Mukherjee, and Omer Karin offer a maths theory for why animal cells fall into a tidy family tree of types, in a 2024 paper. In a growing animal, stem-like cells branch step by step into specialised types, forming a clear hierarchy. The pattern is well mapped, yet what forces it to appear was unknown. Cell identity is set by genes whose switches sit far away, on stretches of DNA called enhancers.

Enhancers compete for a shared pool of helper proteins, and they also cooperate by switching on shared gene programs. The authors model that tug of war and show the hierarchy emerges on its own from those rules. The same setup lets early cells stay primed for several fates at once and lets signals steer them. The theory ties a core feature of animal life to basic gene-control mechanics.
arxiv-2412-12236:
Christophe Grojean and Patrick Janot push back, in this 2024 comment, against a proposed score for judging how green future particle colliders would be. An earlier paper had offered a single metric that mixes a collider's electricity use and carbon footprint, meant to help compare rival Higgs factory designs on sustainability. Grojean and Janot examine the metric closely and find it wanting.

They argue the score misstates reality in several respects. The deeper problem, they say, is the strategy itself. Folding footprint numbers into one multiplier and ranking whole machines by it is fragile at best. Used to argue for or against a particular collider, they say, such a number is worthless. The comment is part of a live debate over how the field should weigh climate costs when choosing its next flagship machine.
arxiv-2412-12336:
Rodolfo Capdevilla and Tao Han wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about how fully the electroweak symmetry returns at very high energy. Far above the scale where the symmetry breaks, its effects should shrink away. Transverse bosons and fermions then act as if the symmetry were intact, while lengthwise bosons join the Higgs as its partner modes.

The authors propose a sharp test based on radiation amplitude zeros, special points where emission vanishes by gauge structure. They study pairs produced with a W boson at the Large Hadron Collider and at future muon colliders. Those channels include a photon, a Z boson, or a Higgs boson as partner. The zeros would measure symmetry restoration in a quantitative way.
arxiv-2412-12536:
Kristijan Kilassa Kvaternik studies trajectories that return to a saddle point in a family of chaotic maps in a 2024 mathematics study. Lozi maps are piecewise linear cousins of the famous Henon map, simple enough for exact arguments yet rich in chaotic behavior. A homoclinic point lies where the stable and unstable curves of the saddle cross, organizing the chaos around it.

Kvaternik maps the boundary in parameter space where such points exist. On that boundary every crossing is tangential or shared along a segment. He proves all homoclinic points there are iterates of two special points, or of points on one special segment, a complete census.
arxiv-2412-12636:
Lao and co-authors present TrainMover, a run-time tool for large model training jobs. Such jobs halt often when chips fail, code breaks, or staff shift the load. Old fixes restart from saved checks or reset the job, and both waste time. TrainMover keeps spare and flex machines ready to take over fast. It claims near no halt time and no extra memory cost.

Three tricks make the swap work. A two-phase step sets up talk groups with small deltas. A boxed warm-up runs with no cross-talk at all. A broad spare plan lets any role fail and still heal. Tests at 1,024 chips show halts of near 20 seconds. The team projects 55 percent less waste than the best known fix.
arxiv-2412-13436:
A sound wave that hugs a crystal's face drags an electric field with it, and the cheap math for that field leaves the magnet out. Takuya Kawada and seven co-authors redo the sum in 2024 without that shortcut. The field they find fades as it climbs off the face, traveling at the speed of sound. Lay a metal film on the crystal and the field seeps in, dying out over a skin-deep span.

In a good conducting film the field's phase twists as it sinks, a twist the old math never showed. The twist and the fade both trace to the magnet the shortcut dropped. The team offer the fuller picture for labs that read spin and charge states through these waves, where a wrong field means a wrong reading.
arxiv-2412-14436:
Eric Modesitt, Ke Yang, Spencer Hulsey, Chengxiang Zhai, and co-authors present a cheaper way to build specialist training data for language models, in a 2024 paper. General models often lack the depth that expert tasks demand, but hand-building expert data sets is slow and costly. Their method, ORBIT, mines noisy web collections for the gems.

As a test case, they sifted a trillion-token educational web set down to a ten billion token astronomy collection. Training a mid-size model on a slice of it lifted its astronomy test score from sixty-nine to seventy-six percent, and judges preferred its answers over the base model's in most comparisons. The same recipe also improved law and medicine data quality. Code, data, and the model were released openly.
arxiv-2412-14836:
Maria Chudnovsky and co-authors extend fast algorithms for finding large sparse subgraphs. Many hard problems ask for the biggest induced subgraph with a stated sparse trait. Logic formulas can express each such trait in one shared language. Graphs that ban a fixed path as an induced subgraph were hoped to make all these problems easy.

A quasi-polynomial method came first, then a polynomial one for graphs banning a six-vertex path. This work pushes the result to graphs banning a seven-vertex path. The catch is that the clique number must stay bounded. With that bound, every problem in the logic family runs in polynomial time.
arxiv-2412-15336:
Zhian Jia presents a 2024 physics paper on topological phases with unusual symmetries. Non-invertible symmetries cannot be undone, which breaks standard group tools. The paper introduces weak Hopf symmetry as a working framework for one-dimensional topological phases. Inspiration comes from symmetry topological field theory. A lattice model, a cluster ladder, is built with two boundary conditions. One boundary encodes the topological symmetry; the other governs ordinary dynamics. The model generalizes the famous cluster state.

The author shows the model carries weak Hopf symmetry, holding both the algebra and its dual. On a closed loop the symmetry reduces to simpler commuting parts. Exact tensor network states solve the model. Theorists get a concrete lattice home for abstract symmetry categories. Every fusion category matches some weak Hopf algebra, so the bridge is general. Solvable models are how exotic symmetry ideas become testable claims.
arxiv-2412-15536:
Justin Dachille, Chao Huang, and Xin Liu ask where to split a neural network between phones and server in split federated learning. Their paper appeared in 2024. In this training style, each client runs the first layers and the server the rest, so raw data stays local. Two variants exist: separate server models per client, or one shared server model. The team analyzed both on paper and tested them on four data sets with two networks.

The per-client variant barely cared where the cut sat, matching the theory. The shared variant swung widely with cut choice. With a well-chosen cut, the shared variant even beat the classic federated averaging method on uneven data. The authors say cut selection deserves the same care as other design choices in split learning.
arxiv-2412-16336:
Gunel Jahangirova and four co-authors audit the benchmarks used to test deep learning fault tools. Their twenty twenty-four paper deals with collections of real bugs in AI systems. New tools for finding, locating, and fixing such bugs prove themselves on these benchmarks, so the benchmarks must be sound.

The team hand-checked four hundred ninety faults from five benchmarks and kept three hundred five for study. They asked whether each bug matched its source, what type it was, and whether it could be reproduced. Only about fifteen percent met their realism bar. Their own attempts to reproduce the faults worked in just over half the cases, a warning for the field.
arxiv-2412-17136:
David Nabergoj and Erik Štrumbelj give the first full match of the many forms of flow-based tools used to speed a class of chance-based samplers. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such flows reshape a target law so a sampler can jump to far zones. Past work picked plain flow forms off the shelf, with no proof they were best. The team tests many flow forms, on many sampler ways and target laws. When the target's slope is known, flow samplers beat classic ones, with the right form and light tuning. When it is not, shelf forms still win. One form, the contractive residual flow, came out best all round.
arxiv-2412-18536:
Jayashish Das and Arnab Kundu drive a two-dimensional holographic field theory and read the response in the gravity bulk. Their paper from twenty twenty-four builds the drive from a deformed rotation algebra's generators. A thermal state starts the run. The event horizon's growth then sorts into three styles set by the drive's class.

One style oscillates without heating. One grows steeply, the heating path. A borderline style grows by power law with a twist. The drive's broken symmetry shows as a flowery horizon pattern, with a full circle symmetry cut down to a finite one. A wide-q limit heals the symmetry back. Curves from the bulk's time-like symmetries have fixed points near the surface that gauges entanglement. Those points can sit outside the expected wedge, a subtlety the authors flag.
arxiv-2412-18636:
Neutrino experiments measure how often these ghostly particles strike a nucleus, and reading the results takes a reliable model of the nucleus. Gonzalez-Rosa and three co-authors test one such model, called SuSAv2, in a 2024 paper against data from two experiments, one using a mostly carbon target and one using argon. The particle energies span a wide range, from tens of MeV up to about 20 GeV.

Across that range, several reaction routes contribute: clean knockouts, paired-particle ejections, resonances, and deep shattering events. The authors compare the model's full predictions with the measured rates to judge where the model succeeds and where it needs work.
arxiv-2412-18736:
Cheng and Zou revisited the hunt for dark matter subhalos in twenty twenty-four using the latest Fermi-LAT catalog. Dark matter is the unseen material shaping galaxies. Simulations say each galaxy's halo should hold many small subhalos, which might glow faintly in gamma rays if dark matter particles annihilate there.

The team refit the spectra of unidentified point sources in the catalog, comparing a standard curve against a dark matter model. Thirty-two sources fit the dark matter model better. Their inferred particle masses ran mostly from thirty to five hundred gigaelectronvolts, with one outlier far higher. None matched candidates from earlier searches, and the authors discuss why. They caution the sources could still be pulsars, so checks in other wavelengths are needed.
arxiv-2501-01436:
Stetz and a large international collaboration report measurements on the radioactive, neutron-rich nucleus tellurium-132. The team studied the strengths of magnetic dipole transitions between excited states of the nucleus. Their goal was to identify the nucleus's lowest mixed-symmetry state, a distinctive excitation in which protons and neutrons move out of step.

The measurements used direct lifetime determination with the Doppler-shift attenuation method, in a two-neutron transfer reaction on a tellurium-130 target. A large transition strength identified the second-excited state as the one-phonon mixed-symmetry state, in agreement with shell-model calculations. The authors also trace how the state's energy and transition strength fall across neighboring nuclei as the proton shell closure is approached. The result gives nuclear-structure theory a firm benchmark in a neutron-rich region that is hard to reach experimentally.
arxiv-2501-01536:
Yury Solyaev and Vasiliy Dobryanskiy present a 2025 engineering paper on finite elements for crack problems. Strain gradient elasticity adds size effects that classical theory misses near crack tips. The simplified version still needs smooth, accurate elements. The authors build triangular elements with continuous first derivatives. The base is a fifth-degree polynomial scheme borrowed from plate bending work. Onto it they graft the known near-tip solutions for gradient elasticity cracks.

The enrichment keeps the smoothness while capturing the crack-tip fields exactly. Amplitude factors and the J-integral, the energy release measure, come out directly. Tests on opening and sliding crack modes show faster convergence. Size effects on those outputs are also measured. Fracture engineers get a tool for small-scale parts where gradient effects are real, like micro-devices and thin films. Direct J-integral output removes a noisy post-processing step that often spoils accuracy.
arxiv-2501-01936:
Vishal Sunder and Eric Fosler-Lussier improve spoken language understanding in a single speech model, in this 2025 paper. Their base model turns speech into meaning directly, skipping a separate transcript step. They add a joint training goal that also teaches the model to spell out words, with that spelling feeding the meaning step. The setup acts like a smooth two-stage pipeline inside one model.

They then align the model's sound features with those of BERT, a text model rich in meaning. A layer that predicts named things from those features conditions the final decoding. The combined tricks lift results well past strong baselines. The system matches much larger models, such as Whisper, while using far fewer parameters. The paper targets voice assistants that must be both accurate and light.
arxiv-2501-02636:
Sellwood and Carlberg revisit a classic puzzle: why some galaxy disks stay smooth while most grow spirals or bars, in a 2025 paper. Spirals and bars are thought to grow from instabilities in the disk. Smooth disks should be stable, yet modelers have failed for years to build a realistic disk with no instabilities. Computer runs kept growing features from tiny noise, even in a model once claimed to be stable.

The authors return to that claimed-stable model, the Mestel disk set in a matching halo. They show that removing the stars on the most nearly circular orbits blocks the slow growth that spoiled earlier runs. The fix offers a concrete recipe for a disk that can stay featureless, and a test case for theories of galaxy structure.
arxiv-2501-03536:
Sheikh, Sahidullah, and Kodrasi survey speech tools for diseases that break down the brain and nerves in twenty twenty-five. Such diseases often slur or weaken speech, which can be a clue to illness. Computers can spot sick speech, read it aloud, and grade how clear it is. The survey sums up the best current methods for each task.

The authors cover ways to find sick speech, boost its clarity, and add more training data. They flag weak points: tools must work in new settings, guard privacy, and show their reasons. They point to future work that mixes speech with other signals. Large language models may also help these tools grow.
arxiv-2501-03936:
Hao Zheng and co-authors automate slide making in this 2025 paper. Turning a document into a good presentation takes content judgment, design sense, and structure. Older tools chased text quality alone and produced dull decks. Their system, PPTAgent, copies how people work: study a model deck, then edit from it.

The agent first sorts reference slides by job and maps their content layout. It drafts an outline and issues edit steps slide by slide. A companion grader, PPTEval, scores content, design, and coherence. Across all three measures the system beat prior tools, the authors report. The edit-based route keeps decks looking designed, not dumped.
arxiv-2501-04936:
Oday Hazaimah studies a class of equilibrium problems with moving constraints in a 2025 mathematics paper. In quasi variational inequalities, the set of allowed choices itself depends on the solution, a twist that fits real strategic settings. He investigates new third-order projected dynamical systems for solving them, in both continuous and step-by-step forms.

The paper analyzes when a gradient-type continuous method stays stable. It then proposes implicit and explicit iterative schemes built on inertial proximal ideas and proves they converge under mild conditions. Applications to generalized Nash equilibrium problems show the point: players whose feasible moves depend on rivals' choices. The work extends the toolbox for game-like optimization.
arxiv-2501-06536:
Adam Nohejl and Taro Watanabe published a 2025 study of how to measure a word’s spread across texts. Word frequency alone says little about whether a word appears in many places or clusters in a few. Dispersion measures try to capture that spread, but few had been checked against real human behaviour.

The authors tested many measures against three outcomes in five languages: how fast people judge a word, how familiar it feels, and how complex it seems. One simple measure, the logarithm of range, beat raw frequency everywhere. It was also the single best partner to frequency, ahead of far more complex rivals. Details like text chunk size and log scaling explain why earlier studies disagreed.
arxiv-2501-06636:
Emiel van Miltenburg reports a survey of a research group on the dual use of tools that write text. The report is from two thousand twenty-five, and the survey ran in the fall of the year before.

The group is the guild for those who work on text writing by machine. A board over the wider field asked each guild to map dual use risks in its area. Dual use means a tool built for good ends can also serve harm. Twenty-three members replied. Van Miltenburg notes that count is too low to speak for the whole guild. Still, the report gives a base for talks to come, and it is open to notes from the group.
arxiv-2501-06936:
Xinru Ji and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on the first fully wafer-scale, factory-ready chip lasers doped with erbium, the element behind fiber amplifiers. Erbium lasers are quiet and stable, but doping the chips used to need ion beams too energetic for mass production. Thinner waveguides cut the needed energy into the range of standard industrial implanters.

Their lasers tune across ninety-one nanometers, covering nearly the whole pair of telecom bands used in fiber networks. Output reached thirty-six milliwatts with an extremely narrow line width. The devices kept working at temperatures up to 125 degrees. The result moves high-grade lasers from lab craft to assembly line.
arxiv-2501-07036:
Pierre Fraigniaud, Minh Hang Nguyen, and Ami Paz wrote a computer science paper in two thousand twenty-five on agreement among networked computers. In set agreement, each node starts with its own input value. All nodes must output values drawn from the inputs, with at most a set number of distinct values across the whole group.

The case where only one value may survive is consensus, the most studied problem in the field. For larger allowances, lower bounds on what is possible have been much harder to prove. Standard proofs lean on heavy topology tools. The authors give a simpler lower bound for networks that change over time, avoiding much of that machinery.
arxiv-2501-07636:
Lingrui Lin and a large team study molecular clouds in the metal-poor outer disk of our galaxy. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A cloud's fate is set by the play of its own gravity, its inner turbulence, outside pressure, and magnetic fields. Past surveys in rich zones found churn and gravity in near balance.

With thin spectral lines that see deep into clouds, they map the outer disk and add data from near dwarf galaxies. A clear trend shows: as metal share falls, clouds slide from churn-held to gravity-won states. In poor zones, churn alone cannot hold a cloud up. Magnetic fields may take that role, which would shape how stars are born there.
arxiv-2501-07936:
Matteo Di Carlo and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on a new finite-volume action for quantum electrodynamics on a lattice. Lattice calculations must correct for the finite box they run in, and the standard action leaves corrections that depend on hadron structure and resist direct evaluation. The new action, called QED with redistributed zero modes, is built to remove those terms.

The authors work out the finite-size effects of the new action on hadron masses and leptonic decay rates, quantities used in precision tests of the Standard Model. They also give methods to remove the remaining shape-dependent terms. The leading leftover error drops a full order, which should cut a stubborn source of uncertainty.
arxiv-2501-08036:
Mainak Bhattacharyya and Ankur Raina improve decoding of quantum LDPC codes by removing check nodes in a guided way. Quantum error correction needs decoders that keep pace with fault-tolerant machines. Message passing is fast but stalls on trapping sets built from short cycles. The pair blend passing with surgical removal of stabilizer checks.

A notion called qubit separation explains when removal frees trapped data. Information measures on qubits and their checks steer which nodes to cut. Tests on generalized hypergraph product codes confirm the design. Trapping sets shrink without heavy extra cost. Decoding success climbs for the min-sum method at the core.
arxiv-2501-08736:
Goswami and Sharma presented Holoview in twenty twenty-five. Holoview uses augmented reality to help students learn human anatomy. In place of flat book pictures, students walk around body data in depth and inspect organs up close. Hand gestures steer the tour. Students can slice cross-sections and use a bioscope view inside body parts.

A light client-server design, with hybrid and foveated rendering, keeps the view real-time on a HoloLens headset. In a user study, people grew their task-specific knowledge by one hundred thirty-five percent. They also felt surer of their grasp of anatomy. Users found picking organs and viewing cross-sections fun and easy to grasp. The work took low mental effort, and ease of use rose over time. The authors argue that hands-on augmented reality, built around users, can lift anatomy learning in a real way.
arxiv-2501-08936:
Blümler and co-authors published a 2025 paper on tiny gas probes that measure magnetic fields with extreme precision at very low temperatures. The probes use helium-3 gas, whose nuclei respond to magnetic fields in a way that can be read by NMR, a radio-frequency technique. They work in fields above a tenth of a tesla, from room heat down to four degrees above absolute zero.

To build up signal, the gas is squeezed to one hundred times air pressure. Pure helium is slow to settle, so the team added materials that speed settling: magnetic additives or silica gel with vast inner surface. A single pulse of the probe can measure the field to a relative precision between one part in ten billion and one part in ten million. Averaging many pulses sharpens it further. Such probes serve physics experiments that must know their fields exactly.
arxiv-2501-10136:
Leonardo Leyva, Daniel Castanheira, Adão Silva, and Atílio Gameiro redesign signal shaping for future wireless networks, in a 2025 paper. In cell-free networks, many small access points serve users together instead of one big tower. Adding radar-like sensing to the same network could aid safety and smart roads, but central planning loads the links that join the points.

Their design splits the planning into two stages shared between the center and each access point. The goal is strong signals for users while keeping enough sensing power at each point. A step-by-step math method turns the hard joint problem into easier pieces. Results land close to the fully central design while cutting the traffic on the joining links. The work targets networks that must scale to many points.
arxiv-2501-10536:
Shane Cooper and Ilia Kamotski analyze band gaps in photonic crystal fibres in this 2025 paper. These fibres guide light through a periodic dielectric pattern. Experiments long showed frequency gaps near one special line in the spectrum. That line belongs to the low dielectric material in the structure.

The authors prove gap existence near that line mathematically. Gaps are described as missing frequencies in the Maxwell spectrum restricted to the line. Results cover one dimensional fibres and a thin inclusion design called ARROW fibres. Asymptotic analysis shows low frequency gaps for ARROW fibres. No special dielectric contrast ratio is assumed, so moderate contrast designs count too. Rigorous backing now supports a widely observed fibre effect.
arxiv-2501-10836:
Prashant Jayannavar and colleagues published a paper in 2025 on teaching software agents to follow spoken instructions. Their setting is a Minecraft building game played by two people. One player, the architect, describes a target structure. The other, the builder, must carry out the directions. The task is predicting the builder's next actions.

The authors rebuilt the task setup and called it BAP version two. They cleaned the test set and designed fairer scoring measures. New measures showed spatial reasoning as the main weakness of current models. To ease scarce training data, they generated synthetic game dialogues. These extra examples taught basic spatial skills. Even strong language models still struggled with the spatial side.
arxiv-2501-13136:
Ramin Mousa and four co-authors build a Bitcoin price forecast tool in a 2025 paper. Bitcoin prices swing hard, which makes them both risky and hard to predict. The team drew on the network's mining power, called hashrate, as an input signal. They also cleaned the price data with a wave based filter that strips noise.

Their model stacks several deep learning networks, including transformer types. It forecasts price moves for one, seven, thirty, and ninety days ahead. Three methods first picked the most useful input features. The model called the next day's move right about sixty three percent of the time. Accuracy rose for longer spans, reaching a high mark at ninety days. Price errors stayed low for daily calls and modest for longer ones. The team says their stack beat older models in past studies.
arxiv-2501-13336:
Xuelong Dai and co-authors clean attacked images with diffusion tools that never touch the model's gradients, in work from 2025. Image classifiers can be fooled by tiny crafted noise, and newer attacks break the mold entirely. Training against attacks costs a full retrain, while older cleaning is slow.

Hostile samples sit near the decision edge and react sharply to pixel nudges, they note. Two prep steps follow. One softens the pixel noise directly. The other restores a sharp, clean-looking image from the degraded one using priors from clean data, rather than painting a new image. The pair defends against both classic noise attacks and free-form ones, at low cost.
arxiv-2501-14036:
Vincent Blot and six co-authors sharpen the count of tiny egg sacs in the ovaries of mice, a key count in the study of how eggs form. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Sharp slide scans let labs count these sacs in a fast, firm way. The hard part is to hold the tool's hit rate high and sure, while it misses few true sacs, so labs can trust the count. The team uses a repeat-test method that gives firm odds on the hit rate. They also pick the cut point for a call with care. Both steps lift the tool's scores and give labs a count they can repeat.
arxiv-2501-14236: Eleftherios Nikolidakis, a solo author, studied a constant tied to the Bellman function of the dyadic maximal operator in two thousand twenty-five. The constant comes from earlier articles on a Bellman function with three integral variables. Part A of the work examines how that constant behaves as its second variable changes, with a focus on monotonicity properties.
arxiv-2501-14836:
Giovanni Ciatto and co-authors reviewed ways to swap knowledge between AI models and human-readable rules in a 2025 paper. Neural predictors work well but stay opaque: no one can read why they answer as they do. Two crafts fight that fog, one pulling rules out of a trained model, the other injecting known rules into one.

The review sets a shared meta-model for both crafts and two sorting schemes for their methods. From an explainable AI view, such swaps can soften the fog while keeping model skill. The schemes let builders compare methods on like terms. The paper maps a field that trust in AI will need.
arxiv-2501-15236:
Banghui Hua and Jiang Zhu release a software package that computes how fast a false vacuum decays, including a correction others skip, in a 2025 paper. Vacuum tunneling sets the pace of early-universe phase changes. The standard route solves the bounce equation for the tunneling path. A renormalization factor on the field can shift both the path and the rate, yet existing tools ignore it.

Their Mathematica package accepts potentials and corrections as plain numbers, no formulas needed. Worked examples show the factor matters. Tricks for the stubborn super-cooled, thick-wall case were built in. Runs take a second for one field and a few seconds for several. The authors aim to make careful tunneling estimates routine.
arxiv-2501-15336:
Raul Alonso, Francesc Castella, and Oscar Rivero build a number theory tool in a 2025 paper, the first in a series. An Euler system is a family of special values that obey strict rules across number fields, and such families can crack deep questions about equations and L-values. Their system is of the anticyclotomic kind, tied to a Galois representation that comes from Hilbert modular forms over real quadratic fields.

The building blocks are cycles named for Hirzebruch and Zagier, drawn from modular curves placed diagonally inside a product with a Hilbert modular surface. The authors prove the norm rules the system must obey and show the classes vary smoothly in p-adic families. They then point to uses of a standard method that turns such systems into results on two major conjectures.
arxiv-2501-16136:
Vivien Vandaele gives a quantum circuit method for multiplying numbers in binary fields with far fewer costly gates, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such multiplication sits at the heart of quantum attacks on curve based codes over binary fields. The costly gate here is the Toffoli gate, and the count matters for real machines.

The method needs a gate count that grows slower than the square of the field size. A twin form runs in straight line depth by spending more helper qubits. For some favored field shapes, such as those set by three term rules, the depth drops to a log scale with the same lean gate count. The author claims the best known trade of space and time for this task.
arxiv-2501-16236:
Jiahao Luo probes the peer network behind Ethereum in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The network links nodes through the devp2p protocol to run shared apps. Forks of the chain and varied client software have muddied that network.

Nodes cannot tell peers from other chains until after a costly handshake, which wastes effort. Client differences also cause failed connections. Luo built a monitor that tracks message exchanges and client states to map these dynamics. The study found discovery waste and client clashes, including timeouts in a major client. It urges that chain and client diversity count in judging the network's health after the merge.
arxiv-2501-17036:
Nikolai Husung works out a fine detail of lattice QCD in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. Lattice QCD simulates the strong force on a grid, and grid spacing leaves errors that shrink as the grid refines. With staggered quarks, one grid flavor choice, the leading error scales with the square of the spacing, dressed by a log-type factor.

Husung derives the exact form of that factor for spectral quantities, for several counts of quark flavors. The key exponents come out negative in each case. He also clears up claims in the literature about which operators belong in the effective action, and flags terms that may matter past spectral quantities.
arxiv-2501-18036:
Eric Switzer and a large team of colleagues demonstrate a two-dimensional discrete time crystal on current quantum processors. A time crystal is a driven system that settles into a rhythm slower than the drive itself, breaking the symmetry of time in a way no resting material can. Earlier demonstrations were mostly one-dimensional with simpler couplings, because bigger systems defeat both classical and quantum simulation. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team combines the newest IBM quantum hardware with advanced tensor network calculations to handle a two-dimensional lattice with realistic Heisenberg-style interactions that vary by direction.

Their analysis maps a rich phase diagram holding spin-glass, ordinary chaotic, and time-crystalline regions. Claiming the middle region truly is a time crystal rests on that combined evidence. The work widens the study of non-equilibrium phases toward interactions closer to those in nature.
arxiv-2501-18636:
Xun Liang and co-authors build SafeRAG, a benchmark for attacks on retrieval augmented language systems, in a 2025 paper. Such systems fetch outside text to ground their answers, but fetched text can be poisoned. Attackers can plant noise, clashing claims, soft ads, or blocking floods.

The team sorted attacks into four families and built test data for each, mostly by hand. Fourteen system parts, from retrievers to filters to the models themselves, then faced the suite. Every attack family hurt service quality, and even crude attacks slipped past defenses. The authors offer the set as a standing security check for builders of retrieval systems.
arxiv-2501-18936:
Minh Le and five co-authors deepen the theory of visual prompt tuning in twenty twenty-five. Prompt tuning adapts a pretrained vision model by adding learnable prompt tokens. It works well in practice, but why it works is still being worked out. A recent link ties prompt methods to mixture-of-experts models, where each attention head acts like several experts.

Seen that way, prompt tuning adds new prompt experts into those structures. The authors find a flaw: those experts are static, so their expressiveness is limited. Their method, VAPT, gives prompt experts more flexibility while keeping the parameter count low. Readers get both a clearer theory of a popular trick and a stronger version of it.
arxiv-2501-19136:
Martin Lemoine builds a theory of how charged particles gain energy in turbulent plasma, in a paper from 2025. Such speeding up shapes cosmic rays and the glow of space objects. Large computer runs have moved the field fast, but a clean theory helps sort out what the runs show. His theory covers the broad class of random Fermi speeding that does not rely on wave resonance.

The theory links the rate of energy gain to the stats of the flow field. It also models how particles move through zones where the flow bends sharply. He then applies it to magnetized turbulence, scale by scale. Speeding peaks where particles get trapped inside a swirl for a full turn. It also peaks where field lines bend hard. The scalings match past computer results well.
arxiv-2502-00236:
Sara Holeman and Sanchayeeta Borthakur wrote a practical manual for reducing telescope spectra in a 2025 guide. The data come from a long-slit spectrograph on a ninety-inch telescope at Kitt Peak, and the processing uses a classic astronomy software package. Raw frames carry instrument fingerprints, cosmic ray hits from the environment, and no wavelength scale until calibration frames supply one.

Step by step, the manual covers removing those signatures and building calibrated images. A worked example ends with a reduced spectrum and an enlarged figure for inspection. Such guides preserve hard-won observatory know-how for students reducing their first galaxy spectra.
arxiv-2502-00436:
Yan, Markovsky, and Lygeros tackle in 2025 how to rebuild true system data when some records have been tampered with. Their method needs no prior model of the system. System behavior is stated through input and output paths, not inner state equations.

Two attack forms are covered, a set count of bad entries, or whole channels that may be faked. Recovery is cast as an optimization task, with conditions that ensure the true path is found. Faster approximations use sparse penalties and keep low cost. The methods extend to noisy data. Sound rebuilt data can then guard later data driven control steps.
arxiv-2502-00636:
Pallis, writing alone in 2025, builds new versions of a favored early-universe inflation model inside supergravity. The base model, from Starobinsky, matches sky observations well. Supergravity is the framework that merges gravity with particle physics here. The inflaton field rolls on a curved geometry borrowed from a class called T-models. Extra symmetry rules shape the setup's equations. A partner field is held steady by a compact extra term.

A slightly broken shift symmetry lets the predictions drift a touch. The key spectral measure then gains a top limit near its observed center value. The surface's curvature stays fixed while other predictions shift. Such tuned variants test how flexible the favored model is. The paper is formal theory for cosmologists. It links geometry choices to numbers telescopes can check.
arxiv-2502-01536:
Shaoting Zhu, Hang Zhao, and four co-authors build photoreal virtual worlds for training legged robots. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents VR-Robo. Robots learn to walk in simulators, but fake-looking scenes leave them blind in the real world. Policies that rely on camera sight suffer most from that gap.

Their loop scans real places, rebuilds them with a splatting method, and drops them into a physics simulator. A robot then learns a sight-based goal-tracking task inside the twin. The learned policy crossed to a real robot using camera input alone. Tests show the twin keeps both looks and touch realistic. The frame may widen what robots can rehearse safely.
arxiv-2502-02836:
Michael Reitz, Stephan van den Wildenberg, Arghadip Koner, George Schatz, and Joel Yuen-Zhou build a quantum theory of surface lattice resonances. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats ranked arrays of metal nanoparticles. Group interplay in such arrays yields sharp diffractive modes with high quality factors. Classic optics covers them well. A quantum account that handles material nonlinearity was missing.

The team couples the lattice to the light field and derives quantum input-output rules in the dipole approximation. Uses follow from it. Outside quantum emitters can couple to the array through the frame. Molecular optomechanics fits too, since sharp modes grip group vibrations well. Arrays of saturable emitters can switch the resonance between transitions. Pump-probe tests could read these nonlinear marks. The work gives a micro-level base with no hand-set environment terms.
arxiv-2502-03136: Yury Neretin wrote a 2025 mathematics note on visualizing completions of free groups. A free group is the most unrestricted kind of group, built from generators with no relations between them. Its pronilpotent completion is a larger structure capturing the group's behavior through a tower of simpler quotients. Such completions are powerful but abstract. Neretin realizes the completion concretely, as a specific subgroup inside the free Lie group, a related and more tractable object. A visible model gives algebraists a firmer grip on its structure.
arxiv-2502-03636:
Jonathan Folkerts lays out a plan to probe the Sun's core with a detector that flies close to the Sun. His paper from twenty twenty-five sums up a talk for the neutrino solar orbiting lab team. Most neutrino detectors sit deep below ground to dodge noise. This plan takes the detector to the signal instead. A special crystal turns some neutrino hits into a train of pulses.

The crystal holds gallium, which neutrinos can leave in an excited state. Split detectors watch for pulses split in space and time. This pattern can cut noise from solar wind and cosmic rays. A small test craft in polar orbit will gauge ray noise past the Van Allen belts. Folkerts weighs what a near-Sun craft could gauge. Direct sight of the core's shape is one open aim.
arxiv-2502-03936:
He and colleagues taught a graph neural network in twenty twenty-five to aim wireless beams in channels where many transmitter and receiver pairs interfere. Beamforming steers each signal toward its receiver, and doing it well under an energy budget is a hard puzzle that grows with the network.

Their network treats the links as a graph and learns the beam directions and powers in two stages, trained jointly without labeled answers. The feature sizes stay fixed no matter how many pairs join, so the same model scales up. Design tricks keep the outputs lean: a hybrid classic scheme trims them, a feature module treats all links alike, and attention heads sharpen the learned patterns. In tests the model came near the best known quality and answered in under a tenth of a millisecond. It also adapted to new network sizes with light retraining.
arxiv-2502-05536:
Rongwei Yang, writing alone, offers a structured theory of subjective experience aimed at the hard problem of consciousness. The 2025 paper asks how felt qualities, called qualia, can arise from physical brain processes. Yang builds the case by analogy with the history of non-Euclidean geometry, where a new framework opened a stuck field.

The theory defines what it means for something to be non-physical, then uses a postulate about awareness to argue that qualia and thoughts are non-physical. A key idea is relative reality: what is real for an observer depends on the observer and the time. A math model in Hilbert space follows, from which a famous quantum equation is derived. The paper closes with a postulate of a qualia force as part of basic reality.
arxiv-2502-05836:
Shubham Kumar Nigam leads a team of six on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It slices Indian court judgments into their rhetorical parts, and releases LegalSeg, the largest marked set for the task.

A judgment mixes facts, pleas, law, and ruling in one long flow. LegalSeg tags each line with one of seven roles, across thousands of documents and well over a million sentences. The team scores a field of models, from stacked recurrent nets to graph nets and a tuned large model. Builds that use wide context and the lines' order beat those that read each line alone. Close roles and skewed counts still trip the best of them. The set lays a firm base for legal text tools.
arxiv-2502-05936:
Yevheniia Kholina and co-authors report a new way that order can form inside messy crystals, in work from 2025. They study Prussian Blue type crystals, which hold many gaps where a chemical unit is missing. The team finds that gaps line up more along the path of growth than across it.

This one-way lining up lowers the symmetry of the crystal, even though its mean form still looks like a cube. When growth runs along a slanted path, the same effect yields domains with a three-way form. The authors argue the effect is broad, since it rests on how crystals grow in general. Steering growth could thus steer symmetry, using known tricks such as growth helpers added to the mix.
arxiv-2502-06036:
Yeimy Rivera and Samuel Badman published this review in 2025. It maps what we can and cannot observe of the solar wind, the Sun's continuous outflow, from its birth in the corona to its sweep through the solar system. Modelers need measurements at the source and along the journey, but coverage is patchy.

The authors audit current remote and in-situ observations property by property: plasma state, magnetic field, composition. Some quantities are watched continuously; others are glimpsed only when spacecraft geometry cooperates. They review recent coordinated campaigns that stitched source and outflow measurements together, showing what integrated science looks like when it works. Upcoming missions promise to make such coordination routine rather than lucky. The paper is written as a planning document for the heliophysics community: it names the gaps that most limit understanding, so future instruments can be aimed at them deliberately.
arxiv-2502-08636:
Xingrui Wang and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on space reasoning in vision models. Models that read images and text do well at flat, two-dimensional relations. Full three-dimensional sense, position plus facing, is far less sure. No test bed graded that skill step by step.

Their bench builds fake scenes with four skill layers, from naming objects to judging facing in space. Seven question types span five levels of difficulty. A new top task asks for full six-part spatial judgment. Tested models faded as tasks hardened, most sharply on depth and facing. A drop-rate score makes the fade easy to compare across models. Bias by object traits showed up too, and echoed in real photos. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2502-08936:
Yu Wang, Chris Ormel, Shoji Mori, and Xue-Ning Bai wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about planet-forming disks. In these disks of gas and dust around young stars, the water snowline is where icy pebbles turn to vapor. That spot is thought to help solids pile up and form the seeds of planets.

Earlier studies often used flat, simple models. The authors instead run two-dimensional simulations that track pebbles, vapor, heat, and light together. They find that vapor released at the snowline drives an outflow and helps ice pile up just outside it. They also describe a water cycle in active disks and a flattening of heat across the line.
arxiv-2502-09436:
Dario Spoljaric, Yashuai Yan, and Dongheui Lee present a 2025 study on teaching legged robots to walk with adjustable joint stiffness. Reinforcement learning can produce lively gaits, but tuning each joint's stiffness by hand eats time. Their method puts stiffness into the learned controls, grouped three ways: per joint, per leg, or a hybrid of both. The robot then sets stiffness as it walks, alongside joint positions.

Per-leg grouping beat plain position control at tracking speed and at recovering from pushes. The hybrid grouping used the least energy. Although training happened only on flat floors, the robots walked well on varied outdoor ground, a sign of strong transfer from simulation. The approach removes a tedious tuning step while keeping results competitive.
arxiv-2502-10136:
Tanja Dravec, Vesna Iršič Chenoweth, and Andrej Taranenko wrote a 2025 math paper on a chase game played on networks. In the cop and robber game, two players move along the lines of a graph, and the cop wins by landing on the robber. Their variant lets the cop win by getting within a set distance instead of landing exactly on the target.

The radius capture number is the smallest such distance that still gives the cop a winning plan. The team prove bounds for it based on the graph's radius and its shortest loop. They also work out exact values for several graph families, including outerplanar graphs and Sierpiński graphs, and for graphs built by combining smaller ones. The results map how the game's difficulty depends on shape.
arxiv-2502-10336:
Finding the closest point on a curved space is a routine step in data fitting, and its difficulty can be counted. Zehua Lai, Lek-Heng Lim, and Ke Ye compute that count, the Euclidean distance degree, for three workhorse spaces. They cover flag, Grassmann, and Stiefel manifolds, plus a key family of subvarieties. Their method also yields formulas for every stationary point, not just the count.

Knowing the count tells solvers how many critical points a problem can have. That shapes which algorithms will finish quickly and which may stall. The closed forms may let some problems skip numeric search entirely. The paper serves the growing field that optimizes directly on curved spaces, from vision to quantum work.
arxiv-2502-10736:
Yu Zhang, Yi Wen, Siying Hu, and Zhicong Lu present SpeechCap, a playful caption system for chat in social virtual reality in two thousand twenty-five. Talk in shared virtual spaces still feels thin next to face-to-face chat. Impact captions, the bold text bursts used in videos, can carry tone and gesture as well as words.

The team first mapped how such captions can vary, with help from four experts in a co-design session. Their working system then turns speech into live impact captions inside VR. Fourteen users tried it in a study. The design let speakers blend verbal and non-verbal cues with ease, and the authors draw lessons on rhetoric, play, and useful ambiguity.
arxiv-2502-11036:
Yuan-chin Ivan Chang surveys five methods for shrinking data down to fewer dimensions, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Lower dimensions ease storage, speed, and plotting of rich data. Three of the methods are kernel-flavored takes on principal component analysis, which chases variance.

The other two, t-SNE and UMAP, guard local neighborhoods and shine at visualization. Each method is weighed on its math, compute cost, strengths, and limits. Trade-offs among global shape, speed, and clarity guide the pick. The survey aims to help practitioners match method to task. Keeping global shape, saving compute, and staying readable pull in different directions across the five.
arxiv-2502-11436:
Sam Lin and colleagues argue that the data inside a prompt deserves the same care as the instructions around it. Most prompt engineering polishes wording or adds worked examples, leaving the raw input untouched. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team instead optimizes the input itself in two stages. Content engineering fills missing values, drops irrelevant fields, and infers extra profile details from what is present. Structural reformulation then reshapes the cleaned content into the layout a given model reads best, since models are sensitive to format.

Across several tasks, these input fixes raised model performance by clear margins, according to the authors tests. Gains came without changing the model or the task instructions. The paper opens a less explored branch of prompt work, treating data quality and presentation as first-class levers.
arxiv-2502-12436:
Wichayaporn Wongkamjan and co-authors build a deception detector in 2025 from games of Diplomacy, the board game of alliances and betrayal. Players chat, make deals, and often break them. The team asked whether an AI can flag a lying offer before it lands.

Their method reads each proposal's terms as logical forms and scores what the deal is really worth to each side, using game-playing agents. Paired with text features, this catches lies with high precision, meaning few false alarms. A large language model, by contrast, flagged many honest messages as lies. The authors suggest such tools could add a moment of friction, a pause that lets users question a deal that looks too good.
arxiv-2502-12836:
Mohammad Feli and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on an AI agent that analyzes wearable heart signals with real tools. Stuffing raw pulse waveforms into a chat prompt overflows the context and invites confident nonsense. Their agent instead delegates the math to proven analysis software.

Built on an open framework, the system pairs a language model orchestrator with data sources and signal tools. It interviews the user, pulls the recordings, runs the estimators, and explains the results. The test case estimates heart rate from wrist pulse signals, checked against chest ECG recordings from a remote monitoring study. The agent's answers were benchmarked against a small general model answering unaided. The authors argue the tool-using pattern is what makes language models safe for physiology.
arxiv-2502-13136:
Zakaria Derbazi studies how transformations affect the shape of a sequence in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. The transforms are given by sign-regular kernels, tables of weights with a strict sign pattern. The traits in question are unimodality, a single peak, and convexity, a bowl-like bend, each also in higher-order forms.

Derbazi proves a sharp split. The transforms keep these traits only for one narrow class of kernels, of order three. For the mirror class, the transforms flip the traits instead. He extends the results to higher orders and to ratios of two transformed sequences. The work builds on classic results by Karlin.
arxiv-2502-13436:
Dimitar Guelev adds preference talk to a logic for games in this 2025 paper. The logic describes what groups of players can force over time in shared game boards. Guelev extends it so formulas can also say which plays players prefer over others.

He gives translations that add the preference operator and later remove it again, keeping truth intact whenever blurred plays form a tidy equivalence. The same trick handles a companion quantifier over sets of plays. With preferences in hand, classic solution ideas like Nash equilibrium become easy to state directly. A further translation lands the whole language in a tree logic with known algorithms, which opens the door to automatic checking.
arxiv-2502-13836:
Peter Carragher and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on how much vision language models lean on memory versus fetched facts. Such models answer hard queries by search plus recall. Fine-tuned models top closed tasks, while broad models do well with no tuning. The trade between recall, reach, and search was not well gauged.

Their gauge flags cases where the answer is right though the search failed. On a known test set, tuned models leaned on recall more and scored higher than search based ones. Image queries drew on recall far more than text queries. The team says future work must weigh recall gaps across data types.
arxiv-2502-14636:
Timo Kuosmanen and Xun Zhou present a 2025 economics paper on whether markets for reused materials could replace pollution taxes. Firms can sometimes turn emissions into saleable goods, a circular economy idea. The authors ask when a price for such secondary materials alone could do the work of a Pigouvian tax on emissions.

The conditions turn out to be very strict. Unless secondary prices jump at once to unreal levels, a positive emissions tax stays necessary. Their preferred policy pairs a subsidy for secondary materials with a tax on uncontrolled emissions, at no net cost to the budget. They extend the model to a data center selling waste heat to a heating firm that is the sole buyer. The extension shows how the policy aligns incentives without a competitive market.
arxiv-2502-14936:
Rezaei and colleagues show in twenty twenty-five how better training data cuts false alarms when neural networks hunt for strong gravitational lenses. These rare bent-light systems are precious for astronomy, but networks flag many fakes. The team stressed diverse, representative training sets, then added data augmentation and model ensembles to tame errors.

Their best setup reached a very low false alarm rate while still catching nearly nine in ten real lenses. That rate was many times better than with the original training set, at a small cost in catches. Checks on a real sky survey dataset confirmed the gains. The authors aim the lessons at coming missions that will scan huge skies for lenses.
arxiv-2502-16236:
Tianyu Wang and co-authors film a light-driven chemical reaction in a 2025 paper on cyclobutanone, a small ring-shaped molecule. A pulse of light lifts the molecule to an excited state, and it then breaks apart in less than a trillionth of a second. The team used ultrafast electron diffraction with very high energy electrons to catch both the structure changes and the electronic changes.

The excited state lasted about 230 femtoseconds before the molecule split. The main path made cyclopropane and carbon monoxide, while a second path made ethene and ketene, and about a fifth of molecules opened their rings instead. The second path also ran faster. The data give simulation builders a strict test for this classic reaction type.
arxiv-2502-17436:
Yichi Zhang and three co-authors widen a way to make new data in twenty twenty-five. Rectified flow learns a path from a plain source spread to real data. The stock form solves one ordinary differential equation in the place field. It picks up just the mean speed field on the way from source to data.

Their ranked form links more than one such law at the same time. Each one lives in its own field: place, speed, rate of speed change, and so on past those. The full chance speed field is kept, and not just its mean. That full view lets the paths used to make data cross as they run. Paths that cross then give tracks that are more straight and cost less to run. The work gives flow fans a rich form that still grows out of the plain, easy to run first form.
arxiv-2502-17536:
Li and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on rebuilding heart tracings from pulse signals for unseen people. Pulse sensors are easy to wear but heart tracings carry richer detail. Public paired datasets lack variety and carry noise. A differential-equation generator first fakes extra paired data. Their model then mixes contrastive, adversarial, and attention parts. It rebuilds tracings for people never seen in training. Accuracy matches or beats prior methods on those unseen cases.

Age and sex sway rebuild quality in their checks. Diverse training data therefore matters, they stress. Non-invasive heart monitoring is the target use. The synthetic data trick widens what models can learn.
arxiv-2502-17936:
Felix Arnold, Maxence Bouvier, and three co-authors speed up digital circuit design in two thousand twenty-five. Their method adds prediction to random search in MIG based synthesis. Good circuits matter for speed, power, and cost. Random search alone can be slow to find strong forms.

A predictor guesses the next state and guides which tries to keep. That loop made synthesis much faster in tests. Circuit size gains also beat past state of the art on a known suite. The team tried many predictor types. More apt predictors did not always mean better circuits. A dose of chance stayed useful in the search.
arxiv-2502-18736:
Nathalie Riche and co-authors turn AI prompts into graspable instruments instead of chat lines. Chat answers arrive as long, straight text that is hard to steer or revisit. Their AI-Instruments embody each prompt as a reusable on-screen tool. Ambiguous intent shows up as several live readings the user can pick among.

Model answers likewise appear as a range to explore, not one verdict. New instruments can sprout from examples or from other instruments. Language models suggest and vary fresh controls on the fly. Four probes in image creation tested the idea with twelve users. Direct handling eased the work of forming and refining intent.
arxiv-2502-18936:
Go Ichikawa and Kenji Mishima observe neutrons surfing a curved mirror in a 2025 paper. A neutron can be trapped skimming a concave surface, held by centrifugal force against the material's pull. These whispering gallery states test quantum mechanics in rotating frames and probe surfaces at nanometer scales.

A pulsed cold neutron beam at a research facility produced the state on a silica mirror. Measured values matched theory within about two percent. The remaining gap traces to tiny edge imperfections in the mirror. Raw sensitivity ran a hundred times finer than that agreement. Sharper mirrors could turn the setup into a search tool for unknown short-range forces. The work confirms a delicate quantum effect with a practical measurement recipe.
arxiv-2502-20936:
Michael Dinzinger and co-authors present WebFAQ, a huge multilingual set of natural question and answer pairs built for training retrieval systems, in a 2025 paper. The pairs come from FAQ annotations already embedded in web pages. After careful filtering and near-duplicate removal, the set holds 96 million pairs across 75 languages, about half of them non-English.

From it, the team built 20 single-language retrieval benchmarks totaling 11.2 million pairs. A multilingual model fine-tuned on the data gained clearly on retrieval tests, and the gains carried to outside benchmarks. The authors also mined aligned bilingual sets spanning over a thousand language pairs for translation work.
arxiv-2502-21236: Daniil Filienko and seven co-authors propose an AI aid for tuberculosis care in a 2025 paper. The disease is the top infectious killer worldwide, and its burden falls hardest on poorer countries. There, few health workers serve many patients, which weakens support and follow-through on treatment. The team suggests adding a language model to a proven digital adherence tool. The model would handle messages with patients, in a human-in-the-loop setup with treatment supporters. The aim is patient engagement and better treatment completion.
arxiv-2503-00136:
Teneggi, Stayman, and Sulam present a method to quantify uncertainty in CT image prediction in twenty twenty-five. Clinicians and regulators need trust in machine learning predictors for patient care. Uncertainty must be stated in terms that carry clinical meaning. Their method adapts uncertainty estimates to each organ and patient.

The procedure builds on conformal risk control, which bounds risk with high probability. A high dimensional version aims for short intervals that still cover the truth. Semantic adaptation adjusts the method to anatomy and organ position. On real CT data, the method gave tighter intervals with valid coverage. It reports uncertainty through features that clinicians can interpret. The authors frame it as a step toward trustworthy imaging tools.
arxiv-2503-00236:
Timothée Crin-Barat, Lorenzo Liverani, Ling-Yun Shou, and Enrique Zuazua study how solutions of one-dimensional hyperbolic systems with relaxation settle down over long times.
