Non-symmetric relaxation breaks the neat form that past stability proofs rest on. Decay can still be forced, but often at the price of extra smoothness taken as given.

The team bring in a frequency-dependent Kalman stability condition and prove an abstract decay result that sits behind a form of inhomogeneous hypocoercivity. Decay rates hinge on how the condition holds across frequencies. They then give an algorithm with wide use that builds Lyapunov functionals for a given system. At times it cancels terms to cut the loss of derivative. New stability results for an acoustics model and a beam model with memory show the method at work.
arxiv-2503-00336:
Brunno Pleffken Hosti and Ângela Cristina Cararo wrote a 2025 paper, in Portuguese, on using space science to teach modern physics. Teacher training in the physical sciences needs fresh links to real research, since modern topics can feel abstract in class. The paper shows how the study of starlight spectra gives those links. It walks through the light patterns of many kinds of space objects, from glowing gas to star surfaces.

The authors explain how spectra reveal what objects are made of, how hot and dense they are, and how they change over time. They aim the text at high school and university physics teachers. Worked ties to topics like blackbody glow and atomic orbits run through the piece. The goal is to help teachers show students the real-world worth of modern physics.
arxiv-2503-00736:
Wenhui Lei and nine co-authors present Shazam, a model that merges many large pre-trained models for disease study from tissue slides. Each base model is strong in a distinct way, since each learned from distinct slide sets. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past merges froze the parts and needed fresh training for each new model added. Shazam instead blends features from many levels while it runs, with weights that adapt to the task. It also learns from the base models on the fly. Across gene map prediction, survival outlook, slide tile sorting, and image based questions, Shazam beat strong single models. The authors pitch live merging as a path that can grow with new models.
arxiv-2503-01636:
Guoming Zhang, writing solo, settles a long-standing question about square roots of rough differential operators. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Kato problem asks whether an operator's square root behaves like a plain gradient. Zhang treats parabolic operators of any even order. Their coefficients may vary wildly in space and time, merely measurable. A Muckenhoupt weight controls the allowed roughness.

The proof covers the weighted problem fully. It also applies inside the elliptic framework as a bonus. Such results anchor estimates for equations of heat and diffusion type. Rough media, where coefficients jump without pattern, are the natural home. Harmonic analysis gains a capstone for higher-order operators.
arxiv-2503-02036:
Ruth Crasto and Esther Rolf tackle, in twenty twenty-five, geographic distribution shift: models trained on data from some places often fail in others. Standard training yields uneven accuracy across continents or biomes. Most fixes use discrete group labels and ignore the coordinates that geo-tagged data already carry. Location-aware models boost overall scores, but their effect on worst-group performance was unstudied. The authors propose a framework that models domain as a continuous latent variable. A location encoder learns that latent from coordinates, and the main predictor conditions on it.

Tests on four geo-tagged image data sets with varied group splits show clear gains in worst-group performance. The framework beat domain adaptation and location-aware baselines. It set new state-of-the-art results on two WILDS benchmark data sets.
arxiv-2503-02436:
Alex Jin and co-authors implement, in twenty twenty-five, a quantum classifier with adversarial defense on a trapped-ion quantum processor. Quantum machine learning promises rich representations and efficient reversible operations. Its robustness against attacks and noise was largely unexplored. Their classifier uses data re-uploading, feeding the same data through a single qubit several times. A new convolutional quantum design builds on that idea. They ran it on real ion-trap hardware, not just simulation.

On the MNIST digit data set, the design showed superior robustness, the authors report. They also quantified polarization noise, where bit and phase errors both occur, in a realistic setting. The classifier stayed robust. The findings speak to the practical security and reliability of quantum classifiers.
arxiv-2503-03736:
Das, Panda, and NaderiAlizadeh tackle packet routing in large wireless networks in twenty twenty-five. Each node in the network knows only local information. Opportunistic routing uses the broadcast nature of wireless links to pick relay nodes on the fly. That lets a packet reach its target through several relays at once.

They frame routing as a constrained learning problem. A state augmentation method turns it into distributed optimization that boosts total throughput. Graph neural networks learn routing policies from the network structure itself. Training uses an unsupervised approach, with no labelled routes. Tests on synthetic and real world topologies beat baseline algorithms. Trials on a real wireless test bed confirmed the gains and showed the policies transfer well.
arxiv-2503-04636:
Open source language models can be copied and misused in silence, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Yijie Xu and co-authors tests ways to mark them. The authors define two abuses, stealing the model as property and breaking its usage terms, then try two marks: one distilled in at answer time, one planted as a backdoor.

The backdoor mark caught property theft well. The distilled mark worked in both cases but faded faster when others fine tuned the model, and it cost more quality. The paper sets out how to judge marks under realistic retraining, and it names stronger marking as the next job.
arxiv-2503-04736:
Joseph Marvin Imperial, Matthew D Jones, and Harish Tayyar Madabushi examine how generative AI fits into industries ruled by formal standards, in this 2025 paper. Standards are the written rules that keep systems compatible, safe, and accurate in fields like engineering, law, health, and education. AI chatbots are spreading fast in exactly those fields.

The authors rate how critical different standards are and grade how well today's best AI models can follow them. They map the challenges and openings in using AI for compliance work, and give practical advice for standards bodies and users alike. Their claim is that tying AI to standards through computing methods can strengthen both rule keeping and daily operations. They expect this topic to sit at the center of trust in larger AI systems.
arxiv-2503-05136:
Ronny Ko writes a beginner's textbook for fully homomorphic encryption, the scheme that computes on data while it stays encrypted. The text from twenty twenty-five opens with the core promise: run operations on ciphertext, decrypt, and get exactly the plaintext answer. Addition and multiplication are the atoms. Subtraction, division, logic gates, and functions like ReLU or sine are built from them, exactly or by approximation.

Applications fill the later chapters: privacy-preserving machine learning where the server learns neither inputs nor answers, confidential blockchain contracts, encrypted database queries, and secure outsourced analytics. Trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy are flagged throughout. A living website version accompanies the text, with a public board for reporting errors.
arxiv-2503-05336:
Laura Weidinger and co-authors argue that testing generative AI systems needs to become a science of its own, in work from 2025. Such systems are now used in real settings, but common tests are fixed lists that may not predict real-world behaviour. One-off audits, they note, rarely scale to wide use.

The authors draw lessons from fields that learned to test safety the hard way, such as transport, aerospace, and drug making. Three lessons stand out. Tests must match real-world use, tests must be refined over time, and shared bodies and norms must run the testing. They then lay out a path toward stricter, more trusted checks. The piece is a call to treat AI testing as a mature field, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2503-05736:
Zhao, Maffa, and Sandstede develop in 2025 a data driven way to trace pattern transitions and their bifurcations. Patterns such as spots, stripes, and spirals appear in nature and in reaction diffusion models. The goal is the boundary between parameter regions where unlike patterns prevail.

Random starts are grown into full patterns, then feature functions measure their shape, such as count and area of components. Those features form a pattern statistic, compared across parameters with a transport distance. Predictor corrector continuation then traces transition curves by maximizing that distance. Examples span uniform states, spots, stripes, and spiral waves.
arxiv-2503-06036:
Chengyu Zhou and Qingguo Li wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on power constructions in domain theory. Domains are structured sets used to model computation, where elements carry partial information. Power constructions bundle sets of elements into single objects, in the style of three classic versions named for Hoare, Smyth, and Plotkin. A consistent version of these, with a partial addition rule, was introduced by earlier authors.

The pair recast consistency as a categorical idea. From that view, they give a general way to build consistent versions of such constructions from simpler ones. They then produce two new constructions over domains. One is a consistent form of the Plotkin index construction. The other is a consistent probabilistic version, suited to modeling random choice. They verify that both new constructions are free, the best-behaved kind in their category. The paper is abstract theory aimed at the foundations of computing.
arxiv-2503-06336:
Jnana Ranjan Das and co-authors present a percolation model of two-fluid flow in a 2025 physics paper. The model is inspired by oil and water moving through rock whose grains differ in how much they attract water. They build the model on a doubled square grid: grains sit on one grid, and the pores between them form the bonds of the other.

A pore bond counts as open when the pull of the two fluids cancels out at that spot. The connected web of open bonds is then the path both fluids can use without a pressure barrier. The authors show this web matches the rims of clusters in a simpler model. They measure its shapes at the tipping point and develop scaling laws. The tipping behavior matches ordinary percolation.
arxiv-2503-07336:
Muhammad Anisuzzaman Talukder simulates a terahertz quantum cascade laser that emits photons in entangled pairs through two-photon transitions. Such sources could improve standard terahertz uses and enable new quantum applications. Their cascaded transitions also create rich, hard-to-predict behavior in time and frequency.

By solving the coupled Maxwell-Bloch equations numerically, the author compares the two-photon device against a conventional one-photon laser. Output intensity is much higher and the spectrum much broader in the two-photon case. A known lasing instability sets in at lower pump current, and more modes lase with greater power each. At high currents, Rabi splitting appears in the emission spectrum.
arxiv-2503-07736:
Tiago Peixoto builds a sampler that maps the full range of networks that could lie behind observed behavior. The paper from twenty twenty-five treats network reconstruction, the task of guessing hidden links from dynamics alone. The task is ill-posed: many networks fit one data set. Most past methods return a single best guess. That hides doubt and rival answers of near-equal weight.

Peixoto's Markov chain Monte Carlo method draws samples from the posterior spread of networks. It works for any generative model, not just one family. For large, sparse networks each step runs far faster than naive designs. Tests on fake and real data show the payoff. Sample spreads expose true uncertainty. A consensus across samples provably beats any single guess. The work reframes reconstruction as a population question, not a point hunt.
arxiv-2503-07936:
Yuanming Wang and co-authors reported this astronomy find in 2025: a radio pulsar, PSR J0311+1402, that spins once in forty-one seconds. Caught with the ASKAP telescope and checked by others, it sits in a gap. Normal pulsars spin in seconds at most, while a new class of slow transients takes minutes to hours and shines too brightly for spin power alone.

The new object looks pulsar-like in its polarization and spectrum. Yet its spin-down places it below the death line, where radio waves should cease. The team read this as proof of a hidden crowd in the mid-range, missed because past hunts were tuned to fast spins. More finds, they say, will map how neutron stars slow and die.
arxiv-2503-08136:
Jeongsol Kim, Bryan Sangwoo Kim, and Jong Chul Ye present a solver for inverse problems in this 2025 paper. Inverse problems ask a model to rebuild a clean image from a flawed one. Flow matching is a newer way to build generative models with differential equations. The team extends diffusion based solvers into that flow setting.

Their solver is called FlowDPS, short for Flow-Driven Posterior Sampling. It splits the flow into a part that estimates the clean image and a part that estimates noise. A likelihood term guides each part. Tests on four linear inverse problems beat prior methods without extra training. The solver also fits inside a latent flow model with a transformer.
arxiv-2503-08936:
Lev Sorokin, Matteo Biagiola, and Andrea Stocco test self-driving software across simulators in this 2025 paper. The head title adds the word Systems: trustworthy autonomous driving systems testing. One simulator can pass a driving aid that another fails. Such flaky results may reflect the simulator, not the car software. Their tool, MultiSim, searches for failures that repeat everywhere.

Each candidate scenario runs on several simulators at once. Scenarios with matching outcomes get explored further, while one-off failures are demoted. Across three lane-keeping systems, the method found many more shared failures than single-simulator testing. A helper model predicts where simulators will disagree, saving wasted runs. Cross-checking, they argue, should be standard practice.
arxiv-2503-09136:
Soumil Kelkar and co-authors treat Earth as an exoplanet to study cloud effects in a 2025 paper. A planet's spectrum is a snapshot that shifts with weather, above all with clouds. That shifting can hide air components and confuse efforts to pin down a baseline atmosphere. Instead of modeling clouds from scratch, the team used real Earth cloud data from a major archive.

Cloud cover and height strongly changed how detectable key gases were, including oxygen, ozone, and water vapor. Varying cover could also confound attempts to retrieve a stable atmosphere for a planet. The findings bear directly on future direct imaging missions hunting habitable worlds. Readers see why weather may be the noise that limits life detection.
arxiv-2503-09436:
Krzysztof Adamkiewicz and co-authors present PromptMap, a new way to work with image generators, in a 2025 paper. Text-to-image tools are now public toys and work tools, but writing a prompt that gets the wanted picture is a skill novices lack. PromptMap replaces the blank box with a map: a browsable landscape of example prompts and their images, grouped by meaning, with zoom that works like a map's.

Users wander the map, find pictures near what they imagine, and borrow the words that made them. The team tested the tool in an online study with sixty people and a closer study with twelve. The map helped users craft prompts by example. The study also showed that language models can build the vast example collections such a map needs.
arxiv-2503-09736:
Colin Fogarty, a solo author, presents a new sensitivity analysis for matched observational studies in a 2025 paper. In such studies, treated and control subjects are paired to mimic an experiment, but hidden bias may remain. Sensitivity analysis asks how strong that hidden bias must be to overturn a finding.

The new method tilts the analysis by the proposed bias strength, for any chosen test statistic. It covers older approaches for some statistics and adds a weighting based method. Unlike the standard approach, it gives closed form answers when each treated subject has several matched controls. The author shows the method improves the design sensitivity, a measure of a study's built in robustness, under many data models.
arxiv-2503-10636:
Ho Kei Cheng and Alexander Schwing diagnose why a trick that speeds up flow-based image generation stops working once conditions enter. Minibatch optimal transport straightens generation paths for unconditional models, cutting inference cost. With conditions attached, the default transport ignores them, skewing the training distribution away from the one used at test time.

Their fix, conditional optimal transport, adds a condition-weighting term to the cost matrix before computing assignments. That closes the training-test gap at its source. Experiments covered discrete and continuous conditions, from a toy moons dataset to ImageNet at two resolutions. The method beat existing baselines across budgets of function evaluations. Code is publicly available.
arxiv-2503-10736:
Pelle van de Bor, John Brennan, John Regan, and Jonathan Mackey try to speed up the chemistry inside galaxy simulations. Solvers such as Grackle work out how gas heats, cools, and changes form as the cosmos evolves, but they eat much of the computing budget in large, sharp models. The team trained neural operators, learning systems that mimic equation solvers, to stand in for Grackle.

The trained models matched the solver's outputs closely, with typical errors under 0.6 dex, though fast-changing chemical states were harder. In large runs they ran up to six times faster. The authors are candid about limits: errors can build up over many steps, and the models need training data that covers the states they will meet. They frame the work as a first step toward learning-based chemistry in space simulations.
arxiv-2503-10836:
Kevin Li and Eric Laber exploit concavity in contextual bandit optimization in a 2025 paper. Bandit problems choose actions step by step as context arrives, balancing learning with reward. In fields such as medicine and engineering, prior knowledge often says the mean reward bends in a concave way as the action changes.

Their algorithm conditions a Gaussian process model on that concavity, using a spline basis that preserves the shape. Regret guarantees are never worse than the standard method, and can be strictly better when concavity informs the problem. Tests, including a warfarin dosing case, cut cumulative regret sharply.
arxiv-2503-11736:
Onur Beker and six co-authors present a new math frame for robots in twenty twenty-five. Robots that touch and push objects face a hard computing problem. Contact makes the math jumpy and hard to smooth out. Simple search methods cope with that roughness but run slowly. Methods that use slope and curve data could run faster, if the contact model allowed them.

The team joins collision detection and contact modeling in one smooth formulation. Unlike older smooth simulators, theirs gives dynamics that are fully analytic in both directions. That opens the door to planning and control that use first and second order data. Readers in robotics get a base for faster work in contact-rich tasks.
arxiv-2503-12736:
Yeon-Ho Choi, Ueejeong Jeong, Jae-Joon Lee, and a large team of colleagues wrote this astronomy paper, published in 2025. It gives an early report on IGRINS-2, a new near-infrared instrument at the Gemini North telescope, built to read the light of planets around other stars.

High-resolution spectra can pick out single molecules in a planet's air and track winds by their motion. IGRINS-2 improves on its predecessor with better light throughput and a shifted red range that catches carbon monoxide more surely. The team tested the new range with an order-drop method. They then pointed the instrument at WASP-33 b, an ultra-hot giant planet, as a showcase target. The paper reports how the instrument performs in its first look and what the added range buys for planet air studies.
arxiv-2503-14436:
Peter Clarkson, Anton Dzhamay, Andrew Hone, and Ben Mitchell found special solutions of a discrete Painlevé equation. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with an equation that rose from quantum minimal surfaces. In the smooth limit it tends to the first Painlevé equation. Yet its start value space matches the fifth Painlevé equation at set terms. Each step of the discrete form is a set mix of shift moves for the fifth.

Some known solutions of the fifth, writ with Bessel functions, give the sole positive solution of the discrete form. Readers in integrable systems get a bridge that lets two Painlevé worlds share their tool kits.
arxiv-2503-14836:
Kunyang Li and co-authors chart the trade-off between accuracy and robustness when fine-tuning models in a 2025 paper. Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a new task, and it is now standard practice. What it does to a model's ability to resist attacks and odd inputs was murky.

Seven tuning strategies were tested across six benchmark data sets. A consistent trade-off appeared: gains in accuracy cost adversarial robustness. Light-touch methods that update only small bias terms won on simple image tasks. Methods that tune information-heavy attention layers won on harder ones. Robustness to shifted data tracked accuracy closely, unlike attack robustness. The authors argue tuning recipes should be picked with robustness in mind, not accuracy alone.
arxiv-2503-15536:
Jayarshi Bhattacharya, Gautam Gangopadhyay, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about heat-driven current in a small quantum system. The system is an oscillator that touches two baths made of fermions, particles of the kind that make up matter. The baths sit at unlike temperatures, so energy flows between them.

The authors derive equations for how the system state evolves and how current depends on settings and bath temperatures. A measure of transport quality matches the classic Carnot limit at high temperature but departs from it when cold. They also study how the current fluctuates over time. The steady state takes a simple bell shape, confirming that the system behaves like a harmonic oscillator.
arxiv-2503-16336:
Srijan Chakraborty and Samir Datta give a parallel algorithm in two thousand twenty-five for a graph routing problem. The task is to find shortest paths between pairs of terminals that never share a vertex, minimizing total length. They restrict it to planar graphs whose terminals sit on two faces, each holding an odd number of terminals.

Their randomized algorithm solves this odd two-face case in polynomial time and even in parallel. The authors call it the first such solution for the problem. The method merges ideas from earlier two-pair and one-face algorithms. Its proof turns a system of equations into triangular form using two involutions, read as a directed acyclic graph. They also give a parallel algorithm for a related variant.
arxiv-2503-17136:
Brihi Joshi and four co-authors present CoKe, a method to grade stories in fine detail in two thousand twenty-five. Grading creative tales is hard, since human raters split on taste. Chain of thought notes can guide a grader's call. Self consistency then pools calls over many notes.

The team finds a flaw in that pooling step. Notes that read well may not lead to good grades. CoKe first makes a chain of keywords, then a rationale. Many keyword sets are tried and their scores pooled. Small tuned graders with CoKe matched human level on a story set. They beat a top large model by a wide margin.
arxiv-2503-18036:
Ian Koot presents a 2025 math paper on how two half-sided setups sit inside one shared space. Such setups, called modular inclusions, arise in operator algebra and quantum field theory. Each carries a rising family of motions, and each motion has its own spectral slices. The author proves that one setup nests inside the other exactly when the matching spectral slices nest as well.

That test turns a hard inclusion question into a spectral one. A second wording uses symmetric inner functions that carry operator values. Worked examples show odd cases the test sorts out cleanly. Tools of this kind help sort the sub-structures inside quantum systems. The result is a bridge between order and spectrum.
arxiv-2503-18836:
Yuxuan Zhang, Jinkui Hao, and Bo Zhou proposed a faster MRI method in 2025. Magnetic resonance scans give doctors detailed images, but full scans take a long time, which hurts comfort and clinic schedules. Recent diffusion models rebuild sharp images from partial data, yet they usually need full scans for training, cost a lot to run, and give no sense of doubt.

Their system trains without full scans, works in two data domains at once, and uses a lighter attention network. At test time it follows several paths, which also supports estimates of uncertainty. On two human datasets it beat rival methods, keeping fine body structures clearer. Hospitals could scan faster without losing detail.
arxiv-2503-19036:
Jonah Reeger reports observations on neural networks for a classic equation in twenty twenty-five. Machine learning is often used to approximate solutions of partial differential equations. Yet the stability of those solutions has rarely been studied in a systematic way. Reeger looks at the advection-diffusion equation as his test case.

He builds a recurrent network that exactly matches a known numerical scheme. The scheme pairs a multistep method with collocation for spatial derivatives. That match lets classic stability tools from numerical analysis apply to the network. It also lets machine learning training methods speed up the linear operators involved. Reeger then reports how varying many parameters affects even this simple linear problem. Readers get a bridge between learned solvers and proven analysis.
arxiv-2503-19436:
Pablo Burset and co-authors present a 2025 theory paper on electron quantum optics with superconductors. Mesoscopic circuits carry quantum excitations that act like optical signals. A time-varying voltage creates those excitations. They scatter coherently off a superconductor interface. The team builds a full Floquet-Nambu theory for this transport. Its core object is a correlation function that tracks the excitations.

The theory predicts the current from periodic voltage pulses. Pulse energy compared with the superconductor gap steers the result. Conditions are given for scattered states to form coherent electron-hole mixes. A purity measure grades how well the outgoing states can carry quantum data. A chiral test system shows the frame at work. Quantum device teams get design rules for electron optics, a field that copies light optics at chip scale.
arxiv-2503-19636:
Pragya Singh, Ritvik Budhiraja, Pankaj Jalote, Mohan Kumar, and Pushpendra Singh study how people feel while giving emotion data in two thousand twenty-five. Body signals such as heart rate can track mood, but the labels for those signals come from the people themselves. How people see the task shapes the labels they give.

Thirty-seven people watched all-around virtual reality videos in a lab while their signals were recorded. Interviews after the sessions probed what shaped their responses and labels. The team found that personal outlook, small design choices, and the lab setup all played a role. They offer advice for building studies around the person, not just the signal.
arxiv-2503-19836:
The ATLAS Collaboration wrote a paper from 2025 measuring how often the Large Hadron Collider makes pairs of heavy tau leptons at high mass. The team used the full run of proton collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts, a hundred forty inverse femtobarns of data. The rate, charted against the pair's visible mass, matched the standard model's forecast. Agreement at the heavy end is itself a tool: new particles that favor the third family of matter would bend that chart.

The authors fit the mass shape while sorting events by jet content, hunting for such bends. Their targets included effective-theory effects, hypothetical leptoquarks, and new Z-prime bosons that couple mainly to third-generation fermions. No signal appeared, so the paper sets tighter limits than before. The bounds even reach the tau's anomalous magnetic moment, a precision quantity where any deviation would be news.
arxiv-2503-19936:
Kelaiti Xiao and colleagues built a benchmark of stylized images that probe abstract visual reasoning in a 2025 paper. VisualQuest holds thousands of non-photographic images across public figures, popular culture, linguistic expressions, and literary works, each paired with questions demanding symbolic, cultural, and language knowledge rather than plain object naming. Captioning skill alone cannot crack a visual pun or an emoji riddle, which is exactly the point of the set.

Ten leading multimodal models were tested. Only two, named in the paper, performed strongly overall, and a small slice of images defeated every model. One leader excelled at stylized public figures, the other at linguistic puzzles. The dataset maps where machine visual understanding still thins out.
arxiv-2503-21636:
Leon Bein, Niels Martin, and Luise Pufahl built KRAFT in 2025, a frame that assigns staff to tasks with the help of a knowledge graph. Firms must weigh roles, skills, case traits, and rules for each open task. Rule lists written by hand are rigid and costly to keep up, while fully auto systems hide why a choice was made.

A knowledge graph stores people, skills, and links in a web that a computer can read. KRAFT draws on that web to propose assignments that fit the case at hand. Each proposal can be traced back through the web, so a manager can see the grounds. The aim is staffing that adapts fast yet stays open to check.
arxiv-2503-23236:
Ismaël Zighed and co-authors build a reduced model for unsteady fluid flows in a paper from 2025. Full flow simulations are costly, so engineers use small models that mimic them. A useful small model must work across settings and report its own confidence. Their model, UP-dROM, is built for changing flows and carries both traits by design.

A variational encoder compresses the flow while measuring uncertainty. A transformer then predicts how the compressed state evolves, guided by outside parameters. The confidence score also guides where to sample new settings cheaply. Tests target more informed decisions in engineering use. The authors stress robustness across regimes as the main advance.
arxiv-2504-00036:
Hido Pinto and Eran Segal present a 2025 paper on using outside biobanks to sharpen disease prediction when local labels are scarce. Medical data sets often lack the disease outcomes a model needs. The authors test whether filling in missing chemical measures from a big external bank can still teach useful biology.

They trained models on their own ten thousand person data set to guess blood chemistry features. Those models then filled the same features for the UK Biobank. Survival analysis on the filled data found disease risk links the raw models had missed. A gene wide scan on key features tied one signal to vascular dementia, they report.
arxiv-2504-00236:
Diffusion models can generate realistic motion, but for robots and other control tasks the motion also has to obey physics. Darshan Gadginmath and Fabio Pasqualetti present a framework that builds the system's dynamics directly into the model's denoising steps. At each step the model predicts a trajectory and then projects it so that it respects the physical constraints, in rhythm with the noise schedule. The result is motion that both looks like the expert examples and can actually be carried out.

The method can produce the most likely trajectories and can even recover trajectories made by linear feedback controllers without being told the dynamics explicitly. Tests cover standard control tasks plus a harder problem that mixes waypoint tracking with collision avoidance in a non-convex setting. The authors argue that weaving dynamics into generation, rather than checking afterward, makes diffusion models practical for planning and control in complex environments.
arxiv-2504-01236:
Stefan Diehl and co-authors argue the case for close ties between a planned American collider and European particle physics, in a 2025 strategy document. The Electron-Ion Collider will probe how quarks and gluons build protons, nuclei, and all visible matter. The project cleared a key approval in April 2024, and its detector collaboration counts about a thousand members. Roughly a quarter of the user group and nearly a third of the detector team are based in Europe.

The document maps the overlap between the collider's questions and the program at CERN. European groups already drive much of the project, and their home experiments stand to gain in return. The authors present the links as a two-way street worth protecting in Europe's strategy update. The catalog record carries a bare date as its title; the text itself is the collider document.
arxiv-2504-01536:
Li and three co-authors mined a star survey for the fossil substructures of the Milky Way's inner halo in twenty twenty-five. The halo preserves debris from galaxies our galaxy absorbed. Using chemistry and motion together can separate these overlapping streams.

Applying the StarGO algorithm in a seven-dimensional space of three chemical abundances, angular momentum, orbital actions, and energy, the team analyzed APOGEE survey data. Known structures reappeared, including the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger remnant and the Sagittarius stream. A new metal-poor group likely ties to a known structure, and a high-alpha group links two streams, Nyx and Nyx-2, supporting a shared origin. Three brand-new candidates showed disk-like motion but dwarf-galaxy-like chemistry, pointing to recent accretion. The authors present the catalog as a step toward reconstructing the galaxy's assembly history.
arxiv-2504-02036:
Nithyanandan Thyagarajan and co-authors published this study in 2025. It borrows a trick from radio astronomy to profile a light beam in two dimensions. Synchrotron facilities need to know their beam's exact shape. Older optical methods need several interferograms or precise knowledge of uneven lighting across the aperture. The borrowed trick uses closure amplitudes, ratios that cancel out lighting errors by design.

With a single interferogram through a masked aperture, the method recovers the beam profile at fine angular detail. Even time-varying lighting does not disturb it, allowing longer averaging and lighter data loads. The team tested it on real data from the ALBA synchrotron in Spain. Results matched existing methods. It is the first real-world use of closure amplitudes for direct beam profiling in optics.
arxiv-2504-02736:
Shang-Qiang Ning, Yang Qi, Chenjie Wang, and Zheng-Cheng Gu link a deep puzzle of physics to topological order in a twenty twenty-five paper. Parity, the symmetry between left and right, is broken in the weak force, and no one knows why. The team asks if a phase of matter could force such a break.

They study a three-dimensional fermionic topological order tied to a known protected phase. In that setting, one form of time-reversal symmetry clashes with the phase and cannot hold. Through a principle that maps the phase to a crystal, parity clashes too. A second form of time reversal stays fine. The work frames parity violation as enforced symmetry breaking.
arxiv-2504-02836: Aurélien Drezet replied to critics of his defense of relational quantum mechanics in a 2025 comment. That interpretation holds that a system's state is defined only relative to another system, drawing sharp objections. Lawrence, Markiewicz, and Żukowski commented on Drezet's earlier defense, disputing its analysis. Here he answers in turn, stating that he refutes their proposed analysis and restates his earlier study to clear the ambiguities in his rebuttal. The exchange belongs to a longer published debate over whether relational quantum mechanics survives its critics.
arxiv-2504-04036:
Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light, and detecting them cheaply at room temperature is a standing challenge. Ryzhii and co-authors propose a detector built from perforated graphene: ribbons of the one-atom-thick carbon sheet linked by narrow bridges. Incoming terahertz waves set the electrons sloshing in patterns called plasmons, which sharpen the response.

Two effects turn that sloshing into a signal: a rectification effect, like a radio diode, and a heating effect in the carriers. The authors compute how sensitivity and detectability vary with wave frequency and with the device's geometry. The two mechanisms trade the lead depending on the design. Their figures suggest the graphene design can rival established terahertz detectors while staying simple and flat.
arxiv-2504-04736:
Anna Goldie, Azalia Mirhoseini, and three co-authors teach language models to reason in steps with synthetic practice data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents SWiRL. Standard training treats each task as one shot. Real agent work takes many steps of thought, tool use, and feedback.

Their method generates multi-step examples with the model itself. Each long run is chopped into single-step pieces for training. Filtering drops the bad pieces before learning starts. Gains appear across math, multi-hop questions, and tool tasks. Improvements run from about eleven to twenty-one percent in relative accuracy. Skills also transfer to tasks outside the training mix.
arxiv-2504-05136:
Yara Elshiaty, Ferdinand Vanmaele, and Stefania Petra prove that a classic optimization method settles down even without the smoothness perks textbooks assume. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The exponentiated gradient method tackles problems over positive values, like those in medical image repair. Standard proofs lean on a strict smoothness bound.

The team reads the method as a walk on a curved space drawn from information geometry. In that view they prove worldwide convergence under weak assumptions. They also show that a standard step-size search ends after finitely many tries. Tests, including a sped-up variant, show the method beating a rival curved-space method. The results matter for Poisson-type inverse problems, where data come as counts. Such problems show up in scans, astronomy, and photon imaging.
arxiv-2504-06536:
Happy Buzaaba, Alexander Wettig, David Ifeoluwa Adelani, and Christiane Fellbaum adapt a large language model for African languages in a paper from 2025. The catalog creator field trails off into affiliation text, but the head byline gives the four authors, and they are the ones described here. Big models often stumble on African languages for lack of training text. The team mixed curated African data with high-quality English educational text.

Their models topped similar-sized rivals on a hard African benchmark, especially knowledge questions. Cross-lingual question answering beat the base model by over ten percent. Translating training text into Swahili showed the content, not the language, drove gains. Models and data are released openly.
arxiv-2504-07736:
After a wildfire, rain on bare slopes can send mud rivers through towns, and the true physics of those flows is too slow to run live. Palak Patel, Luke McGuire, and Abani Patra train a stand-in in 2025: a deep net fed on runs of the slow model. The land is cut into patches, each guessed by the net, then sewn back into one map. A smart spread of training runs covers the knob space with few costly runs.

On fresh knobs and fresh land the stand-in's worst point miss stayed under a tenth. Speed is the point: with the stand-in, dice-roll risk maps that were out of reach now run in fair time. Town planners could weigh many what-if storms, not one. The team frame the net as a lens on the physics, not a swap for it.
arxiv-2504-09236:
Anwesh Ray links graph towers to group representations in a solo 2025 note. Iwasawa theory tracks how number theoretic objects grow in towers. Cayley graphs have their own version, built on graph zeta functions. Their Jacobians grow along towers of covering graphs.

Ray refines that theory using the group's irreducible representations. The Iwasawa polynomial of a tower splits into factors indexed by those representations. Each factor becomes a representation theoretic Iwasawa polynomial of its own. He studies the properties of these finer pieces. The factorization is canonical, not a matter of choices. The analogy between graph zeta functions and number field L functions drives the work. Representation theory thus sharpens an arithmetic style invariant of graphs.
arxiv-2504-09336:
Simon-Christian Klein develops a new recovery method for finite volume schemes in two thousand twenty-five. The method is in the essentially non-oscillatory family, used near sharp jumps. Classic forms pick stencils with divided differences or smoothness gauges. His form rests on a fresh take of the rebuild step.

He states the rebuild as a variational problem with a set of allowed answers. The sign rule of the classic method becomes limits on that set. A guessing step spots where jumps may sit. No tuning knobs remain past order and stencil width. A fixed stencil is used, which eases fast high order code.
arxiv-2504-09836:
Karthik Elamvazhuthi, Darshan Gadginmath, and Fabio Pasqualetti design controllers for nonlinear systems using diffusion ideas in a 2025 study. Instead of steering one trajectory, they steer the whole probability cloud of possible states toward a target set. Their framework is deterministic, even though diffusion usually involves randomness.

First the system is excited with white noise so its reachable region is explored. A feedback law then acts like a denoiser, driving states back toward the desired distribution. The authors give guarantees for systems without drift and for linear time-invariant cases. Score matching supplies the learned ingredient that makes the reverse process work.
arxiv-2504-10036:
Zhengxuan Zhang, Zhuowen Liang, Yin Wu, Teng Lin, Yuyu Luo, and Nan Tang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. Its text presents DataPuzzle, a plea to rebuild language model data analysis as open steps that can be checked, in place of one-shot prompt answers.

The authors argue that fluency hides a structural flaw: proof, thought, and verdict are crushed into one murky reply. Their frame splits a hard query into parts, casts facts into tables and graphs, and gives set roles to agents for pulling, translating, and linking. Each step can be traced and checked. The piece is a blueprint and a call, not a test report: structure, they say, is the path to trust.
arxiv-2504-10536:
Lihong Zhang and Yue Li wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It trains large language models across hospitals without raw records ever leaving home, by fine-tuning only some layers at a time.

In federated learning each site tunes on its own data and shares model updates, not text. Here the rest of the layers stay frozen, so far less data crosses the wire. On a one-billion-parameter LLaMA model the trick cuts traffic by about seventy percent. Scores stay within two percent of central training. Tests on clinical name finding and sorting use the i2b2 and MIMIC-III sets. The method holds up on skewed site data and with privacy noise added.
arxiv-2504-10736: Yakov Veryovkin and Temur Rahmatullaev present a 2025 arXiv paper in group theory, on the lower central series of right-angled Coxeter groups. Each step of the series yields a factor group, and these factors assemble into a graded Lie algebra tied to the group. The authors describe an explicit basis for the fourth graded piece of that algebra, valid for any defining complex. The result sharpens the algebraic picture of a widely studied group family.
arxiv-2504-11836:
James Neill and Rebecca Lester lead a team introducing the Rippler, a sampling algorithm that infers hidden epidemic spread from partial data far more efficiently. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Disease transmission models track individuals switching states, but infections are rarely all observed. Bayesian workarounds are often slow or painful to code.

The trick is to let the transmission model itself propose new histories inside the sampler. Acceptance then judges complete, plausible epidemics at once. Tests on simulated outbreaks showed a good balance of mixing speed and cost. The method was applied to drug-resistant Escherichia coli spread data from Blantyre, Malawi. Comparisons against two standard inference methods favored the newcomer. The authors offer it as a general tool for discrete epidemic models. Public health modelers gain speed without losing rigor.
arxiv-2504-13536:
Arno Fehm and Manuel Bodirsky settle complexity questions over p-adic numbers in twenty twenty-five. The p-adics are a number system built around a prime p, central to number theory. They ask which equation problems over them can be solved in polynomial time. Prior work showed a key satisfiability problem is NP-complete for primes at least five.

The cases of two and three were left open. Fehm and Bodirsky close them: the problem is NP-complete over the three-adics but polynomial-time over the two-adics. They also give polynomial algorithms for linear systems with one-sided valuation constraints. Those algorithms decide satisfiability of linear inequalities as well. Readers get a sharp complexity boundary drawn at the smallest primes.
arxiv-2504-14036:
Mateusz Krukowski, a solo author, presents a 2025 math paper on growth and chance. He studies Darwin-style change in two models. One model grows a group with a cap set by food and space, in the old Malthus style. The other model uses Markov chains, where a system steps between states by set odds. Fixed points of those chains play a key role.

Krukowski proves early results for both models and states open guesses for what may hold next. Computer runs back up the guesses with sample cases. The paper is short and formal, aimed at readers in math and model theory. It links two classic tools that are often taught apart. Readers get a clean starting point, plus clear open problems to test with more proof or more runs.
arxiv-2504-14236:
Galler and Neufeld study light driven currents in two dimensional hexagonal materials in twenty twenty-five. Such materials are explored for spin currents, valley control, and topological devices. Strong laser pulses can drive bulk photogalvanic currents from the two valleys of the band structure. Prior work used multi colour or few cycle pulses for this.

The authors show that single colour elliptical pulses also generate these currents in general. The currents have both parallel and transverse, Hall like, parts. Both parts respond strongly to laser settings, giving control knobs for experiments. The current size varies with ellipticity in a way that reveals the band gap at the valleys. Simulations on hexagonal boron nitride confirm the effects. The work suggests new photocurrent based spectroscopy tools.
arxiv-2504-14736:
Nicolás Gaggion and a large team present ChronoRoot 2.0, a platform for watching plant growth over time, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. How roots spread and change reveals how plants adapt, a key topic for farming under stress. The platform builds on cheap hardware from an earlier version. Its software is much stronger and easier to use. An AI segmentation model now tracks six parts of the young plant at once.

The tracked parts span roots, shoots, and the seed itself. They include the main root, side roots, stem base, leaves, and leaf stalks. The system follows these parts frame by frame as the plant grows. That gives researchers clean growth curves without hand tracing. The open platform targets plant labs that need low-cost, high-throughput phenotyping.
arxiv-2504-15036:
Roy Margalit, Michalis Kokologiannakis, Shachar Itzhaky, and Ori Lahav built a runtime checker in twenty twenty-five for programs running under weak memory models. Modern chips may reorder memory operations, so a program can behave in ways its source never suggests. Race detectors miss some of these behaviors because their own probes add synchronization that hides them.

Instead of hunting races directly, the team checks robustness: whether a program shows only strongly consistent behavior. Their algorithm uses location clocks, a variant of the vector clocks in classic race detection, under a C11-style model. The tool, RSAN, is presented as the first dynamic checker of this property. It can pair with standard race detection for defense in depth. Tests across settings show the approach is practical to apply per program.
arxiv-2504-15536:
Maciej Matys and co-workers flipped the light response of a semiconductor stack from positive to negative in a 2025 paper. Gallium nitride quantum wells normally conduct better under illumination. Adding a superlattice back barrier behind an N-polar well changed the sign: with enough superlattice periods. Infrared light at room heat level made conductivity drop instead. Hot tiny charged bits excited from the 2D tiny charged bit gas fell into traps inside the superlattice.

The negative response exceeded eighty-five percent yield, the largest stated for semiconductors per the authors, and stayed fairly stable up to high temperatures. Such a strong, durable effect suits photoelectric logic gates, optical memory, and infrared sensors that work by darkness rather than brightness.
arxiv-2504-16536:
Petra Hozzová and Nikolaj Bjørner present, in twenty twenty-five, a method to build programs from logical specs when some symbols cannot be used in the result. Program synthesis means auto-building a program that fits a given spec. The banned symbols are called uncomputable here: they may appear in the spec but not in the final function. The authors use SMT solving, a logic engine that checks if formulas can hold. Their core is an algorithm that removes quantifiers using model-based projections.

The method covers functions that are fully or partly defined, in theories of uninterpreted functions and linear arithmetic. Special steps handle cases where the solution is unique. A prototype built on the Z3 solver beat prior tools in tests.
arxiv-2504-17736:
Adrian Esser, Chiara Basla, Peter Wolf, and Robert Riener present an engineering paper from 2025 on wearable robots. Soft suits that help arms or legs move often pull on cables to do the work. The paper gives a full design for a small drive unit that pulls two cables at once.

The authors also set out clear tests for such a unit. They check torque, speed control, noise, cooling, and battery life under load. Their unit is built in parts, so motors, pulleys, and sensors can be swapped to fit a new task. By sharing both the design and the test steps, the paper aims to help other teams build and report on their own units.
arxiv-2504-17936:
Simoni, Riva, and Ping cast open quantum drift for solids from first rules in this twenty twenty-five paper. A bath can bend how a stuff acts when it is pushed out of rest. Rest-only tales miss the fade and blur that a bath brings to such acts.

Inside, a thick-grid frame tracks the stuff's state as the bath pulls on it. Bath pull splits into a clean part from fields and a wild part from shakes. Charge-charge links are kept at the same grade as bath links in the frame. A wild-step set of laws falls out, which trims to a known form at its edge. The frame aims at spin, light, and fact tech uses of such stuffs.
arxiv-2504-19136:
Huiling Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 method for sorting land cover in mixed satellite images. Radar and color images see the ground in unlike ways, and blending them often mixes up shared structure with traits unique to each source. Their method splits each image into two parts in the frequency domain: a phase part shared across sources, and a strength part that differs.

One module aligns the phase parts so shapes line up well. A second module merges the strength parts, weighting high and low detail by need. Tests on two public image sets gave top scores against rival methods. The authors frame the work as a physics-aware path for blending unlike sensors, and they plan to share the code.
arxiv-2504-19236:
Akira Takenaka and co-authors present a 2025 paper on reconstructing particle events in giant liquid scintillator detectors. These detectors, like the JUNO observatory in China, catch faint light flashes from neutrinos. Turning flashes into an event's position, energy, and particle type is the core computing task.

Their algorithm leans on neutron calibration sources rather than generic models. A likelihood method combines the timing and charge seen by each light sensor, using response tables built from neutron captures, cosmic ray byproducts, and laser runs. In JUNO simulations it located events within about four centimeters and kept energy readings uniform to under half a percent. It also rejected eighty percent of alpha-particle background while keeping the signal.
arxiv-2504-20136:
Matilde Brazzini and co-authors trace quasar winds at redshift five in a 2025 astronomy paper. Black hole outflows are thought to shape how galaxies and their central holes grow together. The winds span hot and cold phases across many scales. The team combined several tracers to catch them all at once.

Thirty nine luminous quasars were observed with a VLT spectrograph, six also with ALMA. Absorption and emission lines revealed ionized outflows. Some winds exceed forty eight thousand kilometers per second. Black hole masses ran up to ten billion suns. The holes sit above the local mass relation with their hosts. That matches behavior seen at redshift six. The picture suggests a phase of strong black hole feeding and feedback early on.
arxiv-2504-21736:
Han Wang and three co-authors explain how ocean currents pattern wave heights in a 2025 paper. Currents feed or drain energy from surface waves, leaving patchy maps of significant wave height. Earlier work noted the patches mirror current scales and stretch in odd directions.

A linear map, derived from wave-action conservation, connects wave height to the current field directly. Rotational and divergent parts of the flow act very differently through that map. The spectrum of wave heights follows from the current's own energy spectra. Directional spreading of the waves also enters the relation. What looked like a tangle of effects becomes readable statistics. Forecasters can now predict wave patchiness from current data instead of simulating every crest.
arxiv-2505-00036:
Zhongren Chen and five co-authors set out a frame to judge the risk that chatbots pose to free societies by their power to persuade voters. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Fear has grown that such tools could sway polls at low cost. The team ran two survey tests and a real-world drill. They ask if a chatbot can sway many voters more cheaply than normal campaign work. Their frame splits sway into two steps: a voter must first get the plea, then take it in. Past work used one-shot chats. Their tests use long talks, which is how such tools would be used in real campaigns.
arxiv-2505-00836:
Conor Flynn, Christopher Ebersole, and Edmund Zelnio wrote this 2025 paper on teaching radar image models with fake data. Synthetic aperture radar gives detailed images, but real samples are costly to gather, so trainers lean on simulated images made from 3D models. Simulated and real images differ enough that models trained only on fakes stumble in the field.

The team answer with numbers: they fuse many models, each trained on synthetic data, into one ensemble. The ensemble must also reject targets it was never trained on, a skill called confuser rejection, rather than force a wrong label. The paper tests how well the fused models match the behavior of models trained on measured data. The goal is radar recognition that stays honest about unknown targets.
arxiv-2505-01736:
Han Wan, Rui Zhang, Qi Wang, Yang Liu, and Hao Sun present PeSANet in two thousand twenty-five. PeSANet forecasts systems ruled by partial differential equations. Classic solvers strain when laws are partial or unknown. Learning methods strain when data are scarce and spans mix local with global.

The net has two blocks that split that work. One block bakes physics in as hard rules for local acts. The other works in the frequency domain for long range links. A new attention step ties spectra to each other. Tests show PeSANet beats past methods on all gauges. Its edge grows most in long term forecasts.
arxiv-2505-02536:
Sebastian Kokott, Volker Blum, and Matthias Scheffler present a faster way in 2025 to do a costly step in materials math. The step is called exact exchange, and it helps predict how electrons act in a solid. Doing it over long ranges is exact but slow, so many codes cut it off.

The team extends a screening trick that softens the force between charges at long range. A small math fix-up lets the short-range method stand in for the long-range part. Tests on semiconductors and organic crystals gave energy values close to the full method. The cost stayed near that of the fast cut-off method. This lets big, careful studies run on more modest computers.
arxiv-2505-03136:
Jiaman He, Zikang Leng, Dana McKay, Johanne Trippas, and Damiano Spina read searchers' eyes to guess what they know, in this two thousand twenty-five information retrieval paper. Eye movements track with knowledge and with how people phrase queries, but most work uses gaze fixations and needs more context. This study uses just pupil dilation and gaze velocity, signs tied to memory. It reads how well a user knows a topic and the specificity of their query. No facts on content are needed.

In a lab study with eighteen participants, a gradient boosting classifier called topic familiarity with a macro F1 score of about seventy-one percent. A nearest-neighbor classifier called query specificity at about sixty-one percent. The team also wrote an annotation guideline, fit to question answering, labeling queries as specific or non-specific. The upshots show eye-tracking alone can show cognitive state for search systems.
arxiv-2505-03436:
Gabriella Pinzari, Benedetto Scoppola, and Matteo Veglianti analyze a two-layer model with resonance trapping in a 2025 math study. The model, with two and a half degrees of freedom and forcing that changes with time, was known numerically to capture trajectories into resonance for long stretches. To explain that capture takes a normal form theory adapted to forcing that is not quasi-periodic, which the authors supply.

Seen through that theory, the trapping time comes out exponentially long, with an explicit estimate. Long resonance capture shapes transport in celestial mechanics and plasma confinement, so a proved time scale takes the place of numerical impression.
arxiv-2505-04436:
Michael Anastos, Sahar Diskin, Joshua Erde, Mihyun Kang, Michael Krivelevich, and Lyuben Lichev prove that a randomly thinned hypercube still holds a near-full cycle. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works with the d-dimensional binary hypercube. Each edge is kept by chance with a fixed rate. Past workers long guessed that a low rate would still leave a cycle through near all points.

The team confirms that guess. For any fixed slack, a rate that scales as a constant over d does the job. With high chance, the kept graph has a cycle that misses at most that slack share of points. The rate is sharp in shape: it falls as dimension grows. The result backs a conjecture the authors cite from a recent monograph. It adds a firm stone to the study of random subgraphs of the cube.
arxiv-2505-04736:
Sutapa Dey Tithi and six co-authors tested language models as logic tutors in twenty twenty-five. Intelligent tutoring systems teach formal proof well but lean on rigid templates, limiting personal feedback. Language models promise tailored hints, with risks of hallucination and poor pedagogy. The team measured stepwise proof accuracy across six prompting styles and four leading models on hundreds of propositional logic problems.

One model reached about eighty-seven percent stepwise accuracy, strongest on simpler rules. Its hints, generated for over a thousand real student states, were seventy-five percent accurate. Human raters praised their consistency and clarity but found them weaker at explaining why a hint was given and how it fits the wider proof. The verdict: models can augment logic tutoring, with guardrails.
arxiv-2505-06236:
Jerzy Gorecki, Yuki Koyano, and Hiroyuki Kitahata test a shortcut model for a spinning camphor rotor on water, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Camphor boats and rotors have drawn study for two hundred years: the stuff leaks into the water and pushes the craft along. A full account pairs the motion with fluid flow and camphor spread, a hard sum.

A newer shortcut folds the push into a single energy term, which makes the sums far cheaper. The team tried it on one rotor with a fixed camphor disk nearby as a pest. The shortcut gave results unlike the lab runs. Adding fluid drag to the push term helped, and tracking the camphor spread through time helped more. The authors doubt the shortcut for paired rotors.
arxiv-2505-06636:
Yifan Zeng proposes a security framework for networks of connected robots in a 2025 paper. Robots linked with sensors form the Internet of Robotic Things, used in smart factories and self-driving fleets. An intrusion there can leak data, halt services, or even move machines in harmful ways.

Local robots hold no labeled attack data, and their data must stay private. The framework therefore learns across sites without pooling raw records, and it learns from mostly unlabeled traffic. Contrastive training, which teaches the model to tell similar from different traffic, strengthens detection. Mixed weak and strong data tweaks add robustness. The design targets factories and fleets that need intrusion alarms without giving up data control.
arxiv-2505-06736:
A team of four physicists studied fast flow past a block in a quantum fluid. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a Lee-Huang-Yang quantum fluid in a near flat sheet. Fast flow past a block can spawn rich wave forms. They looked at two kinds: plain light like radiation and slanted dark solitons. Both were worked out by hand and by number runs.

The wave crests of the radiation fit a tweaked form of Kelvin's classic theory. The slanted soliton came from a shift of the one dimensional case into the block's frame. Hand and number results matched well. Readers in quantum fluids get firm laws for waves in a flow that outruns sound.
arxiv-2505-07136:
Mathias Hedegaard Kristensen and Esben Skovsen map the beams of four shop-bought terahertz emitters across a wide band, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The emitters pair light-mixing diodes with silicon lenses. A broadband receiver scanned a square grid to catch each beam's far-field shape.

Beam spread grew with frequency in a steady pattern for all four devices. Ring-shaped diffraction patterns appeared at mid frequencies, blamed on lens aperture effects. The team pulled out hard numbers for spread, lopsidedness, ovalness, and center drift. Such full maps guide lens and package design, they argue, beyond what a single line scan can show.
arxiv-2505-07636:
Radouan Boukharfane studies, in twenty twenty-five, how an oblique shock wave stirs a supersonic reacting shear layer, a flow key to scramjet engines. Efficient mixing at high speed is crucial for scramjets. Shock interactions can enhance it. He ran direct numerical simulations, which resolve the flow in full detail, for four setups: inert and reacting layers, each with and without shock impact. A streaming mode decomposition method extracted the dominant flow patterns and their growth over time.

The shock strongly amplified Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, the rolling waves that mix layers. It excited more unstable modes and sped the growth of the vorticity thickness. Combustion heat release reshuffled energy among modes, boosting high-frequency ones and altering spatial patterns. Distinct frequency bands tied to shock and combustion effects were identified.
arxiv-2505-07736:
Eason Chen and seven co-authors present VTutor, a web platform that lets one tutor watch over many students learning online at once, in this 2025 paper. In hybrid tutoring a human guide supports several students who each work with learning software. Standard meeting tools cannot show the tutor every screen while keeping conversation open, so struggling students get missed.

VTutor shares student screens directly between browsers and adds animated avatar prompts powered by AI. A dashboard lets the tutor spot off task or stuck students quickly and step in. The design draws on research about animated teaching agents to keep students engaged, and it aims to work on weak connections. The authors close with open questions about scaling such AI guided tutoring.
arxiv-2505-08036:
Ze-An Ng studies extreme moves of geometric Brownian motion in two thousand twenty-five. The process is a standard model of growth with random shocks. He looks at its paths when the running peak takes large values. Large deviation theory says such paths tend to a fixed curve.

Ng shows the paths in fact meet that curve in a strong sense. He also gives hard bounds on how fast they close in. He then turns to short life options in finance. New closed form prices come out for barrier options with path based payoffs. Exact forms cover Asian and lookback styles, with error bounds.
arxiv-2505-08436:
Stephen Chege, Louis Bastogne, and five colleagues compute how stretching a ferroelectric crystal changes the inner structure of its domain walls, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The material is lead titanate, and the walls in question separate regions polarized in opposite directions, a one-hundred-eighty-degree flip.

Basic walls of this kind are Ising-like, with polarization shrinking straight through zero. The simulations, based on density functional theory, show an extra Bloch-type component appearing on top under realistic strain. In that component, polarization rotates sideways within the wall plane, driven mainly by lead atoms shifting there. Its size and energy benefit depend sharply on the in-plane lattice spacing. Pulling the crystal, as certain substrates do, strengthens the Bloch part and lowers the wall's energy notably. The findings matter because wall structure shapes how ferroelectric devices switch and store information.
arxiv-2505-08836: Ion Cotăescu, in a 2025 arXiv paper, studies how the null energy condition applies to models of black holes that change over time in flat expanding space. He reports a new identity and uses it to test recent models of such black holes. The condition picks out the models that make physical sense. In those models, the horizons change in line with general black hole theory in frames that use null coordinates, following work by Hayward. The paper is short and focused on this single test.
arxiv-2505-09236:
Bastien Auvray, Julien David, Samah Ghazawi, Richard Groult, Gad Landau, and Thierry Lecroq give the first methods for finding near-matches of Cartesian tree patterns with one flaw allowed. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in string algorithms. Cartesian tree matching compares the tree shape a number string induces, not its raw values. Exact matching was solved; one-difference matching was open.

Their generic method scans a text for spans whose tree sits one difference from the pattern's. Several senses of difference are covered by the same frame. Worst-case cost is stated in text and pattern lengths. On random inputs the method runs in near-linear time on average. An automaton-based variant adapts a known exact method. It can stretch to more than one difference. The work widens pattern search for data where shape matters more than values.
arxiv-2505-09336:
Muzammil Behzad wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It reads facial expressions from three- and four-dimensional face data with no labels, by tying many views of a face to text prompts the model writes itself.

The model, MultiviewVLM, is a vision-language build. Fake labels from made prompts steer the match between face views and mood words. A shared embedding space lines the views up without any hand marks. A new contrastive plan picks steady pairs of like and unlike faces. A smooth loss keeps training calm, and the build scales across machines. In tests it beats the past best methods. The author notes it can shift to other real tasks with small changes.
arxiv-2505-10236:
Rob Bemthuis helps managers choose among the many process models that process mining software produces, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Process mining reconstructs how work actually flows inside an organization, but success breeds overload: dozens of models, each partly right, and no clear way to pick.

His answer is multi-criteria decision making, which scores models on several grounds at once. Hard metrics like fitness and precision count alongside soft factors like cultural fit. An illustrative logistics case uses the Analytic Hierarchy Process to structure the trade-offs. The method aligns the choice with managerial objectives instead of a single accuracy number. Early insights suggest the selected models serve both operations and broader management needs. The study is exploratory, laying a foundation for fuller trials. It reframes model selection as a management decision, not just a technical one.
arxiv-2505-11236:
Rohan Basu Roy and co-authors build ForgetMeNot, a tool that counts the climate cost of so called forever chemicals in chip making, in a 2025 paper. Fluorinated compounds drive key steps of fabrication and linger in the air for millennia, with warming power thousands of times that of carbon dioxide. Sustainability work in computing had counted carbon alone.

The tool blends each factory's practices with hardware specs to estimate the fluorinated output. Checks against real factory data validated its numbers. Runs across processors, memory, and storage show how design choices move emissions. Data center buyers can also pick lower emission servers for a set performance target.
arxiv-2505-13236:
Joseph Ben Geloun and Arnauld Solente extend a branch of field theory in a 2025 paper. In tensor field theory, the quantities that can be measured are built by joining tensor fields in patterns that stay unchanged under a broad group of transforms. In the standard setup, every field in a pattern has the same order, the same number of indices.

Their frame allows fields of mixed orders in one pattern, as long as none passes a set maximum. They then build a group-based method to list all such measurable patterns in a systematic way. The method covers the older counting schemes and matches their results in the cases those schemes handled. Software tools in the paper do the counting in practice, and they turn up new integer sequences not recorded before.
arxiv-2505-13936:
Murad, Dahal, and Rahimi build R1 Translator, a tool that turns brain waves to text. Big word tools have grown fast, yet brain-to-word work lags still. Past tools that read EEG waves to text score low in tests. Their new tool pairs two parts to lift those scores. A two-way LSTM reads the wave codes and holds their order. A pre-trained chain tool then writes the text from those codes.

Wave traits feed the LSTM first in the build chain. Its codes pass to the chain tool for word choice next. R1 tops past tools on ROUGE scores in the runs. Its ROUGE-1 mark hit 38.00 percent in the test set. That beats T5 by up to nine points on the mark. Its word flaw rate also ran low next to peers.
arxiv-2505-14036:
Gyubin Lee and six co-authors find a smarter way to scale diffusion runs in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion models do strong work, from making images to hard tasks of thought. Most ways to scale at run time rest on fixed schedules for the steps that clear the noise. The work spent then cannot shift to match how hard each case turns out to be.

Their plan, ABCD, runs a search through cycles of diffusion that move in both directions. It refines output through those cycles and decides how deep to search and when to stop. Three parts share the load: cyclic diffusion search, an automatic balance of search and use, and thinking time that shifts with the case at hand. Hard cases can draw more run time, and light ones draw less. Tests showed gains across a range of tasks, while the cost stays in check.
arxiv-2505-14536:
Agam Goyal, Vedant Rathi, William Yeh, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It cleans toxic language out of large language models by steering the model's inner activity, using sparse autoencoders to find the exact directions tied to toxicity.

Most detox methods patch the surface and can be dodged by jailbreak prompts. Sparse autoencoders split a model's activity into tidy, readable features. The team found the features linked to profanity and slurs, then pushed activity away from them at three strengths. On two models, strong steering cut toxicity by up to a fifth more than rival methods, though fluency suffered on the smaller model. Standard knowledge tests stayed flat, so the model's skills survived. The paper also warns that overly split features blunt such fixes, and draws lessons for safer deployment.
arxiv-2505-14936:
Salman Habib, Remi Chou, and Taejoon Kim propose, in a 2025 signal processing paper, a cheaper schedule for an interval-based method that rebuilds sparse signals from few measurements. Compressed sensing solves such underdetermined puzzles, and the interval method is prized for its low cost against optimization rivals. Their twist borrows the sequential decoding style of modern error-correcting codes.

Instead of updating every check at once, their scheme visits one check at a time per round. Average message traffic drops, by over a third in some settings. Proofs and simulations agree that accuracy holds steady. The authors offer the schedule as a drop-in saving for interval-based recovery.
arxiv-2505-15236:
Koustav Banerjee, Kathrin Bringmann, and Ben Kane study a counting sequence from combinatorics in a 2025 paper. The sequence u(n) counts unimodal sequences of total size n, arrangements that rise then fall. The authors derive a precise growth formula for it, complete with a guaranteed bound on the error, for sequences admitting exact formulas.

With that formula in hand, they prove the sequence obeys a family of stricter pattern rules, the higher order Turán inequalities, for all n from thirty-three upward. Certain shifted second differences of the sequence also come out positive. The generic method is the point: the same approach should settle such inequalities for other sequences with exact counting formulas.
arxiv-2505-15336:
Hon Ming Yam, Zhongliang Guo, and Chun Pong Lau built a guard for faces against deepfake swaps. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with diffusion based face tools. Fake face tech can bend a person's image with no leave, a clear abuse risk. Past guards lean on spotting fakes after the fact. This team strikes first: they mar the source photo in ways that break later swaps.

Old such guards were made for older build types and fail on diffusion models. New diffusion guards lean on one model's weights and die when the model shifts. Their guard aims to hold across models. Readers who guard their image get a first move defense for the diffusion age.
arxiv-2505-15836:
Aarav Lala and Kalyan Cherukuri published a research paper in 2025 on teams of AI agents that learn together without pooling private data. Their framework uses quantum-inspired networks honed by evolution. Decentralized settings like smart cities and hospitals need decisions that are fast, adaptive, and private. The design borrows superposition and entanglement ideas to widen the search for good strategies.

An evolutionary loop keeps refining agent behavior as conditions shift. Federated learning stitches the lessons together while raw data stays on site. The authors report gains in learning speed and decision accuracy over plain approaches in their tests. They pitch the blend at autonomous systems and other privacy-sensitive, fast-changing worlds, though the evidence is early.
arxiv-2505-16736:
Nicolas Keriven, writing alone in 2025, asks why deep graph neural networks are so hard to train. Such networks pass information between linked points, layer by layer. A known flaw, oversmoothing, washes out point features in the forward pass. In theory, big enough weights could dodge that flaw. In practice, trained networks still smooth too much. Keriven turns the lens to the backward pass, where errors flow back to set the learning steps.

Those backward signals, he argues, also get smoothed away. That backward oversmoothing starves deep layers of useful gradients. The interplay between forward and backward passes is the key mechanism. Nonlinear activation functions shape how the two interact. The paper gives an optimization view of a famous puzzle. It suggests fixes should target training dynamics, not just network shape.
arxiv-2505-17736:
Nilanjan Sinhababu and co-authors steer search rankings with examples rather than fresh training, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Real search must balance pure relevance with goals like diversity and fairness. Those goals hinge on how results interact, and past fixes needed new training for each task.

Their method shows a language-model ranker a few sample rankings that display the wanted trade-offs. The samples come from past queries much like the current one. Gains reached about twenty percent for fairness and over twenty percent for topic diversity. Relevance held steady across the test sets.
arxiv-2505-17936:
Sebastian Gerstner and Hinrich Schütze study single neurons inside language models, in a 2025 paper on how the models work. Most past work judged a neuron by when it fires or by what it writes out. The pair ask a third question: how does what a neuron reads compare with what it writes?

They compare the input and output weights of neurons across twelve models. Some neurons add more of what they detect, while others cut it back. The first kind rules in early and middle layers, and the second kind grows later. The authors tie the first kind to a step in recalling facts. Their view adds a fresh lens for model analysis.
arxiv-2505-18136:
Mykola Trokhymovych, Lydia Pintscher, Ricardo Baeza-Yates, and Diego Saez-Trumper build a vandalism detector for Wikidata in two thousand twenty-five. Wikidata is a vast open base of facts and texts in many tongues. Edits can change both the fact triples and the words. Past guards treated those two sides apart.
