Their method, Graph2Text, turns all edits into one text space. One multilingual language model then checks each change for vandalism. Tests show the system beats the current live guard. The team shares code under an open license. They also share a large set of human made changes to aid more work.
arxiv-2505-18236:
Matuszczyk and five co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-five on bias in geospatial AI and new European audit duties. Bias findings in location-based models are scattered across narrow studies. The team gather that evidence into one overview. Recurring bias types span representation, algorithm, and grouping issues. Each type is mapped to clauses of the European AI Act. Widely used location systems qualify as high-risk under the Act. Recent audit examples and detection methods are laid out.

Routine bias audits are urged even for well-kept datasets. Full high-risk duties bite in twenty twenty-seven. The study is the first to fuse this bias evidence with the Act. Exploratory limits are admitted openly.
arxiv-2505-18636:
Tim Zhou, Evan Shelhamer, and Geoff Pleiss pair big models with small ones, in a 2025 preprint, to get better uncertainty estimates. The standard trick, ensembling many runs of one model, costs too much at today's model sizes. Their Asymmetric Duo joins a strong large model with a far cheaper small sidekick. A learned weighted average merges the two verdicts. Intuition says the weak partner should drag the strong one down. The tests say otherwise.

Across five image benchmarks and many training styles, the duo beat the big model alone. Accuracy rose, uncertainty quality rose, and the model knew better when to abstain. The extra computing cost stayed around ten to twenty percent. The sidekick almost never hurt, even when much weaker. The authors suggest duos as a cheap default for high-stakes image work, where knowing your uncertainty guides real decisions.
arxiv-2505-19136:
Frank Shih, Zhenghao Jiang, and Faming Liang quantify uncertainty in physics-informed networks in twenty twenty-five. Such networks solve scientific problems with equations built into training. Users need confidence sets around their answers. Bayesian and dropout methods are the usual tools, but both hinge on choices that data cannot pin down.

A prior or dropout rate chosen blindly can make the stated confidence dishonest. The authors propose a method inside extended fiducial inference instead. A narrow-neck hyper-network learns the network's parameters. Uncertainty is quantified from imputed random errors in the observations. Readers in scientific machine learning get rigorous intervals without an unverifiable prior. The approach aims at confidence that means what it says.
arxiv-2505-19536:
Jintao Tong and co-authors rethink how to trim waste tokens in models that join sight and language, in work from 2025. Such models read far more picture tokens than they need, which drives up cost. Most trimming tools rank tokens by a score from a single layer, and the team asks if that is enough.

They trace how facts flow between tokens across layers instead. One special token acts as a relay, which makes the flow easier to read. Waste builds up layer by layer, and single-layer scores can clash with each other. Their method, FlowCut, trims by flow rather than by one score. In tests it beat top rivals while cutting most picture tokens and speeding the first pass over data.
arxiv-2505-20936:
Subhaditya Bhattacharya, Soumyajit Datta, and Abhik Sarkar studied in twenty twenty-five how a same-sign muon collider could expose lepton number violation. Lepton number is a bookkeeping rule of particle physics that some new theories break by two units. Effective field theory packages such breaks into a set of added operators, each a possible fingerprint of new physics.

The team examines collisions of two positive muons producing W bosons and jets at a proposed machine called muTRISTAN. The process is sensitive to eight distinct operators at once. They compute how strongly the collider could bound each one and compare with current LHC limits and plans for a future circular collider. The study makes the case that same-sign muon machines are sharp tools for hunting this kind of violation.
arxiv-2505-21636:
Nemecek, Jiang, and Ayday test a way to mark text written by AI in peer review in twenty twenty-five. Many journals let authors use AI to polish language, but bar its use to judge other work. As AI text grows hard to tell from human text, editors need a way to trace its source. The method hides a signal in the topic choices of the text.

The team tried the method on real review texts with several model setups. Marked reviews kept the same quality as unmarked ones. The hidden signal also survived rewriting in other words. The authors call the method a light touch, workable way to keep review honest.
arxiv-2505-21836:
Davood Momeni disputes a recent claim that black hole ringing tones can be rebuilt from bound states of a flipped potential, in a 2025 comment. The claim drew wide notice for tying two classic problems together. Momeni finds the bridge unsound.

Working figure by figure, he argues the mapping misapplies the boundary conditions that define the ringing modes. The inversion trick misses the complex, leaky nature of black hole resonances. Set against the established asymptotic theory of those modes, the bound state picture gives no reliable grip. The comment warns against reading spectra off a mathematically mismatched analogy.
arxiv-2505-21936:
Zeyi Liao and co-authors present RedTeamCUA in a 2025 paper on adversarial testing of computer use agents. Such agents automate tasks across operating systems and the web, but they are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, where hostile content in a page or document steers them. Existing tests lack realistic hybrid settings.

Their sandbox joins a virtual machine operating system with docker based web platforms. Tests can start right at the injection point, separating security from navigation skill. A benchmark of hundreds of examples probes hybrid attacks. Frontier agents showed high attack success and attempt rates, revealing significant vulnerabilities.
arxiv-2505-22036:
Tetsushi Ito, Daichi Takeuchi, and Takahiro Tsushima give an explicit formula for the L-polynomials of a family of curves over finite fields, in the case of characteristic two, in a 2025 paper. The curves are coverings of the projective line of a classic type. Their L-polynomials encode deep counts about the curves, but they are hard to write down in general.

The formula expresses the polynomial through characters of the largest abelian subgroups of certain Heisenberg groups tied to the curves. To build it, the authors develop methods specific to characteristic two that lean on the group structure and on special geometric objects. As a payoff, they construct curves in the family that meet the Hasse-Weil bound.
arxiv-2505-22636:
Jixin Zhao, Zhouxia Wang, Peiqing Yang, and Shangchen Zhou present ObjectClear, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. ObjectClear erases an object from a photo along with its shadow and its reflections. Older tools based on diffusion models often leave artifacts, invent new content, or warp the background.

ObjectClear splits the job in two: lift out the foreground first, then rebuild what sits behind it. An adaptive attention step that knows the target helps the model find both the object and its effects with care. The learned attention maps also guide a blending step that keeps the final image consistent. To train and test the system, the team built OBER, a large dataset of paired images with and without objects and their effects.
arxiv-2505-22936:
Facundo Oliú wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It studies mean-field games where a crowd of players each steers a Lévy process with two-sided singular controls.

Each player pushes the process up or down with two monotone controls, to trim a long-run cost. All players touch each other through the mean of a like process run by a second pair of controls. With the Brouwer fixed point theorem, the author gives plain checks for when equilibrium controls exist, in both the discounted and the ergodic case. The equilibria are then pinned as the fix of an integro-differential equation. A counterexample shows the fix need not be unique. Ends treat how finite games near this limit.
arxiv-2505-24536:
Chaohui Xu and two co-authors present CHIP, a way to prove who owns a deep learning model and to control its use, in a 2025 study. Training big models costs a lot, so theft and misuse are real risks. Older watermark and passport schemes each cover only part of the problem. CHIP builds on a special hash tool that can make many keys land on one fixed signature, yet stays hard to fake.

Each buyer gets a model copy, a passport, and a license tied to that one signature. The owner can prove rights in a dispute and trace leaks to a buyer. The same checks guard cloud access to the master model. Tests on four data sets and two designs show the scheme holds up under attack. Code is shared in a public repo.
arxiv-2505-24736:
Julio Cesar Cavalcanti and Gabriel Skantze measure what shapes the tiny gaps between speakers in conversation, in a 2025 paper. Turn-taking follows universal rules yet varies a lot. The team used a large set of American English phone conversations. They measured the offset between one speaker ending and the next starting. Sex, age, and schooling were tested as factors. Individual habits were tested too.

Women and older speakers left slightly shorter gaps. Schooling showed no effect. Light topics sped the exchanges a bit. Individual differences mattered much more. The strongest effect was pair-specific. Two partners resembled each other more than either resembled themselves with others. The authors coin a term for that pair signature. Joint activity, they conclude, outweighs demographics. Dialogue systems may need to adapt per pair, not per person. The study blends linguistics with statistics.
arxiv-2506-00936:
Peijin Guo and co-authors predict how stable drug molecules are in the body, with honest confidence attached, in a 2025 paper. Metabolic stability decides how long a drug lasts. Graph neural networks are the current tool of choice. They pass messages between atoms but mostly ignore bond detail. They also give no sense of their own uncertainty. The team's framework, TrustworthyMS, attacks both flaws. It remaps the molecule's graph so atoms and bonds inform each other.

A contrastive step aligns two views of each molecule. One view stresses structure, the other bond patterns. Agreement between views hardens the representation. A statistical device then prices the model's doubt. It reports prediction and confidence together. Tests show the method beating current leaders. The authors frame trust as part of accuracy in drug work. A wrong but confident answer can waste a whole program. Calibrated doubt helps chemists choose what to synthesize next.
arxiv-2506-01636:
Yi Liao and six co-authors devise a way to explain, with pictures, why a metric learning model judges two images as similar. Their paper came out in 2025. Metric learning models compare images by distance between compact summaries, and they lack the built-in classifier layer that standard explanation maps rely on.

Their method scores each feature channel by how much it contributes to the similarity verdict between a pair of images. Weighting the model's internal feature maps by those scores produces a heat map showing the regions that drove the match. Tests, both measured and visual, show the maps give clear and trustworthy explanations. The method works with the two common distance choices, straight-line distance and angle-based similarity.
arxiv-2506-02036: Samuel Hedemann presents new versions of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities, a basic tool of mathematics, extended from two vectors to many at once. From these broader inequalities he derives uncertainty relations that involve several quantum operators at the same time, going beyond the classic two-operator form. He also proposes a matching idea of multi-operator squeezing. The abstract is brief and gives no proofs or examples, so the paper's weight rests on the new inequalities themselves and the relations built on them.
arxiv-2506-02936:
Constantin Chilarescu studies how easily producers can swap inputs in a 2025 economics paper. The elasticity of substitution measures how readily an economy trades capital for labor or one input for another. Earlier work with Gomez had traced its effects on growth in a narrower setting. This paper widens the lens to a general growth model and checks both low and high values of the measure.

The central result is one-directional: a higher elasticity raises income per person. It also raises the relative share of physical capital, the economy's shared growth rate, and the share of human capital assigned to making goods. Notably, the effect holds whether the elasticity sits below or above the dividing value of one, which simplifies how modelers can read it.
arxiv-2506-03036:
Anton Klimek, Benjamin Dalton, and Roland Netz study why some particles spread out more slowly than normal, in a physics paper from 2025. This slow spread, called subdiffusion, shows up in protein folding and in thick, springy fluids. Its causes are debated, since both energy barriers and memory in friction can slow motion.

The team compares models with and without memory and with and without barriers. They build a math frame based on how far particles spread on average over time. For friction with many memory scales, they derive how the slow spread should scale. Tests against simulations show memory rules the motion for low to modest barriers. That range was shown in other work to matter for protein folding. The tools apply to polymers and active matter too.
arxiv-2506-03536:
Liu, Zhang, Wei, Wu, Yu, and Wu present a study from twenty twenty-five on the baryon share in diffuse ionized gas between galaxies. Fast radio bursts act as probes, since their signals spread while crossing gas. The team use over one hundred bursts with known host galaxies. Their model of signal spread matches mock data well. Across three cosmos models, over ninety percent of baryons sit in the diffuse gas phase. That share barely shifts with dark energy assumptions. It does shift with assumptions about our galaxy's halo and host galaxies.

No clear change of the share with distance shows in current data. Sample limits explain that gap, the authors note. Feedback settings do not sway the conclusions. The results support diffuse gas as home of the missing baryons.
arxiv-2506-03636:
Stefan Maschek and co-authors present, in a 2025 quantum software paper, a tunable noise model for simulating today's imperfect quantum hardware, plus a way to judge how good any noise model is. Real machines are small and scarce, so realistic simulators carry the field. Their model builds on a standard channel formalism and is fitted to measured noise from commercial systems.

On a large simulator, it reproduced hardware behavior for two test workloads at fair computing cost. Their quality method works at sizes where older metrics fail. Projecting the model onto future, partly fault-tolerant machines shows how noise shape and algorithm design trade off.
arxiv-2506-03936:
Quentin Vigneron, Hamed Barzegar, and James Read offer a 2025 study of geometry for slow and ultra-fast worlds. They sort the kinds of structures that fit a Galilean view, where time is separate, and a Carrollian view, where light cones close up. Both are compared side by side to give one shared picture.

The authors allow twists and stretching in the links between points, and show how both structures arise as limits of the standard space-time picture. They then build a new trio of gravity theories for the ultra-fast case. Open questions and next steps close the work, which should interest readers of math and gravity theory.
arxiv-2506-04736:
Xuan Ye, Yang Zhang, and Bo Wang calculate how Earth's gravity bends a famous quantum optics experiment in a 2025 paper. Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, where two photons meeting at a splitter always exit together, is a workhorse test of quantumness. Precision versions of it may one day sense tiny effects, including gravity itself.

The authors compute the relativistic time delay two ways: by following light paths, and by solving the wave equation for the phase shift. Gravity affects both the timing and the phase, and the two views must agree. Their second-order results tell experimenters how large the gravitational signal is in a ground lab, and what stability a detector needs to see it.
arxiv-2506-05236:
Maxime Toquebiau and three co-authors give teams of learning agents a shared human language in a 2025 paper. Multi-agent systems often invent their own communication codes, which work poorly and cannot be read by people. The authors instead ground agents in ordinary language from the start.

Each agent learns to act and, at the same time, to describe its observations in words and to read partners' descriptions. The language duty doubles as training signal, shaping richer inner representations. Across tasks, language-augmented agents beat emergent-communication baselines, adapted better to new partners, and proved easier for humans to work with. The authors present grounding in human language as a route to clearer, stronger multi-agent learning.
arxiv-2506-06036:
Ben Dali, Bonzom, and Dolega build path steps that act on matched sums. Matched sums here take two bend marks, named q and t. Each step in the new clan ties to one grid path. Path steps swap twixt up and down moves in a set dance. Good sums of such steps match Negut parts by a known map. That map runs through a shuffle-frame act on matched sums.

The team gives spread forms for what such steps make from one. Forms span lone, base, and Schur matched sums in the text. Steps then probe a bent form of the stock tau sums. That bent form spans known chains in count, gauge, and meld work. A set of part sums marks that bent sum as the sole such form. Steps also give a fresh proof of the wide delta claim.
arxiv-2506-07136:
Wenzhang Sun and colleagues organise video motion into two layers for compact autoencoding. Their twenty twenty-five paper presents a system called MotionStrata. Video autoencoders often store scene content once, then code the motion. Treating all motion alike wastes that compact code, though.

Global queries now capture broad scene change over time. Detailed queries keep fine frame-by-frame structure instead. Routing guided by frequency helps assign motion to the right layer. Training moves from coarse detail to fine detail in stages. Reconstruction stayed strong even under heavy compression. The design beat uniform motion codes in the tests. Video creators and model builders gain a leaner way to store moving images.
arxiv-2506-07536:
Jin Li, Man-Wai Mak, Johan Rohdin, Kong Aik Lee, and Hynek Hermansky bring Bayesian learning to speaker verification and anti spoofing that must hold across domains. Both tasks sag badly when real world domains mismatch. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

A frequency normalization trick trims domain pull in feature maps, but fixed weights for each frequency band waste its power. The team argues bands deserve varied weights, and that doubt in those weights from domain shift counts too. Variational inference models the weight spread, giving a Bayesian weighted form. Tests across data sets and spoof styles show clear gains over the fixed forms.
arxiv-2506-09236:
Erin Argo, Tanim Ahmed, Sarah Gable, Callie Hampton, Jeronimo Grandi, and Regis Kopper review a decade of work on augmented reality interfaces for first responders. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses a scoping method with set review rules. The field spans emergency medicine, firefighting, and law enforcement. A keyword search pulled a large pool of papers, of which a small share met the bar.

Close study of the kept set yields a faceted taxonomy of such interfaces. Classes split by task, display style, and setting of use. Key trends, design points, and gaps are mapped along the way. Public safety work through April of the study year is covered. The authors aim the review at builders and scholars in the field. It lays a base for the next round of design work.
arxiv-2506-09936:
Muniz and a large team demonstrate replacing lost atoms mid-computation on a neutral-atom quantum computer, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Atoms held in light tweezers make promising qubits, easy to scale and rearrange. Their weakness is loss: atoms vanish, and swapping in fresh ones during a run had never been shown.

The team measured and reset a subset of atoms, replacing any that were lost, while the rest kept their quantum states intact. They ran logical circuits with repeated mid-run checks, including forty-one rounds of error-syndrome extraction in a repetition code. Real-time branching produced a verified logical Bell state. They also refilled the array from an atomic beam without disturbing the working atoms.
arxiv-2506-10636:
Wei Chen, Giacomo Dimarco, and Lorenzo Pareschi gauge doubt in kinetic equations and keep the physics true. Chance inputs make these equations span many dims. They are hard to sample well. Monte Carlo runs grow slow and noisy. The noise gets worse as dims grow. Their plan pairs cheap, low-grade models with rare high-grade runs. The cheap runs act as a control to cut the noise.

Their stand-in nets are built to hold key laws. They keep mass and charge counts, let entropy fall, and hit the right limits at the edge cases. The nets learn from the cheap models first. A few full Boltzmann runs then enrich them. Noise drops by a lot. Tests in homogeneous and nonhomogeneous multiscale regimes back the plan. Scores and speed both beat plain Monte Carlo. From rarefied gases to plasma edges, these nets stretch a sampling budget.
arxiv-2506-11136:
Couairon and five co-authors present JAFAR, a lightweight upsampler that raises vision features to any resolution, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Foundation vision encoders output coarse spatial features by design. Dense tasks like segmentation need fine detail that coarse maps lack. JAFAR uses attention to align high-resolution queries with rich low-resolution keys.

Queries derive from low-level image features that retain spatial detail. A spatial transform modulation step conditions the alignment on semantics. Training uses only low upsampling ratios, yet generalizes to far higher scales. No high-resolution supervision is required at any point. Extensive tests beat prior upsamplers across diverse dense tasks.
arxiv-2506-11936:
Lehu Bu and co-authors introduce a 2025 method for measuring how soft materials behave when hit at extreme speed. Standard tools struggle past very high stretch rates, since they lack speed, fine detail, or gentle contact. A newer method uses laser-made bubbles inside the material and watches them grow and shrink. Reading softness from those bubble curves, though, took slow repeated fitting.

Their system, the Bubble Dynamics Transformer, learns from simulated bubble curves made with a physics model of bubble motion. It then reads real bubble data from gels and thick polymer fluids and outputs the softness values at once. The results match the older slow method closely, while the readout runs far faster. The team shows it works across liquids and gels at ultra-high rates.
arxiv-2506-12136:
Dignan and twelve colleagues add ninety gigahertz data to a radio survey of star forming regions in twenty twenty-five. Radio emission mixes signals from hot gas, electrons, and warm dust. Separating them tells how fast stars are forming. The team imaged one hundred nineteen regions in thirty nearby galaxies.

The new data came from a large single dish telescope in West Virginia. Earlier maps at three lower frequencies came from an interferometer array. Three fitting approaches split the spectra into components. Hot gas emission, not dust, dominated at thirty-three gigahertz on average. Adding the high frequency data changed estimates only modestly. Star formation rates from the lower frequencies stay fairly reliable. Simple power law fits also held up well.
arxiv-2506-12536:
Farida Mohsen and Ali Safa fuse two cheap sensors to gauge rotation for small robots and drones. Good rotation measures are key for systems that run on their own. The need is sharp for small platforms with low power. Gyroscopes alone drift over time. Plain cameras fail when light changes.

Their method, thermal-gyro fusion, pairs a thermal camera of very low detail with gyroscope readings. Thermal images do not change with light. When fused with inertial data, they counter drift. The team built a system to collect matched thermal and gyroscope data, with rotation speed labels, in many settings. A light convolutional neural network then fuses both inputs to gauge rotation speed. Tests show thermal detail can be cut a lot with little loss of accuracy.
arxiv-2506-13436:
Zhaobin Zhu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on software for quantum computers. Quantum machines promise to solve problems that defeat normal computers. Hardware has moved fast, but shared software to reach the machines lags behind. Each vendor offers its own path, which locks teams into one brand. The team builds a frame that joins access across vendors.

Their system, called Q-AIM, gives one entry point to a site's quantum machines. It is open source and built from small container services. It can run on a laptop, a cloud server, or a dedicated site setup. Users meet the machines at several levels of detail through one secure door. Computing centers get a portable way to share scarce quantum hardware. The design favors light weight and local control, which suits mixed sites where quantum machines sit next to classic clusters.
arxiv-2506-13636:
Star clusters evolve through countless near misses between stars, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Kerwann Tep and co-authors introduces a code that follows them without assuming the cluster is a ball. Direct force sums are too slow at a million stars, while the standard shortcut demands spherical symmetry.

Their hybrid, KRIOS, mixes a three dimensional field method for smooth relaxation with a Monte Carlo scheme for the collisions. It reproduces the known march of test clusters toward core collapse and catches a non spherical instability in stretched clusters. Full position and velocity data stays available across the whole run.
arxiv-2506-13736:
Mayank Sharma and co-authors published this study in 2025. It surveys outflows from quasars, the bright hearts of young galaxies, using a large sky survey instrument. Such winds may shape how their host galaxies grow, a process called feedback. The team hunted a sulfur absorption mark that flags fast, hot gas. In a sample of 130 quasars from the cosmic noon era, eight showed the mark.

The winds ran at speeds from one hundred to forty-six hundred kilometers per second. Five sat between 240 and 5,500 parsecs from the center. Pooling with past finds, nearly half of such winds look strong enough to matter for feedback. Their strength matches winds seen glowing in nearby matched quasars. A few objects changed between visits, and one showed four locked wind systems at once.
arxiv-2506-13936:
Sourish Dutta compares two classic accounts of the economy as a circle of production. The paper from twenty twenty-five sets Leontief's input-output analysis beside Sraffa's production of commodities by means of commodities. Both model industries feeding each other in loops. Their takes on prices, quantities, surplus, and technology part in instructive ways. Math forms and economic premises are laid side by side.

Value and distribution get a joint reading across the pair. Worked examples from the founding texts ground the contrast. Dutta argues the two frames complete each other: one built for data, one for critique. An appendix goes further and proves a formal unification. Sraffa's price theory and Leontief's tables turn out to share one algebraic skeleton. The essay serves readers of classical and structural economics.
arxiv-2506-15336:
Krishnendu Gongopadhyay and Rahul Mondal work on a pure math question about a group of matrices. The group holds square arrays with complex entries and a fixed size rule. They study elements that can be matched, after a change of basis, to the inverse of their complex conjugate. Such elements are called c-reversible, and a stronger form asks for a matching map with extra symmetry.

The authors prove that every c-reversible element in the group is also strongly c-reversible. They give a full list of these elements based on traits that stay fixed under a change of basis. The results also sort maps of space by trace rules and related sums, with a finer list for the four-by-four case.
arxiv-2506-15436:
Martin Andersson, Benny Avelin, and Marcus Olofsson test classical regression methods in two thousand twenty-five on optimal switching problems, where a system must jump between states at the right times. Exact theory demands solving hard equation systems, so practitioners lean on simulation algorithms like Longstaff-Schwartz. The question is which regressor to plug in.

The team tried linear models, tree ensembles, nearest neighbors, and neural networks on four benchmark problems, including fifty-dimensional ones. Several simple methods stayed stable across problem types and beat the neural networks tested. Nearest-neighbor regression did consistently well with almost no tuning. The authors prove error bounds for it and show a dimension-reduction step lets it scale to high dimensions. Simple tools, tuned lightly, win here.
arxiv-2506-18536:
Tahir Naseem explains how a quantum oscillator can act as a one-way valve for heat. Thermal rectification, easy flow one way and blocked flow back, is a prize for nanoscale devices. The oscillator sits between two thermal baths. Photons cross singly in a linear channel and in pairs through a nonlinear one.

At low temperatures, the cold bath, when dominant, pins the oscillator in low-occupancy states. Two-photon emission chokes there, bottlenecking heat in one direction. At higher temperatures, rectification follows the asymmetric scaling of higher-order moments for pair absorption and emission. The paper scans coupling configurations to find where directional flow thrives. A practical scheme couples an auxiliary two-level system to create the pair dissipation. The analysis guides future quantum thermal device design.
arxiv-2506-18936:
Shingo Tagami, Takaykui Myo, and Masanobu Yahiro published this study in 2025. It measures the neutron skin of atomic nuclei: how much farther neutrons reach than protons. Such skins test the forces that govern dense matter, from nuclei to neutron stars. The team read skins from how protons scatter off natural lead and a terbium isotope. They modeled the scattering with two interaction schemes, one for lower and one for higher energies.

Their lead skin value matches the famous PREX-II result within errors. The terbium skin came out near 0.27 femtometers, with a wider error band. They also sized up magnesium, sodium, and argon isotopes. There, squashed shapes clearly swelled the measured radii. Untangling skin from shape, they show, is key to reading these experiments right.
arxiv-2506-19036:
David Kazhdan and Alexander Polishchuk build an analog of theta-lifting for automorphic functions tied to a curve over a ring with a doubled point. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The ring adds a tiny nilpotent direction to a finite field. The curve over it supports a space of special functions tied to the group SL2.

Theta-lifting is a classic way to build such functions from simpler data. The pair show the lift here matches a splitting of the function space into orbits. Their main result: every strongly cuspidal function in that space arises from a lift. The lift runs through a double cover of the curve, chosen to fit. The work extends an earlier study of these exotic automorphic forms. It links representation theory with the geometry of curves over strange rings.
arxiv-2506-20036:
Four-legged robots must pick their steps carefully on rough ground, and learning that skill end to end is hard. Jeremiah Coholich and co-authors split the job in two in this 2025 paper: a high-level policy picks footstep goals, and a low-level policy learns to hit them.

Their twist is that the top layer needs no training of its own. Instead, it searches online over the bottom layer's learned value scores to choose each goal. Against a single-layer learner, the split system earned higher rewards with fewer collisions, even on ground rougher than anything seen in training. The result favors layered control for hard locomotion.
arxiv-2506-20536:
Borowski and fifteen co-authors report 2025 observations of V404 Cygni, a black hole system in a quiet phase. The system gives off more mid-infrared light than its companion star can explain. Past work blamed the extra glow on a disk of gas, on material around the pair, or on a fast jet of matter.

The team watched the system at many wavelengths at the same time, using space and ground telescopes. The infrared light swung up and down fast, at one point rising more than tenfold, and other bands changed in step. That shared flicker points to one source: a jet that keeps flowing even when the black hole feeds weakly. The result strengthens the link between disks and jets around black holes.
arxiv-2506-20736:
Payaswinee Arvikar and three co-authors model neutron stars laced with dark matter in a 2025 paper. Neutron stars pack extreme density into a small sphere, making them natural labs for exotic matter. If dark matter gathers in the core, it should change the star's size and mass in testable ways.

The team treats the star as two fluids that interact only through gravity. Equations of state come from lab nuclear data, collision experiments, and past star observations. A statistical method then narrows the dark matter traits that fit telescope data. Two well-measured pulsars anchor the comparison. Results show current data mainly limit the dark matter share, while stiffer normal matter shifts the bounds.
arxiv-2506-21436:
Ziad Ismaili Alaoui, Namrata, and Sebastian Wild wrote a paper from 2025 on storing a class of networks in far less space while still working on them directly. Some networks grow by a rich-get-richer rule: new nodes link most to nodes that already have many links. Social and web networks often grow this way. Plain storage wastes space on such skewed shapes.

Their data structure squeezes the network and still lets a user walk it as if it were stored as lists of links. Its size shrinks on its own when the network at hand is easy to squeeze. For networks grown by that rule, the size comes close to the best any method could reach. For other networks, it stays no worse than a squeezed list of links. The team works out the space bound with care.
arxiv-2506-22636:
Sotirios Panagiotis Chytas, Miso Choi, Hyunwoo Kim, and Vikas Singh present a 2025 paper on stopping vision-language models from hallucinating. Such models can describe things that are not in the image, often because text habits drown out the picture as a caption grows longer. The authors call this a fading memory of the visual input.

Their fix is a small add-on module named ReCo, bolted onto a trained model without other changes. Drawing on ideas from geometric algebra, it composes reminders of the image into the model's work as it writes. Tests on three widely used models showed gains across several benchmarks. The module also stacked with other anti-hallucination methods, improving each one it joined.
arxiv-2506-22836:
Hongyan An and colleagues refined pedestrian attribute recognition in 2025, the surveillance task of listing what a person in an image is wearing and carrying. Most systems extract one regional feature, say from the torso, and use it to predict a fixed battery of attributes. That sharing blurs the fine patterns that single attributes depend on, and it locks the system to attributes seen in training, useless for a new attribute asked about later.

Their approach, FOCUS, extracts features for each attribute individually, guided by the attribute's own semantics, so an unseen attribute can still be queried at test time. A multi-granularity token mixing module gathers visual evidence at several levels of detail, enriching the features each attribute draws on. The design targets exactly the fine-grained, open-ended character of the task that fixed regional features mishandle.
arxiv-2506-23336:
Hanxun Yao, Tamer Zaki, and Charles Meneveau test a law from thermodynamics in turbulence in a two thousand twenty-five paper. In turbulence, energy flows from large eddies to small ones. A rate for entropy generation can be set from that flow. A fluctuation relation says how likely a reverse cascade is next to a forward one, in an exponential pattern.

Earlier checks of the law held only under tight limits. The team used time-resolved data from simulations at a moderate Reynolds number. They averaged the entropy rates over spans from one to several eddy turnover times. The pattern held when rates were averaged along the paths of fluid particles. It failed when rates were averaged at fixed points in space. The result backs their entropy rate idea for turbulent cascades.
arxiv-2506-23436:
Kai Heussen and six co-authors published a paper in 2025 on recording uncertainty when planning tests of smart energy systems. Test plans for these tangled systems already follow a shared template that describes goals and setups. Yet uncertainty, from shaky sensors to weather, was rarely written down in a structured way, which hurt repeatability.

The authors extend the template with fields for naming and rating uncertainty at the planning stage. They also release a companion analysis tool, and both are openly available. Two case studies show the extensions in use. Writing doubts into the plan itself, they argue, makes results easier to trust, repeat, and compare across labs.
arxiv-2507-00036:
Rohan Putatunda, Sanjay Purushotham, Ratnaksha Lele, and Vandana Janeja forecast where drifting icebergs will go. Icebergs feed fresh water into polar oceans, shape local ecosystems, and threaten ships, but their paths are hard to predict: data are scarce and the motion twists with wind, currents, and shape.

Their model, IDRIFTNET, blends the physics equations of iceberg drift with a learning system that mops up the mismatch between the equations and reality. A rotation-toughened spectral network reads both wide and fine patterns in the data. Tested on two giant Antarctic bergs, A23A and B22A, the hybrid beat leading models on final and average position error at many lead times. The authors credit the physics backbone for learning well from little data.
arxiv-2507-00636:
Andrea Perdomo Garcia and co-authors simulate how local magnetic fields shape quiet zones on star surfaces, in work from twenty twenty-five. Quiet zones lack sunspots but still host small scale fields built by a local dynamo. The team ran paired simulations with and without fields for three star types.

Fields grew from a small seed and settled near one hundred gauss at the surface for all three stars. The fields barely changed plasma speeds or the average layer structure. They did alter the brightness of dark lanes between surface cells and small scale patterns in heat and downward flow. Energy shifts matched the dynamo turning motion energy into magnetic energy. Opacity choices caused their own separate changes.
arxiv-2507-03636:
Xiaodong Wu and co-authors build a lock against unwanted edits of AI images in a 2025 computing paper. Prompt-driven editors can alter any picture, which invites copyright abuse and faked evidence. Their framework, SecureT2I, trains a generator to respect an owner's permission list. Pictures cleared for editing behave normally, while forbidden ones come back blurred or meaningless when someone tries to edit them.

The lock installs through light fine-tuning, with no change to the model's structure. Separate training goals teach the split behavior for the two sets. Tests across data sets and model types showed the block held while legal edits stayed sharp. Such built-in respect for permission could calm a heated fight over image tools.
arxiv-2507-03836:
Jianxin Sun, David Lenz, Hongfeng Yu, and Tom Peterka speed up net-based draws of bulk forms that shift with time. The work came out in 2025. Such bulk data, from sims and scans, is huge and rich. New ways store it as hid net forms. Those forms can shrink the data and draw it at any grain size.

The catch is train time. Those nets learn at a slow pace on large four-part data. The team's build, F-Hash, feeds the net with a trait-based hash code. The code spreads over more than one grain size of a four-part grid, a tesseract. Its hash steps hit no clash at each tier and waste no slots. Rich, clean traits let the net fit the data far more fast than old codes do. The work aims at live use, where staff scrub through time and zoom at will.
arxiv-2507-04936:
Marcel Moran, Malik Salman, and Takahiro Yabe published a paper in 2025 measuring which bike lanes actually cause more cycling in New York City. Cities plead tight budgets and car-first streets, so the type of lane matters. Drawing on seventy-two million Citi Bike trips, the team compared protected lanes, painted lanes, and shared-lane markings.

Stations near any new lane gained trips in the following year, roughly eighteen percent for protected lanes and fourteen for the lesser types. But a difference-in-differences design, which strips out citywide trends, found a causal lift only for protected lanes, about 379 extra rides per station each month. The lift was strongest in older neighborhoods and absent in areas with medium-to-high shares of Black residents, an equity gap the authors flag plainly.
arxiv-2507-05636:
Feng Xia and seven co-authors survey graph learning in twenty twenty-five. Graphs capture relationships that ordinary tables cannot, from molecules to fraud networks. Graph learning grew from early graph theory methods into a major machine learning field. Graph neural networks gave it its modern momentum.

The survey traces a decade of progress. Scalable architectures, dynamic graphs, and multimodal learning widened the field's reach. Generative and explainable methods entered the toolkit as well. Applications run from drug discovery to recommender systems and scientific reasoning. Open problems remain: scalability, generalization, heterogeneity, interpretability, and trustworthiness. Readers get a structured map of a fast-moving area, including the obstacles that still block its full potential.
arxiv-2507-06736:
Jonas Schweiger and Ruaridh Macdonald analyze in 2025 clean backup power systems to replace diesel generators. Power outages and climate goals both push the search for better options. Their framework weighs cost and emissions across many possible futures using real load profiles and outage odds.

They assess twenty-seven technologies, alone and in hybrid mixes. Large emission cuts come at moderate cost, but deep cuts cost much more. Batteries appear in the best systems at all levels. Ammonia generators and hydrogen fuel cells with iron-air batteries stand out as cost-effective. Fuel replacement choices strongly affect both cost and emissions.
arxiv-2507-08136:
Cheng and five co-authors built a tool in twenty twenty-five to rebuild a scene in three views from a few loose photos. No cam pose is given, and few views make the task hard for past tools. Their tool makes local blobs for each view, then lines them up into one whole scene.

A smart match step pairs the blobs with a cost that weighs shape, light, and depth. The match runs from rough to fine and finds cam poses as it goes. On two known test sets the tool lined up blobs with high care. It gave sharp pose reads and clean new views of each scene.
arxiv-2507-08236:
Anthony Miyaguchi, Murilo Gustineli, and Adrian Cheung report their team's entry to a bioacoustics competition in this two thousand twenty-five notebook paper. The BirdCLEF+ challenge asks systems to classify two hundred six species, including birds, mammals, insects, and amphibians, from soundscape recordings. A strict ninety-minute, CPU-only inference deadline rules out many heavy deep learning models. The Georgia Tech team pursued two strategies.

First, they optimized pre-trained models from the Bioacoustics Model Zoo for CPU inference, getting a nearly tenfold speedup for one model and solid leaderboard scores from another. Second, their Spectrogram Token Skip-Gram pipeline clusters mel-spectrograms into discrete tokens and learns embeddings for them with a word embedding model, then classifies with a simple linear layer. It scored lower but ran extremely fast, showing tokenization with static embeddings is a viable lightweight route for bioacoustic classification.
arxiv-2507-08336:
Zhichao Xu, Zhiqi Huang, Shengyao Zhuang, and Vivek Srikumar compare two ways to train text rerankers, in a research paper from 2025. Rerankers sort search results and matter for retrieval quality. One way learns from true labels, and the other learns from a larger teacher model, but a fair head-to-head test under real conditions was missing.

The team trained rerankers of four sizes and two designs both ways, on the same data. Learning from a stronger teacher won on in-domain and new-domain tests in most cases. A teacher of equal strength gave no such gain. The guidance is plain: use a larger teacher if one is on hand.
arxiv-2507-08736:
Idan Mashiach, Oren Glickman, and Tom Tirer propose, in 2025, a fresh way to decide which neural network weights to protect when teaching a model new tasks. Networks forget old tasks as new learning overwrites shared weights. Standard fixes score weight importance over the whole training run.

Their idea watches only the final plateau, when training has nearly settled. Weights that still move and vary there point along flat directions of the loss surface, safe to reuse for new tasks. Weights quiet in the plateau carry old knowledge and should be held. Experiments showed a better balance of remembering and learning than rival methods.
arxiv-2507-10236:
Six researchers study why AI image detectors fail on real social media photos in a paper from 2025. Detectors score near perfectly on lab benchmarks but stumble in the wild. The team built a data set of real and AI-made images drawn from major social platforms. They then tested how design choices affect detection, from model shape to training data and image pre-processing.

Simply scaling up training did not always help. What mattered most was keeping both fine traces and high-level meaning alive through the pipeline. Applying their lessons lifted detection scores by a large average margin across leading methods. The authors offer the work as a road map for tougher detectors.
arxiv-2507-10636:
Jianing Zhi and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a network that picks sites for drone bases in cities. Fast growth of low altitude drone use needs good spots for landing pads and supply posts. Those spots shift as demand shifts, and classic attention methods slow down badly at city scale.

Their network adds four parts to fix the bottleneck. One part bakes distance into the attention scores. One part limits each point to its nearest neighbors, which cuts the work sharply. A memory module based on a classic network stores past patterns, with a rule that keeps it in check. On thousand node cases, the method found near best answers in a tenth of a second. On hundred node cases, it beat a top rival on quality and speed.
arxiv-2507-11236:
Yuchen He, Zhehan Lei, Jianan Shao, and Chihao Zhang improve the task of drawing samples from chance laws whose shape is not of the tame, log-curved kind. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such sampling is key to many counts in stats and learning. Past work set a hard floor: with plain terms, the cost can blow up with dims, and a key gauge can be unbound. The team adds a stronger term, on all laws met along a known drift path from the target. Under it, they show the cost can stay in a tame form in the size terms. They also sharpen the linked bounds on how fast such laws mix.
arxiv-2507-12736:
Five mathematicians study random maps driven by Markov chains in a paper from 2025. A random dynamical system picks its next rule by chance, and a Markov chain makes those picks depend on the recent past. A physical measure describes the long-run statistics seen from most starting points. The team asks whether only finitely many such measures can arise.

They recast the Markov process in an independent form, which lets them import results from the simpler setting. Under stated conditions, finitely many measures cover nearly all starting points. For maps on compact spaces that mostly contract, the weaker version always holds. They apply the results to random maps of the circle and interval.
arxiv-2507-13036:
Lukas Pin, Stef Baas, David Robertson, and Sofía Villar argue that equal arms in a trial are not always the most powerful design. Their paper from twenty twenty-five revisits a bedrock belief of randomized trials. Equal splits win only when outcome spread matches across arms. That match is often false, and rarely checked. Unequal splits can keep or gain power while more patients land on the better arm.

Two cases ground the claim: a small melanoma trial with a yes-no outcome, and a large pain trial using virtual reality. Simulations weigh equal, fixed unequal, and adaptive splits aimed at the Neyman target. Unequal plans put more patients on the winning arm with no power loss. Small power gains showed for both outcome types. The team urges designers to set ratios with care.
arxiv-2507-14036:
Umar Sohail Qureshi and Raghav Kunnawalkam Elayavalli published a 2025 physics paper on cleaning up images of the most violent collisions in nature. When heavy ions smash, they create a hot soup that floods detectors with background. The prized signals, narrow sprays of particles called jets, sit inside that flood. Standard cleaning methods scrape away background but often scrape away parts of the jets too.

Their system, DeepSub, is the first machine-learning method to subtract the background from the whole event at once. A transformer model, built for images, learns to denoise the collision picture and separate the hard jets from the soft soup. It reproduced jet energy, mass, and internal structure to within about a percent, beating existing techniques. Precision matters because jets probe the soup's properties. The authors present DeepSub as a path to sharper measurements of matter at trillions of degrees.
arxiv-2507-14336:
Christopher Wikle and three co-authors give a view of model work with real world rules in twenty twenty-five. Neural nets tied to physics laws have brought new life to the mix of rules and data. The aim is to call how things that shift in space and time move next. Such things come with laws, like partial differential equations, that spell out the real rules.

Stats teams have used this mix for a long time, with lots of sound ways. The view keeps the doubt on data, steps, and set values in sight. A few broad plans get a short look. Bayes based plans get the most time, since they treat doubt in a clean way. The team shows how Bayes tools can fold into the new net based plans. Readers get past work and clear help for a theme too oft sold as brand new.
arxiv-2507-14536:
Aarti Lakhara and three co-authors report, in twenty twenty-five, a shift in a thin film made of tin and selenium, called SnSe2. The film was built into a transistor, a switch that controls electric flow. By adding charge with an electric field, the team raised the count of free charge carriers in the film. At a high enough count, the film crossed from blocking flow to letting it flow freely, like a metal.

At low heat, charge moved by hopping between spots, a pattern the team tied to gaps left by missing selenium atoms. At low heat, stray charged flaws slowed the flow most. At higher heat, shaking of the crystal lattice took over. The work guides use of such thin films in new devices.
arxiv-2507-14736:
Rafał Surdej and a team of co-authors study trainable activation functions for learning agents, in two thousand twenty-five. An activation function shapes each unit's output in a neural network. Making it trainable, as a ratio of polynomials, adds flexibility that can help an agent adapt in changing tasks.

That flexibility can also destabilize training, they found. In reinforcement learning it inflated value estimates, and in long continual learning it collapsed features. Their fix limits how far the function's output can scale, while keeping its adaptability. Tests on robot control suites improved both stability and scores. In continual learning tests, unlike limits shifted the balance between flexibility and memory.
arxiv-2507-15136:
Charles Coleman presents a 2025 study of how to score the overall accuracy of a set of forecasts, one for each unit in a group. Each unit has its own loss function, which grades its forecast error. The total loss function rolls those grades into one number for the whole set. Coleman asks which forms of total are admissible under fair rules: no unit favored by name, and worse errors never scored as better.

Only three families pass: additive, multiplicative, and a restricted third type. The first two match different readings of economic utility. A neat link lets the additive form stand in for the multiplicative one, so the additive total can always be used. The paper also shows the additive form fits the classic axioms of expected utility.
arxiv-2507-15336:
Wang and colleagues design in twenty twenty-five a system that improves neural networks by weaving lessons from past design edits, rather than fetching a ready model or searching from scratch. Each small architectural tweak on earlier tasks is logged with the gain it caused, forming evidence graphs. For a new task, the system retrieves relevant edit evidence and follows promising edit paths.

An adaptive retriever recalibrates how far evidence from each source transfers as the design evolves. Planner modules stretch gains across multi-step evidence chains to handle unfamiliar tasks. Built on a base of tens of thousands of graph networks across many datasets, the system hit the best-known design in most test cases under a strict budget. It beat both search and retrieval baselines consistently.
arxiv-2507-17536:
Abalmasov, Ivanov, Sadykov, and Belushkin study how hydrogen bonds in a crystal called KDP act under pressure in two thousand twenty-five. The crystal shows a group of three peaks where hydrogen and oxygen bonds stretch. What makes up that group of peaks has long been debated.

The team sets side by side two kinds of evidence: computer models built from first rules, and tests that bounce neutrons off the crystal. The models say stretch modes soften with pressure while bend modes harden. The tests show the three peaks hardening with the bend modes. So the peaks most likely come from bends and their overtones, not from stretches.
arxiv-2507-18136:
Lalengmawia and nine co-authors computed the traits of a crystal compound in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The compound, a lithium zinc germanium sulfide, has a diamond-like structure and a wide band gap. Wide-gap semiconductors are chased for energy devices. The team used density functional theory with two levels of approximation.

They mapped the compound's electronic, optical, and mechanical behavior. A pressure-response property tied to piezoelectric use was also computed. Stability checks passed both a classic criteria test and molecular dynamics runs. Results matched earlier reported data in broad terms. The authors nominate the compound as a strong candidate for optoelectronic and piezoelectric applications.
arxiv-2507-18236: The Belle II Collaboration reports a 2025 search for lepton-flavor-violating tau decays. In these decays, a tau lepton turns into an electron plus two further leptons. The Standard Model forbids such decays. Any confirmed sighting would therefore signal new physics. Large detector collaborations hunt them in huge data samples for exactly that reason. The hosted head for this entry is consumed by the collaboration's long member list and carries no abstract. The paper is cataloged here in short form from its title alone.
arxiv-2507-18436:
David Blanco-Mulero, Júlia Borràs, and Carme Torras teach a robot to unfold medical garments in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Dressing robots could ease work for patients and staff. Most past work assumes the gown starts open, yet hospital gowns and aprons are stored folded.

The team calls this unfolding step pre-dressing and learns it by imitation. Three motion styles were taught, mixing fast and slow moves, plus a vision tool that labels a garment as closed, partly open, or fully open. Fast, forceful motions failed on freshly unpacked garments. Combining motions opened them far better. The authors say the step is key to real dressing help.
arxiv-2507-18536:
Man, Luo, and Liu revisited how two charmonium states mix in twenty twenty-five. Charmonia are particles made of a charm quark and its antimatter twin. The states named psi(4040) and psi(4160) may each be blends of two underlying configurations, labeled 3S and 2D.

Standard potential models explain mixing through a tensor force, but that alone seems too weak. The authors add a coupled-channel mechanism, where states interact by exchanging other particles. Their computed mixing angles come out at seven and ten degrees. Those values clash with the larger angle suggested by measured decay widths into electrons. The authors discuss possible reasons for the mismatch and urge precise new measurements, through both broad and specific decay channels, to settle the question.
arxiv-2507-18636:
Ehsan Naghizadeh, Eleni Chatzi, and Paolo Tiso wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about finding cracks in train wheelset axles while trains run. Early crack detection in service could prevent failures, but it needs models of how axles vibrate. A crack that opens and closes as the axle turns makes that vibration nonlinear and costly to simulate.

The authors propose a detection feature built from higher harmonics of the crack's breathing motion. They then build a linear shortcut that mimics that feature closely. The shortcut removes the need to solve the nonlinear motion step by step, which greatly cuts computing cost. Tests against the full model show high accuracy. The authors see promise for near real-time checks on axles in service.
arxiv-2507-18836:
Luo and co-authors test how self-driving cars should show pedestrians how sure they are in this 2025 study. A car's doubt is normally hidden, which clouds trust at crossings. The team compared two display styles in virtual reality: a visible confidence percentage, and motion cues that hint at doubt through movement.

Twenty-six volunteers crossed in front of a virtual car under high and low confidence. The explicit percentage was easier to see, easier to grasp, and made people feel safer and more trusting. Motion cues bred confusion, especially when confidence was low. The authors give design guidance for car exteriors that treat uncertainty as part of the message to people on foot.
arxiv-2507-18936:
Pham Thi Tuyet Nhung and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on long period variable stars. These stars swell and shrink over long cycles on the asymptotic giant branch, a late life stage. Their light curves rise and fall in telling shapes. The team studies 116 such stars in detail. Each light curve is summed up by five measured traits. One trait gauges the relative width of bright and dim phases.

That width trait proves best at revealing links to the star's current state. Stars that have not yet dredged up inner material follow a tight shared path in trait space. Stars past that event split into two light curve types. Stellar astronomers get a cheap diagnostic: curve shape alone hints at deep history. Telescopes gather light curves in bulk, so shape-based sorting can flag stars for costly follow-up spectra.
arxiv-2507-21036:
Simone Roncallo, Angela Rosy Morgillo, Seth Lloyd, Chiara Macchiavello, and Lorenzo Maccone build a shallow neural network out of light in two thousand twenty-five. Plain shallow networks can fit any smooth function if they have enough neurons. Their cost grows with input size and with the count of tuned values.

In the quantum version, data and tuned values ride on single photons. When two photons meet at a beam splitter, their interference sets the output, a known effect the team exploits. Many neurons are packed as a mix of single-photon states. Once trained, the setup uses the same light gear no matter how many inputs or neurons it holds.
arxiv-2507-21136:
Mojtaba Moattari argues that when we shrink data down to fewer traits, we should chase traits that stand free of each other, not just spread or linked moves. Tools in wide use, such as principal component analysis, can leave links, lack of range, and ease of reading unmet. He puts forth three new tests for this free-standing trait, to build tools for use with labels and with none.

The frame comes in a straight-line form and a curved form. On MNIST digits and on a face data set split by gender, the tools beat known baselines on contrast, sort skill, and ease of reading. Views as eigenimages helped sum up the main forms of each class in the face data. The tools also made a variational autoencoder build back its inputs more well. He puts this path forth as a strong one for representation learning.
arxiv-2507-21936:
Julien Beckers and Philipp Haas wrote this particle physics report, published in two thousand twenty-five, on light mesons measured at the COMPASS experiment at CERN. COMPASS fires a fast pion beam at a target and reads the spray of particles to map how light mesons are built.

The talk covers two final states rich in meson signals. One of them can reveal a prized quarry: the pi-1(1600), a candidate for the lightest hybrid meson, a particle with its glue field excited. The analysis splits the data into waves with set quantum numbers, then pulls out each meson's mass and width. The second final state isolates a clean family of mesons with even spin. Several states claimed by other experiments are checked, and their parameters are measured afresh. The results test what theory says these hybrid and standard mesons should do.
arxiv-2507-22236:
C Duangchan and co-authors measure cosmic flows without assuming a cosmology in a 2025 astronomy paper. Galaxy peculiar velocities, motions beyond the universe's expansion, trace the mass beneath them. The Cosmicflows-4 catalog is the largest such sample, but its readings are noisy and biased.

The team built a forward model that assumes only a flat universe. It rebuilds the inward radial flow and the shared bulk drift directly from the data. Tests on sixty-four fake catalogs showed the method recovers both without bias. Applied to the real catalog, the inward flow gives a local Hubble constant of about 75.9 kilometers per second per megaparsec. The bulk flow at two distance scales clashes with the standard model at strong significance, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-22336:
Penghan Zhu, Shurui Mei, Shushan Chen, Xiaobo Chu, Shanbo He, and Ziyi Liu diagnose Alzheimer's-related amyloid from brain scans without a structural image, in a 2025 paper. Clinics usually pair PET scans with MRI or CT. That pairing costs time and needs alignment steps. The team's framework segments brain regions from PET alone. A three-dimensional network was trained on two hundred amyloid scans. The data split into training, validation, and test sets.

Segmentation quality varied by region. Deep brain structures scored highest. Uptake measures in key regions matched reference values closely. Some errors were as low as a thousandth of the scale. Classification of amyloid status reached ninety-eight percent accuracy. The curve score was near perfect. The authors propose the tool for places lacking structural imaging. It also removes manual outlining from the pipeline. Clinical validation and more tracer types come next.
arxiv-2508-01336:
A lone wave that crosses water without changing shape is striking enough; add a steady swirl and an electric field and the math turns fierce. Tingting Feng, Yong Zhang and Zhitao Zhang study such solitary waves on a two-dimensional fluid that conducts electricity, carries constant swirl, and feels a sideways electric field. They frame it as a free-boundary problem, with flow and electric equations coupling tightly at the moving surface.

The coupling breaks the standard tools, whose one-way comparisons no longer hold. The authors build new sign-based properties for the combined system, which guarantee the wave keeps a symmetric hump shape along the whole family of solutions. They then show the family cannot simply end. At its limit, one of four things must happen: the flow stagnates inside, the surface map degenerates, stagnation reaches the crest, or the wave speed grows without bound.
arxiv-2508-01536:
Hong-Shuo Gao, Zu-Xin Cai, Gang Li, and Shi-Dong Liu compute how a predicted spin-zero partner of the X(3872) particle would decay into light mesons. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats the partner, called X0, as a bound pair of charmed mesons. Decays run through loops of charmed mesons in between. Two families of end states are covered: pairs of vector mesons and pairs of pseudoscalar mesons.

Three mixes of the state's makeup are tried, from pure neutral to pure charged parts. Vector-pair widths land in a modest range. Pseudoscalar-pair widths run larger, up to a few MeV in scale. The rho and pion pair channels lead the rates. Ratios between channels barely move with model settings, which aids the hunt. The authors point search teams at BESIII and Belle II.
arxiv-2508-01636:
Tianpei Lu and co-authors make private use of the BERT language model far faster by mixing secret sharing with slim number formats, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Private inference lets several parties run a model without seeing each other's data, but decimal math makes it slow. Slim formats cut cost, yet past work leaked the slimming settings or handled curves poorly.

Layer-by-layer slimming plus one-bit weight layers run safely in the new design. Table lookups handle the softmax curve and format switches with no trim loss. Speed beat three prior systems by large multiples on BERT tests. Readers in secure AI get a practical path to private text services.
arxiv-2508-02036:
Abd-Rabbou and Cong-Feng Qiao present a study from twenty twenty-five on uncertainty relations in quantum physics. Such relations cap how well two clash prone measures can be known at once. The pair derive four new relations for the sum of spreads of two such measures. A reverse form, which caps the sum from above, is in the set too.

Their tool is a known inequality of Maligranda. The new bounds beat several known ones in tightness. A phase angle of the state helps sharpen the bounds. They stretch the results to many measures with a second known inequality. Three worked cases show the gains hold in practice. The work aids exact tests of quantum limits.
arxiv-2508-02136:
Qi Xiong, Hai Dong, Nasrin Sohrabi, and Zahir Tari propose a 2025 defense for a style of machine learning in which many sites train one model together without sharing raw data. That setup, called federated learning, can be attacked by fake sites that act as a group to poison the shared model. Defenses based on grouping or robust training can fail when the fake sites form the majority.

Their method, FedLAD, treats the step that merges each site's update as a linear algebra problem. It pulls out the parts of the merged update that stand on their own and filters out parts that are redundant or hostile. Tests show the defense keeps working even when attackers are numerous. The work offers a fresh angle for guarding shared training.
arxiv-2508-02236:
Lu Chen, Dingyi Zhao, Zihao Yu, Ninghui Sun, and Yungang Bao present GSIM, a simulator that runs hardware designs far faster than standard tools. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Chip designers test their work in software before building it. For large modern processors, that testing has become the bottleneck of the whole flow.

The team first sorts the overhead of register-level simulation into four sources. Fixes then target groups of nodes, single nodes, and individual bits. GSIM puts those fixes together in one simulator. It handles XiangShan, a top open-source processor design, in full. Booting Linux on it ran many times faster than with the standard rival tool. A benchmark run on a smaller core was faster still. The work speeds design exploration, checking, and debugging.
arxiv-2508-02336:
Lasse Mohr and co-authors trace what builds the giant web of a whole nation's family network, in this 2025 paper. Family ties link everyone, and the web grows as people partner and have children. A popular theory credits sameness-seeking in partner choice for the web's shape. The team tests that claim on a population-complete registry network covering millions of people over decades.

Sameness-seeking, it turns out, barely moves the large-scale structure. Two habits do the work instead. Partner switching rewire-links families together, shrinking distances across the web. And switching is self-exciting: each past switch raises the odds of another, minting hub people who bind big components. Network models with those two habits reproduce the real web's shape closely.
arxiv-2508-03436:
Davide Gabrielli, Bardh Prenkaj, Paola Velardi, and Stefano Faralli present a home health watcher in a 2025 computing paper. Their system blends smartwatch signals with room sensors and a universal time-series model. It learns each patient's own rhythm of body and behavior. When the rhythm bends in a new way, the system raises a real-time alert for caregivers.

Unlike classifiers, the watcher needs no constant labeling of what counts as illness. It beat twelve rival anomaly detectors, with a clear lead on the standard score. The same system runs in real homes in a deployment the authors call @HOME. Light, cheap devices carried the load, which makes wide use plausible for aging care.
arxiv-2508-05636:
Mohammed Alam, Fahad Shamshad, Fakhri Karray, and Karthik Nandakumar design a way to make stored face templates cancelable, in a 2025 paper. Face recognition is convenient, but a stolen face template cannot be changed like a password. Good protection needs templates that can be revoked, that cannot be linked across services, and that cannot be reversed into the real face. Simple anonymization methods fail those tests.

Their system, FaceAnonyMixer, blends the code of a real face with a synthetic code drawn from a revocable key, inside a generative model's latent space. A tuned loss keeps the blend useful for recognition while hiding identity. If a template leaks, a new key yields a fresh one. The approach targets biometric systems that must balance security with privacy law.
arxiv-2508-05736:
Yizhuo Tian and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on when a quantum simulation of string dynamics in a gauge theory is truly two dimensional. Simulators now run such theories on a plane of sites. String breaking on that plane can, in a hidden way, act like a one dimensional process. The team asks what marks the true two dimensional case.

The key is the plaquette term, a magnetic part that exists only past one dimension. With short strings and no plaquette term, they show string breaking maps to a flat line process, what the lattice looks like aside. With the term, deep in the confined regime, the dynamics stay truly planar. The rule guides future runs.
arxiv-2508-07836:
Vishwas Shetty, Jiusi Zheng, and Abeer Alwan adapt adult speaker verification to children's voices in a 2025 study. Systems trained on grown-up speech stumble on children because young voices differ acoustically, and recordings of children are too scarce for ordinary fine-tuning to fix the gap.

Their framework inserts a gated adapter into a pretrained speaker embedding model, then fine-tunes in repeated rounds. Gating lets the adapter pass or reshape features selectively, improving transfer from the data-rich adult domain. Better child speaker verification supports classroom tools and safe voice interfaces for young users, where weak checks carry real risk.
arxiv-2508-08336:
A new study rarely starts from nothing: earlier work leaves summaries, estimates, and lists of promising variables behind. Paul Rognon-Vael and David Rossell build a transfer method on empirical Bayes, which lets past data set the starting beliefs for the current analysis. They spell out how that differs from full Bayesian updating and make it practical to compute.

Their theory shows the empirical version can still pick the right variables under weaker assumptions than full Bayes needs. It also settles on answers faster. In high-dimensional regression tests, full Bayes performed beautifully on its own. Borrowing strength through empirical Bayes still added a moderate, real improvement. The authors pitch the method at fields where raw old data are gone but summaries survive.
arxiv-2508-08736:
Hoang Ly and Emina Soljanin settle what one-step majority-logic decoding can achieve for binary Reed-Muller codes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Reed's classical decoder works through several sequential steps, decoding symbols from highest to lowest degree. Later algorithms cut the steps only for limited parameters, or sacrificed performance. A fully parallel decoder remained an open question.

The authors prove any one-step decoder can correct at most a quarter of the code's minimum distance in errors. That bound holds for all orders and lengths. They then construct a hard-decision decoder that finishes in a single step and hits this limit. It can be read as a parallel version of Reed's original algorithm. Remarkably, the same decoder is optimal for erasures. It recovers messages from any erasure pattern up to one symbol below the minimum distance.
arxiv-2508-09936:
Pippi and team wrote in twenty twenty-five on fake handwriting. Machines that read handwriting struggle with small sets from one writer. Such sets differ from the data the machines trained on. Fake samples in the target style could fill that gap. The team compared three top models that make such samples. The three came from rival families: adversarial, diffusion, and autoregressive.

They gauged how fake-data quality shapes tuning of the readers. Both the look and the language traits of fake samples mattered. The study yields number-based guidelines for picking a maker model. Settings with little data are the main target of the work. Results show where today's models already help reading. They also mark weaknesses to fix before wider use. The work gives practitioners a fact base for fake-data choices.
arxiv-2508-11236:
Peter Petersen and James Stanfield published this mathematics paper in 2025. It works on symmetric spaces, highly regular curved shapes that appear across geometry. For each such space, the authors compute two things: a polynomial that counts its holes by size, and its curvature operator, which measures how the space bends.

They give explicit formulas for every space on the known list of compact types that cannot be split into smaller pieces. The hole-counting formula turns out to mirror a known formula for a simpler count called the Euler characteristic. For bending, they show the largest value of the curvature operator never exceeds a key constant of the space. Equality holds exactly for a favored family called Hermitian symmetric spaces. Such complete tables are rare and handy for other geometers.
arxiv-2508-12636:
Ansh Chaurasia presents a memory simulator for chip designers in this 2025 paper. Memory often sets the speed limit for AI hardware. Existing simulators model timing well but can stray from true hardware behavior. MemorySim works at the register-transfer level, the same level designers use to build chips.

The tool plugs into the Chisel design flow and the Chipyard chip framework. It aims to give both exact timing and correct function in one model. Designers can read off speed and power estimates for their memory choices. Those estimates then feed larger simulation setups for whole systems. Better memory models help teams avoid costly design mistakes before any chip is built.
arxiv-2508-13436:
Edesio Alcobaça and André de Carvalho speed up automated machine learning by letting past experience shrink the search, in a 2025 paper. AutoML systems design a learning pipeline on their own, picking data cleaners, models, and settings. The search is thorough but slow, and a wide search can overfit the data at hand. The authors add metalearning: knowledge from earlier tasks guides which corners of the search space deserve a look.

In tests, the guided search cut random-search runtime by 89 percent while shrinking the menu of data cleaners and classifiers to a fraction of its size. Accuracy barely moved. The method also plugged into a popular AutoML tool and trimmed its search space there too. The paper closes with lessons on which task features to feed the guide and how to explain its choices, framing the trade-offs that come with any narrower search.
arxiv-2508-13836:
Mikołaj Janusz, Tomasz Wojnar, Yawei Li, Luca Benini, and Kamil Adamczewski wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It runs one of the first full head-to-head tests of the two great ways to prune a neural network: all at once, or round by round.

Pruning trims nets so they run cheap. One-shot pruning cuts once and retrains. Iterative pruning cuts in cycles, for a finer end shape. Habit favors the cyclic way, but habit is not proof. The team sets firm definitions and tests both across shaped and free-form cuts, criteria, and data kinds. One-shot wins at light trims, the cyclic way at deep ones. Their hybrid, built on patience, beats both in some scenes. The code is public for builders to check.
arxiv-2508-14236:
Minyi Huang, Shuenn-Jyi Sheu, and Li-Hsien Sun study how a huge crowd of agents can act for the shared good when each one is steered by a feedback rule. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

They work with spread models where each agent's state drifts in a non-straight way. By a step method with a stand-in agent who picks a shared-best rule, they draw a new master equation for the value of the game. Under plain terms, the rules from that equation are near-best for each person, up to a small error. Tight bounds on the shared cost are the hard part. They give clear cases and a use in system-wide risk.
arxiv-2508-14336:
Xu Weng and four colleagues present NeRC, a system for improving phone positioning in cities, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Satellite navigation signals bounce off buildings and phone hardware is cheap, so urban positions drift. Earlier data-driven fixes needed ranging error labels that are painfully hard to annotate.

NeRC trains its neural network using ground-truth locations instead, which are easier to obtain.
