A differentiable moving horizon estimator turns measurements into positions and passes gradients back for learning. The authors also propose training with Euclidean distance field cost maps, reducing the need for labeled locations. They evaluate the framework on public benchmarks and their own collected datasets, reporting stronger accuracy in difficult urban settings.
arxiv-2508-15236:
Seven researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on finding cancer spread in lymph nodes without labeled training data. Supervised AI reads pathology images well, but it needs large labeled sets, which are scarce in digital pathology. Unsupervised methods instead learn what normal tissue looks like and flag what departs from it.

Their model joins a diffusion model, which rebuilds images from noise, with a vision-language model guided by pathology words for normal tissue. Guided rebuilds make abnormal regions stand out against the rebuilt normal version. The work targets metastasis in lymph nodes, where early, accurate spotting guides treatment.
arxiv-2508-15636:
Song, Weltevrede, van Leeuwen, Wright, and Keith report that the two magnetic poles of certain pulsars appear to communicate. Knowing where pulsar radio emission is localized would clarify its elusive mechanism. Pulsars showing both a main pulse and an interpulse, one from each pole, offer a test bed. Using FAST and MeerKAT data, the team studied two such pulsars.

In both sources, when emission is bright in one pulse, it is dim in the other. Even split crudely into strong and weak groups, the anti-correlated brightness changes by a factor of two or more. Both also show the same quasi-periodic modulation in main pulse and interpulse, on timescales exceeding one hundred periods. If the interaction happens inside an isolated magnetosphere, either the opposite poles communicate or global changes drive both. Because both sources show it, the authors suggest two-pole modulation is general in interpulse pulsars.
arxiv-2508-15736:
Chong Zheng studies, in a 2025 topology paper, how one discrete Morse function can be morphed into another. Discrete Morse theory simplifies a shape by pairing up its building blocks, leaving a few critical ones that carry the shape's essence. Different pairings give different simplifications, and a shared language for moving between them was missing.

The moves Zheng uses are birth-death transitions, small changes that create or cancel a pair of critical blocks. He proves any two discrete Morse functions on the same finite complex are joined by a finite chain of such moves. As a bonus, the framework yields fresh proofs of several founding results of the theory.
arxiv-2508-16136:
Jaemin Kim, Seungchan Seo, Jiyoung Yun, Benjamin Lienhard, and Joonwoo Bae wrote a 2025 paper on cleaning up the start and end of quantum computations. Preparing a qubit and measuring it are noisy steps, and those errors form a large share of all errors in quantum work. Their protocol repeats the noisy steps to distill clean ones.

With starting errors near five percent, two helper qubits cut the error to about one in a thousand, and four helpers reach about one in a million, they show. The method needs no perfect parts to begin with. It also fits the superconducting qubits used in many labs. Cleaner starts and reads would help quantum algorithms, error correction, and links between quantum machines.
arxiv-2508-16536:
Yun Yang introduces rescaled expansive measures to give a measure based form of rescaled expansiveness for flows, above all with singularities. The goal is fresh tools for entropy and spread in steady time systems. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Matching definitions are set up through reparametrizations of varied smoothness. Under positive entropy, Yang proves that invariant rescaled expansive measures exist. An appendix derives a rescaled form of the Brin Katok local entropy formula for flows. That formula once covered only smooth flows, and now extends to general flows that may hold singular points.
arxiv-2508-17036:
Serhii Volosheniuk and co-authors built a heat engine from a single molecule in a 2025 paper. Ordinary engines burn fuel and move pistons. A particle-exchange engine has no moving parts at all: it harvests the flow of single particles through energy-selective paths.

Their device uses one diradical molecule, a speck a few nanometers wide, held at low temperature. The team measured how it turns a heat difference into useful work, testing quantum thermodynamics where the engine is smaller than the probes around it. Such engines probe the floor of energy conversion and may one day power or cool devices at the molecular scale. The work shows the concept runs in real hardware.
arxiv-2508-17536:
Hyeong Kyu Choi and co-authors pull apart group debates among language models to find which part actually earns the accuracy gains, in a 2025 paper. Multi-agent debate, where models argue over several rounds before answering, is widely credited with better reasoning. The setup blends two ingredients: the debate itself and a final majority vote. The authors tested each ingredient alone across seven language benchmarks.

Voting alone, it turns out, accounts for most of the improvement. The authors explain why with a mathematical model of debate as a random walk of beliefs. In that model, debate by itself cannot raise expected correctness, a property they prove as a martingale result. When they nudged the debate's belief updates toward correction, though, debate did start to help. Their verdict: plain ensembling is the sturdy default, and debate needs steering to earn its keep.
arxiv-2508-17936:
Yury Lysogorskiy and co-authors introduce GRACE in this 2025 paper, a family of all-purpose atom simulators built on graph atomic cluster expansion. Machine-learned potentials that work across the whole periodic table can speed up materials discovery hugely. GRACE models train on several of the largest materials datasets available. In broad benchmarks they set a new best balance of accuracy against running cost among foundation potentials.

The framework also bends well to special jobs. Fine-tuning and knowledge distillation shrink it for narrow tasks without wiping out what it already knew, a common failure called catastrophic forgetting. The authors pitch GRACE as a sturdy base for the next wave of atomistic modeling. High-fidelity simulation across many chemistries is the goal.
arxiv-2508-20336:
Zhou and five co-authors cut brain wave files by shift points, not fixed spans in this twenty twenty-five paper. Brain states do not sit in neat time boxes, yet drill files use them. Fixed cuts can split one state or merge two in a drill file.

Inside, their cut tool starts a new span when the wave's math form shifts. Shift spans then feed drill tools that ask for fixed span lengths. A fake wave forge lets the team test cuts gainst known state shifts. On fit-watch files the new cuts beat fixed cuts in catch truth. The win came with fewer spans to drill on in the same files.
arxiv-2508-21436:
Zhang and five colleagues split word meanings into finer parts inside large language models in twenty twenty-five. Word vectors in these models pack many shades of meaning into one lump. Their model breaks each vector into sub parts, each holding one clear strand of meaning. Brain scans then test if the strands match how the brain sorts meaning.

The split surfaced readable sub strands within broad meaning axes. Polarity, a plus minus split, drove much of the breakdown. Brain maps lined up with the strands in ways that support their reality. The work gives a finer lens on how models and minds organize concepts. It may aid tools that must explain word sense.
arxiv-2508-21536:
Susan Athey, Guido Imbens, Zhaonan Qu, and Davide Viviano introduce an estimator for causal effects in panel data in a 2025 econometrics study. Panels track the same units over time, and a treatment switches on for some units at some times. Their triply robust panel estimator layers three defenses. One is a flexible outcome model with a low-rank factor structure over two-way fixed effects. Another is weights favoring units like the treated ones. A third is weights favoring periods near the treatment time.

Simulations patterned on common study designs test the estimator's performance. Triple protection aims to keep estimates sound when any one modeling choice goes wrong.
arxiv-2509-00036:
Cheng Jin, Zhenyu Xiao, and Yuantao Gu present A-FloPS in 2025, a training-free way to speed up diffusion models. Diffusion models build images by reversing a noise process step by step, which gives top quality but costs many steps. Past speedups tune the solver for that reverse path, yet the path itself can be wasteful.

A-FloPS rewrites the sampling path in flow-matching form, which is smoother to step through. Scores from the diffusion model are mapped by formula to flow speeds, so no retraining is needed. The speed field is then split into a straight drift and a rest part whose change over time is damped. Straighter paths keep accuracy with fewer steps, which cuts the cost of making images.
arxiv-2509-00336:
An B. Vuong, Michael T. McCann, Javier E. Santos, and Yen Ting Lin argue in 2025 that diffusion models do not really learn the score function they are said to learn. The score is the gradient of the log-density of noisy data, a vector field that should be conservative, meaning path-independent. Neural designs in practice do not enforce that trait.

Numerical checks show trained networks break both integral and differential rules that true scores must obey. Yet the models generate remarkably well. The authors recast training as flow matching to the velocity field of a Wasserstein Gradient Flow, which moves a distribution downhill in a space of distributions. That view resolves the paradox and reframes what diffusion training does.
arxiv-2509-00436:
Amanuel T. Getachew, working alone, explores symmetry in parking distributions on caterpillar trees in 2025. Parking functions model cars that drive along a row of spots, each with a preferred spot, and park in the next free one. On trees, the model generalizes to cars that prefer vertices of a branching structure. A caterpillar tree has a central path with leaves attached.

Two statistics are tracked: the count of lucky cars, which park at their preferred spot, and how often each spot is preferred. A first-return decomposition reveals symmetry in their joint distribution. A two-variable analog of the Fuss-Catalan generating function is developed and shown to satisfy a functional equation. The symmetry extends to broader families of statistics.
arxiv-2509-00736:
Anja Haags leads a team of twenty-three authors on charge transfer into ring-shaped carbon molecules. The molecules are nonplanar cycloarenes made on a copper surface. A scanning tunneling microscope with treated tips can identify single molecules. It also shows complex features from electronic effects near the Fermi level. The team set out to explain those features.

They simulate microscope images as weighted sums of molecular orbitals. The weights come from a calculated density of states. The match confirms charge transfer from the surface into several empty orbitals. This holds for kekulene and for isokekulene in both of its bent forms. Photoemission tests on a full layer agree with the result. The method also suits strongly interacting surfaces and low-yield molecules.
arxiv-2509-00836:
Yulin Li, with two co-authors, proposes a motion planning method for robot arms. Classical methods use workspace distance gradients to avoid collisions. They can stall in local minima, though. They can also fail where gradients vanish. Distance fields in configuration space avoid many of these traps. Such fields model distances in the robot's joint space directly.

Their fields give reliable gradients almost everywhere. The team merges them with Model Predictive Path Integral control. Using those gradients, they unify the cost in joint space. They also cut the planning horizon to one step. Computation falls sharply while collision avoidance holds in practice. Tests reach near-perfect success in two dimensions. A seven-degree-of-freedom Franka arm also scores high success. Control runs above seven hundred fifty hertz.
arxiv-2509-00936:
Kishor Datta Gupta leads a team of five authors on UrbanInsight, a framework for smart city digital twins. Cities generate huge streams of data from sensors and cameras. Existing systems struggle with scale, latency, and fragmented insights. UrbanInsight works at the edge, close to where data are made.

The framework blends physics-informed machine learning with multimodal data fusion. Knowledge graphs form the semantic backbone for the data. At the edge, large language models generate context-aware rules. Those rules adapt filtering and decisions in real time. Physics-based methods ground predictions in real-world constraints. Together, these parts move digital twins beyond passive monitoring. They aim at responsive, trustworthy, and sustainable smart infrastructure.
arxiv-2509-01036:
Mohd Yasir Khan, writing alone, studies Vicsek agents in a complex noise environment. The Vicsek model is a standard model of flocking and swarming. Agents align with neighbors amid noise. Khan places a noiseless circular region inside a noisy outer region. Mutually repelling interactions act between the agents.

As outer noise varies, an emergent rotational order appears. It peaks at higher noise levels in their phase plots. Global order follows a U-shaped curve over noise strength. It starts high, dies down, and re-enters at stronger noise. The latter rise is attributed to the rotational order increase. Higher velocities enhance escape rates from the circular region. Slower agents show greater virtual confinement there. A gradual noise gradient reduces both orders, unlike sudden change.
arxiv-2509-01236:
Chain-of-thought prompting, where a model writes out steps before answering, boosts reasoning, but why it works is still debated. Hao Yang, with four co-authors, examines the balance between two forces: what the model learned in pre-training, its priors, and what the prompt itself teaches in context. They analyze the wording of reasoning traces in fine detail.

By adding noisy examples step by step, the team watched how the model shifts between prior knowledge and prompt signals. Models picked up surface structure fast, yet also grasped deeper logic, while leaning hard on priors at first. Enough good examples tipped decisions toward the context. Yang and the co-authors also tested whether prompt design can induce slower, more careful thinking, mapping how prompting shapes reasoning.
arxiv-2509-01536:
Chemistry labs run tangled workflows whose records are hard for machines to reuse, even with digital notebooks. Ebrahim Norouzi, with four co-authors, builds a knowledge graph from Chemotion, a system combining an electronic lab notebook with a repository. The graph follows the Basic Formal Ontology, a top-level scheme for organizing scientific data, and aims to meet the FAIR principles for findable, reusable data.

Experimental metadata were harvested from the Chemotion interface in a linked data format, converted to a standard graph format, and reshaped into the ontology-aligned graph by database queries. The source code and data sets are public. Norouzi and the team present the graph as an integrated, ontology-driven record of chemical research, built to support artificial intelligence driven discovery and reasoning over real lab work.
arxiv-2509-01636:
Tiny particles held in light can twist back and forth. That motion is called libration. Their spectra show puzzling shoulder-like features. Ankush Gogoi, Vikram Pakrashi, and Joanna A. Zielinska present a simulation frame for such spinning systems. It is built on Ito-Taylor expansions for noisy equations. Their test object is a small dumbbell, nearly a cylinder, held in light.

The model captures the particle's nonlinear turning dynamics. It reproduces the shoulder features in the libration spectrum. Those features arise from two motions at play. One is the confined libration itself. The other is heat-driven rotation about the particle's own axis. The authors offer the frame as a practical way to explain such spectra. It helps labs read the motions of levitated rotors from their signals.
arxiv-2509-01736:
Darius A Faroughy, Manfred Opper, and Cesar Ojeda build a model that creates fake but realistic particle jets from collider data. Jets are sprays of particles from high energy crashes at the Large Hadron Collider. Each particle mixes smooth traits, like energy, with fixed labels, like charge and flavor. That mix makes jets hard for standard generators to copy well.

Their transformer based flow learns both trait types at once, joined by a jump process for the labels. Trained on open data from the CMS detector, it makes jets with true looking motion and inner structure. Flavor mix in the fake jets also matches real data. Such models can speed up simulation and help hunt for odd events.
arxiv-2509-02136:
Mohammad Rajabdorri, Bo Zhou, Lukas Sigrist, and Enrique Lobato embed frequency dynamics into the unit commitment problem with a general order model. Unit commitment schedules which generators run to meet demand at least cost. Frequency constrained versions usually lean on first order simplifications or single metrics like the frequency low point. Their model writes time domain frequency response with second order dynamics for accuracy.

Bernstein polynomial approximations turn the differential model into a tractable mixed integer program. A new constraint limits how long frequency stays below a critical threshold, guarding relays and equipment. Data driven links tie the below threshold area to excursion duration. Validation on a Spanish island grid shows stronger frequency security at moderate cost. Low inertia small systems stand to benefit most.
arxiv-2509-02636:
André LeClair wrote a 2025 solo theoretical physics paper proposing that quantum vacuum energy is the origin of gravity. The argument builds a gravitational analogue of the Casimir effect, where vacuum fluctuations create measurable forces between plates.

From that starting point, Einstein's equations are shown to emerge in their Friedmann form, the equations governing cosmic expansion. Newton's constant then becomes environmental, set by the total mass-energy and size of the universe rather than fixed forever. That view reframes the entropy formulas for de Sitter space and black holes. Using a proposed vacuum energy formula tied to the lightest particle's mass, gravity weakens at high energies and the usual big bang singularity is avoided. The author also links the model to the Hubble tension debate.
arxiv-2509-02736:
Markus Clemens, Michael Günther, Timo Reis, and Nathanael Skrepek present a 2025 applied mathematics paper modelling how cable harnesses radiate and interfere electromagnetically, allowing the cables to curve. Standard transmission line models assume straight cables, which real harnesses rarely are.

Each cable follows the telegrapher's equations, the classic transmission line model, driven by signals imposed at its ends. Cables interact through radiation governed by Maxwell's equations, with the coupling entering through boundary conditions on the field. The combined system is energetically consistent: the authors prove a global power balance holds, so energy is neither created nor destroyed by the coupling. The model suits time-domain simulation of realistic wiring in vehicles and aircraft, where curved bundles and radiation both matter.
arxiv-2509-03236:
Ben Chen and 27 co-authors described OneSearch in 2025, a generative framework that rebuilds e-commerce search as one end-to-end system. Online shops usually filter products through stages: recall, pre-ranking, then ranking. Staged designs split computing across steps whose goals can clash, capping overall quality.

OneSearch replaces the cascade with a single learned model. A hierarchical encoding module compresses items while keeping their category structure and distinctive traits tied to shopper queries. User behavior enters as both short-term actions and long-term habits. A preference-aware reward system then fine-tunes results through staged training. In large offline tests and live A/B trials on a major platform, relevance and orders rose while running costs fell by about three quarters. The system now serves millions of users daily.
arxiv-2509-03736:
In a 2025 research paper, James Mooney and six co-authors ask whether language model agents are behaviourally coherent enough to stand in for humans in social research. Agents are often validated because their survey answers match the people they imitate. The authors argue output-level matching is not enough evidence that an agent truly behaves like its assigned person.

Their Latent Profiling framework first elicits an agent's latent profile, its underlying traits, through short surveys. It then tests whether the agent's conversation behaviour follows from that profile, as human behavioural models would predict. Six hypotheses covering preference, openness, and agreement are tested on nine open models. Surface-level trends are copied faithfully. Agents systematically fail the deeper coherence tests, though, even when single responses look convincingly human. The framework is offered as a theory-grounded instrument for building a behavioural science of language models.
arxiv-2509-03936:
Analysing two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy signals from disordered superconductors in two opposite limits is what Naoto Tsuji does in a 2025 physics paper. The technique spreads a material's nonlinear response across two axes, separating effects that plainer spectra blur together. Impurities disorder the superconductor and complicate its signals.

One limit uses narrow-band sinusoidal pulses; the other uses broad-band delta pulses, idealised instant kicks. In the narrow-band case, the signal ties to known third-order responses behind third harmonic generation and the ac Kerr effect. In the broad-band case, signals on the diagonal and horizontal axes instead follow another response, tied to the dc Kerr effect. Tsuji computes those quantities for a lattice model, using BCS mean-field theory with a self-consistent treatment of impurity effects. The two limits show threshold and resonance behaviour at the gap frequency, whose origins trace to quasiparticle and Higgs-mode excitations.
arxiv-2509-04036:
Georgy Lukyanov and one co-author, Anna Vlasova, present a 2025 theory paper on why well-regarded experts often give cautious advice. Their model has an adviser who sees a private signal and a decision maker who picks the safe choice by default. Risky choices happen more often as the adviser's standing grows, and results later feed back into that standing.

Within the model, advice follows a simple cutoff rule based on the signal. When reputation is higher, that cutoff rises under a stated condition, so leading experts experiment less. Pay tied to success shifts how much experimenting occurs. Gatekeeping, meaning control over which advice gets used, changes how much learning follows.
arxiv-2509-04236:
Preetom Borah and five co-authors watch a chemical-warfare stand-in break down inside burning metal powder in a 2025 research paper. The stand-in compound, called DIMP, mimics dangerous organophosphate agents safely. A custom infrared instrument with a spinning mirror tracks the compound's spectrum in real time during each burn. A laser method measures gas temperatures along the flame path at the same time, and standard infrared scans verify the leftover products afterward.

Four powder recipes mixing aluminum, magnesium, and zirconium were ignited inside the heated chamber. A new spectral score rates destruction as it happens. Breakdown strength varied with powder recipe, amount loaded, and gas temperature. Findings guide reactive materials designed to neutralize chemical weapons.
arxiv-2509-04336:
Metha Prathaban and five co-authors port a trusted gravitational-wave analysis method to graphics processors in a 2025 research paper. Hearing a black hole merger is only step one; Bayesian inference then estimates masses, spins, and which theory fits best. The community pipeline bilby relies on nested sampling, a method that peels probability layers inward. The team re-implemented its acceptance-walk kernel inside the vectorized blackjax-ns framework for GPUs.

Aligned-spin black hole analyses ran twenty to forty times faster. Recovered answers and evidence values matched the original CPU code statistically, confirming a faithful port. That clean baseline separates hardware gains from future algorithm tricks. Gravitational-wave teams gain a validated community tool for faster parameter studies.
arxiv-2509-04536:
Oliver Dunn and two co-authors adapt a classical safety monitor for quantum machine learning in a 2025 research paper. Quantum machine learning runs learning methods on quantum hardware, whose outputs are inherently probabilistic. Classical safety tools do not transfer as-is. Their method, Q-SafeML, builds on SafeML, which compares data patterns statistically to judge whether a model's answer deserves trust. The quantum version measures distances over quantum state spaces instead, matching the limits of quantum representation.

That shift makes scoring model-dependent and post-classification, unlike the older dataset-driven design. Drift between training and operating conditions becomes visible. Tests on two quantum model types, QCNN and VQC, showed the monitor supports informed human oversight and safer use.
arxiv-2509-04736:
A smartwatch that recognises activities entirely on the device protects privacy and avoids delays. Taeyoung Yeon, lead author with three co-authors, present WatchHAR, such a system, in a 2025 paper. It combines audio and inertial sensor data to recognise human activities in unconstrained settings.

The team unify preprocessing and inference into one trainable module, gaining a fivefold speed increase. The system keeps accuracy above ninety percent across more than twenty-five activity classes in their tests. It also beats leading models at event detection and classification while running fully on the watch, advancing standalone, privacy-aware activity tracking.
arxiv-2509-04936:
Floating-point arithmetic is famously tricky to reason about, yet little is known about how real code uses it. Andrea Gilot, lead author with two co-authors, close that gap with a large-scale GitHub study in a 2025 paper. They focus on statically typed languages so the study can scale to millions of repositories.

Sampling and filtering follow careful mining practices to avoid bias. The team identify floating-point use from keywords and parse code for constructs such as loops. Their results confirm floating-point code is widespread. They also find literature benchmarks match real-world code in some respects but not others, and they publish a large dataset of extracted functions.
arxiv-2509-05036:
Entanglement embezzlement lets a fixed catalyst state generate other entangled states without being used up. Li Liu investigates the internal structure that makes that trick possible in a solo 2025 quantum information paper. The analysis uses operator algebra tools for systems with no finite dimension cap.

Liu shows that if a catalyst can embezzle a target state, it must contain infinitely many commuting, locally structured copies of that target. That requirement works like a self-test, certifying the hidden copies. The results clarify what any embezzling catalyst must look like inside, and offer new tools for state certification in such quantum systems.
arxiv-2509-05136:
Intermetallic alloys that soak up hydrogen and release it again could store fuel for mobile use. Olivier Nadeau, lead author with five co-authors, compute hydrogen absorption in one such compound from first principles in a 2025 paper. Their multiscale approach first finds absorption sites by geometric analysis. It then characterises them with density functional theory.

Room-temperature Monte Carlo simulations turn those site properties into a full absorption isotherm. The curve matches experimental data well. Accurate results need both hybrid functionals and zero-point energy corrections. Drop either one and the match gets worse. The fully loaded structure expands considerably. That expansion stabilises it at high hydrogen content.
arxiv-2509-05736:
A popular image restoration method can wobble unstably, and Shraddha Chavan with Kunal N. Chaudhury add a stabiliser in a 2025 image processing paper. Regularization-by-Denoising uses pre-trained denoisers as stand-in priors inside reconstruction algorithms, giving high-quality results but sometimes unstable behaviour from the black-box denoiser.

Their fix borrows the Koopman operator, a tool that describes a non-linear system's dynamics through its action on features. In a low-dimensional feature space the operator captures the method's local dynamics. Its spectral radius, a measure of growth, flags instability and drives an adaptive step-size rule. The rule needs no retraining and little overhead, and tests with several denoisers show it works.
arxiv-2509-06036:
More quantizations of the rational numbers exist than the known pair, show Mustafa Topkara and A. Muhammed Uludag in a 2025 paper. Quantization here deforms ordinary numbers into q-versions, following earlier constructions by Morier-Genoud and Ovsienko built from continued fractions. The modular group, the symmetry group behind those constructions, turns out to admit more room.

The authors exhibit a pair of conjugate representations of the modular group and the equivariant maps that respect them, yielding new quantizations beside the known ones. They discuss specializations of these maps and connect the picture to Dyer's outer automorphism and its associated involution of the real line, called Jimm. The results widen the algebraic landscape of quantum numbers and their symmetries.
arxiv-2509-06136:
AI companies' rules for receiving vulnerability reports are audited in a 2025 paper by Yangheran Piao and two co-authors. Security researchers need vendors to welcome and reward reports, especially as AI systems handle sensitive data. The team analyzed the disclosure policies of two hundred sixty-four AI vendors with mixed methods, snapshot and longitudinal, and compared them against hundreds of real incidents and academic articles.

Over a third of vendors had no policy at all, and fewer than a fifth mentioned AI risks. Data access, authorization, and model extraction issues were most often in scope, while jailbreaking and hallucination were usually excluded. Three vendor profiles emerged: proactive, silent, and restrictive. Vendors seem to address AI disclosure later than research and incidents demand.
arxiv-2509-06436:
Long documents defeat language models in the middle, and Song Yu and four co-authors answer with a tree of cooperating agents in a 2025 paper. Information buried mid-context gets underused, trimming risks losing key content, and longer windows disperse attention. Tree of Agents instead splits the input into chunks that independent agents read separately.

Each agent forms a local view, then agents exchange information along tree-structured paths and try different reasoning orders, which cuts position bias and hallucination. Prefix-hash caching and adaptive pruning hold the cost near single-model levels. Powered by a compact eight-billion-parameter model, the system beats multiple baselines and rivals much larger commercial models on long-context tasks, by the authors' experiments.
arxiv-2509-06536:
Tracking objects that streak across an image is benchmarked by Senem Aktas and three co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Fast moving objects blur into streaks, which makes them hard to follow. Several open datasets record such sequences, but their notes about each frame were scattered and incomplete.

The team first writes a shared metadata file in JSON format for four public datasets. They then extend it into a richer file, called FMOX, that adds ground-truth object sizes for the sequences. With that file they test EfficientTAM, a recent foundation model for tracking, meaning a large model meant for general use. Its scores, measured by how well predicted and true paths overlap, compare well with pipelines built specially for these datasets. All code and data files are shared openly for other groups.
arxiv-2509-06636:
Training spiking neural networks with whole numbers only is the advance reported by Ismael Gomez and one co-author in a 2025 neuromorphic computing paper. Spiking networks mimic brain-style pulses and promise low energy use. Standard training methods, though, are heavy in computation and memory.

Their online algorithm mixes precisions: shadow weights are kept at sixteen bits while the weights used for inference drop to eight or twelve bits. Replacing decimal arithmetic with integer arithmetic makes the method friendly to specialized hardware, and memory use falls by more than half. It works for convolutional and recurrent spiking networks alike. On a handwritten-digit task and a spiking speech-digit task, accuracy matched or beat full-precision training, though very low precision and deeper models remain harder.
arxiv-2509-07136:
Jorge V. Rocha's 2025 paper, written with 1 co-author, asks what happens when a self-gravitating material that can stretch and shear collapses under its own gravity. Perfect fluids, which cannot resist shearing, are the usual model for stars. Real neutron stars likely have an elastic crust, a solid layer that can bend and spring back, so elastic collapse is a new case to study.

Using a scale-invariant elastic model, meaning one that looks the same at any size, the authors find steady self-similar collapse patterns and solve for them on a computer. The solutions come in a discrete set, and the study focuses on the main one. Adding elasticity makes the material easier to compress and can produce negative radial pressure near the sonic point. Strong effects can even create a second sonic point, which limits how elastic the material can be.
arxiv-2509-07736:
Benedikt Heizenreder leads a 7-author team in 2025 showing a continuous spectroscopy method based on atom cloud position. The tool is a magneto-optical trap. It uses lasers and magnetic fields to hold cold atoms. Here it runs on strontium's narrow intercombination line. The trap's position depends on frequency. That turns location into a sensitive frequency meter, with a locking range hundreds of times the natural linewidth.

Active feedback on the trap position stabilizes a frequency comb, an optical ruler. The comb in turn stabilizes the trap laser. The frequency sensitivity is insensitive to the effective laser linewidth, the authors show. Instability falls below a few parts in ten trillion after 400 seconds of averaging. That beats hot-vapor modulation transfer spectroscopy. The method offers a broadly applicable route to frequency references at a very high level.
arxiv-2509-07836:
Optimisation problems whose answers are sets, not single points, get a new solution method in a 2025 paper by Suprova Ghosh and 3 co-authors. Their trust-region technique hunts for critical points of set-valued maps built from finitely many smooth functions. Trust-region methods take careful trial steps and shrink or grow the trusted area depending on progress.

A new rule for the reduction ratio keeps the method always descending, and the whole scheme is globally convergent, meaning it settles from any starting point. Each step requires solving a smaller vector optimisation problem, so the method is more than a routine extension of older ones. Set-valued optimisation fits real choices where several goals compete and no single best answer exists.
arxiv-2509-08036:
A long-predicted exotic critical point in quantum Hall bilayers is verified in simulation by Cristian Voinea and 3 co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Two coupled quantum Hall layers can pass continuously between distinct topological phases, the Halperin state and the Moore-Read Pfaffian state. Theory long expected a critical description built from Majorana fermions, particles that are their own antiparticles.

Using fuzzy sphere regularisation, the authors match the low-energy spectrum at the transition to a three-dimensional gauged Majorana conformal field theory. The transition is driven by the closing of the neutral fermion gap, and operator content is extracted in both charge sectors. Confirming the critical theory anchors ideas about topological phases that may one day support fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2509-08136:
M. H. Rayment and 2 co-authors settle a dispute about xenon gas with precise laser work in a 2025 physics paper. They measure a jump between two energy levels of xenon atoms. The light used is in the deep ultraviolet range. Long, clean pulses of that light let them cancel the blur from atoms in motion.

Five common forms of xenon are measured. The values are sharp to less than a millionth of the jump size. Mixed with other precise xenon data, they resolve a clash between recent values of the gas's ionisation energy. The clash was about a thousand times larger than the new error bars. Reference values like these feed plasma work and checks of basic constants.
arxiv-2509-08236:
Ranking methods that reshuffle winners when a new option appears are a known embarrassment, and Lisheng Jiang with 3 co-authors reduce that risk in a 2025 decision science paper. Their target is a hybrid method that combines entropy weighting with TODIM, a multicriteria ranking technique. Rank reversal, where adding an alternative flips the order of existing ones, undermines trust in the result.

An expanded evaluation matrix, padded with virtual alternatives, lowers the probability of reversal. The method is then applied to selecting energy storage technology, a choice balancing cost, performance, and risk criteria. Decision tools used for real investments must not change their verdict because an irrelevant extra option wandered into the spreadsheet.
arxiv-2509-08336:
Atoms diffracting through sub-nanometre holes in an atom-thin sheet are simulated two ways by Eivind Kristen Osestad and 3 co-authors in a 2025 atomic physics paper. Patterned hexagonal boron nitride membranes could advance atom interferometry and atomic holography. Dispersion forces, especially the Casimir-Polder attraction, pull passing atoms toward the membrane and threaten to close the smallest holes.

Solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for helium matter waves gives the quantum benchmark. Transmission rates come out significantly higher in the quantum treatment than semi-classical models suggest, a consequential difference for design. Knowing the true transmission decides feasible hole sizes, and therefore whether membrane-based atom optics can deliver the sensors and holograms promised for it.
arxiv-2509-09036:
Lorenzo Neil and 4 co-authors report new user experiences with secret management tools in a 2025 paper. Developers must protect API keys and passwords, and leaks can cause major harm. Secret management tools store secrets centrally and are widely recommended.

Twenty-one new users were observed doing storage, access, and injection tasks, then interviewed after each task. Even when users found features helpful, remediating a hard-coded secret proved hard. Documentation quality and navigation problems pushed many toward secondary sources or workarounds. Interface flexibility was praised, but help resources often failed to onboard users. The authors argue quick, secure adoption is unrealistic without better help.
arxiv-2509-09736:
Sruthy Jyothi Das and Austin Baty address a background problem in collider physics in this 2025 paper. Collisions of light ions such as oxygen and neon are used to study how quark-gluon plasma behavior changes with system size. While stored in a collider ring, light ion beams can break apart through electromagnetic effects and mix in other ion species, which are hard to simulate exactly.

The authors propose a data-driven way to measure how much this contamination could distort a physics analysis. Their method uses the time pattern of the contaminant ions and their smaller size to set up control regions in real data. A simple model shows the approach is robust, and it can be applied to current and future light ion runs.
arxiv-2509-09836:
Marco Pasini and 2 co-authors build an audio compressor in 2025 that refuses to choose between smooth codes and token codes. Generative models that work in a compressed space need that space to be both tiny and faithful, a hard bargain for sound. Most autoencoders commit to either continuous embeddings or discrete tokens, locking later tools into one style of generation.

CoDiCodec emits both from a single trained model: continuous codes at a very low frame rate and discrete tokens at a modest bitrate, guided by global summary embeddings. A dropout trick on its scalar quantiser keeps the two views consistent under one training loss. It also decodes in parallel for better quality and speed, beating rival compressors at similar bitrates on reconstruction tests.
arxiv-2509-09936:
Saarth Gaonkar and 7 co-authors test a different use of language models in a 2025 paper: writing the solver instead of the solution. Much scientific machine learning trains networks to predict answers directly, which can be fragile. Their SciML agents instead read a plain-language description of an ordinary differential equation and write code that calls proven numerical methods, choosing fit solvers and checking stability.

To measure this skill they built two test sets, one of tricky problems that look stiff but are not, and a benchmark of a thousand varied equation tasks. Newer instruction-following models, given guided prompts with domain knowledge, wrote code that ran and matched reference answers well. Older or smaller models still gained from fine-tuning.
arxiv-2509-10236:
Old simulation code often hides valuable stencil kernels, the repeated neighbor-based calculations at the heart of many scientific programs. Mingyi Li and seven co-authors introduce Stencil-Lifting in this 2025 paper, a system that converts such low-level code into an equivalent high-level domain-specific language automatically.

Their method rests on a hierarchical recursive lifting theory. Nested loops are captured as invariant subgraphs, custom dependency graphs whose parts carry predicate summaries of what they compute. Keeping those summaries consistent yields the loop invariants needed for correctness without outside verification tools. On standard stencil benchmarks and four real applications, the system ran far faster than rival verified lifters, over thirty times faster than one, while keeping the rewritten code exactly equivalent in meaning.
arxiv-2509-10536:
Jean-Pierre Magnot, writing alone, gives Boltzmann machines a geometric upgrade in this 2025 paper. A restricted Boltzmann machine is a learning model whose connections carry numeric weights. Magnot lets those weights take values in abstract groups instead, such as rotation-like matrix groups or even infinite-dimensional operator groups, so the model can encode richer relations between its units.

On top of that change he defines a contextuality index, built from group-valued holonomies traced around cycles in the model's graph. The index measures how inconsistent the local weights are when taken around a loop, a kind of curvature. The paper links the idea to sheaf theory, gauge theory, and noncommutative geometry, with worked examples in finite and infinite settings.
arxiv-2509-10736:
Biobanks hold genomes and health records for hundreds of thousands of people. Yiran Li and three co-authors make Bayesian analysis feasible at that scale, in this 2025 paper. Bayesian hierarchical models can pool information across traits and conditions. Sampling-based inference drowns in high-dimensional parameter spaces, though. Fast approximations ignore the structure of genome-wide problems.

Their adaptive focus strategy works inside a variational inference scheme. At each step, it updates only the blocks of parameters that current estimates mark as relevant. Real biological effects concentrate in a few units, after all. The test bed is protein quantitative trait locus mapping. Data come from simulations and from UK Biobank proteomics. Runtime fell by up to half. Statistical performance held steady. A genome-wide pipeline for thousands of traits shows the approach in full production shape.
arxiv-2509-11036:
Dust in a young planetary system does not simply vanish when it gets hot, and Sheng Xu with four co-authors model that stubbornness in this 2025 astrophysics paper. In the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, grains sublimate, turn to gas, and textbooks treat the process as equilibrium thermodynamics. Their first-principles quantum calculations and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations say otherwise: sublimation is a slow kinetic process.

Binding energies and vibration rates for silicate compositions imply grains survive far longer than local orbital times, persisting in a superheated state. The sublimation front therefore spreads out, its position and shape governed by inward drift and grain growth. Coupled simulations show the front's radius varying fourfold with accretion rate and a bowl-shaped, layered structure. Disk models and observations of inner rims, the cradle of planet formation, need the kinetic picture.
arxiv-2509-11236:
Emre Sahinoglu and Shahin Shahrampour prove learning guarantees on curved spaces in this 2025 paper. Online optimization makes a decision, sees the cost, and adjusts, round after round. On curved spaces called Hadamard manifolds, earlier guarantees for a natural convexity notion worsened as the space curved more, which punished exactly the settings where the geometry helps.

Working instead with horospherical convexity, the authors analyze online gradient descent and prove regret bounds that do not depend on curvature at all. For the plain and strong versions of the notion, the bounds match the best flat-space rates. Experiments on the space of positive definite matrices, covering robust estimation and averaging problems, show the theory at work.
arxiv-2509-11336:
William Farlessyost, Sebastian Oberst, and Shweta Singh propose a smarter way to choose sensors in this 2025 engineering paper. Soft sensors estimate hard-to-measure quantities from other readings. Picking which inputs matter is usually done with linearized statistics. Such statistics miss how influence changes over time.

Their framework uses liquid time constant networks as observers. These neural models have adaptive internal clocks. Each candidate sensor's causal impact gets measured by perturbation. Weak inputs are pruned. The observer is retrained. The cycle repeats until accuracy starts to slip. Three test systems were used. One was a spring-mass-damper rig. A stirred-tank reactor served as another testbed. A predator-prey model with seasonal forcing completed the set. Pruning kept the meaningful sensors and improved accuracy.
arxiv-2509-12236:
David Oprea and David Perkins pair two ideas to solve the minimum set cover problem in a 2025 paper. Set cover asks for the smallest collection of sets that together cover every element. Their new heuristic borrows Wave Function Collapse, a procedure of observing, propagating constraints, and collapsing choices, and applies it to covering.

The resulting algorithm, WFC-SC, quickly finds coverings close to the minimum. The authors then add hill climbing, a metaheuristic that improves a solution by small steps, to escape local optima, solutions that look best nearby but are not global bests. Benchmarks used the well-known OR library from Brunel University. Against other proficient algorithms, their pairing showed a better balance between solution quality and running time.
arxiv-2509-12736:
Water that clings to a condensing surface instead of draining away throttles heat exchangers and water harvesters alike, and grooving the surface can either help or hurt. Matteo Leonard and one co-author settle the question in 2025 with high-throughput condensation tests on plates cut with parallel vertical grooves.

Only the groove spacing varies, and one length rules the outcome: the radius at which droplets detach. Wider spacing than that radius makes grooves passive reservoirs that raise retention. Tighter spacing turns them into active drains that confine droplet growth and cut retention below even a smooth plate. Two simple models capture the switch.
arxiv-2509-12836:
Shreyas Shivakumara, Gabriel Eilertsen, and Karljohan Lundin Palmerius explore combining quality metrics for neural radiance fields in a 2025 paper. Neural radiance fields synthesize new viewpoints of a scene, but judging their output is hard because they produce unique artifacts. No single metric performs well across all datasets.

The authors hypothesize that fusing two successful metrics based on varied perceptual ideas can overcome single limits. They combine a metric for image structure and texture with a video assessment fusion metric. Two normalization strategies and two fusion strategies were tested for their effect on correlation with subjective quality scores. Experiments ran on synthetic and outdoor datasets under three configurations. The detailed analysis compares fusion methods against single scores.
arxiv-2509-13036:
Agnese Bissi, Giulia Fardelli and Mohammad Khansari resum bubble loops in a large-N field theory in 2025. The four-point function of like scalars is the test case. Its dual is a curved space with a quartic term.

A universal part is fixed at each order by tree data alone. That part drives a log growth in spin for paired-trace weights. The pair sums those effects to all orders. A neat curved-space picture emerges. In Mellin space the same part matches chained cuts of bubble graphs. In the flat limit the match is exact.
arxiv-2509-13436:
Evan Eisinger and Michael Heroux ask in 2025 whether research software science counts as metascience, the science of science. Research leans on code, so result trust hinges on software quality, replay, and openness. Class shapes funding and standing, which makes the ask practical.

Definitions and goals of both fields are compared in depth. Shared pledges to replay, openness, and empirical study favor inclusion. A tool focus versus whole enterprise focus favors separation. Verdict: the field is a distinct cross field that aligns with metascience and fits broad definitions of it. Rigor for discovery tools is urged either way.
arxiv-2509-13736:
Muyuan Ma and 4 co-authors propose motion adaptation for exoskeletons via meta-learning in a 2025 paper. An exoskeleton you wear can add to your strength. The hard part is help that fits. Assistance that is personal, and that carries across tasks, has stayed out of reach.

Their approach learns by meta-imitation. At its core sits a neural network built for one task at a time, which predicts how a person's elbow joint will move. Motions of the whole body, captured as keypoints, were pulled from public video and motion-capture collections spanning many tasks. The elbow paths produced there trained the network, inside a model-agnostic meta-learning framework. A few gradient updates are enough to fit it to a new task, or to a user it has never served. A controller that compensates for gravity follows the personal references the network sets.
arxiv-2509-13836:
Weihang Wang and seven co-authors attack object hallucination in large vision-language models in a 2025 paper, the failure where a model confidently describes things that are not in the picture. They suspect the visual encoder, the component that reads the image, because different encoder training styles plant different biases that show up as different hallucination patterns.

To test this they built VHBench-10, a benchmark of about ten thousand samples spanning ten fine-grained hallucination categories, and confirmed that encoders do hallucinate in characteristic ways. Simply fusing encoder features was not enough, so they propose VisionWeaver, a routing network that uses global image features to decide how to combine several specialized visual experts. Hallucinations dropped and overall performance improved.
arxiv-2509-13936:
Harvey Mannering, Zhiwu Huang, and Adam Prugel-Bennett improve diffusion image generation at its very first step in a 2025 paper. A diffusion model starts from random Gaussian noise, and that starting noise quietly shapes the final picture's quality and how faithfully it follows the prompt. Existing ways to pick better noise need extra datasets, extra networks, or costly backpropagation.

Their method, Noise Level Guidance, refines the initial noise by raising the likelihood that it aligns with general guidance, with no added training data, auxiliary networks, or gradient passes. It works for both conditional and unconditional models and accepts various forms of guidance. Across five standard benchmarks, output quality and prompt adherence improved, and the method slots in alongside existing guidance techniques without extra compute burden.
arxiv-2509-14336:
Surajit Chakraborty and four co-authors extend a stress only view of jammed solids in 2025, materials such as packed soft spheres that lock rigid. Jammed solids hold internal prestress from tangled force networks. No stress free starting shape explains their stiffness.

An earlier formulation treated mechanical balance like an electric law for tensor fields with vector charges. Response then matched a dielectric response, how a material reacts to an applied field. The new work adds scale dependent screening with both dielectric and Debye type behaviour. Screening creates a characteristic length in stress correlations and in response to outside force. Simulations of soft sphere packings match the extended picture, giving jammed matter a predictive field language.
arxiv-2509-14636:
Yufei Wei and seven co-authors present BEV-ODOM2 in 2025, a monocular visual odometry system for ground robots that works in a bird eye view. Odometry estimates how a robot moved from camera images alone. Bird eye projection gives a metric scaled ground plane, fixing scale drift and simplifying motion.

Two flaws limited earlier bird eye methods: sparse supervision from pose only training, and information loss when warping perspective images to the ground plane. Their system adds dense flow supervision derived from poses and fuses perspective with bird eye features. Ground truth needs stay limited to poses. Robots gain steadier, scale consistent motion estimates from a single camera, useful where lidar or stereo rigs are too costly.
arxiv-2509-14736:
Tingchun Wang and Jingye Yan propose two numerical schemes for the logarithmic Schrödinger equation in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. That equation models wave behavior with a logarithmic nonlinearity, which becomes singular at zero and usually forces extra regularization tricks. Their linearized finite difference schemes avoid regularization entirely.

One scheme uses a first-order backward difference in time, the other a second-order version, with central differences in space. The authors prove error bounds that hold without any restriction linking time step and grid size. Their estimates improve known convergence rates and also hold in a stronger discrete norm where older results needed grid conditions. Numerical tests confirm the theory, so the schemes offer a cleaner route to accurate simulations of these waves.
arxiv-2509-15236:
Shubham Kavane and four co-authors release a tool chain that builds training data for flow models in a 2025 paper. Learned stand-in models for fluid flow are only as good as the data they train on. Most past studies train on fixed, pre-made sets. Careful work needs data that can be rebuilt and reshaped to order.

ChannelFlow-Tools builds 3D channel flow sets with blocks in the way, all from config files. It makes block shapes from six shape families, turns them into voxel grids with signed gap fields, runs lattice-Boltzmann runs, and packs the output as tensors ready for learning. Shape building is checked to be byte-same across reruns. A full mesh audit checks the set. The open tool chain makes data building a repeatable step.
arxiv-2509-15736:
Gabriel Jarry leads a team that models how much fuel airliners burn as they age. Flight planning and emissions checks both need accurate fuel flow figures. Standard models often miss the wear that builds up as engines age. The team study one Airbus type, using records from about nineteen thousand flights across nine aircraft.

They compare physics based models, simple fix factors, and neural networks. Age enters the networks either as an input or as a scaling bias. Plain models understate fuel use for older aircraft. Age aware fixes and networks cut that bias and sharpen accuracy. Few aircraft and missing upkeep records limit how far the lessons stretch.
arxiv-2509-15936:
Jake Bowhay, Yuji Nakatsukasa, and Irwin Zaid find all the roots of a smooth complex function in a chosen region. Roots of such functions matter across applied math. A rational stand in, built by the AAA method, gives its own roots easily. But some true roots may be missed, with no warning. The trio close that gap.

Their method approximates the function's logarithmic derivative instead of the function itself. They split the search region using a classic counting rule for roots inside a border. That split drives where finer approximations are needed until all roots are certified found. Many ideas also cover poles of related functions. A Python package, skzeros, ships the method.
arxiv-2509-17136:
Yuhao Tian and Zheming Yang pair edge and cloud models for factory inspection in a 2025 paper. Checking products by vision demands high accuracy on tight budgets. Large multimodal models reason well but cost too much to run on every item. Light edge models are cheap but fail on hard cases. Their scene-aware system routes work between the two.

The system cuts runtime by up to about a fifth in tests. Energy per correct decision fell by large margins. Code is shared in public. Scene-aware routing could let factories reserve costly model calls for the items that truly need them, keeping lines fast and power bills down.
arxiv-2509-17236:
Thomas K. Kloster, writing alone, models day-ahead electricity prices across Europe in a 2025 arXiv paper. Prices in each bidding zone form one strand of a large panel, and the strands move together over time. That panel view is often overlooked, and Kloster builds a continuous-time frame that takes it head on.

He writes the panel as an ambit field wrapped on a cylinder, where the cross-section is a circle. Hours of the delivery day map onto that circle in a natural way, which lets dependence live inside the index set with no extra parameters. The field extends space-time versions of volatility-driven Lévy processes long used in energy markets. Pricing formulas for derivatives stay nearly as tractable as in the no-space case. The frame also prices contracts on single delivery hours and spreads between them, and the paper gives a simulation scheme.
arxiv-2509-17536:
Giorgia Peluso and a large team of co-authors ask whether faint black hole activity skews a famous galaxy correlation. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies star-forming galaxies, whose infrared and radio output track each other tightly. Recent work found that heavier galaxies sit lower on that correlation, and one suspect is radio light from active galactic nuclei that standard checks miss.

The team's VLBA programme targeted hundreds of galaxies that show no radio excess at low resolution. Sharp radio imaging can flag a true active nucleus by its brightness temperature. With that census in hand, the authors can weigh how much hidden nuclear activity inflates the radio side of the correlation. The study tests whether the mass trend is a real trait of star formation or a residue of quiet black holes hiding in the sample.
arxiv-2509-17636:
Mohammed Racim Moussa Boudjemaa and four co-authors fix a standard data step that breaks in high dimensions. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies whitening, which standardizes data so later estimation gets easier. For spherical Gaussian mixtures, whitening makes the component means orthogonal, so moment tensors split cleanly and the mixture can be read off.

When data are high-dimensional and scarce, the sample covariance warps, and whitening built on it fails: the means stop being orthogonal. Using random matrix theory, the team derives exact limits for the dot products of the whitened means in that regime. They then build a corrected whitening matrix that restores orthogonality in the limit. Tests show the fix improves estimation of spherical mixtures where the classic step degrades. The work serves latent variable modeling at modern data shapes.
arxiv-2509-17936:
Ksenia Fedosova links shape counts and motion traits for a family of symmetry groups. Her 2025 paper works on Hecke triangle groups and the curved spaces they tile. A key tool is the Selberg zeta function, which packs closed path lengths into one object.

Fedosova shows that object can be matched by determinants of finite matrices. The error in that match is known in closed form and shrinks fast as the matrices grow. With it, she pins the fractal size of the groups to high precision. She also values a twin zeta function at zero and bounds where the main one hits zero.
arxiv-2509-18136:
Suqing Wang and 6 co-authors mine a large data set to link a language model's shape to its scores. Their 2025 study notes that model size and skill have grown fast, while firm facts on which shape choices matter stay scarce. The team built a set of open model shapes and their bench scores.

With that set, they test how each shape choice shifts scores, task by task. Inner-state probes back up the broad trends they find. A short past of the field, and a look at next trends, frame the sums. The set will be shared in public for folk to reuse.
arxiv-2509-18236:
S Stepanoff leads a large team that reports the state of a neutrino observatory built for the highest energies. Their 2025 paper covers the Trinity Observatory, which hunts tau neutrinos in a band far above lab scales. Work goes in three stages, and the first, a demonstrator, went live in fall 2023.

The demonstrator acts as a pathfinder for the full build. Its design feeds the plan for the first full telescope. In hundreds of hours of data, the team found no candidate neutrino event. First results from that run are set out, with the build state at the time of writing.
arxiv-2509-18536:
Small language models gain less from extra thinking time than big ones do. Jin Young Kim and Ji Won Yoon propose CCQA, a reasoning trick built for small models, in this 2025 paper. The idea borrows cycle consistency: a good answer should lead back to the question that was asked. Each candidate answer is checked by that round trip.

For each reasoning path, the method generates a question from the path and its answer. It then scores how close that question sits to the original one. The candidate with the closest match wins. Small models are weak at writing such questions, so a light specialist model does that step. Across eight models and both math and commonsense tests, CCQA beat the best prior methods. The authors offer it as a practical baseline for efficient small-model reasoning.
arxiv-2509-18736:
Online shops rank items in stages: a fast retriever drafts a list, then a slower reranker polishes it. Wenyu Mao and 11 co-authors study the reranker side of that pipeline in this 2025 paper. Most past work taught retrievers to please rerankers. Little work taught rerankers to use what the retriever already computed.

The team shows the retriever's scores carry a signal that has been underexplored. They frame reranking as denoising those scores toward what users truly pick. A naive use of the scores has clear limits, which they prove. Their framework, DNR, pairs the denoising reranker with a noise-making module in an adversarial setup. Three added goals cover denoising, score exploration, and distribution matching. Tests on three public sets and one live industrial system back the design. Retriever scores, handled right, make rerankers stronger.
arxiv-2509-18936:
Arun Kumar Das and two co-authors study a coloring puzzle on graphs that comes from scheduling TV programs. Some points of the graph start out colored, and the task is to finish the coloring under strict rules. Points that share a color must sit far apart, at least a set distance. Each color must also be used an exact number of times, which the authors call demands.

The team focuses on the simplest graph shape, a path. They give an exact fast method when the pre-colored points sit only at the two ends of the path. They also build an approximate method for the general case and prove the full problem is NP-complete, meaning no fast exact method is likely. Further results sort out which versions stay tractable when key numbers are small.
arxiv-2509-19036:
When a molecule sits inside an optical cavity, trapped light and matter mix so strongly that both change character. Yetmgeta Aklilu and three co-authors apply a theory that tracks electrons and photons together over time. Their method joins real-space wave functions for the electrons with photon states counted in a Fock space, a standard way to list light quanta. The goal is to see how the cavity reshapes the molecule itself.

They run the framework on several molecular systems as test cases. By varying the coupling strength and the cavity's tuned frequency, they watch molecular geometry shift. They also track the mixed light-matter energy levels, called polaritonic spectra. A third check looks at how binding between molecules changes inside the cavity. The work gives chemists a tool for predicting cavity effects before building the experiment.
arxiv-2509-19136:
Sébastien Salva and Redha Taguelmimt test whether language-model agents can run software tests that are written as plain English instructions. Such natural-language test cases for graphical interfaces are cheaper to write and maintain than coded scripts. But the instructions can be ambiguous, so an agent may report failures that are not real bugs, a flaw the authors call unsoundness. Rerunning the same test may also give different outcomes, which undermines trust in the results.

Their algorithm adds guardrails and specialist agents that check each step as it runs. They define measures for execution skill and consistency, plus a notion of weak unsoundness tied to industrial Six Sigma quality levels. Across eight public models, the largest, a 70-billion-parameter Llama model, performed acceptably with high consistency. Smaller models showed clear limits, mapping where the approach stands today.
arxiv-2509-19436:
Twisted bilayer graphene's electronic behavior shifts with temperature in ways theorists have struggled to explain as one story. Lorenzo Crippa and eight co-authors present a framework meant to unify the evidence. Their account covers scanning tunneling spectroscopy, quantum twisting microscopy, and thermodynamic measurements on the magic-angle system at once. The key claim is partnership: electron correlations and outside symmetry breaking, from strain and from the lattice relaxing into place, act together rather than as rivals.

That cooperation shapes the spectra, the compressibility, and the entropy in matching ways, leaving characteristic signatures in each probe. By fitting all three kinds of data inside one framework, the authors argue the controversy softens: both mechanisms are needed, and their interplay is the physics. The work targets the long-running debate over what governs flat-band graphene's emergent behavior.
arxiv-2509-19636:
Self-driving race cars can top two hundred kilometers per hour, but testing them eats track time that few teams have. Mahmoud Ali and four co-authors present a slim racing stack built for fast deployment. Their system ran real speedway time trials after only eleven hours of track practice. Total track distance in testing stayed near three hundred twenty-five kilometers.

Peak speed reached two hundred six kilometers per hour. The team reports tracking accuracy, vehicle behavior, and safety margins in detail. A minimal design cut the usual long development cycle sharply. Their lessons target teams that must validate on real cars with scarce access. The work shows that careful integration can matter as much as algorithmic novelty in racing.
arxiv-2509-19836:
Training a language model on million-token texts spreads work across many graphics chips, and the chips spend much time waiting. Ao Sun and six co-authors build BurstEngine to raise that wasted share. Its attention method rings data around the chips in step with the machine's wiring, overlapping talk and math. Memory tricks include selective checkpointing at the sequence level and a fused output head.

Workload balancing handles the varied masking patterns that long texts bring. Together the pieces lift hardware use well past tensor and context parallelism baselines, the authors report. Long-context training feeds document analysis, code bases, and book-length reasoning. A framework that makes such training cheaper widens who can attempt it. The work is systems engineering aimed at a clear bottleneck.
arxiv-2509-20136:
Wei Zhang and eleven co-authors present a benchmark for code-generating language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Current coding tests mostly check syntax and correct execution. Real game development also demands playability, good looks, and engaging interaction. V-GameGym was built to measure that fuller set of skills.

The benchmark holds more than two thousand samples grouped into one hundred themes drawn from real code repositories. A clustering method kept the set diverse and structurally complete. Grading uses an automated multimodal pipeline inside full interface sandboxes. Models must synthesize visual game code, not only plain functions. The analysis shows the benchmark separates plain coding skill from practical game-building ability. It gives developers measurable targets for visual programming quality.
arxiv-2509-20336:
Inside a transformer, graph reasoning leaves traces that Xinnan Dai and five co-authors set out to read in a 2025 arXiv paper. Language models solve graph problems well, yet their internal method was largely unknown. The team studied basic decoder-only transformers with a circuit tracing framework. That lens turns hidden activity into readable reasoning traces.

Two core mechanisms appeared across their tasks. Token merging combines related pieces of the graph into shared representations. Structural memorization stores graph patterns the model can reuse. Both mechanisms supported path reasoning and substructure extraction tasks. The authors measured how each behavior shifts with graph density and model size. The study offers a unified way to interpret structural reasoning in this model family.
arxiv-2509-20636:
Imaging instruments that count molecules pixel by pixel blur competing signals together. Joaquim Valerio Teixeira and three co-authors unmix them with a Bayesian method in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their goal is the relative rate of each molecule across a whole tissue image. Natural sparsity in spatial patterns is the lever: most molecules are active in only part of the tissue.

The framework pairs a heavy-tailed graph lasso prior with a new hierarchical variational family. Inference runs efficiently through automatic differentiation. In simulations, the method beat standard point-estimate practice and gave more honest uncertainty than mean-field approximations. On real imaging mass spectrometry data, it recovered known anatomy more faithfully, removed artifacts, and found active regions the standard analysis missed. The tool suits both mass spectrometry and mass cytometry imaging.
arxiv-2509-20836:
Nachi Avraham-Re'em, Michael Bjorklund, and Rickard Cullman study how often a moving system returns near its start, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their objects are cross sections of probability-preserving actions of unimodular groups, together with the measures living on those cross sections.

The authors introduce an invariant called intersection covolume to quantify how periodic a cross section is. Their main theorem, built on a higher-order version of Kac's lemma, bounds this covolume below by the intensity. Equality holds exactly for actions induced by a lattice, in Mackey's sense. They also show that the natural cross sections of cut-and-project actions, used to model quasicrystals, have finite intersection covolume. The paper runs to twenty-six pages.
arxiv-2509-21136:
Certain brain cells fire both when you wave and when you watch someone else wave; they are called mirror neurons. Wentao Zhu and five co-authors import that principle into machine learning in a 2025 paper for ICCV 2025. Their subject is embodied representation alignment for action understanding and execution.

Machine learning usually treats watching an action and performing it as separate tasks. The authors first show that intermediate representations for the two spontaneously align during learning. They then add an approach that aligns the representations explicitly. The unified view treats understanding and doing as two sides of one representation. Robots and video models alike could benefit, since an agent that represents its own actions like observed ones may learn skills from watching people more directly.
arxiv-2509-21236:
Little red dots, a peculiar class of compact objects found by JWST, may not be as compact as they look. The 2025 paper is by Kelly Whalen and 3 co-authors. These are compact objects seen by the JWST telescope. Their tiny size is often used to argue they host active black holes. The paper tests whether common fitting tools can recover true shapes for such objects.

The team made simulated images that mimic little red dots and fit them with two tools. At low signal levels, the tools failed to recover the input values. Most model versions could not be told apart from a point source at modest signal. A point spread fraction may describe compactness more safely. The authors warn that shape claims for large samples need great care.
arxiv-2509-21436:
Adversarial attacks on AI systems are usually studied as if no human were in the loop. Shutong Fan and 2 co-authors argue that this misses the real risk in a 2025 position paper. In human AI decision systems, people interpret, adjust, and act on model outputs. Trust, expectations, and cognitive habits shape those responses. Feedback loops form that adversaries can exploit.

The authors argue human factors fundamentally reshape adversarial analysis. Robustness evaluation must include the interplay between human behaviour and attack strategies. Fully autonomous analysis cannot capture how a person might amplify or dampen an attack. The paper sets out why human centred threat models are needed. It aims to strengthen the robustness of AI assisted decision making.
arxiv-2509-21636:
Araki Woods factors are von Neumann algebras built from orthogonal representations, deformed by a setting q. Changying Ding and Hui Tan prove form results for the q deformed family in a 2025 paper. Strong solidity is the first property: a strong restriction on how subalgebras can sit inside. The representation is assumed almost periodic and strongly non stop. Results cover the full range of the deformation setting.

Non isomorphism is the second theme. For nonzero q, these factors are not isomorphic to any free Araki Woods factor under stated settings. A nontrivial weakly mixing part, or an infinite dimensional almost periodic part with bounded spectrum, suffices. Such results separate operator algebra families that look similar by construction. The paper advances the sorting programme for these factors.
arxiv-2509-21836:
Ben Abramowitz and Nicholas Mattei ask how decisions should be made and judged when people care about more than the outcome. People also care about how a choice was reached. Their 2025 paper, Axiomatic Choice, builds a framework where formal statements, called axioms, state what a good decision must respect. Such statements can carry ethical limits, not just efficiency goals.

Working inside that frame, the authors define the key properties an axiom can have. They sort axioms into a taxonomy meant to be useful beyond this one paper. They then define a puzzle they call the Decision-Evaluation Paradox. The paper also gives precise meanings to openness and deception when a decision is explained. Finally, it shows the limits of current methods that use axioms to drive choices.
arxiv-2509-21936:
O. Duranthon, P. Marion, C. Boyer, B. Loureiro, and L. Zdeborová study why the softmax attention used in language models works so well. Many theories simplify attention to a linear form, which is easier to analyze but weaker. Their 2025 paper, accepted at ICLR 2026, takes on the real softmax in a clean task: predicting an output that depends on one input token at a random position.

Using tools from statistical physics, the authors describe performance in the high-dimensional limit with a few summary quantities. At the population level, softmax reaches the best possible risk, while linear attention falls short by a fixed gap. They then test other activation shapes to find which properties matter for that success. With limited data, softmax is no longer perfect, but it still beats linear attention throughout. The paper also links the findings to training by gradient methods.
arxiv-2509-22236:
Safety-critical control systems, like those in aircraft, read several redundant sensors and must pick which inputs to trust. Arif Ali AP, Jasine Babu, and Deepa Sara John design the voting unit for that job in this 2025 paper. A voter selects a reliable input from the redundant sources, guided by rules that detect and isolate faulty units. Their work covers the full path: formal requirements, design, verification, and synthesis of a generic voter for a measurement system with any number of redundant channels.

The approach is correct by construction, carried out with the Rocq theorem prover. Instead of testing a finished design for errors, the team builds the design inside a proof environment, so the verified properties hold by the way it was made. The voter is generic rather than tied to one aircraft system, since the redundancy count is a parameter.
arxiv-2509-22436:
What makes a neural ordinary differential equation train well? Tianxiang Gao and 3 co-authors point to the activation function. These models treat a network as a continuous flow, which saves parameters but complicates training. Gradient accuracy and convergence guarantees have lagged behind practice. The team studies how smooth, nonlinear activations shape the training dynamics.

Smooth activations ensure the forward and backward equations each have one solution. Enough nonlinearity keeps the neural tangent kernel stable during training. Together, these traits yield global convergence under gradient descent for wide models. Numerical tests backed the theory. The results give practical guidance for scaling these models.
arxiv-2509-22836:
