Roie Kazoom and 3 co-authors generate adversarial patches that fool image classifiers while looking natural. A patch is a small image region crafted to force a chosen misclassification. Past attacks assumed full model access, lacked a target class, or looked conspicuous. Their framework lets the attacker pick both the input image and the exact target class. A generative U-Net builds the patch, and Grad-CAM guidance places it where the model looks most.

Tests spanned convolutional networks and vision transformers. Attack success and target-class success both ran above ninety-nine percent across settings. The method beat prior white-box and untargeted attacks while keeping patches realistic. It also worked in black-box conditions, a rare combination.
arxiv-2509-22936:
Renewable power makes grid flows less sure, yet grid physics stays nonlinear and hard. Ghulam Mohy-ud-din and 3 co-authors build a stochastic power flow model with safety limits. Chance constraints cap how often limits may be crossed, rather than banning all crossings. Their tool, general polynomial chaos expansion, tracks uncertainty of almost any shape.

The model keeps the full AC power flow equations, not a simplified form. Case studies show it holds operating limits well and tracks uncertainty closely. Next to a fixed-value version, it found more unsafe backup cases. That wider view gives operators better insight into weak spots. The authors frame it as a tool for secure daily operation.
arxiv-2509-23036:
Disorder in one dimension is supposed to trap every quantum state in place. Work by Junmo Jeon, Harukuni Ikeda, and Shiro Sakai shows a way around that rule. Their disorder is hyperuniform, meaning long-wave swings are suppressed. Such a pattern sits between random and periodic. In tight-binding chains, strong hyperuniformity triggers a sharp shift to free-moving states.

Mobility edges appear, which split trapped states from free ones by energy. The team confirm the shift with a fractal dimension measure. Scaling of localization length and transmittance back the same story. Hyperuniform disorder thus gives a general knob for transport control in low dimensions.
arxiv-2509-23236:
Vision-language models invent objects that are not there, and fixing that usually needs costly labels. Mingfei Han and 7 co-authors use the model's own consistency as the teacher instead. Short binary questions draw highly reliable answers from the same model. Long, detailed answers can then be ranked against those short checks. Mismatches become preference pairs for training.

No human annotation or stronger outside model is needed. Benchmarks for object hallucination showed clear gains in factual grounding. Instruction following held up on other test sets. The method scales because it runs on unlabeled data. Self-reflection, the team argue, is a free lunch here.
arxiv-2509-23436:
Long inputs make standard transformer attention costly, since its work grows with the square of the length. Ashkan Shahbazi and 5 co-authors propose LOTFormer, a faster attention scheme built on optimal transport, the math of matching two sets with least waste. Most fast attention only balances each row, so a few tokens can take most of the weight. LOTFormer balances rows and columns at once.

The scheme routes queries and keys through a small learned pivot set, which keeps the plan low-rank and provably balanced. Its cost grows in a straight line with length, and no full attention matrix is ever built. Plugged into Swin, DeiT, and BERT backbones, it gave a strong mix of accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2509-23536:
Finding groups in a network usually starts by guessing how many groups exist. Yuhua Zhang and 3 co-authors avoid that guess with recursive partitioning inside a Bayesian framework. Their method splits the network step by step, so it also reveals layered structure. It fits many existing model-based community detection setups rather than replacing them.

The authors prove consistency under the stochastic block model. Simulations across varied settings show the method works well in practice. They then apply it to California hospital data covering emergency and discharge records from hundreds of hospitals. The result maps regional hospital clusters, which can inform how care regions are drawn.
arxiv-2509-24036:
Fatma Almaz and Handan Oztekin study curves that flow without stretching in a four-dimensional pseudo-Galilean space. Such a space bends the usual rules for distance and angle, so curve theory needs its own frame and formulas. The pair state when these unstretched flows can occur, as equations that link change over time and along the curve.

They also define directional derivatives that fit the frame used in this space and extend its standard relations. The work then turns to bending elastic energy, the cost of curving the path. Energy formulas are given for a particle that moves with the curve. The results add basic tools for geometry in this unusual space.
arxiv-2509-24436:
Yingshi Chen presents an evolutionary framework for training large language models. The model is split into several experts, sub-networks with the same structure but different values. Only one expert trains at each step with the standard optimizer. Then evolutionary moves, crossover, particle swarm steps, and mutation, pull the current expert toward the best expert yet.

The current expert thus learns from the best one's experience, and its loss falls faster. At the end, only the best expert's weights are kept, which greatly shrinks the model for inference. Training also needs much less memory and runs far faster in throughput, Chen reports. The framework is written in C++ and CUDA for easy deployment.
arxiv-2509-24536:
Heavy elements are forged in stars, and the beta-decay rates of waiting-point nuclei set the pace of that forging. Qi-Ye Hu and 2 co-authors compute effective decay rates for the classic waiting points at neutron numbers fifty, eighty-two, and one hundred twenty-six. They work in realistic stellar settings with high temperature, high density, and strong magnetic fields, counting both allowed and first-forbidden transitions and heat-populated states.

Rates for the first two waiting points barely move with temperature, while the third climbs fast. Higher density slows the decays, and very strong fields speed them sharply. Rates can swing by orders of magnitude with conditions, so fixed rates mislead.
arxiv-2509-25636:
Quark-gluon plasma is the hot soup of particles that filled the early universe, and theory predicts a critical end point in its phase map. Yi-Ping Si and co-authors use a holographic model of the plasma in this 2025 paper, tuned with machine learning, to study two signals near that point.

Both the plasma's electric conductivity and its rate of thermal light emission rise most steeply near the change temperature, matching earlier work and, at one setting, lattice calculations. Sharper still, the temperature slopes of both quantities blow up at the critical end point itself. Such spikes could serve as fingerprints when experiments hunt for the point.
arxiv-2509-26436:
Donghoon Kim and co-authors present QuaRTZ in a 2025 paper on compressing diffusion models after training. Such models generate high quality images but cost much compute. Eight bit quantization matches full precision, yet four bit settings lose fine texture because rounding errors grow in dense, small activations.

Their scheme first quantizes at eight bits to handle outliers, then compresses to four bits by suppressing leading zeros, preserving low order bits that carry texture. Theory and tests support the method across activation patterns. On a fast image model, four bit QuaRTZ beat a rival that needed extra full precision branches.
arxiv-2510-00636:
Devoto, Jeblick, and Jégou at Sapienza University of Rome and NVIDIA introduce Expected Attention in this 2025 arXiv paper on efficient language model inference. A model's key-value cache grows with every token and quickly becomes the main memory bottleneck for long contexts. Pruning unimportant cache entries helps, but the natural importance signal, attention from future tokens, does not exist yet when pruning must happen. Fast attention kernels also hide past attention scores from the pruning code.

Expected Attention estimates those future attention scores in closed form, using statistical properties of the model's activations. Each cache pair then gets a principled importance ranking before eviction. The training-free method works during both prefilling and decoding phases. Across benchmarks it beat leading compression baselines in both phases, and the authors release KVPress, a library bundling over twenty compression techniques.
arxiv-2510-00936:
Liu and four co-authors fix cross-resolution person re-identification by panning feature vectors in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer vision. Surveillance cameras sit at different distances, so the pedestrian appears at different resolutions, and matching low-resolution to high-resolution images breaks re-identification. Prior fixes lean on super-resolution or feature compensation, which add machinery and have hit a performance ceiling. The authors borrow an idea from word embeddings, where semantic differences appear as directions in vector space.

They show, with canonical correlation and Pearson analyses, that resolution difference is a direction in ReID feature space. Their VPFA framework models that direction and pans low-resolution features along it toward their high-resolution counterparts. On multiple benchmarks the method beat state-of-the-art systems. It is also lighter and faster than super-resolution pipelines. The finding reframes a stubborn matching problem as simple geometry.
arxiv-2510-01036:
Kankanala develops a generalized Bayes framework for conditional moment restriction models in this 2025 arXiv paper on econometrics. Economists use such models when an unknown structural function must satisfy moment conditions given instruments, as in demand estimation or production functions. The function is nonparametric and the problem is an ill-posed inverse problem, so standard Bayesian theory does not apply directly. Kankanala studies a quasi-Bayes posterior built from Gaussian process priors.

He establishes contraction rates for that posterior and gives conditions for a Bernstein-von Mises theorem, which links Bayesian credible sets to frequentist confidence sets. With optimal weighting, the credible sets achieve exact asymptotic frequentist coverage, extending classic parametric GMM results. An application estimates firm-level production functions from Chilean plant-level data. Simulations show the generalized Bayes estimators comparing favourably with common alternatives.
arxiv-2510-01236:
Swapnil and co-authors teach a vision-language model to reason about skin disease the way a dermatologist does, on a shoestring budget. Medical image models need structured reasoning, but data and compute are scarce in this specialty. Their model, DermIQ-VLM, trains in stages designed for low-resource settings.

A stabilized reinforcement method, GRPO++, first builds diagnostic reasoning efficiently. Supervised tuning adds conversational skill, and preference alignment then corrects factual slips. A knowledge graph stands in for expensive expert preferences during that alignment. Early tests on curated skin data beat standard fine-tuning by a clear margin. Memory efficiency is the headline change inside GRPO++. Knowledge-graph retrieval grounds the conversation in verified dermatology facts. Staged pipelines let each phase fix the previous phase's weaknesses. Low-resource clinics are the intended beneficiaries, not an afterthought. Specialist-grade reasoning need not require specialist-grade budgets to build.
arxiv-2510-01336:
Kumar, Sanghavi, and Das attack the slow half of speculative decoding, the verification step everyone else ignored. A small model drafts tokens quickly, but the big model takes far longer to check them than the drafting saved. Their framework, HiSpec, inserts an intermediate verifier along the way.

Early-exit models, trained to answer from middle layers, are natural intermediate checkers. Bad draft tokens die early instead of consuming full verification. The design reuses caches and hidden states between stages to keep memory lean. Unlike earlier intermediate schemes, no heavy extra training or fragile heuristics are required. Verification can run four times slower than drafting in the motivating example. Early exits skip layer traversal, which is where the savings live. Hidden-state interpretability comes from how early-exit models are trained. Throughput, not just latency, is the target metric for serving.
arxiv-2510-01436:
Du and Kauers reverse a standard construction for differential equations: given a combined operator and one factor, they characterize what the other factor can be. The symmetric product of two operators governs products of their solutions, and computing it forward is routine. Division, recovering a factor, had no comparable theory.

Degree bounds from Newton polygon geometry fence in the possible quotients. A worked example solves a linear system to recover the quotient exactly. The authors prove the procedure finds the global quasi-symmetric quotient. Computer algebra gains the missing inverse operation for a classical construction. Rational-function coefficients keep the operators concrete and computable. Formal series expansions supply the computational playground. Possible slopes read directly off the exponential parts of solutions. Forward products are classical; the inverse direction is the contribution. Symbolic computation gains a genuine division algorithm at last.
arxiv-2510-01536:
Heydari, Bessani, and Nayak design a ledger protocol for the awkward middle scale of a few hundred to a thousand machines. Classic protocols drown mid-size networks in messages, while committee-sampling designs only work with huge populations. Production systems such as Redbelly and Sui live exactly in that neglected middle.

Their protocol, QScale, chains blocks through a leader while sampling keeps each machine's chatter low. Expected traffic per machine grows with the square root of the network size, not the size itself. Best-case finality takes only a handful of rounds. Safety and liveness hold with overwhelming probability under both calm and partly delayed networks. Randomness does the heavy lifting, since sampling spreads trust without flooding the network. Moderate scale is where many real consortium ledgers actually operate. Low latency matters because users abandon slow chains. The analysis covers both timing models.
arxiv-2510-01736:
Gjerver and seven co-authors show how to make engineering standards readable by machines in this 2025 paper. Design standards for piping, materials, and valves still live mainly as long documents and tables. Engineers must hunt through them by hand during plant design. The authors convert that text into modular ontologies, which are structured webs of concepts and rules.

Their modules follow shared modelling patterns and align with an international industrial data ontology. Stored in a W3C-compliant format, the modules can be reused and exchanged between tools. The team tested the approach on a valve selection process for a process plant. Valves and their working conditions became entries in a semantic asset model. Automated reasoning then checked each valve data sheet against the standards. It also judged whether a manufacturer's product type truly met the given specification.
arxiv-2510-01836:
Iso and six co-authors build a new instrument for quantum spectroscopy in this 2025 optics paper. Entangled photon pairs, called biphotons, can probe molecules with linked time and frequency information. Measuring their joint spectrum across distant colors is technically hard. The team combines two very different single-photon spectrographs into one hybrid system.

A fiber spectrograph handles the near-infrared photon of each pair. A delay-line-anode imager captures the visible partner without any scanning motion. Time-tagging every detection lets the system assemble the full joint spectral intensity. The setup also resolves how that spectrum evolves, with timing near one hundred fifty picoseconds. That speed opens dynamic studies of molecules using entangled light. The work bridges pure biphoton sources for communication and the time-resolved needs of spectroscopy.
arxiv-2510-02436:
Schib and co-authors present DIPSY, a global model of companions born by disc fragmentation. Their 2025 astronomy paper is the methods companion to a population study. Disc instability fragments a young gas disc into clumps. Those clumps may grow into planets, brown dwarfs, or small stars. Modeling the full story has challenged earlier codes. DIPSY starts with infall from a molecular cloud core. It follows star and disc growth together in one frame. Fragmentation, clump evolution, and clump interactions all run inside the model. Discs stay round while clumps move in full three dimensional dynamics.

The code unites physical effects never linked self consistently before. Gas accretion and orbital migration of companions are included. A wide parameter space opens for systematic exploration. Earlier precursor studies tested pieces of the machinery. Its predictions can face observations directly. Companion formation theory gains a shared workbench.
arxiv-2510-02736:
Gulati and co-authors survey low frequency radio glow from a sample of eighty seven quasars. Their 2025 astronomy paper uses the upgraded GMRT array in India. The Palomar Green quasars all sit at modest redshifts. Observations ran at six hundred eighty five megahertz. Radio emission appeared in all but three sources. The loud versus quiet split survived at this frequency. Only one quasar changed sides under the new data. About a third of the quiet quasars showed active nucleus radio output. The rest likely mix in star related emission.

Loud and quiet quasars occupied separate tracks on the black hole activity plane. A luminosity gap divided the two families. Quiet sources stayed compact, mostly under thirty kiloparsecs. Some loud quasars showed bent or restarted jets. Leftover diffuse glow hinted at past activity episodes. Low frequencies reveal plasma that higher bands miss. The loud quiet divide looks intrinsic, not observational.
arxiv-2510-02836:
Ppali and co-authors ask whether virtual reality can serve as a quick well-being break at work. Many past tools focused on one fixed activity. Knowledge workers, though, have mixed physical and mental needs. The team built an app called Tranquil Loom. It offers stretching, guided meditation, and free exploration. Users can visit a forest, a beach, snowy scenes, or an abstract space. An AI helper suggests activities based on mood.

The study ran in two phases. Interviews with ten workers shaped the design. Then thirty-five people used the app in daily work. Mindfulness rose after use, and anxiety fell. People liked both the guided and the open options. Many used the app in playful, unplanned ways. The AI suggestions were rarely picked, but they sparked ideas. Workers saw VR as a flexible drop-in tool. They preferred it on their own terms, not as a fixed prescription.
arxiv-2510-03336:
Devahi and a large team present a 2025 arXiv paper on spotting Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive decline from speech. Current diagnosis leans on costly, invasive tests, while speech is cheap to record. The team entered the PROCESS Challenge, which asks models to sort speakers into healthy, mildly impaired, and dementia groups. Their features came from picture description and fluency tasks that patients already perform in clinics.

One feature set measured word use, sentence shape, and filler words in transcripts. Another set used Whisper audio embeddings that capture how speech sounds. An ensemble trained on the word features gave the best sorting of the three groups. Audio based models instead gave the sharpest estimates of standard mental test scores. The two views of speech thus proved to carry different, matching strengths. Cheap speech checks could one day flag patients early, at home or in small clinics.
arxiv-2510-03436:
Emran presents a 2025 paper, published in Icarus, that compares two ways of reading Europa's surface mix from reflected light. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, hides an ocean under ice laced with sulfuric acid compounds. Lab spectra of water ice mixed with a sulfuric acid hydrate give a test bed. One method blends spectra in simple linear shares. The other uses radiative transfer physics for grains mixed at small scales, like salt and pepper.

The physics based method reproduced the lab shares more closely, missing by about five percent or less for the test grains. The linear method missed by roughly five to fifteen percent across the mixtures. Both methods overestimated the acid share and underestimated ice, a bias users should remember. When acid dominated or barely appeared, both methods landed within about ten percent. Europa watchers should favor the physics method, while keeping the simpler one for extreme mixes.
arxiv-2510-03536:
Meng and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on helping language models reason through multi turn medical dialogues. In real consultations, key facts scatter across many exchanges, and models that ace single questions often lose the thread. Their system, TriMediQ, turns each patient answer into triplets of the form subject, relation, object. Those triplets build a patient specific knowledge graph. A small trainable projector then feeds graph structure into a frozen language model at answer time.

On two interactive medical question benchmarks, the method beat five rival systems. Its best gain reached about ten percent in accuracy over a medical dialogue method with a large backbone in the reported runs. Smaller models gained strongly too, which matters for cost. Because the base model stays frozen, clinics can adopt the add on without retraining their whole stack. Explicit graphs also leave an audit trail for why the model reached its answer.
arxiv-2510-04036:
Tapia presents this 2025 arXiv paper on a compact muon detector built to work down a borehole. Muons rain from the sky and pass through rock, so counting them from underground reveals the density of material above. That imaging trick, muon tomography, needs detectors slim and rugged enough for drilled holes. Earlier designs relied on long scintillator bars and wavelength-shifting fibers, which complicate the build.

The new detector couples silicon photomultipliers directly onto small scintillator tiles, removing the fibers entirely. A modular unit packs sixty-four channels into a tube about one hundred forty centimeters long and eighty millimeters wide. It detects muons with efficiency above ninety-five percent across a wide range of incoming angles. Simulations combining hit positions and energy deposits reconstruct direction with a resolution of a few degrees. Tapia argues it offers a cheaper, tougher route to imaging mines, tunnels, and geological structures.
arxiv-2510-04136:
Cappellazzo and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on speech recognition that watches lips as well as listening, at adjustable cost. Audio-visual recognition helps in noise, but language-model-based systems are expensive. Token compression cuts cost only at a fixed rate chosen before deployment. Matryoshka representation learning allows multiple granularities in one model, yet trains each scale independently, wasting cross-scale synergy.

Their framework, MoME, fuses sparse mixture-of-experts routing with Matryoshka representations inside a frozen language model. Top-k routed experts plus shared experts allocate capacity dynamically across scales and modalities. A shared router keeps expert activation consistent between granularities, so compressed sequences inherit knowledge from richer ones. On the LRS2 and LRS3 benchmarks, MoME reached state-of-the-art results across audio-visual, audio-only, and visual-only recognition. Flexible inference-time compression suits deployment on devices with varying budgets.
arxiv-2510-04236:
Liu and colleagues at Meta AI present this 2025 arXiv paper introducing Kaleido, a generative model family that treats 3D rendering as video-style sequence synthesis. Neural rendering has been fragmented across explicit representations like voxels and point clouds, each needing scarce camera-labeled data. Kaleido instead frames view synthesis as a sequence-to-sequence image task. A masked autoregressive design generates any number of target views from any number of reference views, with six-degree-of-freedom camera poses.

A single decoder-only rectified flow transformer unifies 3D and video modeling in one architecture. Kaleido set new state-of-the-art results across view synthesis benchmarks. In few-view settings its zero-shot output substantially beat other generative methods. In many-view settings it matched per-scene optimization quality without any per-scene fitting, a first for generative renderers. Remaining artifacts include texture flickering in high-frequency scenes.
arxiv-2510-04936:
Abigail Hickok and Andrew J. Blumberg work on geometry for data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Curvature describes how a smooth shape bends at each point. Real data, though, often comes as point clouds or graphs, not smooth shapes. The authors ask how two discrete notions of curvature relate on such data.

One notion, Ollivier-Ricci curvature, is defined for edges of a graph. The other is a scalar version built from it, in analogy with smooth geometry. They define the scalar quantity as a weighted sum of the edge curvatures. They then prove it converges to true scalar curvature for nearest-neighbor graphs sampled from a manifold. The work also sharpens known convergence results for the edge notion itself.
arxiv-2510-05236:
James B. Dent, Bhaskar Dutta, and Mudit Rai build a unified theory of black holes born in the infant universe in this 2025 arXiv paper. Primordial black holes could form when first-order phase transitions reshaped the early cosmos. Older accounts leaned on pressure balance or overdensity arguments. The authors instead use Israel junction conditions to track the collapse.

Their framework handles general mixtures of vacuum, radiation, and matter energy inside the bubbles. One application shows exotic Fermi-balls collapsing into black holes even with energy trapped in solitonic cores. Another links multiple hidden-sector transitions to correlated gravitational-wave spectra. The paper maps the resulting black hole mass spectra and dark matter fractions. Several promising parameter regions remain open to current searches.
arxiv-2510-05436:
Wijk and colleagues work on keeping machines safe when their controls have hard limits. Robots and aircraft can only push so hard, since motors and engines have fixed strength. A safety method called backup control barrier functions can guarantee safe behavior within those limits. The catch is speed, since the method solves a hard math problem at every moment.

The authors blend two controllers, a normal one and a verified backup one. Their blend is chosen in the best possible way, and they solve it with a direct formula. They prove the blended controller stays safe and respects the input limits. Tests cover a simple double integrator and a fixed-wing aircraft that must stay inside a fence. The formula beat hand-tuned blending and suits aircraft with weak onboard computers. Future work will run the method on real flight hardware.
arxiv-2510-05636:
Zhou and colleagues map a stubborn nonlinear effect inside silicon nitride microresonators. Photo-induced second-harmonic generation doubles light frequency inside these tiny rings. Textbook wisdom says it needs both harmonics parked exactly on resonances. Their 2025 experiments show it surviving far from that sweet spot.

A pump-probe technique gives enhanced spectral maps of the conversion dynamics. The team pushed pump power high to stretch the thermal tuning range. Generation persisted into a highly detuned state with the harmonic shifted off resonance. That persistence yields an unconventionally broad conversion bandwidth. They also captured detuning-dependent all-optical poling with direct evidence. Nonlinear multi-mode interactions appeared in the maps as well. Efficiency still favors the doubly resonant condition at the thermal triangle's edge. Smaller high-finesse resonators or coupled rings could raise efficiency further. The results open wider bandwidths for integrated second-order photonics.
arxiv-2510-06036:
Yin and co-authors investigate why reasoning models fail to refuse harmful requests in a 2025 study. These models think step by step before answering, and their guardrails often look weaker than those of chat models. The team used linear probes to track refusal intent inside the models as each token was produced.

The probes reveal a pattern the authors call the refusal cliff. Many models spot a harmful prompt and hold a refusal intent through most of their thinking. That intent then collapses in the final tokens, before the answer appears. A small set of attention heads causes the collapse, and switching off about 3 percent of them cut attack success below 10 percent in their tests. Their repair method trains only on the worst cliff cases, matching safety gains with under 2 percent of the usual data.
arxiv-2510-06136:
Wang and Smith of the University of Kentucky ask which hidden geometry explains a network in a 2025 statistics paper. Latent space models place nodes in an unseen space where nearby nodes link more often. Flat Euclidean space is the default choice, yet hyperbolic space often matches real networks better.

Analysts embed shortest-path distances with multidimensional scaling and pick the lower-stress geometry. That comparison ignores sampling uncertainty, so close calls are hard to trust. The authors extend permutation-based hypothesis tests from scaling analysis to network data. They also build a parametric bootstrap generating networks conditioned on observed distances under a Gaussian latent position model. The construction extends the Davidson–MacKinnon J-test to rival latent geometries. In simulations, both improved detection of the true geometry. The gains matter most for large, sparse networks, where naive stress comparisons mislead most easily.
arxiv-2510-06336:
Magalhães Junior, Mezabarba, and Monteiro study the convergence structure every graph carries naturally in a 2025 combinatorics paper. A closure operator extends sets, respects inclusion, and preserves unions. Each graph defines one by adding to any vertex set all its neighbors.

Since closure operators match pretopological spaces, this induces a canonical convergence structure on the vertices. The authors describe that convergence in terms of nets. They relate combinatorial graph properties to convergence-theoretic ones. Ordinary graph features thereby acquire topological meaning. Convergence becomes a statement about neighborhoods and adjacency rather than distances. The work builds a two-way dictionary between graph theory and convergence theory. Each closure step grows a set by exactly one neighborhood layer. Such dictionaries let each field import the other's theorems. It gives students a tangible entry point into abstract convergence spaces.
arxiv-2510-06536:
Jordan Thomas and eight co-authors work on sending quantum signals through ordinary fiber optic cables. Their 2025 paper studies entangled photons, which are pairs of light particles linked in a quantum way. The team sends these photons through the same long fibers that carry fast classical internet data. The hard part is filtering out noise without losing too many of the fragile photon pairs.

In their setup, entangled photons travel alongside 10-gigabit classical data over two 25-kilometer fiber spans. Narrow filters let them raise the classical power to milliwatt levels while keeping the quantum signal usable. The photons sit at a wavelength that suits erbium-based quantum memories. The team finds a trade-off between blocking noise and keeping single-mode purity. Their analysis shows how filter shape, pump power, and pulse width jointly set the final fidelity.
arxiv-2510-07136:
Seif, Koskela, Poor, and Goldsmith study how to group network data without exposing private links. Their 2025 paper joins graph clustering with differential privacy. Spectral clustering groups nodes by the pattern of their connections. In a social network, each link can reveal a sensitive tie. The authors design three ways to hide single links while keeping the groups useful. They weigh privacy, accuracy, and cost 

One method flips some edges at random and then shuffles the network, which greatly strengthens the privacy promise. A second method projects the graph into a smaller space and adds noise there. A third spreads noise across the steps of an iterative solver. The team proves error bounds for how often nodes land in the wrong group. Tests on fake and real networks matched the theory. The results help analysts mine network data.
arxiv-2510-07236:
Jiang, Qu, and Ding catalog the patterns of zeros that an exotic symmetry can force into neutrino mass tables. Their 2025 paper works in the minimal seesaw model, a leading account of why neutrinos are so light. The authors derive them from non-invertible symmetry rules, a modern generalization of symmetry in physics. A doubled version of a cyclic symmetry does the forcing in their construction.

The team lists every possible zero pattern for the four key matrices in the model. They study in depth the patterns with the most zeros and the next tier down. Those sparse patterns still fit the observed pattern of neutrino mixing. The paper connects the surviving patterns to open questions, like the ordering of neutrino masses. Such catalogs help theorists pick models that experiments can actually test.
arxiv-2510-07336:
Randino and co-authors build data-driven models of wind turbines that work both alone and in each other's wakes. Their 2025 paper addresses a control problem. A turbine's power depends on wind speed, rotor speed, and the churned air arriving from upstream machines. Fixed textbook models miss those wake effects. The team fits power maps from data, blending local radial basis bumps with smooth polynomial trends. The maps plug into a simple dynamic model fit for real-time control design.

Wind tunnel tests covered a calm two-turbine line and a turbulent farm mock-up. In the tandem case, a standard rotor controller using the fitted model tracked target rotor speeds better. Power output also held steadier than with textbook or static models. Interpretable models like these let operators squeeze steadier power from farms.
arxiv-2510-07436:
Naskar, Thoppe, Negi, and Gupta remove the guesswork from federated reinforcement learning with temporally correlated data. Their 2025 paper studies temporal-difference learning shared across many agents. Federation promises a speedup proportional to the agent count. Samples from a Markov chain break the independence that classic proofs assume, though. Existing fixes for that problem tune step sizes using unknown quantities like mixing times, which no practitioner actually knows. The team's two-timescale federated method adds Polyak-Ruppert averaging, a running average of iterates that stabilizes the estimate without any problem-specific tuning.

The method provably reaches the optimal convergence rate in both average-reward and discounted settings. Agents may live in different environments and update asynchronously, as real federated systems do. The result is new even for a single agent learning alone.
arxiv-2510-07836:
Wu, Yan, An, and Deng wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on light tetraquark states, particles built from four quarks. Ordinary mesons hold two quarks, so four-quark states test how the strong force binds matter. The authors compute the masses of light states in a non-relativistic quark model. They include pseudoscalar meson exchange. An instanton-induced interaction supplies the spin-dependent part of the force.

Two confinement schemes, the Cornell potential and a linear one, let them check robustness. The computed spectrum lines up with a list of known mesons, from the f0 and a0 families to strange partners. Those matches suggest many observed light mesons may carry tetraquark structure. The authors present the spectrum as guidance for searches. Experiments can target the predicted states and masses to settle which mesons are exotic. The work adds theoretical weight to four-quark interpretations of the meson zoo.
arxiv-2510-07936:
Heintz and a large collaboration wrote this 2025 paper on dust in a galaxy from the young universe. The galaxy, A1689-zD1, sits at redshift just past seven and is magnified by a foreground cluster. Early galaxies have surprised astronomers with how much dust they already hold. This team combined Webb telescope spectroscopy with ALMA observations for an accounting. The galaxy is massive, metal-rich, and loaded with gas.

Despite a large dust mass, its dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios came out about ten times lower than in similar local galaxies. Other metal-rich galaxies at similar redshifts show the same shortfall. The pattern suggests early dust production was inefficient at turning metals into grains. That runs against the expectation that metal-rich gas grows dust faster. The authors call for tracking how the dust-to-metal ratio evolves as the universe ages.
arxiv-2510-08236:
Konrad Löhr, Shuzhou Yuan, and Michael Färber test political bias in chatbots in a 2025 arXiv study. Large language models now shape how many people get news and advice. Hidden leanings in these tools could sway public views and votes. The team used the Political Compass Test, a quiz that places views on two axes, to probe eight well-known models.

All eight models leaned left on the quiz, the authors report. They then gave the models personas, such as age or job, to draw out open stereotypes. They also used quiz versions in other languages to surface hidden stereotypes. Hidden stereotypes, triggered by language choice, proved stronger than the open ones from personas. For most models, the hidden and open patterns matched closely. The authors say this match suggests models reflect their leanings in fairly consistent ways.
arxiv-2510-08536:
Gregor Olenik, Marcel Koch, and Hartwig Anzt rebalance fluid dynamics workloads between processors and graphics cards in a 2025 arXiv paper. OpenFOAM is a widely used open-source toolkit for computational fluid dynamics. Plugin GPU solvers speed its linear algebra, but the CPU still assembles the matrices. When GPUs finish too fast or sit idle, oversubscription and undersubscription waste resources.

The team proposes repartitioning the matrices to better balance CPU assembly against GPU solves. They present a detailed computational model of the split and a novel repartitioning and update procedure. Large-scale CFD simulations evaluated the strategy in practice. The method significantly mitigated the subscription imbalance, they report. Solver performance and resource utilization both improved in heterogeneous CPU-GPU environments. The approach keeps the plugin design, avoiding a full rewrite of the OpenFOAM codebase.
arxiv-2510-08836:
Lin and Yuan tackle a bias that creeps in when some categories vastly outnumber others, in this 2025 arXiv paper on image classification. Real datasets are long-tailed: a few common classes supply most examples, while many rare classes have only a handful. Models trained on such data lean toward the frequent classes and fumble the rare ones. Fixes that simply rebalance the data often throw away useful information.

Their two-stage method guards the information while removing the lean. The first stage learns features using an information-theory argument that, in effect, pulls examples of each class tightly together. The second stage picks training examples by how much they teach, which straightens the skewed decision boundaries between classes. Overall accuracy stays intact while rare classes gain. Across several standard long-tailed benchmarks, the approach set new best results.
arxiv-2510-09136:
Holzleitner and colleagues test a compromise between editors and algorithms at a major Norwegian news outlet, in this 2025 arXiv industry paper. Big aggregators personalize news fully by machine, but legacy outlets guard editorial values and move cautiously. The outlet's site therefore mixes editor-chosen stories with algorithmically selected ones, a strategy the authors call controlled personalization. They evaluated it with a live A/B test, the standard split of visitors into two versions.

Even the modest personalization in the test paid off clearly. Readers shown personalized selections clicked through more often and spent less effort navigating, which suggests the system surfaced relevant stories faster. The personalized mix also widened the diversity of content readers saw and spread attention across more of the catalog. Popularity bias, the rich-get-richer pull toward already popular stories, shrank. The authors conclude that controlled personalization can serve readers and editorial goals at once.
arxiv-2510-09636:
Prarthana Kartholy, Thandi Labor, Neil Panchal, Sean Wang, and Hillary Owusu test an AI advising chatbot for engineering students in a 2025 arXiv paper. Choosing a college major is hard, and traditional advising suffers long waits, intimidating settings, and little personalisation. Chatbots could help, but they can also produce biased answers tied to race, gender, income, or disability, which risks driving students away.

The team built a programme-specific chatbot for the A James Clark School of Engineering at the University of Maryland. They probed it with diverse student queries and scored replies on accuracy, relevance, personalisation, and bias. Mean scores topped nine point five out of ten on the first three measures, and no stereotypical bias appeared. The authors note the small sample and short timeframe limit the conclusions. Even so, they offer the work as guidance for building ethical advising tools that complement human advisors.
arxiv-2510-09736:
Antonio Martínez-Ibarra, Aurora González-Vidal, Adrián Cánovas-Rodríguez, and Antonio Skarmeta map algae in a troubled Spanish lagoon in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Mar Menor is Europe's largest hypersaline coastal lagoon, and severe eutrophication crises have devastated its biodiversity and water quality. Chlorophyll-a signals phytoplankton biomass, so tracking it helps anticipate harmful blooms.

Boat measurements are precise but sparse, so the team turns to Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, corrected with a processor designed for coastal waters. Buoy measurements, aggregated by depth, supply the ground truth for training several machine learning algorithms, including gradient boosting and neural networks, tuned with cross-validation and multi-objective optimisation. Performance depended on depth, with logarithmic error scores starting near zero point three four. The goal is high-resolution, depth-specific maps across the water column, strengthening early warning for eutrophication beyond surface-only estimates.
arxiv-2510-09936:
Aulakh, Nils D. Forkert, and Matthias Wilms model brain change over time in this 2025 arXiv paper on neuroimaging. Brains change structurally across a life, and disease can bend that path. Repeated MRI scans capture the change, but each person's scans come at uneven times and resolutions.

The authors build semi-disentangled spatiotemporal implicit neural representations, models that store a brain's trajectory as a continuous function of space and time. Semi-disentangled means the model partly separates what a brain looks like from how it changes. These representations feed trajectory classification, sorting people by the path their brain follows. The method is designed for the messy sampling of real longitudinal studies, where visits rarely line up across patients.
arxiv-2510-10036:
Pang, Tian, Zhang, and Jiang compute fermionic Love numbers of charged black holes in this 2025 arXiv paper in general relativity. Love numbers measure how much a compact object deforms under a tidal pull, revealing its internal structure. For black holes, the numbers for bosonic fields vanish in general relativity.

Fermionic fields, tied to matter particles like electrons, behave differently: recent work showed they can give Kerr black holes nonzero Love numbers. The authors extend that question to Reissner-Nordström black holes, which carry electric charge but do not spin. A nonzero fermionic Love number would sharpen the contrast between black holes and material stars. It also tests how universal the vanishing theorem really is.
arxiv-2510-10236:
Dhrumil Bhatt, Siddharth Penumatsa, and Vidushi Kumar design a hybrid network protocol for drone swarms in this 2025 arXiv paper on wireless communications. Flying ad hoc networks link drones that move fast and change formation often, with tight limits on energy and compute. Existing protocols usually optimize one metric, such as path length or energy.

The authors integrate medium access control with multi-layered security, instead of bolting security onto a finished design. Their protocol weighs performance, security, and MAC-layer efficiency together, since those factors interact in a swarm. Resource-constrained drones cannot afford heavy cryptography or chatty routing. The hybrid design aims to keep swarm communication both efficient and protected under real flight conditions.
arxiv-2510-10636:
Viktoria Brandt and six co-authors measure a chirality sensitive signal from the heaviest organometallic molecule yet studied this way, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The technique is photoelectron circular dichroism, where left and right circularly polarized light knock electrons out of a chiral molecule at different rates. It is a uniquely sensitive probe of chirality and structure. The team studies a camphor based molecule called HFC and its europium complex, Eu-HFC3.

They discuss keto-enol tautomerism, a structural flip between two forms, in both the free molecule and the complex. Modeling such large open shell systems is challenging, and theory often matches experiment poorly for them. Still, the measured asymmetries reached about 8 percent for HFC and about 7 percent for the europium complex, similar in size to those of much smaller chiral molecules. The authors conclude the technique remains practical for large, complicated chiral systems.
arxiv-2510-10936:
Anirudh Ganesh and Jayavardhan Reddy check whether a landmark neural sequence labeling model still reproduces, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The 2016 model by Ma and Hovy combined three parts: convolutional networks for character level features, bidirectional LSTM networks for word level context, and a conditional random field for structured prediction. It removed the need for hand crafted features and set strong results on named entity recognition and part of speech tagging.

The authors reimplemented the architecture in PyTorch and reran the key experiments. Their implementation successfully reproduces the headline results, reaching an F1 score of 91.18 percent on the CoNLL-2003 named entity recognition benchmark in their runs. They analyze the contribution of each architectural component. They also release the implementation as open source. Reproducibility studies like this one anchor a field's shared knowledge: they confirm which reported numbers new work can safely build on, and they give students a verified reference implementation.
arxiv-2510-11136:
Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions in the universe, and their flickering light sometimes hides a near-regular pulse. Mariusz Tarnopolski searched for such quasi-periodic oscillations, rhythms that repeat at nearly steady intervals, in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. He worked with the prompt light curves of long gamma-ray bursts recorded in the Swift/BAT satellite catalog, building on his earlier study with Marchenko.

Using a wavelet-based approach, a method that tracks rhythms changing over time, Tarnopolski searched 1160 long bursts and found 34 new oscillations, the largest uniformly identified sample of burst oscillations to date. Some signals keep one or more constant leading periods, while others chirp, meaning their period drifts. He examined several possible origins for the rhythms. Non-planar orbits around spinning Kerr black holes, the Lense-Thirring effect, and shock oscillations all remain plausible mechanisms for generating them.
arxiv-2510-11436:
Geodetic VLBI sessions use networks of radio telescopes to pin down Earth's orientation and station positions, but many scheduled observations never survive to the final analysis. Tiege McCarthy and Lucia McCallum quantify that loss and its cost in this 2025 arXiv geodesy paper. They examine a decade of the weekly rapid-turnaround IVS-R1 and IVS-R4 sessions, from 2014 to 2023.

Across 1,030 sessions, an average of 25.3 percent of scheduled observations did not make it to analysis, lost to station outages, sensitivity problems, or source effects. The median precision losses relative to the full schedules were about 19 percent for Earth rotation and station positions, and worse for polar motion. Nutation estimates proved particularly robust to the losses. Several parameters suffer critical degradation, a doubling of their error, at loss rates of 15 to 19 percent, below the decade's median loss.
arxiv-2510-11536:
Studying how programmers really work with AI code generators needs fine-grained records collected without disturbing the coding itself. Manaal Basha and co-authors present CodeWatcher, the tool they built for that job, in this 2025 arXiv software engineering paper. The system watches activity inside the Visual Studio Code editor and logs semantically meaningful events rather than raw screen captures.

CodeWatcher logs events such as insertions made by code generation tools, deletions, copy-paste actions, and focus shifts, each structured and time-stamped so a session can be rebuilt later. Architecturally it combines a VS Code plugin, a Python REST API, and a MongoDB database, all containerized. Developers keep normal workflows while researchers gain continuous usage data. The authors position the infrastructure as support for research on responsible AI, developer productivity, and human-centered evaluation of coding assistants.
arxiv-2510-11636:
Engineering simulation on complex 3D geometry is slow: meshing and solving partial differential equations for every design variant eats the design cycle. Peijian Zeng and co-authors present LRQ-Solver, a neural operator framework that learns to solve such equations directly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The target is computer-aided engineering inside CAD-driven workflows for integrated circuit and system design. 

Two ideas carry the design. A physics-consistency module embeds physical constraints into the learning process, and a low-rank attention module cuts the quadratic cost of attention dramatically by decomposing it through covariances. On industrial benchmarks the solver reduced error by about thirty-nine percent on the DrivAerNet++ automotive dataset and about twenty-nine percent on a 3D beam dataset. It trained up to fifty times faster than baselines and handled simulations with two million points on a single graphics card. They release code for interactive design exploration.
arxiv-2510-11736:
Sahaj Raj Malla tests how well different artificial intelligence strategies play Dhumbal, a traditional draw-and-discard card game from Nepal. The game, also called Jhyap, hides each player's cards, so decisions rest on partial information. Malla's 2025 arXiv paper formalizes the rules and builds agents of three kinds. Some follow fixed rules, some search through possible futures, and some learn from experience with neural networks.

The agents first played tournaments within their own kind, then met in a cross-category championship. Across one thousand twenty-four simulated rounds, a simple rule-based agent with an aggressive style won about eighty-eight percent of its games. It exploited the game's Jhyap declaration, a risky early call that ends a round. The best search-based agent won only about nine percent, and the best learning agent about two percent. Carefully tuned rules, Malla concludes, beat heavier machinery in this game.
arxiv-2510-11836:
Osvaldo L. Santos-Pereira, Everton M. C. Abreu, and Marcelo B. Ribeiro take a fresh look at the Alcubierre warp drive. Alcubierre's 1994 idea bends spacetime into a bubble that could carry a ship faster than light. The bubble's motion is governed by the shift vector in his metric. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines the coupled Einstein equations for the original warp metric, now including a cosmological constant, and seeks vacuum solutions.

Under a suitable ansatz, a chosen simplifying form, the system separates into friendlier pieces. One piece is a Burgers-type equation, famous for describing shock waves in fluids. Another is a heat-type equation, describing how quantities diffuse and smooth out. The authors read this as a hint about the bubble's nature. The spacetime distortion carrying a particle at such speeds behaves like a geometric analog of a shock front. That viewpoint offers a new framework for handling warp speeds.
arxiv-2510-12236:
Currie and Jones model how the deep winds of giant planets fade with depth, in a 2025 arXiv planetary science paper. Jupiter like planets show strong zonal flows, meaning winds that circle along lines of latitude, at their surfaces. Gravity data from the Juno mission suggest these jets reach deep, so a good model must explain both their strength and their gradual weakening.

The authors force the flow in a thin stable layer near the surface, which sets up a meridional circulation much like the Ferrel cells in Jupiter's atmosphere. That circulation creates a horizontal temperature anomaly, and through the thermal wind relation it steadily reduces the zonal winds with depth. Their three dimensional simulations show convection below the forced layer, usually as tall thin cells. When convection drives the fluctuations, the temperature anomaly persists much deeper than when jet shear does, letting the jets extend far into the interior.
arxiv-2510-12636:
Chemseddine and colleagues build generative models from one dimensional noising processes, and then let the noise itself be learned from data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Generative flows turn noise into data through a gradual process, and diffusion is only one choice of how to add that noise. Their framework constructs models from general one dimensional processes, showing the flexibility this allows through examples beyond diffusion.

In the learnable version, the noise distribution is parameterized through quantile functions, which describe a distribution by its percentiles. The construction plugs into standard training objectives, including flow matching plus consistency models. Learning the noise this way naturally captures heavy tails and bounded supports when the data have them, features a fixed Gaussian noise cannot express. Numerical experiments show both the flexibility and the effectiveness of the method, suggesting the noise process should be treated as part of the model rather than a fixed given.
arxiv-2510-12736:
Andronikos and colleagues map how the success of a quantum classifier for Boolean functions depends on how far a function sits from known patterns, in a 2025 arXiv quantum computing paper. Boolean functions assign yes or no values to bit strings, and quantum algorithms can classify them by their structural patterns. The Hamming distance counts how many output values two functions disagree on, a natural measure of closeness.

Extensive experiments confirm that Hamming distance is a central metric for validating nearest neighbors in classifying random functions. The successful classification probability decreases monotonically as Hamming distance grows. However, specific function classes break the pattern, showing internal heterogeneity. The authors show these deviations are systemic and predictable rather than random, and they quantify them. Their main novelty is demarcating exact Hamming distance intervals for the classification probability. Practitioners can use these intervals to endorse a classification result or dismiss it with confidence.
arxiv-2510-13036:
Hatgis-Kessell, Bhamidipaty, and Brunskill repair flawed reward functions with human preferences in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning agents optimize whatever reward they are given, so a misspecified proxy reward invites reward hacking, behavior that scores well while breaking the designer's true objective. Learning a reward from scratch through human feedback avoids the bad proxy but demands costly preference data.

Their framework, Preference-Based Reward Repair, instead learns an additive correction term for the existing reward, depending on transitions, guided by preferences between trajectories. A targeted exploration strategy hunts for the few transitions where corrections matter most. The authors prove a regret bound matching prior preference-based methods in tabular settings. On reward-hacking benchmarks, their approach beat baselines that learn rewards from scratch or patch proxies in other ways. It also needed far less preference data.
arxiv-2510-13236:
Nicolajsen surveys programming language extensibility in this 2025 arXiv overview paper, writing as a newcomer-friendly introduction rather than a manual. Extensibility, the ability of a language to grow new constructs, is, he argues, an overlooked component of conventional language design. The overview grew out of the guide he himself lacked while studying programming languages.

Through a literature review he finds four key extensibility themes: macros, modules, types, and reflection. The analysis then crosses those themes with shared properties. These include parametricism, the ability to parameterize constructs, and first-class citizen behavior, where language constructs can be passed around like ordinary values. By outlining these facets across existing languages and research, Nicolajsen aims to inspire future language designers. He wants them to assess the extensibility of their creations critically, instead of treating it as an afterthought.
arxiv-2510-13336:
Oxley and Kerswell examine how density layering affects brief bursts of growth in streaky shear flows near a wall. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns turbulence, where long streaks of fast and slow fluid sit close to solid surfaces. Recent work had questioned the classic lift-up account of how these streaks sustain themselves. It also showed that removing vertical motion from a model can release far larger growth.

The authors add stable stratification, a layering of fluid by density that naturally damps vertical motion. In their vertical shear case, this layering permits the hugely enhanced growth seen when vertical velocity is removed outright. When layering instead damps sideways motion, growth falls, because the active push-over effect weakens. They also derive a formula for the layering strength that fully stops the favoured growth, and it predicts their full numerical results well.
arxiv-2510-13436:
Yao and co-authors propose a non-standard dark matter model and test it against sky surveys. In their 2025 arXiv paper, dark matter gains an equation of state that grows with the young universe. The design forces dark matter to behave like cold dark matter at the start. Both its pressure-like term and its rate of change vanish at that limit.

The team fits three model variants to cosmic microwave background and baryon acoustic oscillation data. They add three independent supernova collections to tighten the constraints further. For two data combinations, the results favour a negative dark matter equation of state beyond three sigma. That is strong statistical evidence against plain cold dark matter in those fits. Swapping in the new matter also sharply cuts the chance of breaking the null energy condition. Two variants rival the best-known dark energy extension in fit quality.
arxiv-2510-13936:
Fengbin Zhu and a large team of co-authors evaluate deep research agents, AI systems that use language models to carry out extended research tasks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their focus is corporate financial analysis, a demanding test because analysts must recognize data, compute metrics, and then interpret what the numbers mean for a company.

The team built HisRubric, a grading framework that follows the analyst workflow from data recognition through metric calculation to strategic summary, and used it to create the FinDeepResearch benchmark. The benchmark covers 64 listed companies in eight markets and four languages, with more than fifteen thousand grading items. Testing sixteen methods, from deep research agents to reasoning models with and without search, revealed clear strengths and limits across markets and languages.
arxiv-2510-14036:
Qiushi Wu and co-authors introduce BugStone, a system that uses large language models to find hundreds of hidden siblings of a single known software bug, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They call these recurring pattern bugs: the same root-cause mistake repeated across many code segments, often left unfixed after the first instance is patched. Such leftovers are slow to hunt by hand. Public bug reports also hand attackers a pattern to search for.

BugStone combines the LLVM compiler framework with a language model, starting from a patched instance to extract the error pattern, such as an API misuse, then scanning programs for matches. Starting from 135 recurring bugs, it flagged more than twenty-two thousand issues in the Linux kernel; manual review of four hundred confirmed 246 as valid. On a data set of over nineteen hundred security bugs, it reached precision above ninety percent with a cheap model.
arxiv-2510-14136:
David Roqui and co-authors build a lightweight multimodal AI model that predicts how climate change is damaging cultural heritage sites, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Traditional monitoring inspects sites visually or reads environmental sensors, but neither captures how heat and humidity interact with material decay, and heritage data sets are tiny, under a hundred samples.

Their architecture fuses temperature and humidity sensor data with visual imagery. It adapts the PerceiverIO model with a small latent space to avoid overfitting on just thirty-seven training samples. A modified Barlow Twins loss pushes the two modalities to complement rather than duplicate each other. On data from Strasbourg Cathedral, the model reached accuracy near seventy-seven percent, beating multimodal architectures by a wide margin and the unmodified PerceiverIO by a quarter. Sensor data alone scored about sixty-two percent and images alone about forty-six percent, confirming the fusion helps.
arxiv-2510-14336:
Shruti Sarika Chakraborty and Peter Minary redesign graph transformers, the attention-based models for graph data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their architecture is searched rather than hand-fixed, and their decisions can be measured for interpretability. Standard graph transformers commit to one graph network type across all layers and remain opaque about whether their wins come from real patterns or spurious correlations.

Their attention is asymmetric: queries come from node features while keys and values come from graph network transformations. Differentiable architecture search selects the best graph operator at each layer, allowing depth-wise variety inside the attention mechanism. To explain the architectures, they build the first quantitative interpretability framework for these models, based on causal ablation, with metrics for head deviation, specialization, and focus. Across eight benchmarks, the model reached state-of-the-art results on four data sets and stayed competitive on the rest.
arxiv-2510-15236:
Brett Reynolds argues that today's tests for artificial general intelligence grade like a flat checklist, and that this hides what matters. His solo 2025 arXiv paper notes that current evaluations weight every skill domain equally and score systems in one snapshot session. A model can then look strong while lacking memory that lasts, a flaw equal weights cannot expose.

Reynolds proposes treating general intelligence as a homeostatic property cluster: a set of abilities plus the mechanisms that keep them working together under stress. Tests should weight domains by causal centrality, meaning how much each one holds the cluster together. He adds a centrality-prior score borrowed from human intelligence research and a Cluster Stability Index that tracks persistence, durable learning, and error correction across sessions. The paper closes with testable predictions and protocols labs can run from outside the model.
arxiv-2510-15336:
Liviu-Mihai Stan and six colleagues help rescue robots drive through wreckage where some obstacles can be pushed aside and others cannot. Their 2025 arXiv paper adds this judgment to the standard ROS 2 navigation stack using only LiDAR scans, with no camera system or pre-training. The test setting is disaster response inside damaged, cluttered buildings.

One new layer marks any scan return missing from an earlier static map as tentatively movable and prices paths through it cheaply. A second checker compares commanded speed with actual speed. If the robot slows against resistance, the cost rises in steps, and a full stall marks the spot lethal so the planner backs out and reroutes. In simulator trials on a Scout Mini robot, the setup reached more goals with fewer deadlocks than a baseline without the layer. Driving times stayed broadly similar, and the method runs on modest computing hardware.
arxiv-2510-15636:
Black holes absorb and scatter waves that pass near them, and the pattern depends on gravity's rules. Sihao Fan, Chen Wu, and Wenjun Guo compute this for regular black holes in quasi-topological gravity. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats massless scalar waves hitting these singularity-free black hole solutions. Using the partial wave method, they compute total and partial absorption cross-sections for varied parameters. One parameter, alpha, measures the strength of the higher-order gravity corrections.

They find that larger alpha shrinks the total absorption cross-section. They also find that spacetime dimension affects absorption and scattering differently than earlier computations suggested. The comparison highlights how sensitive wave capture is to the underlying gravity theory.
arxiv-2510-16136:
Sayan Deb Sarkar and three co-authors tackle appearance transfer: giving a 3D object the look of another object shown in a photo or described in text. Existing tools falter when the two shapes differ greatly, and simply running a 3D generator on the input produces unattractive results, as the authors demonstrate.

Their training-free method, GuideFlow3D, steers a pretrained rectified flow model during sampling by periodically adding guidance from differentiable loss functions, including a part-aware loss and a self-similarity loss. It moves both texture and fine geometric detail onto the target asset and beats prior methods in tests. Because standard metrics judge this task poorly, the team also ranks outputs with a GPT-based evaluator backed by a user study.
arxiv-2510-16336:
Pachara Sawettamalya and Huacheng Yu sharpen a space-saving method for certifying that a network stays connected. A k-edge connectivity certificate is a small subgraph with a big job. It keeps the full graph's connection strength, up to k edge failures. In a dynamic stream, edges come and go, and memory is tight.

Their simple algorithm stores the certificate using space that very nearly matches the known lower bound. For mid-to-large k it settles the space cost exactly, closing a question open since a 2012 algorithm used more room. For small k, only a tiny doubly-log factor of slack remains. Near-optimal sketches like this let huge, shifting networks be monitored from a trickle of memory.
arxiv-2510-16536:
Niranjana Arun Menon leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on heart risk from mixed body data. Heart disease risk is hard to grade, and clean labelled data is scarce. Their frame joins gene marks, called SNP variants, with heart trace traits from ECG tests. An ECG is a test that records the heart's electric beats. A large language model does the joining.

A clean-up step keeps only labels the model holds with high trust. The model also writes plain reasons for each call, in a step-by-step style. Scores matched models trained on the full data set. That hints at good care tools that need few labels. Clear reasons help doctors judge each call.
arxiv-2510-16636:
Abraham Atsiwo, the sole author, builds a bubble alarm for stock markets in a 2025 study. A bubble is a price surge that outruns real worth, then bursts. His target is the S&P 500, a broad index of US stocks. The frame runs in three steps. Step one flags past bubble spans with a right-tailed unit root test, a stats check for runaway growth.

Step two pulls mood traits from vast sets of finance news text. Mood here means the tone of hope or fear in the news. Step three trains group models on mood traits plus broad economy gauges. Checks with held-out folds show the blend beats solo rival methods. Early alarms could help investors and watchdogs curb risk.
arxiv-2510-16736:
Patrizio Dazzi and four co-authors run exact nearest-neighbor search on FPGA chips to save energy. Nearest-neighbor search finds the closest stored vectors to a query, a core task behind systems that use learned image and text embeddings. FPGAs are reconfigurable chips that can be tuned for one job.

The team offers two designs on one low-level setup. One streams data that cannot fit in chip memory and favors throughput. The other keeps data in memory and favors low delay per query. On public image and text data sets, both beat leading CPU systems on speed and energy use. Reported gains reach a scale-up factor above sixteen for throughput.
arxiv-2510-16836:
Lin Shang and three co-authors map the steady states of the one-dimensional quantum contact process, a model of spreading and recovery with quantum rules. Contact processes show how activity can persist or die out. The quantum version adds coherent effects that change the phase picture.

The team computes the Liouvillian gap in the large-system limit and uncovers metastability, where the system lingers in a state that is not its final one. A mean-field method with a new self-consistent condition sidesteps that trap. Their order parameter shows a saddle-node pattern, marking a sudden, discontinuous steady-state transition, and they extract its point for an infinite system. A cluster expansion result argues against a diverging correlation length near the transition.
arxiv-2510-17136:
Enhao Gu and Haolin Hou speed up image making with a self-check trick in this 2025 paper. Diffusion models build images step by step from noise. A common guide boosts quality but cuts image range. Past fixes used a second, weaker model as the guide, at extra cost.

Their method draws the weak guide from the same model on the fly. A random pass makes a worse guess, which then steers the main pass. The trick adds no extra model and no extra training cost. Tests show strong quality, range, and fit to the prompt at once. The work sets a lean base line for cheap, guided image making.
arxiv-2510-17336:
Flat defects inside a complex metal can decide how strong or brittle that metal becomes. Christina Gasper, with seven co-authors, maps those defects in the tantalum iron mu phase, a tightly packed crystal form found in intermetallic compounds. The team varied the tantalum share across a wide range and combined electron imaging with quantum based calculations.

At low tantalum levels, Gasper and her co-authors saw twin boundaries and flat faults holding thin layers of a related crystal phase. At higher levels, slanted pyramidal twins took over instead. The calculations link that switch to chemical conditions during crystal growth, and the team sketches a full defect map for guiding future tuning of such metals.
arxiv-2510-17436:
Portable scanners that work at very low magnetic field could bring brain imaging to places that cannot afford standard machines, but their pictures are far rougher. Vladyslav Zalevskyi, with three co-authors, tackles the task of outlining infant brain structures in those low field scans. Babies are a hard case in any scanner, because the brain grows fast, tissue contrast is poor, and small patients move.

Zalevskyi and his co-authors train on high field scans that are randomly altered to look like low field ones, a trick called domain randomization. Cleaning the training labels by removing badly matched entries helped further, and merging several models by majority vote lifted the scores again. The combined method placed first on one target structure in a public challenge.
arxiv-2510-17736:
Jun Yan studies when a dense graph must contain every possible spanning tree. A spanning tree connects all vertices of a graph without cycles. A classic result covers trees whose largest vertex degree stays fairly small. Yan asks what happens when that degree grows much larger.

He finds a near-best minimum degree condition for the large-degree case. Minimum degree means the smallest number of edges at any vertex. Past that threshold, the host graph contains every allowed tree. He proves matching statements for random graphs as well. The work sharpens a celebrated theorem by three earlier authors.
arxiv-2510-18036:
Stavros Mitsis, with six co-authors, fits emotion reading onto tiny, low-power hardware that can work in private. Voice and word cues are read together, but most joint systems need strong chips or the cloud. Their redesign joins the two streams late and is tuned for an Edge TPU chip.

A quantized sound model pairs with frozen keyword features from a compact speech network. The whole system runs in real time inside a very small memory budget. Uses the authors name include tension monitoring and calming wearables. Edge computing readers get a working pattern for smart sensing that never sends raw audio away.
arxiv-2510-18136:
Myles B Sherman, with twelve co-authors, describes a search system hunting slow radio bursts with a California telescope array. Most burst searches chase flashes far shorter than a second. This pipeline stretches sensitivity to pulses lasting from a tenth of a second to nearly three minutes, a thousand-fold wider window.

A custom GPU code runs the search in real time on image data. Commissioning tests with steady sources and a known pulsar set the sensitivity limits. An offline survey of the galactic plane then hunted the new class of long-period radio transients. Radio astronomers get a working net for slow cosmic flashes.
arxiv-2510-18836:
Anthony Conway and Daniel Kasprowski classify four-dimensional manifolds with a given boundary. It is a companion study to their work on relative invariants. The central question is extension. Two manifolds may have boundaries matched by a homotopy equivalence. When does that match extend to the interiors? They solve the problem in broad settings. The fundamental groups covered are wide. They include free groups and finite cyclic groups. They include finite dihedral groups and certain solvable groups. Many three-manifold groups are included too.

When the group is also well behaved for surgery theory, more follows. The authors list when a boundary homeomorphism extends to the whole manifolds. A homeomorphism is an exact geometric match. Old theorems are recovered inside the framework. One covers the simply connected case. One covers the circle fundamental group case from past work.
arxiv-2510-18936:
Hamed Jelodar and four co-authors introduce SBAN, a large dataset that links source code, binary code, assembly, and plain language descriptions of software. Each sample carries all four views, which lets models learn how the same program looks at very different levels.

With more than three million samples, split between benign programs and malware, SBAN supports training and testing of large language models for code analysis. Uses range from malware detection and code translation to code explanation and other software mining tasks. Its layered design suits transformer models and other deep systems that learn across data types.
arxiv-2510-19036:
Suswitha Pericharla and two co-authors test whether fine-tuning helps large language models map biomedical terms to standard identifier codes. Linking plain terms to shared codes lets databases work together, but model skill varies a lot across biomedical terminologies.

Fine-tuning a Llama model brought large memorization gains for Gene Ontology terms, up to seventy-seven percent better accuracy, yet little gain for a human phenotype vocabulary. True generalization to unseen terms appeared only for protein-gene mappings. The contrast warns that fine-tuning can teach recall without teaching a transferable mapping rule for new terms.
arxiv-2510-19236:
Annan Yu and nine co-authors examine how quiet design choices bias time series foundation models, rather than chasing another leaderboard win. These general-purpose forecasting models are shaped by details such as patch size, embedding choice, and training objective. Each choice tilts what the model learns about time.

Through theory and controlled tests, the authors show how those knobs change temporal behavior, geometric structure, and how strongly a model snaps back toward average values. Understanding such hidden biases helps users pick and audit models for forecasting tasks where a subtle tilt can quietly distort every prediction the system makes.
arxiv-2510-19436:
Kazutaka Takahashi, Pratik Nandy, and Adolfo del Campo study Krylov complexity when a quantum system's Hamiltonian is deformed. Krylov space, the smallest subspace in which the dynamics unfolds, gives an efficient language for complex quantum motion and a natural way to measure how complicated that motion becomes.

For a class of deformations, the Krylov space itself does not change; only the basis is reorganized, and the generator keeps its three-diagonal form. The deformation parameters then obey generalized Toda equations, classic integrable flow equations. The authors also link imaginary-time evolution to real unitary motion, and point to building solvable models from known ones.
arxiv-2510-19636:
Sahar Maleki and three co-authors test whether a multilayer perceptron neural network fits the contrast responses of local field potentials better than the formulas neuroscientists usually use. Local field potentials record the combined activity of neuron populations in the primary visual cortex, and their tuning curves are broader than those of single spikes. The data come from primate V1 responses to luminance contrast.

The team first sorted the recorded response curves into linear, saturating, and supersaturating types using a monotonicity index. Several identification methods were then compared, including radial basis networks, fuzzy models, and the classic Naka-Rushton function. The multilayer perceptron tuned significantly more recordings successfully across all three types, suggesting it as a better standard tool.
arxiv-2510-20336:
