The Virgo cluster serves as the test case. Its substructure resolves into galaxy groups of varied size, whose members run brighter than the cluster average and each hold an active galaxy. Inside the groups, brighter average magnitude pairs with higher average velocity. The authors read that correlation as evidence of expansion, and the groups as ejections from a central galaxy.
arxiv-2512-19736:
Gongli Xi leads an eight-author team on a practical data problem. Real network shapes are scarce. So researchers make synthetic graphs with set traits, for tests or for release. Past diffusion-based tools had flaws. Some baked the traits in and needed retraining for each new trait. Others steered after training, with no grip on scale or real-world limits.

Their tool, CoPHo, steers the diffusion while it runs. It feeds gradients from a trained graph classifier into the reverse steps. A tool from topology, persistent homology, reads the shape of each draft graph. Those readings act as guide signals at each step. On four data sets, CoPHo matched target traits better than past methods. It also moved well to the QM9 molecule data set. The work was accepted at KDD 2026.
arxiv-2512-19836:
Elisabeth Werner and Diliya Yalikun define new ways to measure the surface of a ball-convex body, a convex shape cut out by balls rather than half-spaces. Their L_p relative surface areas are shown to be valuations unchanged by rigid motions, placing them in a classical family of geometric functionals with well-understood algebraic manners. Inequalities for the new quantities follow.

A monotonicity property of these measures leads the authors to a fresh notion of entropy for ball-convex bodies. They also introduce a weighted ball floating body, a shrunken inner companion shape, and prove that differentiating volume along that shrinking recovers the L_p relative surface areas geometrically. The construction mirrors how ordinary surface area arises from floating bodies in classical convexity.
arxiv-2512-20436:
Muhammad Usman and co-authors segment stroke lesions in diffusion MRI scans with a dual-encoder Transformer. Diffusion-weighted imaging and apparent diffusion coefficient maps show complementary views of acute and subacute damage. Separating them by hand is slow, and lesion appearance varies enough to defeat simple rules.

Working on the ISLES 2022 dataset, the team first benchmarks U-Net variants, Swin-UNet, and TransUNet under one training approach. Transformers beat the convolutional benchmarks. Their proposed design gives each modality its own encoder inside a TransUNet and feeds three adjacent slices for spatial context. The dual-encoder model tops the comparison, reaching a strong Dice score on the test set. Automated delineation of this quality can speed clinical assessment.
arxiv-2512-20536:
Alex Chen Yi Zhang, Pablo Mateu Hoyos, David Brückner, and Gašper Tkačik ask how embryos could read position more precisely by sharing information. Cells infer where they are from morphogen concentrations, but noise limits that readout. Communication between cells offers nonlocal information that might sharpen the estimate.

In a Bayes-optimal approach, the answer hinges on the spatial correlations of the morphogen field and on the structural prior describing the cellular lattice. The authors bound how much positional information nonlocal readout can add. They then exhibit signal-processing methods that nearly achieve the optimum, plus simple chemical reaction schemes that implement them. The theory says correlational information, often ignored, can significantly raise developmental precision.
arxiv-2512-20636:
Dhananjay Saikumar and Blesson Varghese delete whole attention layers from language models using nothing but the weights. Their premise, the attention suppression hypothesis, says some deep attention layers learn during pretraining to mute themselves, leaving the residual stream and feed-forward layers to carry the representation. Those layers should be safe to remove.

Their criterion, Gate-Norm, ranks attention sublayers by query-key coupling and cuts the least coupled, with no calibration data, no forward passes, and no fine-tuning. On a forty-layer, thirteen-billion-parameter LLaMA model the scoring takes under a second. Removing eight to sixteen layers raises throughput by up to about thirty percent while zero-shot accuracy barely moves. The method matches data-driven pruners at a thousandth of the scoring cost.
arxiv-2512-20736:
Hamid Afshar and Mehdi Ahmadi-Jahmani work on Carrollian gravity, a version of gravity suited to settings where light cones collapse and motion behaves very differently from everyday physics. They add matter and a scaling symmetry, then recast the whole setup as a gauge theory, a framework that builds theories from symmetry rules.

Their construction loosens one conformal symmetry and enlarges the set of gravity fields. After fixing the scaling freedom, a few fields govern the theory, including a vector field tied to size changes. Suitable gauge choices then recover several known descriptions, among them Carrollian and Aristotelian pictures. The result unifies views that looked separate before.
arxiv-2512-20836:
Lachlan McGinness asks what a good concept test for quantum computing should contain. Concept inventories, standardized question sets that expose student misconceptions, have improved teaching in other fields. Quantum computing needs one as its workforce grows, but the subject's heavy mathematics raises doubts about what can be tested without it.

McGinness interviewed eight experts across quantum computing, communication, and sensing. They agreed substantial non-mathematical content exists and sketched a first list of key concepts. Building the inventory remains hard: questions must avoid jargon, stay valid, and suit students who have not yet studied quantum mechanics. The paper frames both the promise and the international teamwork the task demands.
arxiv-2512-21336:
Masked diffusion models generate text by unmasking tokens in any order, and Ziyu Chen, Xinbei Jiang, Peng Sun, and Tao Lin show the order matters enormously. They trace output quality to the predictive uncertainty accumulated along a generation path. Their measure, denoising entropy, turns that uncertainty into a number the model itself can supply.

Two algorithms put the measure to work: one picks the best finished path after the fact, the other steers generation live. Both lift accuracy on reasoning, planning, and code benchmarks. The result recasts a weakness of flexible decoding as a control signal. For builders of diffusion language models, path choice becomes an optimizable design decision rather than a coin flip.
arxiv-2512-21436:
Chinmay Giridhar, Philipp Vojta, Zohar Nussinov, Gerardo Ortiz, and Andriy H. Nevidomskyy develop the fusion rules of topological defects in a quantum lattice model. The symmetries are generalized and non-invertible, beyond ordinary group ones. Such symmetries produce exotic phases of matter outside the classic Landau picture.

The test case is a two-dimensional quantum Ising plaquette model with extra subsystem symmetries that act only on lower-dimensional slices. Combining bond-algebraic automorphisms with half-gauging, the authors expose the model's duality symmetry operators as an explicit quantum circuit. The rigid subsystem symmetries restrict how the resulting defects can move. The team then establishes the fusion algebra of these defects, the rules for combining them. They also verify the duality transformation acts as a partial isometry, matching a recent generalization of Wigner's theorem for non-invertible symmetries.
arxiv-2512-21536:
Yuan Li, Qiaoyuan Cheng, and Engui Fan prove that solutions of the Fokas-Lenells equation exist for all time, for a wide class of starting data. The Fokas-Lenells equation is a nonlinear wave equation used to model ultrashort light pulses in optical fibers. Their result covers any initial data in certain weighted Sobolev spaces, which control both smoothness and decay at infinity.

Earlier work by the same team needed extra spectral restrictions on the initial data. The new proof removes those restrictions entirely. It relies on the inverse scattering transform, recast as new Riemann-Hilbert problems, together with Zhou's bijectivity theory for such problems in square-integrable Sobolev spaces. Global existence results of this kind matter because they certify that the model's predictions never blow up in finite time.
arxiv-2512-21736:
Xindi Zhang, Bang Zhang, and their co-authors present SyncAnyone, a system for lip-syncing video to audio in uncontrolled footage. Dubbing demands accurate lip motion, sharp image quality, and preservation of identity and background. The standard training trick, masking the mouth and asking the model to repaint it, breaks the surrounding context and causes flicker and drift.

SyncAnyone works in two stages. First, a diffusion-based video transformer learns masked mouth inpainting, using its space-time modeling to generate audio-driven lip movements. Some artifacts remain around the face and background because the input was corrupted. In the second stage, the team builds synthetic training pairs by lip-syncing source videos to sampled audio, then fine-tunes the model without a mask. This self-correction pass teaches precise lip editing with consistent backgrounds. Experiments show state-of-the-art quality, temporal coherence, and identity preservation.
arxiv-2512-22136:
Mahadev Sunil Kumar and five co-authors present SlimEdge, a way to spread deep neural networks across weak edge devices without breaking them. Edge hardware has little memory and computing power, and devices can fail mid-task. Their method prunes the network in a structured way while optimizing several goals at once, respecting each device's limits and its chance of failing.

They demonstrate the system on Multi-View Convolutional Neural Networks, used for 3D object recognition from multiple camera views. By measuring how much each view contributes to accuracy, they assign pruning budgets view by view. The resulting models meet user-set accuracy and memory bounds even when several devices fail at once. Inference runs up to 4.7 times faster across simulated device setups.
arxiv-2512-22236:
Adrien Pavão ran a simple experiment with an uncomfortable result: people cannot reliably tell AI-generated images from real photographs. Participants in an interactive web test classified twenty images each, drawn from a set of 120 difficult cases. Real photos came from the CC12M dataset, and the fakes were carefully produced counterparts made with MidJourney.

Across 165 users and 233 sessions, average accuracy was 54 percent, barely above coin-flip guessing, and practice brought only limited improvement. People answered in about seven seconds on average, and some images fooled nearly everyone always. Pavão concludes that human judgment alone is becoming insufficient as synthetic media improves, and calls for greater awareness and ethical guidelines around AI-generated imagery.
arxiv-2512-22336:
Mengkang Hu and eleven co-authors present Agent2World, a system that teaches language models to write symbolic world models, the rule sets that planners reason over. Good world models, in PDDL or as executable simulators, are scarce training material, and static validation misses errors that only appear during interactive execution. Agent2World instead grounds generation in feedback from a team of specialized agents.

A Deep Researcher agent searches the web to fill specification gaps, a Model Developer writes the executable model, and a Testing Team runs adaptive unit tests and simulations. The system led its benchmarks at inference time. Its feedback loops also generate multi-turn training trajectories, and fine-tuning on them improved world-model generation by roughly thirty-one percent on average.
arxiv-2512-22536:
Qinglin Zeng, Kaitong Cai, Ruiqi Chen, Qinhan Lv, and Keze Wang present CoAgent, a system for generating longer videos that hold together as stories. Text-to-video models usually render each shot independently, so characters drift in appearance, scenes clash, and the timeline wobbles. CoAgent treats generation as a closed loop of planning, synthesis, and verification, driven by a user prompt, a style reference, and pacing constraints.

A Storyboard Planner breaks the prompt into shot-level plans naming entities, spatial relations, and temporal cues. A Global Context Manager keeps entity memory so appearances persist, while each shot is synthesized under a Visual Consistency Controller. A Verifier Agent checks intermediate results with vision-language reasoning and orders selective regeneration when something clashes. A pacing-aware editor finishes the rhythm and transitions.
arxiv-2512-22936:
Arthur Yaghjian replies to a comment disputing his claim about the classical motion of a point electric charge. The background dispute concerns radiation reaction, the force a charge feels from its own emitted radiation, and whether a consistent causal equation exists after the charge's mass is renormalized. Critics Zin and Pylak objected to how the derivation handles abrupt changes in the applied force.

His answer retraces the derivation, which starts from the motion of an extended charged sphere and takes the sphere's radius to zero. Along the way, the modified equation produces a causal version of the Lorentz-Abraham-Dirac equation. He then addresses the objection directly. Velocity jumps across short intervals near points where the force is nonanalytic do not create delta-function spikes in the radiated fields, contrary to the critics' claim. The reply is short and defensive, aiming to leave the original conclusion standing.
arxiv-2512-23136:
Junyeong Park and co-authors study why Korean students switch into Korean while practicing English conversation with an AI partner. Code-switching is studied in multilingual communities but rarely in learners talking to language models, where its teaching value is unclear. The team built LAKE, a dataset of learner-AI dialogues capturing South Korean learners' Korean-English switching during practice, with hundreds of dialogues and dozens of hours of speech.

A taxonomy of switching functions shows learners reach for Korean to flag unknown words, negotiate meaning, and express culturally marked content. Learners reuse and adapt English expressions the AI partner offered right after their switches, hinting at chances for well-timed vocabulary support. The authors release hours of human-verified code-switched speech and benchmark speech recognition on it, exposing how poorly recognizers handle learner switching. The message for designers: treat switching as a resource, not an error.
arxiv-2512-23236:
Gang Liao and a large Meta team describe KernelEvolve, an agentic system that writes and optimizes the low-level kernels behind recommendation models. Making deep learning recommendation training and inference fast is hard for three stacked reasons. Model architectures vary, kernel primitives vary, and hardware generations differ across NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards plus Meta's own accelerators. KernelEvolve takes a kernel specification and automates generation and tuning across that matrix.

The search is framed as graph exploration with a selection policy, a universal operator, and a fitness function, adapting to runtime through retrieval-augmented prompts. It works at several abstraction levels, from Triton down to hardware-agnostic low-level languages. On the KernelBench suite it passed all two hundred fifty problems, and it achieved full correctness on one hundred sixty PyTorch operators across three hardware platforms. In production, development time reportedly fell from weeks to hours, with speedups.
arxiv-2512-23336:
Marta Pita-Vidal and co-authors review a qubit platform that marries semiconductors to superconductors. Hybrid qubits have emerged as an alternative to established designs because their Josephson coupling is tunable by electric gates. That promises superconducting-style architectures with electric-field control, and a route toward scalable processors with low crosstalk. Quantum information can be stored, for instance, in the spin of a quasiparticle sitting in an Andreev bound state, combining long coherence with fast control.

The review surveys recent advances, from Andreev states in coupled quantum dot arrays to minimal Kitaev chains hosting Majorana zero modes. Hamiltonian-protected designs, which exploit superconducting phase dynamics and discrete charge or flux variables to resist local noise, get equal attention. The authors organize the field by physical mechanism, device implementation, and emerging architecture, emphasizing potential for protected quantum information processing while noting many designs remain at proof-of-concept stage.
arxiv-2512-23636:
Alberto Bemporad releases NashOpt, an open-source Python library for computing generalized Nash equilibria in games where players share constraints. In such games each player's feasible choices depend on the others, so ordinary equilibrium solvers do not apply. The library works from the joint optimality conditions of all players at once.

General nonlinear games are solved as nonlinear least-squares problems, with the JAX library supplying automatic differentiation. Linear-quadratic games are reformulated as mixed-integer linear programs, which also makes it possible to enumerate several equilibria. NashOpt further supports inverse games, where the game is inferred from observed play, and Stackelberg design problems. Examples include game-theoretic control problems built on linear quadratic regulation and model predictive control. The code is public on GitHub.
arxiv-2512-23836:
Dingmin Wang, Ji Ma, and Shankar Kumar study retrieval-augmented question answering, where a language model answers using documents fetched for it. Bigger context windows invite stuffing in more retrieved text, but irrelevant passages actively degrade answers. The authors ask how the retrieved material should be fed to the model, and what models do when the material simply does not contain the answer.

Their adaptive strategy splits the retrieved information into smaller chunks and prompts the model chunk by chunk, with chunk size tuning the trade-off between coverage and noise. Across three open-domain question answering data sets, the strategy matched standard prompting while spending fewer tokens. The sobering finding came from failure analysis: faced with insufficient information, models usually fabricated an answer instead of declining, and that behavior was a major source of error.
arxiv-2512-24036:
Fazlay Ahmed, Qiang Wu, Sushant Ghosh, and Tao Zhu ask whether gravitational waves could reveal small quantum corrections to a black hole's shape. They study a Schwarzschild black hole modified along lines suggested by loop quantum gravity, where one correction parameter changes part of the geometry while leaving the horizon in its classical place.

The team follows a small test particle on repeating bound orbits, sorted by a zoom-and-whirl scheme, and computes the waves those orbits emit. Quantum corrections shift the wave phase, change its strength, and alter its harmonic mix, with richer patterns for orbits that zoom more. The signals land in the millihertz band, inside the reach planned for space detectors such as LISA, Taiji, and TianQin, and for some settings the predicted strain rises above expected detector noise. Periodic orbits, the authors conclude, offer a sensitive test of quantum-corrected black holes.
arxiv-2512-24136:
Matthew Gentry Durham gives a new account of a proof in geometric group theory. The result is joint work with Minsky and Sisto. Mapping class groups admit bicombings. Teichmüller spaces admit them too. A bicombing is a well-behaved choice of paths between points. Its existence has strong consequences for a space's geometry.

The account generalizes beyond those two settings. Any colorable hierarchically hyperbolic space qualifies. Take two points there and form their hierarchical hull. That hull is quasi-isometric to a finite cube complex. The complex is CAT(0) and has bounded dimension. Small changes to the point pair change the cubical structure only slightly. The change is uniformly bounded. Durham stresses that the exposition is mostly expository. Many aspects of the approach are simplified and new.
arxiv-2512-24236:
Lynn Heller, Sebastian Heller, and Claudio Meneses study a degeneration in Higgs bundle geometry. The setting is the moduli space of strongly parabolic Higgs bundles. The bundles live on a sphere with n punctures. A hyperkähler metric, the Hitchin metric, equips the space. Scaling the parabolic weights toward zero degenerates that metric.

Twistor lines organize the analysis. Lines from hyperpolygon spaces appear as limiting initial data. The authors build matching families of connections from them. On shrinking regions, the rescaled metric converges. Its limit is the hyperkähler metric of the hyperpolygon space. That space is the finite-dimensional model of the degeneration. Higher-order corrections also become explicit. They are written with iterated integrals of logarithmic differentials on the punctured sphere. The work links an infinite-dimensional reduction to a concrete finite model.
arxiv-2512-24336:
Sara Geremia, Michael Fop, and Domenico De Stefano find communities in networks where nodes carry attributes. Real communities form through mixed forces. Structure matters: some nodes are hubs, some are leaders. Shared traits matter too, through homophily. Most detection methods treat these forces separately. That limits what they can recover.

Their method, AttDeCoDe, extends a density-based framework. Density is estimated in attribute space rather than from topology alone. Communities then grow around attribute-based representatives. Structural connectivity still constrains the outcome. Leader influence remains visible in the design. A new generative model tests the method. It extends the degree-corrected block model with attribute-driven leader attraction. That model mirrors collaborative research networks. A real application uses Horizon programme collaboration data. Performance matched or beat topology-based and attribute-assisted benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-24536:
Seog-Jin Kim, Xiaopan Lian, Atsuhiro Nakamoto, and Kenta Ozeki prove a graph coloring result about squares of planar graphs. The square joins vertices at distance one or two, so its coloring assigns labels so nearby vertices differ. For subcubic planar graphs, where each vertex has at most three neighbors, seven colors were known to suffice for ordinary coloring.

List coloring is stronger, since each vertex picks from its own list of seven. Earlier results needed no short cycles or large girth. Here only five-cycles are banned. Readers in graph theory get an improvement that widens the family covered by the seven-choosable conclusion.
arxiv-2512-24636:
Tanjum Motin Mitul and three colleagues ask whether AI coding agents care about energy. Agents now write much software automatically. Their own training and running costs are large. Whether the code they produce is energy-aware was unclear. The team examines agent-authored pull requests from a public dataset. Energy-explicit changes were isolated for close study.

Two hundred sixteen pull requests made the cut. Thematic analysis produced a taxonomy of energy-aware work. The techniques applied mostly match established research advice. Encouragingly, agents do show energy awareness in their artifacts. A downside tempers the finding. Optimization pull requests are accepted less often than others. Reviewers cite harm to maintainability as the reason. The study maps both the promise and the friction of energy-aware agent coding.
arxiv-2512-24836:
Sandip Maiti, Debasish Banerjee, and Shailesh Chandrasekharan map the phase diagram of a lattice fermion model that can generate mass in two other ways. Fermions may stay massless, gain mass through spontaneous symmetry breaking with a condensate, or gain mass symmetrically without breaking, a process called symmetric mass generation. Fermion-bag Monte Carlo runs on large lattices chart the edges.

Ordinary second-order critical points separate the phases, and those points appear to merge into a multicritical point with enhanced symmetry when a tuning setting vanishes. Readers in lattice field theory get evidence for how symmetric mass generation connects to standard critical behavior.
arxiv-2512-24936:
Katz searches for periodicity in the fast radio burst source FRB 20240114A, an extraordinarily active repeater. Magnetar models predict a spin period, so thousands of bursts offer a chance to find it. One day of observations held over three thousand bursts within a span short enough that slowing would not smear a period above a tenth of a second.

No significant peak appears in the periodogram of those bursts. Injecting artificial modulation shows an amplitude of about fifteen percent would have been detected robustly. Astronomy readers get a firm null result: if bursts are modulated by rotation, the modulation that day was weak or absent.
arxiv-2601-00236:
Mangilal Choudhary, Vanshika, and Surya test a plasma reactor that cleans dye from water without heat. Textile wastewater is hard to treat by standard means. Non thermal plasma offers a chemical attack route. Their reactor uses a dielectric barrier discharge. A liquid electrode forms part of the setup. Discharge happens after the plasma zone, in a post discharge design.

The team tunes operating settings for stronger dye breakdown. Crystal violet serves as the first test dye. Its reaction kinetics are tracked in detail. Other synthetic dyes then face the same reactor. Those samples model real textile effluent. Results suggest the design can degrade several dyes well. The authors frame it as a primary lab study. Scale up questions remain open for later work. Still, a promising path toward full mineralization appears. Cleaner discharge water is the long term goal.
arxiv-2601-00336:
Siddhartha Paul and Adarsh Vishwakarma use a framework called KMOC, which reads classical physics results out of quantum scattering calculations. Their 2026 paper applies it to electromagnetic observables in four dimensions. The focus is the linear memory effect, a lasting shift left by passing radiation, together with its tail contributions, which arrive later after scattering.

Soft-photon theorems, rules for very low-energy photons, supply the kernel for the radiation. With it, the pair show how memory and tail effects emerge straight from scattering data. They then turn the logic around. Requiring those effects to behave as expected places nontrivial demands on the underlying scattering matrix. The authors read those demands as a form of large-scale causality imposed on it.
arxiv-2601-00536:
Yuelyu Ji, Zhuochun Li, Rui Meng, and Daqing He survey how systems answer questions that need several hops of evidence. A multi-hop question cannot be settled from one passage; the system must retrieve, reason, retrieve again, and know when to stop. Many recent retrieval and agent methods report strong scores, yet the step-by-step process behind them is often left vague.

The authors organize that process along four axes: the overall execution plan, the index structure, how the next step is chosen, and the stop or continue criteria. They map representative systems onto this framework and compare reported ablations on standard benchmarks such as HotpotQA and MuSiQue. Recurring trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, and faithfulness to evidence emerge from the comparison.
arxiv-2601-00936:
M P V S Gopinadh and S Mahaboob Hussain test whether emojis can smuggle harmful requests past a language model's safety training. Adversarial prompts that hide intent are a standing threat to deployed systems, and pictures of symbols are an understudied disguise. The authors built fifty emoji-based prompts and ran them against four open-source models of similar size.

Responses were scored as successful, partial, or failed jailbreaks, alongside safety adherence and response latency. Two models, Gemma 2 and Mistral, allowed about ten percent of attacks through, while Qwen 2 blocked every attempt in the test set. A chi-square test confirmed the differences between models are statistically significant. The study maps uneven emoji vulnerabilities that safety teams should probe before release.
arxiv-2601-01136:
Guoping Zhang surveys and organizes the question of whether the eigenstates of quantum mechanics form a complete set. Completeness means any state can be built from these basic states, a fact that much of quantum theory quietly assumes. Zhang splits the proof by how the potential energy behaves far away, giving eight cases in all.

For each case, the paper offers a theoretical proof or a computer simulation. It also gives a general way to normalize free states, solves for the needed coefficients, and proposes a general set of starting states that makes the proof simpler and more concrete. A spectral function is defined for states with a continuous range of energies. With it, the link between measured probability and the expansion gains a clear meaning as a change between position and momentum views.
arxiv-2601-01236:
Stefan Kiefer and Andrew Ryzhikov ask how large a finite family of rational matrices can be while still multiplying together in a closed way. Such families, called semigroups, generalize the inner workings of simple automata. A classical result from 1962 bounded the size of the irreducible kind, those with no shared invariant subspace, by a fast-growing function.

Using a very different technique, the authors improve that bound sharply, down to three raised to the square of the matrix size. They also show the new bound is close to best possible by building families that nearly reach it for every size. A side benefit is a better bound on the mortality threshold, the number of factors needed to force a zero product in such families. The results clarify the structure of objects that sit at the crossroads of math and computer science.
arxiv-2601-01636:
Atovullaev and 15 co-authors test a shared iron shield that protects light sensors from stray magnetic fields. Particle detectors built from plastic scintillators measure timing, position, and energy loss, and their sensor tubes often sit near strong magnets that distort readings. The usual fix shields each tube on its own.

Their design wraps a whole row of tubes in one common iron enclosure, with individual metal cylinders inside for extra cover. Used in a 2022 experiment at a Russian institute, the setup kept sensor gain and timing sharpness intact. The team argues the shared design is a practical option for future detector arrays in similar settings.
arxiv-2601-02136:
The BESIII collaboration reports a measurement of a rare charmonium process. It runs at Beijing's electron-positron collider. Collisions produce two neutral pions alongside the ψ(3686) state. Energies run from about four to just under five gigaelectronvolts. A large collected dataset backs the result.

The measured cross sections come out at roughly half those of the charged-pion sibling process, exactly as isospin symmetry predicts. Fitting the energy dependence coherently reveals two structures. One known resonance's parameters stay fixed. The Y(4390) and Y(4660) appear at strength above five standard deviations each. Their masses and widths match the earlier charged-channel measurement. Such Y states remain among the most puzzling exotics in hadron studies. Each separate channel tightens their profile.
arxiv-2601-02236:
Diffusion language models could generate text in parallel. Training teaches them small local steps under fixed schedules, though. Fast inference demands long jumps through states never seen in training. Yihao Liang and ten co-authors close that gap with CD4LM. The fix splits into distillation for training and adaptive decoding for inference.

Discrete-space consistency distillation trains a student in a special way. Many different noisy states map straight to the clean distribution. The student grows robust to jumps. Confidence-adaptive decoding then spends computation only where tokens are uncertain. Steps are skipped aggressively without the usual quality collapse. On GSM8K, the system matched its baseline's accuracy. Its speedup topped five times. Across math and code benchmarks, it averaged more than triple the speed with better accuracy.
arxiv-2601-02636:
Byungwoo Kang, Maceo Richards, and Bernardo Sabatini tackle credit assignment, the problem of deciding which neurons and synapses caused a network's output, in a way a brain could plausibly implement. One biological candidate is noise correlation, which estimates gradients by wiggling activity and correlating the wiggles with output changes. It scales badly, because the number of wiggles needed grows with network size. And perfectly round noise also clashes with the fact that real neural activity lives on a low dimensional surface, a manifold.

Their method restricts the wiggles to that manifold. Theory and experiments show the space a gradient lives in aligns with the manifold in trained networks, and that the manifold's dimension grows slowly with network size. Manifold restricted noise therefore estimates credit far more efficiently, improving performance and sample efficiency over the plain noise method.
arxiv-2601-02836:
Klaus Jansen and Felix Ohnesorge give a practical approximation algorithm for moldable job scheduling. Each job can run on any number of identical machines. It runs faster, or at least no slower, as more machines are assigned. Scheduling such jobs to finish as early as possible is hard to solve exactly, so approximation guarantees matter. The best earlier options were a theoretical scheme whose running time explodes as accuracy tightens, a fully polynomial scheme that needs very many machines, and a simpler three halves approximation.

Their algorithm guarantees a ratio near one point four six, improving on three halves, and runs in time that grows gently with the accuracy parameter. Better still, the result covers the contiguous variant, where a job's machines must form a single block. The authors stress practical efficiency alongside the improved bound.
arxiv-2601-02936:
Zhijie Huang and five co-authors probe the magnetism of a layered organic conductor with the long name kappa-(BETS)2Mn[N(CN)2]3, using electron spin resonance. The material draws interest because its molecular pi-electrons couple magnetically to manganese ions. The team measures how the spin susceptibility, g-factor, and resonance linewidth change with temperature and with the direction of the applied field.

At low temperatures the g-factor shifts enormously, with an in-plane pattern that flips as the sample cools. The lines also broaden, and the susceptibility rises with a kink at the phase transition. Careful analysis of the angular patterns points to anisotropic Zeeman effects alongside spin-phonon coupling. The authors conclude there are two magnetically distinct BETS chains and raise the possibility of altermagnetic order.
arxiv-2601-03136:
Selma Wanna and six co-authors audit the language inside datasets used to train embodied AI systems, the vision-language-action models that turn instructions into robot behavior. Language steers these models, yet the instruction text in popular corpora had never been systematically documented. The team measures the corpora along several dimensions, including word variety, duplication, semantic similarity, and sentence complexity.

The audit finds that many datasets rely on highly repetitive, template-like commands with little structural variety, so the range of instruction forms a model ever sees is narrow. The authors present the findings as descriptive documentation rather than criticism. Their aim is to support better dataset reporting, more principled dataset choice, and targeted curation or augmentation that broadens the language these robots are trained on.
arxiv-2601-03636:
Shu Hamanaka, writing alone, rethinks a boundary effect in non-Hermitian physics for systems that are nonlinear. In linear non-Hermitian systems, the skin effect piles states at the boundary, but nonlinear systems have no clean eigenstates to pile. Hamanaka proposes describing the effect through the Koopman framework, which lifts dynamics into a space of observables where functions, not states, carry the behavior.

Using a mildly nonlinear version of the Hatano-Nelson model, the study shows dominant Koopman functions localizing sharply on higher-order observables, unlike the linear case. That lifted piling controls how strongly the system reacts to boundary changes, giving a clear fingerprint of the nonlinear skin effect. The setup gives physicists a faithful language for boundary phenomena in driven, nonlinear devices.
arxiv-2601-03736:
Shuyan Bai and seven co-authors introduce HyperCOD, the first large benchmark for finding camouflaged objects in hyperspectral images. Ordinary color images rely on color and texture cues that camouflage defeats. Hyperspectral cameras record fine-grained spectral signatures instead, offering another way to separate an animal or object from its background, but the field lacked a dedicated dataset to compare methods fairly.

HyperCOD contains three hundred fifty high-resolution hyperspectral images with hard real-world traits: tiny objects, intricate shapes, heavy occlusion, and changing light. The team also adapts the Segment Anything Model into HSC-SAM by reformulating the input, feeding a spatial map to its encoder while using spectral information separately. A shared hard benchmark plus a strong baseline should accelerate work on search, wildlife monitoring, and defense imaging.
arxiv-2601-04036:
David Stap, in a sole-authored thesis, studies how multilingual translation models move knowledge between languages. Such transfer matters most for languages with little paired training text. Stap treats neural machine translation as the main test case for wider multilingual learning.

The thesis examines how likeness between languages shapes transfer and how retrieval or extra supervision can help low-resource pairs. It also shows that fine-tuning on paired data can create unwanted side effects in large language models. Training with more varied languages improves general performance and cuts off-target output, where a model answers in the wrong language. Together the chapters link data makeup and training choices to fairer, sturdier multilingual systems.
arxiv-2601-04336:
William Franz Lamberti, Sunbin Kim, and Samantha Rose Lawrence report a pilot survey of what university students think about generative AI in their classrooms, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Opinion on the technology's proper place in education is divided, and the team set out to take a first measurement that larger studies could build on.

The pilot's loudest finding is about participation itself: only about one invited student in twenty-two responded. the authors flag as a warning about how hard it is to engage students in research about AI at all. Within those limits, the responses sketch student attitudes toward classroom use of generative tools. The authors present the work as groundwork, arguing instructors need such evidence to lead informed, critical discussion of the technology rather than guess at student views.
arxiv-2601-04436:
Kanishk Gandhi, Agam Bhatia, and Noah D. Goodman study what it takes to predict the next line of a conversation, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Guessing what someone will say means modelling how they think, so the team compares training schemes for next-turn dialogue prediction along two axes. Whether the model may think before answering, and what it is rewarded for — a judge model's similarity scores, or the actual words people said.

The judge-based route backfires: scores from the judge climb while the model's grip on real human replies loosens. human raters pick its outputs as human-like less often, especially when the model thinks first. Training directly on the probability of observed replies improves both measures. Best of all is treating the thinking itself as a hidden variable and optimizing a derived bound, suggesting that reasoning helps only when training stays anchored to real dialogue.
arxiv-2601-04636:
Duc Manh Doan and Hung Q. Nguyen test a paradox of quantum nonlocality in a ring of four particles, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hardy's nonlocality argument exposes conflicts between quantum predictions and local hidden variables without inequalities, but it has mostly been studied when every particle is entangled with every other. Their system is sparser: four particles in a cycle, each entangled only with its two neighbours.

That structure, they find, enlarges the set of conditions producing the contradiction with local realism, because excluded states and correlations multiply while each measurement touches only its paired partners. They design quantum circuits matching the cyclic structure and identify the correlation patterns in simulation. Running the circuits on IBM's Brisbane quantum processor is the sobering coda. The hardware results deviate considerably from simulation, a reminder of the gap between nonlocality demonstrations on paper and on present-day machines.
arxiv-2601-04736:
Han Zhu and ten co-authors defend multimodal chatbots against attacks that arrive one innocent turn at a time, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A single malicious image-question pair is easy to refuse; a patient adversary instead rebuilds harmful intent gradually across a multi-turn, multi-image conversation, slipping past per-turn filters. Standard preference training was designed for single exchanges and needs expensive annotation, so it misses these cross-turn dynamics.

The team open-sources MINT-Safe, over eleven thousand multi-image dialogues plus refusal examples built by multi-agent generation with image synthesis. On top of it, TAD-Align trains with a turn-aware reward: rollouts reveal which turns show inconsistent safety behaviour, and optimization up-weights exactly those turns. Across two open multimodal models, attack success rates drop by more than ten points while harmlessness and helpfulness both improve and general capability survives.
arxiv-2601-05236:
M. F. DiScala and 7 co-authors check whether chemical disorder disturbs the nickel ions in a frustrated magnet in a 2026 paper. Their material, NaCaNi2F7, is a rare spin-1 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the pyrochlore lattice, a network of corner-sharing tetrahedra. Sodium and calcium share one site at random, and that A-site disorder could complicate the local electronic and magnetic environment of the nickel ions on the other site.

Using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the nickel edge, they find the nickel electronic structure sits in nearly ideal octahedral coordination, needing only a small trigonal compression to explain every spectral feature. A stable local structure means the material's exotic magnetism can be studied without disorder dominating, keeping it valuable for frustrated magnetism research.
arxiv-2601-05536:
Shreya Shankar and 2 co-authors introduce task cascades, a 2026 framework for cutting the cost of running language models over large document collections. Databases increasingly let users ask natural-language questions over text columns, row by row. A cheap model can handle easy cases, with hard ones passed to an expensive oracle.

Standard cascades vary only the model. Task cascades also vary which part of a document is read and which simpler, related operation is run first. An agent generates hundreds of candidate tasks and assembles them into a cascade. The authors prove optimal selection is intractable, give an iterative builder, and add an accuracy-guarantee extension. Across eight tasks, costs fell by about a third on average.
arxiv-2601-05736:
Mate Krezinger and 11 co-authors present, in a 2026 survey, milliarcsecond-resolution radio images of seventeen blazar candidates at very high redshift. Blazars are active galactic nuclei whose jets point nearly toward Earth, boosting their apparent brightness. Confirming that classification at early cosmic times needs extremely sharp radio imaging.

Using the European VLBI Network, the team imaged compact core and core-jet structures. Archival radio, optical, and X-ray data helped separate true blazars from misaligned jetted sources. Eleven objects showed the Doppler-boosted emission expected of blazars. Five more lacked boosting despite suggestive X-ray data, possibly due to variability, and two looked like non-blazars. The survey grows the imaged high-redshift quasar sample by about a tenth.
arxiv-2601-06536:
Student writing and the feedback on it are usually studied apart. Dennis Zyska and 3 co-authors release Exposía in a 2026 paper, the first public dataset connecting both in higher education. It comes from a computer science course on scientific work, where students draft research project proposals and review each other's drafts.

The dataset holds proposals plus peer and instructor feedback as comments and free-text reviews, reflecting the draft-feedback-revision cycle. Human scores accompany both writing and feedback, graded on a fine-grained pedagogical schema the authors developed. Benchmarking leading language models on scoring proposals and scoring reviews showed different models win the two tasks. Closed models consistently beat open-weight ones, and scoring several aspects together in one prompt worked best, informing classroom deployment.
arxiv-2601-06936:
Jiangnan Biguo and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with unified geometric perspective for Spin-1 systems. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors present a unified geometric approach for spin-1 systems that connects seemingly distinct geometric representations such as the nematic director.

The Cartesian representation and the Majorana stellar representation. Starting from a product state of two distinguishable spin-1/2 particles, we provide a direct way to capture crucial geometric information. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07036:
Wang Yang and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers Mid-Think. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Hybrid reasoning language models are commonly controlled through high-level Think/No-think instructions to regulate reasoning behavior. Yet we found that such mode switching is largely driven by a small set of trigger tokens rather than the instructions themselves.

Through attention analysis and controlled prompting experiments. The authors show that a leading “Okay” token induces reasoning behavior, while the newline pattern following “</think>” suppresses it. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07136: Daniel Liu and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers Large-Scale study on the development and issues of Multi-Agent AI systems. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The rapid emergence of multi-agent AI systems (MAS), including LangChain. CrewAI, and AutoGen, has shaped how large language model (LLM) applications are developed and orchestrated. However, little is known about how these systems evolve and are maintained in practice. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07336:
Alexander Karpov and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers improved lower bounds for the maximum size of condorcet domains. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Condorcet domains are sets of linear orders with the property that, whenever voters’ preferences are restricted to the domain. The pairwise majority relation (for an odd number of voters) is transitive and hence a linear order.

Determining the maximum size of a Condorcet domain, sometimes under additional constraints, has been a longstanding problem in the mathematical theory of majority voting. The exact maximum is only known for n 8 n 8 alternatives. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07536:
Bui Ngoc Thanh Binh and colleagues build security directly into the network path for Internet of Things devices. Their 2026 preprint targets MQTT, the lightweight publish-subscribe protocol that dominates IoT messaging. Edge security for MQTT remains weak, they argue. Cloud intrusion detection adds delay, which real-time control cannot afford.

CPU-bound firewalls and generic software-defined networking controllers lack awareness of MQTT itself. They cannot easily check sessions, enforce topic-based permissions, or spot odd behavior. The authors design a protocol-aware P4 pipeline, using the P4 language for programmable data planes. It aims to catch and blunt attacks at the edge. The work fits systems that need fast, local protection.
arxiv-2601-07936:
J A Silva, F C Carvalho, and Antonio R G Garcia extend a classic gravity scheme to metrics that jump. The Darmois-Israel junction rules match regions of spacetime across a boundary. Their 2026 preprint extends them to metrics that break and jump. The framework is Colombeau algebras of generalized functions. That scheme gives a sound way to multiply and take slopes of singular quantities like distributions.

Junction rules matter where thin shells of matter or sharp edges show up in relativity. Metrics that jump push the standard tools past their safe zone. Products of distributions have no clear sense in classical theory. Colombeau algebras were built to give them meaning. The paper serves those who do math work on relativity. It widens the class of spacetimes whose matching can be treated rigorously. Thin shells sound like a niche case, yet stars and shock fronts can act just like them.
arxiv-2601-08036:
Bonan Kou and coauthors build API guides from the questions that coders ask online. API guides teach coders how to use a library or a service. Many official guides are out of date or leave gaps. Their system, AutoDoc, pulls API facts from Stack Overflow threads. It then builds guides from that crowd based store of facts. Their 2026 preprint appears at a major software engineering conference.

Stack Overflow holds years of hands on fixes that official guides never caught. To mine it turns group problem solving into neat reference material. Fresh documentation could reduce the errors developers make with aging guides. The approach must filter wrong or outdated answers from the crowd. The paper serves scholars of software building and teams who write guides. It treats developer forums as a living source for the manuals they wish existed. The source is vast and fresh, with new fixes added each day.
arxiv-2601-08136: Zeyang Li, Sunbochen Tang, and Navid Azizan present reverse flow matching for online reinforcement learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that diffusion and flow policies are gaining ground for their expressive power. Training them online stays hard for a basic reason. Online learning lacks direct samples from the target distribution. Instead, the target is an unnormalized Boltzmann distribution set by the learned Q-function. Reverse flow matching offers one unified framework for this setting. It aims to train rich flow-based policies from reward signals alone.
arxiv-2601-08736:
Ping Zhao looks again at a known test for data with very many traits. The test uses the sign of each point, that is, which side of the mean it falls on. Past work found the shape of the test score when no real effect is there. Zhao asks if that shape holds under weak rules on how traits link.

He shows the score does not settle to the plain bell shape that many expect. It settles to a mix of a bell shape and a weighted square type shape. That mix shifts how cut off values should be set. A reader who tests high trait data gets a warn. Use of the old bell shape cut off can give the wrong call on chance.
arxiv-2601-09236:
Chaitanya Kharyal, Calarina Muslimani, and Matthew Taylor learn reward rules from human marks given as grades, not picks. In trial learn, a reward rule tells an agent what counts as good. Hand rules are a known choke point. Grades, such as a score out of five, hold more sense than a pick of A or B. They may also ask less of the grader.

The team tests a learn rule based on grade rank and squared gap. It fits a reward that keeps grades in the right order, with right gaps. Past grade learn work was thin next to pick work. A reader in agent train gets a way to use rich grades that folk can give with ease.
arxiv-2601-09436:
M. Napsuciale and S. Rodríguez show a shortcut for a workhorse method of quantum physics. Their 2026 arXiv paper recovers Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory from the supersymmetric expansion algorithm. Perturbation theory corrects known energy levels step by step when a system is slightly disturbed.

The usual route sums over all the states in between, which is slow and prone to slips. The supersymmetric route skips those sums entirely. Corrections to energies and states come out as sums weighted by the chance curves of edge states of partner Hamiltonians. A cleaner formula helps both hand calculation and teaching of the method.
arxiv-2601-09836:
Hadis Rezaei, Rahim Taheri, and Francesco Palmieri build a graded test set for a notorious smart contract flaw. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a risk-stratified benchmark for bad randomness, cataloged as SWC-120, in Ethereum contracts. Many contracts draw randomness from block values such as timestamps or block hashes.

Those values are predictable and can be nudged by miners. The flaw has powered real-world exploits in lotteries and games. A benchmark sorted by risk lets scanner tools prove themselves on realistic cases. Better detection protects users who trust contract code with real funds.
arxiv-2601-09936:
Joaquín Lema builds new surfaces tied to a class of flat bundles. The bundles are G-opers for a complex Lie group G. Past work by Epstein built such surfaces for one group. That group was the group of moves of the complex plane.

Lema lifts the build to groups of adjoint type. For each oper, he makes a matched surface. The surface sits in a space tied to the group. It codes facts about the oper in shape form. Such lifts help link the study of bundles with the study of shapes. They may also aid work on flat links and their moduli.
arxiv-2601-10036:
Hitesh Kumar, Bojan Mohar, Shivaramakrishna Pragada, and Hanmeng Zhan study tree graphs by their top tones. For a graph, the top two tones come from how its nodes link. The sum of the two is named the spectral sum. Trees are graphs with no loops.

The team looks at a mix of the first and second tones. A mix weights one more than the other. They ask which trees make such a mix large or small. Tone sums code facts about links and walks on the graph. Sharp bounds help sort trees by shape. The work fits the wider study of graph tones.
arxiv-2601-10236:
Bohan Zhang, Chengke Bu, and Paramveer Dhillon ask who owns text made with AI help. AI aids cut work and smooth prose. But they can make a writer feel the text is less theirs. That feel can change how much a writer trusts and uses the aid.

The team built an aid that gives line by line tips on call. They test two design picks. One is a coach voice with a set role. One tunes tips to the writer's own style. They ask which picks keep the sense of own work strong. The work gives design rules for aids that help sans theft of voice.
arxiv-2601-10636:
Yazan Alamoudi works on sums that count prime factors of integers, a topic in analytic number theory. The sums weight each integer by the Möbius function and by how many prime factors it has. They link to Alladi's higher-order duality, a known symmetry between small and large prime factors. Getting sharp estimates for such sums is the goal.

Alamoudi uses a variant of the Selberg-Delange method, a classic tool for counting problems with prime factors. He allows the cutoff in the sums to grow with the range, within set limits. The estimates sharpen what is known about these sifted sums. Results like these feed the study of how prime factors are spread among whole numbers.
arxiv-2601-10736:
Johannes Hagel studies when invariant tubes in a dynamical system break apart. The systems come from time-dependent Ermakov-type equations. A tube is a family of paths that the flow carries into itself. Starting from a reference system whose tubes are known exactly, he builds a close geometric picture of the perturbed motion.

The perturbation keeps positivity and works to second order. Hagel then seeks an algebraic test for rupture based on a cubic discriminant. A single formula that flags break-up would be cheap to check in practice. The work serves the study of driven oscillators and traps, where keeping motion inside a tube means keeping the system stable.
arxiv-2601-10836:
Gerhard Krumpl, Henning Avenhaus, and Horst Possegger study how training choices shape out-of-distribution detection. Detectors must flag inputs that differ from what a model was trained on. They are key to safe deployment in open worlds. Yet most work tunes detectors alone, apart from the training pipelines that boost in-distribution accuracy.

The authors ask whether one model can show many behaviors: strong on known data, yet honest about strange data. Their empirical study links training recipes to detector performance. Some tricks that raise accuracy may quietly harm detection. The findings guide teams that need both skill and self-knowledge from the same model.
arxiv-2601-10936:
Piyush Maheshwari, Sheshera Mysore, and Hamed Zamani ask whether instructed retrieval models can really support exploration. Exploratory search has vague goals that shift as the user learns. A retrieval model that follows instructions could adapt results to those shifting intents. Such models promise exactly that skill. The authors test the promise directly.

The study checks whether the models capture user-specified nuance in query intent. It also checks whether results adapt as intent evolves. Exploration is where search tools earn trust: a user who cannot state the goal needs a partner, not a slot machine. The findings guide designers of search for research, shopping, and discovery.
arxiv-2601-11036:
Kecheng Cai and co-authors present a self-augmented mixture-of-experts model for quality of service prediction. QoS prediction asks how a service will perform for a given user: response time, availability, and the like. It is a basic problem in service computing and recommendation. Users and services each carry descriptive features, and past interactions give feedback values.

A mixture-of-experts design lets specialist sub-models handle different user-service patterns. Self-augmentation enriches the data the model learns from. Good QoS forecasts help systems pick services that will not stall. The work serves cloud and platform teams that must match users to services before anyone waits on a slow call.
arxiv-2601-11136:
Martí Berenguer, Johanna Erdmenger, Nick Evans, Wanxiang Fan, and Florian Vasel revisit confinement in holography. They study N=4 super Yang-Mills theory compactified on a spatial circle. At a thermal first-order transition, the dominant bulk geometry swaps. One saddle has a compact spatial circle; the other has a compact Euclidean time circle. Their exchange marks the transition.

The authors frame the swap as a smooth switch-off of confinement. Holography turns a hard gauge theory question into geometry. A clean account of the switch helps physicists read confinement, the force that traps quarks, through the gravitational mirror. The work refines a classic holographic model of the confinement transition.
arxiv-2601-11636:
Gaurav Saini, Bappa Ghosh, and Sunita Chand model Zika spread with memory in time. Their 2026 preprint gives basic checks and numeric studies. Models of outbreaks are key tools for how groups change. They aid prediction and control of outbreaks in practice.

The model tracks Zika virus transmission in two populations. Humans and mosquitoes pass the virus between them. Time terms with memory make past states weigh on the spread. Past states then weigh on how the epidemic moves now. Basic checks test if the model's balance points hold. Numeric studies show the spread under set scenarios. Models with memory can fit real outbreak curves more closely.
arxiv-2601-11836:
Finn Hackett, Evan Wrench, Peter Macko, and their co-authors present a way to check concurrent code as it runs, with no changes to the code. Concurrent systems are hard to check. Rare thread orders can hide bugs for a long time, and most tools need code changes or fake run models.

Their method, called OmniLink in the work, checks real runs against a high level spec in TLA+. A tool that needs no code change can be used on live systems. It can catch rare order bugs that tests miss. The work links formal specs to real code in a new way.
arxiv-2601-12336:
Rakesh Pandey, Aina Palau, Alvaro Sánchez-Monge, and their co-authors study the space round a candidate bloated O-type star, IRAS 19520+2759. Bloated stars are young, swollen massive stars still in their birth cloud. They use high-resolution data from ALMA and the EVLA array.

EVLA radio data in three bands give a spectral index of 0.5. That value fits a thermal jet from the star. ALMA data add the cold gas and dust view. Joint views help show how massive stars launch jets as they form.  Jet signs tell how the young star sheds mass.
arxiv-2601-12536:
Tom de Jong and Martin Hotzel Escardo work in univalent mathematics, a modern foundation for math. They study injective types, objects with a strong extension property. Several big examples were already known to be injective. Those include type universes, reflective subuniverses, and algebras of the lifting monad.

The pair add many more examples, and some counterexamples too. They show the type of ordinals is injective, as are iterative sets and multisets. Pointed directed complete posets also qualify, as do small infinity magmas, monoids, and groups. A catalog of this kind helps type theorists know which constructions are safe. Counterexamples matter just as much, since they mark where the property stops.
arxiv-2601-12636:
Satyaki Roy Chowdhury and three co authors study how a model reads water depth from satellite images. The images come from the Sentinel 2 satellite, and the task is bathymetry, mapping depth under shallow water. Deploying such models robustly across many sites remains a challenge. The team analyze a model that joins a Swin Transformer with a U Net.

They ask how the model infers depth and when its outputs can be trusted. A leave one band out study ranks which spectral bands matter most. The ranking lines up with the optics of shallow water, a good sanity check. Knowing which bands drive a depth call helps users spot bad predictions. The work serves coastal mapping from space.
arxiv-2601-12736:
Qingtian Zhu and four co authors rebuild faces in three dimensions from a single photo. Their system is called KaoLRM. It repurposes a large reconstruction model, retargeting its learned prior for faces. Parametric face models, called 3D morphable models, describe a face with a compact, interpretable parameter set.

Regressors for those models often lack consistency across viewpoints, though. The same face seen from a new angle may yield a different reconstruction. A strong learned prior from a large model could stabilize those estimates. Single view face reconstruction serves avatars, effects, and biometrics. Better view consistency would make all of those uses more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-12836:
Kamaljeet Singh and three co authors design light alloys for beam pipes in particle accelerators. A beam pipe guides particle beams through a detector, and its material matters. The pipe should be light to particles yet stiff enough to hold shape. The team develop next generation ternary magnesium aluminum lithium alloys for this role.

Their objective balances high radiation length with strong stiffness properties. Radiation length measures how much a material disturbs passing particles. Conventional benchmarks are aluminum, titanium, and stainless steel pipes. A lighter, stiffer alloy would sharpen detector measurements near the beam. The work links alloy design with the needs of high energy physics.
arxiv-2601-13236:
Ilias I. Giannakopoulos and co-authors add doubt maps to fast MRI scans. Fast scan tricks cut the time a patient spends in the scanner. As the speed up grows, though, image grade falls. In real care, teams pick slow speeds since no tool checks if a fast scan is still fit to read.

The team gives a per pixel doubt score for each rebuilt scan. A high doubt spot flags where the rebuild may be off. Such a map could let teams speed up when the map stays calm and slow down when it flares. For care work, a sound doubt map may mean more fast scans that stay safe to use.
arxiv-2601-14036:
Maria-Catalina Isfan, Laurentiu-Ioan Caramete, and Ana Caramete run a quantum neural network on cloud quantum machines in 2026. Their network was built for gravitational wave data analysis. The target is the LISA space mission, which will hear low-frequency waves from space. They built the network with the Qiskit library in Python.

They evaluate state-of-the-art cloud quantum computers from big providers. IBM, IonQ, and IQM Quantum Computers are among the named platforms. Running the same network across machines shows where each stands. Gravitational wave work may one day gain from quantum speed on hard data.
arxiv-2601-14536:
Tiantian Yang, Yuxuan Wang, Zhenwei Zhou, and Ching-Ti Liu classify disease from omics data in this 2026 paper. Omics data, such as transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, give critical insights into disease mechanisms and clinical outcomes. They are hard to learn from, though. Their dimensionality is high, sample sizes are small, and the biological networks behind them are intricate.

Graph neural networks offer a promising route, since they can encode feature relationships as graphs from prior knowledge. The team's method, engGNN, uses a dual-graph design. It targets both disease classification and feature selection. Readers get a model that predicts disease while also naming which molecular features drive the call.
arxiv-2601-14636:
Rakshanda Goswami, Pulak Talukdar, Bhoomika Das, Udit Raha, and Fred Myhrer compute a scattering correction in this 2026 paper. Their topic is elastic lepton-proton scattering, a basic probe of proton structure. They present an exact analytical evaluation of the two-photon exchange correction to its differential cross section at low energies. The framework is heavy-baryon chiral perturbation theory, carried to next-to-next-to-leading order with hadronic effects included.

Their analysis focuses on the kinematic regime relevant to the ongoing MUSE experiment. MUSE scatters muons and electrons off protons to test lepton universality. The authors restrict the intermediate states to the dominant elastic channel. The work is pure math. No new lab run is used, but the end terms feed straight into how the MUSE data will be read. Readers get an exact correction term for a precision experiment that compares how distinct leptons strike the same proton.
arxiv-2601-15036:
Dirk Tasche revisits a kind of shift that can hit a dataset between training and use. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with factorizable joint shift. Under this shift, both the input mix and the label mix change at once.

Recent work showed that this shift arises from two shifts in a row. A label shift and a covariate shift can follow each other in either order. Work so far stayed with labels that fall into fixed classes. Tasche takes the idea further and asks what the factorization means for learning in practice.
arxiv-2601-15236:
Anjishnu Mukherjee, Ziwei Zhu, and Antonios Anastasopoulos teach language models a sense of place. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a common flaw: models are trained on text as one global mix. The result is behavior that is geographically homogenized, the same everywhere.

The team studies metadata conditioning as a light fix. They pre-train dozens of small models from scratch on English news text. Each text is tagged with its source URL, country, and continent. The data spans four continents and seventeen countries, and the tags steer the models toward local norms.
arxiv-2601-15836:
Nicola Gallucci and a large team classify health-related radio signals in a 2026 arXiv paper. Wearable health monitors rely on radio links to report data. Reliable systems need awareness of interference around them. The 2.4 GHz ISM band is overcrowded with other devices. In it, low-power medical transmissions are hard to spot. Strong co-channel interference and power asymmetry hide them.

The paper works on SmartBAN signals, a standard for body-area networks. Classifying them under heavy interference is the challenge. A classifier that spots medical traffic can help systems avoid collisions. It can also warn when conditions threaten the link. For patients who depend on wearables, that awareness is a safety feature, not a luxury.
arxiv-2601-15936:
Tessa Wilkie, Idris Eckley, Paul Fearnhead, and Ian Gregory audit a historical health dataset in a 2026 arXiv paper. The data record infant mortality in England and Wales. Counts are kept by local government district. Such records offer insight into how society changed across the twentieth century. Analysis is tricky in practice. District boundaries changed often, so areas do not line up over time.

The authors detect interpolation errors in the counts. Interpolation fills gaps by estimating between known values. Errors there can fake trends in child health. Careful detection protects historians and demographers from false stories. Infant mortality is a sensitive marker of public health. Getting its history right matters for understanding what policies and conditions saved lives.
arxiv-2601-16136:
Diego Céspedes and Sebastián Donoso show a fail case for mean sums along a prime count map. Their 2026 preprint sits in number field maths. The Omega map counts prime parts of a whole number, with repeats. Mean sums along that map were thought to settle at each point. The pair test that hope in the field of number fields.

They show the sums can fail to settle point by point. A clear case uses sums over pairs that feed the map. The fail marks a bound on when such means can be trusted. It guides later work on means along wild count maps. The proof is a warn case in the field.
arxiv-2601-16536:
Yuanhong He and four coauthors tune mixed grade matrix times on Ascend chips. Their 2026 preprint deals with W4A16, a mix of weight and act grades. Weights use four bits while acts use twice times four bits. The mix cuts the store size of large models much. It keeps loss of truth low if the sums run well.

Ascend 910 chips pose hard bounds for such mixed sums. Store moves, not math, oft set the true speed cap. The team maps those move caps and shapes sums to fit. Fit sums would let big models run on less gear. The work serves low cost model use at scale.
arxiv-2601-16936:
Anton Zamyatin, Patrick Indri, Sagar Malhotra, and Thomas Gärtner test a lean team-in-one net. Full teams of nets give sound doubt gauges. But each team mate costs full train time and space. BatchEnsemble packs a team in one base net. Small rank-one tweaks set each mate apart. Their 2026 preprint asks if that pack is truly one model or many.

The team checks doubt skill and spread of calls. Lean teams suit phones and fast apps with tight caps. If the pack's doubt is sound, it saves much cost. The checks show where the pack holds and where it thins. Buyers gain proof for picks in tight spots.
arxiv-2601-17136:
Julian Bellavita and a team of six co-authors speed a famed group-sort tool on GPUs. K-means sorts points in groups by their hubs. It is a core tool in data work of all kinds. Plain K-means can't draw bent group walls. Kernel forms fix that, but cost much more. Their 2026 preprint cuts the talk twixt cores that slows those forms.

Less talk lets GPU cores run near full pace. Bent-wall sorts then run at near-plain cost. Big data sets in shops and labs gain most. Fast sorts feed search, shots, and sales tools.
arxiv-2601-17436:
Anosh Joseph proposes a thermometer for lattice gauge theory simulations. Such simulations model strong-force physics on a grid. Checking their heat is a basic need. His estimator reads temperature from the gradient and Hessian of the lattice action. It is gauge invariant, so it does not depend on gauge choice. It uses configurations alone, with no momentum data.

Those traits let users check thermodynamic consistency in Monte Carlo runs. A bad run can waste vast compute time. A quick, sound check catches drift early. The tool fits the daily flow of lattice work. It adds trust to results that rest on long simulations. Other groups can adopt it with little cost.
arxiv-2601-17536:
Jiaming Liang, Haowei Liu, and Chi-Man Pun measure how easy an image is to attack. Neural networks can be fooled by tiny, crafted changes. Some images fall fast; others resist well. That trait is called attackability. It matters for active learning and for tests of robustness. The authors propose OTI, a model-free measure of it. OTI is also visually interpretable.

A clear score lets teams see why one image is weak. They can pick strong samples for training or audits. Model-free means the score needs no access to the target net. That widens its use across systems. The work helps safety teams spend attack tests where they count.
arxiv-2601-17636:
Aayush Gupta and five co-authors present HealDA, a fix for a weak point in AI weather forecasts. Machine learning weather models now rival top classic systems at medium range. Almost all still need classic data assimilation for start conditions. That tie keeps them bound to costly infrastructure. It also caps their speed and accuracy gains. HealDA stresses the role of initial errors.

Initial errors grow through a forecast and set its fate. Highlighting them can guide better assimilation for ML models. A free-standing ML pipeline would run faster and cheaper. That could widen access to top-grade forecasts. The work targets the handoff where ML still leans on the old system.
arxiv-2601-17736:
Can Liu and co-authors present Athanor, a tool to make static charts interactive by voice or text. Interactivity is crucial for good data visualization. Static charts, though, often lack source code and data. Rebuilding them takes long effort even when code exists. Athanor lets users describe changes in natural language. It applies action modifications to the chart as shown.

A working tool would rescue vast chart archives. News, reports, and papers hold millions of static figures. Users could probe them without the author's files. That widens access for analysts and the public. The work treats the image itself as the interface. Language becomes the bridge to interaction.
arxiv-2601-17836:
Weijiang Lai and co-authors work on faster prediction of what a user will click next. Their 2026 preprint sits in the study of recommender systems. Big language models have shown that scale brings skill, and ad systems want the same gains. But modeling long runs of past clicks is costly, since standard attention grows fast as the sequence grows. That cost blocks use in live products.

The team turns to sparse attention, which lets each step look at only part of the past. Picking the right part is the crux when months of behavior matter. Their method aims to keep the signal from long histories while cutting the compute. Better click prediction drives both ads and feeds.
arxiv-2601-17936:
Antonio Falcó, Daniela Falcó-Pomares, and Hermann G. Matthies rebuild basic quantum gates from group geometry. Their 2026 preprint starts from a known oddity. In the standard circuit model, gates are defined against a chosen split of the system into parts. That split is imposed from outside. The full group of motions, U(2^n), has its own geometry that does not need the split. The authors embed Lie groups in that space to define gates from within.

They then study what the shift buys: geometry, universality, and discretization. Universality asks whether the gates can build any operation. Discretization asks how a smooth group yields a finite gate set. The work gives quantum computing a more intrinsic base.
arxiv-2601-18036:
Asmaul Smitha Rashid and co-authors report a direct sighting of paired electron pairs in a graphene device. Their 2026 preprint studies three-terminal Josephson junctions. Such junctions can host effects beyond the reach of the usual two-terminal kind. The team used spectroscopy to observe Cooper quartet resonances. A quartet is a correlated tunneling event in which two Cooper pairs cross the device together. Seeing it directly is a strong sign of that joint motion.

Quartets are a signature of exotic superconducting behavior. They may one day serve quantum circuits that use multi-terminal tricks. Graphene makes a clean test bed because its traits can be tuned in place. The result adds hard data to a young area of quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-18336:
Isaac Deutsch, Nicolas Moënne-Loccoz, Gavriel State, and Zan Gojcic make 3D reconstruction robust to the way cameras alter photos. Their 2026 preprint presents PPISP. Multi-view reconstruction is highly sensitive to photometric inconsistencies. Camera optics and image signal processing change brightness and color from shot to shot. Past fixes use per-frame latent variables or affine color tweaks. Those lack physical grounding and generalize poorly to new views. PPISP instead compensates with a physically plausible model of the imaging pipeline.

A physical model can correct a new view it has never seen. That is the test that matters for real captures. Better color handling means cleaner models for film, retail, and robotics.
arxiv-2601-18436:
Christos Pandis works on a clean shape task: how large a flat slice through a known shape can be. He takes two shapes in many dims. One is the simplex, a kind of multi-sided spike with equal edges. The next is the cube with a set bulk. For each shape he asks which flat cut gives the most area, and which gives the least.

For the simplex he finds a closed form that gives the slice size for each cut. The same form shows which cuts hit the top and the base of the range. He then turns back to the cube and takes a fresh look at its flat cuts in the plane case. Shape facts like these feed work on data, codes, and the maths of high dims, where slices stand in for views of a full set.
arxiv-2601-18836:
Abdelmalek Boumali, Nosratollah Jafari, and Yassine Chargui build a fresh frame for the maths of a spin-free bit in a trap. Their world gives the rules of speed a Planck-scale twist. The twist bends the link between a bit's push and its speed at the high end. Such twists are guessed from plans that join gravity with the quantum world. They are far past lab reach, but their maths can still be worked.

The team first turn the bit's wave rule into a pair of plain rules that are less hard to solve. They build that turn for both the plain twist and a wide form of it.
