With the pair in hand they study a trapped bit and a bit that hits a step wall at high speed. The work is a maths test bed for Planck-scale claims.
arxiv-2601-18936:
Jialei Liu, C. Emre Koksal, and Ming Shi study choices made at two speeds in networks. Some choices, like how much resource to set aside, move slowly. Others, like which job runs next, must react fast to queues and states. The two speeds interact, and each choice can carry a cost when it switches.

The team frames the slow layer as an online convex problem that learns as data comes in. The fast layer is framed as a constrained Markov choice process. Their setup aims at network resource use where slow plans and fast schedules must fit each other, not fight.
arxiv-2601-19036:
Tianxin Tao, Han Liu, and Hung Yu Ling polish machine captured motion until studios can use it. Motion data feeds games, film, virtual worlds, and robots. Camera based capture now looks good at a glance. But the last mile to real use is full of flaws that break the sense of physical truth.

Their fix is based on physics: it refines raw captured motion so feet, weight, and contact behave as real bodies do. The work was shown as a technical talk at SIGGRAPH Asia. Closing that last mile matters because studios judge tools by shipped shots, not by demos.
arxiv-2601-19136:
Iftekhar Ahmed and six co-authors trace retinal blood vessels without the usual breaks and gaps. Maps of eye arteries and veins help doctors spot body wide heart and vessel disease early. Standard convolutional networks often return broken maps, with gaps where thin vessels fade.

Their module, TFFM, fuses features with an eye on topology, reasoning over a hidden graph of how vessels connect. Joined up maps matter: a break can hide a blockage or fake one. The work aims at vessel maps a clinician can trust for screening, not just pretty pictures.
arxiv-2601-19236:
Zhiyu Yin and eight co-authors define a new video task: filling the gap between two clips. Most video generation starts from text or one image. Real uses like editing and vlogging often need smooth content that joins two clips. The join should look as if one camera shot ran through both.

Their bench, VC-Bench, supplies the data set and the scoring rules for this video connecting task. A shared bench lets rival methods be graded on the same joins. Smooth joins would save editors hours of reshoots and patch shots when two good clips refuse to meet.
arxiv-2601-19636:
Pien Rooijendijk, Christoph Treude, and Mairieli Wessel study how security flaws get named in code reviews. Known flaws carry standard identifiers, such as CVE, CWE, and GHSA codes. These codes link a change to public records about the flaw. Yet how people actually use the codes in practice is poorly understood.

The authors compare pull requests on GitHub written by three kinds of authors. Some are human developers, some are simple bots, and some are autonomous agents. Each group may cite identifiers at different rates and in different styles. Knowing the pattern helps maintainers judge how much to trust each source. It also shows where security practice in open source is strong or thin.
arxiv-2601-19936:
Minseo Kwak and Jaehyung Kim work on detecting whether a text was used to train a language model. The secrecy around massive pretraining corpora raises privacy and copyright concerns. Detection methods usually rely on token likelihoods: text the model finds unsurprising was probably in its training data. These methods overlook how the text diverges from the model's own top prediction.

Their method, Gap-K%, measures that top-one prediction gap. It also uses local correlation between neighbouring tokens. Combining both signals should sharpen detection. Reliable detection tools matter for authors, publishers, and regulators auditing models. The work adds a new signal to a contested measurement problem.
arxiv-2601-20036:
Prosenjit Bose, Guillermo Esteban, and Tyler Tuttle solve a covering problem about points in the plane. Given a set of points, they seek a pair with a special property. Any disk that contains both points of the pair must also contain a fixed fraction of all the points. Finding such a pair means finding a location where disks are forced to be crowded.

The authors present several algorithms for the task. This paper is an extended version of a conference paper on the problem. Problems of this kind underlie facility location and clustering, where coverage guarantees matter. A forced-crowding pair certifies density without checking every disk. The work is a neat piece of computational geometry with clean guarantees.
arxiv-2601-20336:
Murad Farzulla asks whether the claims in cryptocurrency whitepapers predict how the coins actually behave in markets. Projects state their value in whitepapers, making claims about function, use cases, and technical ability. The study checks whether those narrative claims line up with observed market behavior, using factor analysis.

Factor analysis groups coins by shared patterns in their returns. If whitepaper claims sort coins the same way the market does, the claims carry real information. If not, investors are reading stories the data do not support. The test gives buyers a check on one of crypto's main sales tools.
arxiv-2601-20536:
Supriya Pisolkar and Biswanath Samanta give a universal construction of p-typical Witt vectors for associative rings. Witt vectors are a tool that lifts arithmetic from finite fields to richer rings, and they come in many constructions. For a prime p and a ring with unity, the existing constructions all reduce to the classical ones when the ring is commutative.

The authors' construction aims to cover the associative case in one frame. Witt vectors underlie modern number theory and the study of formal groups. A universal construction can simplify proofs and unify a scattered literature.
arxiv-2601-20636:
Claudia Negrete, Attila Kákay, and Jorge A. Otálora analyze the origin of spin-wave nonreciprocity in planar magnetic multilayers. Nonreciprocity means waves traveling one way have a different frequency from waves traveling the other, a property many proposed magnonic devices rely on. The effect is usually blamed on dipolar interactions or interfacial chirality.

The microscopic origin in multilayers, though, remains under debate. The authors study structures without Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and argue for an exchange-dominated origin. Settling the mechanism matters for designing devices that route spin waves like signals on a chip. That is a sharp claim, and one the field can now put to the test.
arxiv-2601-20836:
Erekle Jmukhadze, Sam Olin, Allan MacDonald, and Wei-Cheng Lee study layered materials with exotic electronic phases. Their 2026 paper concerns parallel-stacked WSe2, a moiré material made of two twisted sheets. Such homobilayers are topologically non-trivial in both real and momentum space. They are known to host quantum anomalous Hall states, both integer and fractional. They also support magnetic and superconducting states.

The title names the pair's focus: stripe antiferromagnetism and chiral superconductivity. One phase orders magnetic moments in stripes that cancel out. The other carries current without loss in a handed, chiral way. The paper examines how these phases arise in this material. Such layered systems are a rich test bed for new quantum matter. The work helps map which phases win under which conditions.
arxiv-2601-21036:
Chonghuan Wang studies how to experiment when the treatment itself is a match. The 2026 paper concerns experimental design for matching mechanisms. Matching plays a central role in operations management. It assigns students to schools, patients to care, and users to services on platforms. Comparing a new algorithm with the status quo sounds simple. It is not. Matching interference blocks the naive approach.

In matching, assigning one unit changes what remains for others. A unit placed in one matching may be precluded from the other. That entanglement breaks standard A/B test logic. The paper tackles how to design fair comparisons despite it. Sound experiments are vital before platforms swap their matching rules. The work serves any field where assignments, not doses, are the treatment.
arxiv-2601-21336:
Masato Shirasaki, Ryuichi Takahashi, Ken Osato, and Kunihito Ioka link fast radio bursts to the gas held in galaxy halos. Each burst's signal is spread by free electrons along its path, and that spread can be measured. Galaxies mark where much of that gas should sit.

The team cross-matches a large galaxy catalog with a set of bursts whose positions are known. They measure how the signal spread relates to distance from nearby galaxies. The pattern constrains how much gas halos hold compared with their total mass. That ratio is a key clue to how galaxies keep or lose their gas.
arxiv-2601-21636:
Jan Schuchardt and Nikita Kalinin remove random sampling from privacy accounting for matrix-based training methods. Differentially private training often splits work by random allocation, like balls tossed into bins. A recent method computed the privacy gain by Monte Carlo sampling.

Those guarantees held only with high probability, or needed the mechanism to sit out at random. The authors derive the accounting without sampling, giving firm guarantees. Exact accounting matters because privacy budgets are promises made to real people. A promise that holds only probably, or needs random abstention, is weaker than the ledger suggests.
arxiv-2601-21736:
Michael Hinze, Christian Kahle, and Michael Stahl speed up simulations of heat-like equations with a reduced basis method. Parabolic equations model diffusion of heat and chemicals, and they are costly to solve again for every parameter choice. Their method rests on a space-time least squares form that needs only minimal smoothness.

The authors extend that form to parameter-dependent problems. A greedy routine then picks the most informative snapshots to build the small basis. Fast reduced models let engineers test many designs in the time one full solve once took. That speed is what makes live control and optimization over such equations practical.
arxiv-2601-21936:
Jon Chun, Kathrine Elkins, and Yong Suk Lee build a courtroom inside a computer to test high-stakes decisions. Their 2026 preprint introduces AgenticSimLaw, a multi-agent debate framework aimed at tabular decision making, where choices carry real consequences and must be explained.

Unlike black-box systems, the framework assigns clear roles: a prosecutor, a defense, and a judge, modeled on a juvenile courtroom. The agents follow a structured debate over several turns, and each uses private reasoning strategies. Because every step is explicit, the whole decision process can be audited afterward. Transparent test-time reasoning of this kind could help institutions check automated decisions before trusting them with people's lives and livelihoods.
arxiv-2601-22136:
Gloria Felicia and co-authors argue that catching a rogue agent early is worth far more than catching it late. Agent safety benchmarks usually report simple accuracy: was the violation flagged or not? That scoring lumps together a detector that intervenes in time and one that writes a post-mortem.

A flag at an early step lets someone stop the harm. The same flag many steps later has only forensic value. Their 2026 preprint presents StepShield, built to measure when intervention happens, not just whether. Software agents are gaining real powers. They can move money and change records. Benchmarks that reward early detection push the field toward systems that can actually be stopped.
arxiv-2601-22236:
Noah Rogers and nine co-authors report new telescope data on gas clouds that hold very few heavy elements. Their 2026 preprint is part two of a project that uses the Large Binocular Telescope. The team took spectra with the MODS tool to read the light from these clouds.

From the spectra they work out the heat and density of the gas. They also measure how much oxygen each cloud holds. Such clouds are close in mix to the early cosmos. Clean reads of them help pin down how much helium the Big Bang made.
arxiv-2601-22636:
Mingqian Feng and a team measure the true attack risk of language models when foes get many tries. Safety tests often use one or a few attack prompts. Their 2026 preprint notes that real attackers can sample in parallel, again and again, until a harmful reply slips out.

Attack success grows with tries, so low-budget tests understate risk. The team build a statistical way to estimate risk under best-of-N sampling. Firm risk numbers help labs set honest safety bars. They also help buyers judge a model's true exposure. The work replaces a guess with a measure.
arxiv-2601-22736:
Md Musfiqur Rahman and co-authors from Purdue, Johns Hopkins, and Intuit study a hard problem in causal inference. Working with data from past cases, not new trials, they ask how sure we can be about the best action to take. Hidden factors can blur cause and effect, even when data are endless.

The authors split total doubt into parts, so each part can be judged on its own. Recent work used neural networks to set bounds on causal effects, but that task is often too hard to solve exactly. Clearer bounds help decision makers see what the data can prove, and what it cannot.
arxiv-2601-22936:
Charalampos Anastasiou, Julia Karlen, Yao Ma, and George Sterman make a hard particle-physics calculation finite and computable. They target real-virtual terms, at next-to-next-to-leading order, for collisions that produce electroweak or other colorless states. Such terms mix loop integrals with the phase space of outgoing partons.

Their local subtraction scheme cancels all infrared problem points point by point in momentum space. What remains is a finite integral ready for numeric work in four dimensions. Precise predictions of this kind are needed to match collider data. Subtracting problem points at the integrand level is what makes the combined integral ready for direct numeric evaluation.
arxiv-2602-00036: Keishu Utimula builds LOGOS-CA, a cellular automaton whose cell states and rules are written in plain language and updated by a language model. The idea grows from the Winograd Schema Challenge, where models trained only on text show strong common sense, hinting that human language captures much of the world in fine detail. Freed from numbers and fixed rules, the automaton can run richer simulations, and the author shows it handling a simple forest fire. The paper also reads the system as artificial life research.
arxiv-2602-00136: Ti Ti Nguyen and coauthors study semantic loss in deep joint source channel coding for Earth observation imagery. High resolution images aid monitoring, disaster response, and land use work, but their volume strains satellite links with limited bandwidth, power, and changing conditions. The paper first tests a reconstruction frame, tracking semantic decay under varied compression and signal to noise ratios. It then builds a task oriented frame that joins coding with light, task specific models such as EfficientViT, aiming to preserve meaning that downstream tasks need.
arxiv-2602-00736: Arul Pandian B and colleagues present a new pulsar signal-processing pipeline for the Diamond Array Radio Telescope, based at the Gauribidanur observatory. The array uses 32 off-axis dual-polarised LPDAs for transit observations between 130 and 350 MHz. Custom receivers and real-time tools have been built. They produce transient-buffer voltages and full-polar spectral data. It now observes pulsars daily between 170 and 196 MHz, reducing data almost as fast as observations run. Initial results cover five bright pulsars at 175 MHz, including rotation-measure estimates and single-pulse studies.
arxiv-2602-00836: Tanique Schaffe-Odeleye and colleagues show static methods misestimate dynamic effects, and a COVID-19 lockdown study shows the value. They extend potential outcomes to time series, defining causal effects on whole stochastic processes. Their Dynamic Average Treatment Effect tracks how effects evolve and falls back to the classical average treatment effect after one period. For observational data they derive a dynamic weighting estimator unbiased under ignorability and positivity. When few units are treated, conditional mean trajectories take a linear state-space form, giving a dynamic linear model.
arxiv-2602-00936: Ziqing Xiang introduces natural graph matrices, built from the adjacency matrix by a fixed sequence of basic operations. The class covers adjacency, Seidel, Laplacian, and distance matrices. It answers van Dam and Haemers' 2003 question: a sound matrix exists whose spectrum pins down a random graph up to isomorphism. The proof introduces double algebras, a simple test for spectral ID, shown true for random graphs.
arxiv-2602-01136: Ronald Katende builds one matrix-spectrum frame for steadiness and read-ability in deep nets. Reading nets as data-tied chains of linear maps brings out spectrum numbers that steer touchiness to input tweaks, label noise, and train shifts. A global steadiness index pools Jacobians, weight slopes, tangent-kernel maps, and loss curves into one scale for forward touch, credit steadiness, and tune health. Tests on MNIST and CIFAR sets show mild spectrum tuning lifts credit steadiness a lot, even when broad spectrum sums shift little.
arxiv-2602-01736: Qinwei Ma and colleagues argue that one architecture cannot fit all domains in time series forecasting, as the field hits its limits. General domain architectures grow ever more complex while performance saturates. They offer little to real practice in specific domains such as finance, weather and traffic, where each domain builds its own methods. The authors note that domain methods rarely use recent neural network advances from the time series community. They call for a shift: either deep learning for specific domains, or meta learning for general domains.
arxiv-2602-02136: Yingsha Xie and colleagues ask why safety tuning harms the broad thought skills of large thought models. They blame a gap between the safety traces used for tuning and the target model's own inner style, since most such traces come from other models or human labelers. Their method, called DGR, reshapes and refines an existing safety set so it fits the target model's own spread of outputs. Tests show the safety cost falls while safety stays strong, and just ten samples can switch on sound refusal conduct.
arxiv-2602-02236: Julian Lemmel and others study online fine-tuning of pretrained driving controllers with real-time recurrent reinforcement learning. The method adjusts policy settings each step without backpropagating through time, using memory efficiently. Validation covers CarRacing test and a tenth-scale RoboRacer platform carrying an event camera, fine-tuning a pretrained policy online during real-world line following. To their knowledge, this is the first online reinforcement fine-tuning demonstration with event-camera notes on standard hardware in closed-loop control.
arxiv-2602-02336: Yuan Li and others study uranium shape in uranium-uranium collisions using covariant density functional theory densities. They improve the elliptic-flow ratio, while a deformed uranium configuration gives a larger triangular-flow ratio than a symmetric one. Transverse-momentum ratios remain hard to describe. Variations in gold reference density can shift the triangular-flow ratio as much as the gap between uranium configurations. Both uranium structure and reference density must be managed before quantitative constraints can be drawn from collisions.
arxiv-2602-02836:
Four newly confirmed brown dwarfs are reported in a 2026 paper by Ján Šubjak and 32 co-authors. Brown dwarfs are objects too large to be planets but too small to burn like stars. The team found the four with the TESS telescope and confirmed them with precise velocity measurements.

Three of the companions take more than a hundred days to orbit their stars. That raises the known long-period transiting sample from two systems to five. Comparing eccentricity and metal content across similar objects follows. Long-period hosts tend to be metal-poor, unlike short-period hosts. The pattern suggests brown dwarfs mostly form by fragmentation, like stars.
arxiv-2602-02936:
Whether the universe expands unevenly in other directions is tested by Tanay Gupta and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. The standard model of the cosmos assumes large-scale uniformity. Reports of possible violations motivate models that allow direction-dependent expansion instead, using the eight Thurston geometries, which are uniform but slanted spaces.

Each shape gets extra settings for shear, slant, curvature, and a chosen axis. The authors fit these models to the latest Type Ia supernova data, compiled in Pantheon+ and SH0ES. Supernovae act as standard candles for measuring distances. The fits found mild evidence of large-scale isotropy violation. The paper shows how supernova data can separate these shapes from one another.
arxiv-2602-03136:
Enric Florit-Simon's solo work in 2026 draws a parallel between phase shifts and a famous conjecture about minimal surfaces. De Giorgi conjectured that monotone answers to the Allen-Cahn formula, a model of phase separation, must be one-part in modest dimensions. Florit-Simon studies general answers whose Morse index, a count of unstable directions, stays bounded instead of assuming monotonicity throughout the domain.

Any finite-index answer with bounded energy density in four dimensions turns out to be one-part. Conditional on classifying stable answers, the same holds up to dimension seven. On closed four-manifolds, shift layers behave like smooth minimal hypersurfaces. The rigidity contrasts sharply with three dimensions, where many nontrivial finite-index answers exist with varied end shapes.
arxiv-2602-03936:
A honeycomb magnet that stops magnetizing at exactly one third of saturation puzzles physicists. Amanda A. Konieczna and 2 co-authors explain that plateau in the compound Na3Ni2BiO6 with a first-principles study in 2026. Tests had blamed exotic Kitaev interactions, which tie spin direction to bond direction.

From density-functional math and small-scale modeling, the team extracted the real exchange values. Their model reproduces neutron scattering spectra and the magnetization curve, including zigzag order at zero field. The plateau instead comes from strong out-of-plane anisotropy plus simpler couplings, and a double-zigzag state produces it. Simpler ingredients, it turns out, suffice.
arxiv-2602-04036:
Annie Guo and 1 co-author connect two polynomial families through forbidden patterns. Forest polynomials are a newer quasisymmetric cousin of Schubert polynomials, which encode geometry of flag varieties. Their 2026 paper asks exactly when a Schubert polynomial is itself a forest polynomial.

The answer is pattern avoidance: precisely when the underlying permutation avoids six specific patterns. Schubert members already split positively into forest ones, so the result draws the exact boundary of the overlap. Pattern avoidance controls many Schubert traits, and this adds one more. Such results turn analytic questions about these polynomials into finite checks a computer can run.
arxiv-2602-04236:
One verifier's blind spot need not be everyone's. Mohammadreza Maleki and 3 co-authors propose Cascading Robustness Verification in a 2026 paper. Proving that a neural network resists attack examples is expensive, so users lean on fast but partial verifiers, each with its own shortcuts.

Their insight is simple: an input counts as certified if any method in the cascade certifies it. Chaining verifiers therefore raises measured robustness while keeping costs low. The method is model-blind, no matter how the network was trained. The authors also expose limits of the standard robustness metric itself, arguing the field has been missing certified safety.
arxiv-2602-04436:
Radar can read hand gestures without cameras or wearables, if the classifier is light enough. Towa Sano and 1 co-author use echo state networks for gesture recognition from Doppler radar in a 2026 paper. In-car interfaces and robots need such recognition cheap and fast.

Range-time and Doppler-time maps feed recurrent reservoirs whose states go to simple readout classifiers like ridge regression and random forests. Reservoir computing trains only the readout, slashing cost versus deep networks. On an eleven-class benchmark the method beat existing approaches, and it surpassed deep learning models on a four-class task. Lightweight reservoirs suit always-on interfaces where privacy rules out cameras.
arxiv-2602-04536:
Abdulrahman Alotaibi and 4 co-authors propose a training trick for federated learning in a 2026 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many devices with no central gathering of private data. It struggles when each device's data differ greatly from the others.

Their method, Iterative Federated Adaptation, splits training into generations. At each generation's end, some model parameters are reset to fresh values. The reset parameters are picked at random or from later layers. Forgetting in this controlled way helps the model escape poor fits and keep broadly useful traits. Tests on three image datasets raised accuracy, most when data differed strongly between clients.
arxiv-2602-04636:
Jihee Kim and colleagues present a closeout report in a 2026 paper arguing for a second detector at the Electron-Ion Collider, a planned facility for probing matter's inner structure. One detector is already under construction, but the community sees a second as essential over the facility's multi-decade life.

The report strengthens the physics case, develops a realistic detector concept, and broadens the overall program. The design complements the first detector in reach, precision, and control of systematic errors. Because a second detector would arrive years later, it can adopt technologies not yet mature enough for the first. The document also outlines remaining research and development needs for future teams.
arxiv-2602-04836:
Are AI capabilities really growing exponentially? Haosen Ge, Hamsa Bastani, and Osbert Bastani challenge a prominent report's answer in a 2026 note. The report from Model Evaluation and Threat Research argued for exponential growth since 2019, a claim with major safety and labor implications.

The authors fit an S-shaped sigmoid curve to the same current data. Their fit places the inflection point, where growth stops accelerating, already in the past. They also propose a model splitting capability into base and reasoning components, each improving at its own rate, and prove it supports a near-future inflection. Their stated goal is not a rival forecast. It is showing how fragile the exponential claim is.
arxiv-2602-04936:
Stanislav Byriukov, writing alone, studies exact similarity search in this 2026 algorithms paper. Given millions of sequences, the task is to find the ones sharing the longest common prefix with a query. Approximate methods are common, but some settings demand exact, provable answers.

Byriukov proves a tight lower bound on the memory any exact method needs, then gives a trie-based index whose query time grows only with the sequence length and the number of answers. A second technique, Thermal-Aware Logic, turns the prefix structure into bounded range scans. On a graphics processor benchmark with 20 million items, it used about 308 times less energy per query and cut worst-case latency by a factor of about 329 compared with pairwise comparison. The paper offers exact retrieval for settings where approximations are not acceptable.
arxiv-2602-05036:
Karish Grover and 5 co-authors wrote this 2026 machine learning paper on self-supervised learning for graphs, where models learn from unlabeled network data by solving made-up pretext tasks. Mixing several tasks usually forces every training step to compromise, and the authors name three failure modes: objectives fighting each other, objectives changing usefulness over time, and quiet objectives starving.

Their framework, ControlG, treats the mix as a timing problem instead. It estimates each objective's difficulty and how much pairs of objectives clash, plans budgets with a Pareto-aware rule, and schedules training with a classic PID controller borrowed from engineering. Across nine datasets it beat leading baselines. A side benefit is an auditable schedule showing which objectives actually drove the learning.
arxiv-2602-05336:
Predator-prey models with random noise often add that noise lazily, missing how one predation links both populations. Jiguang Yu and 3 co-authors derive the noise right in this 2026 probability paper. They start from an ongoing-time Markov chain for a Rosenzweig-MacArthur system with four channels. One linked event has a prey death and a predator gain happen at once.

Scaling the chain gives back the standard fixed equations on average, while the jitter forms a reaction Langevin diffusion with an exact state-based spread. The linked event leaves a fingerprint: a negative cross-link between prey and predator numbers. Paths freeze at the first touch of an axis, encoding one-way extinction, and the authors prove the process is well-posed, with moments kept in check. Die-out has positive chance from each inside state, and predator die-out is certain when a stated setting inequality holds.
arxiv-2602-05436:
Harmonic maps that stretch space in a controlled way are called quasiconformal, and their smoothness near borders is a subtle question. Anton Gjokaj and David Kalaj prove a result about such maps between Lyapunov domains, which are regions in space whose borders are smooth in a precise sense. The maps they study also preserve the Laplace equation, a property known as being harmonic.

The authors prove that every such map is globally Lipschitz, meaning its stretch stays bounded right up to the border of the region. Their proof works step by step at the border: a rough bound on smoothness is improved again and again until the gradient stays finite. Along the way they review standard tools from the field, such as how distortion of derivatives behaves and how control at the border spreads inside. The result holds in any number of dimensions.
arxiv-2602-05536:
Merging several fine-tuned models into one is cheap, but shared knowledge can be counted too many times in the process. Yayuan Li, Ze Peng, and 4 co-authors show that when tasks share aligned spectral directions, a plain weighted sum inflates the related singular values. The merged model then leans too hard toward the shared subspaces, a failure mode they call spectral over-accumulation.

Their fix, Singular Value Calibration, is a post-processing step that needs no training and no data. It measures how much subspaces overlap and rescales the inflated singular values to restore a balanced spectrum. Across vision and language benchmarks, the method improved strong merging baselines and set new best results. Applied to Task Arithmetic, it raised performance by a clear margin while changing only singular values. The paper reframes a common merging bug as a spectrum problem. Code is available for others to test the method.
arxiv-2602-05636:
Ontologies lay out the structure of a domain but cannot invent new artifacts, while language models invent freely and often break the structure. Benny Cheung introduces Generative Ontology, a framework that joins the two: schemas written as executable code constrain what a language model may generate, and specialized agents supply the creative roles. The demonstration system, GameGrammar, designs complete tabletop games.

Separate agents act as a mechanics architect, a theme weaver, and a balance critic, each with a professional worry that keeps outputs from going shallow. Retrieval from existing games grounds the designs in precedent. Three studies back the framework: an ablation over many designs shows agent specialization gave the largest quality gains, and schema validation removed structural errors. A benchmark against twenty published board games found structural parity but a real gap in fun. A repeat-evaluation study checked that the automated judge was reliable.
arxiv-2602-05736:
Hexagonal boron nitride hosts two prized features: color centers that emit light one photon at a time, and hyperbolic phonon polaritons that squeeze infrared light into tiny volumes. Jie-Cheng Feng, Johannes Eberle, and 4 co-authors connect the two inside one cavity quantum electrodynamics framework. A single color center becomes a quantum source of the polaritons, something classical near field probes cannot provide.

The authors quantify how strongly the emitter couples to the polariton modes and study two ways to generate them. Spontaneous emission into the phonon sideband can yield single polariton events, and in ultrathin slabs it becomes single mode with an enhanced rate. A stimulated Raman process adds frequency selectivity and a tunable conversion rate, launching narrowband polaritons that travel micrometers as confined rays. A two emitter test is outlined to prove the single polariton character. It frames the platform as a new route to quantum optics.
arxiv-2602-06036:
Large language models write one word piece at a time, which makes them slow. Jian Chen, Yesheng Liang, and Zhijian Liu present DFlash, a way to draft many pieces at once. A small diffusion model does the drafting, while the big model checks the draft in parallel.

Diffusion models can produce a whole block of text in a single pass, so drafting stops being a slow chain. The draft model also borrows context signals from the big model, which helps its guesses get accepted. In tests, answers stayed exact while speed rose more than sixfold. That beat the best earlier drafting method by a wide margin.
arxiv-2602-06136:
Models that adapt on the fly to new data can fix their own drift, but adaptation takes time, and late answers may be useless. Sudarshan Sreeram and 2 co-authors present Tempora, a framework that grades adaptation methods under real time pressure. Standard leaderboards assume unlimited processing time.

Tempora scores methods with three utility measures: hard deadlines for streams, decaying value for interactive use, and budgets for cost-limited settings. Across hundreds of runs with many methods, data sets, and machines, rankings kept changing. The best method under no time pressure often lost once delays counted. No single winner emerged, so the framework helps users pick based on their own time limits.
arxiv-2602-06336:
Targeted ads need user data, but privacy laws increasingly forbid shipping that data to servers. Ahmad Alemari and 2 co-authors present AdFL, a federated learning framework that runs inside the web browser itself. Browsers learn each visitor's ad preferences locally, and only model updates are combined into a global model.

The publisher's server coordinates the learning for people browsing its site. No software install is needed, since the system uses standard browser programming interfaces. Features like ad viewability, clicks, reading dwell time, and page content feed the model. A proof-of-concept predicts ad viewability, tested on two separate data sets from a live website, showing the approach works without centralizing raw user data.
arxiv-2602-06736:
Alexey Basalaev writes a short note in integrable systems, the study of equations with rich exact structure. Work by Dubrovin and Zhang, and by Buryak, shows how certain curved spaces, called Dubrovin-Frobenius manifolds, can build families of such equations. Famous cases, including the KP family, grew out of Saito's classic theory of lone singular points.

The note shows that two more families, the BKP and CKP families, can be built the same way. The new ingredient is an orbifold version of Saito theory, which handles singular points that carry a symmetry group. The build widens the known reach of the geometry-to-family pipeline and ties these families to symmetric singularity theory.
arxiv-2602-06836:
Tonghan Wang and five co-authors ask how a crowd of chatbots might act as a group. Each model in the crowd can lean toward some human groups and away from others, and those leanings shape what the crowd as a whole does. The team treats each model's choice as a mix over human groups, which keeps the math workable where open text would not.

From that setup they work out the stable points where no model gains by shifting its mix alone, under plain shape rules for gains. The result gives plain advice for steering the crowd toward fairer outcomes, as an extra layer on top of tools like RLHF. In a mock social media world, reasoning models in particular left some groups with no model serving them at all, a flaw their steering can avoid.
arxiv-2602-06936:
Edoardo Ballico and Elizabeth Gasparim study vector bundles on Hopf surfaces, a class of compact complex surfaces. They prove that every filtrable bundle on such a surface must have jumps, points where the bundle's structure changes, and that filtrable stable bundles exist with any positive second Chern number. In the opposite direction, they construct irreducible bundles of any rank at least two with trivial determinant, second Chern number one, and no jumps.

Elementary operations at points then let them build torsion free sheaves with higher Chern numbers from stable bundles, showing the new sheaves sit in the closure of the next moduli space. They also introduce very irreducible bundles, whose symmetric powers are all irreducible, and prove a rank-two bundle whose graph contains a component from a surjective map of projective lines is very irreducible. The results map the landscape of bundles on Hopf surfaces.
arxiv-2602-07136:
Tiny neutrino masses and the surplus of matter over antimatter may share one explanation, but the usual version fails if the early universe reheated too coolly.  Rabindra N.  Mohapatra and one co-author add a link that lets right-handed neutrinos break baryon number, opening another route to the matter surplus.

That route predicts neutrons occasionally turning into antineutrons, and the paper derives a cosmological upper limit on how fast that change can happen, within reach of the planned ESS experiment.  Proton stability survives thanks to a symmetry in the model.  The paper is a useful bridge between neutrino theory, cosmology, and an experiment now being planned.
arxiv-2602-07736:
Robots grasp objects more securely when they can spot symmetry axes, since gripping along such an axis tends to balance the load. Omar Tahri uses geometrical moments, numbers that summarize a shape's mass distribution, to detect symmetries and estimate rotations and mirror flips for objects centered at the origin.

The method builds distinctive symmetry measures and works in n-dimensional space, with validation on two- and three-dimensional objects and comparisons against optimization-based methods for finding multiple symmetry planes. The results favor the moment-based approach for robustness. The paper should interest researchers in robot manipulation, shape analysis, and computer vision.
arxiv-2602-07836:
Distributed tuning asks many agents to minimize a shared objective while each sees only its own noisy gradient and talks only to neighbors. Jianhua Sun and two co-authors study this problem in continuous time, where randomness enters through Brownian motion and the communication graph changes over time.

Their recipe blends consensus, which pulls agents toward agreement, with gradient descent on each local objective. Under mild connectivity and convexity assumptions, they prove the agents' states converge in expectation to a common minimizer, using Lyapunov theory and stochastic calculus. A model confirms the theory. The work gives control and tuning teams a rigorous continuous-time foundation for noisy, networked learning.
arxiv-2602-08036:
Graph learning from streaming data must add new tasks without forgetting old ones or replaying private data. Jingtao Liu and Xinming Zhang propose TAAM, a method that guides a fixed graph neural network backbone with lightweight, task-specific Neural Synapse Modulators.

Each new task trains its own modulator, then freezes it as an expert module that adaptively modulates the backbone's computation with node-level attention. New knowledge lives in compact modules, so catastrophic forgetting is avoided without replay, and the paper also addresses the realistic case where task identities are unknown at test time. Graph continual-learning researchers gain a modular, privacy-friendlier alternative to replay-heavy approaches.
arxiv-2602-08136:
Vision-language models resist jailbreaks hidden in a single image, thanks to safety alignment, but what if the harmful meaning only emerges by combining image fragments? Md Rafi Ur Rashid and three co-authors identify exactly that gap: alignment training uses whole images, while pretraining generalizes readily to split inputs.

Their split-image visual jailbreak attacks distribute unsafe cues across fragments so no single piece triggers refusal, yet the combination does the harm. Unlike optimization-based attacks, these transfer well across models in black-box settings. The paper exposes a misalignment between capability generalization and safety generalization, urging safety teams to align on the fragmented inputs attackers actually use, not just clean single images.
arxiv-2602-08336:
Models that both understand and generate images are meant to mix text and vision in one system, but nobody knew how well their words and pictures actually line up. Cheng Yang and nine co-authors build UReason, a benchmark that tests this alignment through reasoning-guided image generation: the model thinks in words first, then draws. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses two thousand hand-checked cases across code, arithmetic, spatial, attribute, and text tasks.

Surprisingly, stripping the reasoning away and drawing from a cleaned-up prompt alone beats reasoning-guided drawing by a wide margin, even though reasoning still beats drawing with no guidance. The intended meaning in the text reasoning often fails to reach the picture. Readers get a sharp diagnostic for the next generation of unified models, and a warning that unified training does not guarantee aligned outputs.
arxiv-2602-08636:
People set behavioral goals every day, from eating better to working smarter, but good intentions need structured support. Michel Schimpf and five co-authors test how chatbots built on large language models can guide goal setting using psychology frameworks. Their arXiv paper reports a preregistered randomized experiment with 543 participants.

Chatbots varied in three design features: guidance, suggestions, and feedback. Goal quality was judged by subjective and objective measures. Guidance alone helps, but adding feedback is what makes the chatbots effective, while adaptive suggestions prove less useful. Readers get concrete design guidance for chatbots that help people actually reach their goals.
arxiv-2602-08736:
Graph coloring questions often turn on whether a forbidden pattern forces a bound on coloring number. Guillaume Aubian and Luis Kuffner construct orientations of rook graphs that dodge one pattern yet break coloring bounds entirely. Their arXiv paper works with graphs whose underlying structure is claw-free.

The orientations contain no directed triangle, yet their dichromatic number grows without bound. That combination refutes a prior conjecture in the literature, and it sharpens an earlier result by Carbonero, Koerts, Moore, and Spirkl. Readers get a compact counterexample with a clear moral: forbidding directed triangles does not tame dichromatic number, even on claw-free ground.
arxiv-2602-08936:
Tiny enzyme-coated particles could one day sense their surroundings and act on their own, if their collective motion can be steered. Jiang-Xing Chen and two co-authors show in simulation how such colloids can be arranged as chemical logic gates, then wired into circuits. The circuits read environmental chemicals as inputs and produce output chemicals as answers.

That chemical computing lets the swarm coordinate: it can spot invasive threats by their signals, then make and deliver chemicals to quiet them. The examples cover threat detection and targeted suppression. The work offers a design recipe for experimental circuits built from self-assembling micromotors that respond to cues without outside control.
arxiv-2602-09236:
Version control in machine design software is plagued by the tangle and linked nature of design data, and Yuanzhe Deng and four co-authors map the trouble in order. Reading 170 online forum threads about version control in modern computer-aided design tools, they spot repeat people-and-tech issues covering version handling, flow, scope, and spread.

The findings feed a broader think on how version control should be designed for design work. They point to tools that better support linking work, cross-team teamwork, and base-level self-checking. For CAD providers, the study offers usable tips; for scholars, it recasts version control as base for product building, not just a file feature.
arxiv-2602-09336:
Standard operating procedures run enterprises, yet language models still stumble on them, mixing up terms, step order, and conditional rules. Siyuan Huang and three co-authors propose FM SO.P, a 2026 framework that trains these skills in stages rather than all at once. Its progressive task mixtures build terminology precision first, then action-sequence understanding, then scenario-aware graph reasoning for conditional logic, each stage adding to the last.

A second novelty is automatic evaluation by three agents that draft scoring rubrics, build stratified test sets, and score answers. The system adapts to each domain's demands, from time rules for motor-vehicle offices to compliance rules for banks. On a benchmark spanning seven domains, from health care to hotels, the team's mid-size model passes nearly half the tests. That matches a far larger baseline model with roughly a tenth of the parameters. The smaller open model also performs competitively.
arxiv-2602-09436:
Hao Wu and three co-authors develop main spectral theory for cyclic joint systems with far-reaching spread over time. Their 2026 paper uses resolvent positive maps and their small changes to set tests for when a main eigenvalue exists. Smooth upper and lower nearby matrix functions then let the main spectrum point stand in for the eigenvalue in telling global dynamics.

That stand-in setup supports studying how the spectrum point moves with settings under broad starting points. For systems with coupled and uncoupled far-reaching terms alike, the authors analyze long-run behavior in spread rate, spread range, and pace. Two models show the theory in action: a Zika virus model and a stem cell model. The paper thus extends spectral tools to far-reaching, cyclic joint systems.
arxiv-2602-09936:
The k-means method groups data by repeatedly refining cluster centers, and Lloyd's version is among the most used. A 2026 paper led by Roy R. Lederman, with five co-authors, proves a stark failure mode in high dimensions with heavy noise. With high probability, nearly every starting split is already stable, so the method simply hands back the split it began with.

That failure bites even when other methods could recover the true clusters with ease. In contrast, the authors prove Hartigan's variant of k-means escapes the trap entirely. The contrast explains why practitioners often struggle with k-means on high-dimensional noisy data, and it draws a bright line between two algorithms that look like close cousins.
arxiv-2602-10536:
Seewoo Lee studies inequalities for many-term math and quasimodular forms in a 2026 paper. The focus is the monotonicity of functions built from a quasimodular form tested on the imaginary axis, scaled by a power of the factor. Such monotonicity questions connect analysis of special functions to deep lattice problems.

As an application, the paper constructs infinitely many positive quasimodular forms of level greater than one. It also gives alternative proofs of modular form inequalities used in proving the optimality of the Leech lattice packing and its universal optimality. The work thus serves both as new math on quasimodular forms and as a streamlined route to results at the heart of sphere packing theory.
arxiv-2602-10636:
Youjun Deng and two co-authors give a stated relaxation tensor for an Earth model in a 2026 paper. The quasi-static extended Burgers model describes Earth's anelastic conduct and its free swings. But no analytical, systematic way existed to compute free-swing key values under this model. Teams lacked a general method for the relaxation tensor itself.

The paper supplies that method for inhomogeneous isotropic models, then applies it to Earth modeled as a homogeneous isotropic unit ball. Integrating by parts under zero initial strain splits the model into two terms, and the authors compute clusters of key values from the resulting form. The work gives geophysicists a concrete tool for studying how an anelastic Earth rings.
arxiv-2602-10736:
Wenlihan Lu and four co-authors predict cellular connectivity for low-altitude drone routes in a 2026 paper. The low-altitude economy depends on steady links for unmanned aerial vehicles, yet pre-flight planning must forecast link quality along routes where readings are sparse. Current radio map methods fail on such thin data.

Their transfer learning system borrows strength from abundant crowdsourced ground signals as auxiliary supervision. General propagation priors learned from simulation, adversarial alignment of ground and aerial feature spaces, and fine-tuning on limited real drone readings bridge the domain gap. Tests on a real-world Meituan dataset show large gains over baselines, hopeful safer route planning for delivery and inspection drones.
arxiv-2602-11036:
Spin glasses hide a tangle of key points that shape their energy landscape. Wei-Kuo Chen and two co-authors study the pure p-spin Hamiltonian with a polynomial possible that breaks rotational symmetry. The random field is anisotropic, so direction matters in a way older symmetric models missed.

Their main result gives the logarithmic limit for the expected count of key points as a variational formula. From it they locate the phase transition point and bound the ground-state energy from above. The paper extends hardness theory for disordered systems to a less symmetric, more realistic possible class.
arxiv-2602-11136:
Who watches the watchers when judges are themselves chance-based? Jiayi Zhou and four co-authors propose FormalJudge, a neuro-symbolic frame for agentic oversight. Language models first turn high-level intent into small, checkable constraints, then prove compliance with Dafny specs and a satisfiability solver.

That two-way Formal-of-Thought design replaces chance-based scores with math guarantees. Tests span behavioural safety, multi-domain constraint following, and deception finding. The frame beats language-model-judge rivals by a clear margin, lets a small judge catch deception from far larger agents, and gains steadily with iterative refinement. The work argues that formal checks can escape the judge's own failure modes.
arxiv-2602-11336:
Traffic density is hard to measure when few cars report positions. Nail Baloul and three co-authors reconstruct density from only the start and end positions of a small probe fleet, generated by microscopic dynamical systems. A machine learning recipe built from scratch turns those sparse traces into an approximate density map.

The approach improves scores despite scarce data, and the authors prove a consistency result: as vehicle count grows, the learned density converges to a well-known macroscopic traffic flow model. The work suits low-penetration probe settings, where full sensor coverage is unaffordable but a handful of tracked cars can still reveal the flow.
arxiv-2602-11436:
Heart MRI slices are uneven, limiting shape analysis. Carolina Brás and seven co-authors train a single neural implicit function on near-isotropic, higher-detail CT angiography data to represent cardiac shapes from MRI at any detail. The method reconstructs right ventricle and myocardium, the latter building both left-ventricle surfaces.

Since high-detail standard segmentations are unavailable, results is judged by extracting four-chamber slices and comparing with standard masks. Similarity scores are strong for the ventricle and moderate for the myocardium, with small distance errors. Measured and descriptive checks show accurate, smooth, anatomically plausible shapes, supporting better cardiac shape analysis from uneven scans.
arxiv-2602-11836:
Urdu is a low-resource language with few effective meaning-based recommendation systems, especially for personalized news. Existing methods lean on lexical matching or generic techniques that miss meaning and falter as query length and information needs vary. Alishbah Bashir and two co-authors propose ULTRA, an adaptive meaning-based recommendation framework built on transformer embeddings with a dual-vector design and query-length aware routing.

A threshold-driven decision process routes short, intent-focused queries to title-level pipelines and longer, context-rich queries to full-content pipelines, matching meaning detail to the query. Optimized pooling moves beyond surface keyword matching toward context-aware similarity search. Tests on a large Urdu news corpus show clearly improved matches across query types, with precision gains above 90 percent over single-pipeline baselines, a strong result for low-resource meaning-based retrieval.
arxiv-2602-11936:
Whether dark energy changes over time is now tested against a pile of late-time data. Tengpeng Xu and four co-authors compare the dynamical w0waCDM framework with the standard LambdaCDM model, using cosmic microwave background data, DESI DR2, SDSS-IV, transverse BAO, and Cepheid-calibrated supernova data. The verdict depends sharply on which datasets are combined.

Microwave background data alone leave a broad geometric degeneracy, while DESI BAO pulls toward weak present-day acceleration. Adding supernova and transverse BAO data instead favors moderate acceleration and eases the Hubble tension substantially. The split traces to low-redshift distance ratios, which differ between BAO datasets below redshift one half. Bayesian evidence follows the same pattern, favoring the dynamical model mainly when supernova or transverse BAO data join, and the standard model for microwave background plus SDSS. Apparent support for dynamical dark energy, the authors conclude, is not universal.
arxiv-2602-12236:
Spiking neural networks promise very low-power vision for event and frame cameras, but they forget old tasks as new ones arrive. Anika Tabassum Meem led this work with two co-authors, proposing energy-aware spike budgeting for continual learning. The frame joins experience replay, tunable leaky neuron settings, and an adaptive spike scheduler that enforces a per-data-set energy cap during training.

Behaviour splits by input type. On frame data, the budget acts like a sparsity push, lifting accuracy while cutting spike rates by up to 47 percent. On event data, a looser budget lifts accuracy by up to 17.45 points with little extra compute. Across five tests, the method gains accuracy while trimming dynamic power, making continual neuromorphic vision more practical.
arxiv-2602-12336:
Representation theory links groups over local fields to functions on related structures, and base change is a key bridge between them. Shenghao Li works alone here, introducing a base change homomorphism for the Bernstein centre of a principal series block, for an unramified group over a p-adic field. The paper then proves that functions related by this homomorphism are associated, in the precise technical sense used in the field.

That association result is new evidence for a conjecture on twisted endoscopic transfer of the stable Bernstein centre, proposed by T. Haines. The same circle of ideas is expected to feed a broader conjecture on test functions for Shimura varieties, due to R. Kottwitz and T. Haines. Readers get a focused, technical step toward two linked conjectures in the Langlands program.
arxiv-2602-12436:
Safety verification for dynamical systems often uses barrier certificates, which are state invariants that prove a system stays safe. Mohammed Adib Oumer led this work with two co-authors, turning to closure certificates, a tool for transition invariants that can verify omega-regular properties including safety. A closure certificate is a real-valued function over state pairs whose zero superlevel set marks an inductive transition invariant.

Finding such a function means fixing a template, such as a polynomial of set degree, and searching by sum-of-squares optimisation. When no function in that template works, the template must change. Interpolation-inspired closure certificates instead use a set of functions that jointly over-approximate a transition invariant, stepping from one-step transitions to two-step, and so on. The team finds these sets by sum-of-squares and scenario programs, and demonstrates them on persistence and omega-regular cases.
arxiv-2602-12736:
Imagine a virus spreading along the edges of a complete network, where each new edge catches fire once it completes a copy of some fixed pattern. That process, called graph bootstrap percolation, has been studied since 1968 for its links to weak saturation. David Fabian, Patrick Morris, and Tibor Szabó survey a fresh question: how long can the spread possibly take before it settles?

Their survey presents a systematic study of that maximum running time and how the chosen pattern shapes it. The behaviour turns out to be surprisingly varied, touching several branches of combinatorics along the way. The authors also collect surprises encountered in the work and open problems that remain, making the survey a useful entry point for readers curious about slow-spreading processes.
arxiv-2602-13036:
Time-domain surveys like the Zwicky Transient Facility find far more supernovae than spectrographs can classify, so photometric sorting must carry the load. A. Townsend and colleagues present a feature-based classifier for ZTF supernovae, aimed at building a photometric Type Ia sample for cosmology. The approach uses the ParSNIP autoencoder to capture light-curve mix, trained on spectroscopically classified ZTF events with realistic noise augmentation mimicking fainter sources.

Light-curve traits feed a gradient-boosted decision tree in binary and multi-class modes, checked on stand-alone fainter data and live alerts with spectroscopic follow-up. Noise augmentation lifts scores markedly for faint events. The binary classifier reaches 98.1% Type Ia recall, above 98% to magnitude 20 with over ten detections, and 95% of sources are classified correctly overall, enabling a large photometric cosmology sample.
arxiv-2602-13136:
Retrosynthesis asks which starting materials could yield a target molecule, and template-free methods treat it as opaque sequence generation. Chenguang Wang and three co-authors argue that atom order in neural representations matters, and build a structure-aware framework around it. By placing reaction-centre atoms at the head of the sequence, the method turns implicit chemical knowledge into positional patterns a model can grasp.

The RetroDiT backbone, a graph transformer using rotary position embeddings, uses that ordering to focus on chemically critical regions. Paired with discrete flow matching, training and sampling separate, and generation takes 20 to 50 steps versus 500 for prior diffusion methods. Results reach 61.2% top-1 on USPTO-50k and 51.3% on USPTO-Full with predicted centres, rising to 71.1% and 63.4% with oracle centres, while a tiny 280K-parameter ordered model matches a 65M-parameter unordered one.
arxiv-2602-13336:
Particles that are not spheres move in surprising ways through viscous fluids, with consequences for microfluidics and drug delivery. This study simulates driven prolate and oblate spheroids inside a square microchannel, using lattice Boltzmann methods backed by far-field theory of wall interactions. It maps how aspect ratio, confinement strength, and fluid inertia shape motion.

In open fluid, speed peaks not for a sphere but for a specific stretched or flattened shape. Under confinement, the best shape shifts toward oblate forms as wall friction dominates, and off-center placement creates two families of oscillating paths, glancing and reversing. Weak inertia breaks those closed loops and spawns new stable points. Aditya Bhowmik leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14136:
Ata Keskin, writing alone, compares a 2026 arXiv set of convex relaxations for AC optimal power flow. The ACOPF problem sets generation and transmission to maximize social welfare under physical limits, but its nonlinear, non-convex equations resist exact solution on large networks. Relaxations offer tractable routes to optimal or near-optimal answers.

The study implements DCOPF, Shor's SDP forms, chordal SDP, Jabr's SOCP, and QC relaxations in one solver-native MOSEK framework, avoiding high-level modeling overhead. Because QC relaxations need angle-difference bounds, quasi-Monte Carlo sampling with Sobol sequences estimates tighter bounds empirically. The unified comparison gives power-system operators a grounded guide to which relaxation fits market-based welfare maximization at scale.
arxiv-2602-14236:
Vishnu Sai and four co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv memory bottleneck in video-language models. The key-value cache grows linearly with sequence length, choking long-form video understanding. Existing fixes mostly evict tokens reactively, after computing full attention matrices, wasting compute.

Their Sali-Cache framework manages memory proactively, before costly attention runs. A temporal filter based on optical flow spots redundant frames, while a spatial filter based on saliency spots visually key regions. On the LLaVA 1.6 architecture, the method reached 2.20 times compression in effective memory use, while holding 100% accuracy on BLEU, ROUGE-L, and exact-match metrics in the reported tests.
arxiv-2602-14436:
Jaehan Im and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv teamwork plan for airport ground jams. Joint virtual queuing lets a central boss cap total pushback flow while carriers keep control over single plane pushbacks. That split caps the boss's power to steer system scores straight.

The non-team plan uses linked equilibrium to give nudge-compatible tips on plane-level pushbacks with no override of carrier freedom. Chance rules handle doubt in carriers' inner cost gauges, giving plain odds guarantees on nudge fit. The boss can thus tune the trust level at which carriers are hoped to heed tips, with a scalable method for working out chance-capped linked equilibria.
arxiv-2602-14836:
Zsolt Lecz and Szilard Majorosi redo laser wake math past the usual shell guess, where a round shell predicts no side push for electrons on the beam line. An exact force law, more broad than the shell law, gives a plain form for the side push of an electron that crosses the pulse.

Non-zero side push shows up for electrons that start on the beam's heart line, and that push lights up the strong wake skew seen in exact work. Electron runs in fierce pulses thus gain a truer, less even tale.
arxiv-2602-14936:
Deshpande and Sawant study two complexes built from a directed multigraph. In one, the faces are directed linear forests: vertex-disjoint unions of directed paths. The other is a related complex tied to directed trees. Their key move is to encode clashes between edges in a plain graph. Under mild acyclicity conditions, each complex then appears as the independence complex of a graph.

That link lets them import known results on independence complexes. From those results they derive graph tests for vertex decomposability, shellability, and sequential Cohen-Macaulayness. They also name forbidden directed subgraphs that block decomposability. Families such as acyclic cases, forests, and cycles are shown to satisfy it, while examples show it fails in general.
arxiv-2602-15136:
Cannella and colleagues justify a finding: a transformer trained on synthetic data performs strongly on empirical Bayes problems. Rather than dissecting the model, they ask why a Bayes estimator, trained under one preset distribution, can adapt to arbitrary test cases. Focusing on Poisson Bayes problems, they identify universal priors under which training yields near-optimal regret across all test cases.

Their analysis leans on posterior contraction, a classical Bayesian effect, showing the trained model adapts to unknown test cases precisely through that effect. The same lens explains length generalization, where test runs exceed training runs, since the model performs Bayesian inference with a general posterior. The paper thus grounds a practical pretraining success in classical Bayesian theory.
arxiv-2602-15436:
Laato and colleagues tackle probing daily social life from old records. Data pulled from text often does not allow scholars to field history or society buffs' queries in numbers. They tackle this puzzle in a hoard of Finn World War II Karelian refugee chats. Earlier work pulled more than 350,000 notes of free-time pastimes and club ties from these chats, giving 71,000 distinct names, too many to probe.

They build a sorting setup catching sides of joining: the kind of pastime or club, how social it is, how often it occurs, and how bodily taxing. They tag a gold-standard set for a solid review, then check whether large word nets can use the same plan. Using a plain polling method across tries, they find an open-weight LLM can mirror pro calls. Lastly, they use the method to tag the 350,000 items, giving an ordered bank for work on mixing.
arxiv-2602-15836:
Liu and colleagues propose EdgeNav-QE, a system joining quantised low-rank adaptation, or QLoRA, with a dynamic early-exit mechanism for large action models on edge devices. Large action models show great promise in autonomous navigation by joining high-level reasoning with low-level control. Yet multi-billion parameter models strain edge devices on memory and latency. By quantising the backbone to 4-bit precision and placing early-exit branches with care, the model stops inference early for simple navigation tasks while keeping full depth for hard decisions.

Tests on Habitat-Sim on Matterport3D, on OpenVLA-7B, show EdgeNav-QE cutting inference latency by 82 point 7 percent and memory use by 66 point 7 percent against full-precision baselines. Navigation success holds at 81 point 8 percent. It also beats a leading static early-exit method by 17 point 9 percent in latency, showing the value of content-aware adaptive computation for safety-critical work.
arxiv-2602-15936:
Hiller and colleagues probe baryon number through missing transverse energy. Quark portal links qqqN with a light singlet fermion N make it testable this way. LHC bounds reach 10 TeV (jet), 8 TeV (top), 11 TeV (b-jet). Rising mass or coupling shortens N life, giving clean displaced vertex signs that urge dedicated searches.

Mesogenesis models with colour triplet scalars narrow to y times 3 TeV with charm, y times 5 TeV without, for couplings y to b and lighter quarks, a HL-LHC window. Rare baryon to meson plus invisible and meson to baryon plus invisible decays complement high momentum searches and may prove baryon number violation. Lambda_c to pion or kaon plus invisible decays carry sizable hadronic uncertainties and need high-luminosity flavour sites like Tera-Z. Top decays to one or two b-jets plus N can reach a few times 10 to the power minus 6.
arxiv-2602-16136:
Hongyeon Yu leads a team of three researchers warning that AI-made web content can break retrieval itself. Search engines and retrieval-augmented systems now draw heavily on text made by large language models. A two-stage failure, called Retrieval Collapse, can then set in. First, AI content dominates results and erodes source diversity. Second, low-quality or adversarial content slips into the pipeline.

Controlled tests cover search-optimized content and adversarially crafted content. In the search-optimized case, a pool about two thirds synthetic leads to far higher exposure in results. Answer accuracy stays stable, yet the state is homogenized and deceptively healthy. Under adversarial contamination, classic BM25 exposes a notable share of harmful content, while LLM-based rankers suppress it better. The authors call for retrieval-aware strategies to stop a self-reinforcing slide in quality.
arxiv-2602-16236:
Matthias Frey and coauthors revisit universal prediction of stochastic sequences over a finite horizon known to the learner. Existing regret bounds for this classical problem hold in expectation. The authors ask whether vanishing regret bounds can also hold with high probability. They propose such bounds, which take a very similar form to prior expectation bounds. For universal prediction of a stochastic process over a countable alphabet, their bound gives a convergence rate that depends on horizon and confidence level. It matches the prior in-expectation rate up to the confidence factor.

They also prove an impossibility result: the exponent of the confidence term cannot be improved without additional assumptions. The pair of results thus pins down what high-probability universal prediction can and cannot achieve.
arxiv-2602-16636:
KyuJung Jun and co-authors offer a frame for breaking ion transport in bulk matter into plain, readable parts. Ion conductors matter for next-generation energy storage, but all-atom dynamics studies have mostly reported one overall transport score. That score hides how charge truly moves. The new frame reads dynamics tracks and splits transport into additive parts tied to real micro events.

Events include single-ion hops, multi-ion hops, and vehicular motion, or shifts between chemically plain coordination states. The parts sum exactly to the Onsager scores from Green-Kubo and Einstein rules. Scanning the sample window shows the time scales where each route rules. Tests on crystals, liquids, and polymers settle old debates on concerted motion and exchange, giving battery researchers a sharper lens on ion flow.
arxiv-2602-16836:
Zhengda Mo and co-authors automate insurance claim handling with a locally deployed, governance-aware language model part. Language models excel at general language tasks, yet use in regulated, data-sensitive fields such as insurance stays limited. Drawing on millions of past warranty claims, the team fine-tunes pretrained models with low-rank adaptation, scoping the model to an early decision module in the claim pipeline to speed adjusters' calls.

The module turns messy claim narratives into structured corrective-action tips. A multi-dimensional test joins automated semantic similarity scores with human judgment, probing both handy value and predictive accuracy. Domain-specific fine-tuning beats commercial general-purpose and prompt-based models by a lot, with about four fifths of tested cases nearly matching ground-truth corrective actions. Insurers get proof that domain-adaptive tuning aligns outputs with real work data.
arxiv-2602-16936:
Zikai Zhang, Rui Hu, and Jiahao Xu propose Fed-PLoRA, a lightweight mixed-resource joint fine-tuning frame for large language models. Federated learning enables joint fine-tuning across distributed clients using low-rank adaptation, preserving privacy by avoiding raw data sharing. Yet deployments struggle when clients hold mixed resources and thus adopt varied low-rank adaptation ranks, causing substantial initialization and aggregation noise that undermines performance.

Fed-PLoRA brings in Parallel One-Rank Adaptation, a new low-rank adaptation variant replacing the classic multi-rank module with multiple parallel one-rank modules. A Select-N-Fold strategy folds untrained modules into pretrained weights before local training. A unified study of initialization and aggregation noise shows how Fed-PLoRA addresses limits of state-of-the-art methods. Extensive tests on varied fine-tuning tasks show Fed-PLoRA consistently beats existing methods, giving joint deployments a practical route to mixed clients.
arxiv-2602-17036:
Rong Fu and co-authors present LiveGraph, an active-structure neural re-ranking framework for exercise recommendation. Digital learning keeps growing, creating demand for smart systems that give each student tailored content. Current exercise recommendation systems have made strides, yet they often struggle with the long tail of student use and with adapting to each student's own learning path.

LiveGraph uses a graph-based method to bridge the gap between active and inactive students while adding a dynamic re-ranking step to foster varied content. By weighting links within past learning, the model balances recommendation precision with teaching variety. Tests on several real-world data sets show LiveGraph beats current baselines in both predictive accuracy and breadth of exercise range.
arxiv-2602-17136:
Jonathan Vahé led a two-author study of how energy changes hands inside turbulent multiphase flows. Kinetic energy and surface energy coexist in such flows, and their conversion could shape the overall energy balance, yet steady flows hide the exchange because both reservoirs stay constant. The authors force the issue by feeding kinetic energy in a fluctuating, time-periodic pattern.

Direct numerical simulations of homogeneous isotropic turbulence under periodic forcing, across varied flow parameters and dense volume fractions, trace a full cycle of injection, conversion, and dissipation. The team recasts the Ka-Pi-bara model in terms of total energy and adds equations for surface energy and its destruction. The model captures non-equilibrium effects, including the phase lag between kinetic energy and dissipation, and linearization reveals the system's key time scales.
arxiv-2602-17236:
Dimitrios Ntalampekos, writing alone, gives a necessary and sufficient condition for mapping a pair of disjoint Jordan regions on the sphere to a pair of disks by a quasiconformal map. When one region is a half-plane, the condition simplifies to a test involving Lipschitz functions.

The results yield two striking consequences. First, all polynomial cusps are quasiconformally equivalent. Second, a quasisymmetric embedding of two disjoint disks extends to a quasiconformal map of the whole sphere, with quantitative control. Combined with the author's earlier work, the paper also delivers a new test for compact sets that are quasiconformally equivalent to Schottky sets.
arxiv-2602-17436:
Yuan Miao led a three-author team on matrix-product operator dualities in integrable lattice models. Matrix-product operators appear in integrable lattice models, notably as transfer matrices. They can also build dualities between models, both invertible and non-invertible, including discrete gauging. The paper studies how Yang-Baxter integrable structures change under such dualities.

The R-matrix from baxterization transforms in a simple way. The authors argue a broad class of dualities calls for an extended R-matrix. That extended matrix meets modified algebraic relations, including a modified Yang-Baxter algebra known from the unitary case. Together these give a structure behind the dual model's transfer matrices that commute. Two case studies test the claims on the canonical XXZ spin chain. One is an invertible unitary operator, the cluster entangler from symmetry-protected topological phases. The other is a non-invertible operator, the Kramers-Wannier duality.
arxiv-2602-17636:
Jiyoung Kim and team improve virtual try-on, where fine garment detail often gets lost, above all in unpaired settings. Past methods fail to enforce person-garment alignment explicitly, and they leave unclear how correspondence arises inside Diffusion Transformers. The paper first probes full three-dimensional attention in such models.

It finds that person-garment correspondence hinges on precise query-key matching within that attention. Their system, CORAL, aligns that matching with robust outside correspondences through two losses: one distills reliable matches into attention, and one sharpens the attention spread via entropy minimization. A vision-language-model evaluation protocol better mirrors human taste. Tests show gains in both global shape transfer and local detail preservation.
arxiv-2602-17736:
Claudio Grimaldi asks whether technosignatures may already have reached Earth without detection or correct identification. In the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, incomplete sampling of the search space is often blamed for six decades without detections. If that account is right, undetected past contacts are possible, and Grimaldi tests what they would imply.

Using a Bayesian inference frame, he estimates present-day detectability given at least one undetected contact over the past sixty-five years, since the first SETI experiment. High detectability for emitters within a few hundred light-years would require implausibly many contacts, beyond even the local habitable planet count. Better odds need tightly clustered emitters or a very recent population boost. If past contacts did occur, the best prospects may lie in searches spanning several thousand light-years, with only a few detectable emissions expected.
arxiv-2602-17836:
Bonaventure Nana and team analyze the nonlinear motion of an upright magnet pendulum driven by two coils. A strong magnet interacts with two coils placed evenly around zero. Forces and torques come from a magnetic charges pull model and an experimentally fitted model, and rest points with their balance are mapped.

When coil currents are minus, the motion energy curve is bistable, even for equal currents and uneven for differing currents or signs. Plus currents yield an even tristable curve for equal currents and an uneven tristable curve for differing plus currents. With sine-wave coil current signals, tone balance math and runs are carried out for this electric-magneto-mechanical system. Results appear as response plots, shift time series and phase portraits. Split diagrams show varied motion with current sizes and rate as controls, including size jumps, hysteresis, many stable states and joint draw points, matched in tests.
arxiv-2602-18136:
Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider and two co-authors solve, in exact form, how a thin fluid layer answers to point pushes and pulls. Their 2026 paper treats a thin layer of chiral active fluid, where spinning parts give rise to odd viscosity, a trait that breaks time symmetry and mirror symmetry. The layer rests on a standard thin lubricating film.

Using a two-dimensional Green's function in wave space, the team writes down full formulas for flow and pressure. The formulas describe how tiny grains and self-swimming specks move and push on each other in such confined chiral fluids. They show how odd viscosity reshapes single-particle motion and group behavior. The results feed directly into models of transport, control, and self-ordering in tiny active fluid devices.
arxiv-2602-18236:
Yi-Zhen Li and three co-authors map the many flow states of turbulent heat convection in a wide, shallow cell.
