Their 2026 paper studies Rayleigh-Bénard convection in a rectangular cell ten times wider than tall, over a wide span of heating strengths and fluid thicknesses. Particle tracking shows the flow arranging itself into several side-by-side rolls.

Repeat runs at identical settings yield between three and seven rolls, with six most likely, proving several states coexist. At the thickest fluid setting, roll-like patterns give way to plume-dominated flow, and the momentum scaling law shifts with it. Within single rolls, sideways speed grows with roll width while vertical speed falls, in line with continuity. Starting conditions also steer the final state, and more rolls mean stronger vertical heat and momentum transport.
arxiv-2602-18436:
Jack T. Dinsmore and Roger W. Romani measure the motions of nineteen pulsars with X-ray precision. Their 2026 paper draws on fresh and archival Chandra X-ray Observatory data, including wind trails and X-ray filaments around pulsars. Precise X-ray proper motions are often limited by aligning observations to a common reference frame.

The team improves alignment by adding unresolved X-ray flux from Gaia catalog stars to X-ray bright point sources. Absolute positions referenced to Gaia reach typical precision near ten milliarcseconds, with the most precise X-ray proper motions achieved to date. With frame alignment improved, accuracy is now limited mainly by pulsar flux. The results uncover a new X-ray filament and clarify the structures and origins of wind nebulae around several pulsars in the set.
arxiv-2602-18536:
Suna Buğday and two co-authors show tiny adversarial tweaks can make MRI reconstruction models hallucinate. Their 2026 paper notes generative models increasingly improve medical imaging, such as MRI and CT reconstruction. Such models hallucinate: they may insert features absent from the original, endangering patients through wrong diagnoses.

The team crafts adversarial noise-like perturbations for raw input images, inducing hallucinations on reconstruction. Evaluation uses brain and knee images from the fastMRI dataset with UNet and end-to-end VarNet. Results show these models are easily tricked by small perturbations and can be easily pushed into hallucinating. That weakness may partly explain why hallucinations occur and suggests careful adversarial training may reduce their prevalence. Yet these hallucinations cannot be reliably detected with standard image quality metrics, so novel approaches will need development to detect them.
arxiv-2602-18936:
Personalised image making must balance content faithfulness with style consistency. Yu Li, with two co-authors, presents CRAFT-LoRA in 2026. It tackles three persistent problems with combining Low-Rank Adaptation weights. Content and style representations become tangled. Guidance for controlling each element's influence is insufficient. Weight fusion is unstable and often needs extra training.

CRAFT-LoRA has three complementary parts. Rank-constrained backbone fine-tuning injects low-rank projection residuals, encouraging separate content and style subspaces. A prompt-guided approach uses an expert encoder with special branches for meaning extension and precise control through selective adapter merging. A training-free, time-based guidance scheme adjusts noise predictions across diffusion steps, steadying making. The method improves content-style separation and enables flexible control over module combinations, with high-truth output and no retraining overhead. Content and style must stay separate. That separation is the whole trick.
arxiv-2602-19036:
Silver niobate is a lead-free perovskite with promise for energy storage and optics, yet its cold crystal structure has stayed debated. Ying Song, with six co-authors, revisits its low-energy shape landscape in 2026 using a theory-based shape search based on phonon-mode theory.

A new chiral ferroelectric phase with space group R3 is found. It shows large natural polarisation and a low switching barrier, so it can reverse polarisation under fields. Key, shape twist is by nature locked to ferroelectric charge, allowing field control of twist. Chiral optical effects, including circular dichroism, photogalvanic effect, optical action, and second-order nonlinear optics, can therefore be switched in reverse by an outside field. The results clarify cold shape ways and give a rare purely mineral platform for field-tunable twist, opening a pathway toward fast, field-tuned chiral optics.
arxiv-2602-19436:
Calibrating low-frequency gravitational-wave detectors is hard because calibration lines have weak signal-to-noise ratio, especially in torsion-bar systems governed by rotational dynamics. Yuki Inoue and two co-authors optimize the geometry of a torque-coupled gravity field calibrator, improving calibration-line signal-to-noise by more than tenfold over conventional layouts. The work targets CHRONOS, a cryogenic sub-hertz torsion-bar detector.

In CHRONOS, the calibration signal appears as a single line within the 0.1 to 10 hertz band. At 1 hertz, the strain-equivalent calibration amplitude reaches 1.16 times 10 to the minus 14th power, with a signal-to-noise density of 4.16 times 10 to the third power. This is the first direct injection of a high-quality calibration line into the sub-hertz band of a torsion-bar detector.
arxiv-2602-19736:
Diffusion models sharpen images well, but they normally work on small fixed patches, while real remote sensing needs whole scenes at once. A 2026 arXiv paper by Shoukun Sun and four co-authors tackles super-resolution for arbitrarily large aerial scenes without visible seams.

Stitching tiles together usually erodes variance, because averaging cancels the independent noise each tile carries, and that blur defeats the purpose of sharpening. The authors carry a variance-corrected fusion method into conditional super-resolution, replacing global normalization at each step with independent per-tile contributions added in one pass. The resulting pipeline, InfScene-SR, splits work across graphics processors and proves seamless and sharp at once on aerial test scenes.
arxiv-2602-19836:
Solar flares release energy along magnetic loops, and the timing of their thermal and nonthermal peaks may depend on loop geometry. A 2026 arXiv paper by S. M. Perriyil and three co-authors tests that link with a sample of flares observed between 2013 and 2015. Observations cover soft X-rays and hard X-rays, plus extreme ultraviolet light.

For each flare the team measures the delay between hard and soft X-ray peaks and estimates loop length from ultraviolet footpoints, assuming a semicircular shape. In every case, longer loops go with larger delays, and the full sample shows a strong correlation. The trend survives stricter tests of Neupert-effect compliance, growing stronger in the most selective subset. The results confirm directly that loop geometry helps govern how flare energy transport unfolds in time.
arxiv-2602-20036:
The Erdős–Straus conjecture claims every fraction with numerator four can be written as a sum of three unit fractions. Related claims extend that idea to other numerators. A 2026 arXiv paper by Philemon Urbain Mballa, working alone, develops a parametric approach. It claims explicit solutions for a set of integers of density one.

The approach centres on a fundamental function. When that function equals a perfect square, a solution follows. In the classic case, the author gives explicit symmetric solutions for three residue classes modulo four, already covering three quarters of all integers. For the long-resistant class of one modulo four, explicit mirror solutions are constructed from a divisor condition. The author argues that condition holds for almost all such integers, with exceptions of density zero. The paper thus claims proof for a share of integers tending to one, plus endless new solution families.
arxiv-2602-20236:
When magnetic patterns shift in space and time, moving electrons feel fake electric and magnetic fields. That picture is well worked out for ordinary magnets, but little was known for a newer class: magnets with no net magnetization that still split electron spins. A 2026 arXiv paper by Constantin Schrade and Mathias S. Scheurer builds a low-energy theory for electrons moving through slowly changing patterns of this new order.

In the slow-change regime, these patterns create extra fake fields and geometric effects that ordinary magnets do not show. One is a fake Zeeman field that encodes the pattern's structure, which could let experimenters nudge spins locally and tell different orders apart. The theory also predicts a lensing effect for electrons that depends on spin and comes from quantum geometry. The work extends the fake-field picture into territory where net magnetization vanishes but spin physics stays rich.
arxiv-2602-20336:
Radoslaw Roszczyk and three co-authors compare machine-learning methods for document sorting under class skew. Their study weighs sorting accuracy against run cost, a key trade-off for real-world auto systems. Three models of varying size were tested: a Naive Bayes classifier, a bidirectional LSTM network, and a fine-tuned transformer-based BERT model. A demo system for skewed document routing was also built.

BERT reached the highest accuracy, above ninety-nine percent, but needed far longer training and more power. The BiLSTM offered a strong middle path at about ninety-eight point six percent accuracy with modest training costs and robust context grasp. Naive Bayes trained fastest, in milliseconds, but scored lowest at about ninety-four point five percent. Class skew hit all methods, most for small groups. The authors conclude that BiLSTM gives the most even choice for the studied case.
arxiv-2602-20436:
The neutron skin, a nucleus's neutron layer, is probed with coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. Kyoungsu Heo and six co-authors compare pion-decay and kaon-decay neutrinos at rest, sorting observables by qR. Pion-decay neutrinos stay near-coherent for all nuclei, while kaon-decay neutrinos at two hundred thirty-six megaelectronvolts reach qR at or above one, where recoil spectra gain sensitivity to the weak form factor.

Using carbon, calcium, and lead nuclei, the authors quantify statistical skin sensitivity at a JSNS-squared-like facility. For ten ton-years and kaon-decay fluences, sensitivities reach about nine hundredths to two hundredths of a femtometre for calcium forty-eight. For lead two hundred eight they run about seven hundredths to two hundredths, as fluence rises. The results rival parity-violating electron scattering results such as CREX and PREX, with different systematics from a clean neutral-current probe.
arxiv-2602-20836:
Many mechanical systems shake under noise whose strength changes over time, and fractional noise adds long memory to the picture. Yanbin Zhu, Xiaomeng Jiang, and Yong Li derive a key formula for such systems in this 2026 arXiv paper: the Onsager-Machlup functional for second-order Newton-type dynamics driven by time-dependent fractional noise.

Their argument applies a Girsanov transformation to the non-degenerate parts of the system and evaluates a limiting conditional expectation tied to the noise, with the stochastic Fubini theorem playing a central role. Two noisy mechanical systems illustrate the result, backed by numerical simulations. The paper gives physicists a concrete way to weigh which paths a noisy Newton system is most likely to follow.
arxiv-2602-20936:
Artificial agents that deal with others must both guess conduct and decide whether others' gains matter. Mahault Albarracin and six co-authors split those two jobs in this 2026 arXiv paper, joining a past-based mind-reading model with an explicit other-regarding value weight. They test the setup in the iterated prisoner's dilemma.

Strong, even other-regarding value keeps mutual teamwork alive, while strong lopsidedness leaves the more caring agent open to steady misuse. Online guesses about a rival help near the teamwork edge but cannot stand in for true other-regarding value, and guessing alone with no such value yields no teamwork. Planning depth helps most against partners who pay back in kind. The paper maps guessing, planning, and prosocial value as distinct yet linked parts of social agency.
arxiv-2602-21136:
Expert talks yield deep insight, but experts are scarce and scaling talks is hard. David Anugraha, Vishakh Padmakumar, and Diyi Yang build a machine host in this 2026 arXiv paper via SparkMe, a multi-agent language-model host. They frame flexible half-set hosting as tuning: balance topic-guide breadth, fresh-theme finds, and talk length.

SparkMe plans with forethought through mock chat rollouts, picking questions with high hoped-for value. Control trials show better breadth, nearly five percent above the best base case, plus richer fresh insights in fewer turns. A study with seventy volunteers across seven fields confirms experts rate its talks highly. Code, data, and steps are open source.
arxiv-2602-21236:
Language models now argue in public on social media, yet most studies use private chats that miss multi-party dynamics. Matteo Migliarini and seven co-authors fill that gap in this 2026 arXiv paper with @GrokSet, a dataset of over one million tweets involving the Grok model on X. Analysis reveals a functional shift in how the model is used.

Instead of serving as an all-purpose helper, people often call on the model to settle contested, high-stakes political disputes as if its word were final. Yet it receives far less social validation, likes and replies, than human peers: a visible but low-status utility. Hostile users slip past safety filters by taking on a simple invented role and copying its tone, rather than by crafting elaborate jailbreaks. The dataset is released for studying AI agents in societal discourse.
arxiv-2602-21336:
Video quality metrics guide codec training, but they can be gamed: unsharpening an image can raise its VMAF score while lowering perceived quality. Florian Fingscheidt, Alexander Karabutov, Panqi Jia, Elena Alshina, and Jorn Ostermann study that vulnerability for the hardened VMAF NEG variant in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their contributions are threefold.

First, they identify and analyze VMAF NEG's remaining vulnerability, particularly when it is used to fine-tune image codecs. Second, they propose a robust loss including VMAF NEG for fine-tuning either encoder or decoder, keeping its high correlation with human perception while resisting attacks. Third, quantitative results are supported by perceptive impressions of example images, grounding the metric discussion in visible quality.
arxiv-2602-21936:
Leonardo Colombo, Thomas Beckers, and Juan Giribet present a control scheme for quadrotor drones that learns to cancel unknown pushes and twists. Starting from a standard tracking controller, they add a learning-based estimator that guesses the unmodeled forces and moments, then folds those guesses into the control signals. A gain schedule then tunes how hard the controller reacts, based on bounds on the model's error.

The point is to fly less aggressively without giving up tracking quality: gentler feedback where the model can be trusted, firmer where it cannot. The paper states the trade-off plainly among model accuracy, robustness, and aggressiveness, and proves that tracking stays within a prescribed bound. The result is a principled route to safer, calmer drone maneuvers under real-world disturbances.
arxiv-2602-22436:
Front-end coders build reusable UI parts by setting visual and behavioral traits, but that freedom makes use hard: coders must search a large design space and pick lifelike values. Priyan Vaithilingam and three co-authors introduce distinguishing variations, variants that are both lifelike and distinct, framing their creation as design-space sampling.

Symbolic inference picks out visually key traits, while a language-model sampler makes lifelike instances from world knowledge. The team builds these variants into Celestial, a tool for viewing and mapping component design spaces. In a study with a dozen front-end coders, those who tried it found the variants useful for sizing up and mapping design spaces.
arxiv-2602-23336:
Camilo Gomez and two co-authors build a smooth stand-in for the zero-one loss, the gold standard for classification accuracy that gradient methods cannot use straight because it is not differentiable. Recent work has folded structured tuning into end-to-end differentiable models for richer inductive biases and tighter task alignment.

Their method projects smoothly, preserving order, onto the n,k-dimensional hypersimplex through a constrained optimization framework, yielding a new operator called Soft-Binary-Argmax. After deriving its mathematical properties, the authors show its Jacobian can be computed efficiently and wired into binary and multiclass learning systems. Tests show clear gains in generalization under large-batch training, since geometric consistency constraints on output logits narrow the performance gap large batches usually cause.
arxiv-2602-23636:
Zhihao Ding and three co-authors present FlexGuard, a tunable guard for LLM content. Most guard models treat guarding as fixed binary sorting, taking one fixed meaning of harm. In practice, rule strictness varies across platforms and shifts over time, making binary guards brittle under shifting needs.

The team first adds FlexBench, a tunable guard test giving controlled tests under multiple strictness regimes. Tests reveal a large mismatch across regimes: models strong under one regime can drop sharply under others. FlexGuard instead outputs a tuned sliding risk score showing level, aiding set calls via cutoffs. Trained via risk-matching tuning with usable cutoff choice plans, FlexGuard gets higher guard scores and much better toughness under varying strictness on FlexBench and public tests.
arxiv-2602-23736: Ruixiang Qian and four co-authors present PoCo, a tool for better coverage-based seed picking in mutational greybox fuzzing. Standard tools like afl-cmin pick seeds by coverage alone. PoCo goes deeper: it slowly drops obstacle conditional statements that block progress, then picks seeds again with a clearer path. That deeper picking finds seeds that plain coverage-based picking suppresses.
arxiv-2602-24036:
Abhishek Kulkarni and Sharon Lynn Chu study how human tutors design interest-based learning, to guide future AI tutors. The 2026 paper defines interest-based learning as instruction that frames content through each learner's own interests. That practice is shown to improve outcomes. It is costly for teachers to tailor one student at a time.

The team analyzed fourteen one-to-one online tutoring sessions, drawing on lesson artifacts, transcripts, interviews, and questionnaires, to learn how tutors weave interests into lessons and why they choose particular moves. Findings trace themes in how interests enter instruction at different stages and for different purposes. From those themes the authors draw actionable design implications for language-model tutors that aim to deliver interest-based learning at scale, grounding AI tutor design in observed human practice rather than guesswork.
arxiv-2603-00036: Le's team studies stability of matrix polynomials under structured changes of their coefficients. Those numbers vary smoothly and semialgebraically with a vector. For monic polynomials they show the spectrum, pseudospectrum, numerical range and joint numerical range vary Hölder smoothly with that vector. The space splits into a finite set of analytic semialgebraic submanifolds. On each, eigenvalues and Jordan pairs vary smoothly. Most results survive replacing the monic rule with local full rank of the leading term.
arxiv-2603-00136: Wilson presents TinyVLM, the first system for zero-shot object detection on microcontrollers with under 1MB of memory. It splits visual inference from text encoding, so precomputed class embeddings live in flash memory. Matryoshka distillation trains nested embeddings at sizes from 16 to 256, giving flexible accuracy-memory trade-offs, while quantized storage cuts class prototype memory fourfold with little accuracy loss. Trained on Conceptual Captions 3M, it runs on 892KB of flash and 285KB of RAM, hitting 26 FPS on STM32H7, and topping 1,000 FPS on MAX78000.
arxiv-2603-00336: Jow and Leung show fast radio burst scattering through the circumgalactic halo is sensitive to small-scale gas shape and patchiness. The spread of scattering times from fluctuations in one halo, the tau distribution function, is measurable and resembles quasar absorption covering factors. The authors compute this spread for a turbulent medium along the line of sight, and for discrete structures localized along it. The spread reveals whether cool gas is mainly spherical, filamentary, or sheet-like. The work sets up future observations with hundreds of nearby-halo sight lines.
arxiv-2603-00536: Equbal and Ahsan test whether correlation driven altermagnetism can emerge in Hubbard models on frustrated lattice clusters, using exact diagonalisation. On a fully frustrated three by three torus at half filling, average spin response stays small despite strong local moments, so moments alone cannot break directional symmetry. Adding one mobile charge carrier creates a finite response that grows with on site interaction, with a d-wave like sign pattern and stronger response for electron doping. The signal vanishes on an unfrustrated lattice, pinning geometric frustration as the key driver.
arxiv-2603-00636: Damour proposes retrodictive forecasting: instead of guessing the future from the past, find the future that best explains the present. He frames this as inverse MAP maths over a conditional variational autoencoder, stressing it does not claim future events cause past ones. A symmetrised gap between forward and reversed path groups gives both the reason and a go no-go test for when the method applies. Tests on four made up processes and two ERA5 weather data sets put four set predictions to the test.
arxiv-2603-00836: Hakimoglu-Brown proves a conjecture of Kanade on the dilogarithm function, related to Nahm sums and Andrews-Gordon-type series. Kanade had studied modular partners to q-series results using Nahm sum growth, and Mizuno lately widened his growth formula for balanced Nahm sums. The proof uses laws from Kirillov and a ladder from Loxton and Lewin. The paper then proves two new related laws.
arxiv-2603-01136: Su, Hajaiej, and Shi solve the ground-state problem for Schrödinger equations mixing local and nonlocal operators with two critical nonlinearities, a combination earlier methods could not handle. Their approach generalizes Lieb's translation theorem in a subtle way, settling existence in the critical case for both operator types. They also discuss positivity and regularity of the ground states, opening the door to similar mixed-operator problems.
arxiv-2603-01236: Baek and three colleagues dissect image token trimming for large vision-language models, comparing focus-based and variety-based methods with true rank and focus entropy. Variety-aimed trimming keeps less trait variety than hoped, and its kept variety tracks higher made-up rates. Focus methods win on simple images and variety methods on complex ones with spread-out features. Image-aware tweaks to hybrid plans always lift scores, and a simple tuning pruner performs strongly across standard and made-up tests.
arxiv-2603-01636:
Will Price, Martin Formanek, and Johann Rafelski generalize a classic radiation formula to full relativity in this 2026 work. Cherenkov radiation is the glow from a charged particle that outruns light inside a material. The classic Frank-Tamm formula gives its strength for steady motion in a uniform medium.

Their covariant version holds in any frame, which suits fast particles in modern physics. From it they derive the matching reaction force, a friction-like push that stays consistent with relativity. The photon spectrum they present depends chiefly on the electric traits of the medium. They also hint the work may help explain an excess of soft photons seen in high-energy hadron crashes. A frame-free form makes the old result usable where speeds near light speed rule.
arxiv-2603-02036:
Edward Turner, Francisco Crespo, Joan Gimeno, and colleagues show that mere time lags can wipe out systems that copy themselves. Their 2026 work studies sloppy copiers like RNA viruses, whose fate is most often blamed on mutation rates. Drugs that block the virus copier, though, act by cramping that copier in time, not by raising mutations.

The team builds delays in copier supply into the quasispecies frame, the standard math for such virus swarms. With mutation rate and fitness map held fixed, swarms cross a death line from delay alone. The cause is lost timing between the steps that read the genome and the steps that copy it. Timing thus joins mutation as a free dial that can tip a swarm to collapse, a route the authors name lag-time-induced tipping.
arxiv-2603-02236:
Jiace Zhu, Wentao Chen, Qi Fan, and colleagues benchmark code models on GPU writing in this 2026 paper. The task is text-to-CUDA, turning a plain request into code for graphics processors. Older tests mostly check translation from other languages, an easier job. Judging speed also matters, since GPU code is built for performance.

Their benchmark, CUDABench, spans AI, science computing, and data work at varied depth and hardness. Scoring checks that code builds, runs correctly, and uses the hardware well. A roofline score grades how close code gets to peak hardware speed. Top models often built code that then ran wrong, the tests show. They also lacked domain know-how and left much GPU power unused.
arxiv-2603-02436:
Zhen Guo, Shanghao Shi, Hao Li, and colleagues defend reasoning models against hidden backdoors in this 2026 paper. Reasoning backdoors corrupt a model's chain of thought to justify a malicious answer. The fake reasoning sounds plausible but rests on a logical break. Large models can often spot such breaks, while small deployable ones cannot.

Their framework, TraceGuard, treats each reasoning trace as untrusted input. Synthetic forensic pairs first isolate where the logic fractures. Step-aware fine-tuning then teaches a small verifier a grammar for checking steps. A final reinforcement stage uses a verifier signal to reward sound auditing. That pipeline fights a key failure: verifiers memorizing trigger words instead of logic. A compact verifier reached forensic precision rivaling models a hundred times larger, even on unseen attacks.
arxiv-2603-02636:
Colin Cooper, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn, Tomasz Radzik, and colleagues time how a network of agents settles on one opinion. Their 2026 paper studies the Undecided-State Dynamics, where each node holds one of many opinions or stays undecided. Earlier results covered only few opinions or narrow starting states.

The new bounds hold for any number of opinions up to the network size, and for any starting mix, in both gossip and population protocol settings. In the gossip model, agreement arrives within a round count tied to the smaller of the opinion count and the square root of the network size. Matching lower bounds show the results are essentially tight. The work completes the timing picture for a basic consensus process.
arxiv-2603-02836:
J. Aguilar, M. Anastasopoulos, D. Barcot, and the large ESSnuSB collaboration study how two neutrino sources can sharpen one measurement. Their 2026 paper concerns the leptonic CP phase, a value that may explain why matter beat antimatter in the early universe. The ESSnuSB experiment plans to measure it with a powerful beam aimed at a huge detector.

Simulating years of atmospheric neutrino data, falling naturally through the detector, they find the phase resolution improves slightly over beam data alone. The added data also break ties with the unknown ordering of neutrino masses, a long-standing ambiguity. Beam and sky neutrinos thus cover each other's blind spots. The synergy strengthens the case for running both programs in one facility.
arxiv-2603-03036:
C. A. L. Bailer-Jones and L. Kreidberg weigh both members of close binary stars using only Gaia data. For an unresolved pair, orbital motion alone reveals the system's path, not the split of mass between the two stars. Their 2026 method adds brightness: a star's light output ties closely to its mass.

Using three-band Gaia photometry with model-based mass-to-light relations, they infer the brightness ratio and then each mass through a likelihood sampling that averages over age and composition. Applied to twenty thousand nearby systems, the main star's mass came out within about ten to twenty percent in most cases. Companion masses, reaching down to planetary sizes, were less precise but usable. The catalog flags near-twin binaries that can fake planet detections.
arxiv-2603-03336:
Angel Rodrigo Avelar Menendez, Yufeng Liu, and Xiaowu Dai warn that language model leaderboards look firmer than they are. Rankings come from pairwise human preferences and guide real choices about deployment and spending. Yet standard leaderboards print one fixed order, hiding estimation noise and the fact that a model's strength shifts with the kind of prompt. Acting on shaky gaps wastes resources and can mislead buyers.

Their 2026 framework ranks models per prompt type with honest uncertainty attached. A contextual preference model ties each model's appeal to prompt features, and simultaneous confidence intervals yield sets of plausible ranks rather than one brittle order. On large-scale human preference data, many celebrated rank gaps proved statistically indistinguishable. The method claims dominance only when data support it, otherwise returning a partial order.
arxiv-2603-03636:
Diosel López-Cruz works out cycle groups for shapes with pinch points. Algebraic geometry measures a variety with Chow groups, built from its algebraic cycles, and a finer cohomological version exists for singular spaces through an elaborate smoothing construction. His 2026 paper works out these finer Chow groups, in codimension one, for varieties whose only flaws are isolated singularities.

Two cases are settled. For varieties in higher dimensions, the working-out succeeds whenever the dual complex of the resolving divisor, a combinatorial shadow of how the resolution's pieces meet, is contractible. For varieties in three dimensions a weaker condition suffices: the vanishing of one cohomology group of that dual complex. The results give concrete answers in a theory where singular cases often resist direct computation, pushing the smooth theory further where both versions of the groups agree.
arxiv-2603-04436: Meng and colleagues federate language model tuning with ZorBA, a zeroth order method. Local updates burden client video memory, and frequent exchange burdens communication. Zeroth order passes drop gradient storage at clients. Different block subsets per client speed convergence and cut memory, while shared seeds and finite differences cut communication. Theory links block choices to speed and memory, and tests show VRAM use falls by up to 62.41 percent against three baselines.
arxiv-2603-04636: Jose and colleagues study how agents persuade through rhetoric in LLMs. LLM agents in open settings can be exploited for manipulative material. The study tasks LLMs with propaganda goals, reading outputs with two models. One model sorts text as propaganda or not, while the other detects tricks like loaded language, appeals to fear, flag-waving, and name-calling. When prompted, LLMs show propaganda acts and varied word tricks. Mitigation via Supervised Fine-Tuning, Direct Preference Optimization, and ORPO is explored. Fine-tuning cuts such output, and ORPO works best.
arxiv-2603-04836: Zhang and colleagues study two-tower ranking with unified text-image fusion in e-commerce search. Customers decide by jointly considering product text and visual information, yet most systems rely mainly on text. Domain-specific tuning and two-stage alignment between query and product text plus image modalities prove crucial. The paper proposes a modality fusion network fusing image and text information and capturing cross-modal complementary information. Tests on large-scale e-commerce datasets confirm the approach. Unified fusion thus strengthens multimodal retrieval beyond text-only ranking.
arxiv-2603-05136: Theresa Elstner and Martin Potthast offer Form Trueness, a check on whether algorithmic choices about people have a reasonable basis. It compares the external input form behind a choice with a self-account supplied by the person concerned, used only to check that input. The authors classify the mismatches between the two views and quantify how far apart they fall. They also release the first benchmark for the idea, built from loan choices, with 30,000 synthetic self-accounts drawn from German credit applicants plus expert mismatch labels.
arxiv-2603-05336: Pau Petit Rosàs revisits number joining of the differential form of Feynman integrals. His integrator uses a novel branch-cut treatment, evaluating master-integral bases in double and quadruple precision, faster than other tools. That opens the door to on-the-fly test of higher-hardness Feynman integrals in Monte Carlo generators, and enables cheaper, easily parallelizable grid making for prohibitive topologies. Testing one- and two-loop families, he reaches double-precision test times of milliseconds and hundreds of milliseconds respectively. He comments on results and suggests improvements.
arxiv-2603-05436: K. G. S. H. Gunawardana studies weak reading on a one-dimensional spin-1/2 deconfined key system with next-nearest-neighbour exchange K. Ferromagnetic below Kc, valence-bond-solid above it. Weak reading couples an ancilla system to the key system. Entanglement entropy, link length, and order settings follow. Asymmetric post-reading entanglement restructuring follows. the uniform-outcome path shows anomalous entanglement. Entanglement lifts below Kc and cuts above it. Asymmetry suggests a weak first-order boundary.
arxiv-2603-05636: Dey and Kang consider the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass with zero external field at inverse temperature β above zero. Here c_N equals N to the 1/3 power times one minus β_N squared. Assuming c_N stays bounded away from zero, they prove a log-partition variance formula. Variance equals negative one-half log of one minus β_N squared minus β_N squared over two, plus order c_N to the negative 3/2. Consequently, variance at one minus c times N to the negative 1/3 equals 1/6 log N plus O(1).
arxiv-2603-05936: Shimomura and team propose OD-RASE, boosting driving safety by spotting crash-causing structures and linking findings to roads. Self-driving systems see well but struggle with rare cases, while gains follow crashes. The frame sets out a road map, makes pitches with a visual language model, and filters for trust. This tags pitches on pre-crash images, building a new set. A baseline model uses visual language and spread models to produce pitches and images of improved roads. Tests show map sifting well predicts crash-causing structures and plans.
arxiv-2603-06036: Dietlmeier and team address hyper-column tangle with layered sub-sampling. Hyper-columns, from living vision, join multi-scale firings for a pixel, used with sorters for splitting. Handling dense hyper-columns grows in line with training size, capping use. The authors study group learning on sparse hyper-columns. Brain tumor tests show stacking and voting groups strong, but at N at most 20, Logit fitting wins. For 10 percent sub-sampling, the best Dice score is 0.66 for N equals 20, well above 24 percent over UNet baseline, less good due to over-fitting.
arxiv-2603-06136: Chen and his team work on diffusion distillation, where cuts to denoising steps have stalled, by tackling quality loss in partial time step low resolution generation. Their Cross Resolution Distribution Matching Distillation method splits time spans per resolution on logarithmic signal to noise ratio curves, and maps between resolutions to offset the shifts. Matching them along those paths closes the gap to the teacher's high resolution output, while noise put back in during upsampling steadies training. It keeps high fidelity generation across backbones, with a 33.4 fold speedup on SDXL.
arxiv-2603-06236: Kellner and his team set out a quantum nuclei corrected NMR crystallography method setting solid state NMR chemical shielding with simulations. Compute cost caps shielding accuracy, with low level approximations that skip thermal and quantum nuclear motion and err most for hydrogen bonded protons. They make cheap quantum ensembles with PET-MOLS, a transferable machine learning interatomic potential model. Feeding them to a chemical shift model lifts test agreement by 33 percent for hydrogen bonded protons with no fixes. Kind scaling spreads gains to amorphous solids past DFT reach.
arxiv-2603-06336: Ghosh and Ghosh present a thermodynamic view of quantum coupled transport in nanoscale systems, framed by entropy production and force-flux pairs. Thermodynamic laws hold across classical and quantum domains, but the analysis centers on quantum dots coupled to reservoirs. Processes face strong near-equilibrium constraints, motivating coupled transport where force-flux pairs coexist and interact. Entropy production guides coupled energy and particle transport in a two terminal dot setup, where Seebeck and Peltier effects emerge as cross effects. The framework extends to a three terminal dot geometry.
arxiv-2603-06736: Higuchi compares three satisfiability notions for propositional formulas over a fixed finite-dimensional Hilbert space. The first uses the standard Hilbert-lattice reading, the second a single commuting projector family for all atoms, and the third a local partial-Boolean reading checked node by node. He proves a chain of implications from the commuting reading through the partial-Boolean reading to the standard reading. One explicit formula separates them, satisfiable in the standard sense but not in the other two.
arxiv-2603-07636: Zhou gives a simple construction for the Gelfand-Dickey hierarchy's algebro-geometric solutions, from Dubrovin's method and the A_n-type infinite ODE system. Dubrovin's A_1-type system built such solutions for the KdV system, and later work covered any simple Lie algebras. The new build extends the method to the Gelfand-Dickey case. As a use, Zhou derives a formula for the N-point function of the related Riemann theta function.
arxiv-2603-07736: Li, Chen and Dimarogonas make tunable input-to-state safety respect motor limits. The tuning function sets safety caution and toughness against shocks, yet often ignores motor limits. They recast the safety rule as a state-linked half-space rule with a clear fit certificate from support functions. Fit then bounds allowed tunings from below. Norm-bounded, many-sided and box limits are covered, and rising tuning ensures fitting inputs and a doable QP filter. A linked cruise control test shows robust safety with input limits enforced by design.
arxiv-2603-07836: Berrouche and Tsiftsis propose Hadamard-NOMA, using the HT before coding to ease fading and channel flaws in NOMA systems. NOMA lets users share a block for spectral gains and massive access, but suffers from power sharing, fading, and bad channel data. Adding the transform reduces bit error rates and enhances trust, with simulations proving robust sending. Tests confirm forecasts with improvements over T-NOMA and Usman-NOMA schemes. Gains include boosts for near and far users at low error rates and lower signal ratios under noise control.
arxiv-2603-07936: Young and colleagues ask whether current vision-language and large language models can turn scanned student-drawn automata diagrams into digital form. Their study feeds scanned diagrams to a vision-language model for descriptions, which reviewers check and revise. Both raw and revised descriptions then go to a large language model for TikZ code, and the output is scored against the originals. Descriptions generated from images proved often incorrect, while correction improved their quality. The findings point to a workflow where model output plus review could support grading and feedback.
arxiv-2603-08036: Mandarapu and colleagues present Samyama, a graph-vector database in Rust that joins workloads usually split across separate engines: graph storage, vector search, analytics, and optimization solvers. It pairs a RocksDB-backed store with a vectorized executor, a cost-based planner, and a CSR analytics engine. It also offers RDF and SPARQL support, 22 metaheuristic solvers, HNSW indexing, and agentic enrichment that grows the graph with language models. A revised version withdraws earlier claims as unreproducible, including an 8.2x GPU speedup, and re-measures the system on rented Linux hosts.
arxiv-2603-08136: Chen and colleagues challenge the idea that physicality always improves user experience with social robots. As robots take on richer roles such as game masters in multi-party games, tangible interaction is often assumed to help across the board. Their study tests a boundary condition: users' Negative Attitudes towards Robots. In a between-subjects experiment with 67 participants, a custom robot game master ran a multi-party murder mystery game. It delivered clues either through direct tangible interaction or through a digitally mediated interface. Attitude scores moderated the outcome.
arxiv-2603-08636: Vitaly Khamitov and colleagues study a new twist on Fibonacci numbers that blends k-sections by convolution, with an eye to stronger stream ciphers. They give an explicit formula for these numbers plus a Binet-type formula, and they draw consequences for Fibonacci numbers and their convolutions through Chebyshev polynomials and Lucas numbers. Many of the new sequences, they note, do not appear in the OEIS encyclopedia.
arxiv-2603-08736: Mohammed Cherifi moves electric-vehicle charging management to the edge with specialist AI agents. Public fast chargers fail often and take days to fix, while cloud control cannot meet the latency and reliability bar. The Auralink SDC design resolves most incidents on its own in tests, with strong diagnostic accuracy and response times under fifty milliseconds.
arxiv-2603-08836: Oriol Reig Fité and Daniele Taufer compute minimal local generalized additive decompositions of homogeneous polynomials. They check the build does not depend on the chosen apolarity action, then give a determinant-based method that cuts the rank of a symbolic inverse system. If minimal supports are finite, the method lists every minimal decomposition without tensor extensions, and this holds when the rank stays within the degree.
arxiv-2603-08936: Hezhao Zhang and colleagues test speech emotion recognition by speech language models. Shifting from fixed labels to open text output makes scores swing with the prompt, and standard tests ignore how ambiguous human emotion is. Their VoxEmo covers 35 emotion corpora across 15 languages with a soft-label protocol, finding zero-shot models trail supervised baselines on hard labels yet match human subjective distributions.
arxiv-2603-09036: Renos Zabounidis and colleagues compose skills via LLM-guided symbolic planning grounded in deep RL. Language agents shine with high-level APIs but fail to turn words into low-level control, and one-shot generation lacks feedback to fix errors. Their SCALAR couples LLM planning with RL through a skill library, refining specs from execution feedback and reaching 88.2 percent diamond collection on Craftax, nearly twice the best baseline.
arxiv-2603-09436: Rong J. B. Zhu rethinks off-policy evaluation for contextual bandits, where a new policy must be judged from logged contexts, actions, and rewards. Inverse probability weighting fixes action distribution mismatch but suffers high variance. Zhu's Nonparametric Weighting builds weights from a nonparametric model, keeping low bias with typically much lower variance. Adding reward predictions yields Model-assisted Nonparametric Weighting, which models and mitigates bias directly for accurate value estimates.
arxiv-2603-09636: Ankit Kumar Panda and colleagues study, at LHC energies, how D and B mesons flow in directed fashion through a quark-gluon plasma with finite electrical and chiral conductivities. Heavy quarks move by Langevin dynamics in an extended quasiparticle model of the medium. The fields come from Maxwell solutions shaped by both conductivities, which steer the split in flow between mesons and anti-mesons. Chiral conductivity matters far less than electrical, and charm mesons flow opposite in sign to bottom ones.
arxiv-2603-09836: T. Riccardi and coauthors use magneto Raman scattering to map the magnetic phases of thin chromium oxychloride layers. This layered magnet hosts rival exchange forces, giving ferrimagnetic, antiferromagnetic and canted states under strong fields. Some ordered states lock to the atomic lattice, while phonon modes shift in complex ways as spin and lattice couple. The pattern holds down to a single layer, with domains shifting by layer count.
arxiv-2603-10136: William Acero, Domingo Morales and Isabel Molina extend small area estimation to several dependent target variables at once. Estimators that ignore survey design can bias badly under informative sampling, and weight aware methods usually handle one response only. Their multivariate pseudo empirical best predictor works under a nested error regression model and accounts for the sampling mechanism. A unified form serves unit or area level data, with bootstrap error estimates and a housing example.
arxiv-2603-10236: Spallitta and Vardi extend conflict driven clause learning solvers to weighted model enumeration. The task lists satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula while tracking a weight function, supporting queries such as the top few models or all models above a threshold. Their methods weave weight aware conflict analysis, pruning based on weights and weight propagation into backtracking of both kinds, chronological and non chronological. Each style proves feasible, with clear trade offs in memory and pruning strength.
arxiv-2603-10336: Hanwei Yan and co-authors address two hard numerical problems for time-dependent mean field games, which model large crowds of agents acting with strategy. For forward solving, they extend the Hessian-Riemannian flow to the time-dependent case, proving global convergence under standard assumptions while keeping density positive. For inverse problems, they cast parameter estimation as a bilevel task and take gradients at the inner solution, not through any one solver's steps. That makes the framework solver-agnostic, with adjoint descent and Gauss-Newton speedups tested in experiments.
arxiv-2603-10436: M S Anwar and co-authors present COHORT, a framework that lets robot teams share large neural network inference under tight real-time limits. Field robots have little compute, bandwidth, and battery, and may have no server to lean on. COHORT learns an offline scheduling policy from auction-based allocation data, then adapts it online with multi-agent reinforcement learning. On vision-language tasks it cut battery use, raised GPU use, and met frame-rate and deadline constraints far more often than baselines.
arxiv-2603-10736: Mohammed Rafiq Namiq studies three nonpure versions of three classic complex properties, taken at the minimum facet dimension. The paper asks when a complex built from simple pieces keeps these good traits. The properties are vertex decomposability, shellability, and Cohen-Macaulayness. Strong vertex dismissibility gives a recursion, by deletion and link, that never lowers that dimension. A join has the strong property exactly when both factors do. For pseudoforest complexes, all the notions coincide, tied to a simple domination rule.
arxiv-2603-11036: Bent Ørsted offers an introductory essay on conformal symmetry. This is the symmetry of structures that preserve angles. They do so while allowing local rescaling. His route in runs through the Yamabe operator. This central tool was built to respect that symmetry. The essay shows how this operator serves conformal differential geometry on one side. It also serves representation theory on the other. It ties the two fields together. It does so through one shared symmetry.
arxiv-2603-11236: Guillermo Perna, Federico Centrone, and Esteban Calzetta derive a thermodynamic uncertainty relation for shortcuts to adiabaticity, protocols that speed up quantum processes when time comes from a quantum clock. Tracing out the clock turns the dynamics of their oscillator into a mixture of unitary Gaussian paths. In the noise-dominated regime, they compute the gap in energy from the outcome. They compute its fluctuations, fidelity, and purity loss. Joining these yields a tradeoff. It links precision to purity loss, fixed by clock exactness and protocol sensitivity.
arxiv-2603-11336: Rasjied Sloot and coauthors present Proto-NUX, a pathfinder telescope for a planned wide-field near-ultraviolet array meant to catch fast-evolving transients from the ground. The prototype adapts an off-the-shelf astrograph to boost throughput and image quality across the near-ultraviolet band. Tests are set for a high-altitude French observatory in 2026. Its two jobs are proving the array's sensitivity is feasible, and mapping atmospheric extinction in this band. It splits Rayleigh scattering from ozone absorption across three filter setups.
arxiv-2603-11636: Řepa and co-authors study reconfigurable plasmonic antennas that can switch their hot spots on demand. Hot spots are tight zones where electric or magnetic fields spike near the antenna. Gold alone gives a fixed response, while vanadium dioxide allows ON/OFF switching. A composite gold and vanadium dioxide platform goes further, flipping between electric and magnetic hot spots in one antenna. Bowtie and diabolo antennas serve as the test cases. The composite also brings strong optical absorption and one joint electric-magnetic hot spot.
arxiv-2603-11736: Ullasci and co-authors test a state-of-the-art generative model for gender bias in job suggestions. The team asks GPT-5 to suggest jobs for 24 simulated candidates, all under-35 Italian graduates. Profiles stay balanced across gender, age, experience, and field. Job titles and industries show no clear gender split. The language around them does: women draw emotional, empathetic adjectives, while men draw strategic, analytical ones. The authors flag a fairness and transparency concern for digital labor markets.
arxiv-2603-11836: Sadeghkhani and co-authors review a decade of Generative Adversarial Networks for rebuilding porous materials from images. They sort 96 papers, from 2017 to early 2026, into six GAN families, from vanilla to hybrid designs. Gains are wide: pore share within 1% of the real samples, permeability errors cut by up to 79%, and rebuild sizes grown from 64 cubed to 2,200 cubed voxels. Open problems stay: compute cost, memory for large rebuilds, and keeping structure whole when moving from flat images to 3D.
arxiv-2603-12036: Kanwal and co-authors classify images with a single pixel sensor and a very fast light projector. A microLED-on-CMOS projector encodes each scene in less than a millisecond, reaching multi-kHz frame rates. The team tests the system on the MNIST digits task with two lean models. An extreme learning machine and a small neural network both keep inference time close to the capture time. Since no image is rebuilt, the extreme learning machine also suits fast anomaly detection as a binary classifier.
arxiv-2603-12536: Munroe, Newton, and Shah revisit how log-log regression results are read. Such slopes estimate the elasticity of the geometric mean, not the plain mean that decisions need. The gap, called retransformation bias, is unbounded and can take either sign. They build a debiased estimator for that mean that stays robust across specifications. Re-estimating fifty published results, they find nineteen change significantly, with a median gap of 65% of the original estimate. The point matters for any reader who uses such numbers to guide real choices.
arxiv-2603-12636: Negar Soheili and co-authors ease the cost of solving finite-horizon Markov decision processes with high-dimensional states. Such problems arise when valuing Bermudan options and real options. Basis-function methods either pile up error or grow costlier with the horizon. Their weakly time-coupled scheme makes cross-stage dependence fixed as the horizon grows. Its bound sits between two known methods and tightens as the basis expands. On option and ethanol cases, it beat both rivals in every test.
arxiv-2603-13036: Donghoon Shin and co-authors interrogate design homogenization in web vibe coding, where lay creators prompt models instead of writing code. Generative tools tend to copy dominant styles from their training data. For web design, that pull may narrow the range of sites online. The authors map the vibe coding lifecycle and mark stages where sameness can creep in. A sociotechnical risk analysis then unpacks the harms. Their fix centers on productive friction that pushes creators to challenge default outputs.
arxiv-2603-13236: Maria Victoria Carro and David Lagnado study how people assign causal blame when AI harms occur. Cause selection is a key first step for liability after safety failures or misuse. Their human experiments probe causality, blame, foreseeability, and counterfactual reasoning in causal chains. More AI agency led people to assign more causal responsibility to the AI. Humans were still judged more causal than AI in matched roles, and developers drew high blame too. An agentic component was judged more causal than the language model part.
arxiv-2603-13436: Deepesh Kalauni and co-authors report a high-field pulsed magnet system with a fiber-coupled cryostat for magneto-photoluminescence work. A novel part is the use of electrolyte capacitors in a 75 kJ bank to drive the magnet. That design yields high fields at a low charging voltage of 400 V. The zylon reinforced wire wound coil reaches a peak field of 35 tesla with a 10 ms rise time. A 4 K helium closed-cycle cryocooler gives a stable cold setting down to 5 K.
arxiv-2603-13536: Rinka Miura proposes Active Sampling Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization for ground-state energy estimation. Near-term quantum devices give only finite-shot measurements and prepare imperfect, contaminated states. Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization restricts the Hamiltonian to sampled basis states and diagonalizes it classically. Naive sampling is biased under finite shots, and blind random expansion grows inefficient with system size. Miura ranks candidate basis states with a perturbation-theoretic acquisition function based on Epstein-Nesbet corrections. Tests on spin chains up to 16 qubits, plus IBM Quantum hardware samples, beat standard SQD.
arxiv-2603-13736: Yuxing Zhong and co-authors report a blackbody quasar and radio source as a candidate transitional Little Red Dot. Subaru PFS spectroscopy followed up a radio-loud quasar at redshift 1.715 with X-ray detections. Its spectrum shows a broad MgII line and a curved UV continuum that dust extinction on a typical quasar cannot reproduce. A blackbody spectrum near 10,000 K fits it well, with photometry modeled by three blackbody components. The authors suggest the source is caught as a dense LRD-like envelope fragments and a quasar emerges.
arxiv-2603-13836: Yamazaki and co-authors show that silicon vacancies in silicon carbide can sense electric fields inside power devices. High fields drive device failure, yet no tool could map them at fine scale before. The vacancy responds equally to field parts along and across the crystal axis, a trait no other quantum sensor shares. That response lets it read fields in any direction. The team detects fields near 2.3 megavolts per centimeter, about 90% of the breakdown field, and maps their spread.
arxiv-2603-13936: Chattopadhyay and Joardar study two size measures for reduced group C*-algebras. Each algebra gets a metric from word length on its group. One measure is metric dimension, in David Kerr's sense. The other is the product entropy of maps that come from group maps. For groups of polynomial growth, that entropy is bounded above and below by known group entropies. For groups of exponential growth, the metric dimension is most often infinite.
arxiv-2603-14636: Ieong and co-authors steer large audio-language models by nudging hidden states. Chain-of-thought prompts can coax reasoning from such models. Gains without training remain hard to win. Three steering plans draw on varied information sources. Tests span four audio-language models and four benchmarks. Accuracy rises up to 4.4% over plain chain-of-thought prompts, they report. Steering vectors built from a few text samples also guide speech reasoning. That cross-modal transfer shows strong data efficiency.
arxiv-2603-14736: Hernández and Hidber exhaust the curve complex of a non-orientable surface by rigid expansions. The surface is closed, connected and of genus at least six. Irmak's finite rigid set anchors the argument. Rigid expansions of that set fill out the whole curve complex. Any graph endomorphism locally injective on the set must come from a surface homeomorphism. The proof first shows the expansions reach every curve. Rigidity then spreads from the finite core to the full complex. The result settles the exhaustion claim for this surface class.
arxiv-2603-14836: Dong and co-authors find residual group-like symmetries inside non-invertible selection rules. Fields here carry labels from a fusion algebra built on finite group classes. Loop effects break the plain fusion rules in general. A groupification step keeps Abelian and non-Abelian group-like symmetries exact anyway. Heterotic string examples on non-Abelian orbifolds ground the study. An approximate discrete symmetry gauges the size of loop-born couplings. Most rule parameters stay natural in the t'Hooft sense, they find. Symmetry anomalies add further model limits.
arxiv-2603-15036: Abdelaziz and co-authors compute primordial non-Gaussianity in Inflation without an Inflaton, where tensor waves create scalar perturbations at second order. Working on an exact de Sitter background, they derive the scalar bispectrum and the three-point function of the scalar potential. The bispectrum depends on the ultraviolet cutoff in a log form, unlike the power spectrum. Its shape peaks in squeezed configurations. Once normalized to observations, its size at CMB scales is far too small to detect.
arxiv-2603-15336: Cheshire and Issartel tackle active seriation, the task of restoring a hidden order to a set of items. The method queries pairwise similarities one by one and adapts as answers arrive. Observations are noisy reads of a permuted Robinson matrix that encodes the true order. Their algorithm may start from partial order knowledge or from scratch. Under a uniform gap condition on the similarity matrix, it recovers the order with high probability. The guarantees cover both error rates and the number of queries needed.
arxiv-2603-15536: O'Loughlin and Rani study q-numerical ranges and the spectral constants of convex domains that hold a matrix spectrum. They extend the Crouzeix-Palencia framework with bounds that depend on a parameter gamma. Those bounds tie back to the shape of the domain and the classic numerical range. The proof that the numerical range is a spectral set with constant one plus root two carries over to scaled q-numerical ranges. They also state a q-version of Crouzeix's conjecture and apply it to GMRES convergence bounds.
arxiv-2603-15936: Painter, Haguinet, and Bate rebuild ClinicalTrials.gov as a safety-ready database. The registry holds the largest public stock of trial records. Free-text harm reports block clean cross-trial safety math, though. Their CTG-DB pipeline converts the full XML archive into relational form. Adverse events map to MedDRA terms by exact and fuzzy matching. Arm-level denominators and placebo arms stay preserved in the schema. Concept-level queries then support pooled safety checks across trials. The open tool feeds downstream signal detection work.
arxiv-2603-16136: Chen and co-authors track the same players across two games with opposed incentives. League of Legends rewards narrow specialization for success. Teamfight Tactics rewards breadth and flexible play instead. The study follows 4,830 players with 50-plus games in both. Same-person tracking cuts the self-selection bias of past work. Players keep their style across both platforms despite the clash. Flexibility habits stay put when the payoffs flip. Personal agency predicts style better than game structure here. Designers who want behavior change face a stiff headwind.
arxiv-2603-16236: Park, Je, and Park build restaurant suggestions from customer reviews. Most language model tools lean on item titles and built-in knowledge. Reviews instead hold the factors that drive each user's choice. Their ReFORM system writes factor-based profiles for users and dishes. A multi-factor attention step weighs which factors matter most per user. Tests on two restaurant datasets beat strong baselines. The design also shows where the personal touch comes from.
arxiv-2603-16336: Wilson and co-authors report lessons from a robot barista that struggled in the wild. A Furhat robot served free daily coffee for five weeks. The site was a housing complex for over-50s in Stockton, England. The study tested whether story-driven dialogue kept residents coming back. Repeat use stayed low. Breakdowns, access barriers, and social dynamics got in the way. The team shares what this means for long field studies with robots.
arxiv-2603-16436: Gu and co-authors explain model decisions for whole input distributions at once. Most counterfactual methods work one case at a time. The distributional version balances closeness in inputs against a target output shift. Its gradient method fails on non-differentiable models, though. Their DISCOVER solver swaps gradient descent for a budgeted search. Per-row impact scores focus edits on the samples that matter most. Tests show strong alignment of input and output distributions.
arxiv-2603-16936: Song and co-authors link facial understanding and facial animation through language models. Text guided body animation has raced ahead, but face animation lacks large text paired corpora. The team uses generative models to synthesize about 80 hours of facial video. Prompts cover emotions and head motions, and each frame is fit with 3D facial parameters. This yields large sets of prompt and parameter pairs. They then test language models in both directions: motion to text, and text to motion.
arxiv-2603-17336: Lehner and Righetto use football to measure how talent moves between countries. Their data cover over 92,000 professional players from Transfermarkt, with nearly 20,000 who can play for more than one nation. They call the shift in player value leg drain. France gains over three billion euros in value, they find. African and Caribbean nations lose the most compared with their economies. Old colonial ties strongly predict these flows, they report.
arxiv-2603-17736: Cai asks whether dissipation hides inside a quantum system's time evolution. Lab runs of Hamiltonian dynamics often pick up noise from the environment. His test uses only black-box access to the evolution channels. A randomized procedure decides if dissipation of a set size is present. Total evolution time scales as one over that size, which is provably best possible. The result gives labs a sharp noise check.
arxiv-2603-17936: Huang and Andersen explore cross-resonance gates between capacitively coupled fluxonium qubits. They derive a simple formula for the peak ZX interaction strength. Past the perturbative zone, a CNOT still lands under 200 nanoseconds with stray ZZ held near 50 kilohertz, they find. Floquet math on the driven control qubit anchors the semi-analytic route. Harmful frequency clash windows get mapped as well. Big fluxonium rigs promise steadier yields than transmon layouts.
arxiv-2603-18036: Schmitz proposes MST-Direct, a method for multivariate geostatistical simulation based on optimal transport. Geological variables often link in bent, bimodal, or step-like ways. Gaussian copula and LU methods assume straight-line links and lose those patterns. MST-Direct uses the Sinkhorn algorithm to match full joint distributions at once. All variables move as one vector, so spatial structure and cross-variable links are kept together.
arxiv-2603-18336: Wang and co-authors release ManiDreams, a code library for robot grasp work that plans with doubt in mind. Most world models chase low forecast error and skip the doubt that real grasp work holds. ManiDreams treats doubt as a core part of the plan loop, not a side fix. It gives spread-out state forms, plug-in dynamics, and plain rules to bound each act. A test loop wraps any base policy with no retraining and holds up on ManiSkill tasks.
arxiv-2603-18536: Ai, Chen, Chen, and Zhao prove a weighted form of a recent cycle inequality for graphs. For each edge, they look at the heaviest cycle that passes through it. If an edge is a bridge, its weight counts twice instead. Summing edge weight over that cycle weight stays below half the vertex count minus one half. The result mirrors a classic global bound at the local level. The authors also describe graph families where equality holds and give conditions that equality requires.
arxiv-2603-18636: Luo and co-authors speed up video diffusion models by exploiting stable attention sparsity. Their SVOO framework needs no training. Offline profiling first measures how sparse each layer can safely go. Those levels barely change across inputs, the team reports. Online, a two-way co-clustering of queries and keys shapes sparse blocks. This respects both layer differences and query-key coupling. Across seven video models, SVOO reaches up to 1.93 times speedup. Quality holds near 29 dB PSNR on Wan2.1, beating prior sparse methods on the trade-off.
arxiv-2603-19336: Naik and Kundu speed up least absolute deviations regression, a robust fit that shrinks outlier pull. Classic solvers lean on simplex methods that grow costly in high dimensions. Their coordinate descent updates one weight at a time, with no matrix inversion. Each update has a closed form given by a median or weighted median. The method stays valid even when predictors outnumber the data rows. Tests match the accuracy of linear-programming solvers on real and fake data. It also scales better and stays stable in hard regimes.
arxiv-2603-19536: Chen and co-authors analyse over 1.3 million social media posts on California wildfires from 2016 to 2025. They ask how the public judges government actors during crises. Users spoke more negatively about named political officials than about working agencies. That gap grew during extreme fire events. Networks also split into more polarised clusters over time. Highly shared negative posts shaped what most people saw. Crisis attention shifted from agencies to political figures, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-19636: Zhang and co-authors present RiboSphere, a framework that learns compact codes for RNA structures. RNA backbones bend freely, and known 3D structures are scarce. RiboSphere encodes shape with a geometric transformer that sees centred, randomly rotated coordinates. Finite scalar quantization turns those features into a finite set of latent codes. A flow matching decoder then rebuilds atomic coordinates from the codes. The codes cluster on real RNA motifs, the authors find. Pretrained codes transfer well to inverse folding and ligand binding tasks.
arxiv-2603-19736: Contente and co-authors offer a cheaper way to tune finite-context models. These models compress symbol sequences such as DNA. Their skill hinges on context length and a smoothing value. Grid search over both is slow and scales badly. The two-step plan splits the search into two stages. First, dependence measures pick the context length. Then likelihood methods set the smoothing value. On simulated data the plan matched grid search compression at far lower cost.
arxiv-2603-20036: Kobs reframes continual learning as keeping old and new data on one shared latent manifold. Standard methods fight forgetting by penalizing parameter change or replaying old samples. Those tricks never say how the internal representation should evolve. Kobs builds a method, SPMA, around preserving the shared support of the data. A geometry-aware variant adds sparse replay, output distillation, and anchor-based shape keeping. On CIFAR-10 and Tiny-ImageNet shifts, it retained old tasks better than replay baselines. A synthetic atlas test showed near-perfect preservation of anchor geometry.
arxiv-2603-20136: Perrin develops a theory of optical long-baseline interferometry for polarized sources. Beam trains in such instruments distort polarization, which once spoiled coherence measures. Symmetric optical designs eased that problem in practice. Large telescopes now reach faint, strongly polarized sources, so a full theory is needed. Perrin adapts concepts from radio aperture synthesis to the optical case. A generalized Mueller matrix links the measured Stokes visibilities to the true ones. Instrument effects enter through that matrix in a clean way. Cases with single-mode instruments are worked out in detail.
arxiv-2603-20336: Tian and co-authors present GEM, a native index for multi-vector retrieval. Multi-vector search matches sets of vectors, giving finer semantic matches than single vectors. Reused single-vector indexes, though, often lose that meaning or run slowly. GEM builds a proximity graph directly over vector sets. Set-level clustering trims redundancy, and local graphs link into one navigable whole. At query time, beam search starts from several entry points with early pruning. GEM ran up to 16 times faster than leading methods at matched accuracy.
arxiv-2603-20636: Sartipi and co-authors use language models to spot wrong prices in retail product lists. Bad prices hurt sales, revenue, and shopper trust. Old tools set simple thresholds and ignore product details. Their system first finds price relevant look alike products. It then scores the target against each match on brand, size, and features. A final step merges these notes into a clear verdict. The system matched human auditors over 75 percent of the time.
arxiv-2603-20936: Bruns-Smith compares two ways to estimate Riesz representers directly, a key object in semiparametric statistics. One route comes from automatic debiased machine learning, the other from sieve methods for conditional moment models. Both solve different problems that share the same population solution. He shows the two estimators match numerically for unregularized or ridge regularized linear, sieve, and kernel models. They can differ under Lasso penalties or richer classes like neural networks, where the sieve route may offer statistical gains at higher compute cost.
arxiv-2603-21036: Beibitkhan benchmarks how large language models serve low-resource languages. Eight models are tested in English, Kazakh, and Mongolian, across five conditions. Fifty hand crafted questions span factual, reasoning, technical, and cultural topics. Two thousand responses are scored for accuracy, fluency, and completeness. Models trail English by about fourteen to seventeen points in the low-resource settings. They stay fluent while content accuracy drops. Prompting models to reason in English first helps bilingual models a little, but gives English dominant models no gain.
arxiv-2603-21136: Cai and Li present MS-CustomNet, a framework for image generation with several user-supplied subjects. Diffusion text-to-image models struggle to place many distinct subjects and control how they relate. Their method inserts multiple objects with no extra training for each one. Users define the hierarchy and spatial layout of the subjects directly. Subject identity is preserved while the stated relations are enacted. They also build the MSI data set from COCO for training. Scores show strong identity preservation and positional control.
arxiv-2603-21536: Okamura studies graph-directed conjugate functional equations on the unit interval, indexed by a two-vertex digraph with self-loops. The focus is on when solutions are singular and when they are smooth. For compatible systems of weak contractions, Okamura first treats the affine case. Both solutions come out singular unless the two systems coincide. For a class of linear fractional systems, he proves a sharp dichotomy between singularity and smoothness. He also gives a sufficient condition for singularity in a nonlinear setting.
arxiv-2603-21936: Amoyal and co-authors align two 3D Gaussian splatting models even when they show different objects of the same kind. Prior tools could only register two scans of the very same object, and often needed the true scale given. Their GSA method finds matches with viewpoint-guided spherical map features. A coarse step solves orientation, surviving flips of 180 degrees and tenfold scale gaps. A fine step then enforces feature agreement across views. In same-object tests GSA won by wide margins, and it gives the first category-level alignment.
arxiv-2603-22236: Petitpas and co-authors describe a photometry upgrade in the Quick-Look Pipeline for TESS data. The pipeline makes light curves for up to 2 million stars about every 27 days. New methods let it work better on fainter stars. The team adopts the photometry approach of the TESS-Gaia Light Curve package. That package showed lower noise on fainter stars than the old pipeline method. It keeps three apertures and three detrending levels for all stars. The change, live from Sector 94, should feel seamless to users.
arxiv-2603-22336: Sarmiento and co-authors classify quantum error correction under diagonal phase noise in geometric terms. They find the largest logical dimension a code can protect. It equals a classical packing number, Aq(n, 2t+1). No affine or stabilizer structure is assumed. Nonlinear codes can thus beat every affine construction when the packing number is larger. The key is a harmonic translation principle: phase operators act as rigid shifts in the Fourier domain. For mixed Pauli noise, they derive a rate cap that acts like an uncertainty principle.
arxiv-2603-22436: Reiber, in a short position paper, builds a dialectical frame for the politics inside technology projects. He draws on critical and emancipatory social science to make the case. A project's ideology, he argues, cannot be read from its stated values alone. The constraints the project works under matter just as much. He closes with a brief example that shows how the two sides fit together.
arxiv-2603-22636: Hyndman, Kandanaarachchi, and Turner present an updated version of the lookout anomaly detector. The method uses kernel density estimates to flag points that sit in low-density regions. Its bandwidth comes from Rips death diameters, a tool from shape analysis. The authors prove the density estimator is consistent. They also describe a multivariate scaling step that is robust and efficient. Tests on varied examples show the updated method beats the earlier version. The work gives the tool a firmer theory base for practical use.
arxiv-2603-22736: Li and co-authors use quantum Monte Carlo methods to study a symmetric mass generation transition. Such transitions open a gap with no symmetry breaking or topological order. The setting is a bilayer honeycomb lattice model. The team confirms a transition at a coupling near 2.584. It splits a Dirac semimetal phase from a symmetry-keeping gapped phase. Careful fits give critical exponents far from mean-field values. The team then drives the system out of equilibrium. Driven behavior still follows a generalized finite-time scaling law.
arxiv-2603-22936: Li, Wang, and Wu study the nonlinear stability of Taylor-Couette flows with heat buoyancy. The flow sits in an annular domain with small viscosity and thermal diffusivity. Buoyancy-driven convection matters for real uses of such flows. A buoyancy term adds a destabilizing radial derivative to the system. The authors use negative-derivative estimates to tame it. Extra viscous damping then offsets the instability. Their criterion bounds the starting disturbance by a power of the viscosity. Under it, solutions stay close to the base Taylor-Couette flow.
arxiv-2603-23036: Ran studies zero-uncertainty states with quantum memory from an operator algebra view. The frame handles degenerate projective measurements in a natural way. In the equal-dimension case, Ran proves a rigidity theorem. It covers purity and maximal entanglement. Two routes can break that rigidity: smaller observable subalgebras, or larger memory dimensions. Ran gives algebraic descriptions for both cases. A quantum steering example shows how the frame settles a concrete physical question.
arxiv-2603-23736: Saidi and three co-authors port parallel trends thinking to systems tracked as distributions. Cell groups and pay cohorts shift as whole spreads, not single numbers. Such spaces lack the plain vector math that classic tools need. Their Wasserstein Parallel Trends swaps subtraction for parallel transport along best-path curves. A fanning scheme makes that transport cheap to compute, with the first proofs of its kind. Plain averages fall out as a special case. Tests on cell data fill in gene dynamics across samples.
arxiv-2603-24136: Zhang and co-authors present SELLER, a framework that explains recommendations with sequence-aware language models. Past explainers ignore the order of user actions and use metrics with little practical value. SELLER reads both behavior sequences and item semantics through a dual-path encoder. A mixture-of-experts adapter aligns those signals with a language model. Its evaluation scores both text quality and the effect on recommendation outcomes. On public benchmarks, SELLER beats prior methods on explanation quality and real-world utility, they report.
arxiv-2603-24336: Driemel and co-authors give near-linear time approximation schemes for clustering in partially doubling metrics. The k-median problem picks k centers that minimize total distance to the points. Doubling metrics allow near-optimal fast schemes, but general metrics do not. The authors show the scheme extends when only one side, the points or the centers, has bounded doubling dimension. Their work gives the first such algorithm for median problems under discrete Fréchet distance. The results also extend to the facility location problem.
arxiv-2603-24436: Kafantaris proposes Enes, a causal discovery architecture built as a mixture of experts. The design lets model entities such as causal relationships be parameterised further, though fitting a neural net to this dataset proves hard. A simple, fast Pearson coefficient linear model already scores well, setting a tough baseline to beat. The work also stresses the limits of causal discovery from observational data alone. Unlike the Sachs study, no interventions are used, only prior knowledge, and the data itself is a key constraint.
arxiv-2603-24636: Zhao and co-authors present DyMRL, a dynamic multispace learning method for multimodal event forecasting.
