arxiv-2604-27936: Sarkar and eight colleagues push animal-sound classification past the human hearing band, where most audio models stop at 8 kilohertz. Animals call well above that range, into ultrasound, so the team splits the full call spectrum into band features and fuses them into one shared picture. Tests show some encoders yield band pictures that barely overlap, sharpening class splits after fusion. Across three data sets, eight ready-made models, and five fusion plans, fused pictures beat both baseband and time-stretch baselines on two sets.
arxiv-2604-28036: Dymetman isolates a single identity for exponential families. It gives a KL difference through the log-partition function and a moment. From that identity plus the plain fact that KL divergence is never negative, he gets a cluster of classic results by direct swaps. These include Pythagorean theorems, convexity of the log-partition function and the Gibbs variational principle. Standard analysis then recovers the gradient formula, the Bregman form of within-family divergence and the fact that the moment map covers all its targets.
arxiv-2605-00136:
Kaituo Zhang and 6 co-authors question a common belief about language model agents: that giving them tools always makes them reason better. When a task contains misleading but related material, tool use can fail to beat plain chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors ask where the loss comes from.

Their framework separates three costs: prompt format, the tool-calling protocol itself, and the real gain from running a tool. Under noise, the protocol cost often cancels the gain, a loss they call the tool-use tax. They add G-STEP, a light gate used at run time, which recovers part of the loss. The broader lesson is that stronger basic reasoning still matters.
arxiv-2605-00336:
Khizar Qureshi and 2 co-authors study how to feed long clinical texts to language models under a strict token budget. Clinical notes are long, mixed, and often repetitive, while the questions asked of them are short and high stakes. Their problem is to choose which pieces of a document to keep so a standard generator can answer within fixed cost and delay limits.

They frame the choice as a knapsack problem and propose an objective that balances relevance, coverage, and diversity. They compare ways of cutting documents into units, from sentences to clusters, plus a routing rule that adapts to the budget. On discharge notes, research abstracts, and a long-text benchmark, no single strategy won everywhere. Selector choice mattered more than unit choice, and one popular quality score saturated while another kept separating good summaries from bad.
arxiv-2605-00436:
Kenneth J. K. Ong studies how the phrasing of a task can plant presumptions in a large language model, quietly bending its decisions. In unpredictable real-world use, such presumptions are a safety and reliability concern: a model locked into an assumed framing adapts badly when the real task deviates. Ong tests the effect with a classic game as the case study.

In an iterated prisoner's dilemma, the models proved susceptible to presumptions in their choices, even when they reasoned step by step before deciding. When the task phrasing was kept neutral, the same models reasoned logically with little sign of the bias. The contrast is the paper's lesson. Careful, neutral task phrasing is not cosmetic; it measurably reduces the risk that a model will answer the task it expected instead of the one it was given.
arxiv-2605-00836:
Hao Xiao compares four classic solvers for the ordinary differential equations used when sampling from flow matching generative models. Sampling cost is dominated by neural network passes, so a better solver can save many evaluations. Xiao derives Euler, midpoint, classical Runge-Kutta, and Dormand-Prince methods from first principles, codes them from scratch in PyTorch, and benchmarks them from toy distributions to MNIST digits.

Runge-Kutta at eighty evaluations matches Euler at two hundred in sample quality. Two further findings stand out. The learned velocity field stiffens sharply near the end of the path, which explains why the adaptive solver spends steps there. The solver gap also widens for smaller or undertrained models, so solver choice matters most when the model is imperfect.
arxiv-2605-01136:
Sanjukta Krishnagopal asks whether thinning a graph changes what a graph neural network learns. Thinning, called spectral sparsification, drops edges while keeping the graph's Laplacian forms nearly the same, and it is often used to speed up training. Krishnagopal instead studies the learned embeddings: does their geometry survive when the graph is thinned?

For networks built on polynomial filters, the paper proves a bound. Any good spectral thinning shifts the filters, the hidden layers, and their Gram matrices by a small amount tied to the thinning error. Distances between points, class means, and covariance structure in the embedding space thus stay stable. Training paths on full and thinned graphs also stay close over finite time. Tests with effective-resistance thinning back the theory: even under heavy thinning, the learned geometry and training behavior barely move, and Gram matrix stability predicts how well neighborhoods and class centers are preserved.
arxiv-2605-01336:
Muhammad Arslan Manzoor and six co-authors build a shared toolkit for judging news outlets by political slant and factual care. Automated checks matter because outlets shape public views at scale, yet the field has lacked one large label set and one broad test of methods.

The team releases labels for about 2,600 outlets drawn from Media Bias/Fact Check. It also builds multi-view profiles for two outlet sets. Those profiles mix link graphs, graphs drawn by language models, articles, and encyclopedia pages. They test many ways to encode and merge these views, including a learning-based merger that tunes itself. Their runs set new best scores on the older ACL-2020 set and strong first benchmarks on the new one.
arxiv-2605-01536:
Cedric Martens, Philip Trettner, and Mikhail Bessmeltsev compute generalized winding numbers, a robust inside-or-outside score for 3D surfaces that may be open, self-crossing, or torn. Geometry tools lean on this score for many tasks, but known methods force a choice between speed and exactness.

Their antipodal method rewrites the number as two plain parts: the signed count of ray crossings with the surface, plus a boundary integral over the surface's shadow on the unit sphere. That split yields a discretization with no costly surface integrals. On meshes it runs over twenty times faster than the quickest exact rivals on a CPU, and on a graphics card it reaches a billion queries per second at full precision. For smooth parametric surfaces it is several times faster than the best prior method at the same precision, and messy topologies need no special care.
arxiv-2605-01636:
Carney studies a spare number system built from a single constant and one operation. The Exp-Minus-Log system, proposed by Odrzywolek, reduces every elementary function over complex numbers to the constant one plus a two-place function that subtracts a logarithm from an exponential. It matches the EL numbers defined by Chow, which formalize the idea of numbers expressible in closed form. Carney asks what this system cannot express, a question the original constructive account left open.

Every number expressible in the system turns out to be computable, meaning a machine could in principle grind out its digits. Chaitin's Omega, the standard example of a real number no machine can compute, therefore cannot appear in it. That gives the system its first formal inexpressibility theorem: a clean boundary between what closed-form expression can capture and what it cannot.
arxiv-2605-01736:
Sixian Zhang and five co-authors build maps that a robot and a large model can both read. Embodied navigation needs the shape of a space and its meaning at several scales at once. Earlier semantic maps traded one for the other. They also needed extra trained adapters before a big model could use them.

Their Gaussian-Language Map stores each semantic unit twice over: a plain-language description and a 3D Gaussian blob, which renders fast and stores small. Geometry stays explicit, and meaning runs from single objects up to whole regions. A Gaussian estimator derives the blobs from dense point clouds by direct calculation, with no gradient training, so maps grow step by step as the robot moves. On object finding, instance finding, and spatial question tasks, the map lifts navigation and reasoning while staying zero-shot compatible with large-model methods.
arxiv-2605-02036:
Saugata Barat and colleagues use the James Webb Space Telescope to read the atmosphere of TOI-1130b, a warm mini-Neptune in a rare two-planet system. Its outer companion is a hot Jupiter, and the pair sit in a two-to-one orbital resonance. Combining two Webb instruments, the team measures how starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere during transit.

They detect water, carbon dioxide, and sulphur dioxide, with a tentative sign of methane. The atmosphere is metal-rich and heavy, with a mean molecular weight well above that of hydrogen alone. Its carbon-to-oxygen share is bounded from above. The authors argue the traits fit formation beyond the water ice line, followed by later movement inward.
arxiv-2605-02136:
C Almeida asks whether the shadow of a black hole depends on the handedness of the light that probes it. In the basic geometric picture, the shadow edge is set by light paths alone and carries no polarisation information. At the next order, the gravitational spin Hall effect adds corrections that depend on helicity, the light's spin sense.

For any still, spherically symmetric spacetime, an exact mirror symmetry in the spin Hall equations forces those corrections to cancel at the capture edge. Both helicities share the same critical impact value, so no splitting occurs. Rotation breaks the symmetry. For a slowly spinning Kerr hole, Almeida derives the first non-zero shift, which grows with spin and falls with frequency.
arxiv-2605-02336:
Partha Sarker, Han Ma, and Urban Seifert study a Kitaev model on a honeycomb lattice, with spin-one moments. Interactions are quadrupolar and depend on the bond. They are also frustrated, which can hide ordered phases and favour disordered quantum states. The authors use several methods and expand around controlled limits.

A variational study in SU(3) flavour theory finds a huge set of classical ground states with the same energy. That suggests quantum effects may stabilise a disordered phase. In a bond-anisotropic limit, perturbation theory gives effective low-energy models that depend on a residual symmetry. A Majorana parton construction reveals an exact gauge structure. It motivates confined and deconfined phases driven by gauge-charge condensation.
arxiv-2605-02436:
Tomaž Fleischman and Ethan Buchman present the Cycles Protocol, a way to clear debts and payments without relying only on cash. In current clearing, trade credit holds a large stock of short-term funds, yet it sits outside formal systems. A key block is novation, the step where a central party takes over both sides of a deal.

Cycles instead maps debts as edges on a shared graph and clears them in closed loops, all at once. Risk stays with the same partners as before, so the method can sit beside current clearing houses. The authors focus on two uses: squeezing balances between clearing members, and bringing trade credit into formal settlement.
arxiv-2605-02636:
Dário Passos reviews why studies of neural networks for near-infrared spectroscopy so often disagree with each other. The technique reads food, farm, drug, and process samples quickly and without destroying them, and deep learning promises better readings. Yet papers conflict on kernel size, depth, preprocessing, model size, and transfer to new settings.

Passos argues many conflicts come from incomplete reporting of conditions, not truly opposed findings. Three moderators organize the review. Spectral signals are indirect and heavily overlapping, shaped by scattering and temperature. Network design should be read through receptive fields, the span of wavelengths a model can use. Validation design can act as a hidden setting, since random splits may reward the wrong traits. The review offers conditional design guidance instead of universal rules.
arxiv-2605-03036:
Prashant Arote and Manish Mishra construct a pinned, canonical Jordan decomposition for characters of finite reductive groups, even when the relevant dual centralizers are disconnected. Jordan decomposition maps each character series to unipotent characters of a smaller group, a core tool in representation theory.

With a fixed pinning, they build an exact bijection characterized by fit with Deligne-Lusztig formulas and Harish-Chandra series. For some disconnected groups, an enriched version records extra Clifford data as well. The construction uses Clifford theory, Weyl group comparisons, and Howlett-Lehrer theory. An application fixes the finite-field input in a depth-zero Hecke algebra comparison.
arxiv-2605-03336:
Alexander Pirker, Robert J. Hayek, Alexander Kolar, Igor Kadota, Joaquin Chung, and Rajkumar Kettimuthu test a centralized, task-based controller for quantum networks against the usual layered design. Layered control adds latency to entanglement requests, and delay degrades fragile quantum states before they can be used.

Simulated with the SeQUeNCe tool, their controller tracks memory across all nodes and schedules jobs offline by priority. Across bottleneck, grid, star, and caveman layouts, caveman and grid designs delivered more low-delay requests but also more heavily delayed ones. Queue behavior stayed robust under high load, supporting the framework's scale potential.
arxiv-2605-03936:
Daniel Drucker and Kyle Mahowald test whether language models can do conceptual analysis, the classic method of proposing a definition and refining it against counterexamples. They set up iterated chains. One model instance generates counterexamples to a proposed definition. Another instance repairs the definition, and the loop repeats. The study covers twenty concepts and thousands of counterexample-repair cycles.

Many model-generated counterexamples were judged invalid by both expert humans and a language model judge, though the model judge accepted roughly twice as many as the humans did. Per-item judgments agreed moderately well across judges. Longer iteration produced increasingly verbose definitions without improving accuracy. Some concepts resisted stable definitions altogether. The repair loop, the authors suggest, hits shrinking returns quickly.
arxiv-2605-04336:
James W. Bono models the contest between a cyber attacker and a defender who both invest in artificial intelligence tools across many attack surfaces. Attack spending helps in two ways: it strengthens attacks directly, and it can erode defence, with that erosion growing as the defender invests more.

Bono derives a closed-form ratio for the relative payoff of attack and defence spending and shows the contest settles to a unique stable outcome. A key factor is how much threat intelligence carries across surfaces. With full sharing, adding more attack surfaces gives the attacker no extra edge at all, because defence on one surface informs defence everywhere.
arxiv-2605-04536:
R. Labouriau develops a shape-based argument for why a smoothing kernel can rescue models from degenerate behaviour. In the framework he uses, a model is described by a distribution paired with a fast-fading kernel. It is not described by a classical density alone.

Labouriau argues the kernel places models in generic position. It does so relative to the loci where parameters cannot be told apart, information becomes singular, or forms fail. Using classical transversality theorems, he proves that for a generic kernel in a rich enough family, the induced feature map avoids those bad strata. He gives checkable rank conditions and verifies them for location families, the log-normal, and graphical models.
arxiv-2605-04636:
Alessio Basti and six co-authors introduce a family of measures for detecting genuine interactions among several brain signals at once, where one rhythm arises as the sum of others. Cross-frequency coupling is a basic mechanism for combining information across timescales. But volume conduction in the skull creates fake zero-delay links. Those links fool standard metrics.

Their antisymmetric polyspectral indices are immune to that instant mixing by design. The authors derive the measures' basic properties. They validate them on simulated cubic nonlinearities. They then apply them to real EEG recordings. There they reveal higher-order links that standard approaches miss. They also discuss personalised brain stimulation as a possible application.
arxiv-2605-04736:
Chiara Vercellino and seven co-authors present a neural approach to embedding a graph onto neutral atom quantum hardware. That layout problem decides whether an optimisation problem can run on the machine at all. In these devices, atoms excited to Rydberg states interact within a blockade radius, so the hardware's connectivity is exactly a unit disk graph.

Computing the connectivity from atom positions is easy. Finding positions that realise a desired problem graph is much harder. The target graph is given as a quadratic binary optimisation matrix. Their method searches for a feasible unit disk arrangement matching that target connectivity. The work addresses a recurrent bottleneck for solving combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom platforms.
arxiv-2605-04936:
Vivien Parmentier and seventeen co-authors report evidence that winds carry chemicals from the hot dayside of an exoplanet to its cooler nightside faster than chemistry can adjust. The planet, NGTS-10A b, is a hot Jupiter with a permanent day and night side. In balance, carbon should sit mainly as methane on the nightside.

Observing both sides with the James Webb Space Telescope, the team found water and carbon monoxide at similar levels on each side. The nightside held far less methane than balance predicts. They rule out odd elemental mixes and vertical mixing as explanations, leaving sideways transport by fast winds as the cause.
arxiv-2605-05136:
Yu-Hsi Chen and Abd-Krim Seghouane build CPCANet, a network that learns shared structure across data domains so models can generalise to unseen domains. Their starting point is common principal component analysis, a statistical method that finds one subspace shared by several datasets. They unroll its classic iterative algorithm into differentiable neural layers, making the search trainable end to end.

The design enforces discovery of a domain-invariant subspace while staying interpretable, and it needs no dataset-specific tuning. On four standard domain generalisation benchmarks, CPCANet reached leading zero-shot transfer performance according to the authors. Because the module is architecture-agnostic, it can be added to existing models as a simple route to robustness under distribution shift.
arxiv-2605-05236:
Haoyang Le and three co-authors coordinate teams of soft robots so they can work in tight, cluttered spaces without tangling around each other and obstacles. Anti-entanglement control for such multi-robot systems is a current research focus in precision manufacturing. Distributed training struggles here because each robot sees only part of a dense, unstable environment, leading to poor learning.

Their topology-driven framework trains a central critic that shares topological state, letting each robot perceive the others' strategies during learning while execution stays distributed and communication-free. An integrated topological safety layer uses topological invariants to judge and reduce entanglement risk. The design aims to keep policies out of local traps that simpler training falls into.
arxiv-2605-05436:
Neural networks quietly prefer simple solutions, a bias called implicit regularization. Joseph H. Rudoler, Kevin Tan, Giles Hooker, and Konrad P. Kording offer a way to measure that hidden penalty for any network. Their tool matches gradients: since regularization pushes updates away from plain loss gradients, the gap reveals the penalty at work.

The method recovered well-known penalties on test networks, including the effect of early stopping. It also worked on arbitrary networks where no formula exists. Applied to dropout, it showed the popular trick quietly acts like a squared-weight penalty, giving practitioners a clearer picture of their choices.
arxiv-2605-05536:
Database engines rewrite queries into faster equivalent forms, but the rewrite rules are usually hand-coded inside each engine. Sicheng Pan and five co-authors introduce Rulescript, a language for writing those rules once and using them anywhere. Rules split into a matching phase and a transformation phase over a core algebra.

Every rewrite is verified formally, so correctness does not rest on testing alone. The team reimplemented thirty-three rules from Apache Calcite and deployed them to CockroachDB and Apache Data Fusion. Only a light adapter was needed per engine, supporting their write-once claim.
arxiv-2605-05636:
Capturing a face's true appearance from casual smartphone photos is hard, because unknown lighting tangles with skin reflectance. Yuxuan Han and six co-authors propose learning a delighting network, which strips illumination away, as a prior for the reconstruction. Studio light-stage systems do this well but are costly and immobile.

Their network trains on both a light-stage dataset and rendered scans. A modulation scheme conditions the network on learnable source tokens, separating each dataset's style from the shared physics of delighting. The learned prior then constrains inverse rendering on ordinary photos, disentangling reflectance from light more reliably.
arxiv-2605-06136:
Lin proposes a new way to judge code written by AI agents. Most coding benchmarks ask only whether generated code behaves correctly, but repositories are increasingly agent-managed: one agent writes a codebase, and later agents must inspect, audit, or extend it. A repository is therefore also a communication artifact, and even behaviorally correct codebases can differ in how clearly they expose intended design choices. Build-and-Find measures whether downstream agents can recover those choices, and how much inspection recovery takes.

For each task, a builder creates a codebase from a hidden specification, while a finder sees only the code plus a question bank traced to the specification. The protocol reports recovery accuracy, repeatability, coverage, and inspection effort, with accuracy and stability gating any reading of effort. Controls and audits tell omitted claims apart from finder failures, and a released task pack supports auditable extensions and private packs.
arxiv-2605-06336:
Toluwani Okunola and four co-authors solve imaging inverse problems whose forward operator is itself uncertain. In computed tomography the projection angles may be off, and in photoacoustic tomography the sensor positions may drift, and methods assuming a known linear operator leave strong artifacts in such cases. The team propose a nonlinear scheme that estimates the image and the operator parameters jointly, at large scale and with bounded memory.

The method joins majorization minimization for nonsmooth regularization with Krylov subspace projection and recycling of past subspaces. Two versions trade roles between image and parameters, one swapping updates and one dropping the image variable outright. Streaming variants process data in sequence for dynamic acquisitions, with plug in temporal regularization. Tests on fan beam CT and photoacoustic problems show high quality images.
arxiv-2605-06736:
Unaza Tallal, Shruti Kshirsagar, and Ankita Shukla propose STDA-Net for sorting sleep stages in brain-wave records from new datasets. Sleep staging models often falter when sensor setups, sampling rates, recording sites, or patient groups change. Most cross-dataset methods feed one-dimensional signals, while two-dimensional spectrogram inputs inside a no-label adaptation framework stayed largely unexplored until now.

Their network extracts features from spectrograms with a convolutional net. It models sleep dynamics over time with a two-way recurrent module, and aligns source and target features through a rival net without labeled target data. Across three public datasets and six transfer settings it hits about eighty-nine percent accuracy on average, beating one-dimensional baselines with lower run-to-run variance.
arxiv-2605-06836:
John Debes and forty-one co-authors describe the Hubble Advanced Spectral Products program, which automatically combines ultraviolet spectra in the Hubble archive. For each target, the program coadds data from two spectrographs across visits and programs, applying a careful multi-stage quality filter. Products exist per grating setting and combined across gratings and instruments, raising signal-to-noise and wavelength coverage.

Whenever calibrations improve or new data arrive, products are regenerated automatically, so the archive always holds the best reduction. The code is also released for astronomers who need custom combinations. The program turns a sprawling spectral archive into uniformly processed, science-ready products for the community.
arxiv-2605-06936:
Pengju Liu and four co-authors introduce PostEDA-Bench, a benchmark for the final stage of chip circuit design. Language model agents are now used to fix design rule violations and meet power, performance, and area targets after design tools run. Earlier benchmarks largely skipped the fixing task.

The benchmark holds 145 tasks in four groups, from basic rule fixing to harder reasoning and multi-goal cases. Testing eight large language models, the team finds decent results on simple tasks but sharp drops on realistic ones. Adding vision helps, and weak trade-off reasoning emerges as the main limit on multi-goal work.
arxiv-2605-07236:
Bai-Hao Huang and Liu Zhao extend a thermodynamic framework for black holes to observers sitting at a finite distance, not infinitely far away. The restricted phase space approach is applied to charged black holes, with and without a cosmological constant. The first law and Euler relation still hold, but only with an added pair of variables.

Those variables describe the pressure and area of the surface where the observers reside. In this local view, ordinary charged black holes behave surprisingly like their cosmological-constant cousins, gaining phase transitions the distant view lacks. Even uncharged holes show a Hawking-Page-like transition locally that the asymptotic description misses entirely.
arxiv-2605-07636:
Sujoy Majumder and two co-authors ask which meromorphic functions can solve certain nonlinear partial differential equations involving both differential and functional operators. The problem is set in several complex variables. It mixes a function of one combined variable with values passed through an entire function. Such problems are tightly constrained by value distribution theory.

Working with a fixed form built from a non-constant meromorphic function and an entire inner function, they pin down the solutions for both constant and polynomial coefficients. The results extend earlier work on meromorphic solutions of such problems from one variable to several. They also display the rigidity that value distribution properties impose on nonlinear problems of this kind.
arxiv-2605-07736:
Douglas Tesch and four co-authors improve online goal recognition, the task of inferring what an agent is trying to do from its partly observed trajectory, in continuous domains. The twin challenges are packing long trajectories compactly and comparing them meaningfully against candidate goals. Earlier methods built custom formats and metrics for the job.

Their method instead borrows path signatures from rough path theory, a compact and expressive code that captures the key meaning features of a trajectory. Paired with dynamic time warping for comparison, the approach beat the state of the art in accuracy and in online planning efficiency, while staying close offline. The result suggests established coding tools from other fields transfer well to this task.
arxiv-2605-08036:
Mads Greisen Højlund, August Smart Lykke-Møller, Henry Moss, and Ove Christiansen make Gaussian process regression exact and fast on very large, high-dimensional data. Standard methods drown in the size of the kernel matrix, and data often arrive on incomplete grids that break older fast tricks.

Their method, CUTS-GPR, pairs an additive kernel with the incomplete grid so the kernel matrix gains a Kronecker-like structure with fast matrix-vector products. Benchmarks reach billions of points and thousands of dimensions. Full runs, including hyperparameter tuning, handled about four and a half million points in five hundred dimensions, plus ten real potential energy surfaces from chemistry.
arxiv-2605-08136:
Pamela Barboza and colleagues benchmark object detection for competitive robotics, where lighting and background shifts can break a vision system mid-match. Transformer detectors are popular, but little is published on how backbone size and environment interact in this setting.

The team trains RT-DETR with four ResNet backbones, from eighteen to one hundred one layers, under the same settings and varies dropout, lighting, and background contrast while detecting round objects. Environment changes mainly moved prediction confidence, while latency stayed nearly flat and accuracy remained high, near or above ceiling in most cases. The results help robotics teams pick a backbone size with evidence rather than habit.
arxiv-2605-08236:
Dan-Dan Liang, Xin Shen, and Zhi Li read the topology of a band structure from the motion of wave packets. Their system is a graphene-like model with an added third-nearest-neighbor coupling, which creates extra pairs of Dirac points that can merge, annihilate, or turn into hybrid and parabolic points as parameters change.

The authors show each structure leaves a dynamical fingerprint. Near a gapped hybrid point, a wave packet performs a one-dimensional trembling motion known as Zitterbewegung. The winding number of a Dirac point follows from the packet's center of mass, and that of a parabolic point from its spin texture, suggesting new experimental ways to characterize topological bands.
arxiv-2605-08336:
Doojin Kim, TaeHun Kim, Jong-Chul Park, and Jong-Hyun Yoon revisit hotspots from light primordial black holes. Hawking radiation heats the nearby plasma far above the background. Earlier studies followed the cooling in flat spacetime. They ignored the growth of the cosmos itself. That gap is what this team sets out to close.

The authors write the diffusion equation for hotspot growth in an expanding universe. They mark where the math holds. Formation survives expansion intact. The radius where expansion overtakes diffusion matches the decoupling radius from earlier work. The heat profile stays nearly unchanged. Cooling changes more. The plateau heat first drops fast. It then follows a new course set by the expansion.
arxiv-2605-08436:
Benjamin Shaffer, Brooks Kinch, M. Ani Hsieh, and Nathaniel Trask learn physics from scattered point clouds without ever building a mesh. Their meshfree exterior calculus equips a neighborhood graph with virtual measures through one sparse solve, producing a discrete complex that conserves quantities exactly and stays differentiable in the point positions.

On that foundation, MEEC-Net learns the unknown physics as a shared flux law on edges, written in a rotation-invariant local frame, so one kernel serves any cloud within the training range. The surrogate transfers across resolutions, geometries, and physical parameters, and the authors prove an error bound that splits cleanly into discretization and kernel parts.
arxiv-2605-08736:
Mustapha Ouchen and two coauthors draw sharp tests from a mirror trait in proton hits. A term that tracks how charged counts stray from a mean law is said to mirror when its scaled input flips. The flip is a neat swap in log terms. Taking the trait as given, the team works out a tower of local rules. The rules bind the spread's slopes at its mean.

The lowest rule fits collider data at a few energies. It fits to a few percent. The next rule stays unclear with bins as they are. Three known cascade models each break the trait. A clean entropy form also comes out. It fits the data's entropy to a fine degree.
arxiv-2605-08936:
Dongcheng Zhang and five coauthors train reasoning models to recover on their own when an attack pushes their thinking onto unsafe tracks. Models can self correct in ordinary tasks, yet under adversarial pressure they rarely climb back, and fine tuning on static expert traces misses the model's own live failure modes. Self-ReSET is a pure reinforcement learning framework that harvests the model's own unsafe trajectories and reuses them as starting states for learning recovery.

Across models and benchmarks, robustness against jailbreak prompts rises significantly, especially on unfamiliar attack styles, while general usefulness holds and data use stays efficient. Analysis shows genuine self recovery patterns emerging: models learn to spot unsafe intermediate states and steer back to benign paths by themselves.
arxiv-2605-09436:
Jiang proposes a non-analytic model for the microscopic origin of the Boson peak, the anomalous vibrational density of states in amorphous solids. It rests on a scalar dynamical matrix for a network of springs and nodes. Disorder splits two ways: varying spring strength and varying coordination numbers, the count of springs tied to a node.

The results say the Boson peak comes solely from fluctuation of coordination numbers, while spring-strength fluctuation only adds damping and barely touches low-frequency density of states. The work turns complexity into simplicity and settles the puzzle of the Boson peak's microscopic origin.
arxiv-2605-09736:
Kamenshchik and two colleagues tamed runaway math for a massless, self-acting scalar field in de Sitter space, the expanding universe of early inflation. Series for correlation functions diverge, so the authors applied their autonomous-equations method to get finite time-dependent functions. Those functions tracked the stochastic theory's time course fairly well.

Applying the same method to Borel-Le Roy transforms and then resumming matched that picture far better. The paper also offers a new way to pull out series coefficients and a fresh derivation of the autonomous equation by truncating Schwinger-Dyson-type equations. Together, the tools give divergent de Sitter series a controlled, finite meaning.
arxiv-2605-10036:
Wang and five colleagues proposed a unified memory approach for 6G agentic AI radio networks, to bridge the cognitive gap in radio access networks. As 6G evolves, the radio access network must pass old tools toward agentic AI able to sense, reason, and evolve. A basic cognitive gap persists in split designs, where links force the radio layer to squeeze high-detail states into low-detail numbers, trapping thinking agents behind a meaning choke point.

The article sketches a shift from link-bound to memory-centric designs. It puts forward a unified memory approach erasing the walls between sensing and thinking by mapping brain-like memory layers onto mixed compute fabrics. New fast links enable a cognitive flow where instant reactions, split-second thinking, and long-term growth share state. By swapping message passing with zero-copy watching, AI agents bridge real-time speed and long-horizon context.
arxiv-2605-10236:
Michal Korniak and five colleagues ask a pointed question about reinforcement learning. That is the field where agents learn by trial and reward. When does sampling past experience unevenly actually beat sampling it evenly? Their 2026 paper studies experience replay, the buffer of past transitions that off-policy algorithms reuse during training.

Across varied settings the authors find three factors govern the payoff. Replay volume means replays per environment step. Expected recency means how fresh sampled transitions are. Entropy means the spread of the sampling distribution. Uneven replay helps most when volume is low, and high entropy matters even at similar recency. Their Truncated Geometric sampler favors recent experience while staying spread out. It lifted sample efficiency in low-volume regimes and stayed competitive when volume was high.
arxiv-2605-10536:
Honghan Wu and four colleagues tackle a problem they call feature density conflict. Rare new ideas in complex, mission-critical domains are often hidden by dense background contexts. Standard sparse autoencoders mix the two regimes, so model capacity is consumed by repeat background variables, smoothing over rare linked interactions. Their 2026 paper introduces the Hybrid Hierarchical SAE, or HH-SAE.

HH-SAE splits manifolds into a nested ladder of three tiers: Contextual, Atomic, and Compository. A low-rank dense layer stiffens and subtracts the contextual background, letting a tiered sparse ladder mine hierarchical innovations. Across varied spaces, HH-SAE splits administrative clinical labels into physiological modes and reaches a peak cross-domain zero-shot AUC of 0.9156 in fraud detection. Removing contextual subtraction collapses use by 13.46 percent, confirming the design is needed. Knowledge-steered synthesis lifts AUPRC by 9.9 percent over the best generators.
arxiv-2605-10636:
Harender S. Dhattarwal and four colleagues show that a usual test fails for CaMnO3 perovskites. Heat storage in oxide perovskites relies on oxygen vacancy formation. Tests have used the single oxygen vacancy energy as the key measure. Their 2026 paper shows it fails.

The pure compound is not the lowest energy state. Vacancies are present at high heat, giving negative single formation energies. Materials with negative values are often left out as unsuitable, yet this reflects a wrong choice of reference state. The authors compute formation energies versus vacancy counts, setting the count as the correct reference point. Curves from this minimum match seen reduction heats. A-site doping with magnesium and strontium acts through strain release and symmetry breaking, while B-site doping with iron and aluminum reshapes the redox setting. A model with configurational entropy predicts equilibrium stoichiometry versus heat and oxygen pressure.
arxiv-2605-11036:
Hyeseon An, Shinwoo Park, Dongsu Kim, and Yo-Sub Han watermark LLM agents by their behavior, not just their text. Agent action trails reveal little about which agent or policy produced them, making origin, ownership, and reuse hard to establish from observed actions alone.

Earlier behavior marks treat each action as a separate trial and break when trails are perturbed, cut short, or misaligned. SeqWM instead embeds signals into history-shaped move patterns and checks trails without relying on position, against random-key baselines. Tests across agent benchmarks and model backbones show reliable detection with utility preserved, robust under damage where round-indexed marks collapse. Agent owners get origin proof that survives messy real trails.
arxiv-2605-11336: Ilya Ilyankou, Stefano Cavazzi and James Haworth map geospatial web search at scale. They use embeddings, a small classifier and clustering on the full MS MARCO set of 1 point 01 million Bing queries. They find 181,827 geospatial queries, or 18 percent, nearly three times the share labelled Location in the original annotations. Costs and prices alone make up 15 point 3 percent of geospatial queries, and much of this practical lookup lies outside what traditional GIS was built to serve.
arxiv-2605-11536: Juhyeon Kim, Wojciech Jarosz and Adithya Pediredla present ToF ReSTIR, a reuse framework for time-of-flight rendering. Current time-of-flight methods cost heavily and scale poorly to complex moving scenes. Adapting ReSTIR reuse ideas to time-resolved light transport, they keep optical path lengths valid through path-length-aware shift mapping. That mapping is a geometric transform built on Newton's method, which adjusts reused paths to meet time-gating limits. The framework supports time-gated and transient rendering at interactive rates.
arxiv-2605-11636: Zhang and five colleagues present Seirênes, an adversarial self-play framework for LLM reasoning. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards advanced reasoning, yet models stay fragile amid distractions. Seirênes trains one model to build plausible distracting contexts exposing its blind spots, and to solve problems by finding the essential task. The competing goals drive a co-evolutionary curriculum. Across seven math benchmarks and scales from 4B to 30B, Seirênes gains 10 point 2, 9 point 1 and 7 point 2 points. Its 4B distractions cut top closed models by 4 to 5 points.
arxiv-2605-11836: Xin Ma and six colleagues explain why lifelong model editing stays stable, finding that tough editors share Lifelong Normalization, which scales value gradients with running means. Drop it and scores fall apart at once, and early edits oddly promote later ones. They give the first theory of this steady loop, proving that with ridge regression it yields updates that grow nearly at right angles over time with bounded norms. Their StableEdit strengthens the loop with warm-up and full whitening, lifting long-run results cheaply.
arxiv-2605-11936: Heejun Kim and seven colleagues test whether soft prompt gains come from learned content or from injection itself. Their Random Soft Prompts append freshly drawn random embedding vectors to the input with no training at all, yet match tuned soft prompts on math reasoning tasks in several settings. Early tokens flatten and reasoning branches, then generation commits to one completion as the effect dilutes. The same trick widened Pass@N with temperature sampling and improved DAPO training.
arxiv-2605-12036: Guojian Li and eleven colleagues address multi-sided speech grasp in speech language models. Current models struggle to split apart micro-acoustic cues, sound scenes, and tone signals, choked by scarce vivid data, missing fine-grained models, and coarse benchmarks. Their data flow extracts a high-quality natural corpus from video sources. FMSU-Bench covers 14 speech trait sides. FM-Speech uses split trait models with stepwise lesson fine-tuning to clearly beat open-source models.
arxiv-2605-12236: Matthew Hong, Jesse Zhang, Anusha Nagabandi, and Abhishek Gupta bridge cloning pretraining and reinforcement tuning for robot policies. Cloning yields narrow action spreads that starve downstream search. Their CSP method injects forward noise into policy inputs, spanning precise copying to broad range. Fine-tuning then uses TMRL (Timestep-Modulated Reinforcement Learning), which adjusts this setting on the fly by shifting the step, giving direct search control. The method lifts tuning speed and enables real-world tuning on hard handling tasks in less than an hour.
arxiv-2605-12436: Eldifrawi, Wang and Trabelsi build a fact-checker that matches how human checkers actually work. Existing automated systems, they note, misalign with practice and cannot keep pace with the flood of online and AI-made content. Their CAAFC system works on claims, chats and dialogues, flags factual errors and hallucinations, and corrects them with actionable reasons tied to primary sources. It also refreshes its evidence with recent, context-aware information, and beats leading rivals across several benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-12536: Kearney proposes a maths bridge between the Free Energy Principle and Integrated Information Theory. The first models self-organisation and learning, while the second offers an account of consciousness built on basic cause and effect. No rigorous mapping has limited their precision and testing so far. Defining information as deviation of real motion from a limited maximum-caliber path ensemble, he derives each cause and effect set of IIT 3.0 from maximum-caliber variation rules.
arxiv-2605-12636: Dorovskiy proves shape stability for generic groups of PC-HC vector fields on the 2D sphere. A sorting of these groups up to mid match near their large split supports is given, based on fixed traits such as layout and key set. The building lemma is proved, and split diagrams for the class are built. The work shows which changes keep dynamics and which trigger splits.
arxiv-2605-12736: Basher and three colleagues present ConRetroBert, a dual-encoder framework for template-based retrosynthesis. Template methods predict reactants by selecting and applying a reaction template, so each prediction traces to a chemical rule. They are often seen as less competitive than template-free models, since template prediction is framed as global classification over a long-tailed library. The team argues that weakness lies in the learning formulation, not templates. They reframe the task as dense product-template retrieval followed by listwise ranking, with contrastive pretraining for a shared space.
arxiv-2605-13036: De Felice and Tsujikawa derive gravitational waveforms for charged compact binaries with scalar hair in Einstein-scalar-Maxwell theories. Compact objects can carry vector and scalar charges, the latter as secondary hair induced by the former. Modelling binaries as charged point particles with scalar-dependent masses, they compute tensor waveforms plus scalar and vector radiation channels. Dipole radiation gives a leading minus-one post-Newtonian correction, and binary-pulsar decay data already bound the single deviation parameter tightly for neutron-star binaries.
arxiv-2605-13336: Konar, Mondal and Sen hunt light scalars in the Type-I two Higgs doublet model at colliders. Extra scalars may be light yet dodge past searches through tiny Higgs coupling and suppressed quark coupling. The authors study electroweak pair production, where heavy scalars decay to light scalars plus gauge bosons, yielding boosted multi scalar final states. Tagging a boosted double b fat jet beside a gauge boson probes heavy scalars up to about 560 GeV at the high luminosity LHC.
arxiv-2605-13536: Qingyun Zou and five colleagues propose HLS-Seek, a quality-aware framework for synthesis code writing from natural language. High-level synthesis turns C and C++ into hardware, with latency and costs set by pragmas. Current training ignores quality of results. Reward-based learning needs only paired rankings. It avoids full synthesis training through a proxy reward with 99.53 percent Pareto score. Monte Carlo dropout switching invokes real builds for unsure cases. HLS-Seek reaches 84.7 percent syntax and 81.4 percent functional correctness, beating GPT-5.1.
arxiv-2605-13736: Slaven Peles and six colleagues port the curved tuning library HiOp to GPU-based chips. The team presents a novel inner point form running fully on GPUs, skipping sparse solvers by shrinking the sparse problem into a dense problem of usable size. That shows inner point methods for sparse problems can run well where over 90 percent of compute power sits in GPUs. The work is driven by optimal power flow problems and uses shared libraries Umpire and RAJA.
arxiv-2605-13936: Jimenez-Gutierrez and five colleagues look beyond public data toward private institutional records as the next frontier for language models. Health and finance data hold deep expertise but cannot be shared, being spread across institutions under privacy and regulatory limits and differing in population, modality and labeling. Their cross-domain benchmark supports federated fine-tuning, adapting models where data stays in place instead of being pooled.
arxiv-2605-14136: Tursynbek and four co-authors offer TeDiO, a training-free fix for shaky motion in text-to-video diffusion transformers. Generated clips often flicker, drift or wobble, and those flaws leave a mark inside the model. Incoherent videos show ragged, fragmented temporal diagonals in intermediate self-attention maps, while stable motion shows smooth band-diagonal patterns. TeDiO rates diagonal smoothness, spots unstable regions, and nudges latents toward coherent frame-to-frame motion. It changes no model weights and needs no external motion supervision.
arxiv-2605-14236: Paschmann and five co-authors reframe pairwise ranking prompting as active learning from noisy comparisons. Pairwise Ranking Prompting elicits preference judgments from a language model, usually aggregated by sorting algorithms. Judgments are noisy, order-sensitive and intransitive, so sorting assumptions fit poorly. Truncating a full permutation to meet a call budget yields no dependable top-K. Active rankers serve as drop-in replacements improving NDCG at 10 per call under call limits. A randomized-direction oracle using one model call per pair turns position bias into zero-mean noise.
arxiv-2605-14936: Leo L. Duan and two others soften projected priors, probability laws forced onto tight sets like sparse vectors or graphs. Exact projection inside every sampling step makes posterior computation costly. Their continuous relaxation instead shrinks the duality gap, the mismatch between primal and dual projection aims, toward zero with a workable prior. The result needs no optimizer inside each update, keeps mass near the exact form, and links to global-local shrinkage priors.
arxiv-2605-15036: Tommy Chin and Sarah Shandera derive closed-form propagators for any part of a closed N-qubit network holding just one excitation. One transition amplitude governs excitation flow, positivity, entanglement entropy, and quantum Fisher information at once. This holds for both positivity notions here, set solely by flow direction, no matter the part size or coherence. For single qubits they map a band of states that stays inside every valid domain yet never occurs in the dynamics.
arxiv-2605-15736: Huanyang Tong and three colleagues present BiomedAP, a dual-anchor frame for medical vision-language adaptation. Few-shot diagnosis is strong yet brittle: prompt shifts can break it. Past frames tune visual and textual prompts apart, leaning on golden prompts. In clinics, noisy descriptions make that split unstable. BiomedAP fuses modalities layer by layer with gated fusion, damping stray cues. A dual-anchor rule pulls prompts toward centers from expert templates and visual prototypes. On 11 benchmarks it tops baselines with competitive accuracy and far stronger prompt-shift robustness.
arxiv-2605-15936: Hao Li introduces state estimation, one pillar of advanced control theory. Control theory is the mathematics behind the hardware, software, and daily run of control systems. He frames control science as a core strand of the third industrial revolution. Its appeal, he argues, lies in joining rigorous know-why with practical know-how for real uses.
arxiv-2605-16036: Van Beekveld and five colleagues offer a primer on the Monte Carlo toolset of high-energy physics. Event generators link theory sums to collider measurements, and a modular set of tools has grown around them over decades. The primer maps matrix-element sums, parton showers, hadronisation models, detector simulation, and stats inference. It aims chiefly at new doctoral students, while serving as a guide for the wider field. The book-style guide walks new readers through the full chain from theory to data in plain steps.
arxiv-2605-16336: Aiersilan, Yousefi, and Pless propose a teacher-run mark to catch word-for-word LLM copy-paste. Post-hoc AI-text checkers prove shaky and punish non-native writers, while output-side marks need maker help. Their input-side mark hides an order inside the visible task prompt, so a model that ingests it word-for-word writes a tag into its reply. Their SteganoPrompt tool encodes payloads in the Unicode Tags block, lives through common copy-paste channels, and carries an always-on school-honesty note.
arxiv-2605-16536: Campos, Baldiotti, and Molina develop a framework for reading Kerr-anti-de Sitter black hole thermodynamics in its many descriptions. All satisfy a first law and the scaling rules of homogeneity. Temperature and angular velocity are frame-bound kinematic quantities from the Euclidean formalism. The pressure-volume term is dynamical, needing a gauge choice for mass and volume. The quantum statistical relation narrows the family to Schwarzschild- and Kerr-matching descriptions. It singles out the co-rotating frame description and the one where thermodynamic and geometric volumes agree.
arxiv-2605-16636: Liu and Pande study a conjecture that F-signatures for complex KLT singularities stay above zero as the characteristic grows large. They prove it for 3D non-weakly exceptional singularities by induction. They also prove it for smooth low-degree hypersurfaces by building isotrivial normal toric degenerations. Their tools draw on K-stability theory and birational geometry, with a matching result for the Frobenius-alpha invariant. The work is pure theory, with proofs only and no lab work.
arxiv-2605-16736: Roy and Nair propose CAB, a training-free sampler that speeds up flow and diffusion image models. Existing acceleration either needs distillation training or relies on high-order solvers that can degrade quality at low step counts. CAB first transforms sampling dynamics to a common rectified coordinate system, then applies a multistep Adams-Bashforth predictor with a correction from past velocity evaluations, adding no function evaluations. It reaches at least third-order local and second-order global error, and improves quality-per-step in the 6-to-20-step regime.
arxiv-2605-16936: Ghosh's team shows interface design can steer the anomalous Hall effect in nickel-based film stacks. Nickel films grown on three oxide substrates feel different strains, and room-temperature Hall tests show the anomalous Hall conductivity shifts with substrate. Calculations show strain alone cannot explain the trend; instead, broken inversion symmetry at the interface drives a Rashba spin-orbit effect that governs the conductivity. The team shows an external electric field can tune the conductivity, pointing toward electrically tunable spintronic devices.
arxiv-2605-17136: Filmus extends impossibility results for group classification, where votes on each object must leave no category empty. Earlier work forced a dictatorship when the outcome always met that rule. He shows the same result holds when the rule need hold only with high probability, as long as voter functions stay far from constant. A parallel result covers grouping objects into equivalence classes.
arxiv-2605-17436: Restrepo and colleagues show that medical context distorts clinical vision-language models on chest X-ray tasks. Testing varied general and medical models on MIMIC-CXR, they find decisions dominated by text even when images are available, swayed by irrelevant clinical history, and flipped by minor prompt rewordings. Three failure modes follow: text over-reliance, spurious history reliance and prompt sensitivity. The authors call for explicit safeguards and stress-testing before clinical use.
arxiv-2605-17536: Geng and Wang revisit global weak solutions of wave maps from Euclidean space into spheres. They prove existence as a singular limit of maps minimizing elliptic variational functionals. The functionals carry an exponential weight in time with a small parameter, and Cauchy initial data serve as the boundary condition. The idea traces to De Giorgi and was used by Serra and Tilli for nonlinear wave equations. The approach also covers SO(m)-target manifolds.
arxiv-2605-17636: Ou and Yang report extended gamma-ray emission toward young massive cluster Berkeley 87 from 18 years of Fermi-LAT data. Young massive stellar clusters rank as significant cosmic-ray accelerators and gamma-ray sources. The hadronic scenario is favored given dense gas and strong winds, and the cluster supplies enough energy to power the emission. A nearby pulsar, PSR J2021+3651, linked to the Dragonfly nebula and 4HWC J2021+3650, lies in the same view. The paper also discusses maximum proton energy and electron energy density for this pulsar.
arxiv-2605-17736: David A. Jorgensen introduces rank varieties for modules and complexes over the generic hypersurface. Each local complete intersection ring has one tied to it. Old support varieties rest on restriction of scalars. The new ones use extension of scalars instead. Jorgensen shows each projective variety occurs as one of them for some finitely generated module. He also checks their basic traits. The paper also looks at how they behave in a range of cases.
arxiv-2605-17836: Zachary Feng and four colleagues prove that certain universal supersingular representations are non-admissible and of infinite length. Working over an unramified extension of p-adic numbers, they study linear groups over finite-field closures. For dimension at least 3, the supersingular representation of a generic weight is non-admissible and infinite in length, under certain conditions. The result extends earlier dimension 2 findings, which covered only the smallest case. Their method uses weight cycling with recent progress on Serre weight conjectures.
arxiv-2605-17936: Benedict Florance Arockiaraj and three colleagues generate universal triggers that read like natural phrases. Existing triggers attack many NLP models with one shared sequence, but they come out ungrammatical and unnatural. The team combines part-of-speech filtering with a perplexity loss to craft sensible triggers closer to natural language. On SST sentiment tests, their triggers drive accuracy as low as 0.04 flipping positive to negative and 0.12 in reverse. Training with the generated triggers lifts accuracy from 0.12 to 0.48, showing defenses can harden models.
arxiv-2605-18336: Saumya Singh's 2026 paper studies plasma wakefields driven by two-colour pulses with Laguerre-Gaussian shape and orbital angular momentum. Using perturbative theory and quasi-cylindrical particle-in-cell simulations, the authors examine how transverse mode structure shapes wakefields in underdense plasma. Drivers with finite azimuthal index give weaker, less regular on-axis fields than plain Gaussian drivers. The shortfall comes not from lost excitation but from energy redistributed toward finite radii. Angular momentum modes create hollow ring-shaped wakes with transverse fields, while mixed drivers sit in between.
arxiv-2605-18836: Minyoung Oh, Najeong Chae, and Jae-Young Sim tackle dataset distillation that must survive distribution shift. Distilled sets pack a full dataset into a compact synthetic one, yet standard methods assume test data match training data. Post-hoc generalization tricks fail here, since synthetic sets lack real data diversity and add heavy augmentation cost. Their Spectral Gradient Surgery separates class signals from domain signals in the spectral domain, reinforcing shared gradients and promoting diversity. Tests show much stronger out-of-distribution generalization, with plug-and-play fit to existing methods.
arxiv-2605-19036: Zheng-Duo Fan, Ashvin Vishwanath, and Zijian Wang argue that a gas of non-interacting anyons carrying one-third of an electron's charge can superconduct through a hidden weak-pairing route. Such anyons arise in doped fractional Chern insulators with three forced pockets. By attaching flux so the average statistical flux vanishes, the authors map the problem onto three kinds of composite fermions in zero effective field, whose statistics supply the pairing glue. The resulting state differs from Laughlin's picture, with an edge signature matching recent numerical results.
arxiv-2605-19136: Anh-Quan Pham brings in interaction-readiness, a measure of whether an object can be run under handling. Modern 3D sets offer rich shape and motion detail but lack the physics needed for stable handling, needing hand work. The thesis proposes a framework splitting it into components, showing failure modes missed by usual checks. It presents a simulator-in-the-loop method generating usable objects from assets, deriving physics and tuning them through sim feedback. Tests show object quality affects stable runs, handling, and policy results.
arxiv-2605-19236: Jeremy Mould and three colleagues test whether hydrogen-survey galaxies in the Zone of Avoidance can sit at Hubble distances for mapping. The Zone of Avoidance cuts through Laniakea, hiding galaxies behind Milky Way dust and stars. New 21 cm MeerKAT surveys fill the innermost gap, and the team adds infrared photometry for 163 galaxies plus 2MASS sources to derive extra speeds. Averaging speeds into redshift bins, they find corrections in the Laniakea region are not too large. Mapping can therefore proceed using the redshift data now on hand.
arxiv-2605-19436: Heakl and team fix a credit problem in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where every token earns the same reward whether it drove reasoning or filled grammar. Their CEPO method asks at each token whether the right answer favors it while a wrong answer disfavors it. Tokens passing both tests mark reasoning steps; the rest count as filler. Wrong-answer teachers come free from rejected rollouts in the batch. On five math benchmarks it beats GRPO at two scales, while distribution-matching rivals fall below the untrained baseline.
arxiv-2605-19836: Anbarloei introduces and studies n-ary S-hyperideals in a Krasner hyperring. Hyperideals extend the familiar ideal concept, sets that stay closed when ring operations are applied to their members, to hyperrings where operations return sets of outcomes rather than single values. The paper develops this multiary S version of the concept for Krasner hyperrings and studies how it behaves.
arxiv-2605-19936: Miletić and Falk track how machine written text is reshaping science writing in language processing papers. From more than thirty seven thousand papers plus three thousand made pairs of human and machine polished lines, they find word use and word sense shifting over time. Machine polished lines lean on set phrase shapes, longer harder words, and less varied word choice.
arxiv-2605-20436: Liu and six co-workers make instance segmentation robust to lighting with a Lighting Convolutional-Attention adapter. Foundation models like SAM generalize well but degrade under varied illumination, and the adapter avoids retraining the heavy backbone. Their dual-branch adapter reads RGB features beside contrast maps, sensing structural change rather than lighting artifacts. Pairwise training penalizes gaps between clean images and their lighting variants, and a new Unity synthetic set tests complex real-world lighting.
arxiv-2605-20836: Mikhail Sidorenko and five colleagues design compact high-frequency one-way devices using nanoplasma-switched time-varying metasurfaces. Time-modulated systems can tailor rate conversion and single-direction propagation, but microwave varactors are limited to a few billion cycles per second of tuning. These switches, two-state devices based on gas discharge in a nanometre-scale gap, open higher operating rates. An analytical design based on the time-Floquet method yields an isolator at 100 gigahertz, studied by maths and by full-wave simulation.
arxiv-2605-21036: A. Bruno and three colleagues develop the quantum theory of a three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator. They study quantum traits of a nonlinear Kerr device driven by a three-photon pump. They derive both exact and near math forms for the ground state of that coupled model. The exact solution appears at an exact spectral degeneracy, while the near case describes regimes where levels nearly meet, with a threefold ground-state set of mixes of three large-scale distinct states.
arxiv-2605-21136: Matthijs Reyers, Niels Hokke, and R. R. Venkatesha Prasad offer a Python simulator for LoRa and LoRaWAN networks that is simpler than existing large C++ tools. Built on an asyncio kernel, it models packet delivery with the capture effect, covers the full LoRaWAN 1.0.4 stack, and can run real STM32 firmware by redirecting hardware calls into the simulation. It ships as a package needing no outside simulation framework.
arxiv-2605-21236: Sophie Rosu and colleagues probe star interiors with apsidal motion in the twin binary HD152248. Stars over twenty solar masses lack a firm rule for boundary mixing and a clear check on inner mixing. The team builds GENEC models with two kinds of angular momentum transport: purely hydrodynamic and magneto-diffusive. They compare single- and binary-star models and test overshooting, metallicity, helium, mass, mass loss, and mixing length. The goal is to pin down inner density structure and boundary mixing from the k-two constant.
arxiv-2605-21436: The Euclid Collaboration validates a redshift-space power-spectrum and bispectrum pipeline on Euclid-like mocks. The pipeline tests primordial non-Gaussianity, a probe of cosmic structure origin. Stage-four surveys like Euclid will measure galaxy clustering at high signal-to-noise, requiring robust joint analysis. It uses one-loop power spectra and tree-level bispectra on Abacus-PNG simulations. It is stress-tested on bias parametrisation, priors, and scale cuts, with null tests without non-Gaussianity.
arxiv-2605-21536: Marios Papamichalis and Regina Ruane study high-volume plaintiff-side counsel in Philadelphia eviction cases. Among seven hundred fifty-five thousand four records from 1969 to 2022, three hundred ninety-six thousand one hundred sixty-three residential cases involve tenants appearing exactly once. Single-appearance cases with high-volume counsel advance more often to writ stages, but no more often to default. Within the same plaintiff and property, no broad premium appears on default, judgment, or fees. Monthly filings rise about two to five percent after adopting high-volume counsel.
arxiv-2605-22136: Karpov and co-authors report mysterious optical pulse behavior in transitional millisecond pulsar PSR J1023+0038, swinging between accretion-powered and rotation-powered regimes. Such pulsars alternate between X-ray binary and radio pulsar states as matter flows from a low-mass companion. The team observes a new regime with a sinusoidal pulse shape and pulsed fraction near 5 percent. After 220 seconds in this regime, with flaring activity, the system returned to normal. Explanations involving pulsar wind interactions are discussed, while a complete picture remains open.
arxiv-2605-22236: Blot, Lewański and Shadrin introduce integrable observables as a new tool for cohomological field theories. They offer an alternative to Witten's psi classes, or descendants in two-dimensional quantum gravity, while keeping integrability intact. Three examples are given. The first two recover the Dubrovin-Zhang and double ramification hierarchies and reveal fresh structure within them. The third builds on the Pi-class and proves its hierarchies match both older ones under Miura equivalence. A short new proof of Witten's conjecture is also included.
arxiv-2605-22436: Costeri studies the Lorentzian Wetterich flow equation for quantum fields on curved backgrounds, within perturbative quantum field theory. Two model classes are treated: interacting scalar fields on hyperbolic spacetimes without boundary, and self-interacting Dirac fields on spin backgrounds. Flow equations and beta functions are derived in the local potential approach. The scalar model also features an uneven potential like the Martin-Siggia-Rose description of stochastic dynamics. This hints at a link with stochastic models. Existence and uniqueness are proved for both models via Nash-Moser.
arxiv-2605-22636: Boudourides builds a three layer framework to test whether language models grasp the web of links inside a field, not just its isolated facts. Comparing model made knowledge graphs with expert encyclopedias across ten fields, he finds a steady relational deficit: models name concepts but fail to reproduce their links. The deficit varies sharply by field and collapses fully in the most specialized domains, suggesting model knowledge is misaligned with expert structure. He argues evaluation must move past simple accuracy toward relational integrity, above all for high stakes use.
arxiv-2605-22936: Lin and seven coauthors present ACALSim, a parallel simulation framework for exploring designs of high-performance computing systems. Its key idea is a pluggable thread-management design, letting developers tailor scheduling to each workload. Event-driven execution, zero-copy shared memory, and two-phase parallel runs complete the design. Built into a GPU simulator, it ran over fourteen times faster than an SST version while using 41 percent less memory.
arxiv-2605-23336: Pednekar and Podder advance a decades-old question about how hard Boolean functions are to approximate with polynomials. They study approximate non-deterministic degree, which forces a polynomial near zero on false inputs and at least one on true inputs. A recent result bounded exact degree by a cube of rational degree, and its authors conjectured a stronger polynomial bound from this new measure. Pednekar and Podder prove that conjecture for monotone and unate functions, bounded-alternation functions, symmetric functions, uniform hypergraph properties, and read-k DNF formulas.
arxiv-2605-24036: McCann defines intent-driven computing, where programs emit intents, values for planned actions, instead of running effects. A governed runtime checks each intent against a policy language, records each call in a tamper-evident ledger before running the effect, the sole path to effects. Moving control from undecidable program semantics to decidable intent data yields event sourcing, replay checks, complete audit, and a clearer view. He spells out the model, builds it for the BEAM virtual machine, and checks key traits in Rocq with no lemmas assumed.
arxiv-2605-24136: Jones-McCormick tackles a hard task: finding distinct basins in high-dimensional Markov processes from sampled paths alone. Inside each basin, motion mixes fast, but jumps between basins are rare. Older tools lean on spatial grids or operator spectra, which turn shaky in high dimensions or twisted basin shapes. The key test: paths from one basin fool a best-possible classifier, while paths from different basins separate cleanly. A neural routine merges candidate samples by that test, recovering layouts where standard spectral and clustering tools fail.
arxiv-2605-24236: Bakagianni and Papadopoulos tackle multi-language paper search, matching short, casual claims to their papers, where related papers act as hard decoys. Their CheckThat 2026 entry studies hard-negative training for multi-stage search. Cluster negatives from candidate sets train dense search and second passes better. Local cluster negatives favour hits, while broader meaning negatives give reach and stable second passes across tongues. Constrained sorting prompts prove the soundest final proof picker. The system, dense searcher plus multi-language second pass plus a tie-breaker, ranked sixth of 37 entries.
arxiv-2605-24436: Jayprakash Nair, Mathew, and Shivashankar Nair propose a latent-yield method for nimble switching. Picking the best method per instance is hard in online settings, where traits shift over time, and judging by instant scores alone gives shaky switching. Their technique folds rewards and fines into a latent yield that triggers use and search, pooling scores across instances. Island models from gene methods let method groups explore side-by-side and exchange score notes. Tests on sorting and robot block dodging show the method works.
arxiv-2605-24636: Junjie Zhao and colleagues introduce GlobalDentBench, the first multinational dental benchmark, spanning 14 specialties across 88 countries and six continents. Its 8,978 expert-validated questions cover multiple-choice, short-answer, and case-based formats at three reasoning levels, from recall to individualized reasoning. Six senior dentists calibrated the construction, with agreement near 100 percent on simpler formats and 96.78 percent on case-based questions. Twelve frontier models degrade stepwise with complexity, and 31.01 percent of real-case recommendations were unsafe, with 4.51 percent risking irreversible harm.
arxiv-2605-25036: Yangneng Chen and Jing Li trace language bias in large vision-language models to modality misalignment during training. Models over-rely on text and neglect images, producing fluent but inconsistent outputs. The authors show that visual instruction tuning and direct preference optimization prioritize textual gains, tilting models toward language modeling over multimodal understanding. They propose fixes: Language Bias Regularization for instruction tuning, and Language Bias Penalty for preference optimization. Regularization lifts results on over ten general benchmarks, while the penalty cuts hallucination, with no extra data or auxiliary models.
arxiv-2605-25136: Rémi Goerlich and colleagues present a study of chirality transfer and odd transport in a chiral active bath. The authors drive a passive tracer through collisions with a non-equilibrium chiral bath, combining tabletop experiments, many-body simulations, and a coarse-grained theory. Collisions pass chiral dynamics to the tracer, which then loops in circles. The same mechanism produces a transverse drift under a constant pulling force. Nonlinear friction proves essential, rectifying chiral fluctuations into an odd response. The results reveal how odd transport arises in chiral active matter.
arxiv-2605-25336: Wen Zhang and colleagues build a mid-infrared ghost imaging system for fast waveforms at single-photon sensitivity. Infrared detectors are too slow and too deaf for such signals. The team converts the light upward in frequency and encodes it with patterns from a near-infrared modulator. Matching intensities against those patterns rebuilds waveforms at 80 picosecond resolution, beyond the detectors' speed and jitter. The system recovers waveforms below 0.1 photons per bit and, with compressive sampling, cuts capture time by over 90 percent. The approach could extend to terahertz sensing.
arxiv-2605-25536: Muslim Chochlov and colleagues gather thirty earlier reviews of language models that write code. Their tertiary study sorts publication trends, effects, use cases, integration hurdles, and future directions through software-engineering knowledge areas and the HELM framework. Benchmark accuracy looks strong, yet support for real-world transfer stays weak, robustness proves fragile, and efficiency limits recur. Economic feasibility, evaluation validity, and socio-technical integration emerge as the main hurdles, pointing toward domain-aware models and shared evaluation standards.
arxiv-2605-25636: Vaso and colleagues study how the form factor of Reggeized tensor Pomeron and Odderon exchange shapes high-energy elastic proton-proton and proton-antiproton scattering. Spin structure enters via stated covariant projectors for spin-2 and spin-3, kept apart from the scalar kernels. That keeps vertex effects apart from trajectory dynamics. They test seven Odderon-proton forms against TOTEM and Tevatron data. Six dipole, polynomial, Gaussian and hybrid forms fit alike, while a one-parameter exponential form fits best. That suggests a peripheral soft Odderon effect.
arxiv-2605-25836: Cheng and colleagues present CTI2TTP, which extracts MITRE ATT&CK techniques from threat reports. Existing methods miss techniques or invent unsupported ones. CTI2TTP first splits reports into atomic behaviors tied to evidence windows. It then proposes candidates broadly, keeping only those backed by evidence and the MITRE definition. The team also releases two evaluation resources. On both resources it beats same-backbone chain-of-thought prompting.
arxiv-2605-26036: Liu and seven colleagues offer CityRep, a shared yardstick for urban representation learning across cities, tasks and data types. City encodings turn complex city life into general vectors for downstream jobs, but current tests cover one or two cities and lean on random splits. Random splits leak nearby data across train and test, inflating scores. CityRep instead uses block-based spatial splits and a unit-agnostic alignment module for varied encodings. Its unified protocol should give fairer cross-city comparisons and firmer support for urban foundation models.
arxiv-2605-26236: In 2026, Ferdinand Paar and four colleagues split co-speech gesture generation into two streams, one carrying meaning and one carrying rhythm, in a system called DuoGesture. A stochastic gate decides frame by frame when meaningful gestures should override beat motion. Motion-grounded conditioning ties semantic choices to movement patterns instead of bare word vectors. An arm-chain beat prior weighted by body measurements steadies the rhythm without dulling meaning. Tests show DuoGesture beating strong baselines on objective scores and human judgments.
arxiv-2605-26536: Prasanna Venkatesan Ravindran, Priyankka Gundlapudi Ravikumar, and Asif Islam Khan ask when ferroelectric-dielectric stacks can hold ideal, domain-free negative capacitance. Tests to date show enhanced capacitance but always with domains present. For given layer widths, the trio claim a key domain-wall energy value exists. Above it, the system holds in a robust domain-free state, resisting domains. Reaching it therefore means learning to control domain-wall energy through theory and experiment, by fast design and engineering of ferroelectrics.
arxiv-2605-27236: Kurchaba and co-authors compare two ways to tell true methane plumes from look-alike artifacts in TROPOMI satellite data. Many plume-like features are not real emissions at all, but artifacts from terrain, surface brightness, aerosols, coasts, or water. Older work used expert-built features with a support vector machine, which drops spatial layout and narrows what the model can see. The authors test feature-based models against image-based networks under balanced and skewed test settings, then use SHAP explanations to guide model choice for live screening.
arxiv-2605-27436: Arijit Ghosh and colleagues test whether the TRIANGLE method aligns modalities beyond cosine similarity. TRIANGLE shrinks triplet areas on a hypersphere to force shared consistency across side modalities. The redo confirms zero-shot gains of about 9 points over pairwise baselines, but fails to redo learning-from-scratch runs, blaming joint optimization instability.
arxiv-2605-27536: Waleed El-Sayed and colleagues tune a diamond optomechanical crystal to an exceptional point, where coupled modes coalesce. Structural symmetry breaking yields two high-frequency mechanical resonances tied to one optical cavity, reached within a stable window below the phonon-lasing threshold. The team sees lopsided sharing of damping and anti-damping between hybrid modes, making diamond crystals a base for non-Hermitian optomechanics.
arxiv-2605-27636: Hadi Bayrami Asl Tekanlou, Mahdi Bakhtiyarzadeh, and Jafar Razmara tackle culture-based question answering for low-resource languages. Their region-aware hybrid retrieval mixes word matching and dense meaning links with local weights, feeding a set prompt to a quantized Qwen3-14B model.
