The team extended an existing model with new temperature relationships, then fed it fine-grained global temperature data. The maps show where temperature should block year-round transmission or mosquito survival. A surprise result: the tiger mosquito Ae. albopictus shows greater capacity for transmission than Ae. aegypti, contrary to explanations for its rare real-world role.
europmc-pmc4189936:
Amal S. Ibrahim, Hossam Kamel, and three co-authors published Egypt's first national cancer counts in the Journal of Cancer Epidemiology in 2014. The country's new registry program gathered cases from three regions, one governorate standing for each, plus national treatment centres and death records.

The age-standardized rate came to 166.6 new cases per 100,000 people. Liver cancer led by far, at 23.8 percent of all cases, followed by breast cancer at 15.4 percent and bladder cancer at 6.9 percent. Among men, liver and bladder cancers topped the list; among women, breast and then liver. The authors project a threefold rise in yearly cases by 2050 as the population grows and ages. They present the figures as a baseline for planning cancer control.
europmc-pmc4215636:
Sudhakar V. Nuti, Karthik Murugiah, and five co-authors reviewed research built on Google search data in PLoS ONE in 2014. Google Trends offers free records of what the world searches for, and health researchers had begun mining it to track disease and behaviour. Standards for such work were still loose.

Seventy studies qualified, and their number grew sevenfold from 2009 to 2013. Infectious disease and mental health led the topics, and most studies described patterns or ran surveillance rather than proving causes. Among surveillance papers, most checked their results against a standard source and correlated well. Yet only 7 percent documented their search choices fully enough to repeat the study. The authors supply a checklist to fix that weakness.
europmc-pmc4242436:
Yuhang Liu, He Yan, and eight co-authors pushed polymer solar cells past a key mark in Nature Communications in 2014. Plastic solar cells can be printed cheaply like newspaper, but their efficiency lagged silicon, and the best recipes worked for one material pair at a time. The blend's inner structure, how polymer and fullerene domains mix, decided performance.

By controlling how the donor polymer clumps as the film dries, using its temperature-dependent aggregation, the team formed nearly ideal blends: highly ordered yet small polymer domains in thick films. The trick worked across several polymer and fullerene pairings, giving efficiencies above 10 percent with fill factors up to 77 percent. Three donor polymers crossed the line. The design rules, they argue, free chemists to invent new materials without losing the morphology that works.
europmc-pmc4256936:
Emily S. Wan, Dawn L. DeMeo, and ten co-authors studied a puzzling lung pattern in Respiratory Research in 2014. Some smokers' breathing tests show a low total output with a preserved ratio between measures, a pattern called PRISm. It is not normal and not classic COPD, and its causes and subtypes were unmapped.

In the COPDGene study of 10,192 current and former smokers, PRISm appeared in 12.3 percent. Its holders reported more breathlessness, walked less far in six minutes, and showed more emphysema and thicker airway walls than normal-test controls. A genome scan found no common variant behind it, though a link with Klinefelter syndrome appeared. Clustering split PRISm into subgroups, one looking like early COPD. The authors frame PRISm as a mixed bag needing separation, not a single disease.
europmc-pmc4258036:
Becky Field, Kate Gerrish, and two co-authors traced how a health framework is actually used in Implementation Science in 2014. The Knowledge to Action framework guides teams turning research into practice, and it is cited often. Citation, though, can mean anything from a passing mention to the backbone of a project.

Searching three databases found 1,787 citing records, and 146 studies that used the framework to some degree. Only ten built their whole project on it, from design to evaluation. All ten used its Action Cycle, and seven also used its Knowledge Creation part. Projects ran in hospitals and universities and targeted patients, the public, and nurses. The authors conclude the framework works in practice, but most citations borrow its name more than its method.
europmc-pmc4273436:
Yoshinori Aso leads a team mapping how the fruit fly brain turns learning into action. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. In the fly's mushroom body, about two thousand smell cells converge on a small set of output neurons, and the team tested what each output type does.

Flies were taught to link odors with reward or punishment, and output neurons were switched on or off. Some types drove the flies toward a cue and others drove them away, and the effects combined across types. The team concludes that the output group as a whole encodes whether a cue is good or bad, and that this balance steers choices based on memory.
europmc-pmc4280536:
Leopoldo Palma, Delia Muñoz, Colin Berry, Jesús Murillo, Primitivo Caballero, and Anne-Brit Kolstø survey the toxins made by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, known as Bt. Their review appeared in Toxins in 2014. Bt forms crystals of proteins that kill insects, and sprays and crops based on it have been used against pests for decades.

The review sorts the toxin families. It covers the crystal Cry and Cyt proteins and the proteins released during growth. It also covers newer finds active against beetles, flies, worms, and even some cancer cells in tests. It sets out how each group attacks its target. The overview shows why Bt remains a mainstay of pest control that spares most other life.
europmc-pmc4305236:
Haibao Tang and eight co-authors present ALLMAPS, a tool that orders genome pieces into chromosomes using several genetic maps at once. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology in 2015. A fresh genome sequence arrives as loose scaffolds, and maps from crosses, physical markers, or related species each suggest a different arrangement.

ALLMAPS computes the ordering that agrees best with all maps together, weighted so that errors in any single map do not wreck the result. The output is a chromosome scale assembly more trustworthy than any one map gives. Plant and animal genome projects, which often hold several half matching maps, are the main audience for the method.
europmc-pmc4330336:
Nicholas J. Croucher and seven co-authors present Gubbins, a program that builds bacterial family trees while stripping out swapped DNA. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Whole genome data sets for bacteria keep growing, and recombination between strains piles dense clusters of changes onto some branches, which distorts a tree built naively.

Gubbins scans the alignment for stretches with unusually dense substitutions, the fingerprints of horizontal transfer, and builds the tree from the point mutations outside them. It repeats the pass until the tree settles. Simulations under realistic settings gave highly accurate trees. Outbreak investigators and evolution researchers use the output to trace how strains recently diverged.
europmc-pmc4338236:
Nandita R Garud, Philipp W Messer, Erkan O Buzbas, Dmitri A Petrov, and Gregory P Copenhaver hunted for the fingerprints of recent adaptation in North American fruit flies. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2015. When a helpful mutation sweeps a population, it can rise on one DNA background. That is a hard sweep. It can also rise on several backgrounds at once, a soft sweep. Standard tests were built for the hard kind.

Theory says soft sweeps should be common when adaptation starts from existing variation in large populations. Scanning fly genomes with new statistics, the team found recent sweeps carrying the soft pattern rather than the hard one. The result supports retooling adaptation searches for species with big populations, flies included.
europmc-pmc4379436:
Clement Blanchet and a team of co-authors described the sample systems at a biological X-ray scattering station, in the Journal of Applied Crystallography in 2015. Small-angle X-ray scattering reveals the overall shape of molecules in solution, at scales from nanometers up. The P12 beamline at the PETRA III synchrotron in Hamburg, run by the European Molecular Biology Laboratory, is built for such work on biological samples, which are often scarce and fragile.

The station pairs bright X-rays with automated hardware and software, so samples are loaded, measured, and processed with little hand work. Sample holders cover many conditions, letting users vary temperature and other settings in one visit. Automation keeps data collection fast and uniform, and built-in processing gives quick feedback on data quality. The design aims to let visiting biologists run complex experiments without being scattering specialists.
europmc-pmc4410136:
Kristin Schmidt, Philip Cowen, Catherine Harmer, George Tzortzis, Steven Errington, and Philip Burnet tested prebiotic fibers on stress and mood processing, in Psychopharmacology in 2015. Gut microbes are now firmly linked to brain function, and probiotics alter anxiety-related processing and stress hormones. Prebiotics, fibers that feed resident gut microbes, had shown effects in rats but not in people. Forty-five healthy volunteers took one of two prebiotics or a placebo daily for three weeks.

After the galactooligosaccharide prebiotic, the cortisol rise on waking was significantly lower than after placebo, marking a calmer stress response. In a computer task, those volunteers also showed less attention to negative over positive information. The fructooligosaccharide fiber showed no such effects. Feeding gut microbes, even without adding live bacteria, reached the brain's stress and emotion systems.
europmc-pmc4439136:
Judith Korterink, Kay Diederen, Marc Benninga, Merit Tabbers, and Lanjing Zhang reviewed how common functional abdominal pain is in children, in PLoS ONE in 2015. These are gut pain disorders with no clear physical cause, including irritable bowel syndrome. Families and doctors need to know how often they occur, where, and in whom, to plan care and research.

Searching five databases to February 2014, the team kept studies of children aged four to eighteen drawn from births, schools, or the general public, and rated their quality. Fifty-eight articles covering a very large number of children were pooled. About one child in eight worldwide met criteria for such a disorder, with irritable bowel syndrome the most common kind. Rates varied widely between studies and were higher in South America and Asia than in Europe in their analysis.
europmc-pmc4471936:
Timothy Grant, Nikolaus Grigorieff, and Wesley Sundquist measured the best radiation dose for cryo-electron microscopy in eLife in 2015. Imaging single particles in ice can reveal molecular structures, but the electron beam damages the specimen as it images, capping the detail reachable. For each desired level of detail there is an ideal total exposure that maximizes image clarity before damage wins.

Using a sharp reconstruction of a rotavirus protein shell, built from movie frames, the team measured ideal exposures across a wide range of resolutions. At low and middling detail levels, ideal exposures were much higher than values from crystal studies and higher than labs generally use. Filtering movie frames by these values improved image contrast and sharpened reconstructions. The authors commend the high-exposure approach especially for small molecules, long the hardest targets for the method.
europmc-pmc4489236:
Itamar Sela, Haim Ashkenazy, Kazutaka Katoh, and Tal Pupko built GUIDANCE2, a tool for spotting unreliable parts of sequence alignments, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Alignments line up related DNA or protein sequences so they can be compared, and nearly every evolution study depends on them. The same sequences, though, align differently under different methods and settings, and trusting a wrong stretch can mislead downstream findings such as claims of positive selection.

Earlier detectors of unreliable regions missed several sources of doubt. GUIDANCE2 accounts for uncertainty in how insertions and deletions arose, in the guide tree used to build the alignment, and in ties between equally good pairwise alignments. In simulations and real benchmarks it beat seven rival methods. It also offers alternative alignments for analysts to test. The method runs as a free web server.
europmc-pmc4595636:
In 2015, a study of gut bacteria living in the outer mucus layer of the large intestine was published by Hao Li and colleagues. The gut lining is coated with mucus made by goblet cells. The inner layer is nearly sterile, while the outer layer holds bacteria. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

The team found that the outer mucus forms its own distinct microbial niche, with communities that differ from those in the gut contents. Even bacteria without special mucus-digesting tools live there. Species in mucus grow and feed differently, using iron and carbon sources from the gut wall. This close layer may shape the whole gut community and how microbes trade signals and goods with the host.
europmc-pmc4598836:
In 2015, a materials study introducing entropy-stabilized oxides was published by Christina M. Rost and colleagues. Mixing many different metal ions onto one crystal lattice creates strong disorder. The team asked whether that disorder alone could hold a new crystal phase together. Their test case was an oxide built from five metal components. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

Heating drove the mix from several phases into one single phase, and cooling reversed the change. Tests showed the metal ions sat randomly and evenly in the single-phase state. A simple heat model matched the behaviour. The results prove that entropy can be the main force stabilizing a crystal, which opens a design route toward new materials with tuned properties.
europmc-pmc4668836:
Sara M. Pires, together with colleagues, released a 2015 World Health Organization study estimating illness and death from nine foodborne diarrhoeal diseases in 2010. Diarrhoea is a major global killer, especially of children, but pathogen-specific totals were missing. The team drew on systematic reviews and applied two estimation approaches depending on country death rates. The work appeared in PLOS Medicine.

The nine diseases caused an estimated 1.8 billion cases and 599,000 deaths worldwide in 2010. Norovirus caused the most cases, at 677 million, and also the most deaths. Enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shigella, and Giardia followed in case counts. Nearly forty percent of cases and forty-three percent of deaths fell on children under five. Regional patterns differed sharply, guiding where food safety effort matters most.
europmc-pmc4702836:
Cricket A. Sloan, Esther T. Chan, Jean M. Davidson, and nine colleagues described ENCODE data at its new portal in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. The ENCODE Project is cataloguing the functional parts of the human genome: which DNA regions regulate genes, which proteins bind where, and which stretches carry chemical marks. The project's third phase widened the assays used and the cell types covered. Nearly five thousand experiments had been released when this paper appeared.

The rebuilt portal lets users search and browse by the metadata describing each assay, and shows where each dataset came from. That design targets reuse and reproducibility, not just download counts. Data also flow to other genome browsers and archives. The portal is built to absorb results from sister projects as well. The paper presents the doorway to one of the largest public datasets in biology, rebuilt so others can build on it safely.
europmc-pmc4751336:
Chen and Schulz systematically review whether information and communication technology can ease social isolation in older adults, a condition tied to worse mental and physical health. The journal page opens with an editor masthead, but the review is theirs. They gather 25 studies published between 2002 and 2015, covering training, internet use, and other digital interventions.

Technology use reliably improves social support and connectedness, and isolation in general, though effects on loneliness are mixed. Benefits fade within about six months after interventions end. The routes of benefit include contact with the outside world, gained support, engaging activities, and confidence. The authors call for stronger study designs.
europmc-pmc4820836:
Emily B. J. Coffey and four co-authors locate the sources of a brain response to sound in Nature Communications in 2016. When a steady-pitched sound plays, the brain answers at the same pitch, a response called the frequency-following response. Clinics use it to study sound processing, and textbooks assigned it to the brainstem alone, below conscious hearing.

Using a magnetic brain scanner that can separate sources, the team found a strong contribution from the hearing cortex itself, stronger on the right side, at the sound's base pitch. The expected deep stations, from the ear nerve relay to the midbrain and the relay to cortex, also contributed. The cortex's share means the response reflects higher processing too, so past readings of it as a pure brainstem gauge need rethinking.
europmc-pmc4931236:
Hyunwoo Yuk, Teng Zhang, German Alberto Parada, Xinyue Liu, and Xuanhe Zhao build soft materials that join hydrogels and elastomers like skin joins its layers. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Hydrogels are wet, soft gels. Elastomers are stretchy rubbers. Hybrids of the two suit soft robots, wearable devices, and tissue engineering, but past versions bonded weakly and were hard to pattern with fine features.

The team's method bonds the two with very high toughness, over 1,000 joules per square meter at the interface. It works with many common rubbers, from silicone to latex, and with tough hydrogels in general. The hybrids can carry tiny fluid channels and electric circuits built in. Showpieces include a stretchy circuit board and fluid chips that react as they bend. The authors present the bond method as a general recipe for soft devices.
europmc-pmc4933736:
Rosemary McEachan and five co-authors pool studies that test the reasoned action approach, a model of why people act. Their meta-analysis appeared in Annals of Behavioral Medicine in 2016. The model splits attitude, social norms, and felt control into paired parts. It then predicts intention, and intention in turn predicts behavior. The team applied the model to health behaviors, both protective acts and risky ones.

Sense of capacity and felt enjoyment of an act linked most strongly to intention. All parts of the model except felt autonomy predicted intention on their own. Intention, capacity, and experiential attitude also predicted real behavior, joined by descriptive norms, what people think others do. The authors conclude the model's parts each add useful signal. They argue it gives health programs clear levers, such as building skills and shifting what people see as normal.
europmc-pmc4964536:
Valentina Turinetto, Emanuela Vitale, and Claudia Giachino review senescence in human mesenchymal stem cells and what it means for cell therapy. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. These stem cells are prized for regenerative medicine and for aging related disease. Therapy needs huge cell numbers, which forces long growth in culture. Over that time many cells senesce, entering a worn, non-dividing state with changed behavior.

Senescent cells lose much of their power to become bone, fat, or cartilage. Their ability to migrate and home to injury sites also fades. Their secreted mix can fan inflammation body wide, blunt immune calming, and even help cancer cells grow or spread. The authors argue therapy makers must watch senescence as a quality risk. Fresh, well checked cell batches, they say, are a condition for the field's promise to hold.
europmc-pmc4987536:
Michael J. D. Daniels leads a large team showing that a class of pain drugs blocks the NLRP3 inflammasome. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Fenamate drugs are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, long known to block COX enzymes. The NLRP3 inflammasome is a protein complex that activates the inflammatory signal interleukin-1beta and is blamed in many diseases. The team found fenamates inhibit it by a separate route, blocking a volume regulated anion channel in macrophages, not through COX.

Two fenamates, flufenamic and mefenamic acid, calmed inflammasome driven inflammation in rodent models. They also protected memory in a model of amyloid beta damage and in a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The authors propose repurposing these approved, widely used drugs as inflammasome inhibitors. That path could reach patients faster than a new compound, they argue, if trials confirm the effect.
europmc-pmc4998136:
Peter R. Shewry and Sandra J. Hey review wheat's contribution to human diet and health. Their review appeared in Food and Energy Security in 2015. Wheat is the top staple crop of temperate zones and demand grows as countries urbanize. Beyond starch and energy, wheat supplies protein, B vitamins, dietary fiber, and phytochemicals, plant compounds with health effects. In the United Kingdom, bread alone provides a fifth of daily fiber intake.

Fiber from cereals links to lower risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer. The amounts of wheat's helpful components vary widely with variety and growing conditions. Fiber content is strongly heritable, which means breeders can select for it. The authors argue breeding should target health traits alongside yield. That way rising wheat consumption could carry health gains rather than diluting diet quality.
europmc-pmc5028936:
Jeffrey Cummings and nine co-authors map Alzheimer's drug development toward 2025 in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy in 2016. National leaders had set a goal to prevent or treat the disease by 2025, and this review asks what that deadline honestly allows. Drug development is slow and failure-prone, so only compounds already in late early testing when the paper appeared could plausibly reach approval in time.

The authors list ways to cut time and risk: sharper trial design, ready registries of well-studied volunteers, and proven biomarkers to track the disease and predict response. They add more sensitive outcome measures and faster review by regulators. All of it needs more funding, shared data, and less fragmented work. Even with reforms, they judge that only a few new disease-modifying drugs could arrive by 2025, which makes starting the fixes now urgent.
europmc-pmc5058336:
Mariet Allen and a very large co-author group release a shared brain dataset in Scientific Data in 2016. Gene studies have flagged many DNA regions tied to Alzheimer's and related diseases, but the flagged variants rarely name the gene they act through. Many seem to work by changing gene expression in the brain. To let researchers test that route, the group pooled its genome and gene-activity data and opened it to qualified scientists.

The release combines genome-wide genotype data from 2,099 people with gene expression measures from 773 brain samples, 186 of them also sequenced for RNA. A separate cohort adds 556 brain samples with RNA sequencing. Donors had Alzheimer's or other neurodegenerative diseases, or were controls. By placing variant and expression data side by side, the set lets outside teams hunt the regulatory variants and real disease genes behind the statistical signals, without collecting a single new sample.
europmc-pmc5064736:
Zhiyong Yang and a wide team of co-authors report a glow-after-light material in Angewandte Chemie in 2016. Some pure organic crystals keep glowing after the light is switched off, an effect called persistent room-temperature phosphorescence, but no shared mechanism or design rule existed. The team proposes that pairing two different excited states in neighboring coupled molecules can steady the glow, and they built molecules to test the idea.

Adding a heavy halogen atom to the coupled units sped the crossing into the glowing state. The result was an afterglow lasting 0.28 seconds with a quantum efficiency of five percent, in open air at room temperature, far beyond the few milliseconds typical for organic materials. Long afterglow matters for displays, sensors, and time-gated imaging that reads a signal after background light fades. The authors present their coupling scheme as a general recipe other chemists can adapt.
europmc-pmc5210636:
Eric W. Deutsch and sixteen colleagues reported on the ProteomeXchange consortium in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. ProteomeXchange, started in 2011, sets shared rules for depositing and spreading mass spectrometry proteomics data, the large data sets that identify proteins in a sample.

Two new members, MassIVE and jPOST, joined the founding PRIDE and PeptideAtlas resources. A shared portal, ProteomeCentral, now searches data sets across all member resources, with better visual displays. Submission guidance was updated to cover four members, and the numbers show a culture shift. More than 4,500 data sets were submitted since 2012, roughly half of them human, with over 900 species represented in all. Journal rules that require public release helped make sharing the norm. Reprocessing of shared data sets is also growing, and the paper outlines next steps.
europmc-pmc5240936:
Michael M. Mendelson and a large consortium linked body mass index with DNA methylation in blood cells in PLoS Medicine in 2017. Methylation, a chemical mark on DNA that tunes gene activity, might connect obesity to heart and metabolic disease, but the direction of cause was unclear. The study hunted for marks that track with body mass across thousands of people.

Across 3,743 participants from two cohorts, with repeat checks in 4,055 more people, 83 methylation sites tied reliably to body mass. Marks near fat-handling genes came with matching changes in those genes' activity in blood. A genetic method that mimics an experiment, Mendelian randomization, tied one site inside the SREBF1 gene to body mass, fat traits, and coronary artery disease. For 16 of the 83 sites, the evidence pointed the other way: higher body mass came first and the mark followed.
europmc-pmc5273336:
Byrom Bramwell, with a spinal cord report by James W. Dawson, published a case of severe spastic paraplegia in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1916, the eleventh of his clinical studies. The patient lived fifteen years with stiff, paralyzed legs and complete inability to walk, watched closely for seven of those years. Bramwell suspected disseminated sclerosis, the disease now called multiple sclerosis, since it often opens exactly this way, especially in young women.

Yet none of the disease's signature signs ever appeared: no eye tremor, no intention tremor, no optic damage, no speech change. Death came instead from diabetes mellitus and boils. Only the post-mortem settled the question. Examination of the spinal cord, pons, and medulla, the only parts available, showed all the characteristic lesions of disseminated sclerosis. The case warns that a diagnosis of primary spastic paraplegia, a very rare condition, should always be distrusted.
europmc-pmc5333436:
Chloë FitzGerald and Samia Hurst reviewed hidden bias among health workers in BMC Medical Ethics in 2017. Hidden, or implicit, bias means snap judgments held outside full awareness, based on traits like race or sex that should not sway care. The pair searched four databases for studies of such bias in doctors, nurses, and other care staff.

They kept forty-two sound studies from a ten-year span. Some used a timed test that exposes snap links between groups and traits. Others gave staff twin case stories that differed in just one trait, and watched the care choices shift. Race and ethnic bias were the most studied, ahead of sex, age, and weight. Most studies found bias present. Every study that checked found higher bias tied to lower quality of care. The authors urge the field to face the problem head on.
europmc-pmc5356236:
Amirhossein Modabbernia, Eva Velthorst, and Abraham Reichenberg reviewed life-setting risks for autism in Molecular Autism in 2017. Genes explain part of autism risk, but work now credits world and body factors for up to half of the spread. The team gathered the pooled reviews on such factors and graded the proof for each, with notes on how each might act.

Some blamed factors came out clean: vaccines, a vaccine preservative, and smoking in pregnancy showed no link to risk. Older parents did show a higher risk. Birth harm tied to trauma or low oxygen also linked strongly. Mother's weight, diabetes, and surgical birth linked more weakly. Proof on diet parts was mixed, though low vitamin D showed in patients. Some heavy metals, most of all mercury and lead, showed links firm enough to merit deeper study.
europmc-pmc5357536:
Vincenzo Monda and co-authors reviewed training effects on gut microbes in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2017. The gut hosts a dense mix of microbes that guard its wall, feed the body, and tune the immune system. Diet, drugs, and illness can shift that mix for good or ill. Fresh work hints that exercise is one more lever on the mix.

The review sums up what is known so far. Training seems to raise the count of helpful kinds, widen the spread of kinds, and help friendly resident microbes grow. Those shifts track with better gut wall health and calmer body-wide swelling. The authors frame the gut mix as a hormone-like organ that answers to body state. They argue that the gains from exercise may run in part through this microbial path, with promise for blocking disease.
europmc-pmc5383336:
Alison A. McBride and Alix Warburton review how human papillomavirus, or HPV, can become part of host cell DNA, in a 2017 article in PLoS Pathogens. In its normal life cycle the virus stays as a small separate ring of DNA in skin cells. Cancers linked to HPV often hold virus DNA built into the cell's own chromosomes instead.

Built-in virus DNA is a dead end for the virus, since it can no longer spread. Yet it can free two viral genes that push cells to grow and lose normal checks. That gives those cells an edge and helps them turn cancerous. The authors explain the main forms this joining takes and why the joined cells grow out over time.
europmc-pmc5386536:
Farhan Basit and his co-authors report a 2017 study in Cell Death and Disease on how blocking part of the cell's energy chain kills melanoma cells. They used a drug that blocks complex I, a key step in how cells burn fuel. The work used skin cancer cells with a common gene change, grown in dishes and in tumors, to trace the death path step by step.

The drug drained the cell's energy charge, raised harmful oxygen byproducts, and sped up removal of worn energy parts. Lowering certain helper proteins blocked the death, while lowering others made it worse. The cells died by two backup routes that do not need the usual death switch. The authors map this chain as a lead for new cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc5394636:
Cordelia E. M. Coltart, Benjamin Lindsey, Isaac Ghinai, Anne M. Johnson, and David L. Heymann review the West African Ebola outbreak in a 2017 paper in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Ebola causes severe bleeding fever with a high death rate. The 2013 to 2016 outbreak was larger than all past outbreaks combined and spread across borders in a new way.

The authors trace the outbreak country by country and in time order, with case counts and the steps used to contain it. They set it against past outbreaks and weigh theories of how it began. Slow detection, weak health systems, and travel helped it spread, while local and world action at last contained it. The paper presses that its hard lessons not be lost.
europmc-pmc5409636:
Maximilian Tremmel, Ulf-G. Gerdtham, Peter M. Nilsson, and Sanjib Saha review the cost of obesity in a 2017 paper in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Obesity rates keep rising, and weighing its full cost can guide policy. The team searched two databases for studies from 2011 to late 2016 that priced obesity for a whole country, counting adults whose body mass index marked them as obese.

The studies that fit showed a heavy cost load in both rich and poorer countries. Yet their methods clashed at every step: which obesity-linked diseases they counted, whose costs they took, and over what span. That spread blocks fair side-by-side checks. The authors call for agreed world methods for such cost work, and for strong steps to prevent obesity and save public funds.
europmc-pmc5424036:
Lambie reviews the grave two-way problem of diabetes in pregnancy. The paper was read to the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society. Diabetes endangers both mother and child. It also blunts fertility. About half of diabetic women stop menstruating. Only a small share of married diabetic women conceive. Insulin could restore reproductive function if organ damage had not gone too far.

Pregnancy, in turn, makes diabetes worse. Sugar tolerance falls early in pregnancy. Gland changes in mid-pregnancy strain it further. A heavy appetite adds to the load. The chief threat is acidosis. It can strike suddenly, even as coma, in pregnant patients. Lambie weighs the rival reports on late-pregnancy tolerance. Some doctors saw a fall, others a rise. He also notes flare-ups after delivery. The paper captures early insulin-era thinking on a rare but deadly mix.
europmc-pmc5433236:
Rath and co-authors hunt the gut bacteria that make trimethylamine, a compound tied to heart disease. Their research article appeared in Microbiome. Gut microbes make trimethylamine from choline and carnitine in food. The body converts it to TMAO. TMAO is linked to clogged arteries and grave heart events. The maker bacteria are rare and hard to spot. Normal gene surveys miss their trait.

The team built databases for the two key maker genes. They screened over 67,000 genomes for candidates. They then built targeted tests for stool samples. All 50 human samples held potential producers. The choline gene showed up in everyone. The carnitine gene appeared in only about a quarter. Producers stayed under one percent of the community in most samples. Many sequences matched no known strain well. Key human producers may still await isolation. The tests give a base for treatments that rein in these bacteria.
europmc-pmc5502436:
Patel and co-authors report an immunology study in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. It tracks the three kinds of monocytes that patrol human blood. Classical monocytes make up about 85 percent of the pool. How the subsets relate, and how long each survives, was unknown. The team used safe heavy-water labeling to follow the cells in people.

Classical monocytes proved short-lived precursors, they report. They can mature into intermediate and then nonclassical monocytes. All three subsets circulate in a steady balance at rest. Widespread inflammation triggers an emergency release of classical monocytes, though. The work gives human monocyte lifespans their first firm numbers.
europmc-pmc5505136:
Mu and co-authors report a mouse study in Microbiome on gut bacteria and lupus kidney disease. Lupus is an autoimmune disorder with no cure. Its kidney form, lupus nephritis, is a leading cause of death in patients. Current drugs suppress the whole immune system and raise infection risk. The team asked whether gut microbes shape the kidney damage.

Lupus-prone mice showed a sharp loss of Lactobacillales gut bacteria, they report. Feeding five Lactobacillus strains improved kidney function and lengthened survival. The bacteria sealed a leaky gut and calmed inflammation. Harmful antibody deposits in the kidney fell as well. The benefit appeared in females but not intact males.
europmc-pmc552336:
Basciano and co-authors present a review in Nutrition and Metabolism on fructose and metabolic disease. Fructose intake has soared through sucrose and corn syrup sweeteners. The liver handles nearly all of it, unlike other sugars. Heavy fructose flow pushes the liver to build fat fast. Triglyceride output climbs as a result.

That pattern breeds insulin resistance in animals and humans, they report. Blood lipids shift toward the profile that clogs arteries. Gut and liver both overproduce risky lipoprotein particles. The authors link the sweetener surge to the metabolic syndrome epidemic. They urge public awareness and curbs on added fructose in packaged foods.
europmc-pmc5561136:
Ambadipudi and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. Their subject is Tau, a protein that forms toxic tangles in Alzheimer's disease. In healthy cells Tau is loose, soluble, and binds to microtubules. What first pushes it toward solid deposits was unclear.

The team studied the repeat region of Tau that binds microtubules. That region can split from solution into liquid droplets. The droplets crowd the parts of Tau that favor amyloid formation. Forms with three and four repeats differ in this behavior. Chemical tags called phosphates push the process further. The authors propose that droplet formation is a step toward tangles. Readers get a fresh mechanism for a known disease protein.
europmc-pmc5578736:
Smith and co-authors report a test of the glymphatic idea in eLife. That idea says fluid flows through brain tissue and clears waste. Water channels called aquaporin-4 were said to drive the flow. The claim drew wide interest for sleep and dementia research.

The team re-ran the key experiments in mice and rats. They tracked glowing sugar molecules after injection into brain fluid spaces. Movement matched plain diffusion, not flow. Deleting the aquaporin-4 gene did not slow solute entry. Stopping the heart and breathing also left local spread unchanged. The authors conclude the evidence favors diffusion. Readers get a careful challenge to a popular brain theory.
europmc-pmc5581336:
Zhang and co-authors report a battery advance in Nature Communications. Zinc-manganese dioxide cells rule the throwaway battery market. Making them rechargeable has been hard. Their new system uses a water-based, mild-acid electrolyte with zinc triflate.

On first discharge, the tunnel-shaped cathode changes into a layered form. Zinc ions can then move in and out of that structure. The electrolyte also helps a protective layer form on the cathode. Cells kept 94 percent of capacity after 2,000 cycles. A pouch cell reached an energy density of 75.2 watt-hours per kilogram. The parts are cheap and safe. Readers see a strong candidate for large-scale energy storage.
europmc-pmc5606636:
Damalas and co-authors review how farmers meet pesticides at work, and how to cut that risk. Their review ran in Toxics. Farmers face much higher doses than people who just eat the food. Contact comes most when they mix, load, and spray. It also comes when they clean spray gear.

Spills, splashes, drift, and faulty gear all add to dose. Skin and lungs are the main routes in. Workers can also pick up residues from crops and soil after spraying. That route is often missed. The review sorts the types of harm pesticides can cause. It then sets out steps to prevent harm. Chief among them are less use and the right protective gear at each stage of handling.
europmc-pmc5683736:
Chin and co-authors report a cohort study in JACC: Cardiovascular Imaging. It links heart muscle scarring with decline in aortic stenosis. Scarring drives the shift from thickened muscle to heart failure. Magnetic resonance scans can map two kinds of fibrosis. T1 mapping shows diffuse scarring as expanded tissue space. Late enhancement imaging marks replacement scar directly. The study enrolled 203 subjects prospectively. Of these, 166 had aortic stenosis and 37 were healthy.

Patients split into three scan-based groups. Half had normal myocardium on imaging. About a fifth showed expanded tissue space only. The rest had clear replacement scar. Worse scarring tracked with more injury and weaker function. Death rates rose stepwise across the groups.
europmc-pmc5752736:
Hugenholtz and de Vos weigh mouse models for research on the human gut microbiota. Mice have served this field since its early days. Turning mouse results into human claims needs care. The review compares gut traits in mice and humans side by side.

Many bacterial genera occur in both hosts, but their shares differ a lot. Only about 4% of bacterial genes match closely between the two. Mouse strain, supplier, and housing can shift the microbes a study finds. That can harm repeatability across labs. The authors urge studies to report and control these factors.
europmc-pmc5753036:
Purlyte and co-authors study how Rab29 switches on LRRK2, a kinase tied to Parkinson disease. LRRK2 faults are a common genetic cause of this illness. Rab29 sits in a genome zone also linked to the disease. The team tested how the two proteins interact in cells.

Rab29 pulls LRRK2 to the trans-Golgi network and boosts its kinase work, they find. Disease forms of LRRK2 are drawn in and switched on more readily. Set spots in LRRK2's ankyrin domain are needed for this grip. Removing Rab29 cut LRRK2 action on Rab10 in lung cells. Rab29 looks like a master regulator of LRRK2.
europmc-pmc5765236:
Jenkins, Barbie, and Flaherty review how cancers resist immune checkpoint inhibitors. These drugs free T cells by blocking CTLA-4 or the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. They have changed care for many cancers. Some patients gain lasting responses, while others never respond at all.

Late relapses also appear after first success, the authors note. That points to acquired resistance on top of inborn resistance. Firm markers to predict response are still lacking. Most mechanism claims rest on early lab work and linked clinical data. The review sorts those claims to guide drug pairing and order.
europmc-pmc5784936:
Tokhi and co-authors review programs that involve men in maternal and newborn health. Such programs run in low and middle income countries. Earlier reviews called male involvement promising but the proof base messy. The team searched for studies from 2000 to 2012 that engaged men during pregnancy, birth, and infancy.

Thirteen studies from nine countries were kept. Programs raised attendance at antenatal care and skilled birth care, they find. Home care and readiness for complications improved as well. Effects on deaths, illness, and breastfeeding stayed unclear. Partner support and joint decisions grew, with mixed effects on women's autonomy.
europmc-pmc5785536:
Carradec and co-authors build a world ocean atlas of genes from eukaryotic plankton. These small organisms drive much ocean life, yet their genes stayed hard to study. The team used data from Tara Oceans stations across four size classes. They clustered the reads into sets of expressed genes.

The catalog holds 116 million unigenes, the largest such set for one biome. It reveals what plankton do across regions and how those jobs map onto geography. Almost half the sequences match no known protein. Many belong to new gene families found only in parts of the ocean.
europmc-pmc5791736:
Smith and co-authors identify CCPG1 as a cargo receptor for eating worn parts of the endoplasmic reticulum. This selective cleanup, called ER-phagy, keeps the organelle's proteins in balance. How it runs in the body stayed unclear. CCPG1 sits in the ER membrane and had no known job.

The protein binds core autophagy parts through two separate motifs, they show. Its gene switches on under ER stress, linking stress to cleanup. In mice, loss of CCPG1 let proteins clump in the pancreas. Stress responses then ran too hot and tissue was injured.
europmc-pmc5862936:
Wagenmakers and co-authors argue for Bayesian inference in psychology. Their article is part one of a series in Psychonomic Bulletin and Review. Psychology papers lean heavily on p values, they note. Those values are often read in ways that mislead. Bayesian methods offer an alternative for estimation and testing. The authors list ten clear advantages of the Bayesian approach.

Among them, evidence can be updated as data come in. Researchers need not know how sampling was meant to stop. Support for the null hypothesis can be measured directly. The authors answer common objections to Bayesian testing. They stress gains for practical, day-to-day research work. A companion part covers JASP software for these methods.
europmc-pmc5938036:
Jeon and Shin explore vitamin D metabolism and function in cancer. Their review appeared in Experimental & Molecular Medicine. Vitamin D is a precursor of a potent steroid hormone. After two steps in liver and kidney, it yields calcitriol. Calcitriol binds the vitamin D receptor and switches many genes. A newer route uses the CYP11A1 enzyme instead.

Vitamin D has many reported anticancer properties, the authors note. Yet its metabolism often goes wrong inside cancers. That failure can blunt its antitumour effects and help cancers grow. The review sums up these pathways and their faults. Knowing them may guide vitamin D based cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc5948736:
Yang and co-authors study how human mesenchymal stem cells change as they age in culture. Their study appeared in Stem Cell Research & Therapy. Such stem cells must be grown through many passages before clinical use. Senescence during that growth can alter their traits. The team passaged bone marrow stem cells up to passage 8. They used two expansion media, one DMEM based and one αMEM based.

Aged cells lost their spindle shape and grew uneven, they report. Growth rates fell over time in both media. Surface marker CD146 dropped with passage only in the DMEM group. Fat cell formation survived at late passage in both groups. Bone formation was clearly compromised in aged cells.
europmc-pmc5953836:
Hellmann and a large team of co-authors seek genomic signs of response to combination immunotherapy in lung cancer. Their study appeared in Cancer Cell. The patients had advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. They received PD-1 plus CTLA-4 blockade together. Predictors of benefit from this pairing were unknown. The team used whole-exome sequencing on their tumours.

High tumour mutation burden predicted better response, they report. It also tracked with durable benefit and longer progression-free survival. The link held apart from PD-L1 expression levels. Low mutation burden meant low response rates despite the combination. The authors argue mutation burden belongs in future trial design.
europmc-pmc5975536:
Moberg and co-authors describe the GRADE Evidence to Decision framework for health system and public health decisions. Their paper appeared in Health Research Policy and Systems. The framework was built within the DECIDE project. It grew from GRADE evidence to decision tables. The team used brainstorming, literature checks, and stakeholder input. An international survey of policy-makers also fed in. Workshops and user testing refined the draft.

All GRADE frameworks share one basic structure, they note. Users frame the question, assess the option, then draw conclusions. Criteria cover effects, cost, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Evidence certainty is often low for such decisions. Monitoring and evaluation therefore matter a great deal.
europmc-pmc5993136:
Cheng and co-authors review lipid metabolism reprogramming in cancer and its possible drug targets. Their review appeared in Cancer Communications. Rewired lipid handling is now seen as a hallmark of cancer. Tumours take up, store, and build more lipids than normal tissue. That supply feeds fast growth and new membranes. SREBP transcription factors sit at the centre of this control. They are strongly raised in many cancers.

A partner protein moves and activates SREBPs, the authors explain. It also senses glucose, linking sugar and fat pathways. Blocking faulty lipid routes has become a promising strategy. The review lists targets and their candidate inhibitors.
europmc-pmc5993836:
Saunders and co-authors explore how saturation is understood and used in qualitative research. Their paper appeared in Quality & Quantity. Saturation signals that more data collection is not needed. It is widely accepted as a guiding principle. Yet its meaning is unsettled and its use is patchy. The authors set out to clarify its nature and purposes. They sort published practice into four distinct approaches.

The approaches differ in logic, from inductive to deductive. They also stress data collection, analysis, or theory to different degrees. Saturation is a prediction about unseen data, they argue. That shaky logic breeds confusion in the field. Use should fit the question and framework chosen.
europmc-pmc6003936:
Nagy, Lánczky, Menyhárt, and Győrffy test the power of small gene bits to foresee liver cancer outcomes, using fresh data sets. Their study was published in Scientific Reports. Many past papers put forth distinct gene bits as outcome marks. Few were ever checked past their own data. The team built a data bank of gene bit levels from shared sources. They drew 223 marked bits from 214 past papers. Tests then ran on two sorts of data.

Some bits did foresee who lived longer, they report. Far more hit that mark in one data sort than the other. Levels in tumours and in healthy liver were far apart for half the bits. The bank lets new claims face fresh checks.
europmc-pmc6008936:
Mohamed-Ahmed and co-authors compare adipose-derived and bone marrow stem cells from the same donors. Their study appeared in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. Both cell types serve regenerative medicine widely. Donor differences often confound head-to-head comparisons. Paired samples from identical donors remove that noise. The team checked growth, surface markers, and differentiation. Fat-derived cells grew faster than marrow cells, they report.

Fat cells also formed fat tissue more readily. Marrow cells won on bone and cartilage formation instead. They deposited calcium earlier and more heavily. Capacity varied strongly between donors in both types. Source choice should follow the target tissue.
europmc-pmc6043636:
Albanesi and co-authors review the interplay behind psoriasis. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease. It involves both genetic and lifestyle factors. Skin cells and immune cells drive it together.

Keratinocytes are the main resident skin cells. They release signals that wake innate immunity. Peptides like LL37 help trigger dendritic cells. Those cells then expand several T-cell types. T-cell signals switch keratinocytes into overdrive in return. The cells grow too fast and mature poorly. They also pour out more inflammatory molecules. This loop sustains the disease over time. Genetic quirks inside keratinocytes add to the imbalance. Readers get a two-way account of skin inflammation.
europmc-pmc6107736:
Feehan and co-authors offer a systematic review in JMIR mHealth and uHealth on how exact Fitbit trackers are. Fitbits are sold to spur daily activity. Yet researchers and clinics now use them to measure health. The review asks how well their readings match trusted lab tools.

The team searched four databases and kept 67 studies. Fitbits met a tight step-count bar about half the time. They tended to miss steps in lab tests and add steps in daily life. They were poor at gauging energy burned in all setups. Sleep time looked close to research tools. The authors say more accuracy work is still needed.
europmc-pmc6249736:
Vasileiou and co-authors studied how interview based health research justifies its sample sizes. Their analysis appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology. They examined studies in three health journals over fifteen years. All used one interview per person. Sample size choice is often debated in qualitative work. Poor reporting of that choice is common across many fields.

Few studies in the sample gave a clear defence of their size. Defence did not depend on how many interviews were done. The journal a study appeared in mattered more. Most defences rested on saturation, the point where new interviews add little. Practical limits were the other common reason. Many authors still called their samples small, as if size alone proved weakness. The team urges fuller, more honest reporting of data adequacy.
europmc-pmc6259136:
Miguel reviews the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions of essential oils. Her short review appeared in Molecules. Essential oils are scented liquids drawn from aromatic plants. Each oil mixes many compounds in varied shares. Food, cosmetic, and health makers all use them. Interest in their protective effects has grown in recent years.

Recent studies link many oils to radical blocking power. Others report calming effects on inflammation pathways. The review surveys the lab tests most used to measure antioxidant strength. It also sets out how some oils may damp inflammation. Major compounds can make up most of an oil, while trace parts still shape its scent. That mix makes each oil hard to judge as a single agent. Miguel's account helps readers weigh the claims with care.
europmc-pmc6260436:
Abiodun and co-authors survey real world uses of artificial neural networks. Their survey appeared in Heliyon. Neural networks learn patterns from data and now serve many fields. The authors sort network types into a clear taxonomy. They then track where each type is used. Uses span computing, medicine, farming, mining, business, and the arts.

Each use is weighed for its gains and its weak points. Methods are compared on speed, accuracy, and scale. Feedforward and feedback networks did best on human problems in their reading. The authors judge them by factors such as fault tolerance and data volume. They suggest that future work blend network types into shared systems. A single method may miss what a mix can catch. The survey gives newcomers a map of a fast moving field.
europmc-pmc6267036:
Roach, Schmidt, and Borneman present a tool that cleans up duplicated parts of genome assemblies. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. The tool is called Purge Haplotigs. Long read sequencing now builds near reference quality genomes. In varied genomes, matching chromosome copies can fail to merge. The assembly then holds both copies as if they were distinct regions. That error distorts later variant and pairing work.

Purge Haplotigs hunts for those doubled fragments and reassigns them. It uses read alignments and repeat notes to judge each piece. Tests used a simulated set and four real diploid assemblies. Processed assemblies held less duplication with little loss of completeness. Paired copies were also matched more often in diploid outputs. The tool runs fast and is free under an open licence.
europmc-pmc6272636:
Franci and co-authors review silver nanoparticles as antibacterial agents. Their review appeared in Molecules. Drug resistant bacteria now threaten many standard treatments. Broad antibiotic use has fed that resistance. Silver has served against infection since ancient times. Nano sized silver brings that old power into new forms.

Silver particles attack bacteria in several ways at once. That breadth may slow resistance. Studies also show action against bacterial biofilms, the tough films germs build on surfaces. The review gathers work on how the particles work and where they fail. Safety, dose, and delivery questions are weighed. Hospitals, wound care, and coatings are possible uses. The authors see nanosilver as one tool among many. It cannot replace careful antibiotic stewardship.
europmc-pmc6279736:
McRae and co-authors report a huge map of gene variants that steer DNA methylation. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Methylation marks help control which genes are active. Variants that shift those marks are called methylation QTL. They may explain disease signals found in non-coding DNA. The team combined family and birth cohort data from about two thousand people.

Nearly 55,000 such variants were confirmed across the two samples. Most acted near their target marks. About two thousand acted at a distance. Distant actors clustered near chromosome ends and on two chromosomes. Marks tied to these variants carried extra weight for several traits. Height and two bowel diseases stood out in that test. The map gives disease genetics a new layer to work with.
europmc-pmc6283836:
Stephansen and co-authors trained neural networks to score sleep and flag narcolepsy. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Sleep scoring now relies on trained staff reading overnight records by eye. That work is slow and varies between scorers. The team used about three thousand normal and abnormal recordings. Their network outputs a full probability trace over sleep stages.

The best model beat every single human scorer in tests. It agreed with the group consensus at eighty-seven percent, scored by the humans. It can also score in five second steps, not just thirty. A marker built on odd stage overlaps caught narcolepsy well. Sensitivity reached ninety-one percent, with specificity at ninety-six. Adding a gene test lifted specificity to ninety-nine. The method could cut clinic time sharply. Home sleep studies might even carry the diagnosis.
europmc-pmc6315036:
Kunitski and co-authors report a molecular version of the double-slit experiment. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. They fired a strong laser field at neon dimers. Each dimer holds two neon atoms side by side. Freed electrons could emerge from either atom. That setup forms two coherent electron sources.

The team measured electrons together with their parent ions. Sorting the ions let them pick the symmetry of the leftover ion. Both interference types then appeared in the electron patterns. The result shows wave behavior surviving strong-field ionization. It extends a classic quantum test to ultrafast scales. Physicists can use it to probe electron birth and motion.
europmc-pmc6351836:
Belfiore and co-authors map Alzheimer's-like changes over time in a key mouse model. Their study appeared in Aging Cell. The 3xTg-AD mouse carries genes for the human disease. It has served labs for almost fifteen years. Reports on its timing of symptoms now conflict. The team rechecked the model at four ages.

Female mice were studied at 2, 6, 12, and 20 months. Amyloid plaques hit the rear hippocampus by six months. By twelve months all mice had hippocampal plaques. Cortical plaques, including in entorhinal cortex, appeared at twelve months. Tau marks showed in every hippocampus by then as well. Inflammation and memory were tracked in parallel. The timeline gives labs a firmer baseline for drug tests.
europmc-pmc6362136:
Rosato and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on a new angle for cancer immunotherapy. Memory T cells left over from past viral infections also sit inside tumors, they note. The team asked whether waking those cells could attack cancers that resist current treatments.

In mice, injecting plain viral peptides into tumors reactivated the antiviral memory cells. The authors report that growth of resistant, weakly immunogenic tumors stopped. The peptide treatment switched on dendritic cells and natural killer cells inside the tumor. It also made resistant tumors respond to PD-L1 blockade. Human tumor samples treated outside the body showed similar immune activation.
europmc-pmc6368436:
Bartel and co-authors present a research article in Science Advances on predicting perovskite stability. For ninety years, chemists used the Goldschmidt tolerance factor, a simple ratio of ion sizes. It sorts perovskites from other structures with only 74 percent accuracy, and far worse for heavier halides.

The team derived a new factor, tau, from data on 576 known compounds. Their factor reached 92 percent accuracy on the same set. It works for single and double perovskites, oxides and halides alike. Because it needs only a chemical formula, researchers can screen candidate materials quickly. The authors present it as a practical tool for materials discovery.
europmc-pmc6372836:
Martino and co-authors present a methods article in mSystems on analyzing microbiome data. Such datasets are sparse and compositional, so standard distance measures can mislead. Rare microbes may matter most, yet abundant ones dominate the usual plots.

The team built a robust Aitchison principal component method, released as the open-source tool DEICODE. It uses matrix completion to handle missing values in sparse count tables. The authors report strong power to separate microbial niches and to rank the features that drive the split. A QIIME 2 plugin makes the method easy to add to existing pipelines. The work targets clearer beta diversity analysis for microbial ecology.
europmc-pmc6389936:
Yu and co-authors report a research article in Cell Death and Disease on a colon cancer drug. Lobaplatin kills cancer cells, but the death route was unclear. The team tested it on two colon cancer cell lines.

Treated cells swelled and grew large bubbles, signs of pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. A protein called GSDME was cut by caspase-3 and opened pores in the cell surface. Removing GSDME changed the death to a quieter form. The authors show this protein decides the drug's death mode. That may affect how the drug stirs immune responses.
europmc-pmc6441236:
Fiori and co-authors pick apart how the fibroblasts that gather around tumors help cancers grow and shrug off treatment, with a shape-shifting switch at the center. Fibroblasts are the most common support cells in solid tumors, reaching up to 80 percent of tumor mass in pancreatic cancer. They talk with cancer cells through secreted signals, small vesicles, shared fuels, and the matrix itself.

Through that cross-talk, fibroblasts can push cancer cells to loosen up and move, switch on survival paths, keep stem-like programs alive, and rewire how cells burn fuel. Newly found fibroblast subtypes make a single attack risky: wiping out the wrong subset could help the tumor. Turning the rich lab picture into plans that work in the clinic remains the unfinished work.
europmc-pmc6450036:
Franzén and co-authors introduce PanglaoDB, a free web database that makes published mouse and human single-cell RNA sequencing data explorable without heavy computation. Hundreds of datasets existed as raw files that biologists could not easily open. PanglaoDB pre-processes them into a uniform, browsable form.

The resource covers more than 1,054 experiments and over 4 million cells across major platforms and tissues. Visitors can query cell types, pathways, and regulatory networks directly in the browser. A community-curated marker collection with more than 6,000 gene-to-cell-type associations supports automatic labeling of clusters. Atlas builders gain a shared reference instead of reprocessing the literature study by study.
europmc-pmc6459836:
Rogers and co-authors show that gasdermin proteins, known for punching holes in the cell surface during pyroptosis, also poke holes in mitochondria and so amplify apoptosis. When caspase-3 cuts gasdermin E, the freed piece homes to the membranes of the power plants and lets cytochrome c escape. That escape triggers the complex that fully switches caspase-3 on.

Cells lacking gasdermin E let out less cytochrome c and switched caspase-3 on weakly under both inner and outer death signals. They also grew faster in culture and in a mouse melanoma model. Gasdermin D did the same trick at mitochondria. A single change at threonine 6, one that acts like a phosphate tag, shut pore formation off, hinting at a natural off-switch.
europmc-pmc6506336:
Kucab and co-authors build a reference set of mutation patterns left by environmental agents, writing in Cell. Tumors carry distinct mutation patterns that hint at what caused them, but proof needs a clean test. The team exposed human stem cells to 79 known or suspected cancer-causing agents, then read the whole genomes of 324 cell lines.

Forty-one agents left clear substitution signatures, and some matched patterns seen in real human tumors. Six agents left double-substitution marks, and eight left small insertions or deletions. Repair systems in the cells stayed fully at work, and one agent could still yield a spread of outcomes through rival repair routes. The compendium gives researchers a lab-made yardstick for judging which agents help drive human cancers.
europmc-pmc6511336:
Weinkove and co-authors review costimulatory domains in chimeric antigen receptor design. Their review appeared in Clinical & Translational Immunology. CAR T cells need costimulatory signals to expand and persist. Designers build those signals into the receptor itself. They borrow domains from molecules such as CD28 or 4-1BB.

Choice and position of a domain shape how the cells behave. Clinical work on anti-CD19 CAR T cells hints at distinct effects. Domains differ in cell kinetics, killing power and safety. The authors compare set domains such as ICOS, OX40 and CD27. They also weigh pairs of domains. Clear winners may depend on the construct and the disease.
europmc-pmc6566436:
Ruan and co-authors review the jasmonic acid signaling pathway, the alarm system plants use against attack and stress, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Jasmonates are fatty-acid-derived hormones. They steer growth and development in calm times, and switch the plant to defense when insects chew, wounds open or pathogens invade.

The review follows the signal end to end. Damage peptides such as tomato systemin and Arabidopsis AtPEP1 trigger jasmonate synthesis; the hormone then travels cell to cell, through the vascular system, and even by air between plants. Receptors catch it, transcription factors relay it, and defense genes switch on. The authors assemble this chain as the shared logic behind plant resistance.
europmc-pmc6573036:
Vianello and co-authors measure what a person actually breathes indoors using a breathing thermal manikin, writing in Scientific Reports. Food and drink dominate microplastic exposure research; air has been neglected. Their manikin inhaled apartment air in three homes while the team counted and identified particles by infrared imaging, down to sizes near a hundredth of a millimeter.

Every sample held microplastics, at roughly 2 to 16 particles per cubic metre of air. True synthetics were only about 4% of all particles caught — most were protein and cellulose — but polyester ruled among the plastics, and plastic particles ran smaller than natural ones. Small enough to inhale, they mark indoor air as a direct exposure route.
europmc-pmc6582336:
Tonkin-Hill and co-authors present fastbaps, a fast Bayesian tool for sorting genomes into population clusters, writing in Nucleic Acids Research. Model-based clustering gives probabilities and honest uncertainty, but full Bayesian methods choke on modern dataset sizes. Their method approximates a Dirichlet process mixture model, letting the data itself decide how many clusters exist, and adds a way to split an existing family tree into clades by model fit.

The payoff is scale: datasets ten to a hundred times larger than rival model-based tools can handle. The authors prove it on an alignment of over 110,000 HIV-1 pol sequences, a workload previously out of reach. On simulated and real bacterial and viral data, accuracy matched or beat slower methods. The R package is open source.
europmc-pmc6598536:
Mohamed and co-authors review immune reactions against PEGylated liposomes. Their review appears in Science and Technology of Advanced Materials. Coating drug carriers with polyethylene glycol should hide them. The coating extends circulation and protects the payload. Yet the immune system often notices anyway. Repeat doses can trigger fast clearance from the blood. That effect is called accelerated blood clearance. It stems from antibodies raised against the carrier.

Another reaction is a pseudoallergy at infusion time. Complement activation drives the flushing and breathing symptoms. The review explains both reactions in toxicology terms. It lists factors that raise or lower the risk. The authors urge immune screening before clinical use. Such checks could make PEGylated drugs safer overall.
europmc-pmc6624636:
Zhai and co-authors test two strains of a gut bacterium against chronic colitis in mice. Their research article appears in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. The bacterium, Akkermansia muciniphila, lives on mucin in the gut. Its type strain has eased obesity and diabetes in animal studies. Whether it helps bowel inflammation was unknown.

The team compared the type strain with a mouse isolate, strain 139. Both strains cut IL-8 output in cultured gut cells. In mice with DSS-driven colitis, both eased colon damage. They lowered TNF-α and IFN-γ levels in the colon. The type strain worked more strongly than strain 139. Only it shrank spleen weight and raised short-chain fatty acids. It also boosted regulatory T-cell formation. Both strains nudged the gut microbiota back toward normal.
europmc-pmc6659036:
Xia and co-authors review T cell dysfunction in cancer immunity and immunotherapy. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Persistent antigen exposure wears T cells down. Dysfunctional cells proliferate poorly and kill weakly. They also carry many inhibitory receptors at once. PD-1, CTLA-4, Tim-3, and LAG-3 mark the state. The tumour microenvironment layers on further inhibitory signals. Different tumours produce distinct dysfunction states. Exhaustion differs from anergy and senescence.

Reactivating these cells has produced real patient gains. Checkpoint blockade against PD-1 or PD-L1 leads the way. Responses often fade, though, as other receptors persist. The review maps hallmarks of the dysfunction. It closes by linking those traits to therapy design.
europmc-pmc6675736:
Battle and co-authors map the global burden of Plasmodium vivax malaria from 2000 to 2017. Their modelling study appears in The Lancet. Vivax is the most widespread malaria species. Its burden had never been mapped at fine scale. The team adjusted routine surveillance data for known biases. Bayesian geospatial models predicted incidence and prevalence. African estimates leaned on falciparum surfaces and ratios. The maps feed the Global Burden of Disease 2017 study.

Global cases fell by 41.6 percent over the period. They dropped from 24.5 million to 14.3 million. The Americas cut cases by over half. South-East Asia and the Western Pacific matched that pace. Europe reached zero cases entirely. Declines stalled recently in many countries, though.
europmc-pmc6694136:
Deelen and co-authors pool genome-wide studies to identify longevity genes. Their analysis appears in Nature Communications. Longevity is heritable, yet gene hunts mostly failed. The team applied a strict phenotype definition. Survival cut-offs came from country life tables. Sex and birth cohort were matched with care. Cases numbered 11,262 past the 90th percentile. The top one percent set held 3,484 cases. Controls totalled 25,483 across twenty cohorts.

APOE dominated the results as expected. The ε4 variant lowered survival odds. The ε2 variant raised them instead. A locus near GPR78 also reached significance. It lowered odds of reaching that age. Gene-level analysis implicated tissue-specific expression. Long life shared genetic roots with health traits.
europmc-pmc6731336:
Palmer and co-authors review cellular senescence as a shared root of aging and diabetes. Senescent cells are worn cells that stop dividing but linger in tissue. They build up with age, obesity, and diabetes. Such cells have been tied directly to insulin resistance, the core flaw of type 2 diabetes.

Senescent cells release signals that inflame tissue and block new fat cell formation. The review surveys their role in the tissues that matter for diabetes. It then covers senolytics, drugs that clear senescent cells, which have entered clinical trials. Clearing these cells might ease several age-linked conditions at once. The authors weigh the early evidence for diabetes care.
europmc-pmc6787836:
Lee and co-authors review nanoparticles for treating infections from multidrug-resistant organisms. Such infections are rising worldwide and often leave few antibiotic options. Nanoparticles attack bacteria in unusual ways. They can slip through cell membranes and disrupt key molecular pathways. Paired with standard antibiotics, they may act in synergy and slow the resistance crisis.

The review classifies nanoparticles that killed resistant organisms in lab tests. The targets include the notorious ESKAPE pathogens, six species behind many hospital infections. How nanoparticles move through the body, and how bacteria might resist them, also get attention. Dose realism is a flagged problem: cell-killing doses in dishes often exceed anything people could take.
europmc-pmc6801136:
Zhang and co-authors assess Akkermansia muciniphila as a promising probiotic. This bacterium lives in the gut's mucus layer. It has been tied to better metabolic function and immune responses. It may also modify how cancer treatment works. Most research so far, though, shows correlation with disease rather than proven cause.

Intervention studies are few and mostly in animals. Human safety and efficacy data remain limited. The review covers the bacterium's traits and safety profile. It weighs its causal links to metabolic disorders, immune diseases, and cancer therapy. Some metagenomic studies found no link at all, a caution the authors note. A critical foundation is needed before it can be declared a beneficial microbe.
europmc-pmc6834636:
Johnson and co-authors test a workhorse method of microbiology, in Nature Communications. For decades, scientists have sorted bacteria by reading the 16S rRNA gene. Cheap machines read only short pieces of it. Newer platforms can read the whole gene, about 1,500 letters long. The team asked how much sorting power that buys.

Computer checks and real sequencing agreed on the answer. Short reads from part of the gene cannot separate close species and strains. Full-length reads, by contrast, resolved single-letter differences between strains. Errors in inserted or missing letters remained a limit. The authors give practical guidance on when each approach is enough.
europmc-pmc6893436:
Uusitupa and co-authors review lifestyle prevention of type 2 diabetes, in the journal Nutrients. Diabetes prevention is a worldwide challenge, and diet sits at its centre. The authors synthesised trial evidence to update European nutrition guidelines. They reviewed randomised trials in people with impaired glucose tolerance, the stage before diabetes, plus one trial in broader metabolic disorder.

Seven trials in all tested whether lifestyle change prevents the disease. Weight loss through a healthier diet, lower in saturated fat and rich in vegetables, fruit, and whole grains, helped, especially with added physical activity. Regular breakfast and less snacking also looked protective in the wider evidence. The review then asks which diet quality is best, and whether prevention also cuts later complications.
europmc-pmc6919336:
Guthold and co-authors pool global data on teen physical activity. Their study appeared in The Lancet Child and Adolescent Health. They combined 298 population-based surveys. The surveys covered 1.6 million students aged 11 to 17. Data came from 146 countries, from 2001 to 2016.

The team report that most teens move too little. In 2016, 81 percent were insufficiently active. The rate was 77.6 percent for boys. For girls it was 84.7 percent. Boys improved slightly over the period. Girls showed no clear change. The authors urge urgent scale-up of known policies. Their benchmark is the WHO target of a 15 percent cut by 2030.
europmc-pmc6954236:
D'Hulst and co-authors find an oxygen sensor that guards muscle-building machinery by an unexpected route. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The protein complex mTORC1 controls muscle mass. How oxygen and nutrients tune it was not fully clear. The oxygen sensor PHD1 drew their attention.

Mice lacking PHD1 had smaller muscles. Their mTORC1 responded weakly to leucine, a key amino acid signal, but normally to growth factors and contractions. Surprisingly, PHD1's usual chemical activity was not the point. Instead, PHD1 binds and stabilizes LRS, the cell's leucine sensor, shielding it from breakdown. That protection strengthens during oxygen and amino acid shortage. Older human muscle showed lower PHD1 levels and weaker LRS activity, hinting at a role in age-related muscle loss.
europmc-pmc7036236:
Yan and co-authors present a systematic review and meta-analysis in Critical Care. They pool global data on survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. All patients in the studies received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR. Survival after such arrests is known to be poor, but estimates vary by place.

The team searched three databases and kept 141 studies. Pooled survival to hospital discharge was 8.8 percent, they report. One-year survival was 7.7 percent. Chances were better when a bystander saw the arrest or gave CPR. Rates were also higher in Europe and North America. Survival rose over the study period, the authors find. They link the gains to wider bystander CPR.
europmc-pmc7058536:
Rodriguez-Martin and co-authors study jumping genes in cancer in Nature Genetics. About half of all cancers carry somatic insertions of retrotransposons, mobile DNA bits that copy themselves into new sites. Their role in causing cancer was unclear. The team analysed retrotransposition patterns across the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes resource to find out.

They catalogued 19,166 somatic retrotransposition events in 2,954 cancer genomes from 38 subtypes, affecting 35 percent of samples. Insertions of the LINE-1 element were the most frequent structural change of any kind in oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and second in head-and-neck and colorectal cancers. Rogue insertions can delete megabase-scale chromosome regions, sometimes removing tumour-suppressor genes, trigger complex translocations and duplications, and start cycles that amplify oncogenes to high levels. The study establishes retrotransposition as a real force reshaping cancer genomes, with consequences for how tumours develop.
europmc-pmc7080536:
Pang and co-authors build a smart wound dressing in Advanced Science. Infection is the most frequent wound complication and a major clinical headache. Ordinary dressings leave healing as a black box: nobody sees infection starting until it declares itself. The team designed a dressing that watches the wound and treats infection on demand.

The dressing has two layers. The upper layer is flexible electronics sealed in silicone, carrying a temperature sensor and ultraviolet light-emitting diodes. The lower layer is an antibacterial hydrogel that releases its drug when ultraviolet light hits it. Wound temperature, a sign of early infection, is monitored live; when needed, the diodes switch on and free the antibiotic in place. Animal experiments showed the system detecting bacterial infection and treating it effectively, with good flexibility and durability.
