The authors offer the design as a proof of concept for monitored, responsive wound care.
europmc-pmc7098036:
Yang and co-authors review traditional Chinese medicine in the treatment of COVID-19, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. At the time of writing, no specific antiviral drug or vaccine existed for the new disease. The authors report that more than 85% of infected patients in China were receiving traditional Chinese medicine alongside standard care.

Because SARS-CoV-2 closely resembles SARS-CoV in spread, genetics, and disease course, the review first weighs the evidence gathered when these methods were used against SARS. It then covers current use in COVID-19 and lab studies of natural compounds that act against coronaviruses. The authors note that many earlier trials were poorly designed, so stronger controlled studies are needed.
europmc-pmc7201936:
Richardson and co-authors use genetics to separate the effects of childhood and adult body size on disease. Their study appeared in The BMJ. It drew on 453,169 UK Biobank participants and large genome studies totaling over 700,000 people. Genetic variants served as stand-ins for body size at different ages. Adult body mass index was measured, while childhood size was self-reported at age 10.

The outcomes covered heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and breast and prostate cancer. The method tests whether early size matters on its own. Or whether it acts only through adult size. Results linked early body size to earlier puberty timing as well. The study shows how genetic tools can untangle life-course causes. Such answers shape when prevention should begin.
europmc-pmc7206536:
Chen and co-authors test two immune checkpoint drugs together in advanced colorectal cancer. Their trial report appeared in JAMA Oncology. Patients had cancer that no longer answered standard treatment. The Canadian Cancer Trials Group CO.26 study randomized 180 patients. Two thirds received durvalumab plus tremelimumab with supportive care. The rest received supportive care alone.

Median survival was 6.6 months with the drug pair versus 4.1 months without. Blood tests for tumor mutation burden refined the picture. Patients with 28 or more variants per megabase gained the most benefit. Most colorectal tumors resist checkpoint drugs, so any gain matters. The results suggest a biomarker can pick out likely responders. The authors support further study of the combination in that group.
europmc-pmc7230636:
Borges do Nascimento and co-authors carry out a scoping review and meta-analysis of early COVID-19 evidence. Their article appeared in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Research on the new virus was piling up without any synthesis. The team searched five major databases for studies through February 24, 2020. Two reviewers independently selected studies and judged bias.

They combined clinical, lab, and chest imaging data across studies. In the lab findings alone, 56 studies covered 58,663 patients. Nearly all confirmed infection by real-time PCR testing. Imaging signs in the lungs marked the severe end of the disease. The synthesis gave clinicians an early pooled picture. It also showed how thin parts of the evidence still were. Later reviews built on this first broad map.
europmc-pmc7243036:
Docherty and co-authors describe the first 20,133 UK hospital patients with COVID-19. Their cohort study appeared in The BMJ. Patients were enrolled at 208 acute care hospitals during the first wave's growth phase. Data followed a shared international protocol for emerging infections. The team recorded symptoms, existing conditions, and outcomes in near real time.

The analysis also explored which factors tracked with dying in hospital. Age and chronic illnesses weighed heavily in such cohorts. A small share of patients had been admitted for other reasons and caught the virus inside. The authors kept them in, judging their effect small as numbers grew. The report became a reference portrait of the disease in Britain. It showed planners who filled the wards and who fared worst.
europmc-pmc7395236:
Paltiel and co-authors model how United States colleges could reopen safely in fall 2020, in JAMA Network Open. Residential campuses pack young adults into dorms and dining halls, a recipe for outbreaks. Their model follows a hypothetical campus of 4,990 uninfected students plus 10 with undetected silent infections.

Symptom-based screening alone could not contain spread, since silent cases seed chains before anyone feels ill. Screening every student every 2 days, even with a test of modest sensitivity but high accuracy on negatives, kept outbreaks manageable at a defensible cost. Isolation dorm space and constant prevention discipline were also required. The paper gave administrators a concrete, if demanding, price for reopening.
europmc-pmc7454936:
Duchene and co-authors ask when SARS-CoV-2 genome data became strong enough for firm family-tree claims. Huge genome sets appeared in near real time, a first for an outbreak. Early data showed little variation, which raised doubts about their power.

The team gathered public genome sets at eight time points. They ran tests for temporal signal, the clock-like buildup of changes. By February 2, 2020, rate and time-scale estimates had become possible. Later sets, with between 47 and 122 genomes, settled on a shared rate. Their origin estimate fell near late November 2019. The authors give steps to check this threshold in future outbreaks. Passing it marks when early genome data can truly guide response.
europmc-pmc7464436:
Primorac and co-authors review knee osteoarthritis, its causes, and care without surgery. It is the most common progressive joint condition. Among adults aged 60 years or more, rates reach about 10% in men and 13% in women.

The disease is not mere cartilage wear from load. It affects all joint tissues, with changes in shape, metabolism, and function. Signals from cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and fat hormones drive the shifts. Blood and joint measures of these signals may mark disease stage. Gene-control marks add a further layer. Care without surgery aims to slow the course and delay joint replacement. Options include platelet-rich plasma and cell-based treatments. Gene therapy may join them in time.
europmc-pmc7591536:
Yee and co-authors show that neutrophils drive ferroptosis in glioblastoma tumor necrosis. Dead tissue in tumors predicts poor outcomes for patients. Its cause was thought to be chronic low blood flow.

In a mouse model, neutrophils matched necrosis in time and place. Removing neutrophils reduced necrosis in the tumors. Neutrophils from brain tumors killed cultured tumor cells. They passed myeloperoxidase granules into those tumor cells. That transfer caused iron-linked fat peroxide buildup inside. Blocking myeloperoxidase cut the killing effect sharply. Human tumor data linked neutrophils and ferroptosis to necrosis. They also linked both to poorer patient survival.
europmc-pmc7604136:
Walls and co-authors design protein nanoparticle vaccines for SARS-CoV-2 that raise strong antibodies in mice. A safe and scalable vaccine was needed to halt spread. Their design uses structure-based methods for the antigen.

Each nanoparticle displays 60 spike receptor-binding domains. They sit in a highly immunogenic array on the surface. Neutralizing antibody levels rose 10-fold above a spike vaccine. That gain came despite a 5-fold lower dose. Antibodies targeted several distinct sites on the antigen. That spread may guard against escape mutations. Binding to neutralizing ratios looked favorable versus patient sera. Yield and stability suggest large-scale making is feasible. Production work toward clinical use had begun.
europmc-pmc7613836:
The SGLT2 inhibitor Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists' Consortium tests whether diabetes changes kidney benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors. Large trials had shown kidney and heart gains from these drugs. No trial was built to split results by diabetes status.

The review found 13 trials with 90,413 participants. After exclusions, 90,409 participants entered the analysis. Of those, 82.7% had diabetes, almost all type 2. The drugs cut kidney disease progression risk by 37%. The relative risk was 0.63 versus placebo overall. Gains were alike with and without diabetes present. Acute kidney injury risk fell by 23% as well. Results held across primary kidney diagnoses in chronic disease trials.
europmc-pmc7683736:
Norat and co-authors review faulty cell power plants in brain disease, plus a bold fix. Mitochondria make the energy neurons need to fire and send signals. Their failure shows up in Alzheimer, Parkinson, and Huntington diseases, and in stroke. Damage leaks membranes and can trigger cell death.

The review sums up the paths by which broken mitochondria drive disease forward. It then turns to transplantation: moving healthy mitochondria into damaged tissue. Early work hints this may restore energy and spare cells. The authors weigh what must be solved before such grafts can serve as real therapy for brain disorders.
europmc-pmc7775736:
Hou and co-authors compare the D614G variant of SARS-CoV-2 with the original form. The variant, a single spike change, has largely replaced the ancestral virus. The team tested both forms in human airway cells and in animal models. They asked if the variant infects better, spreads better, or harms more.

The variant grew to higher levels in upper-airway cells than the old form. Animal tests showed better transmission as well. Signs of worse disease were modest at most. The variant was also more open to neutralizing antibodies. Vaccine candidates in development kept their power against it. The authors read this as evolution for spread, not for severity.
europmc-pmc7778936:
Ghoussaini and co-authors describe Open Targets Genetics, a free online resource that links human genetic variants to the genes they most likely affect. It pulls together genome-wide association study results with functional genomics data. Those data cover gene expression, protein levels, and chromatin contacts across many cell types and tissues.

Users can search the portal by variant, gene, or trait. Tools help rank likely causal variants and genes at disease-linked loci. The resource also offers colocalization analysis across 92 cell types and tissues. Charts such as regional plots and PheWAS plots let users inspect signals in depth. All data are open for bulk download, and a GraphQL API gives programmatic access. The team presents the portal as an aid for finding new drug targets.
europmc-pmc7790836:
Yang and co-authors review drug discovery aimed at G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs. This receptor family is among the most successful drug targets known. Drug design for GPCRs moved from random screening to knowledge-driven work. New insight into receptor structure sped that shift.

The authors give a broad account of the field. They trace how structure and function knowledge guides new drugs. Recent progress is covered in depth. The piece is written for a wide readership in drug discovery. It shows how basic receptor science turns into medicines at a fast pace.
europmc-pmc7858636:
Foley and co-authors present HyPrColoc, a fast method to find shared genetic risk across traits. Genome studies have flagged thousands of disease-linked zones. Which genes and paths sit behind them is the hard part. Colocalization tests whether traits share one cause.

The new method handles many traits at once. One hundred traits can be checked jointly in about 1 second. The team ran it on coronary heart disease and fourteen related traits. They found 43 zones where heart disease shared a cause with another trait. Five zones were new for heart disease. Gene and protein data then named likely causal genes. The tool is offered for wide use in genetics.
europmc-pmc7898236:
Li and co-authors present a review of DNA repair pathways in cancer treatment and resistance. Cells fix DNA damage from inside and outside sources to keep their genes stable. When repair systems go wrong, cancer can start and grow. The review links that biology to how treatment succeeds or fails.

Radiation and many cancer drugs kill cells by damaging DNA. Tumours with faulty damage responses may be extra sensitive to such drugs. Others use repair to resist them. The authors explain the main repair routes and how each is controlled. They argue that blocking repair could make standard treatments hit harder. Inhibitors of repair in both the nucleus and mitochondria are a focus. The review aims to guide new drug design built on this idea.
europmc-pmc7921936:
Niculescu and co-authors present a review of microfluidic devices, covering how they are made and where they are used. Microfluidics handles tiny flows of liquid inside chips with channels at the microscale. The field blends physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science. Such chips can run lab steps in miniature, at low cost and volume.

The review surveys the materials used to build these platforms. It then compares the fabrication methods that shape channels and chambers to a set design. Biomedical uses take centre stage. The chips can prepare nanoparticles and load drugs into carriers. They can also aim drugs at targets, analyse cells, support diagnosis, and grow cell cultures. The authors weigh the strengths of each route. Readers get a full tour of a young but fast-spreading technology.
europmc-pmc7922036:
Gunti and co-authors present a review of organoid and spheroid tumour models. Both models grow cancer cells in three dimensions, closer to real tissue than flat cultures. They differ in their cell sources and in how they are set up. Grown from a patient's tumour, they keep many traits of the original growth.

Spheroids are simpler in structure and popular for drug screening. Organoids match the source tumour in both form and genetics. They can be kept alive long term and frozen in biobanks. Testing chemo-, radio-, and immunotherapies on them may predict how the patient will respond. Chip versions add flow and tissue-to-tissue contact for a closer match to the body. The review compares the models' methods and latest uses. It frames them as a bridge between flat cultures and animal work.
europmc-pmc7946236:
Gibbon presents an address on Samuel D. Gross, the great American surgeon. The address was made before the medical history section of the College of Physicians of Philadelphia on January 19, 1926. No full picture of Gross could fit the space, Gibbon admits. His writings, honours, posts, and societies alone would fill it. He chooses instead a few sides of a full and fruitful life.

Gross shaped the surgery and surgeons of his day more than any rival, Gibbon argues. His influence ran on into later generations. The sources of that power were industry, honesty, and love of his work and his fellow men. Those traits won him respect across the surgical world and love from all who met him. Readers who want dates are sent to Gross's own autobiography. The address is a tribute shaped to stir young doctors.
europmc-pmc8037236:
Munteanu and Apetrei compare the main tests used to measure antioxidant activity. Antioxidants matter from food engineering to medicine, so measuring them well matters too. The authors sort assays by how they work. Some track a transferred hydrogen atom. Others track a single electron. A third group mixes both routes.

Hydrogen-transfer tests include ORAC, HORAC, TRAP, and TOSC. Electron-transfer tests include CUPRAC, FRAP, and the Folin–Ciocalteu method. ABTS and DPPH anchor the mixed group. For each test, the authors give the detection mechanism and best uses. Strengths and weaknesses get plain treatment. Most assays rely on color changes watched by spectrophotometry. The review adds electrochemical sensors as a complement. Paired together, the methods clarify how antioxidants actually work.
europmc-pmc8110536:
Ren and co-authors show that electron spin can speed the oxygen side of water splitting. Splitting water stalls at the oxygen evolution reaction. That step moves four electrons and must make triplet oxygen from singlet feedstocks. Spin rules quietly tax every turn of the cycle. The team used ordered ferromagnetic catalysts as spin filters. A steady magnetic field held the filter in line during tests.

With spin selection active, the reaction ran faster. Non-ferromagnetic catalysts gained nothing from the same field. The authors pin the key moment to the first electron transfer. There, spin swaps coherently between catalyst and bound oxygen. Later steps inherit that fixed spin direction by rule. Hund's rule and the Pauli principle then steer the rest. Triplet oxygen emerges as the natural product. The work hands catalyst designers a new dial. Magnetism joins composition and shape on the bench.
europmc-pmc8189436:
Yanagida and co-authors build a human embryo model from naive stem cells. Human naive pluripotent cells can form the early lineages of the embryo. A brief induction step starts the process.

Within 3 days, the cells self-organised into blastocyst-like structures, called blastoids. Each blastoid held three tissue layers with the right lineage markers. Single-cell gene data matched the natural blastocyst closely. The system is scalable and repeatable. It gives researchers a model for early human development that avoids use of real embryos. Limits of the model are part of the discussion.
europmc-pmc8294036:
Kartikasari and co-authors assess tumour-driven cytokines and devices that detect them for cancer care. The tumour setting breeds chronic inflammation. That state secretes varied cytokines at each cancer stage.

Some cytokines slow tumours, while others help them grow. They act in self and neighbour loops and track with poor outcomes. Because they reach the blood, they may serve as biomarkers. Devices that read them could detect cancer earlier. They could also forecast outcomes and guide therapy. The review weighs the biology and the sensor technology together. Circulating cytokines are the practical target for such devices.
europmc-pmc8527836:
Scheiblich and co-authors show how microglia share the work of clearing alpha-synuclein clumps. These brain immune cells react to misfolded proteins and spark inflammation. Clumps of alpha-synuclein drive Parkinson disease and related disorders. How microglia cope with that load was the question.

Microglia laced into networks through tiny tunnels built of actin. Overloaded cells passed fibrils to fresh neighbors through these links. The cargo was then broken down fast and well. Sharing the load calmed inflammation and helped cells survive. A Parkinson-linked gene mutation broke this strategy. Tests in tissue slices and patient samples confirmed the transfer happens in real brains.
europmc-pmc8898236:
Castiglione and co-authors review blood biomarkers for diagnosing and managing heart failure. Heart failure affects about 64 million people worldwide. Blood tests that mirror the disease's pathways can help clinicians. Natriuretic peptides lead the field. The heart releases them under pressure or volume strain. Their roles in diagnosis and risk sorting are well proven. Newer uses include screening and starting treatment early.

The authors judge other markers against that standard. High-sensitivity troponins and soluble ST2 look most promising. They add risk information beyond the peptides. Galectin-3 and growth differentiation factor 15 follow. Kidney markers matter because the organs fail together. Multi-marker scores may sharpen decisions. Genomic and metabolomic profiling close the survey. The authors weigh guidance value honestly. Peptides as therapy guides still lack firm proof.
europmc-pmc8949236:
Chen and co-authors review cholinergic signaling and its place in Alzheimer's disease. Acetylcholine carries signals for memory and learning. Its loss is the oldest theory of Alzheimer's. Cholinergic neurons waste away as the disease advances. Cognition declines in step. The review connects that signaling system to other risk factors. Faulty cholinergic tone may drive tau changes. It may also feed inflammation and cell death.

The authors first explain the system's normal jobs. They then tie it to the disease's pathology. Plaques, tangles, and synapse loss enter the story. Treatment coverage is current and detailed. Existing cholinergic drugs are weighed honestly. New candidate drugs and strategies follow. No cure exists yet, the authors stress. Their aim is a clear map of one therapeutic road. It remains the road most current drugs travel.
europmc-pmc9180936:
Teleanu and co-authors describe neurotransmitters as key factors in brain disorders of the central nervous system. These molecules amplify, transmit, and convert signals between cells. Hundreds have been found over the past century. They shape emotions, thoughts, memory, learning, and movement.

The review sorts transmitters into canonical and noncanonical groups. Canonical ones include amino acids, monoamines, and acetylcholine. Noncanonical ones include exosomes, steroids, and D-aspartic acid. The authors link disturbed transmitter balance to many neurological and degenerative diseases. New detection methods are briefly covered as well. The closing section weighs ways to restore balance by modulating these substances.
europmc-pmc9221336:
Nassir reviews nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, covering its mechanisms, treatments, and biomarkers. The disease, now also called metabolic-associated fatty liver disease, is among the most common liver disorders worldwide. It grows in parallel with obesity. No drug is approved to treat it directly.

Fat buildup in the liver can progress to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and liver cancer. The review discusses sirtuins as possible treatment targets. It also sums up current diagnostic tools and their limits. Non-coding RNAs are presented as emerging markers for early detection. The author stresses that cheap, accurate, non-invasive tests are crucial. Such tools would speed trials and help validate new treatments.
europmc-pmc9422136:
Li and co-authors survey recent treatment advances for triple-negative breast cancer. This subtype lacks the three receptors that guide care in other breast cancers. It is the most aggressive form and has a poor outlook. Standard care rests on surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation.

The review sorts new options by molecular subtype. Targeted drugs act on DNA repair faults and kinase pathways. Androgen receptor blockers are covered for the subtype that bears that receptor. Cell cycle drugs and agents that cut tumor blood supply also appear. Immunotherapy has raised survival and response in some patients, the authors note. Combo plans that pair these routes are a main theme. The field still lacks options for patients who miss the surgical window.
europmc-pmc9516236:
Jia and co-authors compare techniques for isolating small extracellular vesicles and their clinical uses. These tiny vesicles carry messages between cells. They also look strong as a drug delivery platform. Their mixed sizes and traits are still poorly mapped. That gap slows clinical work.

The review sorts isolation methods by how they work. Ultracentrifugation and size exclusion chromatography are standard routes. Precipitation, ultrafiltration, and immunoaffinity capture follow. Newer options use microfluidics and charge based steps. Each method is weighed on yield, purity, and ease of use. Open questions about the vesicles themselves get a full airing. Storage, dose, and delivery rules lack standards so far. A final part surveys disease diagnosis and treatment uses. Ongoing clinical trials are listed for the reader.
europmc-pmc9829236:
Guo and co-authors review how brain stimulation therapies calm neuroinflammation in anxiety and depression. Mood disorders travel with raised inflammation in the body. Symptom relief often comes with inflammation settling down. Brain stimulation is used when standard care falls short.

Results vary by person, with no firm guide for choices. The review gathers human and animal studies on the theme. It maps inflammation across the circuits tied to both disorders. Seven stimulation methods are then examined one by one. Magnetic and electric stimulation open the method list. Shock therapy, light, and ultrasound methods follow. Deep brain and vagus nerve stimulation complete the set. All were reported to dampen brain inflammation signals. Pro-inflammatory factor release fell under these treatments. The authors propose inflammation marks as treatment guides. Such marks could help match patients to methods.
europmc-pmc9977836:
Long and co-authors present GraphST, a method for spatial transcriptomics analysis. Spatial methods record gene activity with location kept intact. Three tasks dominate: spatial clustering, multi-sample integration, and cell-type deconvolution. GraphST tackles all three in one framework.

The method joins graph neural networks with self-supervised contrastive learning. It pulls nearby spots closer in its learned space and pushes distant ones apart. Tests spanned several tissue types and technology platforms. Clustering accuracy rose by 10 percent over rival methods. Brain and embryo structures were drawn in finer detail. GraphST alone could join multiple slices while fixing batch effects. It also read cell mixes in lymph node and tumor niches well.
expose-et-examen-critique-du-systeme-phr:
Cerise's Exposé et examen critique du système phrénologique tests phrenology on its own terms. Laurent Alexis Philibert Cerise was a Paris doctor. The title page is dated November 1836 and names the publisher Trinquart. A letter to students of the Paris medical school precedes the work.

The title promises a study in four parts: principles, method, theory, and consequences. Cerise examines the system that read character from the skull in each of those frames. His motto is a line from Saint Paul on many gifts and one spirit. The copy later passed through Yale collections, its stamps show. The book is a medical man's measured critique of a popular science. It belongs to the early debate over phrenology's claims.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-10-of: Part 10 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone holds pages the text layer cannot carry. The sampled leaves are handwriting and faint print, broken into stray letters and marks. No name, date, or claim can be pulled from them with trust. The part sits in a vast case record on the Chicago gang leader, kept in thirty-six parts. It must be read on the page image, not from the text here. Its content is not described, because it cannot be read.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-11-of: A section cover opens part 11 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone. The cover marks the set as part 4 of 11 within bureau file 62-39128. Past it sits a routing slip from 1935, sending the file through named staff in Washington. The body, in the text layer, is a narrative in broken type. It tells of a man judged too old for a job he was offered. Names and places do not come through clean. The part is best cited for its frame.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-12-of: Part 12 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone is, in the text layer, lost. Head and middle samples alike are strings of broken marks and split words. No report, letter, or clipping in the part can be picked out with trust. The file around it is the bureau's great Capone record, built over his rise and his prison terms. This part's pages may read clear on their images. From the text that survives here, nothing in them can be stated.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-13-of:
Prison paper opens part 13 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone. A letter from the Director of the Bureau of Prisons in Washington, dated in the fall of 1935, leads the sampled pages. It went to the head of the investigation bureau.

The letter passes on an agent's report. Its subject was a plot to bring goods that were banned into the federal prison at Atlanta, Georgia. Tied to the same matter was a manuscript said to be the story of Capone's life in that prison. The prisons chief hoped the bureau could learn who wrote it. Stamps on the pages date the file's moves to November 1935. The part shows Capone still a live file long after his trial, watched through the walls of his own prison.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-14-of: Handwritten pages fill part 14 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone, and the text layer fails them. Sample after sample comes through as blocks of broken signs, with no line whole enough to quote or sum up. The part sits inside one of the bureau's largest gang files, a record of Capone's career and cases kept across decades. What these leaves hold, a reader must get from the page images. From the text here, no claim about their content can be made, and none is.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-16-of:
A hoax played on a prisoner runs through part 16 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone. The sampled pages hold a typed tale, set down in a rough text layer, about letters Capone wrote in prison. The woman he wrote to, called Ruth in the tale, did not exist.

The tale says Capone had not told her, in the letters he thought he sent, that his love had ceased. When he learned the truth, his pride was cut. The text calls him a genius who had made millions and who saw the prison as a haven of rest. Now, it says, every man inside would learn of the trick, and he felt he must act or lose his reason. The part reads as a kept press or prison tale, filed with the case.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-17-of:
Part 17 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone opens with a section cover: part 5 of 11, bureau file 62-39128. The pages past the cover are rough in the text layer. One tale can be read in part, and it turns on a manuscript.

A man in the sampled text states that he knew nothing at all about a manuscript that had been put to a detective bureau for publication. The words around his denial are too broken to build on. Still, the theme fits the file at this point. More than one part of the Capone record deals with life stories of the gang leader. They were told or sold while he sat in prison. The part is a fragment, and is best used as one.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-18-of:
A letter from abroad sits in part 18 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone. The writer asks what Capone's release would mean to the plain man in America. He hopes for word on the events that led to the arrest, and for tales of the man's early life.

The ask is a working writer's one. He wants press clippings and photographs that English newspaper libraries would be unlikely to hold. He offers to have them copied and sent back within a few days. A signed story, he says, would carry more weight with such proof in hand. The part shows the Capone file used as a source far from Chicago: by the press of another country, as the gang leader's fame outlasted his power.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-19-of:
Press clippings in part 19 of 36 of the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone tell of the day he walked free. Reporters scanned each man who stepped from the train. At the prison's front gate, newsmen waited for the shot they had come for.

The clip says they missed him. An official named Hill had Capone brought to his office and handed him the papers of his release. Capone, the paper says, smiled a yard wide and gave a polite thank you. He left by a rear gate at the far end of the grounds and was sped away by car. The part keeps the press view of a release staged to cheat the press.
fbi-vault-al-capone-al-capone-part-2-of-: Part 2 of 36 in the Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Alphonse Capone is one of the file's large early parts. Its text layer, though, is broken past use. Head and middle samples come through as mixed marks and half-words, with no report or letter legible. The wider file is the bureau's record on the most famed gang leader of his era, from his Chicago years through his prison terms. This part's place in that record is plain. Its pages' content, from the text that survives, is not.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Withheld pages are the whole subject of release 36 of the Special Counsel Mueller investigation records, freed through the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Its deleted-page sheet counts 432 pages withheld in full. The grounds here are near uniform: page after page carries the pair b6 and b7C, the privacy marks. A block in the middle shifts to Referral or Consult, pages sent to another agency for judgment. No interview, memo, or finding is in the part. It is a list of what was kept, with the code for why.
frus-1861-d136:
On 6 July 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 136 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paired letters let Seward sort Paris business point by point. One file might hold law, the next a claim or a name. The second letter of 6 July shows the same neat hand at work in the French file as in the London one. Neat clerk work of this sort kept a vast record clear under wartime strain. A clear record is a gift to every later reader of a crowded year.
frus-1861-d236:
8 June 1861 is the date on a dispatch from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 236 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d36:
Thomas Corwin received a letter from William H. Seward on 6 April 1861, as he set out for Mexico. Corwin was the new American minister to Mexico. The letter is document 36 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mexico mattered to Washington for its long border with Texas and its own deep debts in Europe. Corwin, a famed speaker and former Treasury chief, carried weight in Mexico City. Seward's April letter sent him south with the war only days from its start. Corwin's fame as an orator made him a strong voice with the Mexican government of Benito Juárez.
frus-1862-d136:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 4 September 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 136 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d236:
Two Seward letters to William Stuart bear the date 11 September 1862, and the first is Document 236 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting head of the British legation in Washington that year.

By 11 September, Union and Confederate armies were closing on each other in Maryland, days from Antietam. Foreign policy waited on the result more openly than either side admitted. Seward's letters of that week kept the Department's business with the legation current. So that no small dispute could grow while the great question was decided by arms. The channel stayed open through the whole war, which was itself a kind of success.
frus-1862-d336:
On 20 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 336 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter came late in a heavy month of Paris mail.

Late October found the truce proposal stalled in London and France unwilling to act alone. Seward's letters in this stretch could afford a calmer tone than September's, though the danger was not past. This dispatch shows the Department working to convert a reprieve into a durable result, keeping pressure on Paris while tempers cooled. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d36:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 20 March 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 36 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d436:
Gabriel García Tassara sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. It appears as Document 436 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, out of strict date order in the printed Spanish file.

The printed volume groups letters by subject as well as by date, so Tassara's August note sits among the autumn papers. Its place in the file is a reminder that the Spanish correspondence ran on several tracks at once. Those tracks were Mexico, Cuba, and maritime rights. They also included the daily courtesies between two governments at peace. Reading the Tassara notes in sequence gives a clear view of how a resident minister worked, and how much of foreign policy was routine care.
frus-1862-d536:
On 19 June 1862 Roest van Limburg wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward, ten days after the first burst of Dutch notes. His letter is Document 536 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The mid-June note shows the Dutch business settling into its longer rhythm after the intense first week. Van Limburg continued to represent a government whose ships, colonies, and carrying trade gave it a permanent interest in American maritime practice. Seward's department dealt with The Hague on two tracks, through Pike abroad and Van Limburg at home. The letter belongs to the home track, where questions arrived in writing and were answered in kind, on the record.
frus-1862-d636:
On 8 May 1861 Townsend Harris addressed this dispatch from Japan to the Secretary of State, by then William H. Seward in the new Lincoln administration. It is Document 636 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Harris wrote a month after Fort Sumter, though no word of the war could yet have reached him. His subject was Japan. There he remained the solitary American minister. The address to the office rather than the man suits a dispatch sent across a change of government. His reports from Edo in 1861 describe a treaty system still fragile and a minister worn by isolation and ill health. The letter opens the Civil War-era Japanese file in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d136:
On 28 March 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 136 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A same-day Adams letter sits right after this one in the volume, so the pens crossed in print as they did at sea. Seward's second sheet of 28 March held its own head of the brief, as his pairs always did. Adams would read it ten days on, beside the news of the hour. The letter is a stitch in the tightest-woven part of the file, the spring of 1863.
frus-1863p1-d236:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 14 July 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 236 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d336:
On 10 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 336 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d36:
On 14 August 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to A. Dudley Mann. Benjamin ran the Confederate state office in Richmond; Mann was one of the South's first agents sent to win backing in Europe. The letter is document 36 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mann had roamed the courts of Europe since 1861, seeking a nod for the South's cause. Benjamin's letters kept such agents stocked with claims, facts, and hope. This one predates the others in its group, a look at the South's pitch in the summer of 1862. Printed in the Union's volume, it lets readers hear the other side in its own words.
frus-1863p1-d436:
Secretary William H. Seward wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 1 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d536:
Dated 27 May 1863, document 536 is a letter from F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d636:
Among the day's business on 8 October 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d136: Minister Kirk wrote to the Secretary of State from Cairo on November 17, 1943, five days before the conference opened in his city. The dispatch is Document 136 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Host-city reporting in the final days mixed politics with roofs, guards, and telephones, though this record names no topic. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the arrival run of papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d236:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure B, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Prime Minister Churchill at Cairo. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the short secret paper went directly to the President without Joint Chiefs of Staff approval.

Command questions head the list: the urgency of naming an overall commander, a commander for Overlord, a commander for the Mediterranean, and a unified strategic bomber command in Europe. Other items cover the Rankin plans for a German collapse. They also cover the American refusal to join operations in the eastern Mediterranean and Balkans, Soviet cooperation from bombing to Turkey and Sweden, and American facilities in the Azores.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d336:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a second secret priority telegram from Cairo on 27 November 1943, numbered 10065. It follows his longer report of the same day on the civil affairs talks.

McCloy says he has spoken with the Joint Chiefs and the British, and with Roosevelt, Winant, and Eden as well. If the British confirm the agreement set out in his telegram 10064, he feels the Americans will have gained all they set out to win on civil affairs. He adds a glimpse of the wider conference: though he stood only at the fringe of the strategy talks, every important decision was plainly being held up. All waited until the Eastern conference, at Tehran, reported back. He had been asked to stay on at Cairo pending the party's return.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d36: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 4, 1943, the same day he wrote to Stalin. The Churchill letter is Document 36 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired letters like these let the president keep both allies moving in the same week, a habit of his summit diplomacy. No topic is given in the record. The message can be read in the Foreign Relations volume, where the October papers thicken quickly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d436:
On December 3, 1943, the American and British chiefs of staff met in Cairo. They sat as the Combined Chiefs of Staff. That joint body ran the shared war effort of the two countries. The meeting came two days after the Tehran Conference ended. It came one day before the Second Cairo Conference opened. The State Department later printed the minutes in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Minutes of this kind record who attended the session. They note which plans were argued over. They also note what the chiefs settled. The chiefs then reported those points to Roosevelt and Churchill. Read beside later sessions, the record shows summit work in detail. Broad pledges made at Tehran became orders, dates, and forces. Commands could then act on them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d536:
Prime Minister Churchill opened the new year with a message to President Roosevelt on January 2, 1944. The two men had parted after the Cairo conferences in December, Churchill falling ill on his journey home. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

New Year messages between the leaders set the tone for the decisive year of the war in Europe. Their correspondence now had to turn Tehran and Cairo decisions into the Normandy invasion and the final campaigns. For readers, this letter stands at the hinge of the volume: the summit season behind, and the year of action ahead, in the words of the alliance's most tireless writer.
frus-1944-quebec-d136:
On September 8, 1944, Roosevelt sent Secretary of War Henry Stimson a short memorandum on Italy. It followed General O'Dwyer's report to the president that same day. The supply situation in Italy, Roosevelt wrote, was critical after years of Fascist and Nazi rule and the destruction of battles fought on Italian soil.

The order is direct and leaves no room for delay. The War Department was to take immediate action to make available the additional essential civilian supplies and shipping needed to remedy the condition. The memorandum is a clear example of a briefing paper turning, within hours, into a presidential instruction to a cabinet department.
frus-1944-quebec-d236:
Schoenfeld cabled from London on September 16, 1944, transmitting an appeal from Warsaw's Council of National Unity. Dated September 15 and addressed to Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, the appeal reached London through Premier Mikołajczyk. It was the forty-fifth day of the Warsaw struggle, and the first Soviet supply drop had just brought, in the council's words, great relief.

The council affirmed the inflexible will of Warsaw and Poland to fight to the end. It fervently appealed for continuous dropping of arms, ammunition, and food, for permanent air cover, and for bombing of German concentrations. The enemy was attacking with reinforced formations, and without quick, effective succor a catastrophe might follow. Mikołajczyk noted weather had recently impeded the American shuttle service and British flights from Italy.
frus-1944-quebec-d36:
The American minister in London, named Reed in the heading, wrote to Harry Hopkins on August 29, 1944. A message from an embassy officer straight to the President's aide shows how many side channels fed the White House that summer. It appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Late August was arrangement season: the Quebec Conference was a fortnight off, and London was both a partner capital and a staging post for the journey. Staff messages like Reed's handled the questions that could not wait for the leaders. For readers, the note shows the conference being prepared from the British end of the alliance's wiring.
frus-1945-50-intel-d136: A memorandum of conversation dated 16 April 1948 is the latest-dated paper in the intelligence volume. Memoranda of conversation record a talk between officials, who met, what each side said. What was left open. So that spoken words cannot later be denied. The title names neither party. So the record stands on its date and its place at the volume's end. By then the National Security Act of 1947 had replaced the old system with the Central Intelligence Agency.
frus-1945-50-intel-d236:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Director of the Bureau of the Budget (Webb) on 15 December 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 236, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d336:
A text titled "National Security Council Resolution" bears the date 13 January 1948. It survives in print as document 336 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

The form is stiff because it has to be: each line is a rule that a named office can be held to. For a reader, the gain is precision: this is the rule as the ruled were told to obey it. A formal resolution carries more weight than a memo, since it records a choice the Council itself made and stood behind.
frus-1945-50-intel-d36:
General Hull, the Army's assistant chief of staff for operations, wrote to Lovett on 28 October 1945. Hull had appeared in the Potsdam papers as well, a mark of his wide duties. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Operations and intelligence are the two hands of a general staff. Their chiefs had to agree on how the Army would gather and use secret information. Hull's letter to the air secretary crosses staff lines in a way that shows the question ripening inside the War Department. Readers can watch the Army sorting its own house in these autumn papers, before it faced the other departments across a table. Internal agreement came first; it was rarely easy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d136:
How much should Germany pay, and in what form? A briefing book paper of 16 January 1945, “Reparation and Restitution Policy Toward Germany,” gives the American answer prepared for Yalta. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Reparation, the paper warns, must never be let to wreck wider aims in Germany and Europe. It should take only the surplus above what a minimum German standard of living and prior charges require. Payment should be mostly in kind, over a short span, five years if possible and never more than ten. Labor services are allowed within reason, with a line drawn between active Nazis and passive Germans. Stolen property that can be traced must go back to its owners.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d236:
Moscow gave its side of the Iran oil quarrel in a letter of 28 December 1944 from Ambassador Gromyko. Addressed to the Secretary of State and received in translation, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers an American note of 1 November on the question of Iran.

In September, Gromyko writes, the Soviet government sent an official commission to Iran under Deputy Commissar Kavtaradze. Its task was to negotiate an oil concession in Iran's northern regions. The terms Moscow had in view, he insists, were very profitable and advantageous for Iran. In no degree did they infringe her sovereignty or independence. Prime Minister Saed at first declared his attitude favorable, and the commission began its early work on that basis.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d336:
Germany's treatment headed the plenary session at Yalta on February 5, 1945, and Bohlen's minutes open with Roosevelt framing the day. Political questions on Germany would come first, the President said. The leaders would not roam over the whole map of the world, to Dakar or Indochina. Zones of occupation came first.

Those zones, Roosevelt noted, had already been agreed in the European Advisory Commission. One point stayed open: France wanted a zone of its own and a seat in the control machinery for Germany. He stressed that zones concerned occupation only, not Germany's lasting fate. He then laid a map of the agreed zones on the table.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d36: Roosevelt also wrote to Churchill on 31 December 1944, giving the year two closing messages between them. His letter is document 36 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Paired with Churchill's note of the same date, it shows both leaders ending 1944 in active consultation, already looking toward their January departure for the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d436:
Nine subjects crowd Page's minutes of the foreign ministers' meeting of February 10, 1945. Eden presided. Poland's formula led, then the Declaration on Liberated Europe, Yugoslavia, and reparations. The conference communiqué and the world organization followed. Three frontier questions closed the list, with Iran behind them.

On Poland, Stettinius said the American experts and the President had studied the formula closely. The Americans were ready to withdraw the last sentence, which Molotov had objected to. In return, the President would stay free to make any statement he felt necessary, based on his ambassador's reports. Page records the deal being trimmed to fit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d136:
John Hickerson, acting director of European affairs, routed a small social invitation through Paris on July 11, 1945. His confidential telegram to Ambassador Caffery is document 136 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The message was meant for James Dunn, the assistant secretary traveling with the American delegation.

The British Embassy in Washington had word that Sir Alexander Cadogan, the Foreign Office's permanent head, would reach Terminal early on the afternoon of July 14. Cadogan hoped very much to have an informal talk with Dunn that day. Hickerson asks Caffery to pass the word along. Such quiet advance contacts between the two delegations' senior officials helped shape the conference before the leaders ever sat down together.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d236:
Under Secretary Grew recorded the Italian ambassador's call about declaring war on Japan in a memorandum dated July 6, 1945. The memo is document 236 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Tarchiani came that morning with a secret paper from his government.

The new Italian government had decided in a secret meeting to favor declaring war on Japan, Tarchiani said, and wanted the step approved before the Big Three meeting if possible. The United States favored the move, and Cadogan had said Britain would not object. The Soviet government might have to be consulted. Grew said he did not know whether approval could come before the summit; the matter might have to be discussed there. He promised to explore it at once. Italy did declare war on Japan days later, a step toward regaining standing among the victors.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d336:
Money for German exports opens a quarrel in Clayton's letter of June 18, 1945, to McCloy at the War Department. War Department officers had told the State Department that the Army was not responsible for exports from Germany, except where goods served a direct military need. On that view, the Army could not pay for supplies to raise German output for export.

The question had come up over coal. Europe's freed countries needed far more German coal, and producing it took supplies someone had to finance. Clayton's letter presses the War Department to widen its duty, setting up a State-War fight that ran on into the Potsdam briefing.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d36:
Stalin wants the meeting, and would host it near Berlin: Hopkins cabled Truman from Moscow on May 28, 1945. Another long talk with Stalin had ended that night; details would follow in the morning. Stalin had again said he was anxious to meet Truman at any time wished. In the suburbs of Berlin, he said, there would be adequate quarters for such a meeting.

Hopkins asked whether he should tell Stalin that Truman would like to meet around July 15. Stalin, he judged, would prefer an earlier date, given the many pressing problems to be decided. The cable assumes the Control Council would by then be set up, with American forces in the area. Potsdam enters the record here as a suburb and a date.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d436:
Expulsion of minorities from Czechoslovakia is the subject of a briefing book paper dated June 23, 1945. The Czechoslovak Republic had officially informed the United States that it wished to expel, immediately, the Sudeten German and Hungarian minorities. Washington had voiced sympathy with Prague's concern over its minority problems.

Yet the United States opposed any unilateral action to transfer these minorities. Transfer must wait for a satisfactory agreement with the powers responsible for order and military security in Germany. The paper places the Sudeten question inside the larger problem of German minorities in Poland and other states, fit for the heads of government to settle in an orderly way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d536:
A post-war lend-lease settlement with Britain is missing, a briefing book paper explains, and it gives the reason. No so-called 3(c) agreement for post-war deliveries of lend-lease has been made with the British. When approached informally in 1944, the British indicated they were unwilling to enter any commitment to make post-war financial settlement for lend-lease goods.

That position rested on Britain's hard outlook. The United Kingdom will emerge from the war in a difficult financial position, with limited supplies of gold and dollar exchange. The British should nevertheless be asked to reconsider, the paper argues. American policy holds that lend-lease is not to be used for post-war purposes, so transfers would be interrupted shortly after V-J Day without a settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d636:
A top secret briefing paper on Syria and Lebanon was prepared for Potsdam, dated June 30, 1945. It is document 636 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Levant crisis had just brought British troops into Syria against the French.

The paper notes that London and Paris both want the Levant problem settled. It clouds their ties and blocks a general treaty of alliance between them. Britain had proposed five-sided talks with the U.S., Syria, and Lebanon taking part. Washington agreed, but asked that fair French proposals get preference. France then countered with a call for a broad Near East conference of the five major powers. Washington told Paris it did not think such a wide conference would serve the purpose. The brief readies Truman in case Churchill seeks U.S. backing for a British plan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1036:
Philip Mosely cabled Ambassador Winant from Babelsberg on July 20, 1945, about the additional requirements agreement for Germany. Soviet official Vyshinsky had told him that Moscow approved the agreement, apart from a new title and first paragraph. Those two points should clear shortly, Vyshinsky expected.

Mosely also reports talks with John McCloy and Colonel Cutter on Washington's questions. Their answers stress that Allied representatives means the four commanders, acting both in the Control Council and in their zones. The draft does not assume a central German government exists. Nor can the council act on German property in a power's own country against that power's will, since council rulings must be unanimous. McCloy saw no bar to early War Department clearance.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1136:
Stanislaw Mikolajczyk, deputy prime minister of Poland, sent this memorandum on 24 July 1945. It was the first of three he put forward that day. Mikolajczyk led the non-communist wing of Poland's new joint government, the part that spoke for Poles who hoped for a free vote.

His papers put the Polish case straight before the Potsdam powers. Poland's border and its promised vote were being settled by others, in another country. A deputy premier with no seat at the table had only paper to fight with. This memorandum opens a striking one-day burst of Polish pleading in the record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1236:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the Secretary of State on 16 July 1945, the day before Potsdam opened. The two cabinet chiefs ran the war and the peace talks between them. A letter from the war secretary to the top envoy joined those worlds on paper.

Stimson's concerns spanned the fronts: the forces in Europe and the Pacific war. They also covered the secret work on new weapons, which he alone in the cabinet fully oversaw. His word to Byrnes on the summit's eve helped align the two departments. This message is part of that alignment. It shows the cabinet's senior men closing ranks before the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1336:
General John Hull, the Army's assistant chief of staff for operations, wrote to General Thomas Handy, the deputy chief of staff, on 28 July 1945. Hull ran the War Department's operations desk in Washington. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Staff papers between senior generals show the Army's inner workings while the Potsdam talks went on abroad. Operations officers had to match summit choices with real forces, ships, and plans for the war still being fought against Japan. Readers can follow how orders moved through the wartime Army. The paper trail shows two of its top staff men talking to each other.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-136: Printed after document 710 without a number, this editorial note forms part of the frame of the second Potsdam volume. The Foreign Relations editors used such notes to mark provenance and point out connections. They also flag where a paper survives only in part. The note helps a reader keep bearings among many similar staff documents.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-36:
A United States delegation memorandum sums up the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Its purpose was to fix the afternoon agenda for the heads of government.

Four subjects were recommended in order. First came procedure for peace settlements, hinging on one redrafted paragraph of the Council of Foreign Ministers proposal. The ministers would meet briefly beforehand to try to agree that text. Second came policy toward Italy, on the U.S. paper the President had presented on July 17. Third came the situation in Austria, above all in Vienna. Churchill would speak on it, seeking ratification of the control and zones agreements already approved for Austria. Fourth came the western boundary of Poland, on a Russian paper with a map.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d736:
George Allen, deputy director for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Document 736 is an internal State Department letter from the Potsdam week. Allen's office watched a region the conference touched only at its edges. His letter moved business between two senior desks.

Internal letters show the Department's daily grain. Officers traded facts and asked for calls on live questions. Allen wrote to a man who stood near the Secretary's door. Readers see how a regional office reached the center. The document adds the home front of diplomacy to the summit's brighter stage.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d836:
Elbridge Durbrow and an acting director named Phelps wrote jointly to Emilio Collado on July 18, 1945. Document 836 is an internal paper linking Eastern European affairs with financial policy. The two offices shared problems where politics met money. Their note went to the director of financial and development policy. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

Joint office papers show the Department thinking across its own walls. Eastern Europe's future turned on loans, trade, and aid as much as on flags. Readers see that link being worked at staff level. The document adds an economist's thread to a volume of envoys and generals. Potsdam's choices needed both kinds of mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d936: American staff attached this table to Clayton's statistical paper during the July 1945 Potsdam talks. It values movable factory equipment in Germany at the start of 1945, at prewar prices. Heavy industry, including iron, steel, machinery, and chemicals, totals 6,608 million marks. Only 27 percent of it sits in the eastern zone plus Berlin. Light industry totals 5,686 million marks, with 55 percent in the east. Across all manufacturing, the eastern share comes to about 40 percent.
frus-1947v05-d36:
Secretary of State Marshall wrote this top secret memorandum to President Truman on February 26, 1947. Britain had warned it could no longer carry the cost of aiding Greece and Turkey. Marshall states that Greece faces collapse without fast American help.

An annex from the State, War, and Navy secretaries lists nine steps. They urge telling London yes, seeking funds at once, and drafting a law for aid. Greece's needs for the rest of the year were put near $250,000,000. The memo stands at the start of the Truman Doctrine. The file shows relief policy made in the shadow of a hard winter.
frus-1969-76v01-d36: An editorial note in Volume I of the 1969-1976 Foreign Relations series quotes a Kissinger memo to President Nixon of September 10, 1969. Kissinger doubts that Vietnamization can work on the planned timetable. He says the war cannot be won within two years on current plans. He also doubts that South Vietnamese forces can take over the burden fast enough. Withdrawals, he warns, will feed public demand for more withdrawals. Hanoi, he adds, will not be fooled about Saigon's strength.
frus-1969-76v36:
The energy crisis from 1969 to 1974 is the subject of Volume XXXVI in the 1969-1976 series. Chapters are cut by date, in spans of about a year. Early chapters cover oil import rules and rising worry over supply. The span from October 1973 to March 1974 covers the Arab embargo and the price shock. A short final span runs to August 1974.

Talk records show officials debating how prices set by producer states compound over time. The papers track talks with oil firms, allies, and producer governments. They show energy moving from a trade topic to a top security concern. The volume ends with new consumer-side plans taking shape.
gao-gaoreports-b-295836:
The protest in files B-295836 and B-295836.2 reached GAO's ruling on April 18, 2005, with Hospital Klean of Texas, Inc., as the protester. The Army had awarded Integrity Management Services a contract for hospital housekeeping at Fort Polk, Louisiana. One issue was a late proposal revision from the winner. GAO held the late paper properly taken. The agency had moved the deadline to a Saturday, its own doors were locked that day, and no delivery guidance was posted. The carrier's failed Saturday attempt was the agency's fault, not the firm's.

The revision reached the agency on Monday, the next business day. The award itself withstood the rest of the attack, and the protest was denied.
gao-gaoreports-b-295936:
In GAO ruling B-295936, dated April 18, 2005, Vertol Systems Company, Inc., was the protester. The Air Force had obtained foreign threat systems aircraft for training exercises from an Army office, under the Economy Act. Vertol said a competitive purchase was required, in which it could compete. GAO denied the protest. The Air Force fairly judged that the firm was not a viable rival. Its helicopter could not meet the need for demonstrated airworthiness.

Threat systems aircraft play the enemy in air exercises. A plane that cannot show proven airworthiness cannot fill that role. The Economy Act path therefore stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-296536:
Computers Universal protested the stretch of a sole-source order in GAO decision B-296536, dated August 18, 2005. The holder was abcISP. The buyer was the Veterans Affairs office. The work was tech services in San Diego. The same work was tied up in a live protest fight.

GAO denied the protest. The stretch was short and for a clear cause. It held the work in place while the live protest was solved. A fresh award would then be made. That bridge was sound on these facts. A short bridge to keep key work going can stand. It must be brief and tied to the live fight, as here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296836:
Muddy Creek Oil and Gas protested a Bureau of Indian Affairs call for firefighter meals in GAO decision B-296836, dated August 9, 2005. The firm sent its quote by fax reply. On the face of the quote it had hand-written changes. Those notes changed key terms of the work plan. The agency ruled the quote not fit.

GAO denied the protest. A quote that rewrites key terms does not meet the call. The agency could reject it on that ground. Bidders must take the call as drawn or seek a change first. Hand notes on a quote will not bind the buyer. The ruling is short and stark on that point.
gao-gaoreports-b-297536:
American Material Handling protested an Army award for forklifts for Iraq in GAO decision B-297536, dated January 30, 2006. The winner was JLG Industries. The trucks were rough ground, all-wheel units. The firm had the low price. It said low price should have won. Ship speed was the split point.

GAO denied the protest. The pick lead found the winner's short ship time beat the firm's price edge. That trade fit the tests in the call. The call set a price and tech trade, not low price wins. Fast ship to a war zone can be worth more than a price gap. The pick thus stood on a sound trade.
gao-gaoreports-b-310136:
Firestorm Wildland Fire Suppression, Inc. lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-310136 on November 26, 2007. The Forest Service sought crews to fight wildland fires. The award went to Ferguson Management Company South. The call was set aside for small firms. Crews of 20 were to serve near six national forests.

The loser pointed to bad facts it claimed marred the winner's past work. GAO denied the protest. The agency lacked first-hand grasp of some of the claims. It did weigh in full the facts it did know of. A review is fair when the agency weighs what it knows and lacks a base for the rest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310436:
Recon Optical, Inc. lost its protest. GAO decided B-310436 on December 27, 2007. The Army sought remote weapon stations for armored trucks. A gunner fires the gun from inside the truck. The award went to Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace AS. Recon fought the scores of both bids on each point. It held the high price in the race as well.

GAO denied the protest. Recon's bid drew the low mark on the three top points. It was marked red or high risk on each. The rival bids were both stronger and cheaper. A weak, high-cost bid has no fair claim to a win.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-336:
Intellectual Property, GAO-05-336 of June 17, 2005, is the deep form of work summed for Congress in a fall statement. Patent bids to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office grew from about 185,000 to over 350,000 in ten years. A backlog of about 750,000 bids waits. Bids were set to top 450,000 by 2009. The office has chased a paper-free path for two decades.

GAO grades how far that path has got and what snags it. The plea in the title is for firm craft at the core: clear aims, sound plans, and grip on each build step. Staff strain shares the tale in a twin report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-536:
Risk retention groups, a form of self-insurance for like firms, are examined in GAO report GAO-05-536, released on August 15, 2005. Congress allowed these groups to ease shortages of liability cover. A federal act lets a group form an insurer in one state and sell cover in many. Failures of several large ones raised doubts about how they are policed.

The groups wrote about $1.8 billion of cover in 2003, 1.17 percent of the market. Members gained steady prices and cover shaped to their risks. More groups formed in 2002 through 2004 than in the prior 15 years. About three quarters of the new ones sold medical malpractice cover. Rules differ widely by state. Many groups base in six states that charter them as captives under light rules. Those states may even loosen terms to draw business. GAO found uneven standards for solvency and reporting. It urged common baseline rules and stronger protection for members.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-736:
In GAO-05-736 (July 26, 2005), GAO took stock of share-in-savings contracts for technology work. Under this method, a firm funds a project up front. The agency then pays the firm from any savings the work creates. A 2002 law let agencies use the method and told GAO to judge how well it worked.

GAO found the method had never been used. No such contract had been awarded by late 2004. Rules and guidance from the budget office were still not out, more than two years after the law. The General Services Administration had built tools and training. Few staff used them, and no deal followed. GAO set out why agencies held back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-236:
Spectrum auctions and their future are debated in GAO-06-236, a report issued on December 20, 2005. In 1993 Congress let the Federal Communications Commission sell spectrum licenses by auction. The method assigns scarce airwaves to commercial users. A 2004 law told GAO to study the licensing system. GAO described how spectrum gets set aside for commercial use. It weighed what auctions did to prices, network build-out, competition, and small firms. It also gathered options to run the spectrum better.

Stakeholders strongly back extending the auction power, GAO found. Beyond that point, agreement thins out. Ideas to make spectrum use more efficient draw split views. Clearer rights and more flexible use drew support in parts of the debate. GAO laid the choices before Congress as a matter for its judgment. The report is a map of where spectrum policy commands consensus, and where it does not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-336:
Turning thinned forest waste into fuel and heat is studied in GAO-06-336, a report issued March 22, 2006. Crews thin such stands to cut fire risk. The cuttings — woody biomass — can be burned for energy instead of piled and wasted. The House Resources chairman asked GAO to learn from current users. GAO gathered what helped them and what hurt. Money incentives and cheap supply drew users in. Green benefits added a further push.

Supply gaps and handling costs held users back, GAO found. Burning wood instead of oil or gas meant new gear and higher upkeep. Thin markets may steer wood users toward other fuels over time. Places with strong wood industries nearby fare better. Help works best when sized to each user's scale. The report turns scattered experience into guidance. It shows a waste problem and an energy resource as the same pile of brush.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1036:
Computer control systems behind power, water, and fuel networks are the risk in GAO report GAO-07-1036, dated September 10, 2007. Such systems run core processes in electric power, oil and gas, water treatment, and chemical plants. A break in them could harm public health and safety.

GAO mapped cyber threats and weak points in these systems, and the harm an attack could do. It named hurdles to guarding them. It listed private steps to harden them, and judged public steps for fit. Many efforts are under way, GAO found. Yet hurdles remain before these quiet systems are safe.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-136:
The Internal Revenue Service collects nearly all the money that funds the federal government. GAO audited its books in GAO-07-136, a financial audit dated November 9, 2006. The audit covers fiscal years 2006 and 2005. GAO judged whether the statements were reliable in all material respects. It also judged whether management kept effective internal control. Compliance with key laws and with federal financial system rules was tested too.

GAO found that the financial statements present fairly the agency's position. They conform with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. But the verdict on internal control was negative. Because of material weaknesses, the agency did not maintain effective internal control. GAO cited information security as the most serious remaining weakness. It also told of record errors, such as a $1,694 tax bill entered as $169 million. The taxpayer got notices seeking nearly $200 million before the error was fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-236:
Twenty federal programs help people with disabilities find work, and little is known about some of them. GAO reviewed four of the programs in GAO-07-236, issued January 26, 2007. Three sit in the Education Department, including the Randolph-Sheppard vending program. The fourth buys goods from workshops for blind and disabled workers.
