GAO checked whether each program had goals and measures. It also judged the quality of federal oversight.

One program had no federal performance goals at all, GAO found. That was Randolph-Sheppard, where the agency leans on state self-reports. It does not routinely analyze the data it gathers. Another program's goals long lacked targets to judge progress. Oversight of the other two programs looked more solid. In case files at visited workshops, 11 percent lacked required medical proof of disability. GAO urged stronger goals, guidance, and monitoring across the four.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-336:
Nine of 12 giant Energy Department construction projects ran over budget or behind schedule. GAO diagnosed the pattern in GAO-07-336, a report dated March 27, 2007. The 12 projects carry about $27 billion in total costs. They support weapons work, research, and waste cleanup. GAO surveyed project directors and read project files. It dug into five projects near construction start.

Cost growth hit 8 of the 12 projects, GAO found. Increases ran from $79.0 million to $7.9 billion. Nine projects slipped by 9 months to over 11 years. Weak department oversight fed every troubled project. Builders got approval before designs were complete. Readiness checks for new technology vary by project. No shared scale shows whether a design will work as drawn. One uranium facility needed concrete torn out and redone. GAO urged one consistent readiness method.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-36:
The agency built in 1999 to fix nuclear weapons management still fights security and cost problems. GAO reviewed its progress in GAO-07-36, a report dated January 19, 2007. The National Nuclear Security Administration runs weapons, nonproliferation, and naval reactor work. GAO checked site security surveys and inspections. It interviewed current and former officials. It also reviewed the agency's structure and management systems.

Headquarters oversight of security has improved, GAO found. But the agency cannot show all security goals are met at all sites. Inspectors found physical security flaws at three major sites. Cyber security weaknesses span the complex. Four people have held the top security job since 1999, often in acting roles. Site offices lack staff and training funds. The agency keeps no full tally of security flaws found. GAO issued 21 recommendations across five areas. They span structure, security, and project control.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-536:
One ledger for a 22-agency department remains out of reach in GAO-07-536, dated June 21, 2007. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) opened in March 2003. It inherited a tangle of aging finance systems from its merged parts. Sound, fast financial data is the goal. GAO asked whether DHS had a full plan to reach a single integrated system.

The answer was no. The department had ended its eMerge2 effort, a call GAO called wise. But no defined finance strategy took its place. GAO also weighed what the money spent so far had bought and found the yield thin. Old systems stayed in poor shape. GAO urged DHS to build its plan on proven practice, step by step, with skilled staff. Without that base, the department cannot fully prove where its money goes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-736:
Address lists for the 2010 census are the topic of GAO-07-736, dated June 14, 2007. The Census Bureau asks local, state, and tribal governments to update its address maps. The effort is called the Local Update of Census Addresses program. Good lists help ensure no home is missed in the count. GAO checked the program's status and the bureau's reply to past advice. It also checked plans for areas hit by hurricanes Katrina and Rita.

A dress rehearsal ran on time on most steps. The bureau sent advance letters to local areas in early 2007. Yet its timeline skipped tests of the software local staff must use. Plans for address checks in storm-hit areas still lacked a schedule. GAO told the Commerce chief to test the software for ease of use. It also told him to set dates for the storm area work. The department largely agreed with the calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-836:
Unmanned aircraft and spy assets are studied in GAO-07-836, dated July 11, 2007. Commanders rank intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance high among their needs. The Defense Department buys many such systems, drones among them. GAO asked how well drones are woven into combat operations. It also asked whether tasking weighs all spy assets together. The review drew on data and guidance and on talks with officials. Some of them serve in Iraq and Afghanistan.

The services wrote joint guides for drone use in combat. Those guides omit one key point: advance coordination across the department. Central Command set its own coordination steps for its theater. Services did not always follow them, since some did not know of them. Tasking choices can also miss assets held by other services. GAO urged better coordination of drone deployments. It also urged full weighing of all assets and checks on results. The department generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-936:
Army training for its new brigades is reviewed in GAO-07-936, dated August 6, 2007. The Army is reshaping divisions into modular brigades. It calls the shift its biggest restructuring since World War II. Public Law 109-163 orders a training strategy for the brigades. The strategy must cover five named elements. GAO checked how fully the strategy meets the law. It also tracked rollout steps and hurdles. The strategy's purpose is stated clearly at the top. Goals and measures lag behind the vision, though.

Brigades should reach full mission capability before deployment. That overall goal lacks hard metrics to prove success, GAO found. Commanders judge readiness by professional feel instead. Live and virtual training goals exist for combat brigades. Constructive training goals stay vague in unit templates. Funding models and reporting steps need more work. Goals are not mandatory guides for planning. GAO urged the Army to flesh out the strategy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-136:
Leverage measures in housing programs are probed in GAO report GAO-08-136 (January 18, 2008). Leveraging means using one pot of funds to draw in others. Two agencies report such measures for their housing and development programs. They are the housing department and the Treasury. This study is the second of two on the topic.

GAO examined six programs in depth. It checked how clear the data and methods behind the leverage figures are. It also asked how well the figures show true program results. GAO found that more detail is needed on their accuracy. It also found weak links between the measures and program goals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-336:
The State Department's Antiterrorism Assistance program is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-336, dated February 29, 2008. The program trains and equips partner nations to fight terrorism. GAO reviewed the guidance behind country priorities, coordination with other programs, and how results are measured and reported.

GAO found that policy guidance gave program managers little help in ranking recipient countries, and needs assessments were not used in a steady way. Coordination with other U.S. counterterrorism efforts showed no major overlap. But the department did not systematically assess program outcomes, so it could not judge effectiveness. Its reports to Congress on counterterrorism aid were incomplete and inaccurate. The department generally agreed with GAO's recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-36:
Pandemic flu planning for critical infrastructure is the subject of GAO report GAO-08-36, dated October 31, 2007. Over 85 percent of the nation's critical infrastructure, such as water and power systems, is run by private firms. GAO reviewed joint work in 5 of the 17 infrastructure sectors.

Federal agencies and industry councils had drafted preparedness guidance, named the critical workers each sector needs, and held workshops and some exercises. Work ran largely through sector councils that share information and write sector plans. GAO still saw gaps in facing a pandemic's strain on staffing and services. GAO recommended that the Secretary of Homeland Security push the councils to tackle the full range of these challenges. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-536:
Privacy law for personal data is studied in GAO report GAO-08-536, dated April 19, 2008. The Privacy Act of 1974 anchors federal privacy protection, and the E-Government Act of 2002 requires privacy impact reviews for systems holding personal data. GAO asked whether these laws cover all federal collection and use.

They do not, GAO found. The act's key term, system of records, does not reach all personal data agencies process. Rules on limiting collection and use to a stated purpose are modest, and notice and access rights have gaps. GAO laid out options for Congress, such as widening the act to all personal data held in an organized way. It said Congress, not the budget office, must strike the final balance. The budget office urged a wider statutory view.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-936:
Handheld computers for the 2010 Census are the subject of GAO-08-936, a July 2008 report. Census workers were to use the devices to check addresses door to door. Cost worries led the Secretary of Commerce to redesign the automation effort in March 2008, but the bureau chose to keep the handhelds for address canvassing. GAO studied how the devices performed in the 2007 dress rehearsal.

Field staff hit frequent snags: failed transmissions, frozen screens, faulty map spotting, and trouble with large blocks. The contractor pushed software fixes, yet help desk support fell short and productivity suffered. The bureau and its contractor never fully measured how bad the problems were. With the devices staying, GAO says planning, testing, and clear readiness rules are now critical.
gogol-inspector-general-1836:
Nikolai Gogol wrote The Inspector General in 1836, a comedy play about corruption in a small Russian town. Local officials hear that a government inspector is coming in secret. They mistake Khlestakov, a poor and vain clerk passing through, for that inspector. Gifts and bribes pour in at once.

Khlestakov plays along, boasts wildly, and takes money from everyone. The mayor hopes to marry his daughter to the supposed great man. A letter read aloud at the end exposes the trick, just as the real inspector arrives. Gogol's satire of greed and fear still plays well. It is a peak of Russian comic drama.
illustrated-catalogue-of-the-collections:
James Stevenson compiled this larger catalogue of goods from the Indians of New Mexico and Arizona in 1879. It was printed in the Bureau of Ethnology report in Washington in 1883. A note says it was ready for an earlier report but left out for want of space.

Numbered entries run through pots, baskets, and tools in long series. Zuni baskets of coarse willow ware are noted for shape and use, such as carrying ripe peaches. Figure numbers follow the earlier report, which explains their start point. Readers get a dense record of Pueblo craft as collected then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-gersh:
Aaron ben Gershon Abu al-Rabi of Catania, called also Aldabi, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. A Sicilian scholar, cabalist, and astrologer, he flourished between 1400 and 1450. He was the youngest of five brothers, all rabbinic scholars. He studied at Treviso and knew Arabic, grammar, and the science of his age well.

Travel took him to Turkey, Egypt, Palestine, Damascus, and Kaffa, the entry reports. In Jerusalem he disputed with Karaites and defended rabbinical theology with pride. In Rome, Pope Martin the Fifth received him kindly among his cardinals. His Pentateuch commentary explains some laws as warnings against idolatrous practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-gorion-of-: Abba Gorion of Sidon was a tanna who flourished in the second century. He passed down two sayings to later ages. One was a saying of Abba Saul, and the other a saying of Rabban Gamaliel II. The Gamaliel saying stands at the start of a Midrash on the Book of Esther. For that reason that Midrash is called Midrash Abba Gorion. The entry names no other act or work of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ablat-336:
Ablat was a Gentile sage and astrologer in Babylonia. He was a close friend of Mar Samuel, who died in 254. Their friendship showed that Babylonian Jews and their heathen neighbors could mix socially despite legal limits.

One story shows the care on both sides. As a guest, Ablat would not drink wine before Samuel, knowing Jewish rules on wine touched by idolaters. Samuel had mulled wine ready, which fell outside the ban. The Jerusalem Talmud also preserves a question Ablat put to a Jewish scholar about a rabbinic rule. Ablat was widely liked and respected among the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrogation-of-l:
Abrogation of laws asks when a law of the Torah may be set aside. Deuteronomy xiii. 1 says nothing may be added to or taken from the commands. The Sadducees and later the Karaites read that line in a strict way. They turned down later rabbinic growth of the law. The rabbis read the rule with more room to act.

The entry says the old rabbis claimed power to guard the law with new rules. In hard cases they could even pause or lift a Bible law for a time. Maimonides backs that power in his code. He says a court may act to bring people back to the Torah or to stop a worse harm. Later parts trace how civil law and reform meetings changed practice in Germany and the United States.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achshaph-736: Achshaph was a town named in Joshua xi. 1 and xii. 20. It was the seat of a king in north Canaan. Robinson links it to ruins at Kesaf, a village northwest of Hunin. That site fits the first text well. It fits Joshua xix. 25 less well, since that verse needs a town near the coast. A link with the Aksap of an Egyptian list is not sure. The hosted text gives the two views and leaves the site in doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adoi-836: Adoi was the father of Hananiah. Hananiah was a prince of the captivity, or resh galuta. He worked about the year 700. The name draws note for its form. It shows a Semitic name in Persian dress. At its root stands the known name Ida, or Ada, or Adda. That root shows in Jewish and Palmyrene sources. The tail oi is a Persian mark of fondness. The hosted text gives that word study, the son's rank, and his rough date, and nothing on Adoi's own life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-bardala-936: Aha Bardala was a Babylonian amora of the first generation. He was a contemporary of Abba Areka. The entry states only these two facts about him. It gives no teaching, ruling, or event from his life, so he stands in the record as a named scholar of Abba Areka's generation and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akiba-ben-judah: Akiba ben Judah Loeb was a German rabbi of the early eighteenth century. He lived at Lehren-Steinsfeld, in Wurttemberg. His one printed book was "Ha-Ohel Olam," the Everlasting Tent. It holds novellae on the Talmudic treatise Ketubot, and it came out at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1714. Four responsa of his were bound with it, plus an essay on Seder Zera'im from his papers. He also left two books on Seder Taharot. Those survive only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-balas:
Alexander Balas was a king of Syria who died in 145 B.C. He was a youth of low birth, set up as a pretender in 153 B.C. Men claimed he was a son of Antiochus Epiphanes. His strong likeness to Antiochus V. made the tale believable. Crowned at Ptolemais, his first act was an embassy to Jonathan the Hasmonean.

He named Jonathan high priest and "the King's Friend." He sent him a purple robe and a crown of gold. At the Feast of Tabernacles in 152 B.C., Jonathan put on the high priest's holy dress. That step ended the rule of the pro-Hellenic party in Judea. Jonathan stayed loyal in return. In 147 B.C. he beat Apollonius, who had taken arms against Alexander, and he was given the town of Ekron. At Alexander's wedding in 150 B.C., Jonathan sat beside him in royal purple, with new titles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alimony-1236:
Alimony in modern law is support set by a court. A husband pays it to a wife after a split. Strict Jewish law gave no such court award. The entry says the marriage contract did the same work. That contract is the ketubah. It fixed a sum owed to the wife.

The sum fell due at divorce or at the husband's death. It stood as a first charge on his estate. The entry traces how the payment rules changed over time. It also tells of a sage who housed his divorced wife. She had wed again and fallen into want. A model court writ closes the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alupka-1336: Alupka is a village on the south shore of the Crimea. The Crimea was then part of Russia. The entry knows the village from one old letter. That letter was sent by Joseph, king of the Chazars. He wrote to Hasdai ibn-Shaprut about the year 960. In the letter Alupka stands on a list. It is named as one of the towns that paid tribute to the Chazars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-rab-1436: Rab Amram was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth century. He was a peer of Hisda and of Nahman. His work lies in law more than in tale. Even there he is seldom first with a view. The entry cites tracts where his rulings show. One tale of a clash with Rabbah stands out. Rabbah called him a fool in a hot dispute. A cedar post in the hall cracked at that point. Each man read the crack as a sign for his side.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archisynagogue-:
Archisynagogue means synagogue-chief, the officer who oversaw the religious services of the synagogue. The title can be traced from the time of Jesus to about the year 300, and it occurs several times in the New Testament. His clear task was to pick fit men to read the Law, recite prayers, and preach.

Ancient synagogues had no fixed officers for those duties, so the choice mattered each time. Though the office is so Jewish, its name is borrowed from Greek and was used across the Roman empire, but not in Babylonia. The Jerusalem Talmud adds that in a pinch the archisynagogue had to act as reader himself. He was chosen for piety and good character, the entry says, unlike the archon, for whom standing and influence counted most.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-artom-isaac-183:
Isaac Artom, an Italian patriot, diplomat, and writer, was born at Asti in Piedmont on December 31, 1829. Piedmont's higher schools shut out Jews, so in 1846 he went to Pisa to study law. When revolt against Austria broke out in 1848, he joined the students' battalion under Professor Montanelli, though frail in health, and fought at Curtatone and Montanara. He took his law degree at Turin in 1853.

In 1855 he entered the Tuscan foreign office, and three years later he became private secretary to Count Cavour. Clerical foes attacked Cavour for keeping a Jew as chief secretary, and Cavour answered with high praise of Artom's ability. After Cavour died on June 6, 1861, Artom served at Paris as secretary of legation in 1862 and rose in the foreign service. He died at Rome on January 24, 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-ben-levi-:
Asher ben Levi, also known as Abd al-Masih, is a legendary boy convert and Christian martyr. The tale places him toward the end of the fourth century at Sinjar, between Nisibis and Mosul in Mesopotamia. Born to Jewish parents, the boy lived shunned by his Christian and Zoroastrian playmates. They let him eat with them only after baptizing him themselves, since the village church stood far off.

They gave him the name Servant of the Messiah and pierced his ear for an earring. His mother hid the change from his father, a rich head of the Jewish community. On a Sabbath feast the boy refused to eat with Jews, and the secret broke. He ran to the well of his baptism, where his father killed him. Merchants later reported light and sweet scent over his grave.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asshur-2036:
Asshur was a city that once served as the capital of Assyria. The entry says it was likely the first important town built by early colonists who probably came from Babylonia. One early ruler, Shamshi-Adad I., built a temple there to Anu and Adad about 1820 B.C. The site now lies under a mound called Kalah Shergat on the Tigris.

About 1300 B.C. Shalmaneser I. moved the capital to Calah. Tiglath-pileser I. later made Asshur the capital again, before it moved for good to Nineveh. The entry also gives the rabbinical view. There Asshur was a pious man who left his homeland to avoid taking part in building the Tower of Babel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augustine-2136:
Augustine was the greatest of the Latin church fathers. He was born on Nov. 13, 354, at Tagaste in Numidia. He died at Hippo on Aug. 28, 430. After a wild heathen youth he joined the Manichean faith. Nine years later, in 386, Ambrosius converted him to Christianity. He became a priest in 392 and a bishop in 395.

The entry stresses the contrasts in Augustine. He mixed wild fancy with sharp logic, hot prejudice with fine care, and mystic feeling with hair-splitting argument. His "Confessions" looks inward as few books do. His letters, sermons, and polemics fight for strict Church doctrine. On Judaism the picture is mixed in a curious way. His picture of God bears a Hellenic cast gained through Neoplatonism. Yet his thought also shows hard legal lines that the entry calls Jewish, most plainly when he argues against Judaism itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ba-al-and-ba-al:
Ba'al is a wide-spread Semitic word. Its root most nearly means possess in English. So Ba'al, usually rendered lord, is more exactly possessor or owner. Speech uses it for the owner of a house or of goods, and for a husband. The word also builds loose phrases: a ba'al of dreams is a dreamer, and a ba'al of wings is a bird.

When a god is called a ba'al, the entry argues, the title means owner of certain things, not ruler of men. That sets Ba'al apart from Adon, a word of personal rule. In Babylonia the same word, Bel, named a great national god of Nippur. His name later passed to Merodach of Babylon. The entry then asks how Ba'al worship reached the Hebrews. It answers that farming Israel learned it from the Canaanites of the soil, whose feasts were bound to the land they worked.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-joseph-233: Joseph Baer founded a firm of booksellers at Frankfort-on-the-Main. Born in the last half of the eighteenth century, he died in 1851. He began with a small second-hand book stall at Bockenheim in 1785. After many blocks he won citizenship at Frankfort and moved his trade there. The entry says the business grew into one of the greatest in Germany. Great libraries, among them the Imperial Public Library of St. Petersburg, drew rare works from it. For its centenary in 1885 the firm issued a catalogue of 10,000 works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bandmann-daniel:
Daniel E. Bandmann was a German-American actor born at Cassel, Germany, in 1840. He first acted at the Court Theater in Neu Strelitz at eighteen, mostly in German versions of Shakespeare. In 1863 he left for the United States and played an English part at Niblo's Garden on Jan. 15. He then toured the country for five years, with Shylock as his most loved role.

Early in 1868 Bandmann reached London and played at the Lyceum. Parts in "Othello" and, in 1873, Hamlet followed, with a tour of Australia between. Since then his stage work has been mainly in the United States, where he bought a ranch. In 1901 he appeared in vaudeville in a shortened "Merchant of Venice." The entry gives his roles in strict date order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnave-antoine:
Antoine Pierre Joseph Marie Barnave was a French politician, born at Grenoble on October 22, 1761 and guillotined in Paris on November 29, 1793. Of a Protestant family, he was educated in the law at home. At twenty-two he was known as a political orator. In 1789 the Tiers état elected him deputy to the States General, and he soon led the popular party.

Having suffered under restrictive laws as a Protestant, he pleaded the cause of the Jews at the Assembly. On December 23, 1789, his great discourse defended them against the abbé Muray and the bishop of Nancy. Both men had tried to check the complete emancipation of the Jews. Barnave, with Mirabeau, carried his followers in their favor and helped greatly toward the final triumph of justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-adolph-273: Adolph Beer was an Austrian colonel born in 1833 at Prossnitz, in Moravia. He died on Oct. 2, 1888, at Leibach, in Carniola. Trained at a school for military cadets, he left with a lieutenant's rank. He then taught at military academies in Moravia and at Cracow. In the war of 1866 he won praise for holding the frontier fort of Olmütz against a night surprise by Prussian troops. The entry calls him one of the first Jews in the Austrian army to reach the grade of colonel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-benven: Benvenida Cohen Belmonte was a poetess who lived in London at the start of the eighteenth century. She was a sister of a well known patron of letters in that city. Her verse sang the praise of a famed book of lives printed at London in 1720. She also wrote a poem in honor of Samuel Nassy of Surinam, across the ocean. No birth or death dates are given for her in this brief entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedikt-rudolp: Rudolph Benedikt, an Austrian chemist, was born at Döbling on July 12, 1852, and died in Vienna on Feb. 6, 1896. He trained at the Polytechnic in Vienna, where he became an assistant teacher of technical chemistry in 1872. A post in analytical chemistry followed in 1876, and in 1890 he rose to full professor. His chief work dealt with man-made dyes and came out in 1883. The entry also lists his journal pieces on salts, boric acid, and halogen compounds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berechiah-i-r-3: Berechiah the First was a Palestinian scholar of the third century, always cited by that name alone. Once he is called Berechiah Saba, the Elder, to set him apart from a later namesake. Nothing is known of his life, and little of his teaching survives. One debate of his turns on the worth of Torah study, where a single passage of the Law is prized above all this world. The entry notes a doubt from one scholar over whether this Berechiah existed at all as a separate man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-eduar:
Eduard Bernstein, a socialist leader and editor, was born in Berlin in 1850. He began as a bank clerk and joined the Social-Democratic party in 1872. In 1878 he left business to edit party papers from Switzerland. When Bismarck's anti-socialist law forced the party press abroad, he ran its organ at Zurich and then at London.

After the law fell in 1890 he wrote for Berlin and London journals. His book of 1899, on the grounds of socialism and the tasks of social democracy, stirred debate across Europe. Even foes praised his talent and clear thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezai-2636: Bezai was a family named in Ezra and Nehemiah. Its members numbered 324. They returned from exile with Zerubbabel. Ezra gives that figure in his list. Nehemiah's parallel list agrees. The name also appears among covenant signers. There it may mark the clan's leader. First Esdras calls that leader Bassai. A clay tablet from Nippur bears the name Besai. The entry notes that find as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bisliches-or-bi:
Mordecai Loeb Bisliches edited valuable medieval Hebrew works. He was born at Brody at the end of the eighteenth century. He died about 1851. He married at thirteen, a fact he bitterly lamented. After divorce and his children's deaths he moved to Paris. Business prospered for him there. His leisure went to Hebrew manuscripts. He collected more in Holland and Italy.

Back home he prepared eight works for print. His brother Ephraim helped him. They include Abravanel and Palquera editions. Naḥmanides' novellæ also appeared under his care. His own catalogue described eighty rare manuscripts. Zunz and Sachs annotated that catalogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenthal-oska:
Oskar Blumenthal was a German author and playwright born at Berlin on March 13, 1852. He studied in Berlin and Leipsic and took his doctorate in 1872. He then edited verse journals before moving back to Berlin.

As critic for the Berliner Tageblatt, Blumenthal won praise for wit and fairness. In 1887 he opened the Lessing Theater and ran it till 1898. He also ran the Berliner Theater for a year. His many comedies include joint works with G. Kadelburg. After 1898 he wrote full time. Named plays include Der Probepfeil of 1882 and Die Grosse Glocke of 1887. He also edited the works and papers of Grabbe in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bodo-11836:
Bodo was a bishop and chaplain of Emperor Louis the Pious. After a loose life at court, he made a pilgrimage to Rome in 838. On that journey he was converted to Judaism and took the name Eleazar.

Bodo married a Jewish woman and went into military service at Saragossa. He urged the Moorish rulers to oppose the Spanish Christians. In 840 he traded letters with Pablo Alvaro of Cordova, a baptized Jew. Each man tried in vain to win the other back. Many of their letters survive. The Spanish Christians, the entry adds, asked the king of the Franks for aid against the pressure he urged on them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boniface-viii-b:
Boniface VIII, born Benedict Gaetan at Anagni, was the one hundred and ninety-eighth pope. He was elected on Dec. 24, 1294, and died in 1303. He followed Celestin V., who had resigned after six months.

Boniface held kindly feelings toward the Jews, the entry says. An Inquisition rule of 1297 let accusers stay hidden from persons of influence. Jews were classed among the powerful, so a mere charge could doom them. On appeal, his bull of June 13, 1299, declared most Jews unimportant. Only those of known influence stayed under the rule. His own physician was a Jew named Isaac.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandes-ludvig-:
Ludvig Israel Brandes was a Danish physician born in Copenhagen on Oct. 26, 1821. He died there on Sept. 17, 1894. He took his medical degree in 1850 after service as an assistant surgeon in war.

Brandes rose to chief physician at the Almindelig Hospital in 1863. He gained the title of professor in 1869. His energy went largely to good works for the sick and aged. In 1859 he helped found a Copenhagen home for incurables and the aged. He also founded a society for seamstresses and served the Jewish congregation. From 1873 he worked to raise the training and standing of nurses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-broker-3736:
Broker names a middleman who brings buyer and seller together, or a paid agent who acts for another person. The entry gives the Neo-Hebrew word as sirsur. It traces the term through the Mishnah, the Babylonian Gemara, and later codes. One Mishnah case asks who bears the loss when a package of oil or wine breaks during measuring.

Maimonides is cited for the rule that a paid agent who departs from his orders must cover the loss. Further rulings bar a broker from selling goods to himself, set his pay, and make him answer for goods lost or stolen. The entry also notes the matchmaker, or shadkan, as a lawful kind of broker.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burger-hugo-pen:
Hugo Lubliner, who wrote as Hugo Bürger, was a German dramatist born in Breslau on April 22, 1846. He reached Berlin at twelve and began writing short plays at seventeen. One early comedy of 1865 was well received. He ran a textile business and traveled for it, until a hit comedy in 1873 turned him fully to the theater.

From 1876 to 1891 he wrote about fifteen comedies and dramas, some with partners. A four volume collection of his plays came out in Berlin in 1881 and 1882. He also wrote two novels about Berlin in the empire years. The entry praises his mastery of stage effects. It also credits his sharp eye for the weak spots of modern social life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cardozo-david-d:
David de Jahacob Lopez Cardozo, a Dutch Talmudist and communal worker, was born in Amsterdam on May 21, 1808, and died there on April 11, 1890. He studied at the bet ha-midrash Ets Hayyim and under Rabbi Berenstein at The Hague. He gained his Morenu diploma in 1839.

That same year Cardozo became ab bet din of the Portuguese synagogue of Amsterdam. In 1852 he rose to ab bet din and preacher there. He served as dean of the middle classes of Ets Hayyim for nearly half a century. He founded a society for study of Jewish law and its commentaries. Decorated with the Royal Order of the Lion, he retired in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castrojeriz-413: Castrojeriz is a town in southern Castile, eighteen miles west of Burgos. Jews lived there from the time of Moorish rule. A charter of 974 ordered that killing a Jew be punished like killing a Christian. In 1035 Ferdinand I settled Jews left from Mercatello there, after forty Jews had been killed in that place. In 1106 townsmen from Castro attacked Castrojeriz Jews, killing and robbing many. The king and queen barred further harm under heavy penalties. Charters for the Jews were confirmed in 1234. In 1474 the community paid 1,100 maravedis in taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chimham-4336: Chimham was a son of Barzillai, who had supported David during his exile at Mahanaim. After Absalom's death, David invited Barzillai to spend his last days with the king. The old man declined and sent his son Chimham in his place. Jeremiah xli. 17 names a camp of Chimham near Bethlehem. From that mention, the entry infers that David gave Chimham land there. The land seems to have passed to his descendants under his name. Targum, Rashi, and Ḳimḥi support that reading of the Samuel passages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cock-4436:
Cock, the male of the domestic fowl, probably came from India and reached Palestine by way of Babylonia and Greece. When it arrived stays unclear, since Bible mentions are doubtful. The entry works through Hebrew and Aramaic words that rabbis linked to the bird, weighing each claim against Talmud and Midrash.

In rabbinic writing the cock bears a Babylonian name and counts as a common yard bird. Yet breeding cocks was banned in Jerusalem while the Temple stood, since scratching birds might stir up ritually unclean matter. Pages follow on white cocks in pagan sacrifice, the idol Nergal read as a cock, and lore about crowing at dawn. Folk beliefs about demons with cock's feet close the piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohnfeld-adalbe: Adalbert Dorotheus Solomon Cohnfeld, a German author, was born in Pyritz, Pomerania, on Aug. 3, 1809. He died in Berlin on Jan. 20, 1868. He lived at Breslau in his early years and became a physician. Fame came through editing instead. He ran a north German journal for the theater. His books include two novels from 1837 and 1838. A full history of the Prussian state followed in 1840. A life of Frederick William III came in 1840-41.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-consumption-tub:
Consumption, an infectious disease caused by the tubercle bacillus, is studied here through one question: how often does it strike Jews? Crowded, badly aired tenements feed the bacillus, the entry notes, and Jews crowd the great cities. Tailoring and other sitting trades, favored by Jews, raise the risk, as do marriages between kin.

Yet the numbers surprise. Jews form the shortest and narrowest-chested people in Europe by the measures quoted, with the lowest index of vitality. Still, census tables place deaths from consumption lowest among Russians and Hungarians, read here as Jews. Dr. Maurice Fishberg tested the figures in New York's ghetto ward by ward. The entry reports his work as backing the census, while noting that other writers disputed the base counts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-converts-to-chr:
Converts to Christianity, Modern counts Jews who left their ancestral faith after the age of Mendelssohn. Estimates cited here run from over 100,000 to as many as 250,000 for the nineteenth century. Russia and England each get large figures. The entry ties the waves to set times, such as the Mendelssohn era and the anti-Semitic years after 1880.

The bulk is a long list of named converts, each with dates and a field. Painters, poets, doctors, judges, and scholars appear side by side. Names range from Heinrich Heine and Karl Marx to Benjamin Disraeli and Felix Mendelssohn-Bartholdy. Readers can scan it as a quick who-was-who of that shift.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-boaz-: Boaz's son David was a Karaite scholar who flourished in the tenth century. He was reported to be fifth in descent from Anan, the founder of Karaism. The chronicler Al-Hiti names him under the year 993 and lists three works by him: commentaries on Ecclesiastes and on the Pentateuch, plus a treatise on the Pentateuch's basic principles. Only a fragment of the Pentateuch commentary survives, in manuscript at St. Petersburg. In it David often attacks Saadia without naming him, calling him simply "this man."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deckert-francis:
Francis Deckert was a clerical anti-Semitic agitator born at Vienna in 1846. He joined the anti-Semitic movement as a writer and political speaker. When the liberal press exposed his shady business deals, he struck back with a pamphlet claiming to prove a ritual murder at Trent. He also got a convert to publish a fake account of a murder in Russia.

A libel suit followed, and on September 15, 1893, Deckert was fined 400 florins. He kept preaching against the Jews in his magazine. The city of Vienna even gave him its Salvator gold medal in 1899. He died at Vienna on March 21, 1901, leaving money to charity without regard to religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-carolin:
Caroline Deutsch was a German novelist born at Namesto, a small Hungarian village, on February 23, 1846. Her father was a rabbi, and German language and culture ruled the home. She wrote verse while still very young, some of it printed in Berlin papers. In 1870 she qualified as a public teacher and took a permanent post on the "Jüdische Presse" of Berlin.

Caroline Deutsch later wrote chiefly for the "Hamburger Nachrichten." Her novels are mostly set in Hungary and picture the life of the Hungarian peasant and small tradesman. She married in 1875 and, though her legal name became Caroline Weiss, kept writing under her maiden name. Novels named include "Ueber Klippen" of 1894 and "In Letzter Stunde" of 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drumont-edouard:
Edouard Adolphe Drumont was a French anti-Semitic author born at Paris on May 3, 1844. His family came from Lille, where they painted porcelain. Left to earn his living at seventeen, he turned to letters. He wrote for several leading Paris papers.

In 1886 Drumont published La France Juive, in two volumes. The entry treats it as the start of the anti-Semitic movement in France. It ran through more than one hundred editions and many translations. Drumont founded the daily Libre Parole in September 1892. His Panama writings earned him three months in prison. He later sat as a deputy from Algeria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edrei-5436:
Edrei was an ancient city in the Jordan valley, now Der'at, southeast of Muzerib. Egyptian inscriptions may name it as Otara. In the Old Testament it ranks with Ashtaroth as a capital of King Og. There Og met defeat in battle.

Edrei marked a bound of Israel's conquests and lay in Manasseh's land beyond Jordan. Then it vanishes from the record for ages. Under Rome it passed from Syria's province to Arabia's. Eusebius calls it Adraa, and it held a Christian bishop's seat. Jews driven from Medina by Mohammed settled in part at Adra'at. Its underground dwellings still strike travelers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-eliezer:
Eleazar ben Hisma was a tanna of the second century. He was a pupil of Joshua ben Hananiah and of Gamaliel the Second. The Mishnah keeps several of his rulings on law. He debated points with Eleazar ben Azariah and with Akiba. One rule of his guards the pay of a hired worker.

The entry also shows his skill in homily and in science. With Joshua he gave a figure for why Amalek attacked Israel. Israel without the Law, they said, is like a reed without water. He could near count the drops in the ocean, men said. Gamaliel gave him a paid post in the academy, for he was poor. Eleazar had his own scale of worth. Law on birds' nests is core matter, he said. The stars and geometry are but spice to wisdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-solo:
Elijah ben Solomon was the famed Gaon of Wilna. He was a Lithuanian Talmudist, cabalist, grammarian, and mathematician. He was born at Wilna on April 23, 1720. He died there on Oct. 9, 1797. As a small child he showed rare gifts of mind. At seven he was said to know whole tractates by heart. From the age of ten he studied with no teacher at all. As a young man he wandered through Poland and Germany. He came home to Wilna in 1748.

Even before he turned twenty, rabbis sent him hard points of law. He never sat in a regular school as a pupil. That lack kept his mind free of the bent ways of his day. The entry calls his method his chief merit as a scholar. He brought true language study to the Talmud and its books. He aimed at the plain sense of each text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-s-chair-:
Elijah's Chair is a seat kept at every circumcision. Jews hold that Elijah, the angel of the covenant, attends the rite. He is set at the right hand of the godfather. The entry traces the custom to a tale of his zeal. In the days of Jezebel the rite faced a ban in the north. Elijah hid in a cave and pled with God. God then ruled that no circumcision take place without him.

Some read that rule as a prize for his zeal. Others read it as a guard for Israel's sake. Elijah must see in each case that the covenant holds fast. The law code Shulhan Aruk backs the custom in set words. A bench seat or a stand-alone chair must be kept for him. The circumciser names the chair in his prayer before the rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-errera-abrao-58:
Abrao Errera was an Italian banker and deputy born December 8, 1791. He died at Venice on December 25, 1860. His family traced its line to Benjamin Errera, who came from Aleppo to Venice about 1700. Tradition linked the family to the Herreras expelled from Spain in 1492.

Errera sat on the Chamber of Commerce and helped found the Stabilimento Mercantile at Venice in 1852. He served on the city council for years and sat in the National Assembly in 1848-49. During the siege of Venice he was one of five men on the Committee of Public Safety. For thirty years he led the Jewish community and directed its Talmud Torah school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exeter-5936:
Exeter, county seat of Devon, England, enters the record with a Jew fined 10 marks about 1181. The king took charge of his bonds for that sum. Under King John, Exeter Jews paid a tenth of debts recovered in court. One, called Deulecresse le Eveske, lent money to the Priory of St. Nicholas.

Later in the thirteenth century Exeter kept an archa, a debt chest, with two Christian and two Jewish record keepers. Its Jewish keepers were charged with forging a charter in 1275 and cleared. At the expulsion the king seized debts owed to about thirty-nine Exeter families, totaling 1,058 pounds and 542 quarters of corn. A small new community arose in the late eighteenth century, worshiping in a synagogue founded in 1763.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-firman-joseph-t:
Joseph Firman the Elder was a Greek rabbi and author who lived in the sixteenth century. The entry, citing Solomon Cohen, calls him a native of Seres in European Turkey. From there he went to Salonica and became rabbi there. Later he moved to the Morea in Greece.

He took charge of all the communities of that peninsula. He left many decisions that were never printed. His name appears in the responsa of Moses di Trani and Jacob ha-Levi. It also appears in those of his pupil Solomon Cohen. A grandson bore the same name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flour-10836:
Flour is the finely ground meal of any grain. The earliest way to crush grain was pounding in a mortar. That gave coarse grades of grits. Finer flour was ground between two stones. The Israelites used a mill from early times. Each household made its own flour. So the law barred taking a poor man's hand-mill in pledge. The heavy grinding work fell to women, female slaves, and captives.

The mill had two round stones. Grain was fed through a hole in the upper stone, which turned on a peg. Barley and wheat were the chief bread grains, and wheat was the finer food. A sifted fine flour was prized at twice the price of barley. In ritual use, fine flour was the rule. Barley flour served for one offering only, that of jealousy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-formstecher-sol:
Solomon Formstecher was a German rabbi born at Offenbach on July 28, 1808. He died there on April 24, 1889. He took his doctor's degree at Giessen in 1831. In 1842 he became preacher in his home city, in succession to Rabbi Metz. He held that office until his death. Through his long ministry he worked to fit Jewish religious and social life to modern civilization. He pressed those aims at conferences of German rabbis.

His chief work, printed in 1841, sets out the principles of Judaism in a system. It argues that Judaism arose of necessity and grows toward a universal religion for civilized mankind. Against paganism, it holds God apart from nature and beyond doubt. So it rejects any god-making, any emanation, and any dualism. The book ends with a history of Judaism. Other works include twelve sermons, a book on Mosaic religious teaching, and a novel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furstenfeld-643: Furstenfeld is a town in Styria, Austria, where Jews began to settle in 1278. Rudolph of Habsburg had granted the town trade rights in 1277. He also confirmed for Jews the privilege letter of July 1, 1244. The favor lasted only a short time. In 1312 a charge that Jews had killed Christian children and harmed the host set off an attack. Many Jews were burned or killed. In 1496 all Jews were expelled from Styria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gesenius-heinri:
Heinrich Friedrich Wilhelm Gesenius, a Christian Hebraist born at Nordhausen on February 3, 1786, died on October 23, 1842. He taught at Heiligenstadt in 1809, then became a theology lecturer at Halle in 1810. He stayed there until his death. His sway over Hebrew study and Old Testament reading was vast. He helped set both on a firm word-study base.

His Hebrew word book of 1810-12 became the standard work in Germany and the English world. His Hebrew grammar of 1813 ran through twenty-seven German editions. A great thesaurus, finished by Rodiger in 1858, joined word book and concordance in one. His Isaiah version and comment of 1820 rest on word study alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goitein-baruch-:
Baruch Goitein, called Benedit, was a Hungarian rabbi. He died at Högyész on Nov. 16, 1842. He had held that town's rabbinate for many years. His book "Kesef Nibḥar" appeared at Prague in 1827-28. It sets out 160 principles of rabbinical law. It gives their Talmudic sources and their uses in real cases. The entry praises its clear handling of a tangled subject.

Goitein retired in 1841. His son Hermann followed him at Högyész. His grandson Elijahu Menahem came next. The notice extends to the generation after that. One great-grandson, Hirsch, served as rabbi at Copenhagen. He wrote on optimism and pessimism in Jewish religious philosophy. Another, Eduard, held a Bavarian rabbinate. He wrote on punishment in biblical and Talmudic law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goudchaux-miche:
Michel Goudchaux was a French statesman. He was born at Nancy on March 18, 1797. He died at Paris on Dec. 27, 1862. He began as a banker in his home town. Paris received him in 1826. His honesty and charity made him vice-president of the Central Consistory. He helped found the "National," a paper for the working classes.

He fought at the barricades in the July Revolution of 1830. In 1848 he took the finance portfolio in the provisional government. He resigned after ten days, then returned under Cavaignac. He sat for Paris in the Constituent Assembly. In 1857 voters elected him deputy. He refused the oath to Napoleon III and never took his seat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guizolfi-giexul:
Zacharias de Guizolfi was a fifteenth-century prince. He ruled the Taman peninsula on the Black Sea's east coast. He descended from Simeone de Guizolfi, a Genoese Jew who gained the rule in 1419. In 1482 the Turks drove Zacharias from Matriga to the island of Matrice. He asked Genoa's Bank of St. George for 1,000 ducats to keep his Gothic allies.

Czar Ivan III invited him to Russia in a letter of March 14, 1484. Zacharias set out but was robbed and tortured by the waywode of Moldavia. Guides were promised again and again. In 1496 they waited for him until Dec. 6, but unrest among his people held him back. After eighteen years he never reached Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggites-7036: The Haggites are known from a single line. The name is the tribal name of the descendants of Haggi, second son of Gad. It rests on Numbers xxvi. 15. The Vulgate gives the name as Agitae, and the Septuagint gives it in Greek form. The entry adds nothing further: no land, no acts, and no later history are recorded for the Haggites here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanukkah-4236:
Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication, also called the Feast of the Maccabees, runs eight days from the twenty-fifth of Kislew and is kept chiefly as a festival of lights. Judas Maccabeus and the elders instituted it in 165 B.C. to mark the dedication of the altar, three years to the day after Antiochus Epiphanes had set a pagan altar on the altar of burnt offerings and sacrificed to his idol.

Josephus took the lights as a symbol of the liberty won that day. The Talmud instead ties the eight days to the one small cruse of consecrated oil, found sealed and unpolluted, that burned for eight days until new oil could be made. The entry also covers the Shammaite and Hillelite dispute over lighting eight lamps down or one lamp up, the festival liturgy, and its mention in John x. 22.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hapax-legomena-:
Hapax legomena are words or forms that occur once only. The entry counts about 1,500 of them in the Old Testament. Only about 400 are strict hapax legomena. These are new coinages. Or they are forms whose shape or sense cannot be derived from other stems. The other 1,100 occur once as forms. Yet they connect easily with common words.

Some are ordinary words that chance never repeated. Others cluster where the matter is unusual. Job is one such place. The animal lists of Leviticus xi and Deuteronomy xiv are others. So is the cargo list of Ezekiel xxvii. The entry then lists the strict hapax legomena book by book. It starts with Genesis, with gopher-wood and pistachio-nuts. A summary table of the counts follows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hausen-moses-be: Moses ben Asher Anshel Hausen, born at Copenhagen in 1752, was a Danish Talmudic scholar. He died on June 28, 1782, still a young man. A sermon commentary on Genesis, printed at Hamburg in 1787, is put under his name. The entry flags a dispute over that book. Two catalog makers give it to a Meir ben Isaac of the same city. Azulai says the printed work names no author at all. Nothing else about Hausen's life is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazzan-hebrew-a:
Hazzan names a communal official in Jewish life. The word likely comes from an Assyrian term for an overseer. In the Talmud it covers overseers of a city, a court, the Temple, and the synagogue. The synagogue hazzan brought out the Torah scrolls and put them away. He sounded trumpets to mark the start of holy days.

Over time the office grew. By the geonic age the hazzan read the Torah and led the prayers. He blew the shofar and sometimes acted as the congregation's scribe. In Poland and Germany singers stood at his sides to support the chant. The long article traces each duty with its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heart-hebr-leb-:
Heart, in Bible thought, is the seat of the inner life. The Hebrew writers gave the heart the work that later thinkers give the mind. Knowing, feeling, and willing all sit there. A person thinks in the heart, and speaks to the heart when thinking alone. Understanding is called having a heart.

Feeling fills the heart too, from hunger to joy, fear, and remorse. Resolve also starts there, so a vow or a free gift rises from the heart. The entry gathers many verses to show each use. It notes that love with all the heart means a choice the whole being backs. Animal hearts, by contrast, lack reason.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heller-isidor-7:
Isidor Heller, born on May 5, 1816, at Jung-Bunzlau in Bohemia, was an Austrian author. He was studying for the rabbinate when restlessness drove him to France in 1837. There he joined the French foreign legion. After many adventures he came home and took up magazine work at Budapest.

Politics drove him from Hungary in 1848 and from Berlin in 1852. He became private secretary to an Austrian minister and traveled with him to Constantinople. Back in Vienna he founded papers and wrote books on Prague, Austria, and the times. Illness ended his active work, and he lived his last years in seclusion. He died on Dec. 19, 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzfeld-jacob-: Jacob Herzfeld, born at Dessau on Jan. 3, 1769, was a German actor and theater manager. After studying medicine at Leipsic, he turned to acting and debuted in Vienna. In 1791 he joined the Hamburg theater under Schröder. He became assistant manager in 1798 and manager of the Stadttheater in 1812, holding that post until death. The entry says his fame rests more on management than acting. He corresponded with Goethe and Schiller. He died at Hamburg on Oct. 24, 1826.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-joseph-v: Joseph von Hirsch, born at Würzburg on July 2, 1805, was a German banker and father of Maurice de Hirsch. He entered his father's bank after his studies. On his father's death in 1841 he took charge of the firm. He was chief builder of the Bavarian Ostbahn railway. He also joined forest, farm, and factory ventures. As head of charities, he set up hospitals during the cholera outbreak of 1854 and paid for their upkeep. He died at Munich on Dec. 9, 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-pulgar-isaa:
Isaac ben Joseph ibn Pulgar was a Spanish philosopher, poet, and controversialist of the first half of the fourteenth century. Where he lived is not known. He warmly defended Isaac Albalag and finished his translation of Al-Ghazali. He had been a friend of Abner of Burgos. When Abner converted and sent him an anti-Jewish work, Pulgar answered with a stinging satire in verse.

His chief book, Support of Religion, argues in dialogue across five books. It strikes at apostates, skeptics, astrologers, literal and allegorical Bible readers, and deniers of the soul's survival. Pulgar denied that the single soul is immortal. Only the universal soul lasts, he held. Laws exist for man's sake, not God's, so virtue carries its own reward and sin its own misery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaiah-book-of-:
The Book of Isaiah article is a long survey of the biblical book's contents and makeup. Its opening claim is that variety is the book's chief note: variety of tone, style, thought, and setting. The heading presents the book as one vision about Judah and Jerusalem. The survey then shows how later parts widen that frame far beyond the heading's promise.

Chapters xiii to xxiii speak to foreign nations and were likely added after the first plan. Chapters xxiv to xxvii judge the whole earth; the entry calls them a mosaic of fragments, swinging between judgment and salvation. Chapters xxxvi to xxxix speak of Isaiah in the third person and match II Kings closely. Chapters xl to lxvi stand against a ruined Jerusalem and a captive people. The article walks through the book section by section on that basis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-javal-ernest-le: Ernest Leopold Javal, a French administrative officer, was born at Paris on Sept. 25, 1843, as a son of Leopold Javal. He served as a lieutenant in the Gardes Mobiles during the war of 1870-71. From 1877 he held a string of subprefect posts, and in 1881 he became prefect of La Creuse. In 1885 he took charge of the national school for deaf-mutes in Paris. From a long visit to America he brought back new methods there, among them hand training and speech teaching. He died at Paris on Sept. 1, 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-exponent: Jewish Exponent is a weekly paper printed in Philadelphia and Baltimore since 1887. The Jewish Exponent Publishing Company founded it. Charles Hoffman serves as editor, with Ephraim Lederer as his associate. The entry says the paper stands for American Judaism in its broadest sense and acts as the organ of the Jewish Chautauqua Society of America. Its church stance is conservative, and it looks with warmth on the Zionist movement. The notice is brief and gives no word on size, price, or readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-john-of-giscala:
John of Giscala, also called Johanan ben Levi, came from the small Galilean town of Giscala and played a big part in the great war against Rome from 66 to 70. Poor and weak in body at first, he was no eager fighter. Josephus, his mortal foe, paints him as greedy, bloody, and a ready liar, but the entry warns that portrait may be strongly colored.

When foes burned his town, John armed its people, beat the attackers, and rebuilt Giscala finer than before, with walls. Fighters gathered to him by the thousand. Money from oil sales paid his troops, and grain stored for the emperor went to his walls. His clash with Josephus, then governor of Galilee, grew from those acts into open enmity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ibn-hasa: Joseph ibn Hasan was an Arabic author of the fifteenth century or earlier. In 1467 he wrote Muhsin al-Adab, a work on culture cast in fifty kasidahs, a form of Arabic ode. Steinschneider held that the book was adapted from the Sefer ha-Musar of Isaac ibn Crispin. The entry is among the shortest in this group. It gives no birthplace, no life story, and no other works. Its whole notice rests on one line in Steinschneider's work on Arabic books by Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jude-der-9036: Der Jude was a weekly magazine published at Altona in Germany by Gabriel Riesser. It ran from April 10, 1832, to December 31, 1833. Its chief aim was to press for the social emancipation of the Jews of Europe. It printed full accounts of the debate in the English Parliament during 1833. That debate took up the proposed removal of the legal disabilities on Jews. The entry is very short, signed only with initials, and gives no word on the paper's other contents or writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judgment-divine:
Divine judgment is God's final decision, as Judge of the world, on the fate of men and nations by their deserts. Justice stands so deep in Judaism, the entry says, that every ill was read as the fruit of God's judgment and every evil deed as sure of its payback. The Flood, Sodom, Korah, and Egypt's fall are all shown in the Bible as such judgments.

The end of history was pictured as God's judgment on all nations, to be held on earth. Later writings split the judgment in two: one at the start of the Messianic kingdom and one at its close, the Day of the Great Judgment. That last assize sends souls to Paradise or to Gehenna. The entry closes with the season of repentance, which eased Jewish dread of that day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judo-german-lit:
Judaeo-German literature begins, in its earliest known piece, with a prayer book rendering of the fourteenth century. Two moral works of the fifteenth century stand at its early peak. Most early books in the tongue, though, were translations, above all of the Bible and the prayers. With the Baba Buch in the early sixteenth century came translations from other tongues, and the literature proper began.

The Ma'aseh Buch, a set of tales from Talmud and rabbis, came out at Basel in 1602 and was even rendered into German by a Christian. Works on customs and prayers were much loved, though rabbis fought prayers in the vernacular. The entry's later sweep reaches the modern Yiddish writers: folk poets, novelists, and playwrights whom it calls still unexcelled in their fields.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kairwan-arabic-:
Kairwan is a city in the regency of Tunis. It lies thirty miles inland from Susa. It stands about eighty miles south of the capital. Only Tunis is larger in the country. The city was founded in the year 670 as a fortified camp. Jews from Arabia, Egypt, and Cyrene came to it at once.

The entry follows the community through its best years. From the late eighth century to the early eleventh, it stood high among the Jews of the East. It had a synagogue, a seminary, and a poor fund. Its scholars wrote to the geonim of Babylon. Teachers such as Isaac Israeli and Ḥushiel b. Elhanan made it a center of Talmud study. The article ends with decline, raids in 1050, and hard years under later rulers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-katz-albert-923:
Albert Katz was a rabbi and author born on July 17, 1858, at Lodz, in Russian Poland. He studied at the yeshibot of Lublin and Wilna. In 1881 he went to Berlin, where he still lived when the entry was written. He preached at Fürstenwalde from 1883 to 1886. He then served a Berlin congregation for a year. From 1887 he gave all his time to writing.

Katz helped to found Berlin's society for Jewish history and literature. He also helped to found a union of literary societies at Hanover in 1894. He served that union as secretary. His books treat the blood libel and the true Talmud Jew. Others deal with the Jews of the Caucasus and of China. A set of his stories also appeared, at Prague in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ketubah-or-ketu:
A ketubah is a Jewish marriage contract. It sets down a sum owed to the wife. The sum falls due at her husband's death or on divorce. The rabbis set up the rule to check free divorce. No consent of the wife is needed for a divorce, so the debt guarded her. The least sum was 200 zuz for a virgin bride. For other brides it was 100 zuz.

The long article prints the full form of the contract in English. It then explains the lien the ketubah lays on all the husband's land. A wife could lose her claim for set faults, which the entry lists. It could also be gathered many years after a death or divorce. The last part traces old forms and ornaments. Italian contracts of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were the most richly adorned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kir-9336: Kir was a people and a country subject to the Assyrian empire. Scripture names it as the place the Syrians came from before settling north of Palestine. Tiglath-pileser sent his prisoners there after the conquest of Damascus. Isaiah mentions Kir together with Elam. The Septuagint omits the name in that passage altogether. The entry ends plainly: so far, the place has not been identified.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohut-alexander:
Alexander Kohut, a rabbi and Orientalist born on April 22, 1842, at Felegyhaza in Hungary, died in New York on May 25, 1894. He came from a family of rabbis and learned late, reaching age eight without Hebrew or Hungarian schooling. After gymnasium study and Talmud work he went to Breslau. He took a doctorate at Leipsic and a rabbinical diploma in 1867.

Kohut's life work was his Talmud dictionary, the Aruch Completum. Begun from seven manuscripts of Nathan ben Jehiel's ʿAruk, it ran to more than 4,000 double-column pages across 1878-92. In Hungary he held pulpits at Stuhlweissenburg, Fünfkirchen, and Grosswardein. In 1885 he became rabbi of Congregation Ahavath Chesed in New York and helped found the Jewish Theological Seminary there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krefeld-4736:
Krefeld, a Prussian factory town near Düsseldorf on the Rhine, saw its first known Jewish settler in 1617, Jacob of Mörs. Growth was slow. In 1702 the town passed to Prussia with the community still small. A synagogue built at the Jews' own cost came in 1765. Only eleven families, about seventy people, lived there in 1780.

Full rights arrived under French rule, then narrowed again after Prussia returned in 1814. A new synagogue was dedicated on June 17, 1853. Rabbis named run from Löb Karlsburg in 1808 to J. Horowitz, in post since 1869. The entry closes with a town count of 106,928 people, including 1,800 Jews, and notes craft and school aid societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krysa-judah-lob: Judah Löb ben Nathan Krysa, a Frankist leader who lived in Galicia in the eighteenth century, served as rabbi at Nadworna. He joined the Frankist movement as soon as it arose and became its leader. Sent to speak for the sect against the Talmudists, he made a Christian confession of faith on May 25, 1759. He read the cross as a sign of a trinity named in the Zohar. He also claimed that the Talmud orders the use of Christian blood. In 1759 he embraced Christianity, like Jacob Frank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lapwing-9636: Lapwing is the Authorized Version's rendering of the Hebrew word dukifat, listed among unclean birds in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The Revised Version's hoopoe has the backing of the old Greek and Latin versions and is now widely taken as right. The hoopoe winters in Egypt and returns to Palestine in spring. It feeds on insects in dung heaps and wet ground. Talmud reading takes the bird as the mountain cock, tied to the Shamir legend and to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-sylvain-98:
Sylvain Lévi, a French Orientalist, was born at Paris on March 28, 1863. He studied at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes and won his agrégation in 1886. He taught Sanskrit there from 1889, and added lectures on the religions of India. In 1894 he became professor of Sanskrit at the Collège de France.

Lévi's "Théâtre Indien" of 1890 is the standard work on its subject, the entry says. He also wrote on sacrifice in the Brahmanas and edited Sanskrit texts. In 1897 the state sent him on a mission to India. He has led both the Paris linguistics society and the Société des Etudes Juives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewysohn-ludwig: Ludwig Lewysohn, a German rabbi, was born on April 15, 1819, at Schwersenz, Posen. He died at Stockholm on May 26, 1901. He studied Oriental subjects in Berlin and took his doctorate at Halle in 1847. In 1848 he became preacher at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. In 1851 he was called to Worms, and in 1859 to Stockholm. He served at Stockholm until 1893, when he resigned. His books treat the grave inscriptions of Worms and the zoology of the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-moritz-1013:
Moritz Löw, a Hungarian astronomer, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Mako, Hungary, in 1841, he studied at the universities of Leipzig and Vienna. He earned his doctorate from the University of Budapest in 1867. After graduating he worked as an assistant at the Leipzig observatory.

The article records his move to Berlin in 1883. There he became a section chief in the Prussian geodetic institute, with the title of professor. His work joined astronomy to land surveying, fixing exact positions and pole heights. The entry lists his main writings, on planets, passage instruments, and surveys in East Prussia, Helgoland, and the Harz mountains. He died at Steglitz, Berlin, in 1900. Short as it is, the entry preserves a Jewish scientist's place in German state science.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabees-the-g:
Maccabees, the name of the Hasmonean family, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The entry explains that Maccabeus was first the surname of Judas alone. He was the third son of Mattathias and the family's most heroic warrior. After he took command, his name spread to all his kin and followers. Hence the title Books of the Maccabees.

The article then hunts for the name's origin. Scholars read it as the hammer, a title earned by Judas's heroism. Others link it to the banner of the tribe of Gad, or to initials of a verse from Exodus. One view takes it from a word meaning the extinguisher. The entry admits the question stays unsettled after all these efforts. It also notes the Talmud never uses the name, calling the family simply the Hasmoneans. The piece shows how a famous name can resist every explanation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-of-mers:
Menahem of Merseburg was a German halakist of the first half of the fifteenth century. Isidore Singer and Gotthold Weil profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob Weil praised him as a great and prominent scholar. His collection of legal notes was printed as an appendix to Weil's responsa. It was treated as authoritative across the communities of Saxony. It covered marriage law, the civil code, and communal taxation.

His boldest act concerned the law of mi'un. Under that law, a girl married in her minority could dissolve the union on coming of age, without a divorce. Her mother or brothers had made the marriage. Menahem judged the practice immoral. He repealed the law on his own authority. The next century set that ruling aside. The entry praises his range. Where German Jews of his day debated petty liturgical questions, his book engages everything that concerns Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molo-francisco-:
Francisco Molo, a Dutch financier of the seventeenth century, is sketched by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1679 he settled in Amsterdam as financial agent of John III, king of Poland — though De Barrios, his contemporary, called him a Spanish Jew. His ability made him a power at The Hague.

The Dutch state thanked him with two years' exemption from taxes. His influence with the States General was so great, the entry claims, that Louis XIV was enabled through Molo's mediation to conclude the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697. A short entry, resting on Dutch histories — Koenen, Lamberti, and Wagenaar — for a backstage figure of European diplomacy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-musaf-11236:
Musaf is the additional offering, and the additional prayer that replaced it, in Jewish worship. Cyrus Adler and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. In the Temple, extra sacrifices followed the morning offering on Sabbaths, New Moons, and festivals. When the Temple fell, prayer took their place.

The article sets out when Musaf is said, soon after the Torah reading, and how the rabbis made it a duty for every person. Its middle blessing quotes the day's sacrifice from the Book of Numbers. For the New Year it grows into the longest prayer of the year, with the kingship, remembrance, and shofar verses. Through it all runs a prayer for the Temple restored.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nassau-11336:
Nassau was a German dukedom later joined to Prussia. Its entry was written by Gotthard Deutsch for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article traces Jewish life there from early medieval times. A Jew named Levi of Lorch is named in a record from 1266. In 1865 the dukedom held 6,995 Jews among 465,636 people in all.

Medieval attacks hit towns such as Limburg, Diez, and Montabaur. Jews there paid special taxes for many years. Those taxes ended in the early 1840s, step by step. Nassau then set up district rabbis and a school for Jewish teachers. Full religious freedom came in 1848, with more gains in 1861. The entry names rabbis such as Abraham Geiger of Wiesbaden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nemenyi-neumann:
Ambrosius Neményi was a Hungarian writer and lawmaker. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Peczel in 1852. Until 1871 he bore the family name Neumann. He studied law at Vienna and Paris.

Neményi worked on the staff of the Pester Lloyd. In 1884 his district sent him to Parliament. He served on committees for economics, transport, and finance. He was secretary of the budget committee as well. His books treat Rabelais and parliamentary discipline. Others cover Hungary's railways, its state, and its offices. From 1896 he edited the Pesti Napló as chief. He died in Budapest on Dec. 13, 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nieto-isaac-115:
Isaac Nieto was haham of London's Portuguese congregation. Joseph Jacobs and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1702, son of David Nieto. He died at London in 1774. In 1733 he was appointed hakam ha-shalem officially.

He gave up that post in 1741 and went abroad. Home again in 1747, he worked as a notary. The congregation recalled him as ab bet din in 1751. A violent dispute over court titles soon arose. He resigned by letter on March 17, 1757. That July he was barred from acting as assessor. His lasting work is his prayer-book translation. Its two volumes ground all later English versions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nyari-alexander:
Alexander Nyári was a Hungarian critic of art. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1861 at Zala-Egerszeg. He trained at Vienna and gained a diploma in building in 1884. He then went to Paris and Berlin. There he read in thought and the past of art.

Nyári took his doctor's degree at Leipzig in 1891. His state sent him to hunt for fine old works in Hungary. He sought art from the days of King Matthias. He later held posts at the state museum in Budapest. He also taught the past of art at a trade school. In 1894 he took charge of the state art hall. His chief books treat a portrait painter and a great church.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-morri:
Morris Simeon Oppenheim was an English lawyer in London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in London in the year 1824. He died there on January 3, 1883. His father was clerk to the Great Synagogue.

Morris served as clerk to a Jewish school group first. While in that post, he read for the bar. He was called to the bar in the year 1858. He worked as a pleader on the south east circuit. He gave much time to the work of his flock. In 1869 he joined the Board of Deputies. He sat on its law and Parliament groups there. He wrote on the marriage laws as they touched Jews. He drafted the by-laws for the joint synagogues of London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pastoureaux-119:
The Pastoureaux were bands of French shepherds who rose in religious frenzy. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry covers two outbreaks, one in 1251 and one in 1320. Both waves turned quickly to violence against Jews.

In 1251 a leader called the Master of Hungary preached a crusade in Picardy. His followers attacked towns and robbed Jews at Bourges. The 1320 wave was far worse in the south. Mobs killed the Jews of Toulouse and destroyed many communities. The violence spread into Spain before the King of Aragon crushed it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perjury-12036:
Perjury is the breaking of an oath or a solemn lie. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible counts it among the greatest sins.

Yet the Bible sets no human penalty for perjury. God himself is left to punish the liar. A false oath in court or trade is still banned. The rabbis later sorted the sin into four classes. Each class carried its own set punishment. A witting liar faced lashes, an unwitting one an offering.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-behrendt-1:
Behrendt Pick was a German scholar of ancient coins. He was born at Posen on December 21, 1861. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Mommsen himself had trained Pick at Berlin. His doctorate in classical philology came at Berlin in 1884.

On Mommsen's advice Pick chose inscriptions and coins. He taught archaeology at Zurich from 1889. In 1893 he moved to the ducal library at Gotha. He later directed its great coin collection. He also lectured on coins at Jena from 1896. His chief work catalogs the coins of Dacia and Moesia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahabi-david-12:
David Rahabi was an Indian calendar maker from Cochin. Joseph Jacobs and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there in the mid eighteenth century. His father Ezekiel was a wealthy merchant.

The article says David took over the family business in 1771. He still found much time for study. His fame rests on Ohel Dawid, printed at Amsterdam in 1785. That work deals with the origin of the Hebrew calendar. A brief source note ends the entry. Readers meet a merchant scholar whose one book treated a hard dating topic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ricchi-raphael-:
Immanuel Hay Ricchi was an Italian rabbi, cabalist, and poet born at Ferrara. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Sources give his birth as 1688 or 1693. He was killed near Cento on February 25, 1743.

The article says he lost his father as a small child. An uncle and then a cousin raised the orphan. He studied Talmud under Nathan Pinkerle at Alessandria. He tutored in wealthy homes across northern Italy. At Venice he opened a school of his own. Triest ordained him rabbi in 1717. Love of Cabala drew him to Safed in 1718. There he studied Luria and Hayyim Vital. An epidemic forced him back to Europe in 1720. Pirates captured his ship on the voyage home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenbach-hyman: Hyman Pollock Rosenbach was an American journalist in Philadelphia, born there on September 16, 1858. Cyrus Adler wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Rosenbach worked for the Public Ledger and other city papers before his early death in 1892. In 1883 he published The Jews of Philadelphia Prior to 1800. The entry calls that book one of the earliest works on American Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rules-of-hillel:
The Seven Rules of Hillel are the classic guides for interpreting Scripture in rabbinic Judaism. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Hillel I gave them to the sons of Bathyra as chief guides.

By these rules, laws are drawn out of the Torah's own words. One argues from the lesser case to the greater, or back again. Another argues by analogy between passages sharing a word or phrase. Others apply one passage's rule to its kin, or read the general by the particular. The last rule reads a passage by its own context.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomon-max-130:
Max Salomon was a German physician born at Sleswick on April 5, 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree in 1861 after study at Heidelberg, Berlin, and Kiel.

Salomon served as a Prussian army surgeon from 1866 to 1870. He then practised at Hamburg, and from 1874 in Berlin. His history of glycosuria runs from Hippocrates to the nineteenth century. Other works treat diseases of the nervous system and of the lungs. A late book fights tuberculosis as a disease of the people. Berlin conferred on him the title Sanitätsrath, a medical councilor's rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-nath: Samuel ben Nathan was an amora of the early part of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He appears mostly as the transmitter of sayings of Hama b. Hanina, in Shabbat and elsewhere. Once the direction reverses: Hama passes on a tradition of Samuel's own.
