Yufei Mandy Wu and co-authors published this study in 2023. It studies asylum-seeking mothers in a community program called Welcome Haven. The program mixes social support with nature-based activity. Questionnaires measured wellbeing, self-belief, basic need satisfaction, and stress. Interviews then explored how the mothers experienced the workshops. Feeling connected to others stood out as the strongest predictor of wellbeing.

Stress that adapts rather than crushes carried the effect of need satisfaction into wellbeing. Attending the program came with lower stress and higher wellbeing. Mothers described belonging built through contact with fellow asylum seekers and staff. Access to information and chances to speak for themselves added a sense of power. The authors warn that structural pressures of resettlement dwarf what any program can lift. Still, connection and stress relief are levers worth funding.
pmc-10672636:
Thomas Edison dela Cruz and co-authors compare five Usnea lichens from the northern Philippines as possible sources of new drugs against hard-to-treat bacteria, in a 2023 study. They gathered 46 lichen samples, named each species by its form and chemistry, and tested extracts against the ESKAPE group of drug-resistant germs plus standard test strains and a yeast.

The extracts worked best against Gram-positive bacteria, including strains that resist common drugs. Chemical tests found 24 lichen acid peaks, and one test that pairs a thin-layer plate with live bacteria pointed to three acids as the active ones. The results mark these common lichens as a promising place to hunt for fresh antibacterial compounds.
pmc-10687436:
Wu Xiang and co-authors published a mini-review in 2023 on fecal microbiota transplantation as a novel strategy for treating Alzheimer's disease. In the transplantation, gut microorganisms from a healthy donor are transferred into a patient's gut. The gut microbiota is now known to influence how Alzheimer's disease begins and progresses.

The review summarizes the mechanisms by which the transplantation may help. The pathways named include reducing inflammation, regulating the amyloid-beta protein that marks the disease, and strengthening synaptic plasticity, the connections between nerve cells. Two further pathways run through short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbes, and through histone acetylation, chemical tagging that controls gene activity. The authors hope the transplantation will earn a place in both the prevention and the treatment of the disease. It is presented as a fresh, low-risk addition to the tools available.
pmc-10689836:
Zhe Wang and three co-authors untangle activity and obesity causation in a 2023 genetics paper. Does inactivity cause obesity, or does obesity cause inactivity? Mendelian randomization uses genes as natural experiments to test direction. The team drew on their own genome wide study of leisure activity and screen time.

Simple analyses suggested effects running both ways. Adding years of schooling into the model changed the picture. More moderate to vigorous activity then caused lower body mass. Higher body mass caused more screen time, not the reverse. Schooling itself raised activity, cut screen time, and lowered weight. The results single out education as a quiet driver of the whole web. Activity promotion still earns support as a cause of leanness.
pmc-10691736:
Carlos Gómez-Gallego and Hani El-Nezami open a journal topic on shaping gut microbes for better health, in an editorial from two thousand twenty-three. Gut microbes affect digestion, immunity, and body chemistry. Shifts in the mix have been linked to a range of diseases, though proof can be hard to repeat.

The topic gathers fifteen papers on ways to shift the mix. Tools range from diet and live microbe foods to stool transplants. Gains were reported for immunity, weight, diabetes, and gut disorders. Stool transplant success hinged on dose, route, and donor choice. The editors stress care fitted to each person, since mixes vary so much.
pmc-10693636:
Kaiyuan Liu and colleagues published a computing study in 2023. They built a program that reads new peptides from scratch. Peptides are short chains of amino acids. Lab instruments produce spectra from these chains. Finding the sequence without a database is hard. Older programs often miss or misread many spectra. The new program is called PepNet. It uses a fully convolutional neural network.

PepNet takes a spectrum in and returns a sequence. It also returns a confidence score for its answer. Training used millions of spectra from human peptide libraries. Tests beat two leading older programs on accuracy. PepNet also ran much faster on graphics processors. It found sequences that database searches had missed. Proteomics labs could use it beside standard search tools.
pmc-10694136:
Młynarek-Żak and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three on two new aluminum-rich glassy alloys. Aluminum metallic glasses are hard to form, limiting their use. The team cast two alloys mixing aluminum with nickel, iron, and yttrium. Bulk ingots turn out fully crystalline under X-ray checks. Rapidly spun ribbons of the same mixes form glassy structures instead. Element maps show even spread across ribbon cross-sections. Neutron tests reveal tiny crystals inside the glassy ribbons.

Heat scans mark where each ribbon starts to crystallize. The two mixes crystallize at different temperatures. Structure is checked by several microscope and diffraction tools. The work updates knowledge on low-aluminum glassy alloys.
pmc-10695136:
Richard Gammon leads a team of ten authors reviewing patient blood management as, in part, a supply strategy: every transfusion avoided is a donated unit preserved. The review walks through donor screening and selection worldwide, noting how questionnaires and physical exam rules tightened over the past decade for donor and recipient safety. Transfusion practice challenges get equal attention.

Two pressures dominate: the COVID-19 pandemic's disruption of the blood supply chain and an aging donor base. The authors promote autologous donation and other conservation strategies as buffers. Replacement donor policy and upper age limits, they argue, should follow local demography, and hospital executives must champion the program for it to work. Stewardship of donors and of patients is presented as one job.
pmc-10696236:
Tarapon Setthawong, Theerawech Namwongsa, and Chinnakhet Ketsuwan report a new way to remove a large stone from a urine tube. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Big stones in the ureter can cause sharp pain, infection, blood in urine, and harm to the kidney. A scope through the tube is the favoured route, but it can fail when the stone load is large.

They treat one patient with a mini scope system that works from below, with a vacuum to clear debris. The tool was first made for kidney work through the skin. Here it clears the whole stone in one go. The patient heals in full, with no ill effects.
pmc-10698036:
Thapa and co-authors study how SAM and SAH balance sets worm lifespan. Adding SAH extends life in model organisms. The team built worms with a fault in the AHCY-1 enzyme. The fault mirrors a human disease change at the same site. It should slow SAH breakdown and raise its level.

Mutant worms aged more slowly than normal worms. Their SAM fell while SAH rose a moderate amount. Long life needed AMPK, its activator VRK-1, and DAF-16. The authors say the SAM to SAH ratio may set lifespan. The model can probe methionine metabolism in aging.
pmc-10700036:
Ritah Bakesiima and colleagues follow refugee teenagers using modern contraceptives in northern Uganda. Their prospective cohort study from twenty twenty-three sits inside a larger trial. Teenagers show the lowest contraceptive adherence worldwide. Refugee adolescents face extra barriers that were poorly documented.

Nearly three hundred new users joined at Palabek refugee settlement. Follow-up visits ran at one, three, and six months. The study measured who kept using their chosen method. Reasons for stopping were recorded at each visit. Predictors of steady use were tested with standard models. The parent trial studied peer counselling for contraceptive acceptance. Results can guide family planning services in refugee settings.
pmc-10704736:
A natural sugar can switch on the cell's recycling system, but the sugar dissolves so eagerly in water that little reaches its target. Yuan Zhong and co-authors pack it into tiny gels in a 2023 study aimed at clogged arteries.

Their nanogels carry the sugar, trehalose, chemically bound and then releasable, making up more than half the particle weight. The spheres stayed small, even-sized, and stable in blood-like fluids, and they did not burst red blood cells. In fatty foam cells, the gels revived recycling and helped clear lipids. In mice prone to artery plaque, treatment shrank plaques while recycling markers rose. The work offers a delivery route for a promising but slippery compound.
pmc-10705136:
Qiuxia Wei and co-authors review how well deep learning reads medical images to diagnose the main form of liver cancer, in this 2023 paper. They searched five databases for studies published before July 2023. Eligible work built or used deep learning to spot this cancer in scans or other medical images. From forty-eight candidate studies, thirty gave data firm enough to pool.

Across those studies, the models caught about eighty-nine percent of cancers and cleared about ninety percent of non-cases. The summary accuracy score was high. Results held up across scan types, including ultrasound, magnetic scans, and CT. The models also matched clinician-level performance in the comparisons made. The authors warn that varied reporting and study differences may inflate the numbers, and they urge stricter reporting rules.
pmc-10706836:
Cathryn Payne and a team of co-authors studied whether fear of harm shapes how adults buy hair products, in two thousand twenty-three. Many personal care products carry chemicals that can disrupt hormones. The survey covered adults linked to a university in the Northeast of the United States.

More than five hundred people rated their concern about product harms. Those who strongly agreed that consumers should worry were far more likely to use healthy product apps. They also more often read ingredient labels and looked for natural or non-toxic labels. The authors suggest that raising awareness of product harms could nudge shoppers toward safer choices.
pmc-10707736:
Chengyun Tao and colleagues test how repeated heating and cooling cycles wear down cement concrete. Bridges and highways endure both cyclic vehicle loads and temperature swings for decades. The study subjected concrete specimens to a typical temperature range and up to three hundred temperature differential cycles, then measured axial compressive strength, ultrasonic properties, and compressive fatigue life.

Strength did not decline monotonically. It first increased, rising by about a tenth at sixty cycles, then returned to near its initial value around one hundred twenty cycles. Thereafter it fell steadily, down about a fifth by three hundred cycles. The non-monotonic pattern suggests early cycles can densify or cure the material before thermal microcracking dominates. For infrastructure in swing-prone climates, thermal cycle count becomes a durability variable of its own.
pmc-10709436:
Ter Wee and colleagues test in twenty twenty-three a hidden flaw in scans used to spot loose knee implants. The scan method loads the shin bone from side to side and measures implant shift. But load also bends the bone itself, which could inflate the shift reading and blur the line between loose and fixed implants.

Using donor legs with knee implants, they scanned each leg first loose, then cemented fixed. The bone's top moved notably against its base under load. Shift readings against the whole bone overstated movement for fixed implants. Measuring against the top part of the bone alone cut that error. Telling loose from fixed improved once bone bending was taken into account.
pmc-10709936:
Ye Yang and co-authors study a small peptide in the fluid around human eggs that helps those eggs mature, in a 2023 paper. Lab maturation of eggs is a tool in fertility care, but it works less well than hoped. Since eggs grow bathed in follicular fluid, the team compared the fluid's peptide mix between ripe and unripe follicles to find what helps.

One peptide stood out: C3a-peptide, a fragment snipped from a complement protein of the immune system. In cultured human and mouse eggs, it pushed more eggs to reach the mature stage. It did so by gathering the cell's actin skeleton and helping the chromosome spindle move into place. It did not raise the rate of chromosome number errors, a key safety point. The authors propose the peptide as an additive to improve lab egg maturation.
pmc-10710636:
Ryo Mizuta and nine co-authors look for immune structures inside glioblastoma, a deadly brain tumor, in a 2023 study. In other cancers, clusters of immune cells called tertiary lymphoid structures mark a better outlook. Whether such clusters form in brain tumors, and what builds them, was unknown.

The team stained tumor samples from 54 patients and found the structures in five of them. Fresh samples from twelve patients showed that tumors with the structures held more T and B immune cells. Gene readouts from 43 cases showed stronger immune activation signals where the structures were present, including a T cell marker and a chemical call signal. The study is a first step toward coaxing these helpful clusters to form in brain tumors.
pmc-10713536:
Novo and seven co-authors hunt gene marks tied to low blood lime in fresh-calved dairy cows in this twenty twenty-three study. At first milk, cows lose lime fast into the first feed and the milk that follows. Cows that can not keep up fall ill with milk fever or a mild form of it.

Inside, blood lime was gauged in more than two thousand cows in the first three days past birth. Gene codes were filled out in two steps from chip data to full code reads. Top marks sat in or near genes for lime balance, D-vitamin haul, and fuel use. Some sat near guard genes as well. The work lays a base for breed and care tools to cut the ill.
pmc-10716136:
Wolfgang Simeth and a large team of co-authors built a fine scale model of a heavy fermion magnet. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, deals with CeIn3, a cerium compound. Heavy electron metals mix two natures: electrons that roam and electrons that sit. That clash spawns odd states, from strange superconductivity to hidden order. A full microscopic account of such a magnet has been a long stand challenge.

The team gives a Kondo lattice model tuned to this compound's facts. Reads from neutron and other probes set its terms. Readers in quantum materials get a base model for a class of metals whose states still spawn debate. Such a model can test which forces spawn the odd phases.
pmc-10723036:
Giacomo Marino and a team of co-authors present a data hub for diabetes research, in two thousand twenty-three. Gene activity data sets on diabetes are produced fast, but much of that published data goes unused for new discoveries. Their hub gathers hundreds of curated data sets behind a friendly web portal.

Each study in the hub has its own page with plots, gene difference analysis, and single-gene lookups. A chatbot built on a large language model helps users pick the right tool for their question. A further module pairs gene sets from the data with like sets in the literature and drafts a possible explanation. The code and site are public.
pmc-10732136:
Maria Chiara Storer, Katarzyna Zator, Derek Reynolds, and Christopher Hunter turn charge maps of molecules into point models of weak bonding, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Each point marks a spot where a molecule can grip a partner, with strength values matched to lab measures. Polar spots come from sharp charge peaks, and flat spots from orbital clues.

The point model feeds a liquid model that predicts how compounds split between oil and water. Over fifteen hundred compounds were predicted with small error. Crystal maps built from the points also price each grip in a complex. Readers in drug and solvent design get a compact way to price weak bonds.
pmc-10735336:
Tam Perry, Kent Key, Elena Flores, Vanessa Rorai, and Jamie Mitchell describe recruitment struggles in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Their subject is a health research registry meant to connect Black older adults in Flint, Michigan with university studies. A Community Advisory Board partnered with three local universities, backed by a National Institute on Aging grant. The team launched free community health programming and a Participant Research Pool for non-invasive studies.

Despite monthly virtual seminars, a new website, tailored print and video materials, and a research symposium, enrollment stayed severely low after a year. The authors conclude that more frequent in-person programming, stronger use of board members' networks, and more traditional advertising are needed to reach the target population.
pmc-10735536:
Narda Ipakchi, a solo author, presents work in 2023 on state plans for aging and long term care in the United States. Strong long term services and supports systems need lasting plans, the author argues. Multisector Plans for Aging are state blueprints, often led by a governor, that guide policy, programs, and funding over ten or more years toward aging well in the community.

More than a dozen states and the capital district have such plans or are building them. For the first time, a national state scorecard gives states credit for having one. The presentation reports scorecard findings on these plans and discusses their wider role in state leadership on aging.
pmc-10736036:
Jaesung An and Soonhyung Kwon study how older adults read a stressful event as either a spur or a burden, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. They build on a stress model that ties this reading to traits like optimism, hardiness, and a sense of control.

Little past work had tested that model in older people. The authors ask whether a sense of control, optimism, social support, and spiritual belief shape how older adults respond to a stressor. They also ask whether free-time pursuits change those effects. Daily leisure matters here because it supports control, good mood, and bounce-back strength in later life. pmc-10736136:
Mercedes Sotos Prieto, Javier Maroto-Rodriguez, Mario Delgado-Velandía, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It asks whether living a full Mediterranean lifestyle, not just eating the diet, protects older adults in Spain from becoming frail.

The team followed 1,880 adults aged sixty and over for about three years. A twenty-seven-item index scored food choices, habits around meals, and daily life such as activity, rest, and social time. Frailty was counted when a person met at least three of five signs, like exhaustion, weakness, and slow walking. Over the follow-up, 136 people became frail. Those in the middle scoring group had slightly lower odds than the lowest group, and the paper tests the top group and each part of the lifestyle in turn. The work weighs lifestyle as a whole against frailty.
pmc-10736636:
McGuire and Holt described in twenty twenty-three how to build lasting public health programs for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. No proven way exists yet to prevent these conditions. Public health can still slow their impact through risk reduction, early diagnosis, and better training for front-line health workers.

Programs last when they change systems, environments, and policies, not just habits. That approach widens uptake, extends program life, and links efforts across regions. The authors draw on BOLD programs, a United States effort to build dementia infrastructure, for examples. Their talk covers raising awareness, spotting disease early, and coordinating with aging services, including support for dementia caregivers. Partners from many sectors are part of the model.
pmc-10736736:
Joan Davitt and co-authors describe how Maryland built a research partnership to improve adult protective services, in a 2023 paper. The service guards older and disabled adults who may face harm or neglect. The state office joined with a university school of social work. Their shared aim was a steady review process that checks quality and fixes weak spots.

The partners had to build logic models, pick fair measures of success, and turn office records into data fit for study. They also had to win support from state and local staff. Staff shortages, weak technology, and tight access to records slowed the work. The paper shares the tactics they used, as a guide for other states trying the same link.
pmc-10737136:
Miseon Kang, Seolah Lee, Jungup Lee, and Hyo Jung Lee asked what carries the benefit of digital skills into life satisfaction for older adults, in this 2023 study. Using technology well in late life is widely praised, but the path from skill to happiness runs through other factors. The team used a 2020 Korean survey of 1,680 adults aged fifty-five and over.

Digital skills raised life satisfaction mostly through the benefits people felt they got from going online. That middle step was stronger for older adults who lived alone, as if online benefits filled a gap left by a quiet household. The direct link between skill and satisfaction, though, held only for those living with others. The authors say family setup should shape how digital help for seniors is designed.
pmc-10737436:
Seaman and seven co-authors ask how well health teams use full health checks for older adults with cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-three. These checks cover many needs at once, from mood to strength to daily tasks. The team spoke with doctors and nurses who care for these patients.

They held eight long talks, each about an hour, and read the notes with care. Staff said the full checks help a lot and should be used for all new patients. In real life, time is short, so staff use brief screens instead. That means some needs get missed. Strong team leads and good support made full checks more likely to happen.
pmc-10737636:
Hoang Nguyen and four co-authors read how Asian Medicare patients are sent to skilled nursing care after hospital stays. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, used the twenty nineteen national Medicare data. Past work found Asian residents of such homes the most frail and the most clouded in thought of all groups. If send rates drive that was not known. The team set Asian rates next to Black, Hispanic, and White rates for six base ills.

The ills ran from bone breaks and heart failure to sepsis, in patients age sixty-six and up. Asian patients had the second lowest send rates for near all ills. Joint replacement broke the run. Readers in elder care get a gap that may mean Asian elders reach such care late and more frail.
pmc-10738136:
Nahyun Kim and co-authors study how online contact shapes grief after losing a spouse in a 2023 paper. Widowhood is among the most painful of adult experiences, and support from family and friends is a known buffer. But support now flows through phones and platforms too. The authors ask whether social media communication changes the link between widowhood and depressive symptoms.

They separate four kinds of online contact: direct messaging, social media, video sharing, and community forums. Using a large Korean survey from 2021 with over five thousand respondents, they test which kinds soften, or fail to soften, the widowhood effect. Different channels may play very different roles in mourning. The findings can guide support programs toward the channels that actually help.
pmc-10738336:
John Fitch, Rachel Williams, Dennis Myers, and Michael Devin compared home sensors with caregiver surveys in a paper from twenty twenty-three. Their sensor system tracks daily activities in the home around the clock. The survey asks caregivers each month how well a person manages daily tasks such as washing, dressing, and cooking.

The study followed more than a hundred pairs of care recipients and caregivers for up to eighteen months. Sensor scores matched survey scores well. The system could even detect a one-point change in basic and in more complex daily task scores. The authors note limits in comparing live sensing with surveys filled in from memory, and they propose new measures for later study.
pmc-10739036:
Victoria Steiner and seven co-authors report early results for a play device for people with dementia in a paper from twenty twenty-three. The device, called the Tovertafel, projects games onto a table. It comes from the Netherlands and aims to spur social, physical, and mental activity through play.

Residents with moderate to severe dementia played in short group sessions on weekdays for four weeks. Staff saw more engagement during the games. Tests showed fewer memory-related problem behaviors and less apathy during the play period than before it. Mood and disruptive behavior did not change in a clear way. The authors see promise but call the results early.
pmc-10739536:
Ashley Morgan and co-authors study in 2023 whether older adults accept hard strength training at home after injury. The program uses short bursts of hard effort with everyday movements, mixed with easy recovery periods. A physiotherapist leads it by video call.

Early interviews with eight participants, aged fifty-five to eighty-one, show a positive view overall. All reported enjoyment or that the program met their hopes. Some exercises were liked more than others. No technical problems arose, and many valued the convenience of an online format. Most preferred shorter work intervals with short rests.
pmc-10741736:
Chandrashekar Murugesh Yavagal and co-authors tested ways to clear a hardy germ from infected baby-tooth root canals in the lab, in a study published in 2023. The germ often survives standard cleaning and can spoil treatment. The cleaning fluid under study is a bleach-like solution used in dentistry, in both liquid and gel forms.

Extracted teeth were infected for a month, then cleaned in groups: plain salt water, the fluid, or the gel, each with or without light from a small laser. The gel paired with laser light left no growing germs at all. Laser use clearly improved cleaning over the same rinse without it. The authors back the gel-plus-laser pairing as an effective choice for children's root canal care.
pmc-10742136: Alessandro Vittori argues, in a 2023 editorial, that pain care for children needs action now. Pediatric anesthesia, the field behind children's pain control, faces growing needs for deeper specialization. The piece calls on the field to treat children's pain as a distinct discipline deserving trained experts, rather than a scaled-down version of adult care.
pmc-10742736:
Marta Labrador leads a team profiling young teen gamers in this twenty twenty-three study. Concern is growing about gaming that slips out of control, yet the line between keen play and problem play is blurry. The team studied school students in Madrid aged twelve to sixteen.

Three quarters of the students, more than fifteen hundred in all, said they played video games. The team sorted players into profiles by their habits and looked for traits tied to problem gaming. Drawing these profiles helps schools and parents spot risky patterns early, without treating all gaming as harmful.
pmc-10747236:
Kim and a team of colleagues tested whether a protein called USP11 predicts prostate cancer outcomes in twenty twenty-three. USP11 protects PTEN, a tumor suppressor that restrains a major growth pathway. The team asked whether staining levels in tumor tissue track with how advanced or dangerous a cancer is.

Tissue microarrays from cancer patients and normal controls were stained and scored by a pathologist blinded to outcomes. Cancer tissue stained more weakly than nearby benign tissue. Weaker staining went with higher PSA levels, higher Gleason scores, and more advanced stage. Patients whose tumors stained positively enjoyed better clinical and biochemical recurrence-free survival. The authors conclude USP11 staining intensity is a valuable prognostic factor that reflects both recurrence risk and disease aggressiveness.
pmc-10747936:
Valentin-Adrian Niță and co-authors tested a sensor kit that coaches fencers on balance in real time, in a study published in 2023. Fencing rests on poise and fine movement control. Their kit reads a fencer's sway live and feeds it back by sight or by touch vibration. Thirty fencers trained for five weeks in three groups of ten: plain training, sight feedback, and touch feedback.

All groups gained, as five weeks of drills would give. The sight feedback group gained most, about fifteen in a hundred, and its gain alone cleared the statistical bar. The plain and touch groups gained under five in a hundred each. The authors say live sight of one's own sway is the active ingredient. The kit could fit into club training with ease.
pmc-10750436:
Qiu-han Zheng and six co-authors test a herb pair gainst joint flare ill through web math and lab proof. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Web reads drew eighteen like parts and thirty-four core marks for the pair, with flare and two growth paths in play. Fit runs showed two plant parts bind flare marks tight.

In rats with joint flare and in dish cells, the pair cut paw swell and joint scores by dose. Flare parts in blood and cells fell. A growth path was hushed, and scar parts in joint cloth fell as their guards rose.
pmc-10754236:
Alhabter, Qureshi, and Ullah tour right and law frames for far rehab care in one gulf state in this twenty twenty-three review. Far care grows fast, yet its right and law base lags the tech. Rehab's wide scope adds its own snags to that lag.

The frames they set could serve kin states in the zone as well. The tour backs set rules ere far rehab spreads more wide.
pmc-10759636:
Thilipan Thaventhiran and co-authors test in 2023 a smartphone app that measures children's height at home to flag abnormal growth. The app uses augmented reality and reference algorithms to score height against population norms. It notifies families when thresholds suggest abnormal growth patterns that need clinical review.

The study enrolled 145 children at a London hospital. App measures by the study team showed no appreciable bias versus a clinic stadiometer. Differences stayed within about two centimeters either way. The methods correlated highly, with no extra bias for younger or shorter children. A parent subset also measured at home.
pmc-10763836:
Mahmut Gorkem Gurcinar and three co-authors report the care of a teen boy whose collar-bone joint slipped out of place to the back. Their case report is from two thousand twenty-three.

Such slips are rare, yet they can kill: the joint sits by windpipe, food pipe, nerves, and blood paths. The boy, in his early teens, took an elbow blow to the bone in a football game. He came in with pain, a gap at the chest, and a numb arm. Plain films can miss this harm, so a scan showed the slip in full. The team then eased the joint back in place with the boy asleep, in a surgery room.
pmc-10771036:
Yasuyuki Goto and co-authors review how Leishmania parasites steal iron and heme from the hosts they infect, in this 2023 paper. The single-celled parasites live inside immune cells and cause leishmaniasis. They cannot make heme or store iron, so every atom must be scavenged.

Inside the host's digestive sacs, the parasites also face oxidative attack, which their iron-based defense enzyme counters. The review traces the routes that move iron and heme from host stores into the parasite. Each route is a possible drug target, since blocking supply starves the invader. The authors map what is known and where the gaps sit.
pmc-10847236:
Kayleigh Hood and Laura Hurley study how serotonin shapes response to calls in mice. Their work deals with male mice and female voice signals. Social setting can strongly shape how a call is heard.

pmc-10875136:
Svajone Bekesiene and her team rank which bounce-back skills troop training should teach first when time is short. Their 2024 study uses a fuzzy choice method to bring a troop training plan up to date.

pmc-10875736:
Jeong Eun Cheon, Jeongwoo John Kim, and Young-Hoon Kim ask if wives' hair span and worth tie to wed sex pace. Their survey head is dated twenty twenty-three. pmc-10876036:

pmc-10937436:

pmc-10986236:

pmc-11438936:
Karina Sato-Espinoza and co-authors review how liver transplant care has changed as fatty liver disease has grown. pmc-11532336:

pmc-11532536:

pmc-11533336:

pmc-11534236:

pmc-11534636:

pmc-11535536:

pmc-11536636:

pmc-11538336:

pmc-11538436:

pmc-11538536:

pmc-11547136:

pmc-11569236:

pmc-11575036:

pmc-11575936:

pmc-11576836:
Istvan Pocsi, Jan Dijksterhuis, Jos Houbraken, and Ronald de Vries review fungi that thrive where water is scarce. pmc-11577736:

pmc-11578036:

They test the model on drop sizes seen in trade wind clouds over the Atlantic. Small drops enrich much more than plain drying would predict. pmc-11579936:

pmc-11580636:

pmc-11584636:

pmc-11585236:

pmc-11586236:

pmc-11597136:

pmc-11603136:

pmc-11603336:

pmc-11603636:
Sijiao Wang and co-authors show that blocking a cell stress axis eases acute lung injury in mice. The IRE1α-XBP1 path is one of three arms of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response. pmc-11603836:
Seyyed Mohammad Hashemi and co-authors tested two blood ratios as signs of metabolic syndrome in a 2024 study in southern Iran. The syndrome bundles risk traits that raise the odds of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. A cheap blood sign that flags it early would help clinics screen crowds.

pmc-11604936:

pmc-11605536:

One group, called WNT, has a good outlook when treated well, so missing it is a real risk. The team sorted two hundred forty-four cases from forty-three sites in Japan. The WNT group made up thirty-nine cases, and all tested cases in it shared two clear gene signs. The authors say mixing several test types finds WNT cases well. That helps clinics plan care and future trials.
pmc-11605836:
Priya Martin and co-authors published this survey study in 2024 on medical students in rural Australia during the COVID-19 years. Most past work took one snapshot at the pandemic's start. By 2022, far more students had cared for COVID patients than in the first year. Worry about missed learning peaked in 2020, then eased but stayed real. Fears that grades had suffered ran high in 2020 and again in 2022. Later students saw a wider range of cases and more community-based work. pmc-11607236:
Bum Ho Jeong and eight co-authors build a photonic synapse that can tell red, green, and blue apart. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. A net then reads test colour images with high truth.
pmc-11607336:
Sarkar, Chuang, Mohammed, and Jiang compare de-identified and synthetic clinical notes for privacy, in work from twenty twenty-four. Removing names and identifiers is the standard way to share medical records for research. Synthetic data, generated to mimic real data, is a newer alternative.

Large language models now make synthetic clinical notes plausible. The team demonstrated weaknesses in de-identification of real notes, where residual details can re identify patients. They then tested whether synthetic notes keep research utility. The comparison asks a practical question for hospitals: which sharing route protects patients while still letting science proceed.
pmc-11607836:
Yangyang Xue and co-authors sort lone lung spots in breast cancer patients, in work from 2024. A single lung nodule in such a patient may be a fresh lung cancer or spread from the breast, and the right call steers care. Two blood markers split the groups, as did sugar uptake strength and spread signs on scans. Three traits on CT, tied to lumpy, spiky, and pleat-pulled shapes, marked fresh lung cancer. The top trio for a firm call joined uptake strength with two shape signs. The authors back fused reads.
pmc-11608236:

pmc-11608336:

pmc-11611936:
Yue Yuan, Gang Zhao, and Yang Zhao offer a two thousand twenty-four review of energy failure in Alzheimer's disease. The disease's causes remain unsettled, which slows treatment design. Many studies tie its progress to the brain's failing fuel use.

The authors gather pathways linking lower glucose use to memory loss. Faulty insulin signaling inside the brain also features. Damaged mitochondria, the cell's power plants, are cast as a central player. Their failure may feed several other disease steps at once. Readers get a structured case that fixing brain energy could matter for prevention and therapy.
pmc-11614736:
Ke Wang and three colleagues published a health services study in two thousand twenty-four on what Chinese patients with chronic disease want from local clinics. Help getting referred appointments came second, and traditional Chinese medicine services third. All six features swayed choices to some degree. Willingness to pay differed between patient types. pmc-11616136:

pmc-11616836:

Diagnosis combined heart tracings, symptoms, and vessel imaging. Follow-up lasted a median of several years per patient. The authors pair their series with a literature review. Rare-event data like this guide emergency decisions.
pmc-11617236:

pmc-11618436:

pmc-11636036:

pmc-11638636:

pmc-11640236:

Sixty-five components drove the scent, by strength mathematics. Most piled up as grains matured. Two components topped the strength list. Six components separated the ripening steps cleanly, which marks them as stage signs. Three more separated scented brown rice from plain. The team says the readings can guide breeding of fragrant rice and choices of harvest time.
pmc-11640336:

At two days, the tube test gave the strongest signal for the parasite mix and matched the standard test well. The authors back the two day tube form for clinic use. It is faster and cheaper than the standard form.
pmc-11640736:

pmc-11641436:
Baldaev and co-authors describe genes for key enzymes in the sea cucumber Eupentacta fraudatrix. The enzymes, oxidosqualene cyclases, turn straight-chain triterpenes into ring-shaped ones. Those products are the starting point for other active compounds the animals make, some of medical interest.

Two such enzymes, parkeol synthase and lanostadienol synthase, were known from related sea cucumber genera. The team examined the gene structure behind these enzymes in this species. Knowing the gene layout helps trace how sea cucumbers build their triterpenoids. It also aids comparison across species that make unlike sets of these compounds.
pmc-11641536:
Sreelatha Thonthula and a large team of co-authors test a violet plant extract for skin hydration and barrier strength. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The skin's outer layer guards against water loss, and its health sets how soft and firm skin feels.

In human skin cells, the extract raised two helpers of moisture: a surface receptor and a water channel protein. The channel rose by seventy-eight percent. The extract also matched glycerin on water vapor loss and lipid order tests. A deep chemical scan then cataloged the plant's contents. Twenty-nine compounds were found, fourteen of them reported for the first time. The authors tie the hydration effect to specific plant chemicals.
pmc-11642336:

pmc-11643136:

pmc-11644736:

The team pulled loop cases from a known capture of device malware traffic. Nine learning models were trained to spot the loop patterns. A boosting model called XGBoost came out on top across the scores. Its precision and recall both ran high. The study argues loop shape itself is a strong tell for this attack kind.
pmc-11644936:
Junxuan Li and six colleagues let self-driving cars pool their views to complete occluded street scenes, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A single vehicle cannot see past trucks and around corners. Connected vehicles can share sensor data. But to align the features in that data is hard.

Their two-stream method splits partner vehicles' features apart and lets them interact. A custom attention module lets the host car query the most similar local features from its partners. It does so in place of assuming perfect synchronization of the feeds. The fused features give rise to a three-dimensional occupancy map. That map carries semantic labels for what sits in each place. Two multi-vehicle datasets benchmarked the approach for the team. Cooperative perception holds out the hope of safer autonomy. That holds if alignment errors do not invent phantom obstacles, or wipe real ones out.
pmc-11645036:
Anedito Zico da Costa and co-authors published a study in 2024 on air quality in the Cabo Verde islands. Cheap sensors can blanket a country with live air data where lab stations are few. The team placed sensors across the islands to track dust and traffic gases.

The sensors read fine and coarse particles plus a traffic gas, after tuning against known values. Dust levels passed world health limits in all regions across the year. The capital, Praia, often showed the worst air, above a high daily mark in the dry season. From November to March, Sahara dust blown in on a known wind raised levels further. Other towns stayed lower and steadier. The authors back wider sensor nets paired with reference stations.
pmc-11647636:
Tangui Barré and seven co-authors survey people with Parkinson's disease in France about medical cannabis and cannabidiol. Their survey was published in twenty twenty-four. Cannabis products might ease symptoms, but trial results conflict, and French law keeps cannabis illegal outside a narrow experiment that excludes this disease.

CBD products, by contrast, are legal and widely sold. The nationwide online survey asked patients how acceptable they find therapeutic cannabis and CBD. It also probed knowledge, information hunting, and barriers to self-medicating. Statistical models linked traits with acceptance levels. The authors aim to inform whether medical cannabinoids deserve a formal place among Parkinson's treatment options in France.
pmc-11648536:
Abdulaziz Al Taisan presents a 2024 case report on a flap that partly lifted after successful eye surgery. A twenty-four-year-old man developed a full-thickness hole in his macula, the eye's central vision spot, after a blunt injury. His sight worsened before surgery. Surgeons removed the eye's gel and laid an inverted flap of the inner limiting membrane over the hole, sealing it with gas. The hole closed, and scans showed the flap hinged in place.

Three months later he returned with a central floater, though his sight had improved. Scans showed the flap partly detached. The author warns that such flaps can peel loose once the gas fades, even after a clean closure.
pmc-11650836:
Jeremias Krause and co-authors present a 2024 paper on CNVizard, a small interactive app for exploring copy number variants in genome data. These variants, missing or doubled stretches of DNA, are read from sequencing in clinics and labs alike. Good annotation and clear pictures are essential, and spotting a variant inside a single gene part matters for diagnosis, yet many open tools fall short somewhere.

Built on a lightweight web framework, the app lets users browse variant calls interactively instead of wrestling static files. It joins rich annotations with direct views of the data. The authors aim to cut the formatting and plotting chores that slow genetic testing after the calling step.
pmc-11651136:
Jian Lin and co-authors publish the protocol for a trial combining a Chinese herbal granule with a standard Alzheimer drug in a 2024 paper. The degenerative disease causes progressive memory and thinking loss, and cases are rising with population aging. Earlier studies suggest combining traditional and Western medicine helps.

The multicenter, pragmatic randomized trial will assign nearly four hundred people with mild to moderate disease to the combination or control care. Outcomes track changes in cognitive scores, daily function, and safety. The protocol sets out eligibility, dosing, and analysis plans in advance of results.
pmc-11652436:
Gustavsen and coauthors check if old colon cancer patients in Norway get fair care. Standard care is surgery, then drug treatment to kill stray cancer cells. Rules say that drug care should start within six weeks of surgery. The team asks if wealth or place of birth change who gets it on time.

They used state records for patients aged 70 or more from 2011 to 2021. All had stage III colon cancer and major surgery. The team weighed age, health, income, school, and home region. Their goal was to find gaps in care that health leaders can close.
pmc-11653536:
Alan Schwartz, Saul Weiner, and Molly Harrod report, in 2024, that paying trial recruits more can sometimes lower the total cost of recruiting. Money is often used to draw participants, but studies disagree on the best amount. Within a larger implementation study, the team compared four recruitment approaches, three of them phone-based with different payment levels.

Bigger payments did raise sign-up rates, as expected. The surprise was time: recruiters needed far less time to win agreement when the payment was larger. Those time savings made the larger payment cheaper overall than the smaller one. The authors suggest pilot-testing payment levels, since a sweet spot may exist.
pmc-11653636:
Heini Sofia Rossi and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on which newborn foals with pneumonia leave the hospital alive. Pneumonia is a leading killer of sick neonatal foals, and prognostic signs were poorly charted. Reviewing fifty foals under a month old at a referral hospital, the team tested clinical and laboratory variables against survival to discharge.

Two findings stood out early on. A fast breathing rate on the first hospital day raised the odds of death with every step up, and a positive blood culture multiplied the risk about twelvefold in single-variable analysis. When everything competed together, only the breathing rate survived as an independent predictor, with a cutoff near fifty-five breaths a minute marking the danger line. Standardbred foals fared better, and every extra hospital day lowered the odds of dying.
pmc-11653836:
Baldoni and seven co-authors assess health literacy in people with and without Chagas disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. Chagas disease is a neglected infection that affects vulnerable people. Most patients have low ability to understand health information, which complicates long term care.

The cross sectional study compared health literacy between patients found through blood donation screening and people without the disease. Links with social, clinical, and quality of life traits were tested. Low literacy can hide behind normal clinic visits for years. Measuring it points to where simpler materials and teach back methods are most needed.
pmc-11654136:
Yan Xu and three co-authors report a warning sign that appeared during a child's spine surgery. Their 2024 case report covers a seventeen-year-old with scoliosis and a sunken chest. Prone positioning can squeeze the chest and disturb circulation in such patients. Low blood pressure is the usual first alarm.

Here the exhaled carbon dioxide fell first, then pressure dropped and resisted treatment. Chest imaging showed a narrowed space between sternum and spine. Turning the patient onto her back restored circulation at once. Sixteen minutes later, side bolsters spread the load and surgery resumed safely. Watching the breathing gas may catch chest compression before pressure crashes.
pmc-11654436:
Gustavo Rodrigues leads a team of twelve authors hunting the Nellore cattle genome for variants behind reproductive losses, traits that decide a beef herd's economics. Four traits were analyzed in experimental selection lines: conception success, pregnancy loss, stillbirth, and calf death before weaning. The data covered over thirty-seven hundred cows with seventeen thousand reproductive records, plus nearly twelve thousand calves. About thirty-eight hundred genotyped animals carried over three hundred eighty thousand markers.

A weighted genome-wide scan ranked the genomic windows explaining the most genetic variance for each trait. Genes in the top windows were annotated and checked against biological process terms and metabolic pathways. The study starts mapping zebu reproductive genetics, which European-breed research cannot simply be copied onto.
pmc-11655536:
Nianhui Yang and thirteen co-authors test a drug against myeloma in a 2024 paper. Multiple myeloma, a plasma cell cancer, remains largely incurable. Cancer cells pump out protons through a surface exporter to survive. A blocker of that exporter, hexamethylene amiloride, had shown anti tumor effects elsewhere.

Myeloma patients with high exporter levels fared worse, the team first showed. The blocker slowed myeloma cells and triggered their death in dishes. Patient bone marrow cells responded the same way. Part of the kill ran through a factor that boosts lysosome production. In mice, the drug shrank the disease meaningfully. It also killed cells resistant to a standard drug and boosted that drug's effect. The exporter is proposed as a fresh myeloma target.
pmc-11655636:
Iftekhar Showpnil and co-authors show, in a 2024 study, how long-read genome sequencing can resolve complex rearrangements in rare genetic syndromes. Standard tests can spot that a DNA segment is lost or gained, but not how the pieces are joined. The team sequenced the full genomes of two patients, using reads long enough to span the breakpoints.

In the first patient, the reads revealed a reshaped chromosome 8: a 3.43 Mb duplication at one end linked to a deletion of 7.25 to 8.21 Mb at the other. In the second patient, they found a small moved segment plus four gaps of very different sizes. Both structures had been missed in their full form by earlier tests. The authors stress how varied such rearrangements can be. They argue that long reads should be used when standard tests hint at a rearrangement they cannot solve.
pmc-11655836:
Liana Arakelyan and co-authors assemble a large open data set on how toxic ionic liquids are to cells, in work from twenty twenty-four. Ionic liquids are tunable salts used from synthesis to batteries and medicine. Their harm to living cells is the flip side that needs mapping.

The set covers over twelve hundred liquids and nearly thirty-nine hundred data entries drawn from one hundred fifty-one papers. Each entry records the substance name, formula, registry codes, structure string, weight, and toxicity value. Test details like cell line, assay, and exposure time ride along, with a link to the source paper. The authors offer the set for hunting structure activity patterns and the features that drive cell harm.
pmc-11655936:
Donglan Yuan, Zhiqiang Lu, Xindan Xu, and Wei Liu build a nanoparticle that delivers chemotherapy and heat together to thyroid tumors, in this 2024 study. The particle starts from polydopamine, a sticky, light absorbing polymer. A standard drug, doxorubicin, is attached through a bond that breaks in acid, and a targeting peptide called RGD decorates the surface.

Under near infrared light the particles heated solutions within five minutes. In dishes, the targeted particles plus light killed ninety-two percent of thyroid cancer cells. In tumor bearing mice the particles gathered at tumors, lingered there, and with light they strongly slowed tumor growth, without evident toxicity. The authors propose the design as a candidate path toward clinical use against thyroid cancer.
pmc-11656236:
Navanya Raveendran and co-authors grow a battery material straight on metal foil in a 2024 study. Lithium-ion batteries need anodes, the negative pole, with high capacity. Molybdenum disulfide has a layered form and high promise, but it is often pasted on with binders that add dead weight. The team grew it in place instead, by chemical vapor deposition.

Thin sheets of the material stood upright on molybdenum foil, with a second molybdenum oxide grown inside them. The oxide formed first, then partly turned into the sulfide under sulfur vapor. The hybrid passed ions and electrons fast, thanks to the oxide's conductivity and the sheets' exposed edges. It stored a high charge for its area with no binder or extra carbon. The authors say such direct growth suits compact, high-power cells.
pmc-11656336:
Christina Blagojevic and co-authors ask how often people carrying drug-resistant germs go on to develop infection with the same germ, in a 2024 study. Carriage often comes first, but the size of the later risk was unclear. Using health records for all of Ontario, Canada, the team followed nearly 70,000 people with a positive surveillance test for one of four resistant pathogens over five years.

About 16 percent later developed an infection with the same organism, typically within about two months. The rate swung by germ: near 3 percent for one, above 20 percent for two others, and about 18 percent for resistant staph. Carriage found in a hospital carried higher risk than carriage found elsewhere. The authors say these numbers can guide who gets watched or treated early.
pmc-11657136:
Shiyan Zhang and co-authors measure in 2024 the worldwide toll of age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for 204 countries, they tracked cases and years of healthy life lost from 1990 to 2021, then projected to 2050.

Total cases of low vision and blindness from the disease more than doubled, reaching about 8.1 million in 2021. Yet rates per person, adjusted for age, fell, showing the rise is driven by growing, aging populations. Burden climbed with age, ran slightly higher in women, and weighed heaviest on poorer regions. The model expects about 13.9 million cases by 2050.
pmc-11657536:
Jesús Martínez-Puc leads a team on women in stingless beekeeping in Yucatán. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with meliponiculture in Mexico. The craft predates Spanish arrival in the region.

The peninsula links the bees to Maya culture and medicine. Interviews were held with producers across three states. Referral sampling found the producers for talks. Traits and roles of women were compared with men. The team guessed women's share would run lower. Home and community duties were the stated reason. Interviews spanned about two years of field work.  Three peninsula states formed the study area.
pmc-11659336:
Farm runoff carries phosphorus into streams, where it feeds harmful algae growth. Jack Dekle, William Strosnider, and Sarah White test a low-cost filter pairing for pulling that phosphorus out in a 2024 study.

Their setup joins an iron oxide filter, which grabs phosphorus, with a pine bark unit that strips nitrogen. They ran the pair in both orders on a steady flow of mock farm return water. The iron filter cut phosphorus levels in both spring and fall runs, and did best in cooler months when wetland plants take up less. Recycled iron media still worked well. The authors see the filter as a handy partner for plant-based water treatment.
pmc-11664736:
Chan-Young Kwon surveyed young adults in South Korea in 2024 about anger and suicidal thoughts. South Korea has the highest suicide rate among rich nations. The study focused on millennials and generation Z. It centered on hwa-byung, a culture-bound anger syndrome. Suppressed anger and body heat sensations mark the syndrome. An online survey gathered over four hundred fifty participants. None had a past mood disorder diagnosis. Questions covered suicidal thoughts, anger, stress, and depression.

Over a third reported some suicidal ideation. The group with such thoughts scored higher on every strain measure. Anger syndrome symptoms differed sharply between groups. Final models kept three linked factors. Syndrome symptoms, depression, and in-the-moment anger each mattered. Body symptoms like chest pressure tracked thought severity closely. The author urges prevention policy that includes Korean medical approaches. Larger national samples must confirm the findings, the author adds.
pmc-11665636:
Gutama Ibrahim Mohammad, Tom Michoel, and Thomas Lengauer predict the inherited part of gene expression using whole regulatory networks, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Standard prediction uses only DNA variants near a gene. The omnigenic view says distant variants matter too, acting through networks of other genes.

Their method first predicts expression from local variants. The leftover error is then modeled from the genotypes of the gene's network parents and grandparents in causal and co-expression networks rebuilt from genomic data. Adding both predictions gives the final estimate. Better expression prediction strengthens association studies that link genes to disease without measuring tissue directly. Networks, in this approach, are not decoration but machinery.
pmc-11667136:
Ahmed AbuRaed leads a team on long COVID talk on Twitter across regions. Their study from twenty twenty-four covers Canada, the US, and Europe. Social media holds rich data on public views and feelings.

Long COVID has grown into a chronic ill that hits many lives. Its story shifts as knowledge of it grows over time. English tweets from the three regions were gathered for study. Topic models and sentiment tools mined the tweet text. Region splits in talk could guide public health plans. Tailored plans per region are the wider goal.
pmc-11668636: William K Miller and three colleagues describe a wire-guided biopsy route to the cavernous sinus, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. A fifty-three-year-old woman had double vision and headache from a skull-base tumor wrapping her carotid artery. Standard needle passage through the dura failed. A guide wire pierced the membrane first, and the needle followed its track. Sampling succeeded without complications. Pathology returned a grade two chondrosarcoma. The team calls the trick simple and cheap for hard-to-reach lesions.
pmc-11671236:
A plant hormone called cytokinin can both help and hinder a plant fighting bacteria, and timing may decide which. Xiang Wang and eleven co-authors followed the hormone's signaling through the stages of a wilting disease in a model plant's roots, in a 2024 study. Turning the signal up sped cell death, wilting, and bacterial growth, yet eased some root-growth effects.

Turning the signal down blocked root hairs, death, and colonization. A sprayed dose of the hormone helped root hairs at low strength and hurt at high strength, while hastening death and suppressing side roots. The authors conclude the hormone's role depends on cell type and infection stage.
pmc-11672336:
Hui-Bin Xue and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four on predicting whether stomach cancer will spread to distant sites. Such spread, called distant metastasis, shapes treatment and outlook. The team built a personal risk chart, called a nomogram, that mixes scan-based measures with clinical facts.

They studied three hundred one patients, split into training and test groups. From CT scans they extracted hundreds of image features and kept fifteen that mattered. Age, tumor grade, and nodal stage also predicted spread on their own. Models that joined image scores with clinical facts were judged on accuracy, calibration, and benefit for patient care. The authors present the joint chart as a tool to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-11673236:
Alexis Merculief, Monica Tsethlikai, and Felix Muniz study what helps or hinders the thinking skills of urban American Indian children, using an Indigenous connectedness framework. The frame sorts children's worlds into connecting and disconnecting forces across family, community, land, ancestors, and spirit. The team gathered reports from 156 parents and ratings of children's executive function, the mental skills behind planning and self-control.

Cultural connection protected the children. Parents who engaged with cultural beliefs and practices, and who knew their tribal history, had children with stronger executive function by both parent and child reports. Discrimination and neighborhood risk pulled the other way. The authors argue that resilience research with Indigenous families should start from Indigenous theory, where culture is a source of strength, not an afterthought.
pmc-11673336:
Body-made bubbles called extracellular vesicles could carry cancer drugs straight to tumors, sparing healthy tissue. Alessia Brancolini and Riccardo Vago test how to load such bubbles with chemotherapy drugs in a 2024 study.

The team simply soaked the bubbles with four different cancer drugs and measured how much each one took up. A light-based method, calibrated drug by drug, let them count the load with high sensitivity. Loaded bubbles were then tried on cancer cells and compared with free drug. The goal was a loading recipe that keeps the bubbles intact and the drugs active. A gentle soak that works would make vesicle delivery far easier to scale for clinics.
pmc-11673636:
Aarthi Jeganathan and eight co-authors test a plant extract delivered in chitosan nanoparticles against breast cancer in rats, in a two thousand twenty-four drug-science paper. The extract comes from the roots of Alstonia venenata, a Western Ghats plant rich in alkaloids.

Tumors were induced with the chemical DMBA in female Sprague Dawley rats. Nanoparticle-loaded extract greatly reduced tumor volume, burden, and incidence, letting its compounds out slowly. Treated animals showed improved blood and tissue readings, and antioxidant defenses rose while lipid peroxidation fell sharply. The nanoparticle form beat the plain extract at slowing tumor progression. The authors call for work to single out the active compounds and their mechanisms.
pmc-11674536:
Eylem Gul Ates, Gokcen Coban, and Jale Karakaya present a 2024 journal article on telling COVID-related strokes apart with machine learning. The team extracted radiomic features, numeric texture measures, from brain MR images of 57 stroke patients treated in Ankara between March 2020 and September 2021. Thirty had tested positive for COVID-19 and 27 had not.

Several feature selection methods and classifiers were compared. Without selection, a neural network reached an accuracy score of 0.857 on the standard curve measure. A recursive selection method with a nearest-neighbor classifier did best at 0.882. The authors present the models as diagnostic aids for a hard distinction.
pmc-11674736:
Josgrey Navas-Acosta and a large team of co-authors trace how adult B cell leukemia returns after treatment in this 2024 paper. The disease is B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Over 40 percent of adults relapse, and the paths to relapse were poorly understood. Samples were sequenced at diagnosis and again at relapse.

The study covered 44 adult patients. Four main genetic routes to relapse emerged. One route kept a high risk profile centered on the IKZF1 gene. Others gained RAS mutations or TP53 changes. Patients with the Philadelphia chromosome gained mutations in ABL1 that resist drugs. Most patients with the high risk profile at diagnosis kept it at relapse. The map can guide targeted follow up testing.
pmc-11675336:
Xiaolei Guo and co-authors toughen a common hydrogel with a silicone-based second network, then give the worn-out sensor a second job, in this 2024 study. Plain PVA gels are soft and weak. Threading a springy polysiloxane mesh through them lets the gel shed energy through dense breakable bonds, and its strength can be dialed across a wide range.

The finished gel also conducts well and senses strain with a clean signal, suiting it for wearable motion sensors. When the sensor dies, the same material scrubs metal ions out of water as an adsorbent. The authors present the full arc, from stronger gel to recycled water cleaner, as a model for less wasteful soft electronics.
pmc-11675836:
Anita Pichler and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of Merlot wine aged in toasted oak barrels versus steel tanks. Barrel toasting shapes colour, aroma, and antioxidant power. Vintages from two harvests let the team separate vessel effects from year effects.

Wines aged twelve months across several barrel types and one steel tank. Basic chemistry barely moved, while phenolic compounds changed significantly. Colour pigments fell as polymeric colour rose in both vintages. Element levels shifted with vessel, time, and starting composition. Winemakers gain evidence for matching barrel toast to desired style.
pmc-11676136:
Permatasari and five co-authors model a combined chemical reactor in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The system joins two reactions in one unit. One breaks ammonia to free hydrogen. The other uses hydrogen and carbon dioxide to make methane.

A membrane that lets hydrogen pass links the two sides and boosts performance. Two catalysts drive the separate reactions. The team built a one dimensional computer model and checked it against lab results. They varied layout, catalyst place, heat transfer, and membrane flow to find the best setup. Placing each reaction on the right side mattered most. Models like this guide clean fuel and carbon use design.
pmc-11676336:
Bryce Kille and co-authors wrote this 2024 paper on a core task in DNA sequence analysis. Many tools sample short DNA chunks called k-mers instead of reading every chunk. Good sampling schemes keep few chunks while still catching at least one in each short window of the sequence.

The team proved a lower bound on how few chunks any forward sampling scheme can keep. For small window and chunk sizes, the bound is exact in a common case. Their result shows that top current schemes sit much closer to the best possible density than was known. For one standard setting in the minimap2 tool, the best scheme is at most 3 percent denser than ideal, down from a past gap of 50 percent.
pmc-11676436:
Sun and four co-authors report a lab study from twenty twenty-four on a treated fluid that may fight lung cancer. The fluid is made by exposing a growth liquid to cold plasma, a charged gas. The team tested it on a lung cancer cell line grown flat and in balls. Ball growth mimics real tumors better than flat growth does. They checked cell life, movement, and spread in both setups.

The fluid cut cell life, movement, and spread in both flat and ball growth. It also blocked a shift that helps cancer cells spread, and it kept tumor balls from forming. The harm ran through reactive oxygen, a cell stress agent. Effects were stronger in flat growth than in balls. The authors call the fluid a hopeful new lung cancer tool.
pmc-11677336:
Hao Su and three colleagues published a machining study in two thousand twenty-four on honing hard steel valve sleeves. Servo valve sleeves need extreme precision, yet their hard steel resists cutting. Two grinding stone types were compared for speed and finish.

Electroplated stones removed material two and a half times faster than sintered stones. Sintered stones, though, left a smoother surface. The team proposed a two-step method: electroplated stones for bulk removal, then sintered stones for finishing. That sequence lifted overall efficiency by about one and six tenths times while keeping the finish. The authors see wide use for the approach in precision hydraulic parts.
pmc-11678336:
Maria Jesus Rojas-Lechuga and co-authors pooled survival data for a rare nose cancer in a 2024 review. This melanoma grows on the wet lining of the nose and nearby air spaces. It is rare, fast to spread, and hard to treat, so patients face poor odds in most past reports.

The team searched the main health databases by set rules and kept studies that report five-year survival. They then pooled the rates to give one weighed view of outcomes. Such a pooled figure helps doctors counsel patients with honest odds. It also sets a bar that new care plans must beat to prove their worth.
pmc-11678436:
Rapson Gomez and co-authors re-evaluate a common symptom checklist in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The checklist has ninety items covering many kinds of distress. The team asks whether its scales can measure the broad spectra in a modern hierarchical model of mental disorders.

More than fifteen hundred adolescents in Athens, Greece, completed the checklist and a personality survey. One model, grouping scales into body, internalizing, and hostile spectra, fit the data well. A second model adding a detachment spectrum did not hold up, since two scales performed poorly. The authors conclude that seven of the checklist scales suit the hierarchical model, but the paranoia and psychosis scales do not.
pmc-11678536:
Mpho Tawana and co-authors pool studies of a gut parasite in South Africa in a 2024 review. The parasite, Cryptosporidium, infects both animals and humans and spreads through feces. The team gathered prevalence studies published between 1980 and 2020.

Across studies, pooled prevalence came to about 22 percent in animals and 18 percent in humans. Test methods differed sharply in yield, with gene-based methods finding the most cases. Cryptosporidium parvum was the most common species in both animals and humans. Rates were highest in KwaZulu-Natal and North West provinces. Some provinces lacked studies at all, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-11678836:
Giulia Franceschi and five co-authors review hands-on care plus exercise against exercise alone for vague hip ills. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Whether manual care adds to exercise is a live split in the field. Guides lean against it for hip arthritis, while groin pain work hints it speeds a sport return.

They gather the trials of the past two decades under a set review frame. No clear gap shows between the two paths in most reads. Early hints favour the pair for pain, range, and patient joy, while one study favours exercise alone for life quality. For hip arthritis, no mid- or long-term gain from hands shows. More sharp trials are due.
pmc-11679336:
Chang An and colleagues measured genome sizes and ran first-pass genome surveys for nine common Chinese medicinal plants, each from a different plant family. Medicinal plant research lags behind crop science because basic genome information is missing for many species. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team used flow cytometry, which estimates DNA content from stained cells, and shallow sequencing surveys. The list runs from small genomes under half a billion letters to one giant genome several times the size of the human one.

Three of the sizes had been reported before, and comparisons show earlier numbers sometimes disagree, which the authors blame on method and sample differences. They advise using more than one measurement approach for reliability. For species with wide size variation or doubled chromosome sets, they recommend dedicated ploidy checks before deeper sequencing.
pmc-11679436:
Hailong Xu and six co-authors published this study in 2024. It tests boards made by blending wood flour into a common plastic. Two tree species from China, Masson pine and Chinese fir, were mixed in seven ratios, from all pine to all fir.

The team measured color, density, water swelling, strength, stiffness, and how the boards sag slowly under a steady load. More fir flour generally raised strength and stiffness, though slow sag also grew. The boards' spring-like stiffness rose with fir share, while energy loss fell. Several math models were tried against the data. A refined mixture model matched the strength results best, and a modified time model matched the sag results best. The findings help builders pick a wood mix for panels that must hold up outdoors.
pmc-11679536:
Aishwarya Rajakumar and co-authors study protein tags in heart cells under low blood flow stress in a 2024 paper. Heart disease tied to blocked flow can upset cell balance and harm heart function. Using newborn rat heart cells as a model, the team measured a chemical tag that attaches to proteins. They mapped tagged sites with lab tests and mass based tools.

Tag levels fell under stress compared with normal air conditions. Among many tagged sites, most proteins lost tags and a smaller set gained them. Changed proteins clustered in cell metabolism, muscle structure, and movement, with one key enzyme complex hit hardest. Pathways that make cell fuel from sugar were also affected. Readers see how tag shifts may reshape heart cell work during stress.
pmc-11681936:
Xiaohong Jin and co-authors present a deep learning model, described in the head as a 2024 paper, to predict how small protein chains bind larger proteins. Such pairs matter since chain-based drugs are on the rise, with more approvals each year. Lab tests of these pairs are slow and costly, and classic sim methods eat compute with modest accuracy.

Their model rests on a transformer design, the frame behind many recent AI gains. It trained on 19,187 pairs with both sequence and shape data, mixing local sequence features with global shape features. A rebuilt shape network in a lean order cut the compute the task needs. The model hit 0.855 accuracy, which beat the next best model by a wide margin. Some of its fresh picks match past lab proof, which backs its use in drug hunts.
pmc-11683636:
D Sharda Devi and Nihar R Mohapatra used computer modeling to improve the electrical contacts of transistors built from a single layer of tungsten disulfide. Such devices need contacts that pass positive charge carriers well, and plain metal contacts resist this because the energy levels get pinned at the surface. The pair tested halogen atoms, iodine and fluorine, placed either inside the layer or resting on its surface.

Atoms inside the layer pushed behavior the wrong way, while atoms on the surface helped. The pinning effect still limited the gain, so the team added thin sheets of graphene or boron nitride between the layer and the metal. A fluorine-covered sheet with graphene and platinum gave a strong contact with a much lower energy barrier.
pmc-11689136:
Zhe He and five co-authors ask how older adults can better grasp lab test results online. Their twenty twenty-four project had two parts. First, they surveyed two hundred seventy-six patients with long-term illness. Most said lab results were hard to read, and most wanted a doctor to explain them. Skill with numbers and past portal use shaped test scores.

Next, they tested four large language models on lab questions taken from a public Q and A site. Both a model judge and health experts rated one model, GPT-4, best for help, safety, and right facts. Still, all models at times gave wrong claims, so care is needed.
pmc-11689336:
Ad Maulod, Malcolm Ravindran, and Yunjie Wong study how older people in Singapore use and claim public open spaces, in a 2024 paper. Open spaces help older residents build friendships and express themselves, yet residents have little say in how the spaces are designed or run. Rules on their use can also put older people off.

Drawing on interviews with more than 200 older people across several studies, the authors find a felt lack of control over local spaces and programs. Many avoid the new senior centers, seeing them as places for the sick and frail. Still, residents find creative ways around the rules, holding the activities they want in shared spaces. The authors argue that freedom in public space is a core part of aging well in place.
pmc-11689536:
Raven Weaver and co-authors compare what college students and teachers think about discussing suicide in class, in a study from 2024. Suicide is a leading cause of death among young adults and the highest risk sits with older adults. Learning about it in class could help students respond well in life and in future care jobs.

The team surveyed 313 students and interviewed 27 faculty who teach death and dying courses. Most students wanted to learn more about suicide, and 86 percent wanted to know what help exists for people at risk. Faculty, by contrast, often avoided the topic, felt unready, or feared it would worsen students' distress. The authors urge joint course design, trauma-aware teaching, and better links to campus and outside support.
pmc-11689636:
Alison Chasteen, a solo author, presents a 2024 symposium summary on ageism. Age prejudice was named over fifty years ago. Its impact grew clearer during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The symposium gathers many methods to show how wide ageism runs. Talks use deep interviews, social media scraping, and experimental surveys. Facets range from group labels and media images to beauty standards and thoughts of suicide.

One talk tests how words like elderly and senior citizen color views of older people. Another reads online reaction to a reality dating show with older stars. A further talk weighs how to confront ageist comments. Readers get a tour of a bias that hides in plain speech. The range of methods is the point: ageism shows up in data of every kind, from posts to lab tasks.
pmc-11690336:
Jennifer Reckrey, Emily Xu, Deborah Watman, Sasha Perez, and Emily Franzosa wrote a research paper in 2024 about home care for people with dementia. The paper asks how paid home care workers try to give care that fits each person, not just the disease. It draws on interviews with workers who help clients in their own homes.

The team re-read twenty-two interviews and sorted what they heard by a known frame for person-centered dementia care. Workers knew their clients well, built close ties, and found ways to meet each person's needs. Limits on their role, tense ties with family caregivers, and fixed agency care plans often got in the way. The authors say workers should sit on care teams and get training in this kind of care.
pmc-11690436:
Gina Tucker-Roghi and three co-authors lead a session, in twenty twenty-four, on teaching geriatrics across health fields. Care for older adults draws on many trades, they note, so training should too. Their session shows how to find partners and resources in a school and its town. It shares the work of teachers at several schools who did just that.

Speakers tell how they built joint networks and wove aging content into other fields. They also tell how they drew in people who did not see aging as their field. Tactics include cutting stigma and acting fast on local chances. The aim is staff in all fields who are ready for older patients.
pmc-11691136:
Emily Winters and Tessa McCoy published a review in 2024 covering ten years of research on biomarkers, measurable signs in the body that point to Alzheimer's disease. Clear biomarkers matter for detecting the disease early and tracking how it progresses over time.

The pair searched major databases for studies published from 2012 onward. They report strong progress in brain imaging techniques that target amyloid-beta and tau, the two proteins linked to the disease. Blood-based biomarkers have also advanced quickly, because blood tests are inexpensive and noninvasive. Long-term studies that follow people over time, and imaging that combines more than one method, gave a fuller picture of how biomarkers change. Machine learning tools found new biomarker patterns in the data. Large international collaborations, the review notes, helped drive much of this growth.
pmc-11691336:
