Six researchers test a tryptophan by-product as a treatment for aging mice in a paper from 2024. The compound, xanthurenic acid, falls in the blood as mice age. Its parent pathway is known to shift with age in harmful ways. The team gave the compound to aged mice and tracked broad health measures, from strength to bone and muscle state.

Treated mice showed lower levels of inflammatory signals in blood. They gripped harder, moved more, and endured longer than controls. Their bones had better fine structure and their muscle fibers were larger. Muscle tissue showed less oxidative stress and fewer aging markers. The authors propose the compound as a candidate for healthy aging research.
pmc-11691736:
Shu Xu and Haowei Wang studied how vision trouble shapes the activities older adults value in a 2024 paper. Vision loss is common in later life and is tied to doing less overall. Far less is known about which activities people with poor sight still prize and manage to keep.

Using a national aging survey from 2022, the team covered close to six thousand older adults with and without visual difficulty. They compared activity preferences and actual participation, and probed barriers such as transport, health, and the pandemic. The results can guide services that protect the activities elders care about most, rather than pushing generic activity for its own sake.
pmc-11692136:
Hiroshi Yamamoto and three co-authors follow older hospital patients for nine years in a 2024 study. They tested memory at admission with a short recall test, since dementia drives death and illness in this age group. Over six hundred patients aged sixty-five and up were tracked from admission to the end of the follow-up window.

More than half died during follow-up. Memory problems at admission predicted worse survival, even after other factors were counted. Patients who could not complete the test fared worst of all. Poor nutrition, pneumonia, and having cancer also cut survival clearly. The authors argue for early mental checks in acute geriatric care, alongside nutrition and infection care.
pmc-11692536:
Huiru Song and Hong Mi evaluate Qingdao's long-term care insurance and set it against systems abroad, in this 2024 paper. Qingdao was the first city in China to fully roll out such insurance, so its design carries lessons for the rest of Shandong Province and beyond. The policy splits benefits into medical services and nursing services, each with a yearly fee cap.

The paper lays out those caps for employees and residents and weighs how the scheme supports healthy and fair care for older people. By comparing Qingdao with programs in other countries, the authors judge where the city's model is strong and where it may need change. The study aims to guide regional growth of long-term care policy in China.
pmc-11693236:
Diane Berish and co-authors present a 2024 conference abstract on whether a smart lighting system was installed as designed in nursing homes. The system floods rooms with bright light by day and dims at night to steady residents' body clocks. The team checked delivery two ways: spot measurements in rooms twice a week, and light sensors worn by residents around the clock.

Daytime delivery hit its brightness and circadian targets on both checks, and residents got far more day light and less night light than in the control period. Nighttime levels, though, ran brighter than target. The authors flag night dimming as the fix for the next round.
pmc-11698036:
David Cohen and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on a protein that, against its family's reputation, calms the squeeze inside epithelial cells. Its family was known for building stress fibers and boosting the pull of the cell's motor proteins. Working in a standard kidney cell line that forms sheets, the team found this member, Borg5, doing the opposite. Cells without it failed to settle into the neat column shape of a mature sheet.

Without Borg5, the side walls of the cells lost their actin cortex. Cells grew leading-edge skirts and radial stress fibers, and their top faces lost their even shape. Borg5 keeps a set of scaffold proteins from colocalizing with the cell's rails. It also binds the cell's main motor protein. The model: Borg5 restrains the scaffolds' boost to the motor.
pmc-11701636:
Members of the UniProt Consortium describe the Universal Protein Knowledgebase as it stood heading into 2025. UniProt aims to give users a complete, high-quality, and freely open set of protein sequences. Each entry is labelled with what is known about what that protein does.

Their update explains ongoing changes to the resource and how it is run. Proteins sit at the center of most cell work, so a trusted catalogue underpins research from medicine to farming. Keeping the record accurate and free ensures that small labs share the same base knowledge as large institutes.
pmc-11707436:
Yuka Shinohara and Masahide Oki review, in a 2024 paper, a through-the-gullet route to diagnosing sarcoidosis, the inflammatory disease that seeds clusters of immune cells in the chest's lymph nodes. Proving the diagnosis needs tissue, and the classic bronchoscopic routes often come back empty. A needle passed through the esophagus under ultrasound guidance, sometimes using the bronchoscope itself through the food pipe, reaches the same nodes from the other side.

Gathering the published record, the authors find the esophageal route answers in seventy-five to one hundred percent of cases. Its bronchoscope variant reaches seventy to eighty-six percent, both well above the older lung routes. Harms so far are few: rare node infections settled with antibiotics, a bleed, sore throats. They recommend the route especially for patients whose cough or weak lungs make the airway approach hard, noting that lung doctors can perform it themselves.
pmc-11709336:
Katie Bretland, Li Lin, Sarah Terrill, and Christine Dengler-Crish tested whether a cell-grip protein family shapes early tau disease differently in male and female mice. The mice carry human tau and develop tangles like those in dementia. Earlier work showed the exercise hormone irisin protected young females but not males. Here the team measured the grip proteins, called integrins, in the hippocampus of four-month-old mice after a month of irisin or plain injections.

Young female tau mice already showed disturbed integrin levels that males lacked. Irisin lowered the integrins and calmed a related growth pathway in females, with no effect in males. Removing the ovaries erased irisin's protection in females. The authors conclude that integrin function influences early tau mechanisms in a sex-specific way. They argue dementia research must hunt for causes separately in each sex, since the same treatment can act through different biology.
pmc-11709836:
Natalie Phillips, Paul Best, Nicole Grant, and Ameera Kabir study sense loss in older adults at risk of dementia, in work from 2025. Hearing, sight, and smell loss are each common in later life, and each links to higher dementia risk. The team asks how often these losses occur together and what they mean for the brain.

Data came from a large Canadian study of aging and dementia. Groups ran from healthy adults to people with Alzheimer's disease. Full normal senses were rare and grew rarer as risk rose. Smell loss was the most common fault, then hearing loss. In early memory loss, hearing loss tied to changed brain network links. In those with felt decline, smell loss tied to smaller memory centers in the brain.
pmc-11709936:
Stacey Piotrowski and co-authors study Alzheimer-related blood markers in marmosets with a herpesvirus infection in a 2025 paper. One idea about Alzheimer disease holds that microbes help trigger or drive its damage, and herpesviruses draw interest because they hide in the body for life. Marmosets carry a related virus much like the human Epstein-Barr virus.

The team drew blood from more than two hundred animals in two research colonies during routine health checks. They measured plasma levels of amyloid pieces and three markers of brain cell injury or stress, and they screened blood cells for the virus's DNA. The work tests whether long-term infection in this primate model tracks with the blood signs used in Alzheimer research.
pmc-11710036:
Ignazio Piras and co-authors share a 2025 conference abstract on gene risk scores and health traits in a large United States cohort. Genes drive much of Alzheimer's risk, but changeable factors matter too. The team scored each person's gene-based risk, then searched medical records and body measures for traits that track with that score.

Nine conditions tracked with the score, led by hypothyroidism. People with the thyroid condition carried lower gene risk scores on average, and a thyroid hormone measure pointed the same way. Eighteen body measures also tracked with the score, including height and blood pressure. A United Kingdom cohort of about 390,000 people confirmed the thyroid link.
pmc-11710136:
Teresa Parrao and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on who joins and who leaves a Chilean aging cohort. The GERO cohort follows community elders aged 70 and over in Santiago who report cognitive complaints but have no dementia. Such cohorts lose members over time, and the losses can skew results.

Recruiters approached 17,759 households and enrolled 291 people. Before the first follow-up, 102 withdrew, about a third of the group. Those who stayed were younger and scored better on thinking, daily function, and complex task measures. The authors use these patterns to guide how future cohorts should recruit and retain members.
pmc-11710236:
Ada J Lin and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on how an Alzheimer's antibody drug helps clear amyloid. The drug, aducanumab, was the first of its kind to win limited approval, in 2021. The team grew human microglia, the brain's immune cells, from stem cells and watched them work in flat cultures and in small balls of brain tissue.

In flat cultures, the drug made microglia swallow amyloid faster and in larger amounts. It also cut the share of dense, clumped amyloid inside the cells. In the tissue balls, the drug did not lower total amyloid but blocked larger clumps from forming, which may aid later clearance.
pmc-11710436:
Anu Kumar and co-authors report a 2025 study of driving in older adults with and without brain amyloid build-up. Driving is a hard daily task, and shifts in it may flag early risk of decline. The team asked if body signals during driving differ by amyloid status.

They studied equal groups of amyloid positive and negative adults over age sixty five. All drove the same fixed route while video and watch sensors ran. Staff marked key road events in the films, then compared heart and skin signals. Amyloid positive drivers showed higher heart rates at some turns and ramps. They also showed lower skin response at exit ramps. The authors propose these signals as early risk marks.
pmc-11710636:
Dylan Guan and co-authors present a 2025 study of blood vessel risk and early signs of decline. Some older adults report worse thinking or show mild behavior change before any clear loss. The team asked if vessel risk factors track with those early signs.

They used survey data from a large online study of aging in Canada. Weights, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and smoking formed the risk list. Scores came from scales for daily thinking and behavior change. Each risk factor but past smoking tracked with worse daily thinking scores. Diabetes and active smoking showed the largest links. The authors say vessel health may shape early signs often blamed on Alzheimer disease alone.
pmc-11712436:
Jonathan Gallego Rudolf and co-authors link brain rhythms to tau spread in a 2025 study of symptom-free older adults. Tau is thought to travel between connected brain regions, and amyloid may speed that travel by making neurons overactive. The team worked with eighty-four adults from the PREVENT-AD cohort, all with a family history of Alzheimer's disease.

Brain activity was read with a magnetic scanner, and amyloid and tau were mapped with PET scans about four years apart. Each person's tau hot spots sat mainly in temporal and rear midline regions. Regions wired to those hot spots in the theta and alpha rhythm bands gained tau faster. The link held only in people with high amyloid. The authors say rhythm wiring may chart the paths tau takes.
pmc-11712636:
Yashu Vashishath and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a learning model that predicts thinking test scores from blood data. The model reads three layers of biology at once: gene variants, gene activity, and chemical marks on DNA. Most models use one layer, but the layers shape each other, so the team fed them in as a stacked set.

Hundreds of gene variants tied to test scores anchored the search for nearby marks and genes. The stacked model forecast scores on four standard tests with modest error. It beat simpler models the team tried as yardsticks. A blood-based forecast could one day flag people who need a full memory work-up.
pmc-11713036:
Erica Dove and co-authors present a 2025 study that asked people with dementia to test exercise video games and say what works for them. Such games can raise activity levels, but only if the systems are easy to use for people with thinking difficulties. The team wanted end users to judge the games directly.

Thirty-two people at four Canadian day programs played games on several systems once a week for six weeks, thinking aloud as they played. Gesture-based systems proved easier than those needing handheld controllers and button presses. Frustration, confusion, and tiredness were common reasons to stop, which gives designers clear points to fix.
pmc-11713236:
Maria Eriksdotter draws on a Swedish national registry to describe how dementia unfolds in real care, in this 2025 paper. The registry, called SveDem, has logged people at diagnosis since 2007, with yearly follow-ups. It now holds records for more than one hundred twenty-two thousand people.

Eriksdotter explains why such data matter as new antibody drugs enter use and need long-term tracking. Findings from the registry show that deaths in dementia have fallen over ten years, in part as drug use changed. Alzheimer's disease showed the best survival, while Lewy body and Parkinson's dementia showed the worst. The paper shows what routine care data can teach.
pmc-11713436:
Elizabeth Golembiewski and co-authors describe how patients and other key voices helped shape a diabetes study, in a paper from 2024. The study compares drugs for type 2 diabetes using records from routine care, not a trial. Such data are rich but complex, which makes outside input hard to arrange well.

The team formed an advisory group of twelve people. It included people with diabetes, doctors, health system leaders, and a payer voice. The group changed key choices, such as who counts in the study, and added a study aim on what patients prefer. A survey found that members were glad with the process and wanted to stay involved. The paper offers a model for similar studies that use routine care data.
pmc-11713536:
Prevot and co-authors test a brain-calming drug in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 paper. The drug fine-tunes a receptor that quiets overactive brain cells. In aged mice it had earlier eased memory trouble and reversed cell shrinkage.

Two mouse types were used, one that builds amyloid and one that builds tau tangles. About a dozen mice per group got the drug by mouth daily for four weeks. Tests then covered working memory and other thinking skills, plus signs of cell growth. The authors ask whether the drug rescues thinking in both models, which would support trials in people.
pmc-11713636:
Katherine Murphy and co-authors study a fat sensor in the brain in a 2025 Alzheimer's paper. The sensor, called Ffar4, responds to fats from food such as omega-3 oils. When it switches on, it helps make fat-based signals that calm swelling in tissue. Alzheimer's brains hold too many of the harsh signals and too few of the calming ones.

The team searched health records linked to gene data for ties between this sensor and illness. They also used a mouse model of the disease to check brain tissue. Their work asks whether turning the sensor on could restore a healthier balance of signals. If so, the sensor could become a drug target for brain swelling in dementia.
pmc-11714036:
Jaclyn Eissman and co-authors hunt for gene spots that steer body chemistry, gene use, and DNA marks in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. The study focuses on Caribbean Hispanic adults from the Dominican Republic and New York, a group often left out of gene research. Each layer of data can hint at how the disease takes hold.

The team held full gene reads, gene use data, and DNA marks from 750 people, plus body chemistry reads from 272 people. They scanned millions of gene spots for links to thousands of small body chemicals. Many strong pairs turned up. Path checks pointed to heart and brain blood vessel routes, which the authors say may play a bigger part in the disease than once thought.
pmc-11714736:
Mohammad Chowdhury and co-authors present a 2025 count of who might qualify for new Alzheimer's drugs in Alberta, Canada. The new drugs can slow the disease, but they need a lot of clinic time and staff. Planners must first know how many people could even be offered them. The team used health records for the whole province. They found more than seventy-seven thousand people newly named as having dementia over nine years.

The average age at that point was just over eighty, and most were women. About one in five had a cause other than Alzheimer's disease for their dementia. Among the rest, close to two in five had health problems that would bar the new drugs. In the end, about half of all dementia cases might qualify on paper. The count helps the province plan clinics, scans, and staff ahead of demand.
pmc-11714836:
Reem Neal and co-authors report a 2025 study of how kidney function relates to spinal fluid marks for Alzheimer's disease. Their sample held nine hundred and seventy older adults from two studies at one research center. Just over half had mild loss of thinking skills. Blood and spinal fluid were taken at the same visit. Kidney health was gauged from a standard blood test score.

All three fluid marks moved with kidney score in this sample. One mark rose as kidney scores rose, while two forms of tau fell. The links held no matter what a person's thinking status was. They were stronger, though, in people with mild loss of skills. The authors warn that kidney health should be kept in mind when fluid marks are used to screen people for trials or care.
pmc-11715036:
Daniel Alcolea and a large team of co-authors report in 2025 long-term blood and spinal fluid marker changes in Down syndrome. Alzheimer's disease is the main cause of death in adults with Down syndrome. Their Barcelona cohort tracks markers over time across disease stages, from no symptoms to dementia.

Participants gave at least two samples over follow-up. Blood markers for brain damage rose faster in more advanced stages. A tau marker rose in early symptomatic stages as well. In spinal fluid, two markers rose faster at advanced stages, while one amyloid ratio stayed flat. The patterns may help stage disease in this population.
pmc-11715236:
Lim and Park use in 2025 machine learning to find which personal values shape the lifestyle of older adults in South Korea. Lifestyle reflects the person, yet values behind it are rarely studied. They surveyed 300 adults aged 55 and older who live in local communities.

Profile analysis split the group into a healthy type, near half, and an unhealthy type. The split showed most in social relationship traits, with the healthy type more connected and active. A value profile tool fed the learning model. The authors rank which values carry most weight for each type, to guide programs that support healthy aging.
pmc-11715336:
Alberto Jose Mimenza and three co-authors check how well spinal fluid tests, brain scans, and clinical judgment agree when sorting out memory loss, in this 2025 study. Telling Alzheimer's disease from other dementias is hard, and guidelines endorse biomarker tests to raise certainty. The team reviewed patients worked up at a national institute in Mexico between 2018 and 2023.

Seventy-seven patients had both the fluid markers and a glucose based brain scan. The two test families agreed in eighty-eight percent of cases on Alzheimer's versus other causes. Agreement between the first clinical impression and scan patterns was only moderate. Nearly half the patients had their diagnosis changed once the biomarkers came in. Where doubt remains, the authors advise using both tests rather than either alone.
pmc-11716236:
Satya VVN Kothapalli and co-authors report a 2025 study on a scan dye used to find tau tangles in the living brain. Tau tangles are a sign of Alzheimer's disease, but the dye also sticks in deep brain areas rich in iron. That extra sticking can blur the line between real damage and a false signal.

The team scanned 68 adults, some healthy and some with disease plaques, with both the dye scan and a scan type that senses tissue loss and iron. Tissue loss in side and top brain areas tracked with higher dye reads. A joint model with loss and iron terms fit best in the inner side brain. The work helps sort true tangle signal from iron effects.
pmc-11716536:
Sofia Fernandez-Lozano and eight co-authors published a study in 2025 on the chain linking amyloid, tau, shrinkage, and memory loss in early Alzheimer's disease. All four move together, but the order of cause and effect is hard to prove. The team modeled the chain directly in people who were still healthy or mildly impaired.

They used a Canadian cohort with memory tests, MRI scans, and two kinds of PET scan across 333 visits. A region-selection method picked the brain areas where amyloid and tau mattered most for memory. The models then tested whether tau and hippocampal shrinkage carry amyloid's effect into memory loss. Tracing this chain shows where a drug might break it.
pmc-11716736:
Federico d'Oleire Uquillas and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2025 on the cerebellum and healthy brain aging. This structure at the back of the brain is best known for movement, and aging studies have largely ignored it. The team asked whether its size tracks thinking skill and protection against decline.

They pooled data from three big cohorts, including more than forty-five thousand people in the UK Biobank. Better thinking scores went with denser tissue in the cerebellum, as strongly as in the cortex. Its rear parts mattered most and aged unevenly. The results argue that this overlooked region helps explain why some minds stay sharp.
pmc-11726836:
Agata Jabłońska-Trypuć and co-authors test two plant hormones on human skin cells grown in the laboratory. The hormones, kinetin and benzyladenine, belong to the cytokinin family and are already known to benefit skin. Using fibroblasts, the cells that build skin's scaffolding, the team measured growth, movement into a scratch wound, and production of protein and collagen at two doses of each hormone.

Both compounds pushed the cells to multiply and migrate faster and to synthesise more collagen, the protein that gives skin its strength. The authors read the results as a sign of genuine therapeutic potential for skin disease and aging. They are careful to bound the claim: these are dish experiments, and the compounds now need molecular study and testing in living skin before any medical promise can be made.
pmc-11728436:
Akihiko Asao and co-authors studied shopping help and decline in older Japanese adults in a 2024 paper. Staying able to run one's own daily life keeps care needs down as people age. Shopping is a key such task, since it mixes planning, travel, and money handling in one trip.

The team drew on records for older residents who get light support under Japan's long-term care insurance. They asked whether those who get help with shopping show more decline in daily function than those who shop alone. The cross-check can hint at whether help marks decline or eases it. Such hints guide how support plans are drawn for aging towns.
pmc-11728636:
Lei Xu and co-authors review how to clean soils polluted with heavy metals, in a 2024 paper. Industry and farming have spread metals like lead and cadmium into soils worldwide. Cleanup methods fall into physical, chemical, and biological families, plus mixes of them. Each family has strengths and weak points that the review sets side by side.

The authors also look at how cleanup success is judged, a weak spot in the field. Standards and scoring methods for cleaned soil are still not settled. That gap makes it hard to compare projects or trust claims of success. The paper maps open questions and likely paths ahead. It aims to help future cleanup studies and field work choose methods and prove results more soundly.
pmc-11730436:
Urvi Vashistha and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, whether a gene variant in an immune signal raises gum disease risk in Indians. Periodontitis, the severe form of gum disease, grows from bacteria, immune response, and environment together, and the signal IL-1 alpha is a prime suspect in the immune part.

The team gathered Indian case-control and survey studies on two variants of the gene. Across regions of India, the links pointed in mixed directions: some studies found risk, others none. Their verdict is that the correlation lacks solid evidence in this population. The review maps where Indian data exist and where larger, better studies are still needed.
pmc-11732336:
Atsushi Yamaguchi and co-authors report a pancreatic cancer that seeded separate spots inside the duct branches, in this 2024 case report. Acinar cell carcinoma is a rare pancreatic tumor that seldom enters the main duct. A sixty-year-old man's checkup scan found a head mass about thirty millimeters wide. Juice drawn from the duct showed no cancer cells, yet surgery went ahead on suspicion.

The removed tissue confirmed the rare cancer, with invasion of the main duct. Oddly, tumor implants sat in several branch ducts downstream, with clear gaps between them and the main mass. No link connected the deposits. The authors warn that such implants can linger in the leftover pancreas after surgery and seed relapse. Follow-up plans, they say, should allow for that route.
pmc-11739536:
Yoshihito Mima, Tsutomu Ohtsuka, and Yuta Norimatsu report a green nail in a man taking a psoriasis drug, in a case report published in twenty twenty-four. Green nail usually comes from a common bacterium and favors damaged nails, psoriatic nails, or hands kept wet. The drug, deucravacitinib, blocks a signaling enzyme and clears psoriasis well.

The patient, a man of seventy-two, developed the green nail four months into treatment. His nails had shown no psoriasis before the drug began, so the team suspects the drug played a part. They trace a possible route: the blocked enzyme carries signals for a protein that helps fight this bacterium. No earlier case tied the drug to green nail. The report asks clinicians to watch for it.
pmc-11753336:
Marty and co-authors teach in 2024 a constraint solver to pick good values during search, rather than hand crafting that rule. Constraint programming solves hard combinatorial problems well, but its branching heuristics take expert time to build. Learning based variable rules exist, while value rules were scarce.

Their generic method joins deep Q learning, a tailored reward, and a graph neural network that handles mixed graph forms. Tests on graph coloring, independent set, max cut, and vertex cover rivaled classic impact and activity rules. Fine tuning a trained model on a new problem class is also explored in the paper.
pmc-11772336:
Jiatong Shan and six co-authors pool trials of skin-based vagus nerve stimulation for Parkinson's disease. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-four. The noninvasive therapy is proposed as an add-on, but its worth had never been tallied.

Six databases were searched for randomized trials. Six trials with one hundred and seventy-six patients qualified. Motor outcomes led: sign severity, mobility, balance, and gait. Thinking, mood, sleep, and side effects were also tracked, split by treatment length and medication state. Bias was scored with a standard tool. The pooled results give clinicians a first quantitative read on a therapy patients can apply at home.
pmc-11782036:
Esophageal cancer patients get chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, and how much the tumor shrinks forecasts their outlook. Zhifu Chen and eleven co-authors hunted for blood or tissue markers of that shrinkage in a 2024 study of 60 patients. They compared tumor regression grades against patient features and survival, and mined public gene data from before and after treatment.

A third of patients saw the tumor vanish entirely under the microscope, and three fifths responded strongly. Poorly differentiated tumors and invasion into nerves or vessels predicted weak shrinkage, and weaker shrinkage meant shorter survival. Three candidate genes emerged, with protein checks tying them to outcomes.
pmc-11805236:
Sameep Singh and co-authors review low level laser therapy in dentistry in this 2024 paper. The therapy uses low power light on tissue. In dental care it is used to cut pain and swelling and to speed healing. The review covers a wide range of dental uses.

Conditions discussed include jaw joint disorders, mouth sores from cancer care, and pain after surgery. The therapy also helps in orthodontics by speeding tooth movement and easing pain. The authors present it as a non invasive option that fits well with standard care. Readers get a broad summary of where the method helps and how it is applied.
pmc-11870136:
Avijit Avasthi and Bhumika Rathore estimate dental caries in adults attending a dental college in Himachal Pradesh, India. Their cross-sectional study, published in 2025, uses the CAST index, which records caries severity in more detail.

About thirty percent of adults had experienced tooth loss, and a similar share had lesions reaching dentin. Nearly thirty percent had lesions attacking the pulp, with no significant gender pattern. Caries severity worsened with age. Only a small share had received restorative care for caries. The authors argue the CAST index gives fuller knowledge of severity and changing oral health than the older decayed-missing-filled index alone.
pmc-11888636:
When a heart stops in hospital, the share of time rescuers actually spend pressing on the chest is called the chest compression fraction. Higher shares mean better blood flow, and guidelines want at least sixty percent. Chanjal and co-authors measured this share in fifty cardiac arrests at a large hospital in South India and looked for what drags it down.

The average share was about 72 percent, comfortably above the target. Diabetes was the most common illness among the patients. The share fell as resuscitation attempts ran longer, and it also dipped for daytime events, when defibrillators were used, and when more team members took part. The authors argue that watching these patterns can help teams keep compressions going with fewer pauses.
pmc-11891636:
Surbhi Sharma, Andrea Belluati, Mohit Kumar, and Shikha Dhiman build droplets that form and dissolve on command, steered by enzymes, in this 2024 paper. Living cells run many enzyme networks at once to raise and retire compartments. Copying that timing in a test tube has been hard.

Their network pairs enzymes that fight and enzymes that mind separate jobs. One enzyme grows a polymer chain; the chain then clumps with ATP, the cell's fuel, into droplets called coacervates. Other enzymes burn or rebuild the fuel, so the droplets swell or vanish on a schedule the team sets. The droplets also ran chemistry inside themselves, acting as tiny reactors, and they picked which cargo to take up as they formed. The authors frame the system as a step toward artificial cells with timed compartments.
pmc-12339136:
Shu Wang, Yin Jiang, Anchao Yang, Fangang Meng, and Jianguo Zhang review the growing world burden of diseases that wear the brain away, above all Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. World burden data show steep rises, tied to aging populations. The recent pandemic may have added to the toll.

The review covers the scale of the rise and the unmet needs in care systems today. It weighs the special strain the pandemic placed on patients and families. It also sets out policy and practice ideas for doing better. The authors call for joined work across medicine, research, and policy to lift life quality for patients and caregivers.
pmc-12411036:
Fan Jiang and five co-authors published a 2024 mapping study of research on Aspergillus in respiratory medicine. Aspergillus is a common fungus that can cause serious lung infections, especially in people with weak immune systems. The team used bibliometric tools, which chart who publishes what, where, and how often.

Their search of English papers from 1975 to 2022 found 1,065 articles with over 41,000 citations. The United States led output, and one author, Denning, published most often. Hot topics included disease spread, a blood test marker, and chronic lung infection. Two themes, allergic and invasive lung disease, were still active in 2022. The map helps new researchers see where the field is heading.
pmc-12480136:
A 2024 Korean health report follows rates of felt depressive symptoms among teens from 2014 to 2023. A case counts when deep sorrow or despair kept a student from daily life for two weeks. The figures come from a national youth risk survey run each year.

In 2023 the rate was lower for boys than for girls, a pattern seen across the decade. Rates moved up and down over the ten years without a clear lasting shift. Middle school and high school students showed much the same rates in the final year. The brief report gives school and health officials a compact trend line for planning support, broken down by sex and school level.
pmc-12539536:
Wu and co-authors report in 2024 that a protein called TBC1D15 holds back cleanup activity in microglia, the brain's immune cells, in Alzheimer's disease. Cleanup there clears amyloid plaques, but reports on its level over time conflict. Their work tracks that change and the protein's role in it. The head gives 2024 as the publication year.

Cleanup rose in three month old disease model mice, then fell by twelve months. The protein sat high in microglial lysosomes in the disease state. Silencing it cut cell swelling and amyloid uptake in a cell line, while raising cleanup pathways. A protein chain tied to lysosome swelling is proposed, and targeting the protein is offered as therapy logic.
pmc-12660736:
Guangtai Shen and co-authors present a 2025 study of thyroid surgery done through a cut under the chin. Thyroid cases rise, and patients care about neck scars. The under-chin route aims to beat the mouth route's limits. Records cover 95 patients done at one center across two and a half years, picked for small benign lumps or early cancers without spread. One more case switched to open surgery for bleeding.

Runs spanned part cuts, lobe cuts with node clears, and three full gland cuts. Mean time ran near 160 minutes. No lasting nerve or gland harm occurred; two voice nerve palsies faded with rest. Looks pleased patients strongly. A hidden scar route held its safety in this run.
pmc-12661836:
Ping-Tao Tseng and co-authors weigh whether two popular diabetes drug classes raise the risk of gynecologic tumors. Their 2025 network meta-analysis pools ninety-one randomized trials with well over two hundred thousand participants. Concerns about cancer potential had circulated for both classes, but no agreed answer existed for specific regimens.

The analysis compares many drug variants through their shared trial controls, counting tumors in women as the main outcome. Only one regimen, a high weekly dose of one drug, showed a significantly raised overall tumor risk against controls. Dropout rates served as a stand-in for acceptability, and a second statistical approach checked the findings. Regimen-level answers help prescribers balance metabolic benefit against rare harms.
pmc-12663436:
Paulene Pineda and a large team present a near-complete cattle X chromosome in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The cattle genome guides breeding and the study of ruminant biology, but gaps remained. Their assembly runs from telomere to telomere and resolves both parental copies. It adds a large stretch of sequence missing from the standard reference. With it they found hundreds of new protein-coding genes and many more structural variants.

The X chromosome's centromere drew special interest. It proves to be a natural neocentromere, a centromere that formed at a new spot. Its repeats and chemical marks differ sharply from those of other chromosomes. The finding offers a rare natural case for studying how centromeres are born. Livestock genomics gains a sharper reference as well.
pmc-12664136:
Dzifa Kwaku, Dusty Van Helden, Joan Dao, John Osborn, and Matthew Johnson map how electrical stimulation of the renal nerves changes kidney blood flow in pigs. Their physiology paper showed up in two thousand twenty-five. Overactive renal nerves drive drug-hardy hypertension, and killing the nerves is irreversible.

Hook electrodes around the renal artery-nerve complex delivered frequencies from twenty to fifteen thousand hertz. Low frequencies made sustained cuts in renal blood flow. High frequencies caused immediate drops that adapted over time. Kilohertz stimulation also left a carryover effect, blunting the kidney's response to later low-frequency stimulation. The frequency-dependent picture guides future bioelectronic treatments that modulate rather than destroy the nerve.
pmc-12666136:
Teshager Tessema and six co-authors review heart care outcomes in eastern Ethiopia in a 2025 study. Acute coronary syndrome, a sudden cut in blood flow to the heart, is a leading killer. No prior work had covered their region. They read records for hundreds of patients admitted to public hospitals over five years.

About a quarter of patients had a poor outcome, including deaths in hospital, referrals upward, and patients leaving against advice. Most patients were men, and only a small share arrived within half a day of symptoms. Arriving very late, very weak heart pumping, and signs of poor blood flow on heart scans each predicted poor outcomes. The authors urge faster presentation and care.
pmc-12670736:
Abdelmonam Hagag and co-authors pool trials of tenecteplase, a clot-busting drug, for stroke patients treated late, in a 2025 review. Standard stroke care favors early treatment, but many patients arrive after the usual window. Evidence for this drug at a set dose in the late window was thin. The team searched three databases for randomized trials comparing the drug with best medical care.

Eight trials with 3,068 patients entered the analysis. The drug did not raise the share of patients with excellent or favorable recovery. It did improve early neurological scores. Brain bleeding with symptoms, though, occurred more often in the drug group. Results looked better in trials that left out patients who could also get a clot pulled out by catheter. The authors call the balance mixed and urge care in patient choice.
pmc-12691336:
Marta Kloch and co-authors compare the Y chromosome in European bison, American bison, and domestic cattle. Their 2025 study measures the male chromosome's size and its dark-staining region in cultured blood cells. Such measures can reveal how closely related species have drifted apart.

All measured traits differed between species in clear ways. The dark-staining region content was the strongest separator, with area and length next. A grouping analysis split cattle cleanly from the two bison, while the bison sat close but separable. A classification method sorted samples with high accuracy, erring only between the two bison. The work gives conservation and breeding science a hard measure of difference among these cattle family members.
pmc-12692136:
Garduño-Torres and ten co-authors show tuberculosis bacteria infect human belly fat cells and switch on dormancy genes, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Latent tuberculosis is usually blamed on immune granulomas alone. Fat cells may shelter bacteria away from immune surveillance instead. Cultured visceral fat cells are infected with two bacterial strains.

About thirty-nine percent of fat cells are invaded within three days. Bacteria express virulence and dormancy genes inside the cells. Inflammatory signals rise, one fivefold with the virulent strain. Patient biopsies show bacterial transcripts in over two-thirds of cases. Belly fat emerges as a hidden reservoir for latent infection.
pmc-12692236:
Emily Laveriano-Santos leads a team of fifteen authors who map what shapes hormone metabolism in late pregnancy, across two Spanish cohorts. Steroid hormones steer a healthy pregnancy. But their metabolite patterns and what drives them were not fully charted. Urine samples from over twelve hundred women in the third trimester were run through targeted mass spectrometry.

Fifty metabolites resolved into thirteen hormone groups, plus ratios and estimated enzyme activities across the steroid pathways. Elastic net regression in the first cohort put forth dozens of clinical, lifestyle, and social determinants. Ten such links held up in the second cohort. Body mass index stood out, tied to higher corticosteroid and androgen measures. The shortlist that held up is what the study leaves behind.
pmc-12696136:
Grischa Ott and six co-authors test how far nerve-growth-factor-treated PC12 cells really go toward turning into synapse-forming neurons, in a two thousand twenty-five neuroscience paper. The rat tumor cell line is a workhorse model of neuronal differentiation.

Over twenty-one days the treated cells gained electrical excitability, neurite outgrowth, presynaptic-like shapes, and clustering of synaptic proteins. Endocytosis took place in neurites, but the coupled recycling of freshly retrieved vesicles, the heartbeat of synaptic transmission, was absent. No true synapses formed. The authors conclude differentiation stalls short of presynaptic competence and warn modelers to respect that limit when choosing PC12 cells for synaptic research.
pmc-12699036:
Cemre Baykan and Alexander Schütz test how people move their eyes to check what they cannot see in a 2025 study. Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, and the brain fills that gap with a best guess. The authors ask whether searchers aim their gaze at that spot to test the guess, as they do for other unsure areas.

In a one-eye search task, hidden targets sometimes sat inside the blind spot. The first eye jump did not favor the blind spot when targets could appear on either side. When targets always came on the same side, people learned to look there first. The authors say the brain's fill-in guesses are not tested by default. Context, once learned, can still tune the search.
pmc-12700336:
Williams, Bimali, Garza, and a large team ask what registered nurses need to care well for Black patients with heart failure. Their cross-sectional study is from two thousand twenty-five. Black patients face higher rates of hospital stays for heart failure and longer stays. Good nursing care has been linked to far fewer stays and returns.

The team surveyed two hundred nurses drawn from those who cared for many such patients. Nurses were split by whether their patients stayed ten days or less, or more than ten days. The survey asked how much each work task counts and how well it is done. Seventeen needs set the two groups apart. The authors say that fixing those needs, by training or new steps, may cut length of stay.
pmc-12701936:
Syed Billal Hossain and five co-authors use machine learning to predict trauma stress after breast removal surgery in Bangladesh, in a 2025 study. The condition, post-traumatic stress disorder, is common after mastectomy but little studied in low-resource settings. The team surveyed one hundred thirty-eight survivors at three hospitals. They recorded social, health, and treatment facts and scored stress with a standard checklist.

A feature-picking method named schooling, income, and shifts in family behavior as key predictors. Ten learning models were then raced, and the random forest model won with accuracy near eighty-nine percent. About a third of the women met the bar for the disorder. Urban and younger patients faced higher risk. The authors offer the model as a cheap screen for clinics with few mental health staff.
pmc-12706936:
Reza Tayefeh Davalloo and five colleagues tested whether shining a diode laser inside a root canal weakens the bond of a fiber post. Fiber posts restore teeth after root canal treatment, and lasers are used to disinfect the canal. Whether that disinfection step harms later bonding was the question. The twenty twenty-five laboratory study used thirty-six extracted single-rooted lower premolars. Teeth were divided into four groups combining two resin cements, with and without laser treatment.

After ten thousand heating-cooling cycles that simulate aging, push-out bond strength was measured on a testing machine. The four groups differed significantly. Electron microscopy examined one specimen per group at the cement-dentin interface. Results guide dentists on pairing laser disinfection with cement choice, so posts stay anchored instead of loosening after treatment.
pmc-12707436:
Freddie Seba and co-authors describe teaching generative AI inside two health informatics master's courses, at Chicago and San Francisco, and measure what students gained. The assignments assumed no technical background. Students researched the tools' basics, used them on real projects, and reflected on the experience, while tests before and after the semester tracked their knowledge.

Knowledge scores climbed at both sites, from 81 to 93 percent in Chicago and from 77 to 80 percent in San Francisco. Reflections showed students most engaged by the tools' essentials, by how AI reshapes information work, and by the changes it brings to health care organisations, with ethics a recurring concern. The authors offer their design as a transferable way to build AI competence, judgement, and critical thinking in graduate students of any background.
pmc-12708636:
Kumar, Kumar, Chauhan, Saini, and Kumar use computational drug repositioning to predict multi-target epilepsy treatments, in a study from twenty twenty-five. A third of epilepsy patients resist current drugs. All approved drugs are screened for brain permeability and similarity to epilepsy drugs. Docking tests them against three seizure-related target proteins.

Forty-six drugs bind better than the standard drug for each target. Three candidates bind the right pockets without severe seizure-related side effects. Simulations show all three bind stably over time. Oxaprozin looks most stable and leads the candidate list. Preclinical trials are warranted before any clinical use.
pmc-12709736:
Fumitaka Obayashi and co-authors plan faster recovery for older patients after major mouth cancer surgery in this 2025 study. The operation rebuilds the jaw area with tissue moved from elsewhere, a heavy burden at any age. Sixty-one patients were reviewed for what delayed recovery and stretched hospital stays.

Older patients stayed longer, started eating later, and suffered more aspiration pneumonia than younger ones. Yet within the older group, age itself was not the culprit: delayed oral feeding predicted long stays. Swallowing problems interfered with the recovery bundle. The authors conclude the program is safe for older patients and that feeding support deserves priority in tailoring it.
pmc-12710436:
Jacques Delabie and co-authors census ants across the three layers of an Amazonian rainforest, in work from twenty twenty-five. The layers are the ground litter, the understorey, and the canopy. Ants fill many roles in each layer, from hunters to fungus growers.

Two methods did the sampling: litter extraction for ground ants and direct watch on cut branches for tree ants. Near five hundred species from seventy-seven genera turned up over about three hectares. Trait data on diet, nest site, and colony size sorted species into seven clusters. Those clusters lined up well with the three forest layers. Army ants and fungus growers each formed clear groups. The census matches patterns seen in Central American forests.
pmc-12713236:
Dengkai Huang, Wenjun Xu, Marco Helbich, and Xiaochun Yang reviewed how city design shapes jogging, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their evidence comes from tracking data that runners share by choice on fitness platforms. Running is widely pushed for public health, but past reviews had not pooled effect sizes.

From nearly two thousand papers, a few dozen fit the rules, and a smaller set could be pooled. Building density showed the largest link to running, ahead of mixed land use and water features. Parks nearby and transit density mattered little. Green and blue features of nature tied steadily to more running, while slope effects varied by place. The authors flag weak spots, such as reliance on a single platform's data.
pmc-12716836:
Franka van der Linden and co-authors present a new calcium sensor for live-cell imaging in this 2025 paper. Sensors that glow when calcium rises are workhorses of cell biology, but most switch between a bright state and a dim one. The dim state gives a weak signal, which hurts precise measurement.

While tuning a sensor of a different color, the team found a green version that stays bright in both states. Calcium still changes how long its glow lasts, by more than a billionth of a second, so lifetime imaging can read the level. The sensor, named G-Ca-FLITS, is about as bright as widely used sensors and barely reacts to acidity. With it, the team tracked calcium in cell compartments, saw uneven bursts inside mitochondria, and tested lifetime imaging in fruit fly brains.
pmc-12717036:
Si-Jia Sun and co-authors trace a driver of aneurysm in a 2025 study of the belly aorta. A swelling of that vessel can burst fatally, and cell aging inside the wall plays a part. The team focused on a fiery form of cell death tied to a pore-forming protein, GSDME, and asked whether it switches on aging in the wall.

In mouse models and patient tissue, that death pathway was active in damaged walls. Mice lacking the protein aged less in their vessels and developed smaller aneurysms. Restoring the protein only in muscle cells brought the disease back, while an anti-aging drug pair erased it. Cell-level data showed the protein reshapes muscle cells and immune states. The authors name it a master switch and drug target.
pmc-12717636:
Xueqin Guo and six co-authors grade how well junior intensive care nurses spot and answer a patient's decline. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Fast catch of decline is key in such units, and new nurses are the weak link to train. They survey nurses at five top hospitals in China with a set form that spans six skill fields.

Scores run fair overall, with hands-on emergency work the low field and decision calls next. School level, years on the job, and drill in decline watch all move the score. The team urges managers to build those levers into training, so young nurses act faster and surer at the bedside.
pmc-12718236:
Dina El-Sayed and four colleagues describe two new viruses that kill a crop germ causing soft rot, in a twenty twenty-five study. The germ, Pseudomonas marginalis, rots potatoes and other vegetables. Viruses that infect germs, called phages, may serve as green pest control. The team detail the two phages' toughness, genes, and power against the rot.

Both phages bore wide acidity ranges and heat up to forty-five degrees, but sunlight harmed them. Their genes held no sign of risk traits for farm use. Each phage alone held back the rot on potatoes. Together they cut disease severity by more than eighty percent. The pair form a new branch among their virus class.
pmc-12718536:
Bella Zhong and co-authors warn about missed causes of low blood sugar in babies in a 2025 article. Young children slip into low blood sugar more easily than adults, especially when illness cuts feeding, and doctors often blame simple starvation ketosis. That quick label can be wrong: deeper metabolic causes are missed in up to twenty-eight percent of cases.

One trap is that babies can hide the problem. A child who feeds very often, for instance by frequent breastfeeding, may keep sugar levels afloat and mask an underlying disorder until a longer fast exposes it. The authors urge clinicians to look past the first easy explanation and weigh such confounders closely in young children with repeated episodes.
pmc-12719236:
Hossein Hemmati and co-authors report a 2025 journal article on a womb artery blocking treatment for two rare ectopic pregnancies. Pregnancies in the cervix or in a cesarean scar can bleed heavily, and saving the uterus matters. The team reviewed one year of cases at a single referral center treated with GELFOAM embolization.

Among 41 patients, the uterus was saved in 40, a success rate of 97.6 percent. No procedure-specific complications occurred, and one patient developed a blood collection after surgery. The single failure came in a late-arriving case and needed surgery. The authors call for larger studies with longer follow-up.
pmc-12721336:
James Vu and co-authors present a 2025 case report on a perforated duodenal ulcer in a patient with severe liver disease. People with cirrhosis often get peptic ulcers, and a hole in the gut wall is a grave complication. Surgery is usually the fix, but this patient was too ill for an operation.

The ulcer burst after an upper endoscopy done to check for swollen veins. The team treated him with antibiotics and drainage tubes placed through the skin. They also placed a fully covered metal stent inside the duodenum to seal the leak. He recovered without surgery. The case shows a nonoperative path that other teams can weigh when surgery is too risky.
pmc-12721736:
Baik, Jeon, Yoo, and Kim compare in 2025 two single drug options for long term care of chronic heart artery disease in Korea. A 2024 European guideline newly backed one drug class as a sound swap for aspirin. They tested that advice in a nationwide claims database.

Patients had stents placed from 2019 to 2023 and were checked 18 months later. Of about 127,000 patients, two thirds took the newer drug alone and one third took aspirin alone. After matching, about 42,700 pairs were compared over a median of three years. The newer drug did not cut the combined risk of death, heart attack, stroke, or major bleeding.
pmc-12722536:
Michelle Jerry and co-authors published this training study in 2025. It tested a thirty-minute virtual reality module that teaches standard infection precautions to staff in long-term care homes. Five facilities took part, and thirty-four health care workers completed the training wearing head-mounted displays. The team gathered surveys, interviews, and the performance data the headsets recorded during the sessions.

Participants stayed engaged and reported enjoying the module. The headset data did more than confirm completion: it pinpointed where learners stumbled, marking the exact skills that need reinforcement. The authors conclude that virtual reality can strengthen competency-based training for infection control in care homes. They present the work as early evidence rather than a verdict, but the combination of immersion and automatic performance tracking is the point.
pmc-12722936:
Fares and Champeroux argue in 2025 that heart safety testing of drugs should reach beyond rhythm risk alone. The field grew from rules on drug induced heart effects that standard toxicology can miss. Reflex systems often mask those effects, which may show only in a brief window.

Modeling now lets key blood flow measures be assessed, not just pressure. The authors urge a full framework that links lab QT data to clinical risk and borrows concepts from clinical research. The end goal is to guard not only trial volunteers but also patients with heart disease, who are most exposed to such effects. The piece marks 25 years of guidelines.
pmc-12723836:
You and five co-authors tested in twenty twenty-five a Chinese shot used for other cancers as a care for prostate cancer. They first used web tools to list its parts and the genes those parts touch. That list was matched to genes tied to this cancer to find shared hits.

Near fifty shared gene hits came up, with a few core ones in growth and defense paths. In lab cells the shot slowed growth, spurred self-death, and calmed a key growth path. In mice it shrank tumors and woke defense acts. Dock tests showed parts fit their gene hits well. The team sees a sound base for more work.
pmc-12724236:
Xu Wang and co-authors study a rare kind of stroke that harms eye movement, in a paper from 2025. The stroke strikes a thin bundle of nerve fibers that links the two eyes, called the medial longitudinal fasciculus. When it is the only site harmed, the signs can be mistaken for other eye or balance problems.

The team reviewed more than fourteen thousand stroke cases at one hospital over four years. The rare form made up a very small share, with just twenty-four cases. Most patients were men, and most showed the classic eye sign. First clinical reads missed the true cause in about four in ten cases. Early scans missed cases as well. The paper maps where the lesions sat and urges care with first reads.
pmc-12729236:
Bruno Basil, Winifred Adiri, Ejike Lawrence Ugwu, and Ngozi Ijeoma Okoro pool the evidence on whether low vitamin D travels with fatty liver disease in people who have type 2 diabetes. The vitamin's deficiency is a plausible, fixable contributor to liver fat, but the diabetes-specific literature disagrees. Their search of records from two thousand to twenty twenty-five found ten qualifying studies covering over four thousand participants.

Most studies came from Asia and the Middle East. Pooling showed patients with fatty liver disease had significantly lower circulating vitamin D than those without, with roughly a half-standard-deviation gap. Liver status came from imaging, elastography, or biomarker scores. The authors flag the geographic narrowness as the evidence base's main weakness.
pmc-12729336:
The authors ask how reading comprehension supports word problem solving in Hebrew speaking students, in this 2025 study. Fourth graders and eleventh graders, about forty in each group, took tests of comprehension, applied mathematics, memory, and fluency in reading and arithmetic. Hebrew's rich word structure makes it a telling test case.

Comprehension and problem solving correlated strongly at both ages, but the machinery differed. Among the younger children, arithmetic fluency partly carried the link: skill at computing let understanding become answers. Among the older students the link was direct, with working memory mattering less, as computation had become automatic. The authors propose a developmental scaffold model and urge curricula that teach comprehension strategies as part of mathematics, not beside it.
pmc-12729436:
Rocha and six co-authors tracked inflammation and oxidative stress during drug treatment of uterine infection in dogs in twenty twenty-five. Pyometra, a pus-filled uterus, is usually treated by surgery, but medical therapy with the hormone blocker aglepristone offers an alternative for open-cervix cases. The team compared aglepristone alone against aglepristone plus a prostaglandin drug.

Ten affected dogs, five per group, gave daily blood samples for liver tests, acute phase proteins, and redox markers. On aglepristone alone, albumin and a key antioxidant enzyme rose while protein oxidation fell steadily. Adding prostaglandin changed the marker pattern, raising lipid oxidation and C-reactive protein, which muddied judging treatment success. Albumin proved a sensitive marker of effectiveness in both protocols, the authors conclude.
pmc-12729636:
Olga Kostyunina and co-authors review low-coverage genome sequencing for cattle in a 2025 survey of the field. The method reads each stretch of DNA only once or twice, which keeps costs low. Software then fills the gaps by matching the reads to a reference panel of fully read animals. The review weighs how accurate that fill-in is and what affects it, drawing on papers found in two large databases.

Fill-in accuracy turns on read depth, panel size and mix, and the choice of software. The cheap reads can catch rare and breed-specific variants that older chip tests miss. Hard spots remain, above all for large structural changes in the genome. The authors back wider use in breeding, paired with better panels and long-read data for the hard cases.
pmc-12730036:
Judging a pet's quality of life shapes hard choices in the clinic, yet standard scoring tools for it are seldom used. Friederike Rhein, Rebecca Klee, Balazs Albrecht, and Stephanie Krämer surveyed and interviewed vets and assistants across Germany about how they assess quality of life in small animal practice. They asked who knows the tools, who uses them, and what helps or blocks their use.

Formal scoring turned out to be rare outside research studies. Lack of time, low awareness, doubt that the tools are needed, and unease with squeezing a personal judgment into a fixed form all held vets back. On the plus side, users valued clear records they could track over time and better talks with clients. The team urges work on spreading the tools, not just building them.
pmc-12730736:
Manuel Airoldi and colleagues study a rare inherited illness caused by faults in a gene named TANGO2, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Only about one hundred cases are known worldwide. Two siblings carried the same pair of gene faults, yet one became very ill and the other stayed well. The team wanted to learn what else in the body explains that gap.

They combined gene reads, gene activity data, and symptom records into linked maps for each sibling. The ill sibling carried extra common changes in a gene tied to blood fats, plus shifts in genes for growth and energy use. The well sibling carried a change that may protect gene control. Fat handling in the body stands out as a key path in this illness.
pmc-12731636:
Harmen Krugers, Marian Joëls, and Ursula Stochaj reviewed when the stress response helps and when it harms, in twenty twenty-five. The review draws mainly on experiments in male animals. Its core claim is that calling a stress response adaptive or maladaptive depends on context: the task at hand, the state of the animal, and its recent and distant stress history.

Behavioral examples carry the argument. Brain studies give it a base: past stress reshapes how brain cells and circuits answer a new challenge, a kind of built-in re-tuning. Many effects now read as harmful may in fact be fits to the world the animal's history led it to expect. Trouble comes when the world shifts and the tuned response no longer fits. The authors say grasping this link may help prevent and treat stress-linked mental disorders.
pmc-12732836:
Zou and co-authors review protein markers that may help detect head and neck cancers earlier and judge their course. These cancers form a varied group, and the mouth form is the most common. Its rate has risen in recent years. Tobacco and alcohol can drive changes in the mouth lining that turn malignant over time. Even curable early cases are often found late, so outlook has barely improved in decades.

Markers tied to how these tumors grow could flag change before it turns invasive. The review focuses on altered patches in the mouth that precede cancer. It surveys proteins most strongly linked to tumor development. Better markers could sharpen both screening and follow-up.
pmc-12733836:
Su-Young Kim and co-authors found a gentle way to make collagen scaffolds last longer in the body. Collagen membranes guide tissue and bone regrowth, but they dissolve quickly, and the usual chemical crosslinking can poison cells or stiffen the material. The team instead mixed in L-serine, a common amino acid whose side chain forms hydrogen bonds. Scaffolds with up to forty percent serine were tested in mice under the skin.

Moderate serine kept collagen's natural triple-helix shape, while the highest load formed crystals. The treated collagen remained far larger after implantation than untreated collagen, though a commercial membrane lasted longest of all. The authors present serine mixing as a simple, water-based tuning knob for how fast collagen resorbs. They call the data preliminary and ask for tests with real membrane designs and clinical uses.
pmc-12734336:
Agnieszka Ćwiklińska and co-authors check how well labs agree on cholesterol results measured by direct methods. Their 2025 study uses an international external quality program for lipids. LDL cholesterol is a main risk factor for heart disease, and universal cut-offs guide treatment, so lab results need to line up.

The analysis covered years of samples made from fresh, unprocessed human serum from single donors. Spread between labs ran near nine percent at the median. Within-method spread varied by maker, from tight to wide. Method group averages also differed from each other. Such gaps can push the same patient over or under a treatment line depending on the lab. The authors document the current state of harmonization as a base for fixing it.
pmc-12734636:
Xiaomei Wan and co-authors review engineered geopolymer composites in this 2025 paper. These materials pair the stretch and fine cracking of engineered cement composites with low carbon geopolymer binders. The review ties recipe to two outcomes, strength and ultimate tensile strain. Studies with strain above two percent are collected and compared.

One recipe family stands out in the data. Fly ash blended with slag works best as precursor. A sodium hydroxide and water glass activator in stated ranges follows. Polyethylene or PVA fibers near two percent add the ductility. Fine silica sand completes the mix. Curing choice depends on the precursor blend used. The synthesis gives designers tested proportion ranges instead of single study claims.
pmc-12736136:
Xiukun Zhong and co-authors automate the sizing of supported nanoparticles in electron microscope images using a pretrained general segmentation model, in a 2025 paper. Manual sizing is slow, and these images suffer from low contrast, noise, and busy backgrounds. Their method applies the model with no task-specific training, then cleans the output with their own processing chain.

Tested on ruthenium particles on a titanium oxide support, the pipeline reads scale bars, refines shapes, and separates touching particles. Size estimates landed within 3 to 5 percent of reference values, and each image took under a minute. Both marks beat manual annotation and classic threshold methods by wide margins, the authors report.
pmc-12736336:
Deepika Pantham and co-authors test a targeted nanobubble drug for melanoma in this 2025 paper. Paclitaxel fights melanoma growth, spread, and blood vessel formation, but doses are harsh. A second molecule, ICOS-Fc, attacks tumor cells and their support environment. Their carrier is a chitosan nanobubble loaded with a low drug dose and coated with that molecule.

Cell tests measured survival, migration, and invasion of melanoma lines. Mouse experiments used a melanoma strain carrying a common mutation. Tumors were tracked for growth, cell division, and vessel markers after treatment. The design aims to concentrate drug action at the tumor while sparing the body. Combining a cytotoxic drug with an immune related targeting molecule is the central bet. Results span both human and mouse models.
pmc-12736436: Marco Donald Migliore, writing alone, explains a method for sampling an electromagnetic field in a clear, intuitive way. His 2025 article covers optimal field sampling, a technique for choosing where to measure a field so the readings capture it well. The stated goal is to show the physical reasons behind the sampling strategy as it is used along observation curves, rather than to present new data.
pmc-12740936:
Jun Seok Lee and four co-authors test whether worsening motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease march in step with worsening bladder problems. Urinary dysfunction is among the disease's most burdensome non-motor symptoms, yet its tie to motor stage was poorly quantified. Two hundred twenty-three patients at one university hospital completed validated overactive bladder and prostate symptom questionnaires, scored against their Hoehn and Yahr motor stage.

Bladder scores and dissatisfaction rose significantly as motor stage advanced. Splitting patients at stage two showed the late group already significantly worse on overactive bladder scores, probing how early the divergence starts. The retrospective design shows association, but the authors argue bladder screening should scale with motor severity.
pmc-12741436:
Ibrahim AboGhayyada and co-authors report a rare gene disorder in a girl aged three. The disorder blocks plasminogen, a protein that clears fibrin, so stiff membranes form on body surfaces. Her eyes grew woody membranes, the most common sign of the illness. Scans also showed fluid build-up in the brain from before birth, with fused chambers and a missing brain bridge.

Gene tests confirmed the type one form of the disorder. The pure form of the missing protein was not on hand for care. She was treated with fresh frozen plasma, eye care, and seizure drugs instead. Plasma held her eye and brain state steady, though shunt fixes kept her in hospital. The case shows plasma as a workable option where drugs are scarce.
pmc-12742136:
Claire Dossier and a large team set out the plan for a trial in children whose kidneys leak protein and keep relapsing, in a twenty twenty-five protocol paper. These children often depend on steroid drugs to stay well, and a drug called rituximab is used to hold the disease off. A newer drug, obinutuzumab, beat rituximab in lab and animal tests. The trial tests whether one low dose of the newer drug keeps children well for longer.

Children in the trial get one drip of either the new drug or rituximab, and neither families nor staff know which. The main check is whether a relapse comes within twelve months. The team also tracks time to first relapse, total relapses over two years, and side effects such as infections and low antibody levels.
pmc-12748836:
Mariam Okhovat and co-authors catch Alzheimer's changes in mouse brains before plaques appear in a 2025 study. They use a knock-in mouse carrying a humanized version of the amyloid gene, which develops amyloid damage on a predictable schedule. Knowing what flips first, before symptoms, is the key to early intervention.

The team profiled the brain and blood at early and later stages on three levels: how open the DNA is, which genes are active, and where chemical tags sit on the DNA. Big gene activity shifts showed up before plaque deposition, even though the hippocampus kept its usual cell mix. Changes in blood hint at early signals that could one day be read without touching the brain. The work maps the disease's opening moves in a faithful model.
pmc-12750736:
Chuning Yang and eight colleagues compare two hormone plans used to ripen eggs in fertility treatment, in a twenty twenty-five study. Both plans stop the egg from releasing too early. The classic plan uses a blocker drug, while the newer plan uses a progestin and is simpler and cheaper. The team followed patients at a Shanghai hospital who later received frozen embryo transfers.

After matching patients on age, weight, and hormone levels, near two thousand patients were compared. The authors focused on pregnancy rates and on the health of babies born. They weighed whether the newer plan matched the classic one on both counts. The study adds safety data for a plan that could cut cost and side effects for many patients.
pmc-12751436:
Anisa Brar, Anjali Issar, Thaisa Tylinski Sant'Ana, and Tatyana Mollayeva wrote a systematic review in 2025 on sex, gender, and clinical outcomes. They asked if sex and gender change how sick people get and how they heal. Past work gave mixed signs, and each study used its own way to score sex and gender.

The team searched five study lists for work on adults with set measures. Just 19 studies passed, with more than 600,000 people in all. Four looked at sex traits such as testosterone. The rest, 15 in all, looked at gender traits such as gender identity and roles. One such trait was adherence to masculine norms. The results did not line up, and most links stayed weak. Only links of testosterone to depression and erectile function held up with fair trust. The team blames the wide mix of measures for that weak base.
pmc-12752036:
Shahrooz Nemati and co-authors test a school program that teaches social and emotional skills to children with learning disorders, in a 2025 paper. Such students often struggle with runaway feelings and stress on top of their schoolwork. The program trained self-awareness, control of emotions, and getting along with others. The team wanted to know whether twelve sessions could ease distress and poor emotional control.

The study involved 32 students in grades four to six who had diagnosed learning disorders. Half received the training at school, and half served as a comparison group. Both groups took tests of depression, anxiety, and stress before and after, plus a questionnaire on emotional control. The trained group improved sharply on both measures, with large effect sizes. The authors suggest such training belongs in support plans for these students.
pmc-12752436:
Gustavo Marquezani Spolador and colleagues propose trigger points for sending patients with inherited metabolic diseases to palliative care. The link between that care and these diseases matters in the clinic, yet the two are still joined only in a limited way. Blocks include poor grasp of the link, slow will to refer, limited resources, and no rules on who is eligible.

The team drew on past work and on the pathophysiology of the diseases. They set out three pairs of illness paths. One pair covers intoxication disorders, such as organic acidurias and urea cycle disorders. A second covers energy disorders, from fatty acid oxidation defects to select mitochondrial diseases. The third covers disorders of complex molecules, with storage disorders and trafficking defects. They set referral triggers against those paths, starting at diagnosis, and covering times of doubt about the outlook. The frame gives teams firm times to start palliative care.
pmc-12753636:
Arthur Dyer and a team of co-authors tested lab models of tumor-linked immune cells in a 2025 paper. Macrophages that live inside tumors can blunt the body's attack and weaken immunotherapy. The old habit of sorting them into two simple types no longer fits what doctors see in patients, so better dish models are needed.

The team bathed human macrophages in fluid from tumor cell lines and checked whether the cells turned suppressive and held back T cells. They profiled what the tumor fluid carried and how the macrophages changed, in both their proteins and gene activity. They also compared the models with fluid drawn from ovarian cancer patients. The work points to which dish setups best mirror real tumors.
pmc-12754936:
Sindhu Vasireddy and seven co-authors compare preventive drugs for vestibular migraine, in a review published in twenty twenty-five. The condition brings repeated attacks of vertigo and harms quality of life. Many drugs are used to prevent attacks, but few have been tested head to head, so doctors lacked a clear ranking.

The team searched four large databases for trials and strong observational studies up to early twenty twenty-five. They merged direct and indirect evidence in a network analysis. The main outcomes were how often vertigo struck each month and scores for handicap from dizziness. The review weighs both benefit and safety across the drug options. It aims to give clinics a firmer base for choosing treatment.
pmc-12767236:
Sen Zhou and seven co-authors search for gene markers of diabetic kidney disease in a 2025 study. The markers sought sit in pathways that break down polyamines, a family of cell chemicals whose leftovers can harm kidneys. Whether those genes mark the disease was unknown.

The team mined public gene datasets from patients and controls, crossing disease-linked changes with the polyamine gene set. Machine learning screens and accuracy curves narrowed the field to three genes. The three took part in several biological pathways and tied into immune cell patterns in the tissue. Drug guesses were also made from the markers. Lab tests on patient samples confirmed the genes' altered levels. The trio may seed future blood or urine tests for early kidney damage.
pmc-12769636:
Yaqi Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of web-like traps spilled by white blood cells in lung infections. When neutrophils fight germs, they can cast out DNA webs that trap the foe. In excess, the webs may mark worse disease. The team enrolled 120 patients with lung and blood infections from 2022 to 2024 and read gene activity in their blood cells.

Web-forming genes switched on early in pneumonia and sepsis. One signal protein, IL-8, tracked web output most tightly and ran far higher in sepsis blood. Web gene levels rose with standard severity scores. Two web-linked genes also ran higher in sepsis than in plain pneumonia. The team built a forecast model from the web genes. Such marks could help sort patients by risk at the door.
pmc-12771136:
Anita Paiva and six co-authors reported a chest tumor that came back far away, seeded by its own biopsy, in a case report published in 2025. This tumor type grows slowly but can spread. A 75-year-old woman arrived with painful lumps outside her chest, eight years after her type A tumor was removed. Her scans in the first five years had shown no return.

Detective work on her history tied the lumps to the needle path of the biopsy before surgery. Cells shed along the path had grown where the needle went. The authors note that today such clear-cut chest lumps are often not biopsied at all, because of this risk. They urge longer monitoring past five years, and care for the needle tract in plans.
pmc-12772536:
Holly Blake and her team test lead-role training made to help Black and minority ethnic staff move up in the National Health Service. Their 2025 study uses more than one method and looks at two state-wide lead-role plans.

Staff on the plans spoke of blocks set by the way the service is run and of race bias in its rules that kept them from top roles. An online poll and talks heard views from staff on the plans who came from ten ethnic groups. Views of the plans were good all through, and the plans gave a safe space where staff could share what they had lived through. Trust in self and drive to seek growth grew once staff took part.
