Most staff won real steps up in their work life. The team says such plans are prized and help cut the race gap in top lead roles.
pmc-12775536:
Ali and four co-authors hunt for stress biomarkers in rainbow trout, in work from twenty twenty-five. Climate driven stressors threaten fish growth, survival, and farm output. Reliable molecular markers would improve stress management and help fish adapt.

Trout were exposed to five stressors: high and low temperature, crowding, salinity, and low water quality with reduced oxygen. Full transcript profiling captured gene responses to each. Machine learning then picked signature genes that best mark stress type and load. A biomarker panel could let farms detect stress early, before growth or survival losses appear.
pmc-12779436:
Sun and four co-authors compare insulin resistance scores and erectile problems in work from twenty twenty-five. Insulin resistance, where the body responds poorly to insulin, has been linked to erectile dysfunction. Several simple scores estimate it from routine tests, but which links best was unclear.

The team used data from a United States health survey in the early two thousands. More than seventeen hundred men were examined. Four scores were tested with weighted models that account for survey design. Only one score held a clear link in their results. The work is a snapshot in time, so it shows links, not cause, but it can guide which score clinics track.
pmc-12780236:
Guilherme Costa Alvarenga and co-authors map the best jaguar habitat across the cat's whole historic range, in this 2025 paper. Jaguars suffer from hunting, habitat loss, and broken-up forests, so planners need to know where good habitat remains. The team fitted models to GPS tracks from 172 jaguars in eight countries, the largest such dataset yet. Fifteen landscape measures fed the models at several scales.

Jaguars picked rich habitat near water and shunned farms, dense settlement, and livestock country. The suitability map predicted known densities well. Conservation units and protected areas held most top habitat on a third of the range. The Amazon and Mayan forests stood out as strongholds, with the Pantanal, Chaco, and Cerrado also shining. Small unprotected patches punched above their size.
pmc-12780436:
Mary Shepard, Lydia Binelli, and Ikenna Okereke review how openly asbestos levels are reported in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Asbestos exposure causes lung disease and cancers, and deaths linked to it have risen over time. Knowing where levels are high helps protect workers and the public. Yet rules for measuring and publishing asbestos levels differ widely by country. Some places rely on laws, others on community pressure.

The review sums up current monitoring and reporting practice around the world. It compares how legislation has shaped asbestos use and openness in different settings. It also notes where reporting still hides risk from those most exposed. Public health advocates and regulators can use the survey to press for clearer disclosure.
pmc-12781536:
Emily Gregg and co-authors gather expert clinicians to draft shared working definitions for Sjogren's disease care, in work from twenty twenty-five. The autoimmune disease varies widely between patients, and clinics judge it inconsistently. Common terms lack fixed meanings in daily practice.

Eight seasoned clinicians from several countries gave interviews, then refined draft definitions in a group workshop. Seven themes surfaced, from classification and activity to severity, progression, and remission. Agreement failed on four themes. Severity alone split four ways: damage, symptom type, irreversibility, or symptom load. Similar terms for body wide spread were used inconsistently. The authors offer their drafts as a first step toward unified routine assessment.
pmc-12781736:
Guo and co-authors weigh how low activity shapes heart disease deaths worldwide. They used Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2021. Death rates from heart disease tied to low activity rose over that span. The yearly rise averaged 0.70 percent across the period. The team also ran a genetic test called Mendelian randomization.

The genetic test linked more activity to lower heart attack risk. The odds ratio was 0.17 in their main model. Yet the genetic tools varied a lot, which weakens the estimate. The authors urge wider promotion of daily activity. They also call for larger studies with stronger genetic tools.
pmc-12784036:
Gadis Meinar Sari and co-authors compare a herb extract with vitamin C in rats stressed by hard exercise in two thousand twenty-five. Hard training raises oxidative stress, which can upset bone turnover and speed bone loss. Vitamin C is a common shield, but high doses can backfire, so a plant option is of interest.

Fifty-four male rats swam under load for four weeks and got water, herb extract at three doses, or vitamin C by mouth. A stress marker in blood rose in all groups, most at the high herb dose and with vitamin C. The share of spongy bone improved in treated groups, based on leg bone and blood samples. The herb thus helped bone while its stress effects were mixed.
pmc-12785036:
Lucas Bickmann, Matias Rodriguez, Xiaoyi Jiang, and Wojciech Makałowski introduce a tool that sorts jumping genes by type, in a 2025 paper. Jumping genes are DNA stretches that copy and move within a genome. They make up a large share of many genomes and shape how genomes evolve. Their variety makes them hard to sort with older tools.

Their tool, TEclass2, uses a lean transformer model that reads DNA in short chunks. It sorts shared sequence forms into sixteen families. Tests show it sorts more accurately than earlier tools, and users can retrain it on their own data. A web version with ready models makes it quick to use. The authors aim to strengthen genome notes for many research groups.
pmc-12793036:
Maedeh Akbari and colleagues compared taste preferences between obese and non-obese older adults in the Iranian city of Zanjan. Taste leanings shape food choice and may feed weight gain, yet data in the elderly are limited. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team surveyed adults over sixty with a validated food questionnaire covering six taste families: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, savory, and fat. Body mass index was related to each taste score, and the two weight groups were compared directly, with a look at sex differences.

Higher body mass tracked with stronger liking for salty and fatty tastes and weaker liking for sweet, bitter, and savory tastes. Obese participants likewise scored lower on sweet and savory and higher on salty and fat. Among obese participants, women leaned more toward savory taste than men. The authors suggest taste-aware diet advice for older adults.
pmc-12793636:
Malaria kills many children in South Sudan, and knowing which patients face the highest risk can guide scarce care. Loro Gore Lado Jumi and Altaiyb Omer Ahmed Mohmmed studied six thousand four hundred ten children treated at a Juba hospital in twenty twenty-one. Records covered ages from one month to fifteen years. About four point seven percent died. A survival model weighed age, weight, drug choice, and other illnesses.

Older age slightly raised the risk of death, while higher body weight lowered it. Quinine treatment linked to lower risk than artesunate in this data. Children with no other illness had about half the risk of those with one. The authors offer the pattern for triage planning, with care about reading drug effects from records.
pmc-12796336:
Javier Sastre Toraño and a team of co-authors present a method to read sugar chain structures from scratch in a 2025 paper. Glycans, the sugar chains on proteins and in milk, carry biological messages, but chains with the same parts in different arrangements are hard to tell apart. Sorting them usually needs a library of costly synthetic standards.

Their method breaks chains into fragments, identifies the pieces, and assembles the sequence, using ion mobility and mass data. Each new fragment identified joins a reference database, which grew from nineteen standards to 332 entries as the work proceeded. They applied it to sugars in human milk and to chains on manufactured therapeutic proteins.
pmc-12799736:
Drouillard and a large team tested in twenty twenty-five if a locked pair form of a signal protein is safe in live animals. The protein, CCL20, calls defense cells to a spot through its switch. Locked pairs can block that switch with more aim than broad drugs.

They gave the locked form by shot each day for two weeks at doses that had helped in skin ill tests. No weight loss or broad defense loss was seen. Blood, urine, and organ checks were near normal at most doses. The top dose grew the spleen a bit, and one dose mildly shook a cell-aid path. The team sees a wide safe range.
pmc-12804836:
Lucong Zhang, Jinghai Sun, Peng Jiang, and Hui Li redesign the moving cabin of the world's largest single-dish radio telescope, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The cabin holds receivers above the giant dish and must aim finely. A new design hangs the cabin's fine-tuning gear on steel cables in place of rigid arms.

The cable layout cuts weight sharply. Modeling under cable tension limits then tuned the structure for load and sky reach. The new cabin carries more receiver weight and tilts to wider angles. Wider reach opens more sky near the galactic center, the team notes.
pmc-12805736:
Mengyao Hao and co-authors test whether silencing one receptor can ease pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that scars the lungs and destroys the air sac walls. Attention fell on a receptor called S1PR3, which sits on the cells lining the air sacs and rises after injury. The team asked whether it helps or harms the barrier those cells form.

Gene data from patients and from mice with drug-induced lung scarring both showed the receptor switched on strongly. Mice bred to lack it in their lung lining developed far less scarring, with less inflammation, less collagen buildup, and a tighter barrier. Blocking the receptor with a drug or with gene silencing raised the levels of proteins that seal the gaps between cells. The authors conclude that this receptor weakens the air sac barrier during fibrosis.
pmc-12807936:
Amon Bwalya and six co-authors send mystery shoppers into Zambian farm supply shops and pharmacies to see how freely cattle antibiotics flow without prescriptions. Udder infection, mastitis, is the test case. Unregulated antibiotic sales feed resistance that crosses into humans through food, contact, and the environment.

Two hundred twenty sellers across six districts were visited by simulated farmers between late twenty twenty-four and mid twenty twenty-five. Roughly a third were agro-veterinary shops and two-thirds retail pharmacies. The study measured how many dispensed antibiotics for mastitis with no prescription and which drug classes moved most. Mystery shopping captures real counter behavior rather than self-reported practice. The findings feed Zambia's antimicrobial resistance policy debate.
pmc-12809936:
Peng-Ching Hsiao and co-authors test what carries stress into lower disaster readiness among nurses. Nurses anchor disaster response, yet strain erodes their readiness. A survey of 476 registered nurses fed a mediation model. Stress, self-efficacy, family support, and readiness were all scored by standard scales.

Stress linked to lower confidence and thinner family backing. Readiness rose with confidence and support, and fell with stress. Bootstrap tests show self-efficacy clearly carried part of the stress effect. Family support, while welcome, carried no firm share of it. Training and drills that build confidence are the suggested lever.
pmc-12812036:
Naoto Inoue, Tomohito Ijiri, and Toshiaki Suzuki examine in 2025 how pushing with the arms affects the middle phase of standing up from a chair. That phase, from seat-off to peak ankle bend, demands peak muscle effort to lift the body's center while keeping balance. Upper limb support may matter most there.

Ten healthy young men performed the movement with and without arm pushing. Joint angle changes and muscle activity were compared between conditions. Arm pressure links to angle changes were also tested. The study clarifies how arm support reshapes leg demand during a daily movement that many patients struggle with.
pmc-12812436:
Abimbola O Kolawole, Fahd Mohamed, and Denise Mourad offer a two thousand twenty-five narrative review of income-related gaps in aortic aneurysm screening among American women. Aneurysms rupture more and kill more in women, yet screening programs target men. Money and education may widen the detection gap further.

Four databases were searched for United States studies across three decades. Eligible work linked screening or outcomes to at least one social factor. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently. The synthesis gathers determinants of missed screening and proposes equity-centred strategies, from outreach design to coverage policy, for a high-risk group.
pmc-12812736:
Shiqiang Wu and co-authors test three blood markers of bone turnover as predictors of bone loss and repeat fractures, in work from twenty twenty-five. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises fracture risk. Markers of bone build up and break down could flag risk sooner than scans alone.

One hundred eighty patients and eighty healthy controls were compared. All three markers ran higher in patients and rose further in those with fractures. Higher markers tracked lower bone density at the spine and hip. Each marker stood as an independent risk factor for a second fracture. Joined with density scans, the trio predicted risk with high accuracy. The authors back adding them to clinic risk tools.
pmc-12813936:
Cooper and Sejka report a rare synovial sarcoma growing from the falciform ligament in the abdomen, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. Synovial sarcoma is an uncommon soft tissue cancer of youth, usually in limbs. Its aggressive course makes early recognition vital. This case involves a sixty-four-year-old man with a large upper belly mass.

The mass extends into the chest and involves the heart sac. It invades the liver and front chest wall and has spread to the lungs. The tumor arises from the falciform ligament, a fold that anchors the liver. Pre-surgery chemotherapy shrinks the main mass only partly. Spread progresses meanwhile, which rules out surgical removal. The case stresses vigilance for atypical sites.
pmc-12815536:
Jesse Hill and seven co-authors checked how well emergency doctors followed a fast chest pain protocol in five Canadian city hospitals, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The protocol uses a sharp blood test for heart injury to sort patients by risk and speed safe discharge. The team reviewed more than fourteen thousand adults who came in with suspected heart-related chest pain and had the blood test.

Only about a third of patients got care that matched the protocol. High-risk patients were handled by the book nearly all the time. The gap sat in the middle group, where only about one in five matched the plan, above all when the first blood value fell in a gray zone. The authors say the middle path needs clearer rules or better support at the bedside.
pmc-12817436:
Ahmed El Ghoneimy and co-authors report a hip shelf surgery in kids whose thigh bone heads died as a side ill of leukemia care. The surgery builds a bone shelf to cover the soft head. It is known from a hip ill of youth, but not from this cancer-tied one. The team read all such cases at their center from 2017 to 2024 with at least a year of checks.

Fifteen kids, four with both hips hit, gave nineteen hips to grade. Hip scores rose from a mid of seventy-four to a mid of ninety-six after surgery. That jump cleared the stats bar by a wide edge. Half the hips read at the two safest grades for joint wear. Three hips had ills: two lost the graft and one caught germs. The shelf may guard such hips from bad wear, the team say.
pmc-12817536:
Emil Danehorn and four co-authors asked what Swedish students meet during a term abroad, in a study published in 2025. In one school year, 20,000 Swedes chose a term in a distant country. Earlier hints said such students drink more and take more sexual risks abroad. The team held in-depth interviews with eleven who had completed a term away and sorted their accounts by theme.

Stress from heavy workloads ran through the accounts, and culture gaps both annoyed and charmed. Homesickness and minor illnesses showed up too. On sex, the students spoke of care and protection with casual partners. Drinking was social and mild for most, not wild. Some met theft or harassment and took steps: locked doors, no walks alone, and buses over taxis. The authors flag the risks of the term for schools to plan around.
pmc-12820136:
Maureen Makama and a large team of co-authors scope what is known about menstrual changes caused by contraceptives in poorer countries. Their review appeared in 2025. Such changes, from skipped periods to heavy bleeding, are a leading reason women abandon contraception. The team searched nine databases for studies from 2000 to 2024 and gathered 321 studies across 44 countries. Reported rates of changes ranged from zero to ninety-four percent, varying sharply by method.

Two in five reports never even defined what change they counted, hampering comparison. The review also mapped health effects, treatments, and the barriers women face in getting help. The authors urge standard definitions and better counseling, so a predictable side effect stops ending contraceptive use by surprise.
pmc-12821936:
Sydney Bouder, Lia McNulty, and Daehyoung Lee look at insomnia, gaming habits, and health as seen by the subjects, in autistic adults. Their 2025 cross-sectional study also takes in adults with mild intellectual disability at the same time.

One hundred seventeen people filled in standard self-report forms. The forms gauged how bad insomnia was, how they played games, and how they saw their physical and mental health. About a third said their insomnia was moderate to severe. A smaller share may have met the marks for gaming disorder. Time spent on games each week was higher for those with mild intellectual disability. It was also higher for males than for females. How people saw their mental health was linked, in a negative way, with some of the study scores. The team works through links that could guide help for sleep and for wellbeing.
pmc-12824236:
Hamza Rafeeq and three colleagues published a feed technology study in two thousand twenty-five on protecting helpful enzymes. Microbial enzymes help animals digest feed, but they are costly and fragile. One bacterium can make four at once if conditions are tuned.

The team optimised production of protein, fat, fibre, and starch enzymes from Bacillus subtilis. After purifying them, they packed the enzymes into alginate beads. The beads widened the range of acidity and heat the enzymes could handle. After a month in the fridge, packed enzymes kept sixty to seventy-four percent of their activity, against about a third for free ones. Animal feeding trials are still needed.
pmc-12827336:
Jianqing Wu and co-authors release a structured dataset of the Italian railway network, joining train operations with schedules, in a 2025 paper. Railway data is valuable but usually messy or partial, which limits research use. Their dataset covers several train types, station locations, distances between stations, weather conditions, and timetable information, all cleaned into a consistent form.

The authors aim it at studies of large networks and dynamic systems: mining travel patterns, analyzing network shape, and tracing how delays spread. Practical uses include timetable design, resilience testing, and smarter scheduling for real operations.
pmc-12827636:
Yahya Shabi and co-authors present a study, published in 2025, of antibiotic resistance in skin and soft tissue infections at a large hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. These infections are common and costly, and treatment grows harder as germs shrug off standard drugs. Local data with fine detail by germ and sample type were scarce.

The team reviewed nine years of lab records, covering 6,760 wound samples. They tracked which germs appeared and how often each resisted key antibiotics, split by specimen type and infection depth. The long window lets trends show through year-to-year noise. The authors offer the survey as a base for local prescribing rules and stewardship.
pmc-12830636:
Daegwang Choi and co-authors report a highly coherent organic laser built on a patterned surface that needs no etching, in a 2025 paper. Surfaces of this kind can trap light in bound states, which makes them fine platforms for tiny, sharp lasers. Past etch-free designs used plain polymers and stayed passive, meaning they did not lase.

The team patterned the surface straight onto an organic crystal material with a tidy, stable structure. The laser fired in a tight beam with a spread of only 0.2 degrees. Its line width hit the limit of their measuring gear, and its coherence lasted about 20 picoseconds. The authors credit the pairing of the surface design with the material's uniformity.
pmc-12830736:
Minutes count when an ambulance races to a patient, and heavy rain may steal those minutes in ways emergency planners rarely measure. Athicha Uttajug and co-authors measure them in a 2025 study of dispatch records from fifteen cities in southern Japan. They matched a large set of rainy-season calls over seven years with hourly rain records.

The middle call took eight minutes to reach the patient. Past a sharp rain threshold, each extra unit of rain added close to a minute of delay on average. Bad cases, the ones needing long hospital stays, felt rain slowdowns at far lower rain levels. Light cases waited longer once the rain grew extreme. The authors warn that storm plans for ambulance fleets should treat heavy rain as a real drag on care.
pmc-12830936:
Abdulwahab Alamri and Ahmed Alafnan ran a computer study in 2025 on tiny ring sensors for diabetes checks through breath. A compound called indole in exhaled breath may serve as a sign of the disease. The pair tested three ring forms built from carbon, from boron and nitrogen, and from aluminum and nitrogen.

They used quantum math tools to model how indole sticks to each ring and how the grip changes each ring's traits. The boron and nitrogen ring gripped indole the most strongly and held it the longest, which marks high sensing power. The aluminum ring scored in the middle, and the plain carbon ring gripped the least.
pmc-12836436:
Nada Faquir and co-authors report a case of massive stomach bleeding traced to tuberculosis in the chest, in a 2025 paper. A 43-year-old man arrived vomiting large amounts of blood and in unstable condition. A scope found a large ulcer in the mid-esophagus that was actively bleeding, an unusual site with an unusual cause.

Imaging showed a complex lesion linking the esophagus to the chest cavity, plus a weakened bulge in a nearby artery. Ordinary biopsies kept coming back blank, until a needle sample taken through the airway showed the dead-tissue inflammation typical of tuberculosis. Blocking the artery stopped the bleeding, and standard tuberculosis drugs followed with a good recovery.
pmc-12837436:
Kwang-Min Kim and colleagues published an animal model study in 2025. They studied severe hydrocephalus in newborn rats. Bleeding in preterm infant brains can block fluid flow. The swollen brain condition may need surgery to survive. Older models produced only mild swelling in animals. The team wanted a model matching human severity. They injected blood products into pup brain ventricles. Saline, hemoglobin, iron, and red cells were compared. Brain scans tracked ventricle size over several weeks.

Iron caused the most severe ventricle swelling overall. The effect matched the serious human condition closely. Other blood products caused weaker effects by comparison. Microscopy showed damage to ventricle lining surfaces. The study points to iron as the key driver. A faithful severe model can speed treatment testing. Future therapies can now be screened more realistically.
pmc-12837536:
Charmayne Mary Lee Hughes mines police records to chart violence between partners in Los Angeles, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Police data cover whole populations and record when, where, and how abuse happens. Yet researchers rarely use them beside surveys and clinic studies. This work gives them a full workout.

Across four years, from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-three, the city police logged close to seventy-five thousand such incidents, about fifty-one a day. Most happened in homes, and women were the victims in over three quarters. Physical abuse dominated, usually without a weapon. A seasonal time model found steady rhythms month to month, with no clear pandemic-era jump. The author offers the patterns to health, police, and community groups.
pmc-12838036:
Wei Luo and co-authors sort older adults in Fujian by how they seek health care in this 2025 study. China's coverage and clinics have grown more equal, yet health gaps persist. The authors suspect the remaining divide runs through behavior: what people actually do when they feel ill.

They surveyed 1,500 older adults in two cities about five habits, from checkups and online care to delaying treatment and self-medicating. Statistical grouping found three types. One group manages health proactively, mixing prevention with digital tools. A second leans on primary care but skips prevention. A third waits, delays, and treats itself. Membership tracked income, schooling, registration status, and self-rated health. The authors argue that behavior now carries inequality forward, and that help must be tailored by type, from digital access to health literacy.
pmc-12838736:
Jung-Mei Tsai and three colleagues run a pilot study on thinking skills and brain activity in autistic youth, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Autistic young people often struggle with executive function, the mind's control system, but the brain basis is unclear. Thirty matched youths, half of them autistic, did a Flanker task that tests focus amid distraction. A light-based brain scan read activity in the front and side regions during the task.

Both groups answered at like speed and accuracy. Yet autistic youths varied much more from trial to trial, and their daily control-skill ratings were far worse. Brain activity patterns also differed between groups. The authors say steady responding, not raw speed, may be the key gap to target.
pmc-12839836:
Juliana Montoya Montoya and co-authors present a 2025 mouse study on whether transplanted gut microbes change the course of colorectal cancer. Gut microbe balance is swayed by diet and weight and is thought to shape this cancer's growth. The team gave human gut microbes to mice in which colon cancer had been chemically triggered.

Mice received microbes from healthy donors or from cancer patients, alongside control groups with no transplant. Transplanted mice, above all those given patient microbes, showed more cell division, more abnormal growth, and stronger changes in gut immune tissue. Several immune signal levels also shifted in both transplant groups. The study marks gut microbes as real actors in tumour dynamics.
pmc-12844236:
Wang, Wang, and Shen build a chip system that cleans and completes camera images at once in twenty twenty-five. Phone cameras capture raw images with noise and with color gaps at each pixel. Filling the gaps and removing noise takes costly math. The team designed a lean network and a chip plan that can be set up in varied ways.

Their network uses partial filters and views the image at more than one scale. That cut the model's size and math load by more than three quarters. On a standard photo test set, image quality beat the best past design. The chip ran more than twice as fast and can adapt to many small devices.
pmc-12847936:
Chenqi Fang and a team of co-authors chart world river levels from satellites, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Most rivers lack gauges, so the team used radar altimetry at nearly forty-seven thousand virtual stations. Records ran from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-four.

Median level swing worldwide came to 3.76 meters. Levels fell across the Americas' centers and western Siberia, and rose across Africa, Oceania, and much of Asia and Europe. Yearly seasons sharpened in most basins even as peak-to-trough range shrank. Extreme level events surged after twenty twenty-one, the team warns.
pmc-12849336:
Anwar Nader AlKhunaizi and Areej Ghalib Al-Otaibi listen to care staff who helped design a new birthing room. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Birth is run by hormones led by oxytocin, and strange, tense rooms can blunt that flow and slow contractions. Calm rooms built for birth can cut stress and help mothers.

They interview doctors and midwives at a state hospital in Saudi Arabia. One core theme emerges, a supportive room for natural birth, with four subthemes. Staff feel the old space fought their values, praise the new room's privacy, note shifts in midwife work, and give ideas for change. They urge leaders to spread the redesign to other hospitals.
pmc-12854336:
Poojari and Ismail blend a decision tree with logistic regression to predict heart and liver disease in twenty twenty-five. Trees overfit by lumping all cases in a branch. Regression misclasses often in wide data. The hybrid aims to keep both strengths.

Simulations across sample sizes put the hybrid ahead of five rival models. Real data backed the claim, with top accuracy on both disease sets. One set was balanced, the other skewed, and the hybrid handled both. That frees users from hunting for balance fixes. Early flags could sharpen care choices, the authors argue.
pmc-12857136:
Xiaojuan Yin, Jing Ruan, and Wulin Ma study AI and language learning in a 2025 paper on Chinese students of English. Generative AI tools are now common in language classes, yet most research tracks skill gains, not feelings. The team asked how such tools affect students' enjoyment of learning English, and whether gender, skill level, or time using the tools matters.

Ninety-eight university students took a survey after a twelve-week program, and ten were interviewed. Enjoyment sat at a medium level, with the teacher-linked part scoring highest. Gender and English level showed no firm effect, though men and weaker students reported slightly more enjoyment. Usage length is also weighed in the results. The study adds an emotional angle to debates on AI in class.
pmc-12859836:
Yanshuo Ye, Yiyang Jia, and Wei Li identify a stiffness-driven gene marking metastatic colorectal cancer. Their study from twenty twenty-five names the gene TAGLN. Stiff tumour surroundings push cancer cells toward spread. Public cancer data first linked high TAGLN to poor survival.

Lab work showed extra TAGLN speeds identity change and migration. Gene profiles tied it to matrix rebuilding and cell adhesion. Stiff artificial matrices switched the gene on in cells. Its levels rose from normal tissue to tumours to metastases. Related cross-linking and transition mediators moved with it. TAGLN may serve as both warning marker and drug target. Mechanical forces join genes in explaining metastasis here.
pmc-12884436:
Lai Wei reports on the 2025 FELASA congress, the European gathering for laboratory animal science, held under the theme of reducing severity in animal research. Sessions ranged across the 3R principles of replacement, reduction, and refinement, with talks on immunology challenges, AI-driven animal monitoring, and sterile surgical technique.

Two lectures stood out: one tracing the origins of zoology, and an award-winning talk on squid welfare. The meeting cut waste, ran a networking app, and paired exhibits of new technology with hands-on workshops. The report closes on the congress push for openness and cross-field teamwork in humane, rigorous animal research.
pmc-12906736:
Chetan Bohara and six co-authors present a 2025 study of deaths from natural causes in an intensive care unit in western Nepal. Intensive care saves many lives, but death rates stay high where resources are thin. Local data on who dies and why are needed to plan better care.

The team reviewed one year of records, through 2024, at a teaching hospital in Lumbini. They included every ICU patient who died in hospital with a complete record. Data covered age and sex, other illnesses, lab values, and use of breathing machines. The study gives special weight to differences between men and women and the conditions that traveled with each death.
pmc-12909236:
Andrea Pissatto Peres, Maressa Caldeira Morzelle, and four co-authors improve kefir by adding plantain peel. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses the green peel of a cooking banana. Kefir is a fermented milk drink made by grains of bacteria and yeast. The peel is a waste part rich in fiber and health-active compounds.

The team tunes the mix with a grid of tests, varying peel and grain amounts. The milk was fermented a few hours at room heat with some sugar. They track makeup, microbe life over three weeks of storage, and taste. The aim is a drink that uses farm waste and gains extra health value.
pmc-12913936:
Phan Nhan and four co-authors read the full genome of a new duck virus strain from Vietnam, in a study published in 2025. The virus affects Muscovy ducks, causing joint pain, weak immunity, and farm losses. Its spread in the region was known, but no full genome from Vietnam existed. The team took liver and spleen tissue from sick ducklings and sequenced the whole strain.

The genome ran to ten segments and matched the known structure of its family. Family trees for all ten parts placed it in the new duck lineage, close to recent Chinese strains. One part, S1, varied most between strains, with hot spots in a spike protein that the team read as immune-driven drift. A single change in one part may be a local marker. The authors call for steady genome monitoring and vaccines fitted to the region.
pmc-12920536:
Azlan and co-authors test a mushroom blend in rats with blocked brain blood flow. The blend, called NevG, mixes three medicinal mushrooms. Forty male rats were split into five groups of eight. Stroke was induced in most groups, and three groups got the blend by mouth for 28 days. Doses were 250, 500, and 1,000 mg per kilogram.

The blend cut dead brain tissue by 32 to 58 percent. Maze tests showed faster learning, with escape times down 25 to 46 percent. Rats also stayed longer on a spinning rod and moved better in open tests. Stains of the hippocampus showed healthier nerve cells. Blood markers of swelling fell as well in treated rats.
pmc-13053236:
Zenghui Zhao and ten co-authors published a poultry science study in twenty twenty-six testing a fermented herbal product, Bazhen San, in the diets of older laying hens. Hens late in lay often produce fewer, poorer eggs. The team compared the fermented product against plain feed and the unfermented herb mix.

One hundred fifty seventy-week-old hens were split into five groups for the feeding trial. Every supplemented group laid more eggs and used feed more efficiently than controls. The middle fermented dose beat the unfermented mix and also improved yolk color and Haugh units. Blood tests showed stronger antibody levels and lower inflammatory markers, supporting benefits for immunity and gut health.
pmc-13059836:
Yagana Samim and Nicholas Spence set out a plan to review how ethnic groups decide when to have children. Their protocol, from twenty twenty-five, takes an ethnological lens. Past work groups people by broad race labels. That hides the cultural logic inside each group's choices about timing and spacing of births.

The review will ask what social and structural forces shape those choices. It will also draw out the cultural reasoning people give. The setting is the United States, chosen for its mix of peoples and rich data. Birth timing is an overlooked corner of family decision research. The map they build can guide fairer health policy.
pmc-13107136:
Xin-Xing Luo and co-authors update, in 2026, the taxonomy of a young cockroach genus. Unihamus was carved out of a broader group only recently, and its species and anatomy stayed poorly documented. The team redescribes the founding species and adds three new ones, each named and diagnosed in detail.

Males and females of each species were matched using DNA barcodes, avoiding the classic trap of describing the sexes as different species. High-resolution photographs support the diagnoses. The authors also look ahead at what a distinctive internal structure might reveal in future work on this small genus of the cockroach family Blattidae.
pmc-13127736:
Baudolino Mussa and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six comparison of European guidance on peripheral vein catheters. These small tubes are placed in huge numbers, and complications are common. Clinicians need clear, shared rules for preventing and handling problems.

Six reference documents were searched for agreed key terms. A matrix showed where guidance agreed and where wording blurred. Few documents covered these catheters at all, and none followed the standard evidence grading framework. Terminology differed enough to confuse practice. The authors propose fixes so European guidance can speak with one clear voice.
pmc-13134936:
Christoffel Roche McDuling, Ellie Georgiou, and Carina Labuschagne report a 2025 case study of sarcoidosis found only in the spleen. Sarcoidosis is a disease of unknown cause that forms small clumps of immune cells in organs, most often the lungs. Disease confined to the spleen is extremely rare.

The patient was a young woman with vague belly complaints and an enlarged spleen of unknown cause. In a region where tuberculosis is common and looks much the same, the team faced a hard diagnostic path. They combined clinical review, blood tests, imaging, and tissue study to narrow the cause. The case shows the value of removing the spleen by keyhole surgery, both to settle the diagnosis and to treat. The authors stress that no single test suffices here.
pmc-13153236:
Water trapped inside very thin glass tubes can stop acting like a liquid, and An Wei-qing, Yue Xiang-an, and Zou Ji-rui report a striking case in 2026. Inside silica tubes far wider than the usual nano scale, the water held a firm shape across a broad span of heat and cold. It could be sliced by a focused beam and bent under stress rather than flowing away.

Light and magnet probes showed the trapped water's bonds and motion differ from both plain liquid and ice. The key, the team finds, is the tube wall: a dense coat of water-loving groups on the silica grips the water hard. Sourness of the water shifts the effect, and the change can run back and forth. The result widens the known map of where confinement remakes a fluid.
pmc-13155336:
Mareike Körner and co-authors report a 2026 ocean study from the northern Gulf of Mexico. In coastal water, layers of different density can block mixing between the surface and the bottom. Low oxygen near the bottom harms sea life, so how water moves across those layers matters a great deal.

Detailed observations showed slanted bands of overturning water that link the surface to the bottom. These bands are the mark of symmetric instability, a flow pattern driven by wind and currents. The motion kept going for two days after the wind stopped. It carried far more water up and down than plain turbulence did. The findings suggest this process helps air out low-oxygen bottom water in coastal seas.
pmc-13157436:
Yunfei Dai and Jing Fei set out unmet needs in the care of small cell lung cancer. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. This cancer is fast and harsh, though immune drugs plus chemo have lengthened life. Three gaps stand out: spread to the brain, life quality, and proof from real-world care.

Brain radiation can ward off spread but can harm thought, all the more in the old. New scans and focused rays spare the memory zone and cut that harm. New drugs reach the brain and shrink tumours there at high rates. Early comfort care and symptom control guard life quality. Real-world data can guide personal care, but its uneven quality is a block.
pmc-13158336:
Xinlei Wang, Zhongyang Wang, and Keyan Cao propose a method for classifying functional brain networks that accounts for both direction and change over time. Their paper came out in 2026. Classifying these networks supports diagnosis of neurodegenerative disease and decoding of brain activity.

Traditional networks only measure static correlations between brain regions, ignoring which region drives which. Their framework models directed propagation, the causal flow between regions, within dynamic graphs that evolve over time. On real datasets, the method beat current state-of-the-art approaches by several percentage points of accuracy. The authors argue that direction and dynamics carry real diagnostic signal that static correlation misses. Better classification could sharpen tools for disease detection and brain research.
pmc-13161536:
Byung-Jo Kim introduces a review that recasts star-shaped brain cells as lead actors in multiple sclerosis. The disease was long read through immune cells alone, with astrocytes cast as bystanders. New tools that read single cells and map tissue have changed that picture. Astrocytes now appear as active regulators that can worsen or repair damage.

Kim weighs what the shift means for treatment. Animal models defined many astrocyte subtypes, but how far they match human disease stays unsure. Late-onset and progressive forms raise the stakes, since aging and inflammation feed each other there. Patients with late onset reach disability steps faster than same-age peers. The editorial argues that closing the gap between model and human is the field's next task. Astrocyte types could then become drug targets.
pmc-13163036:
Ali and co-authors compare rectal and infrared temperatures across goat body surfaces in a 2026 study. Rectal measures are standard for checking animal temperature, but they require restraint and carry contamination risk. Infrared imaging is non invasive and less stressful. The team studied eighty four healthy goats, recording rectal temperature plus infrared readings from forehead, ears, eyes, feet bands, shoulders, and mouth lining.

All infrared measures rose and fell with rectal temperature. The strongest link was with the maximum infrared reading of the right eye. That single measure explained about forty percent of rectal temperature variation in their model. The authors suggest eye imaging could serve as a non invasive gauge in goats. Readers learn which surface site tracks core temperature best.
pmc-13164936:
Ahmad and six co-authors reviewed in twenty twenty-six a new class of catalysts that mix many main parts in one phase. Such mixes can speed the split of water to make green hydrogen gas. Plain catalysts are held back by slow pace, short life, and high cost.

The mixes offer wide choice of parts, tuned charge states, and gains when parts work as one. Gaps stay in how to find the true live sites and guess long life. The review maps new design and make steps and their link to acts. It ends with seven grand blocks and fixes for each in the path to real use.
pmc-13167036:
Mario Koddenbrock and co-authors present a 2026 study using synthetic images to train foundation models to outline microtubules. Cell scientists still trace these cell filaments by hand for hours. No large labelled dataset existed to judge machine methods fairly.

Their system made true-to-life microscope images with perfect ground truth built in. Nine methods were benchmarked, both untouched and lightly tuned. Most older and foundation methods fell short of the accuracy the task needs. One recent text-prompted model, tuned on just ten synthetic images, matched or beat human-grade results. Synthetic training data may unlock automated cytoskeleton analysis.
pmc-13177836:
Sam Paplauskas, writing alone, revisits the belief that genetically uniform host populations suffer bigger epidemics, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. That wisdom sits at the base of crop monoculture warnings and backs conservation arguments. The evidence base outside plants was put to a fresh test here.

Two hundred eleven effect sizes from two past syntheses were merged with no duplication. Epidemic size was found to track parasite genetic diversity, and host diversity too, as the old rule said. But that rule held in the main for parasites tied to a single host species. Parasites with a broad host range acted in an unlike way. The author frames a diversity-uncertainty model for this, since predicting severe outbreaks takes both sides of the host-parasite genetic equation.
pmc-13179236:
Derluyn and colleagues test a fast field tool that checks how fast stone soaks up water, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Workers press a wet sponge to the stone and weigh how much water moves. Lab tests use a slow rise test on small blocks instead. The two methods agree in broad terms, but their numbers do not yet match well.

The team used beams that can image water inside stone to watch the sponge test live. They saw that water does not sink as deep as it spreads on the face. That breaks the old rule used to turn sponge data into a soak rate. Their new rule tracks flow in three ways at once. It brings field and lab numbers much closer.
pmc-13179636:
Hanbazaza and Alaklabi test in 2026 a nutrition teaching program for low income Saudi families. Poor food skills can deepen food insecurity, so teaching aims to lift security, literacy, and diet at once. The single arm study ran from June to August 2024.

Seventy three adults took the first survey, and 67 finished the last. Food insecurity scores fell by a clear margin after the program. Food literacy scores rose by a larger margin. Diet gains held for fruit, meats, legumes, and breads after strict statistical checks. The authors read the short term gains as support for teaching based aid, while noting the lack of a control group.
pmc-13179936:
Knee arthritis involves the bone under the cartilage, not just the joint surface, so some doctors inject that bone directly. Yazan Abu Salem and co-authors reviewed the evidence on three such injections: calcium phosphate, platelet-rich plasma, and stem cells. They gathered twenty-four studies with one thousand one hundred nine patients, followed for about thirty-eight months on average. Five studies were randomized trials. Quality of the studies was scored with standard tools.

Most studies reported less pain and better function after treatment. Results for calcium phosphate varied widely, with knee replacement rates from about one to forty-five percent. Plasma and stem cell studies looked safer, and stem cell relief lasted up to fifteen years in one report. The authors warn that study quality was modest overall.
pmc-13185036:
Josh Courtney McMullan and co-authors report a 2026 study of how patients view preparation programs before ovarian cancer surgery. These programs blend exercise, food advice, mental support, and medical tuning to get patients fit for a big operation. The question here is whether patients find such help welcome and usable.

The team interviewed 21 patients with advanced ovarian cancer at several UK centers. All had been referred to a National Health Service preparation program before planned surgery. The talks covered how the program was introduced, whether patients felt they needed it, and what helped or blocked them from taking part. Four main themes emerged, starting with timing and the amount of information given. The results should guide the design of future programs in other countries.
pmc-13185636:
Jingkang Zhang and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six review of finding important microbes in meta-omics data, from classic pipelines to deep learning. Sequencing whole communities reveals who is present, but the keystone and rare members matter most. Standard pipelines struggle with tangled ecological relationships.

Deep learning can extract features on its own and model nonlinear links. It can also fuse several data types together. Obstacles include uneven datasets, poor transfer between ecosystems, and hard-to-interpret outputs. The authors propose a unified learning framework and chart what must improve before ecologists can trust it widely.
pmc-13187536:
Javier-David Lopez-Morinigo and nine co-authors tracked insight in first-episode psychosis over its first month of care, in a study published in 2026. Insight, a patient's grasp that they are ill, cuts two ways: it tracks with better treatment gains but also with low mood and risk of self-harm. Their data came from a large trial with 443 first-episode patients, scored at the start and at week four.

At both points, better insight tied to more remission, less illness severity, and better daily function. At the start it also tied to more low mood, self-harm markers, and worse felt quality of life; by week four those links were gone. Gains in insight tied to good outcomes and to no harmful outcomes at week four. The authors say early work on insight is safe to push.
pmc-13191536:
Xiaolong Zhou and co-authors find an energy sweet spot for stirring crude oil during desalting, in a research paper from 2026. Refiners wash salt from crude by mixing in water, and stirring strength shapes how well salt leaves. Speed and time alone describe the mixing poorly.

The team built an energy-structure-performance frame, tracking droplet sizes and computing input energy from flow numbers. Near fifty joules of input, desalting peaked, mirroring the average droplet size curve. In that window droplets merge well without shattering into stubborn emulsion. The method gives operators a physical dial for tuning mixers and saving energy.
pmc-13193936:
MRI texture features can help predict survival in throat cancer, but scanners at different hospitals speak different dialects. Wei Pei and co-authors test a statistical fix called ComBat in a 2026 two-center study.

The study covered 573 patients with locally advanced cancer of the nasopharynx. One hospital's stronger scanner set the reference; the other's weaker scanner data were adjusted with ComBat. Before adjustment, texture features split clearly by hospital, a sign of batch noise. After adjustment, the features lined up far better. A model mixing texture and clinical factors was then built to predict survival. Harmonized data, the authors suggest, let small centers pool scans with big ones.
pmc-13194336:
Upfill-Brown and co-authors test whether waiting longer for spine surgery harms older patients with unstable back fractures. The best timing for patients with no nerve injury was not well set. Data came from a national surgical quality database covering 2012 to 2023.

The study included 976 patients aged sixty or older who had fixation surgery. Mean wait was 2.8 days, give or take two days. Delay did not raise thirty-day death or major problem rates. Waits past four days did raise the chance of discharge to a facility, not home. Models adjusted for patient and clinical traits.
pmc-13197536:
Germán Ortuño-Hernández and colleagues hunted genes behind apricot skin color in a 2026 study. Skin color drives buyer choice and price, yet judging it in the field is slow and weather-bound. DNA markers could let breeders screen young trees fast.

The team focused on a known color region on chromosome three. Inside it sits a gene that helps control carotenoids, the pigments that tint fruit. They built two marker types from variants in that gene. One single-letter marker sorted orange from yellow fruit with full accuracy in a test cross and high accuracy across fifty-seven varieties. A repeat-length marker also scored well. Both tools can speed apricot breeding.
pmc-13198636:
Elabbass A Abdelmahmuod and Tarik Elhadd present a 2026 case series linking acromegaly to blood clots and strokes. Acromegaly is a rare hormone disorder that creeps up slowly and often goes years undiagnosed. Clues may come from vascular events first, as in these three cases.

One man was diagnosed after a lung clot. A second, younger man had clots in both lungs and a delayed diagnosis. A third man's mini-stroke led to finding a small pituitary tumor behind the disorder. All three improved with therapy, in symptoms or lab values. The authors urge doctors to weigh acromegaly when clots or strokes lack a clear cause.
pmc-13199836:
Arianna Morena and a large team published a study protocol in two thousand twenty-six on genetic causes of cardiac arrest in the young. In patients under fifty, inherited rhythm and heart muscle diseases are a leading cause of out-of-hospital arrest. Population-level genetic estimates were missing.

The GenetiCA study will enrol all such cases across Italy's Lombardy region. Blood drawn during resuscitation feeds a broad gene panel for inherited arrhythmia syndromes and cardiomyopathies. Clinical, outcome, and air pollution data are collected alongside. Relatives of carriers will be offered counselling and heart checks. About five hundred seventy-five resuscitated cases are expected from the regional registry. The main goal is the share of arrests explained by inherited disease.
pmc-13201536:
Skin stiffened by systemic sclerosis is usually considered permanently scarred, and a 2026 study authored by Aleix Rius Rigau asks whether immune cell therapy can reverse that damage. The research article examines skin biopsies from patients treated with CD19 CAR T cells, which remove B cells from the body.

Analyzing samples from the CASTLE study and named patient use, the team applied advanced tissue imaging and in situ hybridization methods. Treated skin showed recovered surface papillae, fibroblast populations shifted back toward a healthy state, and signs of blood vessel repair were also visible. The results suggest deep B cell depletion may allow fibrotic skin to genuinely remodel.
pmc-13202036:
An engineered immune signal paired with a checkpoint drug is tested in advanced skin cancers in a 2026 phase 1/2 study led by Carlos Rojas. The article tests pegenzileukin, a modified interleukin-2 designed to activate killer immune cells while avoiding one receptor linked to toxicity, along with cemiplimab in melanoma and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

Forty-six patients joined the multicenter, open-label study across dose escalation and expansion groups. At the chosen dose, tumors shrank in a substantial share of patients in both cancer cohorts, and many responses lasted at least twelve months for those who responded. Five dose-limiting toxicities occurred in four patients, and the pairing now warrants further study.
pmc-13203236:
Łukasz Jankowiak and co-authors test if Poland's Cistercian monasteries still shelter richer bird life than the farmland round them. Sacred sites are often thought to be refuges for wildlife in worked landscapes, but any effect may reflect the habitat kept there. The team ran five-minute bird counts at 234 points across 23 plots. Active Cistercian plots were matched with control and former-monastery plots.

They logged 133 breeding species, most of them common farmland and town birds. Monastery status did not explain bird diversity or species counts, nor did counts inside versus outside the grounds. Both rose instead with the mix of the landscape: more grassland, more town edge, and more varied farming meant more birds. The lesson for policy is plain: what guards birds here is a varied landscape now, with meadows, hedges, and mixed farms, not the age or sanctity of a site.
pmc-13204136:
Diana De la Merced-García and co-authors (2026) review how calcium signals steer the building of the cerebral cortex. Calcium inside cells is a classic messenger, but here it also shapes the cell skeleton directly. During development it guides stem cell choices, cell division, neuron migration, and wiring. The review gathers animal and cell studies on the proteins that read calcium. Calmodulin and its kinases, S100 proteins, cadherins, centrins, and sensors such as STIM1 all appear.

These readers act inside tiny calcium zones that flare briefly in one corner of a cell. From there they tune the microtubule tracks that move nuclei, set spindle angles, and grow neurites. When the calcium code breaks, the cortex can form with the wrong architecture, feeding developmental disease. The authors propose that cells translate calcium rhythms into skeleton changes. Their framework links a fast chemical signal to the slow construction of the brain.
pmc-13205136:
Children born without a thymus cannot build a working immune system, and a 2026 study authored by Samantha Cresoe-Ortiz examines what shapes recovery after thymus implantation. The research article evaluates outcomes of allogeneic processed thymus tissue therapy, the approved treatment for congenital athymia, focusing on T cell reconstitution.

The authors tracked shifts in T cell subsets and their function after implantation in treated children. Immune reconstitution showed no link to T cell function measures, immune suppression, or HLA matching between donor and recipient. Younger age at implantation was linked to better immune rebuilding, which supports treating eligible children as early as possible.
pmc-13205836:
Tadashi Nakagawa and Makiko Nakagawa propose an explanation for why the same gene fault can leave one child's development nearly untouched and another's severely impaired, in a review published in 2026. Brain development disorders are famous for this spread of outcomes, and gene catalogs alone do not explain it. The authors turn to ubiquitin, the cell's tag for managing proteins.

Tagging is not a single switch but a layered system: which sites are free, which taggers are active, which removers oppose them, and which prior marks prime the protein. Those layers can differ by person, cell type, age, and setting, yielding a personal tagging landscape. The review argues that such differences translate gene variation into varied outcomes. Grasping that interplay could guide future treatments.
pmc-13206036:
Yue Sun and six co-authors report a 2026 study of what happens when a fiber called resistant dextrin is added to wheat foods. Plain wheat staples are low in fiber and can raise blood sugar fast after a meal. Adding soluble fiber is one way to improve them.

The team tested how the fiber mixes with wheat starch and with gluten, the protein that gives dough its stretch. At a dose of six percent, starch set more slowly and aged less over two weeks. The fiber held more water in gluten but made the protein net looser and weaker. The study tracks these changes from small bonds up to the look of dough and bread.
pmc-13207036:
Dawid Plutecki and co-authors pool data on Meckel's diverticulum in a 2026 review. This pouch in the gut is the most common birth anomaly of the digestive tract. It arises when a fetal duct fails to close in the first weeks.

The team searched eight databases up to March 2024 and kept 172 studies with usable data. The pooled prevalence was about 1.6 percent. In children, nausea and vomiting were the most common symptoms. In adults, wound problems and leaks after surgery led the outcomes list. The review maps anatomy, symptoms, and stray tissue types found in the pouch.
pmc-13207936:
Augustine Oviosun and co-authors published an animal study in 2026 on a plastic chemical and male fertility. The chemical leaks from many plastic goods and can disturb hormones in the body. It has been tied to harm in the testes of male animals. The team tested a plant compound found in citrus peel as a shield.

Forty-two male rats were split into six groups for eight weeks of daily dosing. Rats given the chemical alone lost testis size and had lower hormone levels. Their sperm-making cells thinned out and stress markers in tissue rose. Rats dosed with the plant compound first kept near-normal tissue and hormone levels. The authors credit the protective effect of the compound to its action against cell stress.
pmc-13208236:
Yueh-Chang Lee leads a team of sixteen authors turning human skin-related fibroblasts into retinal progenitor-like cells using chemicals alone, no genetic editing. Direct reprogramming could supply cells for eye therapy at scale. Their starting cells came from Tenon's capsule, the tissue around the eye.

A defined small-molecule cocktail pushed the fibroblasts toward a retinal identity. Marker proteins, gene activity, and full transcriptome profiles shifted toward neural and retinal programs, including the VSX2 marker. The converted cells, unlike their parents, responded to glutamate with calcium signals. Transplanted into rat eyes by two routes, the cells survived a month and produced localized structural changes. Imaging, electrical recordings, and tissue analysis tracked the grafts.
pmc-13208636:
Yongdong Yan, Daniel Mishael, Chunhua Lu, and Lei Tan study how salt water creeps into jointed concrete in this 2026 paper. Chloride attack corrodes the steel inside coastal structures, and joints are weak points. The team cast beams with no joint, a smooth wet joint, or a roughened joint, then bent and soaked them in strong salt water for nearly a year.

Salt piled up most at the joints, above all the smooth kind, and bending load sped the creep as tiny cracks opened. A crystalline waterproofing additive fought back: at one percent of the mix, it cut the spread rate at the joint by about a tenth. The authors offer the dose as a sweet spot of cost and protection.
pmc-13209436:
Two natural compounds are pitted against chemotherapy damage to the testes in a 2026 rat study headed by Faruk Saydam. The research article contrasts melatonin and the plant flavonoid apigenin to shield rats from paclitaxel, scoring oxidative stress, DNA damage, cell death signals, and sperm-producing tubule health across seven groups.

Paclitaxel raised lipid peroxidation, drained a key antioxidant, and visibly wrecked the seminiferous tubules of untreated rats. Melatonin repaired the redox balance and preserved tissue structure best in the noted checks. Apigenin also cut that damage and improved tissue scores, though it lowered those defenses in otherwise healthy animals, an effect that depends on context, the authors flag.
pmc-13210236:
Cremated bones remember what the living ate, and a 2026 archaeology study authored by Maura De Coster reads diet in Roman Nijmegen from strontium chemistry. The research article measures isotope ratios and concentrations in human remains from rural, urban, and military sites in the Lower Rhine borderlands of the Netherlands.

Town and garrison groups carried higher strontium concentrations, a pattern the authors link to heavier use of salt-preserved, salt-rich Roman provisions. Northern communities instead showed steadier concentrations with narrowing isotope ranges, hinting that older local habits, possibly including earlier salt traditions, persisted beside the empire. Dietary change under Rome, they conclude, was negotiated locally rather than imposed uniformly on everyone.
pmc-13211236:
Audrey Rah and Yuhua Chen present a two thousand twenty-six study on detecting stress in virtual reality from skin signals. Sweat-driven skin conductance hints at stress, but body heat changes distort it. Their method tries to separate true stress signals from heat effects.

Using a public wearable dataset, they matched temperature shifts against conductance patterns. Two correction models adjusted the signal, one simple and one adaptive. The adaptive model produced clearer condition-specific patterns. Temperature features themselves proved reliable markers. The work aims at virtual reality systems that read user stress without mistaking warmth for emotion.
pmc-13211636:
Marta Leiva and co-authors review eye care without antibiotics in a 2026 paper for veterinary medicine. Rising bacterial resistance pushes vets to cut antibiotic use, above all in routine first-line care. Antiseptics for the eye surface have stepped into that gap, active against bacteria, fungi, viruses, and protozoa, with little risk of breeding resistance.

The review weighs antiseptics for surgery preparation and for mild surface disease in animals. Benefits and limits are sorted by setting, and daily practice uses are described. The authors note a lack of protocols tuned by species, disease, and context. They call for studies to set those protocols, so antiseptics can safely shoulder more of the load now carried by antibiotics.
pmc-13213536:
Eygló Ingólfsdóttir and co-authors ask whether aerobic exercise affects memory, attention, working memory, and fatigue after acquired brain injury. Their 2026 pilot is a single-blinded, randomized controlled trial. Twelve participants with moderate to severe stroke or traumatic brain injury, at least three months past the injury, took part in an outpatient rehabilitation programme. Half did 30 minutes of aerobic exercise three to four times a week for eight weeks.

The other half received routine physical therapy, and both groups kept their rehabilitation plans. Cognitive and endurance tests ran before, after, and at a three-month follow-up, with brain imaging at the start and end. Group differences in cognition, fatigue, and brain change were not significant. One demanding processing speed test rose in the exercise group. A simple search test rose in the control group. The team calls for a larger trial.
pmc-13213836:
Felix Neubauer and a team of co-authors make metal-organic framework recipes machine-readable so results can be reproduced and mined. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. These sponge-like crystals depend on fine procedural detail for yield and purity.

The team built a data model that captures synthesis steps and characterization in a standard form. Recipes flow in from tables or electronic lab notebooks, get checked for errors and gaps, and convert into exchange formats. A decision tree then reads X-ray patterns to find which settings control crystal phase and yield. Two framework systems prove the pipeline works. The authors offer the model as a modular base that other labs and AI tools can extend.
pmc-13217436:
Juhui Chen and co-authors present a 2026 prospective study of anaesthesia technique for liver cancer surgery, comparing general anaesthesia alone against general anaesthesia combined with an epidural. Patients chose their approach after consultation, so the comparison is observational rather than randomized.

Among 106 patients, the combined group needed slightly less intravenous opioid during surgery and reported less pain a day later, with median scores of 2 against 3. Their thinking scores on the first postoperative day were better, median 26 against 24, and they left hospital about four days sooner, near sixteen days against twenty. Adverse events were also fewer, 6.38 percent against 20.34 percent. The authors read the pattern as favouring the combined technique while calling for randomized confirmation.
pmc-13218036:
Tanwei Yuan and co-authors examine, in a 2026 cohort analysis, whether blood-based epigenetic scores of body mass predict survival after colorectal cancer. A single weight measurement at diagnosis can mislead, because the disease itself often causes weight loss before diagnosis. Scores built from DNA methylation patterns may capture long-term body fat exposure more steadily.

The analysis drew on 2,126 newly diagnosed patients in the German DACHS study, comparing five methylation-based body mass scores against self-reported weight history. The scores tracked reported body mass across many years, yet they pointed in the opposite direction for survival: higher methylation scores meant higher mortality risk. The strongest score, built from 135 marker sites, carried the clearest signal, and most links appeared in patients whose blood was drawn before chemotherapy or radiotherapy. The authors suggest such scores could sharpen risk grouping beyond reported weight alone.
pmc-13218636:
Thomas Vingerhoets and co-authors review whether oral corticosteroids given after knee surgery ease pain and speed recovery, in a 2026 systematic review. Total knee arthroplasty relieves arthritic joints but leaves pain that drives opioid use and slows rehabilitation. Steroids given intravenously around surgery help early pain, but the value of oral steroids afterward was unsettled.

Searching five databases and registries, the reviewers assembled twelve studies, with four randomized trials covering 380 participants forming the analysis and the rest used for sensitivity checks. Oral steroids cut cumulative opioid use in the first forty-eight hours by roughly nine oral morphine equivalent milligrams. Their effect on pain at rest at the same point was uncertain, with confidence intervals spanning benefit and none. Certainty of evidence was graded, and safety outcomes such as surgical site infection were tracked. The authors present opioid sparing as the clearest gain, short of proof on pain itself.
pmc-13219536:
Vani Chalageri and many colleagues published a 2026 study on care for fever and malaria in parts of India where the disease is common. India aims to wipe out malaria by 2030. To hit that goal, health teams need to know where people seek care and where gaps remain.

The study surveyed households across malaria-endemic states. It asked how families handle fever, which clinics they use, and what steps they take to prevent bites. Bed nets that carry insecticide, known as LLINs, get a close look as a core defense. The authors map use of services against need. Their findings point to where outreach and supplies should go next.
pmc-13222636:
Zihuan Li and co-authors chart how HIV and other sexually transmitted infections burden women of child-bearing age worldwide, in a 2026 analysis of Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2021. Incidence, prevalence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years were tracked by age, region, and development level using trend regression.

In 2021 the combined category produced hundreds of millions of cases in women aged fifteen to forty-nine. Other infections supplied almost all new and existing cases, while HIV supplied almost all deaths and disability. HIV incidence fell steadily across the decades, whereas other infection rates crept slightly upward. The authors warn that HIV progress must not be mistaken for control of sexually transmitted infections overall.
pmc-13224236:
Haman Nassourou Oumarou and four co-authors report on surgery for glioblastoma in a study from twenty twenty-six. Glioblastoma is the most common and most aggressive brain tumor in adults. Outcomes stay poor even with mixed treatment. The study was done at Yaounde General Hospital.

The team looked back at records for thirty-two patients who had surgery with confirmed tumor tissue. Cases ran from twenty eighteen to mid twenty twenty-five. They describe how patients were found, treated, and how they lived after surgery, including quality of life. Standard tests compared groups and survival curves. The work gives a clear local picture where published data have been scarce.
pmc-13226136:
When a clot suddenly starves a leg of blood, doctors race to clear it, usually by sucking the clot out through a catheter. Langford Green, Georges Jreij, Julia Rosenberg, Justin Robbins, Richa Kalsi, and Khanjan Nagarsheth report four cases where that suction method failed. In each, they turned to a mechanical system, Artix, that breaks up and removes the clot instead.

All four patients kept their legs at thirty days. Blood flow grades were good in every case, and three of the four vessels stayed open at thirty days. No problems tied to the device appeared. The team backs the system as a safe rescue when suction fails, and suggests trials of it as a first choice.
pmc-13226236:
Saravanan Sengunthar, Diganta Sarkar, and Pravin Jadhav model a 2026 trade study on how tariff cuts would affect India's exports of AYUSH products. These goods come from traditional systems such as Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy. Eight importing countries take about half of those exports. Using a partial-equilibrium simulation tool, the team tested lower-tariff scenarios across nineteen product codes.

Cheaper duties generally lifted trade, but the gains were uneven. In some categories, imports simply shifted between suppliers rather than growing, a pattern called trade diversion that can leave India worse off. The authors advise selective, product-by-product tariff reduction paired with regulatory alignment, rather than a blanket zero-tariff policy across the whole AYUSH range.
pmc-13230236:
Shintaro Yamada and colleagues report in 2026 that a fat-like signaling molecule reduced stroke damage in mice by protecting blood vessels. After a blocked brain artery, the blood-brain barrier often leaks and worsens swelling and injury. The team gave lysophosphatidic acid right after the blockage and checked the brain two days later.

Treated mice had much smaller damaged areas and less swelling than untreated animals. Barrier leak tests showed tighter vessels, and a key sealing protein stayed in place in vessel walls. Cell data pointed to one receptor, LPA4, sitting on vessel cells in the injured zone. Mice lacking that receptor gained no benefit, which ties the protection to that pathway.
pmc-13231036:
Francesca M Genoese and colleagues link in 2026 anxiety and depression feelings to knee pain months after ligament surgery. One hundred thirty-one people, mostly in their late teens, joined three to twelve months after a first anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Short standard forms measured anxiety and depression, while a knee score captured pain levels.

Age, sex, and time since surgery together explained very little of the pain differences. Anxiety scores alone added a large share of explained difference, and depression scores added a smaller but clear share. People reporting worse mood symptoms tended to report worse knee pain in that later recovery window. Screening mood alongside pain could help clinicians plan support well beyond the early rehab phase.
pmc-13231536:
Christina E Lundberg and colleagues compare in 2026 obesity risk patterns between Canada and Sweden using a global health study. Both rich countries share similar social systems, yet obesity runs far higher in Canada. Records covered nearly ten thousand adults aged thirty-four to sixty from both countries.

A machine screening method flagged ultra-processed food intake and overall diet quality as the chief drivers of obesity risk. The highest processed food group carried more than double the obesity odds in both countries. Among women, rural living, low income, and unskilled work tied to obesity much more strongly in Sweden than in Canada. Canadian men ate more processed food than Swedish men. One-size policy fits neither country well.
pmc-13232136:
Teagan S Mullins and Jeremy Hogeveen gather in 2026 brain scan studies on how teenagers process rewards in the cerebellum. Teen reward drive is usually blamed on fast-growing motivation circuits outpacing slow control circuits in the front brain. The cerebellum, a back brain structure tied to learning from errors, is often left out of that story.

Nineteen scan studies fed a combined map of reward anticipation and reward receipt in healthy teens. While teens waited for rewards, cerebellar activity looked much like adult patterns across many zones. When rewards arrived, teen activity spread widely, while adult activity narrowed to one central strip. Wide teen responses may reflect active learning machinery still building the forward models used for adult self control.
pmc-13232536:
Sara Jarmakiewicz-Czaja and colleagues measure in 2026 blood immune signals in bowel disease patients whose symptoms had settled. Their group held one hundred thirty-two patients in clinical remission plus twenty-nine healthy controls. Eight cytokines, the signaling proteins that steer inflammation, were compared between patients on anti-TNF biologics and patients on standard drugs.

No clear gap appeared between treatment groups for any of the signals measured. Profiles also separated patients from one another poorly while disease stayed quiet. Blood cytokine levels, the team suggests, do not simply mirror which drug class a patient takes. Longer studies that follow the same patients could show whether these signals warn of relapse or fading drug response.
pmc-13233436:
Li Jiang and co-authors present a meta-analysis the catalog lists under 2026. Thoracic surgery often needs one lung rested while the other breathes. The double-lumen tube is the standard tool for that split. A video version adds a built-in camera, so staff can watch its position continuously. Whether the camera version truly helps patients was unclear. The authors search seven databases for randomized trials up to July 2025.

Trials are pooled with standard meta-analysis software. The main outcome is intubation time. Stability checks and publication bias tests guard the pooled result. Anesthesia teams get a verdict built from trials rather than vendor claims. Tube misplacement is a real danger in chest surgery, and continuous sight could prevent it. A pooled answer also tells hospitals whether the pricier tube earns its place in the tray.
pmc-13234136:
Saad M Darwish, Noha A Bagi, and Noha A El-Shoafy published a 2026 education technology study on grading essays by computer when judgment is fuzzy. Automated essay scoring struggles because language is ambiguous and reasonable readers disagree. Existing systems built on knowledge ontologies, structured maps of a subject, handle that vagueness poorly. The authors upgraded the approach with type-2 neutrosophic sets, a mathematical tool that grades truth, falsity, and indeterminacy each with its own uncertainty band.

Their pipeline extracts concepts from essays, scores them with ontology rules, then stretches the scoring with the neutrosophic layer to weigh doubtful evidence more honestly. Tests on benchmark essay datasets showed the enhanced framework beating conventional methods on robustness and interpretability. The authors pitch the design for assessment settings where answers are rarely simply right or wrong.
pmc-13234236:
Yuna Suzuki and colleagues published a 2026 muscle lipid study on how membrane fats remodel when muscle shifts toward fast-twitch fibers. Fast and slow fibers carry distinct glycerophospholipid recipes, and slow shifts were known to rewrite them. The team used clenbuterol, a drug that drives fast-twitch conversion and growth, in mice and profiled the fats in two leg muscles.

Treated muscle gained fast-twitch share and bulked up. Its membranes held more of a palmitate-bearing phosphatidylcholine and less of the stearate-bearing version, in both muscles studied. Genes for the enzymes that choose which fatty chain gets attached changed in step, including one called GPAT3. The authors conclude that lipid remodeling is a genuine part of how muscle retools its identity, not a bystander effect.
pmc-13234736:
Ansingkar and coauthors link groin wound harms to long-term health risks. Groin cuts expose a key leg artery in many vessel surgeries. Blood pools, fluid pools, infection, and wound splits can follow. Their long-term toll past the wound has stayed unclear.
