The team used a large national health database for the study. Patients with wound harms were matched to like patients without them. Harms were tracked against grave outcomes over time. Those outcomes held lung failure, kidney failure, and stroke. Heart attack, leg loss, and death were also tracked. Wound harms tracked with higher rates of most outcomes.
pmc-13235336:
Laura E. Kusumo and co-authors tested in 2026 whether voluntary running eases depression-like behaviour caused by high blood sugar in mice. Diabetes raises depression risk, possibly through brain inflammation and loss of a growth factor called BDNF. Male mice received a chemical that damages insulin production, then lived with or without running wheels for about seven weeks. Behaviour tests and brain tissue measures compared the groups.

High blood sugar produced depression-like behaviour across several tests in the animals. Running improved performance in the forced swim and splash tests specifically. Exercise also raised BDNF expression inside the brain in the results. Other behaviours, including nest building and marble burying, did not respond to running. A marker of inflammation in the cerebellum likewise stayed unchanged with exercise. The authors argue exercise helps a subset of symptoms and suits combined treatment.
pmc-13236036:
Yinghua Wang and Xuan Pan review the many jobs of YY1, a transcription factor doubling as a chromatin architect, in the blood stem cells that seed the entire immune system. Beyond switching genes on and off, YY1 helps organize the genome's three-dimensional folding and belongs to the Polycomb silencing machinery.

Recent work shows YY1 keeps blood stem cells quiet, self-renewing, and able to engraft, in both fetal and adult life. It wires long-range DNA contacts with structural partners and coordinates metabolism with gene programs. Its activity fades with age, paralleling stem cell decline. The authors suggest that understanding YY1 could reveal how blood aging begins and how to slow it.
pmc-13236536:
Hui Liu, Xunqian Yin, Wenshan Duan, and Haiqing Sun developed in 2026 a two-step test for Epstein-Barr virus DNA that works without complex laboratory machines. The virus infects most adults for life and is linked to several cancers. Standard detection needs specialized instruments, which limits testing where resources are scarce. Their method first copies the target at constant temperature, then uses a CRISPR enzyme to cut reporter molecules for a readable signal.

Fluorescence readout detected the virus across a wide range down to about one hundred copies per reaction. No false signals appeared from the other viruses tested for cross-reaction. A paper strip version gave visible positives only at higher virus amounts in comparison. Early testing on patient blood samples caught every positive by fluorescence, while strips missed a few low cases. The authors call for larger clinical studies and a more sensitive strip.
pmc-13238236:
Kluge and colleagues report a child whose adrenal disorder arrived by an unusual genetic route. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency is normally inherited when both parents carry a faulty CYP21A2 gene copy. In a small share of cases the parents are not carriers at all, which usually points to a fresh mutation in the child.

This case came from uniparental isodisomy: the child received two copies of one parent's chromosome segment, and none from the other parent. Hidden in those doubled copies sat the faulty gene. The report urges genetic teams to test for this route when carrier testing of parents comes back blank, since it changes recurrence advice for the family.
pmc-13238636:
Min Sun, Yuanzhi Wang, Yuqing Zhang, and Xiaojuan Wang published a study in 2026 mapping how stomach cancer changes as it spreads. Metastasis drives most deaths from this cancer, but the cell-level script of the journey was blurry. The team sequenced single cells from 131 samples: healthy stomach tissue, primary tumors, and metastases in lymph nodes, liver, ovary, and the abdominal lining.

Eleven major cell types filled the atlas. Killer immune cells thinned out in lymph node metastases while exhausted helper cells piled up, and regulatory cells concentrated in primary tumors. One gene, NAP1L1, switched on in tumor cells at every metastatic site. Silencing it in simulation disturbed the cells' grip and adhesion machinery and woke other spread-promoting genes, marking it as a driver worth targeting.
pmc-13239036:
Morio Kosokabe and colleagues reported in 2026 how a thin, steeply angled video laryngoscope blade secured the airway of a 14-year-old girl with a giant facial rhabdomyosarcoma. Her tumor limited her mouth opening to two child finger-widths, the worst grade for expected intubation difficulty, and she was scheduled for tumor debulking under general anesthesia. The team prepared several devices and fallback plans.

When standard options became untenable, the team switched to the GlideScope Spectrum LoPro blade and completed oral intubation while she kept breathing on her own, without complications. Its angled shape improved the view of her vocal cords. The authors present the case as the first report of this blade succeeding in a child with a difficult airway. Careful preparation, they stress, made the save possible.
pmc-13239336:
Radiation for breast cancer cannot fully spare the lung behind it, and a 2026 prospective study by Farzaneh Allaveisi and co-authors asks which dose measures best predict the harm. Forty eight patients with node negative cancer had lung perfusion scans before treatment and again six to nine months after.

Standard measures like mean lung dose may miss how uneven the dose is inside the lung. The team added a heterogeneity aware measure and compared all of them against scan changes and lung inflammation. The goal is a sharper warning system, so planners can steer dose away from the lung parts that matter most.
pmc-13239536:
Marloes van Mourik and co-authors explore a two-level gel system for repairing joint cartilage in a 2026 laboratory study. Cartilage cells normally sit inside a soft personal shell called the pericellular matrix, and copying that softness while keeping the whole implant stiff enough for load could improve engineered tissue.

The team placed cartilage cells either straight into a stiff gel or first inside soft microgels nested within the stiff gel. Samples grew for twenty-eight days in pig cartilage defects under moving compression. Encapsulated cells spread their new matrix more evenly through the tissue depth. Progenitor cells from cartilage matched ordinary cartilage cells, offering a possible alternative cell supply.
pmc-13239636:
Łukasz Białek and colleagues compare surgical repairs for urethral narrowing that follows prostate surgery in a 2026 multicentre study. Scarring after transurethral resection of the prostate can block urine flow, and urethroplasty, surgical rebuilding of the tube, remains the definitive fix for repeat cases.

Three Polish reconstructive centres reviewed 147 men treated between 2015 and 2022, with an average age of sixty-nine. Most strictures sat in the bulbar section, while penile ones ran longer on average. Half received a joining repair that cuts out the scar, while others received augmentation that widens the tube with added tissue. Follow-up tracked freedom from further procedures.
pmc-13240136:
Seniczak and five co-authors asked what shapes Arctic soil life in this study from twenty twenty-six. Tiny mites and springtails drive soil processes in Svalbard, but surveying them is slow and costly. Plant maps are far easier to draw. The team tested whether plant communities could stand in for the soil fauna.

They sifted one hundred seventy-two soil samples from thirty-three sites across eleven plant classes. Nearly one hundred eighty thousand microarthropods turned up. Place mattered more than plant type for the mite and springtail mix. One harsh southern site explained most of the mite variation. Plant classes proved only weak proxies overall. The authors caution against skipping soil sampling on the strength of vegetation maps.
pmc-13240536:
Liancheng Guan and colleagues offer a 2026 review of vitamin D receptor signaling in aging skin marked by inflammation and cell senescence. The receptor helps keep skin tissue stable. The authors gather evidence on whether adjusting its activity could treat age-related skin disease.

The review explains how the receptor changes gene activity through chromatin effects, direct gene control, and helper proteins. Protective actions include calming a major inflammatory pathway and slowing cell aging programs. Separate sections cover skin surface cells, immune cells, connective tissue cells, and stem cells. Treatment options range from vitamin D based products to plant compounds and new delivery systems. Gaps include tracking receptor activity in older skin.
pmc-13240636:
Fonteyne and colleagues at the University of British Columbia interviewed Canadian youth about apps designed to help them quit vaping. Most young people who try to quit do so without support. Seventeen youth aged sixteen to twenty-four, all app users, shared their experiences. Interviews took place across three provinces in fall 2022.

Three themes emerged, starting with quitting on one's own terms: personal motivation mattered most. Views on in-app communities split, with some valuing peers and others preferring privacy. Tracking, encouragement, and game-like features made apps feel like pocket-sized partners. Youth asked for tools that feel genuine and support relapses without judgment.
pmc-13240836:
Stem cells offer one of the few hopes for repairing brain injury, where current care cannot regrow tissue. Chen Xiong and co-authors map the research field itself, counting and charting 8,785 publications from 2009 to 2025. Their bibliometric study uses standard mapping tools to reveal who publishes, where, and on what.

Output grew in a straight, steady line across the period. China and the United States lead the field, with the University of California system and Harvard as top institutions. Two scholars stand out as the most prolific. Current hot topics include tiny cell-released packages called extracellular vesicles and the role of brain inflammation. The authors intend the map to guide planning, teamwork across fields, and the move toward patient care.
pmc-13241336:
Sixten Borg and co-authors publish a 2026 cross-sectional survey of quality of life among people living with or beyond cancer in southern Sweden. Participants had breast, prostate, lung, or colorectal cancer diagnosed one to two or five to six years earlier. A standard European questionnaire measured their wellbeing.

More than two thousand people responded. Scores were worse for younger respondents, those with several other illnesses, and those with lung or colorectal cancer. Overall, respondents matched published values for the general Swedish population. The team presented results in several formats, including scale scores and problem ranges, and found the formats agreed. Care could improve by focusing on the subgroups that scored lowest.
pmc-13241536:
Wahba's team in Damietta made a new Schiff base ligand and its metal partners as hopeful germ-fighting agents. The ligand was built by joining two ring-shaped blocks into a four-toothed binding pocket. Copper, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and uranyl versions were prepared. Each compound was profiled with light-based and physical methods.

Metal binding sharply boosted the action over the free ligand. The uranyl and copper partners killed bacteria most strongly, while the manganese partner scavenged radicals best, acting like a superoxide dismutase mimic. Biofilm growth in three germ species fell by up to half. Docking runs against key germ proteins favored the cobalt and uranyl partners.
pmc-13241936:
Kelly L Harper and co-authors describe a 2026 protocol for a pilot trial of expressive writing for sexual minority veterans. Those who are gay, lesbian, bisexual, or otherwise sexual minorities face extra stress tied to their identity. That stress raises rates of depression and anxiety, yet few tailored treatments have been tested in veterans health care.

The writing program asks participants to write about minority stress experiences, while a comparison group writes neutrally. A small open phase first refines the program with ten people. A pilot randomized phase then enrolls fifty-four veterans, with checks at the end of treatment and three months later. Interviews will capture satisfaction and practical issues. Results will shape a full trial.
pmc-13242036:
Giovanni M Saladino and co-authors report a 2026 study using focused ultrasound to deliver nanoparticles into glioblastoma brain tumors. The blood-brain barrier blocks most agents from reaching these tumors. Sound waves with microbubbles can loosen that barrier briefly and locally.

The team first mapped sound pressure fields in simulations and healthy mice. Tumor-bearing mice then received ultrasound aimed at the tumor, followed by an approved iron oxide nanoparticle. Imaging showed clearly greater nanoparticle buildup in treated tumors than in untreated ones. Tumor tissue opened at lower pressure than healthy brain, hinting at a selective window. Tissue checks found no extra acute damage from the procedure. The authors frame the method as a measurable delivery platform.
pmc-13242436:
Sabera Sultana and co-authors measured how long COVID affects everyday quality of life among adults in Japan. Their analysis, published in Quality of Life Research in 2026, drew on the CARE Japan cohort followed through 2022 and into 2023. More than twelve hundred participants rated their health with the SF-12 survey. The team compared people reporting long COVID with those without it and sorted symptoms into patterns.

People with long COVID scored clearly lower on quality of life than those without it. The gap was widest for participants who already had lung disease. Symptom patterns fell into three groups, and every group fared worse than the comparison group. Being female, younger, underweight, or having a prior mental health condition also tracked with lower scores. The findings argue for support aimed at the most affected patients.
pmc-13242636:
Miles Tran and co-authors present EmbAlign, software that names the cells of a worm embryo from a single snapshot. In Caenorhabditis elegans, every cell's lineage is known, but naming cells in a new embryo usually takes long live imaging and tracking. EmbAlign instead registers the snapshot in 3D against a spatiotemporal atlas of reference embryos. An iterative Sinkhorn alignment then settles each cell's identity, robust to the embryo's pose and natural shifts in cell position.

The method reached 96.9% accuracy up to the 190-cell stage. A built-in diagnostic layer scores how trustworthy each call is. The output turns raw spatial data into lineage-aware datasets, ready for studies of how embryos vary. A tool that reads the tree off one still image speeds every experiment that asks which cell did what.
pmc-13242836:
Dennis J Head, Jay D Raman, and Roderick K Clark report a 2026 United States cohort study of complications after hydrocelectomy, the standard surgery for fluid swelling around the testicle. European series had reported complication rates, but American data were missing. A national health network supplied records spanning two decades.

Over twenty-seven thousand patients were included. About thirteen in a hundred had some complication within ninety days, with most arising in the first month. Emergency visits, readmissions, and reoperations each affected a small share. Bleeding caused a quarter of surgical complications, while most were inflammatory or unspecified. Patients with hypertension, diabetes, or clotting defects faced more trouble. The authors recommend close first-month follow-up, especially for higher-risk patients.
pmc-13243136:
Liangliang Niu and colleagues describe a 2026 surgical method for a rare and severe eye injury. In these cases the choroid, a layer that feeds the eye, tears away from the wall after major trauma. Their method sews the layer back in place with fine double-armed sutures during repair surgery.

The report covers eight patients treated at a Fudan University eye center in early 2025 after open globe injuries. Three eyes had tearing around the full circle of the choroid. After about seven months, sight had improved a little on average and eye pressure had risen slightly. Every eye was saved, and none shrank away, which supports the method for the worst injuries.
pmc-13244936:
Enya B Vroom, Erin P Finley, and Jennifer Sharpe Potter gather advice on medication care for stimulant use disorder in a 2026 study. Stimulant problems are rising in the United States, yet few patients get treatment. No approved medication exists, even though some drugs show real promise in trials.

The team ran seven focus groups and four interviews with 12 patients and 13 providers. Advice fell into three classes: building capacity, joining services together, and improving how change is rolled out. Training to cut stigma, adding peer workers, and shared care plans all featured. Regular team meetings and links across sites were urged to break down silos. The guidance aims at care that patients help shape.
pmc-13245436:
Jirapat Wonglhow and colleagues compare chemotherapy paths for a rare bile duct area cancer in a 2026 study. Ampullary cancer grows where the bile and pancreatic ducts meet the gut. Proof for the best first drug mix in advanced cases is scarce.

The team reviewed 97 patients treated at a university hospital in southern Thailand from 2005 to 2024. Among those who got drug care, gemcitabine-based mixes faced off against fluoropyrimidine-based ones. Survival with and without disease spread landed close for both families. pmc-13246636:
Duoduo Wang and colleagues read gene activity in a medicinal plant struck by a virus in a 2026 study. Emilia sonchifolia is a tropical herb valued against inflammation and tumors. Plants with yellow vein symptoms were found in a nursery in Guangxi, China, in 2021.

pmc-13246736:
Caenen and co-authors published this correction in Scientific Reports in 2026, fixing numbers in their paper on measuring heart stiffness in pigs. Later analysis uncovered an error in the imaging sequence's pulse repetition frequency, the rate at which the scanner fired its pulses.

pmc-13248236:
Ali Hassan and Younis compare power talk in two medical television shows in this 2026 study. One is Balto, an Egyptian comedy from 2023, and the other is The Resident, an American drama from 2018. In Balto, senior doctors assert rank playfully, and interns answer with softened or ironic lines. pmc-13248336:
Ayodeji and a large Nigerian team measured vitamin D in mothers and newborns in Ilorin, reported in 2026. Cord blood usually carries less vitamin D than the mother's blood, but the size of that gap was unclear in sub-Saharan Africa. The authors warn that a mother's good result cannot stand in for her baby's, which matters for supplement policy in the region.
pmc-13248836:
Shuangshuang Miao and co-authors review freeze-made porous materials for tissue engineering in a 2026 survey. Scaffolds for regrown tissue must mimic body structure, keep cells alive, and let nutrients pass. Ice templating shapes such scaffolds by growing ice crystals through a mix, then removing the ice.

pmc-13249136:
Jean Claude Makenga Bof and Daniel Muteba analyze filariasis care coverage in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in a 2026 national study. Coverage varied sharply by province, with some high-burden areas served worst. Many patients dropped out between being found and being treated. The authors tie coverage to program and system factors.
pmc-13249936:
Kraus and colleagues tested a simple blood ratio as a fortune-teller after heart attack, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. The Augsburg registry held nearly five thousand patients, aged twenty-five to eighty-four, who suffered a first heart attack between 2010 and 2017. The ratio divides platelet counts by white cell counts from the admission blood draw, and the team tracked deaths over a median of close to five years.

More than twelve hundred patients died during follow-up. The highest platelet counts alone predicted worse survival, but the ratio told a subtler story, with middle ranges faring best and the lowest range worst. The authors propose the cheap, routine measure for sorting patients into closer or lighter follow-up.
pmc-13250436:
Chen and colleagues sort donated human knees by how they share load between cartilage and the meniscus during walking. Their 2026 Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine laboratory study ran forty-four cadaver knees through simulated gait. Force maps across the top of the shinbone revealed each knee's loading pattern.

Where load concentrated, peak stress moved with it, sitting under the meniscus in meniscus-dominant knees. Knees that loaded through cartilage directly showed higher peak stresses on the inner side of the joint. The authors say this hidden variety may explain why similar knee injuries and repairs turn out so differently.
pmc-13250636:
Michael Palace built a computer model of one of nature's tightest partnerships for this 2026 paper. Fig trees depend on tiny wasps to pollinate them, and the wasps, which live very briefly, depend on figs flowering in a steady relay across many trees.

The model places single trees and wasps on a map and tracks male and female flower phases separately. It searches for the smallest tree population that keeps wasps alive in every run. How far wasps can fly turns out to be central to survival. The tool also maps which trees exchange pollen, letting researchers test how spacing and timing keep the partnership alive.
pmc-13251036:
Liu and co-authors search for why the new drainage opening after tear duct surgery sometimes scars shut again. Their 2026 BMC Molecular and Cell Biology study compares nasal tissue from thirty patients after endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy, half with re-blockage and half with lasting success. The operation treats chronic tear sac inflammation and constant tearing.

Forcing extra RBM39 in lab-grown vessel cells sped their growth, while silencing it slowed them. A cell-adhesion pathway looked like its likely route of action. The authors nominate RBM39 as a candidate target for keeping the surgical opening clear, pending causal proof.
pmc-13251436:
Jane Symington and co-authors study how immune cells shape a dangerous fungus after its spores are breathed in, in this 2026 paper. The fungus, Coccidioides, causes Valley Fever and can be life-threatening even in healthy people. In soil its spores grow into threads, but in a host they swell into a round parasitic form called a spherule. Heat and carbon dioxide can trigger that switch in a dish; host triggers were unknown.

Blocking the swallowing step blocked the switch, so contact matters. Gene readouts found a core set of genes active in spherules, plus others switched on only near immune cells. The work shows the host helps trigger the parasitic form.
pmc-13251836:
Zijing Wei and a large team review the reviews on artificial intelligence for evidence synthesis in a 2026 paper. Summarizing all research on a question is slow, manual work, and findings can age before they appear. Software vendors promise that AI tools will speed each stage, from searching to writing, but proof of readiness has been scattered.

Searching three databases for reviews published between 2020 and May 2025, the team found twenty-one studies covering forty-six tools. Ten tools reported results for screening titles and abstracts, and all reached at least ninety-five percent sensitivity in some setup, meaning they missed very few relevant papers. Two products, DistillerSR and EPPI-Reviewer, supported the broadest range of tasks. For stages beyond screening, such as data extraction and synthesis, solid evidence was scarce. The authors conclude that supervised AI screening is ready for use, while the rest needs more proof.
pmc-13252036:
Büyükbezirci and colleagues test a back nerve block for shingles patients whose pain resisted the standard drug pregabalin. Their 2026 Journal of Pain Research study follows thirty herpes zoster patients, a group at risk of postherpetic neuralgia, a stubborn nerve pain. Patients whose pain settled on pregabalin alone formed one group; the rest received an erector spinae plane block.

Pain and sleep interference scores improved significantly over time in both groups. The block did not measurably cut the rate of postherpetic neuralgia at three months, though. Immune cell patterns differed, with the blocked group showing lower T-cell and natural killer cell levels at follow-up. Patients who escaped chronic pain started with higher levels of one bright natural killer cell type, hinting at protective immunity.
pmc-13252736:
Guangyu Zhang and colleagues track grass growth on the Tibetan Plateau in this 2026 study. The high alpine grasslands feed herds and store carbon, yet how climate change and human activity each shape their yearly growth was unsettled.

Satellite-based estimates from 2000 to 2022 separated the whole plant community and three plant groups: sedges, grass-like plants, and broad herbs. Total growth slipped slightly, sedges gained, and the other groups declined. Human activity was the dominant driver over more than half the area, ahead of climate alone. Which plant group steered local change varied by place. The authors offer the maps for targeted grassland care.
pmc-13254336:
Anika Shimonty and Lynda Bonewald review irisin and bone in a 2026 paper, with a focus on sex. Irisin is a protein released from muscle during exercise that sends signals to fat, brain, heart, and bone. Its bone effects can look positive or negative depending on context and on sex.

The review covers irisin's action on the three main bone cell types, plus mouse models and human studies. Sex differences also appear in Alzheimer's disease responses to irisin, the authors note. They argue sex must be weighed carefully, especially if irisin is ever used as a therapy.
pmc-13255036:
Kathleen N. Dollman and colleagues used advanced X-ray imaging in a 2026 study of growth in early archosauromorphs, the reptile group that later produced dinosaurs, birds, and crocodiles. The fossils came from Driefontein Farm in South Africa's Karoo Basin, dating to the Early Triassic. Growth speed matters because it ties into body size, maturity, and metabolism.

Synchrotron scanning let the team read bone microstructure without cutting the fossils. The bones showed that both fast and slow growth strategies already existed side by side in these early forms. Later lineages, the authors argue, inherited this variety rather than inventing it anew. The findings push the roots of the modern bird-versus-crocodile growth contrast deep into the group's early history.
pmc-13255936:
Jessica Prunaretty and co-authors report a 2026 implementation study of an artificial intelligence workflow that reconstructs the radiation dose prostate cancer patients actually receive each day. Body shape shifts between sessions, so delivered dose can drift from the plan. Their software builds synthetic CT images from daily scans, outlines organs automatically, and recalculates dose.

The team analyzed 800 treatment sessions from 20 patients. Dose to the target volumes stayed consistent with the plan overall. Some sessions, though, delivered higher-than-expected dose to the rectum or bladder. In two patients, the excess traced back to the software misdrawing the bladder's outline. The authors support AI monitoring as a safety net while insisting that expert eyes still verify its work before anyone acts on it.
pmc-13256436:
Simela Kirimlidou and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of help for nipple trauma in breastfeeding women, a common cause of pain and early weaning. Following standard review guidelines, they gathered twenty-two studies published between 2020 and 2026 testing treatments and support strategies.

Interventions ranged from topical natural products, including olive oil, expressed breast milk, coconut oil, beeswax preparations, and lanolin, to nipple shields and hands-on education in feeding technique. Several topical options eased pain and supported healing, though results varied by product and study. Education and professional support improved technique, experience, and how long women kept breastfeeding. No single fix worked for everyone. The authors recommend combining topical care, technique coaching, and personal support, tailored to each mother, and ask for stronger trials.
pmc-13257236: Elvira Yunita and co-authors issue a 2026 fix to their 2025 review on a vitamin E fraction as a brain guard. The notice is a correction only. One cited paper had been pulled by its publisher. It is swapped for a 2020 Brain study on cell damage in a gene-linked form of Parkinson disease. The authors state that their findings stand as before. The editor passed the change, and the first article has been updated.
pmc-13257836:
Zhiyu Qiao leads a 2026 study of origami structures printed from rigid and flexible plastics together. Miura-ori folding promises deployable designs, yet the seam between hard and soft phases usually tears first. Four hinge geometries were printed and loaded in tension and compression to compare stress transfer and failure.

An interlaced hinge with deep embedment stopped early seam failure best. Failure moved into the flexible rubber itself, a healthier sign than separation. Stretch before breaking more than tripled as embedment deepened, while peak strength held steady. The dual-material structure also beat a single-material version on compression capacity and stretch by wide margins. Deployable-structure designers gain a concrete hinge recipe. Solar arrays, shelters, and medical devices that fold flat all depend on exactly this joint problem.
pmc-13257936:
Steve Williams and co-authors present a physics-based way to predict how fast cracks grow under repeated loading. Engineers usually fit such growth with a simple empirical line on a log plot. Their 2026 method instead builds the forecast from smooth-specimen fatigue data and stresses ahead of the crack.

Stress profiles came from two-dimensional models of a notched edge crack across full load cycles. Feeding those into a damage model produced growth curves for the superalloy RR1000 at three load ratios. Predictions matched experiments well at two ratios and captured the steeper slope at the third. The method was then extended to sudden overloads.
pmc-13258036:
Zhendong Weng and co-authors review wandering ions in layered hybrid perovskite structures in a 2026 article. These soft crystals can be tuned molecule by molecule, yet heat, light, and voltage push their ions around. That movement can blur a sharp interface, grade it gently, alloy it, or even program a working junction.

Fabrication routes are sorted by the interface profile each one creates at birth. Heat-driven halide motion in and across layers is mapped, along with spacer molecules that block intermixing. Electric fields can steer ions deliberately inside devices. Design rules close the review, treating migration as both a failure mode to suppress and a tool to exploit. Solar and light-emitting device engineers gain a mechanistic playbook for stable, layered perovskites.
pmc-13258136:
Subin Lee and co-authors review polymer nanocarriers designed barrier by barrier for targeted drug delivery in a 2026 article. A swallowed or injected carrier must survive body fluids, dodge clearance, gather in diseased tissue, cross cell walls, and release cargo on cue. Each barrier demands its own engineering answer.

Nanoparticles and micelles anchor the carrier survey, with surface chemistry treated as the master control. Stimulus-responsive designs that open under acidity, enzymes, or heat receive special focus. Applications span cancer drugs, genes, proteins, and vaccines. Translation issues close the review, from body compatibility to factory reproducibility and regulation. Formulation scientists gain a checklist organized by obstacle rather than by material, which matches how delivery projects actually fail in development.
pmc-13258736:
Yubang Dong and coauthors survey sensor tools for finding tumor markers in a 2026 review. Blood based liquid biopsy promises cancer checks without tissue samples. Sensors must catch tiny amounts of tumor cells, DNA fragments, and vesicles in that blood.

Electrical sensors lead on precision and small device size for clinic side testing. Fluorescent sensors excel at tracking several markers at once and at imaging. Other families covered include Raman, microfluidic, and gene editing based designs. Current work pushes toward combined testing and smarter data analysis. Diagnostic developers gain a structured comparison of what each sensor family does best today.
pmc-13258936:
Xin Li and coauthors improve microscope depth measurement from focus stacks in a 2026 imaging paper. Shiny surfaces and weak texture warp the focus curve and break simple peak finding rules. Their learning system was trained on synthetic distortions modeled from real optics.

Attention modules reweight the parts of each focus curve most hurt by distortion. A validity output guides smoothing only where depth estimates look trustworthy. Error on a shiny free form test surface fell by more than a third against a strong prior method. Flat region noise on silicon wafer data fell by about half. Precision inspection gains a depth tool that survives difficult surfaces.
pmc-13259036:
Jinling Feng and colleagues trace aging chemistry in ancient camphor trees during a 2026 study. Leaves came from trees spanning ten to over eight hundred years of age. Polyamines and plant hormones were measured and related to tree age with several statistical methods.

Most measures shifted with age, though three hormones stayed flat. One polyamine fell with age while a cytokinin hormone rose. A free salicylic acid measure tracked closely with the senescence turning point near four hundred fifty years. A three part model predicted tree age reliably. pmc-13259136:
Leyan Li and colleagues simplify wheat cell transformation and warn about protein location errors in a 2026 methods paper. Their shortened method works across wheat varieties and yields clean microscope images. Tag position proved decisive, since a badly placed tag can hide a location signal. Wheat researchers gain both a faster protocol and clear design rules.
pmc-13259336:

A modified kinetic law fit crosslink growth best among three candidates. The full model cut prediction errors by over nine tenths against a traditional approach. Accuracy held at temperatures left out of training. Propellant stockpile managers gain a life assessment tool with physical meaning.
pmc-13259436:

Rehabilitation programs gain sensor backed evidence for adding mental load to gait practice.
pmc-13261136:
Min Chen and a large group of co-authors write a 2026 comment on steering open-source AI toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. pmc-13261336:

pmc-13261536:

pmc-13262536:

pmc-13262736:

pmc-13263136:

pmc-13263336:

pmc-13263436:

pmc-13263536:
Fatemah Aryan and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 on parasites living inside brown rats in a city district of eastern Kuwait. pmc-13263936:

That change would affect treatment choices and trial endpoints.
pmc-13264036:

Child brain doctors wrote the most prescriptions in both groups.
pmc-13264136:

The authors argue that less treatment is often more, reserving combinations for clearly high-risk cases.
pmc-13264536:

pmc-13264936:

pmc-13265236:

The results support further development.
pmc-13266636:

Those two forms thrive in low-oxygen tumour environments. Binding to red blood cell enzymes explains the drug's known pooling in whole blood. pmc-13266836:
Farah A Abdallah and co-authors trace in 2026 how esophageal cancer returns after combined chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery meant to cure it. pmc-13267536:
Nobuyuki Takeyama and colleagues report a 2026 imaging study of two cases of ovarian clear cell carcinoma. This ovarian cancer type often grows as a large one-sided mass. Tissue study matched the stripes to alternating bands of tumor cells and dead or fibrous tissue. The living rim sat at the edge of each mass with its own signal traits. Both patients had full removal surgery, and final staging was early. The authors offer the striped pattern as a diagnostic clue.
pmc-13267836:
Qiannan Li and colleagues present a 2026 computer analysis of immune genes in chronic lung disease. COPD involves lasting airway inflammation, and a T cell type called Th17 may help drive it. Both ran lower in COPD samples, a result confirmed by lab tests on fresh samples. Higher levels of both tracked with lower Th17 cell presence. pmc-13268636:
Parnnate Wongsirisakul and colleagues present a 2026 survey study of social conditions in patients with both type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. pmc-13269436:

Sensors based on electricity, light, vibration, or gas offer fast, portable, and cheaper checks for use in the field. The review gives special weight to gases given off by growing mold as an early warning sign. The authors see real-time sensor checks as a strong path to safer food and feed.
pmc-13269636:

pmc-13270236:
Nadja Morello and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on whether MRSA bacteria, a drug-resistant hospital germ, are losing sensitivity to chlorhexidine, the antiseptic used to clear them from patients. pmc-13271236:

pmc-13271836:

pmc-13272036:

pmc-13272236:

pmc-13272336:

After nine days his pain had resolved and neck movement had improved across all directions.
pmc-13272536:

Choices for partial tears varied more, and university surgeons used some added patches and treatments more often than others.
pmc-13272936:

Phone apps for self-screening, remote counseling, and prediction models offer scalable help, though privacy, fair access, and cultural fit remain concerns. pmc-13273136:

Results will judge feasibility and early effect.
pmc-13273236:

It avoids thermal contrast limits and allows finer spatial detail than current thermal sensors.
pmc-13273636:

The team enrolled 403 participants and tested them for malaria. About 70 percent owned a bed net, at 70.2 percent. About two thirds, 66.5 percent, used a net on a regular basis. Malaria was found in 3.7 percent of participants. Most infections, 60 percent, were caused by Plasmodium falciparum. Infection was more common in rural residents. It was also more common in people who owned no net. The authors urge wider net access and steady use.
pmc-13274136:
Monika Kisielewska and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article on why melanoma, an aggressive skin cancer, so often outlasts modern drugs. Melanoma cells flip between fast-growing states and slow, invasive, drug-resistant states as MITF activity rises and falls. Signals driving the flips include inflammation, low oxygen, support cells, stiff tissue, and shifts in how cells burn fuel. The authors map how these cues connect. Targeting the switch itself, they argue, may help stop cancers from dodging therapy.
pmc-13274236:
Melkamu Dugassa Kassa and Jeanne Martin Grace present a 2026 systematic review on folding chronic disease care into primary healthcare in low-resource countries. Long-term diseases such as diabetes and heart disease kill heavily in poorer nations, yet front-line clinics are built mainly for infections and emergencies. The reviewers searched six databases plus grey literature for studies since 2016.

Twenty-three studies met their criteria. The main barriers were too few trained staff, weak buildings and equipment, patchy access to essential medicines, and split governance. Patients' low awareness and cultural hurdles added friction. What helped included shifting tasks to community health workers, strong policy backing, financial incentives, better information systems, and community engagement.
pmc-13276036:
Bassant Hamed and co-authors report a 2026 experiment on strengthening concrete beams with greener materials. Reinforced concrete carries much of modern building, but making steel bars uses huge energy. The team tested fabric-like geotextiles and steel wire mesh, plus tiny carbon tubes mixed into the concrete.

Seven small beams were bent until they failed, comparing plain and strengthened versions. Some had mesh or fabric buried inside; others wore it wrapped around the outside. Every strengthened beam carried more load than the plain one, with gains up to about forty-five percent. Beams also bent much farther before breaking and soaked up more energy. Buried wire mesh gave the highest load, while an outer fabric wrap gave the largest bend.
pmc-13276136:
Kieran Seay and colleagues report a 2026 biomarker study of hormone treatment for a precancerous womb condition. Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia is rising in younger women, and many want treatment that preserves fertility. Progestin therapy spares surgery, yet a large share of patients never respond fully.

Women who failed to respond had lower starting levels of progesterone receptor A in gland and support tissue. A receptor ratio at or below one also matched resistance, while another receptor showed no early link. The authors stress that this small exploratory study needs larger prospective testing.
pmc-13276336:
Jiale Chen and co-authors introduce a 2026 image model for outlining apple leaf pests and disease spots. Orchards pose hard conditions: lesions blend into leaf texture, leaves overlap, and plain colour photos miss subtle signs. Accurate outlines help growers judge damage and target treatment.

Against a strong baseline, the model gained roughly four points on precision, recall, and overlap scores. The authors present the gains as a step toward dependable orchard monitoring in messy real settings.
pmc-13277636:

After tuning, both tests showed good specificity, sensitivity, and repeatability, detecting very small amounts of target DNA. Early tests on clinical samples found the target bacteria as expected. The assays are a base for fuller validation, the authors say. Faster, combined testing could support better antibiotic choices and disease control on farms.
pmc-13278236:

pmc-13278336:
Kyu-Ho Yi leads a 2026 cadaver study of a little-known scalp muscle called the temporoparietalis. The team dissected thirty embalmed cadavers, studying both sides of the head, for sixty sides in total, and graded the muscle as thick, indistinct, or absent.

The muscle was present on about sixty-two percent of sides. Only about seventeen percent were visibly thick, while about forty-five percent were faint and about thirty-eight percent absent. It is not a constant structure, the authors stress. Expecting this variation may help surgeons read dissection planes and plan operations around the temple region.
pmc-13278736:

pmc-13279436:

pmc-13279636:

pmc-13280336:

pmc-13280436:

Against the pill, the chest strap estimates showed a small mean bias, near a sixth of a degree low for continuous data. Rank correlations sat in the mid range. pmc-13280536:

pmc-13280636:

pmc-13280736:

pmc-13280936:

pmc-13281236:

pmc-13281336:

The authors stress that pet movement across borders can carry such parasites into new lands. Their note is short and serves as a watch alert for vets and labs. It backs gene tests when travel history hints at imported worms.
pmc-13281536:

pmc-13282336:

pmc-13282436:

pmc-13282636:

pmc-13282736:

pmc-13282836:

pmc-13283136:

Late follow-up occurred in 13 percent of cases in the study. Early scopes were most common when only low-risk growths were found. Patients with high-risk growths often waited too long instead. pmc-13283236:

Healing time, surgery time, hospital stay, and return to work also matched closely. Major problem rates did not differ clearly in the pooled data. pmc-13283536:

pmc-13284436:

pmc-13285536:

pmc-13285636:

pmc-13285736:
