The arrangement placing gp96 first, then calreticulin, then E7 scored best. The researchers built that construct's gene in a plasmid and produced the fusion peptide in E. coli Rosetta bacteria, purifying it under native conditions. They present the expressed peptide as a promising candidate for further HPV16 vaccine development.
pmc-13400436:
Alexandra A Cordeiro and a binational team compare, in 2026, COVID-19 antibody rates in people with and without HIV during the first pandemic year in Haiti and Tanzania. Most earlier data came from wealthy countries, and results from other settings conflicted. Antibodies show who has met the virus, even without symptoms.

Across both countries, people living with HIV had lower rates of antibodies against the virus than people without HIV. In Haiti, antibody rates rose faster in the group without HIV. In Tanzania, the gap also favored the uninfected group. The findings add low-income country data to a mixed global picture and raise questions about exposure, immune response and protection in this population.
pmc-13400536:
Manar M Ellaban and colleagues survey, in 2026, mental health among international medical students at Ain Shams University in Egypt, comparing those from conflict zones with peers from calmer regions. Medical study abroad is stressful, and students from war-affected areas may carry added trauma.

Of 310 students surveyed between late 2024 and early 2025, over a third met thresholds for extremely severe depression, and even more for extremely severe anxiety. About one in five met criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder, with the complex form slightly more common still. Students from conflict regions scored worse on every measure. The authors call for trauma-informed counseling, peer support and targeted services for this high-risk group.
pmc-13400736:
Ebrahim A Ramadan and co-authors design, in 2026, a hybrid neural network that finds and outlines faults in solar panel arrays from inspection images. Faulty cells waste energy and money, so spotting them early matters. Their model blends convolutional networks, which excel at local detail, with transformer networks that read wider context.

Four image collections were used, from drone thermal views to cell-level electrical glow images with many fault classes. On the thermal set the model located faulty cells with accuracy near ninety-nine percent and solid overlap scores. On a two-class cell dataset it approached perfect detection. Performance dipped on the hardest multi-class sets but still beat comparison models, supporting use across inspection styles.
pmc-13400836:

Crucially, alliin raised the receptor that pulls cholesterol from blood while lowering the protein that destroys that receptor, a pairing confirmed by targeted tests. The authors position alliin for further study in lipid disorders.
pmc-13400936:

A reinforcement learning method rewarding both correct symptom calls and sound reasoning beat standard fine-tuning, with relative gains over ten percent in mid-sized models. Structured rationales added further gains, especially for symptoms needing context, and pushed models to cite relevant evidence.
pmc-13401536:
Kazuya Takeda and colleagues measured radiotherapy use in the final 30 days of life among cancer patients in Japan. pmc-13401736:

The patient, a 42-year-old woman who had given birth twice, had lived with an elongated swelling on her left labia majora for ten years.

Ultrasound suggested an ordinary fatty lipoma. Wide local excision removed the tumour, and tissue examination delivered the true diagnosis. pmc-13401936:

Twenty-nine pooled mixtures were split and incubated at five temperatures from refrigeration to 50 degrees, then measured over 28 days. The standard buffer lost significant haemoglobin from day ten at room temperature and from day three at every higher temperature. The new buffer held up better by comparison in the results that follow. Statistical modelling separated which variables, temperature, time, or buffer, drove the degradation.
pmc-13402036:

pmc-13402236:

pmc-13402336:

pmc-13402436:

pmc-13402936:

pmc-13403136:

pmc-13403636:

pmc-13403736:

pmc-13404036:

pmc-13404636:

pmc-13404836:

pmc-13405036:

pmc-13405236:

pmc-13405636:

pmc-13405736:

pmc-13406136:

pmc-13407736:

pmc-13407936:

pmc-13408136:

pmc-13408336:

pmc-13408636:

pmc-13409036:

pmc-13409236:

pmc-13410036:

pmc-13410536:

pmc-13411636:

pmc-13411736:

pmc-13412236:

The authors offer the measurements as training and injury-prevention benchmarks.
pmc-13412536:

Hospital stay length tracked the number of operations closely, rising as surgical burden grew. With no comparison group, the authors keep their reading descriptive and urge coordinated specialist care.
pmc-13413236:

pmc-13413636:
Tae-Young Kim and colleagues mine public data in 2026 for the story of ZBTB40, a little-known gene switch, in liver cancer. They used the TCGA liver tumour set and web tools built for gene work. pmc-13413836:

pmc-13415336:

pmc-13417936:

pmc-13418436:

Ultrasound imaging shows heart motion, and damaged regions move abnormally after a heart attack. Their pipeline cleans each video frame, segments the left ventricle wall, and extracts motion and area change features for classification.

Noise filtering and fuzzy clustering segmentation did much of the groundwork. The authors propose the system as real time decision support, pending clinical validation.
pmc-13418536:

pmc-13418736:

pmc-13419236:

pmc-13419336:

pmc-13419936:

pmc-13421236:

pmc-13421536:

pmc-13422336:

pmc-13422936:

pmc-13424236:

pmc-13424436:

pmc-13425036:

pmc-13425536:

pmc-13425836:

pmc-13426136:

pmc-13426236:

pmc-13426936:

pmc-13427236:

pmc-13427436:

pmc-13427836:

pmc-13427936:

Three showed no slope change, three showed a marked slope fall, and two showed a slope flip. pmc-13428036:

pmc-13428436:

pmc-13428736:

pmc-13429136:

pmc-13429736:

Nonlinear performance analysis then judged how the damaged building behaves under shaking. Owners and engineers get a case study in judging a wounded building, not just designing a new one, with downtime and repair in view.
pmc-13431036:

pmc-13431436:

pmc-13431736:

pmc-13431836:

pmc-13432936:

pmc-13433336:

pmc-13433836:

pmc-13433936:

X-ray tests showed pure rhombohedral crystals, while electron images showed a shape shift from flat hexagonal plates to grainy nets as nickel rose. Electric tests showed current flipping from n-type to p-type at nickel shares of 0.06 or more, as defect sites raised hole counts. Heat flow fell from 1.7 to 1.0 watts per metre-kelvin at 350 kelvin, as disorder scattered heat waves. Device teams get a defect-tuned mix for cold-temperature power harvesting.
pmc-13434036:
Atrial fibrillation, a common irregular heartbeat, is seen more often in people with lower income and schooling. Shangcai Xie, Xia Zhao, and Menghui Mao ask whether social position itself causes the rhythm problem. They use a genetic method that treats inherited variants as natural experiments, drawing on very large British and Finnish data sets.

Genetic signs of area deprivation showed no link to the heartbeat risk. Genetic signs of household income also showed no link. But genetic signs of more years of schooling pointed to a clearly lower risk in both data sets. The authors read this as evidence that education, rather than income or neighborhood, may itself protect against the condition. They note the finding could guide prevention efforts toward learning and its downstream effects on health.
pmc-13434236:
Fan Zhang and coauthors warn in 2026 that use of a common pain drug in pregnancy may raise joint risk in sons. Rats got the drug on days 10 to 12 of pregnancy, and the young were checked at birth and at week 12. Cartilage forming cells in dishes were studied in the same project.

Sons showed weaker cartilage growth, more breakdown, and more joint wear after running. Daughters showed a brief change at birth only. Low oxygen drove extra sugar burning in the cells, which raised a chemical mark on a growth gene. Blocking that gene path eased joint harm in sons. The rat results urge care, not panic.
pmc-13434636:
Md Shafiquzzaman and coauthors test an iron net that cleans arsenic from groundwater in 2026. Plain iron slowly rusts and grabs arsenic, but two common water guests, phosphorus and silicon, get in the way. Bench tests varied the dose of each guest while tracking arsenic loss and iron wear.

Arsenic uptake slowed as either guest rose, and phosphorus hurt more than silicon. The guests coat the iron with crusts and steal binding sites. Fine spectra show arsenic fully shifts to its safer form before it sticks. Rust cycling drives the cleanup, the team concludes. Field users should test for phosphorus before sizing a unit.
pmc-13435436:
Zeliha Yarar's team compared thyroid problems in 2026 between adults with inborn errors of immunity and healthy controls. Faulty immunity and hormone glands interact, but thyroid rates in these rare immune disorders were not well mapped. Forty patients and 65 controls all had thyroid ultrasound plus blood tests for function and autoantibodies, with autoimmune thyroid disease judged by antibodies, function, and scan signs.

Nodules were no more common in patients than controls, yet autoimmune thyroid disease was nearly twice as common in patients, and their thyroid glands ran smaller on average. The authors back routine thyroid scans and antibody checks in this group. Immunologists get a practical screening case from a small but complete case-control study.
pmc-13438736:
Saranya Kattil Parmbil and colleagues synthesized a family of twenty-one new compounds aimed at monoamine oxidase B, an enzyme breaking down dopamine in Parkinson's disease. Existing blockers often lock onto the enzyme for good and carry side effects, so reversible, choosy ones are wanted. Their 2026 study built indole-based molecules tethered with a propargyl arm and screened each against both forms of the enzyme.

Most compounds preferred the B form, as hoped. The leader, coded PSH18, blocked it at sub-micromolar strength and was forty-two times choosier for B over A. Tests showed it competes for the active site and lets go again, the reversible profile the field wants. A membrane assay suggested it can cross into the brain, and computer forecasts raised no red flags. The authors offer the scaffold as a lead worth refining, not a drug, with animal work still ahead.
pmc-13438936:
Ali Shalash and colleagues map what they call the Parkinson pandemic, charting the disease's growth across every world region. Parkinson's is now the fastest-growing neurological disorder, with prevalence more than doubling between 1990 and 2015. Their 2026 narrative review sets out why the burden climbs, why it climbs unevenly, and what coordinated action could blunt it.

Aging populations and longer lives drive much of the rise. Industrial exposures join in places: pesticides, air pollution, and heavy metals. Even falling smoking rates play a part, since smoking oddly tracks with lower risk. Regions differ in genes, lifestyles, city growth, and, above all, in access to diagnosis, medicines, and specialist care. The authors argue for tailored regional strategies not one global script: chase local drivers, raise awareness, diagnose earlier, guarantee drug supplies, support caregivers, and curb toxic exposures. Framing the growth as a pandemic is deliberate, a call for planning and funding.
pmc-13439336:
Natália Guimarães Melo and colleagues report a 2026 study of the 'Move and Play Programme', a set of short videos that teach parents activities to support baby development at home. For such videos to spread, they must be clear, practical, and trusted. The team asked the two groups who judge them best: child physiotherapists and parents.

More than two hundred physiotherapists and one hundred parents watched the videos and rated them online. Both groups judged most videos fully adequate in presentation, content, and clarity of goals. The therapists said the videos help guide home activities and talk with families. Parents said the videos built their confidence to do the activities on their own. Most in both groups said they would recommend the videos to others.
pmc-13439436:
Xiaocheng Lan and co-authors map the tiny pockets around platinum trapped inside a zeolite catalyst, explaining selective chemistry in 2026. Zeolites are crystals laced with channels that can cage metal particles and steer reactions. How molecules actually reach the caged metal was poorly charted in three dimensions. The team combined careful synthesis, reaction tests, and atom-level modelling using MFI zeolites, a common industrial type, and the conversion of unsaturated aldehydes as a probe reaction.

Two access routes emerged: through the channels, or through a pocket the authors call a molecule-well. The well presses on arriving molecules so their oxygen end, not their carbon chain, touches platinum. That pose favours making unsaturated alcohols, the prized products, over side products. The work ties pocket shape directly to catalyst behaviour and gives designers a concrete target to engineer.
pmc-13439936:
Tian and co-authors track how the decision between two DNA repair outcomes shifts as a worm's germline grows. Their 2026 paper studies meiosis in Caenorhabditis elegans, where the enzyme SPO-11 deliberately breaks DNA. Early breaks are repaired into non-crossovers, while later breaks become crossovers, the exchanges that shuffle genes between generations, contrary to the standard model of a late, uniform choice.

The team measured the growing germline in early adulthood and found expansion of the pachytene stage drives that growth. Nuclei surprisingly slowed as they moved through prophase. The late, crossover-fated region stayed the proximal half of the pachytene zone as it enlarged. The switch point coincided with the peak in RAD-51 repair foci, which held steady at the middle of the region, suggesting a mid-pachytene signal times the transition.
pmc-13440536:
Niu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a class of tiny materials called nanozymes for brain and spinal cord disorders. Nanozymes are man-made particles that act like enzymes, the proteins that speed up chemical reactions. The review covers stroke, brain and spinal injury, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike natural enzymes, nanozymes keep working in harsh tissue and can clear reactive oxygen, which damages cells. Their many active sites let them act on several disease steps at once, and they cross barriers that block most drugs. The authors cite gains in nerve protection and regrowth in lab and animal studies. They also flag weak points: safety data are thin, and few designs have reached human trials. The review maps what must be fixed before clinic use.
pmc-13441036:
Elahe Gharehkhani and colleagues pair a natural growth-control protein with a standard bowel cancer drug to see whether the drug works harder, reporting cell work in 2026. Irinotecan treats advanced colorectal cancer, while IGFBP-3, a binding protein governed by p53, can push tumour cells toward death. SW480 cancer cells received each agent alone and together. Combination software scored whether the pair cooperated or merely added up.

The pair scored as truly synergistic, killing more than either alone. Combined treatment raised cell suicide rates, froze more cells at the pre-division checkpoint, and flooded cells with damaging oxygen radicals while draining their antioxidant store. Death-promoting Bax rose, while protective Bcl2 and the growth driver beta-catenin both fell. The authors propose IGFBP-3 as a chemo-boosting partner, with safety checks on normal cells still owed.
pmc-13442436:
Thomas Steadman and Steven O'Reilly probe a sugar-burning enzyme called PKM2 in systemic sclerosis, a skin-hardening illness, in a 2026 study. Blood and skin cells came from people with early diffuse disease and from healthy donors. The team asked whether PKM2 runs high in the illness and whether it helps drive scar tissue growth.

Blood tests showed more PKM2 in patients than in healthy donors, and skin cells from patients held more as well. A scar signal, TGF-beta1, could switch PKM2 on in healthy skin cells. Forcing PKM2 into its four-part form cut the shift toward sugar burning and lowered scar mesh output. The pair read PKM2 as both a blood mark and a lever on cell fuel choice, a lever that drugs might one day pull to slow scarring.
pmc-13442836:
Charitini Stavropoulou and Ian Viney test what early grant wins do for later careers in United Kingdom medical research in a 2026 study. Data came from the Medical Research Council, with won and lost bids weighed alike through score matching. Outcomes spanned later grant cash, paper counts, and cite marks that track reach.

Winners in both sexes pulled more later grant cash than losers. Women who won gained cites past women who lost, with stronger field-relative cite marks as well. Men who won showed no clear edge in papers or cites over men who lost. The pair reads early cash as a stronger lever for women in this pool. Funders who weigh first grants may shift long careers more than they know, the authors suggest.
pmc-13443036:
Mika Simonen frames a journal collection on animals and social contact in a 2026 editorial. Seven papers in the set span a wide arc of views. Some start with human voices and how people grasp animals. Others watch the shared space where species meet, with no voices at all.

The last papers let animal acts speak, through direct or indirect signs. Simonen sorts the field into three nested rings: broad human-animal studies, contact studies, and a tight focus on social bonds. That last ring gives the collection its name and its aim. Growth in the field shows in fresh methods that treat animals as true partners in contact. The editorial invites readers to track how each paper shifts who counts as a social actor.
pmc-13444336:
Li and colleagues named a new genus of leafhopper, Mencius, from South China in 2026. Leafhoppers are small plant-feeding insects, and this group sits in the subfamily Ledrinae. Specimens were collected in Guangxi and studied under a stereomicroscope, with male genitalia dissected and drawn. The genus holds two species: one moved from another genus, and one newly described.

Mencius adults are large for the group, yellowish green, and about ten to fifteen millimetres long including the wings. The authors separate the genus from close relatives Petalocephala and Platycephala by a mix of traits. Key marks include a long process on the male pygofer and slender processes on the male aedeagus, a genital structure. They supply a written key, full descriptions, drawings, photographs, and distribution data for both species.
pmc-13445936:
Gizamba, Ruddell, and Klausner applied machine learning to Los Angeles County surveillance and census data. They sought neighborhoods at elevated risk of hepatitis C among adults aged 18 to 39. They used first-time positive RNA tests reported from 2020 to 2023. Thirty-one area-level variables covered poverty, healthcare access, and opioid-related harm across 245 zip code areas.

Forty-nine areas sat above the 80th percentile of predicted rates. They were classified as very high risk. They were scattered across the county rather than clustered in one district. Nine variables mattered most. The leaders were the share of families below the federal poverty line, the share of residents aged 18 to 39, and households without a vehicle in each area. Opioid emergency visits, new HIV diagnoses, and opioid hospitalizations followed in importance, along with distance to substance use treatment. The authors offer the map for targeting elimination interventions.
pmc-13446036:
Erin E. Alpaugh and colleagues chart why patients cleared for a spinal cord stimulator trial never reach the trial, in a 2026 chart review from one center. The trial, a short test of the pain device, must come before a permanent implant. Knowing where candidates stall could widen access to the therapy.

Charts spanned a decade and held 358 candidates, of whom eighty-four, near a quarter, never went ahead. Medical reasons led the blocks, followed by patient choice, insurance or money strain, scan findings, and mental health concerns. About a fifth of all candidates stalled for reasons apart from scan findings. One pain condition, complex regional pain syndrome, was the sole patient trait tied to stalling in the adjusted model, a clue for process fixes.
pmc-13447236:
Patricia Borges de Souza and fellow editors introduce a 2026 collection on neuroendocrine tumours, growths arising from hormone-making cells across the body. Once thought rare, these tumours are found more often as imaging and awareness improve. Their behaviour varies widely, so matching treatment to each patient's tumour biology remains an unfinished goal.

Papers in the collection show imaging shifting from simple detection toward measuring tumour traits that may predict response. One team built an explainable computer model that separates aggressive from calmer pancreatic tumours on routine scans, showing which features drive each call. Other work spans molecular drug studies and team-based care. Together, the editors argue, better sorting of patients by biology and imaging is steadily reshaping care for these uncommon cancers.
pmc-13447336:
Benedetta Tessa and coauthors measure a 2026 study of which user traits foretell how people react after a large Reddit oversight step. The team studied 753 social, word, link, and mind traits for 16,800 users, framing forecasting as counting of total conduct shifts under spread change.

Posts and venom shifts proved surely guessable, while joining range shifts dodged forecasting. A small trait subset helped time and again across tasks, and with care picked traits beat both single groups and the full set. Oversight plans should therefore tailor to user traits and to the set conduct aimed, the authors argue.
pmc-13447436:
Guangrong Deng and colleagues compare non-drug options for sleep and work stress in night-shift nurses through a 2026 network analysis of trials. Irregular shifts scramble sleep and raise anxiety, low mood and fatigue. Many drug-free approaches compete, from ear-point patches to scent oils, and head-to-head trials are rare, so indirect ranking fills the gap.

Eighteen trials with over fifteen hundred nurses were combined in a Bayesian network, a method that ranks options through shared comparisons. Structured sleep programmes ranked best for overall sleep scores, while mindfulness training ranked best for sleep length. Ear-point therapy led for depression, a talk approach led for anxiety, and a floral oil led for fatigue. Every ranking rests on indirect evidence with no closed loops, so the authors label results exploratory.
pmc-13447836:
Zachary Paikin and colleagues turn a fat damage product into a precision crosslinking tool for protein mapping in 2026 chemistry work. When fats oxidise under stress, a reactive compound called 4-ONE sticks to proteins, yet which residue pairs it joins and how structures change stayed hard to define with standard methods. The team recasts that damage chemistry as a designed two-step linker between two amino acid types.

First attachment to cysteine wakes a hidden aldehyde, which then rings shut with lysine into a stable link under body-like conditions. Uses shown include peptide stapling, selective protein modification and proteome-wide hunting for reactive sites. A later oxidation step makes the link break predictably inside a mass spectrometer, naming the exact paired residues. Tests on the human proteasome, the cell protein shredder, sharpened confidence in mapped links.
pmc-13448036:
Chen and colleagues reported a 2026 study of spine infection after a common bone procedure. Vertebral augmentation injects cement into cracked spine bones to ease pain. Infection after the procedure is rare but serious when it strikes. The team drew records from four hospitals over seven years.

Among 7,797 procedures, 42 infections occurred, a rate near one in 200 cases. Four traits raised the risk on their own in matched comparisons. Lung infection before surgery and low blood protein each raised risk sharply. A fluid sign on MRI and cement leaking into a disc also raised risk. Most infected patients needed a second operation, so early risk checks matter. Screening for these traits before surgery can guide simple steps that cut that risk.
pmc-13448136:
Luo and colleagues trace how colorectal cancer spreads to the liver in this 2026 study. An amino acid transporter called SLC7A5 pulls tryptophan into cells, and its role in metastasis was unknown. The team combined public datasets, patient samples, cell experiments, and mouse models. They measured the transporter across normal tissue, primary tumors, and liver metastases. They also tested what happens when it is blocked.

Levels of the transporter rose step by step from normal tissue to primary tumor to liver metastasis, and higher levels meant worse prognosis for patients. The transporter fed production of two tryptophan breakdown products that switch on the AhR receptor, driving growth and spread. Blocking it reprogrammed nearby immune cells toward fighting the tumor, and pairing its inhibitor with an anti-PD-1 antibody shrank tumors synergistically in mice.
pmc-13448336:
Dalton and colleagues examined how often palliative care, treatment focused on comfort and quality of life, reaches patients with metastatic spine disease. Their 2026 conference report covers 265 patients reviewed by a brain and spine metastases board between 2018 and 2020. The team compared who received hospital-based palliative visits and who received clinic-based visits, and what factors shaped that use.

Dalton found no differences in consultation rates by gender or race, while clinic palliative visits varied by insurance type and by the original tumor type. Patients who had surgery or radiation within a month of board review were notably more likely to get clinic palliative care. Patients seen by hospital palliative teams had much shorter survival than those who were not, likely because the sickest patients get referred first. the authors say argues for widening access earlier in care.
pmc-13448636:
Nayeong Kim and co-authors achieve nickel-catalysed coupling of unactivated alkyl halides with alkynyl halides through ligand-controlled sequencing in 2026 chemistry work. Joining a carbon triple bond directly to a saturated carbon is valued in drug and product design, yet mismatched reactivity and self-coupling have long blocked the pairing of these two electrophiles. Pre-made metal-based partners were the usual workaround.

A three-pronged ligand forces the nickel catalyst to engage the alkyl partner first, before activating the alkynyl partner, reversing the usual order. Primary, secondary and even tertiary alkyl halides coupled well with wide tolerance for other functional groups. Self-coupling by-products stayed suppressed because activation order, not matched reaction rates, enforced selectivity. Controlling activation sequence is presented as a general plan for other mismatched couplings.
pmc-13450236:
Aurio Fajardo-Campoverdi, Adrián Gallardo, and Ângelo Roncalli Miranda Rocha write in 2026 to complete a picture left lopsided in a trial comparing two breathing supports for patients with carbon dioxide retention. The original crossover study found high-flow nasal oxygen non-inferior to mask ventilation in easing diaphragm effort, and read ventilation's rise in end-expiratory lung volume as unwanted. The letter writers noticed this variable was the only one of eleven never given the Bayesian analysis applied elsewhere.

Reanalyzing averages for fifteen patients, their Bayesian model agrees with the reading. It gives a 97.8 percent probability that ventilation raises lung volume more than high-flow at fifty liters, and 99.5 percent against the thirty-liter setting. Their sensitivity analysis traces how that confidence moves when the error model grows heavier tails, a stress test for a widely spread subgroup. They argue the claim deserved the robustness check as its siblings.
pmc-13450536:
Linfei Ye and a large team test in 2026 a Chinese version of a scale that asks pregnant women what stops them from being active. The work took place in China in late 2023 and drew 448 women who were expecting a child. The scale was translated by a set procedure once the first author gave consent.

The final form holds 28 items in four groups, and expert ratings scored each item high for fit. Factor checks kept the four groups, which together explained close to two thirds of the spread in answers. Repeat scores held steady over time, so the authors offer the scale as a sound tool for clinics and studies in China.
pmc-13451836:
Pityrigkas and colleagues report a patient whose rare muscle eye brain disease adds two new variant pairings to the known genetic picture. The disease stems from faulty sugar coating of a protein that anchors muscle and brain cells, and it most often traces to the POMGNT1 gene. Their 2026 case report combines brain scans, electrical tests of the brain, tissue study, and gene sequencing for a patient followed from childhood into adult life.

The patient had floppy muscles and slow development from infancy, then lost motor skills over time and developed eye faults. Seizures began in childhood and grew into drug resistant epilepsy, meaning standard drugs failed to control them. Scans showed a smooth brain surface and small brainstem and cerebellum, signs typical of the disease. Sequencing found two POMGNT1 variants paired together, and a mix of four seizure drugs at last brought seizures under control.
pmc-13451936:
Zhang and colleagues ask whether being married protects the aging mind, and whether that link differs for men and women. Their 2026 study uses the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, a long running survey of midlife and older adults. The team modeled time to cognitive decline, meaning a clear drop in thinking skills, while adjusting for age, schooling, smoking, drinking, activity, and sleep.

Across all adults, marriage showed no firm link to decline once those factors were counted. Split by sex, though, married men faced a lower risk of decline than unmarried men, while married and unmarried women did not differ. Age stayed a strong predictor of impairment in every model. The authors suggest that support inside marriage may not reach men and women in the same way, and they urge work on marital quality and day to day emotional support.
pmc-13452236:
Passakorn Kingwascharapong and Anurak Uchuwittayakul compare in 2026 two ferments of capsule waste gel, one sweetened with sugar and one with half the sugar swapped for inulin fiber. A gut-friendly germ did the fermenting. Three wide scans, of proteins, small molecules, and fats, read what the swap changed outside the cells.

The two ferments split cleanly on all three scans. The inulin batch ran higher in four proteins tied to sugar hauling and core cell work. Hundreds of small molecule and fat features also split the pair, most in sugar and fat paths. The authors call the set a first map for turning pill plant waste into valued ferments.
pmc-13452336:
Wei-Chih Lin, Stephane Gorsse, and An-Chou Yeh curate in 2026 a data set of how heat-proof alloys rust at high heat. Such alloys serve in jets and power gear, and their surface loss sets their life. The team drew trials from 62 papers across 1956 to 2023 and added fresh runs from their own lab.

Each row logs the alloy mix, heat level, hours exposed, and weight change per area in air, plus the source. All sits in one matched format in an open store. The set is built for data-led study, score checks of past models, and learning-based design of alloys that shrug off hot air longer.
pmc-13453036:
Shixian Liu, Kaixuan Wang, Hao Chen, Ziming Wan, Lei Dou, and Shunping Li ask whether a three drug mix for advanced breast cancer is worth its price in the United States. The mix adds inavolisib to palbociclib and fulvestrant for tumors with a PIK3CA gene change. Their 2026 study models costs and health gains over 15 years from the payer's point of view.

The model gives the three drug mix 1.99 life years and 1.43 quality adjusted life years, a measure that weights years by health. The extra cost came to about 211,640 dollars, which works out near 148,417 dollars per quality adjusted year gained. That sits just under the 150,000 dollar bar the study used for good value. Repeated checks with varied inputs kept the verdict steady, though the chance of clearing the bar was only about 55 percent.
pmc-13453736:
Sven Richter and nine co-authors test how operating room lights disturb a laser based tool that reads tissue chemistry during brain surgery. The tool, Raman spectroscopy, picks out tumors by their faint light scatter, so stray light is a real threat. Their 2026 study ran the tool on rat brain and human tumor samples in a mock operating room under varied lights and gear.

Ceiling lights raised the background glow, but a simple cover blocked the effect and left clean spectra. Surgical lights were harsher, flooding the camera sensor outright. Screens, the exoscope, and navigation gear left patterned marks that math cleanup could strip away. The tissue's own glow mattered most of all, sometimes swamping the signal in low glow tumors. The authors give practical rules for keeping the tool honest in a lit room.
pmc-13454036:
Gregor Mattert and six co-authors probe which factory settings shape the quality of natural killer cells grown for cancer therapy. These immune cells can kill tumors, yet making enough of them at high quality stays hard. Their 2026 study uses a design of experiments plan, a structured way to test many settings without running every mix.

Primary NK cells from two donors grew under varied process settings, each tied to quality traits such as yield, purity, and killing power. The planned runs let the team separate each setting's effect and spot settings that interact. From the data they built a statistical model that predicts the largest count of living cells a run can reach. The authors offer the model as a guide for tuning cell production lines before costly scale up.
pmc-13454536:
Xingyu Li and seven colleagues review, in 2026, how nerves help breast tumors hide from the immune system. Immune escape blocks lasting gains from modern immune drugs, above all in cold tumors that immune cells barely enter. Evidence from cancer neuroscience casts nerves as active managers of the tumor's neighborhood, not passive wiring.

The review traces several routes. Stress nerves use adrenaline-like signals to calm immune attack and remodel tissue. Sensory nerves release messengers that help wall tumors off from immune cells. Some nerves even form synapse-like contacts with tumor cells and pass them fuel or signals. Whole-body loops through the brain and stress hormones then reset immune thresholds. The authors close with drug ideas already on pharmacy shelves, such as beta blockers, that might cut these neural lifelines.
pmc-13454836:
Koichiro Hori and six colleagues examine, in a 2026 case-based article, a heart pump that can end up supporting patients with no path forward. The Impella pump steadies people in shock after heart attacks, buying time for the heart to heal. Some patients never recover enough, yet cannot or will not accept a transplant or a permanent pump.

Two cases show the trap and two ways out. In the first, the team set the pump as a time-limited trial with an exit plan agreed in advance, then shifted to comfort-focused care. In the second, a stronger pump restored the patient's clarity, and the patient declined long-term options, choosing planned withdrawal and end-of-life care. The authors urge early team deliberation and palliative care involvement, so stopping support honors the patient's own goals.
pmc-13455136:
Khaled Saed and others told of non-stop chyme reinfusion in 2026, with the Veraflo set in an open belly with duodenostomy. A forty-seven-year-old man had many belly ops past sulfuric acid intake, with dead tissue that forced full stomach removal and most jejunum removal, which left the belly open and the gut split.

The team used the 3M Veraflo wound vac set to draw gut juices non-stop from the duodenum and feed them with enteral feed through a Y-join into the near ileum. Special chyme sets exist, but this use dodged the split gut to feed a gravely ill man well. Surgeons gain a novel work-around for feeding when the gut is split.
pmc-13455236:
Huicheng Han and Changwook Lee built a flow model for MOBA games in 2026, to test how game tricks drive player stay-through via skill feel and flow. MOBA games need steady player counts for fair matches and lively groups, yet player churn stays a hard woe. How picked game tricks turn into long stay-through via mind routes was not fully known.

With stimulus-organism-response theory plus self-determination and flow theories, the team built a chain model. Clear goals, instant feedback, and prize systems lift stay-through intent via skill feel and flow feel. Cross-section survey data from five hundred eighty-four active MOBA players were tested by factor checks and structural equation models. Bias-corrected bootstrap tests checked chain effects. Hierarchical regression checked task-complexity moderation. Game makers gain a checked path from tricks to stay-through.
pmc-13456936:
Yao and Zhang built in 2026 a machine learning tool that flags type 2 diabetes patients at high risk of nerve damage in the feet and legs. The injury, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, causes pain and numbness. Catching risk early matters because nerve damage is hard to reverse. The team tested five learning methods on hospital records and turned the winner into a bedside chart.

Records from 180 inpatients fed the work, about half with nerve damage. Six factors stood out as predictors, led by years lived with diabetes, a long-term blood sugar measure, and protein in urine. The winning method, XGBoost, sorted held-out patients with high accuracy, beating regression and other models. An explanation tool showed which factors drove each score. The authors caution that other hospitals must test the tool before wider use.
pmc-13457036:
Xinyu Liu, Jingjing Liu, and Chang Xu review, in a 2026 article, how to step down blood-thinning therapy safely after a heart attack treated with a stent. Two antiplatelet drugs are standard after the procedure, yet staying on both raises bleeding, above all in East Asian and high-risk patients. The authors searched three databases for trials from 2018 to April 2026.

The strongest path is stopping early. Landmark trials support one to three months of dual therapy, then a single strong agent alone, cutting bleeding without more heart events in chosen patients. One month proved safe even for high bleeding risk in a dedicated trial. Two shortcuts failed: dropping aspirin within four days missed its safety bar, and early clopidogrel alone raised ischemic risk. The review favors ticagrelor alone after at least a month, with switching and gene-guided plans still on probation.
pmc-13457336:
Martin Fried and colleagues compare two ways of joining small bowel loops in jejuno-ileal bipartition, a metabolic operation for mild obesity with type 2 diabetes. The standard route uses staples, cutting openings in the bowel, while the magnetic route squeezes two swallowed magnets together across the bowel walls until a connection forms. Their 2026 non-randomized study matched adults with body mass index between 30 and 40 by age and sex, following them for one year.

Neither group saw a trocar-site infection or a severe device-related event. Adjusted one-year figures showed the magnetic group slightly heavier, 93.3 kilograms against 91.3, yet with strikingly better blood sugar: HbA1c 41.5 against 56.2 millimoles per mole, fasting glucose 5.4 against 8.6 in the stapled group. Non-inferiority was met for body mass index, HbA1c, and fasting glucose, though not for weight itself. The authors call the magnetic technique safe, anatomy-sparing, and potentially more acceptable for patients.
pmc-13457436:
Trygve Syversveen and colleagues test whether a mid-procedure CT check improves ultrasound-guided liver tumour burning in a 2026 study. Thermal ablation of small colorectal liver metastases needs a clean margin, yet ultrasound alone can miss the edge, and local regrowth rates vary widely. The team reviewed 152 ultrasound-guided procedures in 137 patients from 2018 to 2021, comparing 62 procedures with CT control that allowed immediate re-burning against 90 without it.

Local progression after procedures fell from 22.2 percent without CT to 8.0 percent with CT, and per lesion from 16.6 to 4.5 percent. For tiny tumours of 10 mm or less that ultrasound showed clearly, both approaches did equally well, with regrowth at 2 percent versus 0 percent. Complications stayed minor and similar. Centres with CT available gain a case for routine checks, while ultrasound alone may still suit small, well-seen lesions.
pmc-13457636:
Irene Suilan Zeng and colleagues show how to run sophisticated well-being research without interviewing a single teenager. New Zealand's Integrated Data Infrastructure links administrative records with survey data under strict privacy controls, offering a cheaper route around traditional fieldwork's low response rates. Their 2026 methods study links the 2018 General Social Survey with Ministry of Education records for school-enrolled youth aged 15 and over.

The team asks whether path analysis and Bayesian networks can handle the linked data and the survey's complex sampling design, using calibrated replicate weights and bootstrap resampling. In the weighted path model, life satisfaction carried the strongest link to mental well-being on the WHO-5 index, at 0.36, followed by perceived health at 0.34, ease with cultural identity, and trust in the education system. Feeling life is worthwhile connected only through life satisfaction. The authors conclude the paired methods make rigorous, representative inference from integrated population data.
pmc-13457836:
Yajie Zhou and colleagues built a prognostic score for clear cell kidney cancer from genes related to bone morphogenetic proteins, growth signals that guide cell identity. Their 2026 study combined tumor gene data with patient records to find which of these messages best predicted survival. The search produced a nine-gene signature, including L1CAM, CLIC5, PLG, and CA8, that split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with clearly different outcomes.

Patients in the high-risk group survived significantly less time, and a combined chart adding the score to standard clinical factors predicted outcomes with an accuracy measure of 0.747 on the usual curve scale. High-risk tumors also carried more mutations overall and showed immune patterns dominated by antibody-producing cells. Drug-sensitivity profiling suggested the two groups respond differently to specific compounds.
pmc-13457936:
Maung and colleagues validated the European SCORE2 risk calculator in 2026 in two contrasting cohorts, one in Mexico and one in Portugal, to test whether a tool built on European data travels. SCORE2 estimates ten-year risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular disease from age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol. The Mexican cohort held over ninety-five thousand adults and the Portuguese about twelve hundred, each followed for roughly a decade.

The tool separated risk levels sensibly in both places, with event rates near one percent in low-risk groups and up to nine percent in high-risk ones. Accuracy was modest to acceptable in Mexico, where calibration was good with slight overestimation at the top, but weaker in Portugal, where overestimation at high risk was larger. Nearly all flagged patients were true negatives in reverse: the negative predictive value topped 98 percent. The authors advise recalibration before local use.
pmc-13458036:
Du and a large team identify a driver of immunotherapy resistance in lung cancer in this 2026 study. Anti-PD-1 drugs release the brakes on immune cells, but many non-small cell lung cancers do not respond. The team compared tumors with several large-scale profiling methods. The surface protein CD155 was abnormally high in patients who responded poorly. High levels also tracked with worse prognosis.

CD155 switched on a signaling chain that raised sugar-burning proteins, pushing tumor cells toward glycolysis, a fast but inefficient way to make energy, and fueling their growth and spread. Removing CD155 with gene editing suppressed these traits. In mice, a virus-delivered silencer against CD155 shrank tumors, and combining it with the anti-PD-1 drug pembrolizumab worked better than either alone while drawing more immune cells into tumors.
pmc-13458336:
Julia Papail and colleagues show staph sacs trigger bone cell immunity without needing to enter the cell in a 2026 study. Staph harm partly travels in shed sacs, yet how those sacs act on bone cells was unclear. Sacs from the resistant N315 strain, purified and profiled, carried proteins, fat proteins, DNA, RNA, lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan, and were tested on MG-63 bone-like cells.

Sacs engaged TLR2 and switched on Toll-like receptor, NF-kB, JAK-STAT and inflammasome genes, confirmed by protein changes, interleukin-8 release and caspase-1 switch-on. Although sacs entered cells by dynamin-driven cell entry to late cell sacs, blocking uptake left gene responses intact. Bone infection researchers gain evidence that surface sensing, not cargo delivery, drives this immune response, with clues for blocking sac spotting.
pmc-13458436:
Sebastiaan Dolman and seven co-authors published a 2026 study tracking how cheese enzymes cut the main milk protein during ripening. The cut of alpha-S1 casein into its I-form shapes early texture, and rennet enzymes, called chymosins, differ in how fast they make it. Using intact-protein liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry, the team followed the cut through mozzarella ripening, comparing cow and camel chymosins.

Cow chymosins cut much faster than camel ones at every stage sampled. The method also picked out and counted phosphorylation variants of the proteins. The authors say the approach gives cheese makers a fine-grained view of enzyme behavior. That matters because enzyme choice writes itself into texture and quality long before the cheese is eaten.
pmc-13458636:
Navid Roessler and colleagues ask whether two earlier milestones can stand in for survival after salvage prostatectomy, the last-chance surgery for prostate cancer returning after radiation. Trials would finish far sooner if biochemical recurrence-free survival or metastasis-free survival could replace overall survival. Their 2026 analysis gathers 879 hormone-sensitive patients treated at 13 centers and tests surrogacy at two levels, the single patient and the center.

At the patient level, metastasis-free survival tracked overall survival strongly, with a Kendall's tau of 0.85, while the biochemical measure reached only 0.63, below the strong-link bar. At center level the picture fell apart: three-year values of either endpoint explained just 15 to 21 percent of the gaps in five-year survival, nowhere near enough. The authors conclude biochemical recurrence should never serve as a surrogate here, metastasis-free survival needs proving first, and quality-of-life outcomes deserve equal weight in salvage trials.
pmc-13459236:
Yulin Cui and co-authors built two vaccines against Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite that infects roughly a third of humanity, and compared them head to head in mice. Both vaccines used a stitched together antigen combining pieces of three parasite proteins known to provoke protection. One version delivered the blueprint as messenger RNA inside fatty particles, the modern mRNA vaccine format; the other delivered the ready made protein. In their 2026 study, mice received two doses and then faced challenge infections with two parasite strains.

Both vaccines triggered strong antibody and cell based immune responses with a protective Th1 bias. The mRNA version produced higher levels of those proteins and more of several key immune messenger molecules than the protein version. Both prolonged survival after challenge with the virulent strain. Against the moderate ME49 strain, the mRNA vaccine protected every mouse, a 100 percent protection rate that beat the protein vaccine.
pmc-13459436:
Jemima Collins and co-authors examined how pain relates to neuropsychiatric symptoms, such as agitation and apathy, in people living with dementia at home. Their 2026 study recruited thirty five patient and caregiver pairs, with patients averaging eighty years old. People with dementia rated their own pain on several scales. Partners completed a standard inventory of behavioral symptoms, letting the team check whether the pain scales agreed and whether troublesome pain tracked with worse behavior scores.

Two thirds of the patients, 66 percent, reported troublesome pain on the rating scale used. The pain measures agreed well, with a kappa statistic of 0.70 between the two main scales. Overall behavior symptom scores, however, were not significantly associated with troublesome pain. Only disinhibition stood out: it appeared in 44 percent of those with severe pain versus none without, and in 38 percent with multisite pain versus none with single site pain.
pmc-13459536:
Panja and colleagues build the first full map of a chemical tag called AMPylation in yeast mitochondria, the cell parts that make most energy. AMPylation attaches a small molecule, AMP, to proteins and can switch their behavior. Yeast has one known tagging enzyme in mitochondria, Fmp40. Their 2026 study uses mass spectrometry, a tool that weighs molecules, to compare normal yeast with yeast missing that enzyme.

Normal mitochondria carried the tag on 124 proteins, while mitochondria lacking Fmp40 still carried it on 41 proteins, implying at least one more tagging enzyme exists in yeast. Seven parts of ATP synthase, the motor that makes the energy molecule ATP, bore the tag. Changing one tagged site on the delta subunit altered the motor's activity and its coupling to oxygen use. This held under both sugar burning and breathing conditions. The authors link the control to keeping membrane voltage steady.
pmc-13459836:
Michael Oraebosi, Connor Baucom, and Ruifeng Cao review in 2026 how the body's daily clock governs glucose control, and what that means for type 2 diabetes. Blood sugar handling rises and falls across each 24-hour cycle, steered by a hierarchy of internal clocks. The review walks through clock roles in the pancreas, skeletal muscle, liver, and fat tissue, the organs that together balance glucose.

Evidence linking clock disruption to obesity and diabetes is then weighed, including the metabolic harm of mistimed living. The closing section considers chronotherapy, timing drugs, food, or light to match body rhythms. With diabetes prevalence climbing worldwide, the authors argue that when treatment happens may matter nearly as much as which treatment is chosen.
pmc-13459936:
Valentina Shamoun, Feras Shamoun, Kevin Ghajar, Laxmi Dongur, and Petros Konofaos review in 2026 the surgical options for intercostal neuralgia, a stubborn nerve pain running along the ribs. This pain often follows chest surgery or nerve injury and resists ordinary care. Searching three databases through March 2026, the authors gathered studies on operations and outcomes, viewing the field through plastic and peripheral nerve surgery.

Cutting out the damaged nerve segment remains the best-studied operation, with success above 80 percent in several series. Freeing a compressed nerve helps selected patients, while scope-based removal and radiofrequency ablation ease pain with smaller procedures. Newer reconstructive methods give the cut nerve somewhere to go, aiming to prevent painful neuroma, though evidence rests on small groups so far.
pmc-13460536:
Mikko Hallman reviews how inflammation drives the dangerous early deliveries and lung problems of extremely premature babies, and which treatments can calm it without causing new harm. Babies born before twenty eight weeks now survive from twenty two to twenty four weeks, but chronic lung, body, and brain problems have barely decreased. In his 2026 review, Hallman traces how infection and inflammation trigger both premature labor and the forced maturation of immature lungs. He then weighs the anti inflammatory tools on hand before and after birth.

Standard drugs that delay labor are effective for stopping contractions but toxic to very premature newborns, he notes. Animal studies point to gentler options: blocking inflammatory receptors or replacing missing natural defenses prevented inflammation driven early delivery in the experiments reviewed. Antenatal steroids mature the fetus yet excess doses impair growth and brain development, so dosing needs refinement. Routine care likewise needs gentler calibration.
pmc-13461436:
Kaori Kondo and a large Japanese team report in 2026 a leukemia that changed its identity mid-treatment. It switched from B-precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia to acute myeloid leukemia after the targeted drug inotuzumab ozogamicin. Such lineage switches are rare and usually ominous. To learn how the switch happened, the team sequenced bone marrow samples taken at several points across the illness, comparing mutation patterns between the lymphoid and myeloid phases.

The two phases shared ancestral mutations yet carried distinct private ones, and the myeloid phase gained fresh TP53 and SMC1A mutations while dropping some earlier ones. That pattern favors selective expansion of a minor pre-existing subclone with myeloid potential, squeezed forward by immune pressure from the drug, rather than one cell simply changing costume. The authors urge genomic monitoring during targeted therapy.
pmc-13461536:
Natalija Kecman and colleagues report a single-center study from 2026 on risk scoring in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow. They ask whether a disease-based staging system and a patient fitness score work better together than either one alone. The disease score is the second revision of the International Staging System, known as R2-ISS. The fitness score comes from the International Myeloma Working Group frailty scale.

Records covered 371 people diagnosed between 2018 and 2025, grouped at diagnosis by stage and by frailty. Treatment response was seen in 275 of 340 people who could be assessed. Higher stage went with lower response rates and shorter survival, while fit patients lived longer without the disease getting worse. Combining both scores separated survival groups more clearly, and frailty was the strongest single predictor in the adjusted model.
pmc-13461636:
Liliana Bevilacqua and colleagues report two Italian patients whose severe myasthenia gravis crises eased rapidly on zilucoplan, a self-injected complement blocker. Myasthenia gravis weakens muscles, and a crisis means breathing failure or fast worsening toward it.

One patient was in full crisis on non-invasive ventilation; the other was sliding toward crisis with worsening throat weakness. Both had failed steroids and immune globulin treatment, and one had also failed several biologic drugs. On daily under-skin zilucoplan at 32.4 milligrams, both improved fast and strongly, then held lasting remission with no side effects. Bevilacqua suggests starting complement blockade early could stop a slide into full crisis, pending larger prospective studies.
pmc-13461836:
George Rakovich sets out, in a 2026 technique paper, a back-side approach for removing single right lung segments through camera ports. Removing one segment rather than a lobe is harder surgery, because small airways and vessels branch in complex ways. Most surgeons approach from the front, digging through lobe grooves to reach those vessels. For several segments, the root structures sit at the back, making the front route awkward.

The paper gives anatomy-based reasoning and a step-by-step method for the segments whose roots lie behind: S1, S2, S6, and S10. Coming from the back gives direct access to those roots. Work from behind disturbs fewer tissue planes and avoids digging in the grooves. The author argues the route may cut air leaks, shorten hospital stay, and leave cleaner planes if later surgery is needed. The method fits standard camera surgery and robotic approaches.
pmc-13461936:
Haoran Wang and colleagues report, in a 2026 study, that the amino acid cysteine may hold back mouth cancer known as oral squamous cell carcinoma. Tumor cells often rewire amino acid use to grow and spread. The link between blood amino acid levels and this cancer risk was unclear. The team used a genetics-based method mimicking a natural experiment, then confirmed the signal in cells and mice.

Higher cysteine levels went with lower cancer risk in the genetic analysis. In the lab, cysteine slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion. Feeding cysteine to mice carrying tumors shrank tumor growth. Gene scans showed the effect ran through a gene, GLDC, whose activity cysteine appears to regulate. The authors conclude raising cysteine intake might improve outlook and could help prevent this cancer. They frame it as a new treatment avenue needing clinical testing before any advice to patients.
pmc-13462436:
Tianying Li and colleagues present, in a 2026 case report, a 55-year-old kidney transplant patient whose bladder cancer had spread. His cancer carried extra HER2 gene copies, a growth driver. He received a donor kidney in 2019 for end-stage kidney failure and stayed on immune-suppressing drugs. Two antibody-drug conjugates, delivering cell-killing payloads to HER2-tagged cells, were used in turn as resistance grew.

The first conjugate shrank his lung spread, yet caused nerve damage in his limbs. Standard chemotherapy and an immune drug helped only briefly before the cancer advanced again. The second conjugate, carrying a different payload, produced a striking response: liver spread shrank, brain lesions partly cleared, and lung inflammation was suspected. Through it all, the transplanted kidney kept working. The authors suggest switching payloads can outflank resistance even in transplant patients, while urging longer follow-up.
pmc-13463036:
Chaloemphol Kaewthep and colleagues designed a solar-powered wireless charging system in 2026 for driverless electric cars in remote places. Off-grid sites lack reliable mains power, which stalls electric fleets where roads are long and grids are thin. The system harvests sunlight and beams power without cables, following the SAE J 2954 wireless charging standard.

A 3.3-kilowatt prototype was built and tested in simulation and in hardware, reaching high charging efficiency while running on sunlight alone. The work targets islanded sites such as remote depots, where plugged charging is awkward and diesel is costly. Wider use could cut transport emissions, though cost and weather limits still need real-world trials at scale.
pmc-13463536:
Zhao and co-authors turned in 2026 to lactylation, a recently discovered chemical tag that lactate leaves on proteins. They asked whether it could help predict outcomes in bladder cancer. The team measured the tag in tumor tissue and cell lines. They grouped cancers by related genes in a large American atlas cohort. Machine-learning methods then shrank the signal down to a compact risk score.

The lactylation tag proved far more abundant in bladder tumors than in normal tissue. The final score rested on just three genes: AHNAK, ALDH1A1, and CALR. It separated patients into risk groups with different survival outlooks. The groups also differed in immune cell makeup. They differed in likely response to immunotherapy and chemotherapy drugs as well. The score kept its predictive value in outside datasets and in single-cell data. Lab tests on the core genes supported their role in the disease.
pmc-13463736:
Zoha Majeed and colleagues asked in 2026 whether cancer itself raises stroke risk in people with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that can throw clots. Standard stroke scores guide blood-thinner use, but they were built without cancer in mind. Using a large research network, the team matched 234,428 patients with both conditions against the same number with fibrillation alone, tracking outcomes to five years.

Stroke odds ran about twice as high with cancer at three months, at an odds ratio of 2.092, and stayed higher at six months, one year, and five years. Death and major bleeding also ran higher with cancer throughout. The pattern backs adding cancer to stroke scores for this group, though trials must test whether score changes lead to safer thinner choices.
pmc-13464436:
Soomin Lee and four co-authors compare four cooking methods for fillets of sevenband grouper, a prized farmed fish. Boiling, steaming, oven cooking, and microwave cooking each change weight, texture, color, and flavor in their own way. Lab tools read scent and taste profiles alongside flesh structure under the microscope.

Oven cooking drained the most moisture, while boiling drained the least and gave the softest bite. Steaming kept the firmest texture of all four methods. Scent tools split moist-heat fish from oven fish cleanly, and taste tools found extra sourness after oven and microwave runs. Wide gaps between flesh fibers in oven fish matched its heavy moisture loss, which guides cooks and processors alike.
pmc-13464736:
Xu and colleagues in China built in 2026 a smart screen for germ killing chains that might beat drug proof staph. Such chains, short protein strands, can punch germ skins, but some also burst red blood cells. The team fed a learner near four thousand known chains. Each was coded by plain traits: charge, grease load, and build. A strict test hid whole kin groups at train time.

The strict test cut the scores, as the team warned. Germ kill calls still held fair skill, and blood burst calls stayed strong. Charge and a water shy face drove kill power, while plain grease drove blood harm. The screen ranked twenty chains, all close kin of known strong ones, as lab leads.
pmc-13465236:
Wei and co-authors built in 2026 the Archaeal Viral Genome Database, a census of viruses that infect archaea. Archaea are the ancient single-celled organisms of hot springs, salt lakes, and other extremes. Their viruses are far less studied than those of bacteria. The team sifted more than 64 million candidate viral genomes from public data across eight habitat types. They verified 3,708 archaeal viral genomes, from tiny strands to giants of 188 thousand letters.

About 93 percent belonged to the tailed virus class that dominates bacterial viruses too. The genomes carried about 129,000 genes in total. They included metabolic helpers and anti-CRISPR weapons, raw material for ecology and biotechnology.
pmc-13466036:

It also avoids tilting the patient steeply head-down. Both traits are advantages for fragile bodies.

Those reports describe fewer early complications and shorter hospital stays, with faster recovery on the single-port approach, with the largest gains in the frailest patients. All three studies were retrospective, however, and most changed the access route along with the robot, so credit cannot be assigned cleanly. The authors frame the benefit as an early signal needing confirmation.
pmc-13466236:
Katarzyna Adamczewska and co-authors survey neck and back trouble among young female show jumping riders, in a 2026 cross-sectional study of 353 athletes aged twelve to twenty-five. Riding loads the spine again and again, and the group wanted to know whether skill level changes the burden. An anonymous online survey went out during major competitions in Poland.

Riders split by age band and by amateur or advanced status, answering standard disability questionnaires for the lower back and neck. Advanced younger riders reported somewhat worse back scores than amateurs, though the gap just missed statistical significance. Older riders showed no clear gap, and neck scores did not differ meaningfully between groups either.
pmc-13467436:

In calcium-free fluid, where normal synaptic transmission had stopped, burst stimulation still produced depression in the population response, with three separable components the authors tease apart. Recordings from single cells showed the bursts also changed how CA1 pyramidal neurons fire, slowing their electrical spikes. A neighboring cell type, stratum oriens interneurons, showed no such change, so the effect was specific to the pyramidal cells.
pmc-13467536:

Cai found three methods converged on the same axis: the lysosome system ranked first among pathways where genes and proteins disagreed. Most protein ageing signals sat in the module that sets lysosomal breaking-down capacity, while the sister proteasome system stayed untouched. Extra tests backed a protein-side origin. pmc-13467736:

The authors propose the material as a candidate for gout treatment research.
pmc-13467836:

The team asked how self-efficacy relates to quality of life. Self-efficacy is a person's confidence in managing their illness. They also asked whether daily self-management behaviour carries part of that effect.

The study covered 189 patients at one community health centre. Confidence, self-management, and quality of life all correlated positively. Each pair moved together. Modelling showed self-management partly carried the link. It accounted for roughly thirty-nine percent of the physical health effect. It accounted for forty-one percent of the mental health effect. This supports nursing approaches that build patients' confidence first.
pmc-13467936:

Mice received the yam compounds for seven days before the injury was induced, at a dose of 400 milligrams per kilogram. The team then checked heart function, tissue damage, and a wide panel of body systems.

Pretreatment clearly softened the cardiac dysfunction on ultrasound and tissue examination. The study also tracked blood markers of heart injury, oxidative stress measures, inflammatory signals, the fine structure and energy output of mitochondria, and the makeup of gut microbes. The multi-angle design tests the idea that the yam compounds protect through the gut-heart axis and through mitochondrial rescue at the same time. That pairing is worth knowing for a widely eaten medicinal food.
pmc-13468636:
Ana M. Džamić and co-authors compare in 2026 four Serbian species of bugle, genus Ajuga, collected from different localities, profiling their chemistry and effects on living cells. Ajuga reptans carried the highest total phenolics, at 120.52 milligrams per gram dry weight, and led in four antioxidant tests and in strength against microbes. Ajuga laxmannii held the most flavonoids and the best antifungal activity, while Ajuga genevensis blocked tyrosinase, a skin-darkening enzyme, most strongly. pmc-13469436:

Because the maturation step, from the germinal vesicle stage to metaphase II, runs with the egg's genes switched off, it depends on reshaping RNA messages. The team profiled eggs at both stages with sequencing and network analysis, then checked findings with PCR.

Eggs with and without the syndrome looked identical before maturation, differing in 35 genes, but diverged during it, with 292 differences. Two failures appeared: energy-production messages that should have been cleared lingered, while identity genes the egg must keep were lost too fast. The authors frame PCOS egg failure as a maturation-triggered collapse of RNA housekeeping.
pmc-13470136:
Manne and colleagues in India reported in 2026 a late flaw of fake hips: metal grime that stains and kills tissue round the joint. The state, metallosis, grows when parts rub and shed metal bits. Their patient, a man of 45, had a hip swap ten years back. He came in with worse hip pain, a limp, and a short leg after a fall. Scans showed the metal ball had drifted up and in, a sign read as bone loss.

The true cause showed in surgery. Tissue round the joint was black with stain, and the ball had worn through its plastic cup and shell. Shed metal, not bone loss, had wrecked the joint. Tissue tests backed the call. A fresh swap set him right: he walked pain free on a firm joint. The authors urge teams to weigh metallosis when a fake hip fails.
pmc-13470336:
Mousa Khalafi compared workout modes in 2026 for lowering swelling markers in breast cancer patients. Signals drive cancer growth, and regular training cuts swelling in general, but mode-specific effects on fat signals were unmapped. Pairwise and network meta-reviews pooled 24 random trials with 1,192 patients through January 2025.

Workouts overall cut IL-6 and leptin clearly, with weak trends for TNF-alpha and C-reactive protein, and no effect on IL-10 or adiponectin. Hard burst training cut IL-6 most, while joint training cut TNF-alpha. Mode thus matters for swelling control, though larger trials must confirm which plan helps which patients.
pmc-13470636:
Donninger and co-authors investigate how losing two tumor suppressor proteins drives kidney cancer, in this 2026 study. The target is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common form of the disease. One protein, VHL, is lost in most of these tumors. The second, RASSF1A, is switched off even more often. The team found the two proteins bind into a single complex.

In matched kidney cancer cell systems and engineered mice, the researchers added both genes back. They also knocked them down in combination. Restoring both proteins suppressed three-dimensional cell growth. It made cells more sensitive to drugs that trigger cell death. Losing both sped growth up instead. In mouse xenografts, losing VHL alone started no tumors. But it accelerated growth of RASSF1A-deficient ones, with richer blood vessel formation. Dual loss in whole animals produced no tumors. Further genetic hits therefore appear necessary.
pmc-13470736:
Shashi Prakash Dwivedi and co-authors are the subject of a 2026 retraction notice issued by the journal editor. Their study examined an aluminum silicon magnesium composite reinforced with a high entropy alloy powder. The original article, published in April 2024, covered the internal structure, interfaces, mechanical strength, and wear behavior of that composite. The notice withdraws the paper from the record.

According to the editor, the paper showed a pattern of heavy and improper citation manipulation. Concerns also arose about who should answer for the work across a set of related publications, including a second article named in the notice. Those integrity problems, the editor states, undermine the reliability of the work as a whole. The retraction took effect on July 31, 2026, a little over two years after publication.
pmc-13471036:
Qi-Lu Yuan and colleagues tackle in 2026 a long standing puzzle in liquids that cool toward glass: why particle diffusion and flow fall out of step. In many such liquids, diffusion follows a fractional power of viscosity rather than the classic inverse rule, and the exponent varies by material. Blame usually falls on patchy dynamics, clusters of fast and slow particles that grow as the liquid cools.

Working across many simulated glass formers, the team computed the energy barriers that govern motion at high temperature, before patchiness sets in. Those activation free energies, they argue, already encode the decoupling seen later on cooling. If correct, the exponent stops being a fitting curiosity and becomes predictable from high temperature behavior. The study offers a route to forecasting how a new glass former will age.
pmc-13471436:
Najar and colleagues reviewed how surgeons decide when a child's blocked intestine, caused by masses of Ascaris roundworms, needs an operation. Their 2026 prospective study covered children aged 2 to 16 presenting with intestinal obstruction at a hospital in an endemic region between May 2022 and May 2025.

Of 190 children with obstruction, 120 cases, or 63.2% of the total, were caused by ascariasis, with boys outnumbering girls two to one. Conservative care with fluids and observation was tried first in 80 children, and 65 of them, 81.3% of those tried, recovered without surgery. Operations were still needed in 55 children, and postoperative complications affected 14.5% of the surgical group.
pmc-13471736:
Yu, Voss, and Medford present an improved method for calculating the energies of molecules and materials in this 2026 computational physics paper. The random phase approximation is an accurate but demanding quantum method, and its results depend on the starting orbitals used. Their version, optRPA26, generates those orbitals with a specially tuned hybrid functional and scales the resulting correlation energy by a constant.

Across benchmarks covering molecules, bulk solids, and surfaces, average errors stayed small. Reaction energies were off by about five hundredths of an electronvolt. Cohesive energies were off by about seven hundredths in their test sets. It also handled adsorption of small molecules on metals and oxides accurately, and correctly predicted which crystal phase was stable in metal oxides and magnetic metals. The approach runs inside standard implementations of the original method.
pmc-13472836:
Varoni and colleagues introduced in 2026 a journal collection on veterinary drug development, drug residues, and emerging contaminants. The editors stress how wide the fields now reach: food safety, drug resistance, environmental risk, and One Health, the linked health of animals, people, and ecosystems.

One study printed gabapentin chewable tablets for small animals in 3D. The lower-dose version stayed printable and accurate after two weeks in a fridge, while the higher-dose one formed crystals. Another report describes a Siamese cat that survived four times the intended dose of a chemotherapy drug. Lipid emulsion, plasma exchange, and supportive care saved it. The editors present the collection as a map of a field now central to safe food and better animal medicines.
pmc-13473336:
Lin and colleagues built in 2026 a combined risk index for heart patients who had a stent fitted. It joins a blood measure of inflammation and sugar control with a scan measure of leftover artery narrowing. Even with good care, many such patients still face heart attacks, strokes, or death. The team asked whether pairing the two signals predicts risk better than either alone.

The study followed 1,468 patients treated at one center, checking them for major bad events over a median of two years. About one in eight patients suffered death, a heart attack, a repeat procedure, or a stroke. Risk climbed steadily as the index rose, even after other factors were weighed. pmc-13473536:
