Both scores improved clearly at every check. Four in five patients had at least half their pain gone at one month, and three in four kept that gain at six months. By twelve months the success rate had fallen steeply. No serious side effects were seen.
pmc-13591336:
Iseult Browne, Monica Esteban Garcia, and Alicia Okines review treatment for metastatic triple negative breast cancer in this 2026 paper. This cancer lacks estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors, which removes many drug targets. It kills a disproportionate share of breast cancer patients. The last decade brought major new options, though.

Immune checkpoint drugs and antibody drug conjugates changed the standard of care. PARP inhibitors serve patients with certain inherited mutations. The review weighs each class, its biomarkers, and its resistance paths. Tumor biology and the surrounding microenvironment are covered as well. A framework for choosing and sequencing treatments by biomarker is proposed. The aim is practical guidance in a fast moving field.
pmc-13591636:
Yuansheng Shi and a large team of co-authors craft a battery cathode by gentle chemistry in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lithium-rich layered cathodes promise high energy, but how they are made decides how long they last. A sodium-based precursor can swap its sodium for lithium at room temperature.

The room-temperature product kept a clean layered structure and delivered high capacity. After four hundred cycles it held over eighty-eight percent of its charge. The same material baked at high temperature kept barely half. Heat drove manganese ions to wander, jamming lithium's paths and waking damaging oxygen activity. The authors say synthesis history is a design lever for metastable cathodes. Gentle routes may beat brute heat for sustainable batteries.
pmc-13591736:
Yu-Sha Zhang leads a 2026 case report warning that a heart attack's ECG pattern can point to the wrong artery. A 46 year old heavy smoker arrived with five hours of chest pain. His tracing showed the classic lift in the lower leads, which usually means the right or side artery is blocked. Heart enzyme levels at first sat in the normal range, deepening the puzzle.

Vessel imaging instead found the front artery fully blocked near its start. That artery wrapped around the heart's tip and fed the lower wall, which explains the false signal. After flow was restored, the lower lift faded and front changes appeared. Zhang and the team urge reading tracings as a moving story, not a single frame.
pmc-13591836:
Takasuke Asakawa, writing alone in 2026, asks whether uric acid in blood truly tracks metabolic risk in slim working women, or merely rides along with weight. Uric acid has been linked to insulin trouble and poor blood fats. His group held 630 women with body mass index under 25, drawn from routine work health checks. A ratio of triglycerides to HDL cholesterol stood in as a rough risk marker.

That ratio rose across higher uric acid bands at first glance. Once age, blood pressure, habits, and body size were factored in, the uric acid link faded away. Body size and weight gained since early adulthood carried the stronger ties. Asakawa calls uric acid a shadow of deeper metabolic state in this group.
pmc-13592536:
Bennett and colleagues argued that brain-wasting diseases should be understood as a breakdown of talk between the nervous and immune systems, in a 2026 essay. Studies now show immune cells stationed at the brain's borders and entering the tissue, acting as guards that shape nerve-cell strength and repair.

Bennett groups the field into lenses: outside-in signals, in which adaptive immune responses from the rest of the body engage the brain. Inside-out circuits are those in which the brain's cells direct communication. And gene-regulatory programs lock immune states in. Faulty immunity is cast as a cause alongside nerve-cell fragility, not a side effect. The authors point to the Alzheimer's antibodies as evidence that tuning this dialogue can change a disease. They call for treatments that restore immune balance or reset the epigenetic switches, chemical marks that hold cell states and guide behavior.
pmc-13592636:
Chunmeng Wang and four colleagues build a network that fuses several exposures of one scene into a single wide range image. Older fusion methods tend to lose fine detail, global structure, or true color. Their design runs three branches in parallel: one reads local features with attention, one reads global links with a transformer, and one restores natural color. Merging blocks blend the first two branches' weight maps before guided filtering lifts them to full size.

Against nine rival methods on three datasets, the network topped most detail and human perception scores and placed second on a structural similarity measure. Gains over a leading transformer method reached about twenty percent on one visual quality score. Wang and the team present the three branch split as the fix for detail and color losses.
pmc-13592736:
Chloe A. McGhee-Deakin and three colleagues rethink how brain size differences are measured in RASopathies, a family of genetic disorders hitting a growth signaling pathway. Youth with these conditions show odd total brain and deep brain volumes, but standard fixes assume each region scales in simple proportion. Their allometric approach instead models curved scaling norms. Scans covered 132 affected youth, mostly Noonan syndrome, plus 80 matched controls.

Deviations clustered by gene: thalamus in one condition, several striatal regions in the commonest Noonan gene group, and ventral striatum in another. Simple linear fixes tended to inflate regional gaps, while a few effects survived every method. Girls showed somewhat larger deviations in early checks. McGhee-Deakin and the team urge curved scaling as the default lens for such scans.
pmc-13593636:
Maria Cláudia Soares Cruz Coelho and a team of co-authors tested whether Pornunça hay can replace Tifton 85 hay as the roughage in feedlot lamb diets. Thirty-six young Santa Inês male lambs spent 71 days in confinement while the share of Pornunça in the roughage rose across four groups, from none to complete replacement.

Lambs on the Pornunça diets ate more dry matter and organic matter, though they digested protein and fiber less well. Final weight, daily gain, and feed conversion stayed the same across groups, while hot and cold carcass weights and yields rose as Pornunça increased. Meat color, tenderness, water holding, and basic composition did not change. On that basis the authors recommend swapping Tifton 85 hay fully for Pornunça hay for feedlot lambs.
pmc-13595136:
Yu and Qian ask whether job loss links to depression in different ways for women and men across countries. Their panel study covers 18 large economies from 2010 to 2023. The outcome was the national rate of years lived with disability from depression, split by sex. The exposure was the national jobless rate for ages 25 to 64, also split by sex. Data came from global burden and labor sources.

The team used mixed models that allow each country and year its own baseline. They adjusted for income per person, inequality, and health spending. The design lets them test if the job-depression link is stronger for one sex. Results bear on how downturns shape mental health policy.
pmc-13595336:
Emilie MacInnis and co-authors review what everyday contact with animals does to the human microbiome, in this 2026 scoping review. Pet keeping and similar non-work contact may seed or shift our microbial communities, with knock-on effects for body and mind. The team searched six databases and screened nearly three thousand papers against strict rules. Thirty studies compared people before and after animal contact, or against people without it.

Twenty-four of the thirty found a real change in microbiome makeup after animal interaction. Reporting quality was uneven: many papers skipped contact length, animal species, or lab details. That patchiness limits firm conclusions. The authors urge future studies to report both the animal contact and the microbiome methods in full detail. The field, they say, is promising but under-documented.
pmc-13596736:
Michael Shimelash and others reviewed dementia-friendly hospital care in two thousand twenty-six. People with dementia fill many hospital beds. Their results are often poorer than others. Friendly care is still applied in patches, though. The review gathered staff-reported barriers and helpers. A set of ideas about behavior sorted the findings.

Sixty-five studies entered the review. Reviewers coded hundreds of single factors. Barriers slightly beat the helpers found. Repeat bundles crossed several theory domains. Study quality was mostly high overall. Hospital leaders gain a clear map for doing better. Knowing what blocks staff matters most. The work can then target real blocks, not guesses.
pmc-13597836:
Christian Atkins and co-authors examined the brains of Cavalier King Charles Spaniels with a skull malformation that squeezes the brain, in a study published in 2026. In this breed the condition is nearly universal, and it often brings fluid-filled cavities in the spinal cord and swollen brain chambers. Those changes cause pain and nerve signs, yet the tissue-level effects were poorly described.

Nineteen donated dogs were split into those with and without the cavities and swelling. Affected dogs showed far more new blood vessels around the brain's chambers, thicker vessel walls, and stronger activation of support cells. The authors link the pattern to long-term pressure strain and low oxygen. The findings may point toward future markers or treatments for a breed-wide welfare problem.
pmc-13598136:
Hiroki Tanaka and co-authors used cryo-electron microscopy to watch how the HIV drug lenacapavir sabotages the virus's shell during the late stage of replication, when new viruses assemble and mature. The drug's early-stage actions were already charted; its late work was not, and the team imaged capsid lattices formed inside virus-like particles with the drug present.

Cores built under the drug leaked their reverse transcriptase enzyme while keeping integrase and the viral RNA, leaving the particle unable to copy itself properly. Viruses produced this way showed sharply reduced infectivity and poor integration. The authors say the distorted geometry explains the drug's second punch and points inhibitor designers toward the seams between hexamers.
pmc-13598536:
Yan-Dong Wang and three colleagues published a field study in two thousand twenty-six on spraying for tick control outdoors. Ticks spread serious diseases at gatherings and disaster resettlement sites. The team tested a microcapsule insecticide spray in open field plots.

Three sites each had a sprayed plot and an untreated plot, with tick counts taken by cloth flagging. The spray, a lambda-cyhalothrin formula, was applied once at a set strength. Kill rates stayed between eighty and one hundred percent on most checks over four weeks. Tick numbers held low for about three weeks despite animals roaming through. The authors offer the method for outbreak settings where crowds gather outdoors.
pmc-13598736:
Mohammad Momin Iqbal and four co-authors measure healthy lymph nodes near the pelvis in dogs from CT scans, in a 2026 study. Vets use these nodes to stage cancers, so knowing the normal size range matters. The team reviewed scans of seventy-one dogs and measured three node groups on each side. They recorded width ranges, margins, counts, and density, and checked how size tied to body traits.

The main node group showed up in nearly every dog, most often on both sides. The smaller groups appeared less often. The short width stayed under ten millimeters in all but one node, which fits the standard cut for a healthy node. Node size grew with body weight and with the width of the main artery. The authors back the short width as the yardstick for judging treatment response in dogs.
pmc-13600736:
Emmanuel Peña Gomez-Portugal and two colleagues describe folding a diaphragm through a chest scope to stop liver-driven fluid flooding a lung, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. Hepatic hydrothorax fills the chest with fluid from portal hypertension. Diuretics and salt restriction fail in a fifth to a quarter of cases.

Their patient was a sixty-four-year-old woman with cirrhosis. It came from primary biliary cholangitis, and she had severe breathlessness. Her effusion was transudative in kind. That fit the diagnosis of exclusion in her case. The team performed thoracoscopic diaphragmatic plication. They joined it with chemical pleurodesis for the fix. That tightens the diaphragm, so fluid cannot pile up as freely. The technique is put forth as an alternative for such cases. pmc-13601236:
Yan Wang and five co-authors dissect why a toad lily's leaves carry dark spots, cell layer by cell layer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Spots could come from more purple pigment, less green pigment, or both, and adjacent tissues on one leaf offer a clean comparison.

Gene activity split the three sampled tissues cleanly, with nearly fifteen hundred genes differing between spot and neighbor. A chlorophyll-breakdown gene candidate ran hot in spots. Pigment-building and transport genes rose there too. The authors conclude the spot is mostly a green-loss patch with a remixed purple recipe.
pmc-13601736:
Jing Han and nine co-authors read the full mitochondrial genome in children with leukemia to explain uneven harm from a key drug, in a 2026 journal article. The drug, methotrexate, can injure the brain, and Hispanic children face a higher risk. The power plant genome is passed from the mother and varies by ancestry.

The team read that genome in 94 children, 62 of them Hispanic. They found nearly thirteen hundred variants, about one in eight of them new. Two genes that help cells make energy linked to brain harm after strict checks. Mixed copies of the genome were more common in harmed children. A risk model with the gene data sorted cases better than clinic facts alone. The authors call for a check in a fresh group.
pmc-13603236:

pmc-13603836:

Finally, four hundred ranch cows were bred with one recipe or the other, and pregnancy at fifty days was scored. The design lets lab measures answer to real fertility. The design lets lab measures answer to real fertility on the ranch, not just microscope scores.
pmc-13604336:

pmc-13605036:

pmc-13607336:

pmc-13607836:

pmc-13610436:

pmc-13610636:

pmc-13612336:

pmc-13612836:

A change-point method marked where trends bent. The chart lets policy makers judge whether reforms moved safety in the right way.
pmc-13613136:
Olayemi Dudu and five co-workers set the best water and heat prep for quinoa flour and tested it in bread. Quinoa is rich in food worth but its flour acts in odd ways in bake work. Dry heat swayed the flour's traits most. Treated flour took in more water and oil and packed in a more dense way. Melt and thick scores fell, a sign of less stale drift. pmc-13613536:

The authors propose a dual influence, direct on the pacemaker and indirect through nearby fat.
pmc-13614936:

pmc-13617236:

One hundred seventy-six parents reported on one hundred eighty-seven children.

Sensory processing challenges were common and near-universal among children with autism in the group. The authors recommend routine checks for sensory issues and pain so treatment can target participation and quality of life, not just gait.
pmc-13618336:

Tuning the method's strength yields several possible solutions, and common practice keeps one as the true resonance and discards the rest as fake. He shows that several solutions can be acceptable approximations of the same resonance at once. That ambiguity, he shows, injects more uncertainty into energies than basis set limits or the electronic structure method itself. Proposed fixes, including larger basis sets, subtracting the potential's energy part, and adding a real perturbative potential, all fail to remove it. He concludes the method keeps its proven merits for anionic resonances, but the multiplicity stands as a critical unsolved problem.
pmc-13619036:

pmc-13619436:

Low back pain was the most common sign, and the lower spine was hit most often. Gene-based tests on tissue samples found the germ most reliably. A two-drug pairing was the most common treatment.
pmc-13619636:

They ran a pot experiment crossing three soil mixes with three watering regimes. One mix added mushroom residue with peat and sulfur. Stems were wounded and infected on purpose. The residue mix produced the lowest soil acidity reading and the richest nutrients. A gene marking the germ's attack machinery fell most in that mix, and gall severity dropped from a disease index of about sixty-five to about twenty-four. A nitrogen process in the soil rose too, but it did not explain the milder disease. The authors credit the acidity shift for weakening the germ.
pmc-13620136:

The viral protein gathers the double-stranded RNA at the cell's edge, hiding it from defenders, yet the interferon alarm still sounds, preserving the built-in immune stimulation. The authors propose building B2 into future self-amplifying vaccines and therapies.
pmc-13621336:
Wataru Yoshioka and eight colleagues compared two shapes of plastic stent for draining bile ducts blocked by cancer low in the duct. One difference stood out: no curled stent migrated, while seven straight stents slipped out of place. Overall side effect rates also looked similar. pmc-13621536:
Pernel Roberts and co-authors hunt the equipment failures that quietly wreck teaching sessions at a medical simulation centre, in a 2026 study. Leadership set the severity anchors by consequence. The work covers the first half of a standard improvement cycle, defining and measuring the problem so fixes can follow. Small numbers, the authors suggest, still teach big lessons.
pmc-13621936:
Claus Thomas and nine co-authors study, in twenty twenty-six, worms in the gut of a common African mouse and a drug used to treat them. The mouse, the multimammate mouse, is widespread in sub-Saharan Africa. It is eaten in some places, so worms in it raise food safety and health concerns. Little was known about its gut worms or how they respond to ivermectin, a common worm drug. The team caught ninety adult mice.

Stool tests found five types of gut worms. The most common was a tapeworm found in about four in ten mice. Mice were split into treated and untreated groups. Egg counts in stool were checked every two weeks for eight weeks to gauge drug effect.
pmc-13622336:
James H Acuff and co-authors ask how serious blood infection with Streptococcus mitis group bacteria really is. These bacteria normally live in the mouth and throat and were long dismissed as harmless, except when they infect heart valves. Better lab tools now identify them more often, which raises the question of when a positive blood culture signals true disease.

The team reviewed records for 253 adults treated at three hospitals in the Texas Medical Center between 2017 and 2025. The most common setting was low white blood cell counts, a state that weakens infection defences, followed by pneumonia and heart valve infection. Only about a quarter of cases were judged contamination, meaning stray bacteria from sampling rather than disease. Cases called real infection usually grew bacteria in several blood bottles, while contamination usually meant one bottle. The authors conclude that most such infections deserve prompt treatment.
pmc-13623136:
Shauna A Rasmussen leads a rat study of classic galactosemia, an inherited disorder where the body cannot process the sugar galactose because an enzyme called GALT is missing. Harmful sugar by-products build up before birth, yet babies do well at first, which puzzles doctors. The team used rats lacking GALT to test whether the mother's genes change the picture.

Breeding crosses produced affected pups carried either by affected mothers or by carrier mothers, who keep some enzyme activity. By-products in the fluid around pups stayed high in affected litters but rose in steps as the enzyme supply fell. They were lowest with a carrier mother, highest when mother and all siblings lacked the enzyme. Growth delay appeared only in that worst-supplied group. A carrier mother protected growth despite moderate by-product levels. The authors suggest human babies carried by carrier mothers may gain protection before birth.
pmc-13623536:
Elisa Zoe Battistelli leads the authors of a protocol for a pilot study testing whether intensive care survivors can report their quality of life by phone surveys over time. Quality of life after critical illness matters to patients, yet trials measure it clumsily, often once and by interview. The pilot sits inside a platform trial of intensive care treatments.

The plan enrols one hundred trial participants who will answer a standard survey, delivered by text message, every month from six to twelve months after entering the trial. The team will track how many join, how many keep answering, how fast answers come, and how much reminders matter. Survey results will be compared against a telephone assessment at six months, both for the group and person by person. Plotting the monthly scores as curves should reveal recovery shapes. Special analyses will check whether deaths among dropouts bend the picture.
pmc-13623636:
Qinghua Zhao leads a team that published a 2026 report of X-ray detectors made by rubbing a lead-free crystal film onto ordinary office paper. The crystal, a caesium bismuth bromide perovskite, avoids the toxic lead found in many high-performing detector materials. The challenge was a cheap, scalable way to lay it down on a flexible base.

The dry abrasion method needs no solvents or heat, and it works at room temperature on biodegradable paper. The finished detectors sensed X-rays strongly, and narrowing the gap between electrodes pushed sensitivity to among the highest values reported for thin-film devices. Imaging tests resolved fine detail, and the paper devices still worked steadily after more than a month in open air. The authors present the platform as a green route to cheap, bendable detectors for medical and security scanning.
pmc-13624036:
Quinn Johnson and colleagues run decompression experiments to learn how bubbles are born on crystals inside rhyolitic magma, the thick, silica-rich melt behind many explosive eruptions. Bubbles drive eruptions, and crystals give bubbles an easier birthplace than the melt alone. The team mixed hydrated melt with crystals of two minerals at two size ranges and dropped the pressure.

Bubbles appeared on both crystal types at pressure undershoots far smaller than bubbles in pure melt would need. Tiny crystals hosted about one bubble each, while bigger crystals hosted more, in line with their larger surface area. Raising the pressure drop also packed nucleation sites closer together, which the authors explain as a race between bubble birth and water diffusion in the melt. They built an updated equation that folds crystal surface area into bubble counts, plus a spreadsheet so other researchers can run their own eruption conditions.
pmc-13624236:
Carl P C Chen and Areerat Suputtitada published a 2026 ultrasound study testing whether rolling a patient onto their side widens the safety gap for a common nerve block near the collarbone. In the supraclavicular block, the needle targets nerve bundles that sit close to the membrane around the lung, and puncture there is a feared complication. The gap between that membrane, the pleura, and the nerve bundle is the margin measured.

Ninety adults, including pain patients, neck patients, and healthy volunteers, were scanned at the end of a breath out in three positions: half-reclined, tilted partway, and fully on the side. The safety gap grew at each step and more than doubled in the full side position in every group. Heavier patients showed wider gaps in the side position, age made no difference. The authors propose position as a free adjustment that could make targeting safer.
pmc-13624436:
Jianwu Long, Jinli Zheng, Shiyi Chen, Peng Ou, and Xianzhou Lu present a 2026 study of conversion therapy for liver cancer that cannot be removed at first. Conversion care aims to shrink a tumor until surgery becomes possible. The team compared a drug pair with a procedure that blocks the tumor's blood supply and delivers drugs through it.

They looked back at 153 patients treated at one hospital from 2023 to 2024. One group of 79 got the drug pair; 74 got the vessel procedure. The study compared response rates, tumor marker levels, tumor shape and blood flow, and side effects. The drug group showed a higher response rate, the authors report.
pmc-13625536:
Jun Ohnuki and Kei-ichi Okazaki present, in twenty twenty-six, a tweak to AlphaFold3, a leading AI tool that predicts protein shapes. Proteins change shape to do their work. The tool can miss shape changes that are triggered when a drug or partner binds. The authors treat its shape-making process like a random sampling walk. They add a push that keeps predicted shapes apart from each other. That push forces the tool to search a wider range of shapes.

Their method, called AF3-ReD, found many shapes at once for motor, kinase, and transporter proteins. The shapes matched real lab structures well, down to the pose of bound partners. It even found transporter shapes that postdate the tool's training data.
pmc-13626636:
Vaccines against human papillomavirus are built from empty virus shells that train the immune system, and modified shells may also ferry drugs or genes into cells. Morgan Williamson and co-authors present a new way to build such shells for the HPV16 type in this 2026 study, tagging the two shell proteins with halves of a glowing marker.

When the proteins join correctly, the marker lights up, so assembly can be watched live. Their shells clumped less and yielded more particles than standard builds. The built-in glow could also help sort good particles from bad ones, easing both vaccine production and future delivery research.
pmc-13627236:
Nobuaki Yoshikura leads a large Japanese team describing a rare autoimmune attack on balance. Antibodies against a brain receptor called mGluR1 can inflame the cerebellum, the coordination center, causing ataxia, and nearly all published cases came from Western countries. Their laboratory found twelve positive patients among 699 screened between 2018 and 2025, and the team set their charts beside forty overseas cases.

Three quarters of the Japanese patients had one-sided limb clumsiness, a pattern rarely noted abroad, though uneven record-keeping may explain part of the gap. Spinal fluid inflammation ran milder in Japan, and two patients fell ill within a month of COVID-19. Every patient received immune therapy, mostly steroids, yet only a third of those followed long-term regained independence, a sobering recovery rate for a treatable disease.
pmc-13627936: Melissa de Waal and a large consortium present the genome sequence of a small fruit-eating bat from Central and South America. This 2026 genome note reports an assembly from a single male Dermanura phaeotis. The genome spans about two point two billion bases. Most of the assembly is organised into thirty chromosome-like scaffolds. Both the X and Y sex chromosomes were assembled. The work forms part of the Bat1K effort to sequence all bat species' genomes for comparative research.
pmc-13628036:
Andhika and four colleagues interview dementia caregivers in Indonesia to design a support app in twenty twenty-six. Dementia cases in the country are rising as the population ages. Home caregivers carry much of the burden with little systemic support. No local app had been built with users involved in its design.

The team interviewed health workers, charity staff, and thirty-five caregivers. Caregivers lacked knowledge of dementia symptoms and care steps. They also faced stress, trouble monitoring their relatives, and barriers to health services. The team mapped those needs to app features. Proposed features include diaries, music playlists, community forums, and games for patients. Education videos and psychological checks support the caregivers themselves. Ease of use and information quality shaped acceptance.
pmc-13628136:
Jiang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how artificial intelligence is reshaping antibody drug development by judging developability, not just binding strength. A lab antibody that grips its target tightly can still fail as a medicine if it clumps, thickens, dissolves poorly, or provokes immune reactions. Testing all that in the lab is slow, so teams now train models to predict these traits early.

The review surveys the data sources behind such models and the main predictor types for traits from clumping to shelf stability. It then covers methods that balance rival goals at once, including Pareto and Bayesian optimization, active learning, and models that generate new candidates to order. Special sections treat two-armed antibodies and nanobodies. The authors argue these tools serve best as guides that rank experiments, not as stand-ins for testing.
pmc-13628736:
Su-Yuan He and three colleagues asked whether a combined blood index can flag which atrial fibrillation patients will relapse after catheter ablation. Their 2026 retrospective study followed 591 patients for one year after radiofrequency ablation, an operation that scars small areas of heart tissue to restore normal rhythm.

The index blends inflammation and metabolic markers from C-reactive protein, triglycerides, and glucose readings. Ninety-two patients suffered a late recurrence, and higher index values tracked that risk closely, staying predictive after statistical adjustment for other factors. Extra analyses suggested the index adds information beyond standard predictors. The authors propose it as an inexpensive aid for spotting patients who need closer follow-up after ablation.
pmc-13629336:
Chotprom and colleagues develop smart packaging that both preserves chicken meat and visibly reports its freshness, in 2026 food science research. Their film combines gelatin and alginate, natural gelling materials, with lemongrass essential oil as an antimicrobial. A second element uses anthocyanins, the pigments in butterfly pea flowers, as a color indicator. The film changes color as meat spoils, giving a real-time freshness signal without opening the pack or running laboratory tests.

The active film extended the refrigerated shelf life of broiler breast meat by 3 days in the storage trials reported. Its color shifts correlated strongly with two standard spoilage measures, total volatile basic nitrogen and rising pH, as the meat aged. Lemongrass oil gave the film strong antimicrobial activity against the microbes tested. Chotprom argues such proactive packaging could cut food loss across the poultry supply chain by flagging spoilage at a glance.
pmc-13629836:
Lokeshwar Bhenderu and co-authors mine two decades of device recalls in brain surgery in a 2026 study. Neurosurgery leans ever more on devices, and recalls of faulty ones have risen with that reliance. The team searched the United States regulator's open recall database for 2003 to 2022. Recalls were sorted by device type and cause, with expert checks.

In all, four hundred twelve recalls of neurosurgical devices appeared. Counts climbed until 2013, then fell through 2022. General neurosurgery devices led, followed by stereotaxic and functional ones. Most recalls were class II, the middle severity grade. The top causes were process errors, design flaws, and component or material faults. Labeling problems came next, and marketing issues were rarest. The authors say the patterns point to where safety work should focus.
pmc-13630936:
Rui Cheng and six colleagues systematically compare three surgical approaches for a bile duct cancer, in a review published in two thousand twenty-six. Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma grows where the liver's bile ducts meet. Radical resection is the main hope of cure, but it is demanding surgery.

The team searched six databases, including Chinese sources, for direct comparisons. Robotic, laparoscopic, and open operations were weighed in pairwise meta-analysis. Evidence directly comparing laparoscopic with robotic surgery proved scarce. The overall evidence network was sparse, so network meta-analysis served only as an exploratory extra. The review maps what is actually known about minimally invasive options for this cancer. It also flags how thin the comparative evidence remains.
pmc-13631036:
Chaiane Goulart Soares and seven colleagues review the pulp of Butia palms. The genus holds about two dozen subtropical species native to southern South America. Their aromatic fruits are eaten locally but barely studied. The review gathers proof on makeup, health effects, storage, and food uses.

Across species the pulp supplies fibre, minerals, and vitamin C. It also gives carotenoids and phenolic compounds, with mostly unsaturated fats. Values swing with species, ripeness, and growing conditions. Lab and animal studies suggest protective, calming, and blood sugar benefits. None are confirmed in people yet. The pulp has been trialled in drinks, dairy products, and frozen desserts. The authors flag how much remains unknown. It runs from spoilage behaviour to nutrient uptake.
pmc-13631236:
William J Flerlage and twelve colleagues characterise a previously unrecognised population of neurons inside the mouse lateral habenula, a small brain hub for stress and disappointment, published in 2026. These cells make corticotropin-releasing factor, the classic stress signal, and the team mapped them with high-resolution imaging, gene probes, and viral tracing.

Most of the neurons were of the excitatory type, with a front subpopulation also carrying inhibitory markers. Switching them on did not change reward seeking or anxiety behaviour, but it pushed threatened mice toward passive freezing, stretching escape times in males and shelter stays in females. The sexes also differed in cell numbers, excitability, and wiring. The authors frame the circuit as a sex-specific dial on defensive strategy.
pmc-13632436:
Hakeem Hamdan and co-authors model an oxygen supply pipeline and test two ways to control it, in a 2026 engineering paper. Pipelines that carry pure oxygen must hold steady flow and pressure, yet they face sudden changes at valves and key points. Poor control is both wasteful and risky.

The team first runs the system with standard feedback controllers, the kind long used in industry. They then add a predictive method that looks ahead and plans each move before acting. In simulations with abrupt shocks to the system, the predictive method held pressure steadier and coped better than the standard setup. The authors argue this should give operators more confidence when running real oxygen pipelines.
pmc-13633336:
Andrea Spinelli and four colleagues studied root canal sealer that squeezes past the tooth root tip. The material, a premixed bioceramic sealer called NeoSealer Flo, sets by absorbing moisture. Dentists worry about how extra material behaves outside the root. The team filled thirty-two extracted human teeth with enlarged tips and sorted them into four conditions. The setups varied by canal moisture and by sponge support around the tip, mimicking tissue.

Standard X-rays were taken right after filling and again at one and four weeks. The bright area inside the canal stayed nearly unchanged in every group. The bright patch beyond the tip behaved differently by condition. It grew most in dry canals with sponge support and barely moved in moist ones. The authors note that X-ray change alone cannot prove swelling, dissolving, or merging with tissue. Keeping sealer inside the root remains the goal.
pmc-13634436:
Angelina Collins, Thais Gift, Edward Kim, and Ian Robinson analyze the effect of vedolizumab on bowel urgency in ulcerative colitis, in a research paper from 2026. Urgency, the sudden need to reach a toilet, is among the most burdensome symptoms of the bowel disease. The drug is used for moderate to severe cases, but its effect on urgency had not been isolated.

Data pool more than twelve hundred patients from three phase three trials of the drug against placebo. Three questionnaire items form an urgency score, and full resolution means no symptoms on all three. Outcomes at one year compare score change and resolution rates. Groups split by past drug exposure and disease activity add detail.
pmc-13634536:
Huimei Wang and co-authors studied a fat-making enzyme that limits fat storage in chicken liver cells in a 2026 paper. The enzyme, PCYT2, is a key step in building a major membrane fat and shapes overall lipid metabolism. It changed sharply in chick livers around hatching in the team's earlier work, hinting at a developmental role.

Working in primary liver cells from chickens, they raised the enzyme's level and watched fat accumulation fall. The effect ran through the Notch signaling pathway, a cell communication system. Fatty liver is a costly problem in poultry farming, and the same pathways matter in human metabolic disease. The study names a lever for leaner birds and fresher insight into liver fat control.
pmc-13635036:
Näslund and colleagues ran a 2026 proof of concept study on a gentler way to track blood oxygen in the body. Mixed venous oxygen saturation shows whether oxygen delivery matches what tissues use, but measuring it needs a catheter in the lung artery. The team tested light based sensing on the breastbone of pigs instead.

In fifteen anaesthetised pigs, Näslund lowered oxygen with low oxygen gas mixes and removed blood in two stages. Light readings from the sternum were calibrated against catheter samples from the lung artery. The two measures moved together in each animal, with agreement on change direction reaching eighty-seven percent across the tests. Only severe blood loss broke the pattern, so the authors back more technical work on the approach.
pmc-13635136:
Daniel Boesch and co-authors explain how an enzyme seals DNA breaks inside the nucleosome in a 2026 study. DNA is wound around protein spools into nucleosomes, and breaks occur constantly from oxidation and repair work. Ligase IIIα performs the final sealing step for many single-strand breaks.

How it works on DNA wrapped in chromatin was unknown. The team combined biochemical assays, molecular simulations, and cryo-electron microscopy to watch the enzyme engage a nick in a nucleosome. Their picture reveals how the enzyme reaches and closes a break despite the tight packaging. The mechanism anchors understanding of the last step of a major repair pathway.
pmc-13636036:
Andy Bridger and seven colleagues describe a software pipeline that turns neutron measurements into maps of crystal orientation inside solid materials. Texture, the statistical alignment of tiny crystals, steers strength, stiffness, and conductivity in metals, ceramics, and rocks. Neutron beams can read texture deep inside whole engineering parts without cutting them open. The team's workflow lives inside the Mantid analysis framework and handles planning, calibration, and data processing in one place.

The pipeline converts time-of-flight diffraction data into corrected pole figures, the standard charts of crystal alignment. Its outputs plug directly into popular texture software for deeper analysis. A test on an aluminum alloy dataset already analyzed by an older tool gave matching figures and texture components. The new workflow adds flexible detector grouping and lets users study how shorter measurement times affect quality. The authors aim to streamline texture work across neutron facilities.
pmc-13638336:
Huihui Song, Roberta Piroddi, Philip McHale, and Benjamin Barr report a study from two thousand twenty-six on the effects of a two thousand seventeen cut to disability benefits in England. The reform lowered weekly payments for some recipients judged able to do some work. With health-related joblessness rising, the team asked what the cut did to poverty, mental health, and employment.

Using a national household panel from two thousand ten to two thousand nineteen, they compared people with long-term conditions against suitable controls. Among those who left employment, poverty risk rose by about five and a half points after the reform. New poor mental health rose by about nine points in that group. Employment moves themselves did not shift clearly. Scaled nationally, the toll is large.
pmc-13639036:
Emilija Aleksandrovic, Shaneann Fross, Samantha Golomb, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It shows how the first ovarian cancer cells to seed the belly cavity pave the way for the cells that arrive later, a first come, first served pattern of spread.

The team built a tool, MetTag, that barcodes single tumor cells and stamps each batch with its release time. Barcodes showed early clones dominating sites across the cavity, and removing pioneers shrank the growth of later arrivals. Pioneer cells ran a gene program centered on interferon-gamma, an immune signal. Knocking out its receptor in pioneers cut the metastatic burden sharply. The signal, working with local immune cells, shields floating tumor cells from a death that normally strikes detached cells. The authors name a brief window when blocking this pathway might stop spread.
pmc-13641536:
Hiroaki Miyauchi led a 2026 study asking which blood calcium measure best reflects true calcium physiology in patients, judged against the heart's QT interval. About half of blood calcium circulates as active ionized calcium, while the rest binds protein, and formulas that correct total calcium for albumin have been used for decades. Yet corrected calcium often disagrees with ionized calcium, raising doubt about whether correction helps or harms diagnosis. Prior work mostly compared measures against each other, not against a clinical outcome.

The team studied adults at Keio University Hospital who had simultaneous ionized calcium, total calcium, albumin, electrolytes, and electrocardiograms within two hours of blood sampling and before treatment. They excluded patients with pacemakers, atrial fibrillation, advanced heart block, wide QRS, cardiac arrest, or acute coronary syndrome. Because calcium shapes heart muscle contraction, QT length offers a meaningful test of which measure tracks physiology.
pmc-13642036:
Marie-Odile Baudement and thirty colleagues present a study of how gene control changed after the salmon family copied its whole genome. Salmon did this more lately than most backboned animals. So they give a clearer view of how copied genes and their switches drift apart.

The team built 771 data sets from embryos and adult tissues of two fish, Atlantic salmon and rainbow trout. Change followed rules set by tissue type and by stage of growth. The tightest control sat at one key embryo stage. Kept switch pairs and jumping DNA both shaped which gene copies stayed on. The open data also serve fish farming and wild stock care.
pmc-13642236:
Roman Delucenay-Clarke and fourteen colleagues present a 2026 research letter on noninvasive spinal stimulation for weak breathing in obesity hypoventilation syndrome. In this disorder, obesity combines with blunted central breathing drive, and no curative treatment exists.

The team had earlier shown that gentle direct current applied over the upper neck spine raised diaphragm excitability and breath size in healthy people. Here they test the same trans-spinal approach in mice modeling the syndrome's central breathing failure. The letter frames stimulation-induced plasticity as a possible route to restore ventilation without drugs or machines, pending what the animal results show.
pmc-13643436:
Ahmed A Hassan and two colleagues report a 2026 case from a child with Shone's complex, a set of left-heart defects. The case used a third heart valve placed inside two earlier ones. Severe mitral valve disease in small children is hard to treat. Few valve options fit, and children outgrow them.

The boy was six years old. He got his first Melody valve as a baby. A second valve went inside it at age two. The valve failed again four years later. Widening it with a balloon made the leak worse. So the team placed a third valve through the leg, guided by a wire rail through the chest. The pressure result was good.
pmc-13644936:
Yuming Sun led a 2026 modeling study of how better outbreak operations could help stop vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 in Nigeria. The novel oral vaccine, used in over two billion doses since 2021, reverts less often than its predecessor, yet outbreaks persist in some countries. The team adapted a transmission model for Nigeria from 2024 to 2028, testing whether prioritizing under-vaccinated people for the novel vaccine and adding vaccination rounds could break transmission.

Only the idealized strategy, prioritizing the lowest-immunity people with five rounds per response, achieved interruption. Prioritizing by prior outbreak-vaccine history shrank outbreaks while using fewer doses, but prioritizing by routine inactivated-vaccine history backfired, enlarging outbreaks and dose use. The authors conclude that reactive response alone may fall short in high-risk settings, since needed improvements could exceed program capacity. Polio planners get a case for pairing smarter targeting with routine immunization expansion.
pmc-13645936:
Rodriguez and co-authors dissect an iron enzyme in this 2026 biochemistry study. The enzyme helps make ergothioneine, a protective antioxidant that bacteria and fungi produce and humans must eat. The enzyme EgtB welds a sulfur bond between two building blocks using oxygen, and the team used spectroscopy and rapid kinetics to watch its active site reorganize as ingredients arrive.

Working with the enzyme from a heat-loving bacterium, they showed iron loading and then step-by-step substrate binding each reshape the metal's setting and stabilize the protein. Activity peaked at neutral pH 7.0 in their stopped-flow readings, and reaction speed scaled with oxygen levels, evidence of tightly coupled oxygen handling. Mass spectrometry confirmed the oxygen-dependent sulfoxide product. A practical warning emerged too: the common laboratory habit of leaving a purification tag attached plainly weakened the enzyme's activity and stability.
pmc-13648836:
Oleg V. Kim and five colleagues find when platelet parent cells first learn to squeeze blood clots. Platelets are the cell shards that seal wounds. Their parents, called megakaryocytes, grow in the marrow and shed them into the blood. The team raised these parents from human stem cells in steps.

Plain stem cells could not squeeze at all. Blood starter cells already pulled on clot strands when roused, though weakly. The pull came from the subset pledged to the platelet line, and wiping that subset out erased the pull. Grown parents pulled far harder and faster. One surface switch, flipped on by the pledge, drove the act. The team calls squeeze power an early badge of the line.
pmc-13649436:
Kun Wang and six colleagues gathered case data on 279 people with a rare hormone condition that blunts the making of a potent male hormone before birth. The cause lies in changes to one gene, and the outward signs vary a great deal. Reports came from 36 lands, most of them in Asia.

The team found 78 distinct gene changes, with one change the most common of all. Children who got the same faulty copy from both parents had more severe signs than those with two distinct faults. Some gene changes tied to higher or lower odds of specific signs, such as a cleft in the urine tube. The authors show that gene type alone does not set the outcome.
pmc-13651436:
Seeta Devi, Roshan Yadav, Joyce Robert Mathivanan, Sonopant Joshi, and Bhagyashree Jogdeo tested hybrid machine learning models for early lung cancer prediction in twenty twenty-six. Late diagnosis makes this cancer a leading cause of cancer death, so data-driven prediction is a live goal. Their data set held one thousand patient records with twenty-five candidate factors drawn from medical records.

After cleaning and trimming, eighteen factors stood out, spanning symptoms, lifestyle, and exposures. Age, passive smoking, obesity, smoking, and coughing blood all tracked the disease strongly. Many models, from decision trees to random forests, hit perfect scores on the test metrics, while deep learning and bagged models scored near ninety-seven percent. The authors say machine learning, above all support vector machines, holds strong promise for early prediction from structured records.
pmc-13651536:
Alicia M Kirk and ten colleagues unravel how a bacterial enzyme performs one of chemistry's rarer tricks: attaching a nitro group to an aromatic ring. The enzyme, a cytochrome P450 from the pathway that builds the antibiotic rufomycin, nitrates a tyrosine inside a five-piece peptide, and the details matter because the product feeds the fight against tuberculosis.

Test peptides, simulations, quantum-level modeling, and a fresh crystal structure of a sister enzyme converged on one actor: a histidine sitting inside the peptide substrate itself. Its presence is required for clean nitration. The protonation state of a key iron-oxygen intermediate appears to decide whether the reaction yields the wanted nitrated tyrosine or wasteful nitrate instead. Sequence differences between enzyme cousins and the peptide's own shape jointly tune the outcome. The authors say the mechanism explains the family's behavior and could guide engineered nitration chemistry.
pmc-13664836:
Ma and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on a citrus peel extract that may guard kidneys in mice. Fat-rich diets can pile fat in kidneys and harm them over time. Gut germ shifts are tied to that harm. The team fed mice a fat-rich diet with or without the peel extract. Treated mice gained less kidney fat and showed less swelling and scarring. A stress-response gene in the kidney rose with treatment. Fat making in the kidney also fell.

The extract reshaped gut germs, boosting helpful types. When germs from treated mice moved to new mice, the kidney gains moved too. That transfer points to gut germs as the path of benefit. The authors propose the extract as a preventive option worth more study.
pmc-13671036:
Michael Nikolovski and co-authors present a 2026 study that tests natural variants of a metal-carrying protein called ZIP8, which moves metals such as manganese and zinc into cells. Genome data now lists far more variants than labs can judge one by one. Most variants of this clinically important carrier had never been checked.

The team built a workflow that pairs a laser-based metal reader with scaled-up cell tests. They screened thirty-three natural variants sitting in the part of the protein that faces outside the cell, measuring how much metal each version let in. The screen found disease-linked variants and versions that get stuck on their way to the cell surface.
pmc-13671236:
Junhyeong Lee, Dokyoon Kim, and Seunggeun Lee set out a deep learn frame that lifts gene risk scores through bent-line and doubt-aware work on what each gene form does. Their 2026 study grows a known straight-line model with notes on gene work.

Score ways in use tend to take notes as linked in a straight line to gene acts. They pass by doubt and bent-line rules for gene work. The new group of models gauges each gene form's share of passed-down traits and its doubt as one. Both go into a Bayes score model. Through lots of smooth and ill traits in a state biobank, it made smooth trait guesses more good by near ten in each hundred past the straight base. Gains were most large where tie signs bunched. Spread ill traits did more good with the old way.
pmc-13672336:
Harvey and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-six on chemical tags on DNA in brains with Lewy body disease. Lewy bodies are protein clumps tied to Parkinson's disease and a form of dementia. The team pool data from over twelve hundred brain samples across cohorts. They scan several cortical regions for tag shifts tied to clump load. Twenty-four loci shift firmly with rising clump burden. Two loci sit in genes tied to immune and vessel roles.

Enrichment checks highlight nerve junction traits among the shifted loci. Tag profiles overlap across Lewy, Alzheimer's, and Huntington's diseases, yet top loci stay disease-specific. Genetic risk variants link to tag control near a key Lewy gene. The authors map shared and unique marks across brain diseases.
pmc-13672936:
Alvaro Oleart and Noah Anton Schmitt studied how a major newspaper framed two assault claims. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at opinion pieces in The New York Times. One claim was made by Christine Blasey Ford against Brett Kavanaugh in twenty eighteen. The other was made by Tara Reade against Joe Biden in twenty twenty. Both came in the wake of the MeToo movement.

The first case framed such violence as a broad social wrong and backed those who spoke out. Yet it lacked a lens on how race and class cross with sex. The second case framed the claim through Biden's poll hopes and used sexist frames to brush it off. Readers see how one paper can shift its frame by who stands accused.
pmc-13676836:
Aydin Genc and co-authors test whether hesperidin, a citrus compound, protects rat kidneys from the chemotherapy drug vincristine. The drug is widely used but can damage kidneys at higher doses. Twenty-eight female rats split into four groups: control, hesperidin alone, vincristine alone, and both drugs together. Treatments run for seven days. The team measures kidney function markers, oxidative stress, cell death and recycling genes, and tissue damage.

Vincristine raises urea and creatinine, boosts fat oxidation damage and DNA harm, and weakens antioxidant defenses. It also turns on cell death signals, increases recycling activity, and suppresses a key growth pathway, leaving severe tissue damage. Adding hesperidin softens all these effects. It restores antioxidant capacity, lowers inflammatory signals, curbs cell death, and adjusts the recycling genes. The authors trace protection to two named signaling routes.
pmc-13677036:
Leone and colleagues argue that health data systems in sub-Saharan Africa cannot see people displaced by climate change. Health records and movement records grew up as separate systems. Each is blind to the other's people. That blind spot, the authors say, blocks climate-ready health policy.

The team drew on three streams of proof: health outcomes of movers, system performance, and theory on counting people. Routine systems record only about one death in ten in the region. Facility-based records catch visits, not populations, and surveys sample by home address. Against that base, climate-linked movement ties to hunger and other harms. The authors press for systems that count movers as a real population. Without that, planners build for a public that is partly invisible.
pmc-13679236:
Aldakhil and five co-authors studied a leaky heart valve condition in twenty twenty-six that arises when the heart's upper right chamber stretches in people with a common rhythm disorder. The leak, in the tricuspid valve, was long blamed on the lower chamber, but this atrial form follows a different path.

The team reviewed one hundred fifty-two patients with the rhythm disorder who had heart scans between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-five. One hundred twenty had at least a moderate leak, and the rest served as a comparison group. The leak group showed bigger upper chambers and weaker squeezing of the right side. Over about six years, forty-five percent of the leak group died. One measure, how well the upper right chamber stretches as it fills, predicted death on its own. The authors say that measure could guide risk checks.
pmc-13683036:
Kimberly Rivera-Caraballo and eight co-authors armed a tumor-killing virus with a decoy to block a growth signal, in a study published in 2026. The virus treats hard brain tumors, but earlier patient samples showed it wakes a signal path that feeds stem traits and spread. Their decoy is a loose form of the key signal, which soaks it up and blocks the path in tumor cells.

The armed virus slowed its own growth in the dish yet still killed tumor cells well. Gene readings showed the path and vessel growth shut down. Fuel paths warped too, and oxidative waste rose. Immune cells grown with armed kills turned to an inflammatory form. In mice the armed virus shrank tumors and extended life past the plain virus.
pmc-1934936:
Winter, Vinegar, Nahal, and co-authors present a browser that turns large biology datasets into pictures researchers can explore. Microarrays and other high-throughput tools produce vast tables of gene activity. For scientists who are not computing specialists, such output can overwhelm rather than inform.

Their Electronic Fluorescent Pictograph browser shows data as visual displays that can be browsed and probed. Pictures help users spot patterns and form new hypotheses without deep coding skill. Tools that open big data to bench scientists widen who can take part in genome-era research.  Colour-coded displays let users compare tissues and conditions side by side.
pmc-2689936:
Howie, Donnelly, and Marchini present a flexible and accurate method for genotype imputation in large association studies. Imputation fills in unmeasured DNA variants by matching a person's measured variants to fully typed reference panels. Most studies then relied on the HapMap reference set.

Newer panels, typed densely on several platforms, were becoming available as the authors wrote. Their method was built to use such richer references well. Accurate filling-in lets studies compare results across different genotyping chips and boosts power to find variants linked to disease, without retesting every participant.
pmc-2835736:
Price, Dehal, and Arkin present FastTree 2, a tool for inferring family trees from very large sequence alignments. Their first FastTree could handle alignments with hundreds of thousands of sequences. Speed came with some loss of accuracy, which the new version aims to recover.

Improvements sharpen the tree search without sacrificing the ability to scale. Earlier versions relied heavily on simple neighbour swaps to refine trees. Better accuracy at the same scale matters for tracking fast-spreading microbes and for studies that compare thousands of species at once.  Microbial ecologists use it to track thousands of species in one alignment.
pmc-3276136:
Catchen, Amores, Hohenlohe, and co-authors present Stacks, software for building and genotyping genetic loci from short-read sequences. New sequencing gave chances to genotype individuals quickly and cheaply. Progress was hindered, though, by a lack of software to call tens of thousands of genotypes across hundreds of individuals automatically.

Stacks builds loci from scratch, without needing a reference genome, and scores each individual's variants. That opened population genetics for species never sequenced before. Ecologists and breeders use it to map traits, track parentage, and measure diversity in wild populations.  Fisheries and crop wild-relative studies both picked up the system quickly afterwards.
pmc-4330336:
Croucher, Page, Connor, and their colleagues presented Gubbins in 2015 for bacterial genome analysis. New sequencing tools made whole genome alignments common for evolution studies and outbreak work. Such data often contain stretches gained by horizontal transfer, where bacteria swap DNA directly.

Gubbins finds those recombinant stretches quickly and accounts for them when building family trees. Without that step, swapped DNA can distort the tree and hide the true pattern of spread. The tool handles large samples fast enough for routine outbreak use. Public health teams use it to trace how bacterial strains emerge and move between people.
pmc-5333436:
FitzGerald and Hurst reviewed implicit bias in healthcare professionals in 2017. Implicit biases are associations outside conscious awareness. They can tilt judgment against a person for traits that should not matter, such as race or gender.

The review weighs the studies on whether doctors and nurses show such bias toward patients. If doctors and nurses carry the same biases as the general public, care may differ by patient group without anyone intending it. The authors weigh study quality and what the findings mean for training and practice. Their synthesis informs efforts to make diagnosis and treatment more equal.
pmc-5993836:
Benjamin Saunders, Julius Sim, Tom Kingstone, and colleagues examined the idea of saturation in qualitative research in 2017. Saturation is widely taken to mean that new data would add nothing new. Funders and reviewers often demand it as a quality sign.

The authors show the term hides several different ideas that are often mixed up. They sort these into types and ask when each one fits a study design. Vague use lets weak sampling pass as rigorous. Clearer language would help researchers defend sample sizes honestly. The paper is now a common citation when methods sections mention saturation.
pmc-6249736:
Konstantinos Vasileiou, Julie Barnett, Susan Thorpe, and coauthors studied sample size in interview research in 2018. How many interviews are enough is a debated and practical question. Many tools promise to justify a number, but their logic often stays vague.

Reviewing past studies, the authors find that saturation is the most common defense, yet it is often claimed with little proof. Typical interview studies cluster in a modest range of sizes. The paper urges researchers to explain their reasoning in concrete terms. Reviewers and funders can use it to spot empty claims about sample adequacy.
pmc-6315036:
Maksim Kunitski, Nicolas Eicke, Pia Huber, and coauthors reported a quantum interference experiment in 2019. The double-slit experiment is the classic display of wave-particle duality. Interference appears when no record shows which path a particle took.

Working with the neon dimer under strong laser fields, the team watched photoelectrons interfere like waves from two slits. The molecule's two atoms act as the pair of slits. Careful measurement kept the which-way record hidden, so fringes survived. The result gives a clean atomic-scale test of a foundational quantum idea. The authors discuss what such interference means for telling which slit a particle passed through.
pmc-6450036:
Oscar Franzén, Li-Ming Gan, and Johan Björkegren built PanglaoDB for single-cell data browsing in 2019. Hundreds of single-cell RNA studies have been published across human and mouse tissues. Most sit in archives as raw files that few can easily open.

PanglaoDB processes those studies into a uniform form and serves them on the web. Users can search a gene and see which cell types use it, tissue by tissue. Curated marker lists help name clusters in new data. The resource turns scattered public data into a quick reference for cell-type questions.
pmc-6834636:
J Spencer Johnson, Daniel Spakowicz, Bo-Young Hong, and coauthors evaluated 16S gene sequencing for fine microbe identification in 2019. The 16S gene has anchored bacterial analysis for decades. Reading the full gene only recently became practical at scale.

Through computer simulations and real sequencing tests, the team judged how well species and strains can be told apart. Full-length reads do far better than the short fragments long in use. Some close relatives still blur together. The results guide labs choosing between cheap short surveys and richer full-gene studies. Mock communities with known members gave the team ground truth for judging each approach.
pmc-6919336:
Regina Guthold, Gretchen Stevens, Leanne Riley, and coauthors pooled data on teen physical activity in 2020. Activity brings many health gains for young people. The World Health Organization set a target to cut inactivity among teens by a set share within a decade.

Pooling hundreds of school-based surveys, the team finds most adolescents worldwide do not move enough. Girls are less active than boys in nearly every country. Trends barely improved over the study years. The authors call for urgent action in schools and city design, since adult habits often start in these years.
pmc-6954236:
Gommaar D'Hulst and colleagues reported how the oxygen sensor PHD1 controls muscle growth signaling in 2020. The mTORC1 pathway is a key regulator of muscle mass. How oxygen and nutrients tune it was not fully understood.

In mice lacking PHD1 in muscle, growth signaling faltered and muscle mass fell. The effect ran through stabilization of an enzyme that charges transfer RNA with leucine, not through the classic oxygen route. Leucine is itself a growth trigger, so the link closes a neat loop. The work reveals an unexpected way oxygen sensing shapes muscle.
pmc-7243036:
Annemarie Docherty and a large team of co-authors reported in 2020 on more than twenty thousand patients admitted to hospitals in the United Kingdom with COVID-19. Their prospective cohort study used a shared clinical protocol from an international respiratory infections consortium and the World Health Organization. The patients were enrolled during the fast growing first wave of the outbreak.

The authors describe who these patients were, what symptoms they arrived with, what other health problems they carried, and how their hospital stays unfolded. Because every site recorded the same details in the same way, the study gives one of the earliest clear pictures of severe COVID-19 in Britain. It helped doctors and planners judge what hospital care the pandemic would demand.
practical-phrenology-1836:
Silas Jones published his Practical Phrenology in Boston in 1836, from the house of Russell, Shattuck. Williams, sold by the principal booksellers in the United States, and entered for copyright in Massachusetts in 1835. The title page, worn in transmission, still shows its essentials plainly. Phrenology, the reading of character from the shape of the skull, was then sweeping America as a practical science of self-knowledge, and Jones wrote for the market it created.

Practical was the selling word: not the theory of Gall and Spurzheim in the abstract, but a manual for examining heads and drawing conclusions about talents, tempers, and callings. Books like Jones's taught parlor phrenology to thousands and filled the lecture halls where itinerant professors mapped bumps for a fee. Modern readers meet in it a complete, confident system that science later discarded entire, preserved at the height of its American vogue.
pushkin-captains-daughter-1836:
Alexander Pushkin published The Captain's Daughter in 1836, his perfect historical tale of Pugachev's rebellion in Russia. The tale tests young Pyotr Grinyov's honor in the Cossack rising of 1773 to 1775. Pushkin researched the rebellion in archives and on the ground, then distilled it into limpid prose fiction.

Grinyov, sent to a remote fort, is saved in a blizzard by a guide he rewards with a coat. That guide is Pugachev, who later spares the fort's survivors for the young officer's sake in war. Grinyov's love for Marya, the captain's daughter, drives rescues, trials, and a plea to the empress herself. Pugachev is drawn with respect, a rebel of charm, cruelty, and a strange rough honor in arms. The tale's economy and fairness set the pattern for the Russian historical novel.
qu-est-ce-que-la-phrenologie-ou-essai-su: Qu'est-ce que la phrénologie is a French work on phrenology. Its opening pages survive here only as a garbled library scan. Stamps of the Yale Medical Library are legible. A digitization notice is legible too. The title itself begins the book. The rest of the title page is broken type. It cannot be read with confidence. No author, place, or date is claimed for it.
remarks-on-the-erroneous-impressions-and:
H. G. Wright of Edinburgh published this twopenny pamphlet in 1836 against the hostility then felt toward science, and toward phrenology above all. His title names its target: false impressions and a spirit of hostility, chiefly among the religious public. John Anderson of Edinburgh and Longman of London sold the piece.

Wright opens by granting that phrenologists cannot answer every passing objection flung at their science. Yet when weightier arguments appear, he says, the world should be shown how little ground they have. The present moment, with feeling running high against the spread of scientific knowledge, seemed to him the right time to reply.
richardson-dictionary-1836:
Charles Richardson published his New Dictionary of the English Language in 1836, built on a bold new method. Where Johnson had defined words in his own phrases, Richardson built every entry out of quotations from real writers. The historical method, showing a word's life through its uses, here reached English lexicography a generation before the Oxford English Dictionary was planned.

Each word is followed by dated quotations that trace its meanings from early use toward Richardson's own day. The reader sees the definition emerge from evidence rather than from one man's authority. The book was the nineteenth century's great rival to Johnson, and its two heavy volumes sat in every serious library. Our words are explained here by the writers who used them best. Richardson's faith in quotation became the method of all later historical dictionaries.
selections-from-the-phrenological-journa:
Forty pieces from the first five volumes of a journal of phrenology, the study of mind through the skull's shape, make up this 1836 gathering. George Combe, James Simpson, and Dr. Andrew Combe wrote most of the pieces. The title page names them as the chief hands behind the work.

Phrenology drew wide crowds in its day, promising a science of character read from bumps on the head. Papers here argue that case in earnest terms for new readers. The book preserves an early, confident stage of a field that later science set aside, yet one that shaped talk on schools, prisons, and self-knowledge.
senior-outline-science-political-economy:
Senior published his Outline of the Science of Political Economy in 1836, the fullest system of his teaching. The book began as an encyclopaedia article and grew into the clearest classical treatise after Ricardo. Senior aimed to state what the science is, what it assumes, and what it may conclude.

He builds the whole doctrine from four plain premises about wealth and human desire, reasoning by strict logic. Value, wages, rent, and profit are drawn out in order, each term defined before it is used. Senior also separates the science from the art of policy, a distinction later economists prized. The Outline became the handbook of the deductive school and a model of economic reasoning for a generation. Mill's great treatise followed its plan more closely than Mill ever quite admitted.
soviet-constitution-1936:
The Soviet Union adopted a new constitution in 1936, with Joseph Stalin as its presiding name. Soviet spokesmen praised it as the most democratic constitution in the world. It arrived at the very height of the Great Terror, when show trials and arrests were sweeping the country. The gap between text and terror was the point its critics seized on.

On paper the charter guarantees work, rest, education, free speech, and the vote for every citizen, priests included. It describes a federation of republics with an elected Supreme Soviet at its head. In practice, the Communist Party's grip, mentioned in a single article, overrode every promise. Foreign admirers quoted the rights; Soviet citizens learned not to test them. The constitution of the purges' apogee remains the classic case of rights proclaimed by a state that honored none of them.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5036:
Calvin Coolidge gives six yearly addresses, from December 6, 1923, to December 4, 1928, parted by three stars. The first opens with a death. Since the close of the last Congress, the nation has lost President Harding, whose kindness, humanity, greatness, and character the world knew. He has left his mark on the past, Coolidge says, and made justice more sure and peace more fast.

The flood of honor paid as Harding was borne across the continent to rest at home showed the place he held in the people's hearts. Those who worked with him, Coolidge says, could not take up their office again without a pause to bind themselves anew to the country's service in his memory. Under a head for foreign affairs, he adds that peace reigns in all parts, to be kept by granting full justice to others and asking it of them.
statistics-of-phrenology-being-a-sketch-: The opening of this record holds no page of the book itself. What survives at the front is the standard wrapper Google Books placed on its public-domain scans. The notice explains that the volume was copied from a library shelf copy whose copyright had expired. The record is Statistics of Phrenology, dated 1836 in the record's title. Beyond the wrapper, nothing of the book's text is visible in this record, so its contents cannot be described from it.
texas-declaration-independence-1836:
The Texas Declaration of Independence was made by the delegates of the people of Texas in general convention at the town of Washington on March 2, 1836. It states the case for breaking from Mexico in a long chain of charges.

The delegates charge that Mexico's rule no longer guards life, liberty, or property, the ends for which rule exists. They say the federal republic of their sworn charter has been crushed into a central armed despotism ruled for army and priesthood. Petitions were spurned and the men who bore them thrown in cells. Readers get the founding paper of the Republic of Texas, cast in the style of the American declaration of 1776.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum:
Volume 3 in this second listing of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XVIII to XXIII, printed at Dublin in 1839. The contents promise detachment duty in an assize town, a day in Dublin, a night at Howth, a journey, and Calais. Chapter XVIII opens with Fitzgerald hiding in his room.

Fitzgerald fears to venture out, lest he be recognised and prosecuted for abduction, so no explanation of that morning's events will be needed from Harry. Harry keeps his own secret too. An order to march on detachment duty, which would usually make him miserable, arrives almost as a relief. Anyone who knows army life, he remarks, knows how unpleasant such a chance can be. The volume's numbering clashes with another record also called Volume 3, a defect worth noting. Within its own pages, Lever continues the episodic garrison tale toward Dublin and the Channel crossing.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Vol. 1, No. 36 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated July 15, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium list of books. A subscriber who secures one new subscription may choose any one of them. They are printed on extra laid paper, bound in red buckram with gilt top. The list names Andersen's Fairy Tales and Haggard's Allan Quatermain. It names Adam Bede and Black Beauty.
the-harmony-of-phrenology-with-scripture: The title page can be read as The Harmony of Phrenology with Scripture, a work that links the study of the mind known as phrenology with the Bible. The pages around the title are badly garbled, with broken letters and marks that give no clear author, date, or chapter text. Only the title page is legible here, so no further claims about the argument can be grounded in what is present.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
John Ormsby translated this stretch of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Volume 2, Part 36. Chapter sixty tells of what happened to Don Quixote on his way to Barcelona. On a fresh morning promising a cool day, he leaves the inn after first learning the most direct road to Barcelona without touching Saragossa.

His aim is to prove a liar of the new historian who, they said, abused him in print. Six quiet days pass with nothing worthy of record. Then night overtakes him in a thicket off the road. A wish to clear his name in print, a rare concern for a false book, now steers the last journey of the knight.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, October 25, 1828, No. 337, prints a correspondent's letter on the Cheese Wring in Cornwall. The writer prefaces his view of the stone pile with Cornwall's early importance. Antiquaries identify the county with the Cassiterides, the tin islands. Vallancey is cited proving Phoenicians traded there for tin before the Trojan war, and Ezekiel's Tarshish passage is read as pointing to these shores.

Herodotus candidly confessed ignorance of the Cassiterides, though Homer mentions the metal. Knowledge of Britain, the letter argues, faded until the islands dwindled into a visionary, fabled land. The Phoenician departure severed the link of history. Such deep antiquity frames a granite oddity for the surrounding peasantry's legend-haunted memory. Readers get a Cornish landmark approached through scripture, Homer, and the tin trade rather than geology.
the-pawns-count-pg9836:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published The Pawns Count in 1918. This record opens directly with Chapter One, without the foreword that stands in a second record of the same book. The scene is the lobby of a fashionable London restaurant, where Pamela Van Teyl points to a French notice warning that enemy ears listen.

Pamela tells her companions that, except for the wounded among them, the notice is the first thing that makes her realize England is at war. Captain Richard Holderness calls the warnings rot, fed up with them in France. John Lutchester, raising his eyeglass, allows that some service men do talk too much on leave. The spy tale begins in small talk.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona-pg2236: In this edition of Shakespeare's early comedy, Launce and his dog Crab steal the show from the two gentlemen's romantic tangle. Valentine, Proteus, and the ladies of Milan play out love's follies while the clown and his cur get the biggest laughs. Youthful, sunny, and full of charm.
tholosan-ut-magorum-et-maleficiorum-erro:
Claude Tholosan lays down the law on witches in his Latin tract of near 1436. Tholosan was a judge in the Dauphine, in the hills of France. His tract's name means on the false claims of mages and witches. It is one of the first to make a bold claim. Witches, it says, fly to a sabbath rite and make pacts with the Devil.

He writes from trials at his own bench. The claims here fed the great hunts that came next. The text, in Latin, is a root source of the hunts. Its cold tone chills.
timon-of-athens-pg1536: William Shakespeare's Life of Timon of Athens is laid out here through a contents list of acts and scenes, plus its cast. Timon, a noble Athenian, is attended by his steward Flavius and servants. Apemantus the churlish philosopher and Alcibiades the captain stand among the company. Scenes move from Timon's hall to a senator's house, the senate, woods and caves near the shore, and finally Timon's tomb before Athens's walls. Only the scene list and cast are included in this record, so Shakespeare's lines themselves are not shown.
tob-0036:
